en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
17. The Book of the Forties [521] 1.
The Commentary on the Tesakuṇa Jātaka.
“I ask you about Vessantara”—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove, as an exhortation to the King of Kosala.
For when the king had come for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma, the Teacher addressed him:
“Great King, a king must indeed rule his kingdom according to the Dhamma; for at whatever time kings become unrighteous, those appointed to serve the king likewise [become so].”
At that time, having exhorted him according to the method of the suttas found in the Catukka-nipāta, saying,

"They become unrighteous," and having explained both the danger and the benefit regarding going on a wrong path and not going on a wrong path, he detailed the danger in sensual pleasures by way of the passage beginning,
"Sensual pleasures are like a dream," and said: "Great King, for these beings—
“There is no pact with Death, no bribe can be accepted;
there is no battle, there is no victory—all are subject to the realm of Death.
For those departing for the next world, there is no other support whatsoever except for the wholesome karma performed by oneself.
It is not so. Thus, this transitory manifestation must inevitably be abandoned; it is not fitting to practice negligence by relying on fame.
One must remain heedful and rule the kingdom according to the Dhamma.
In ancient times, even before the Buddhas had appeared, former kings stood by the counsel of the wise, ruled according to the Dhamma, and departed filling the city of the gods.”
Having spoken thus, being requested by him, he related a story of the past:
"In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, he was childless; though he longed for it, he obtained neither a son nor a daughter.
One day, having gone to a park with a great retinue, he spent part of the day there."
Having played in the park, he had a bed prepared at the foot of the auspicious *sāla* tree;
after sleeping for a short while, he woke up, looked at the *sāla* tree, and saw a bird’s nest there. At the very moment of seeing it, affection arose within him.
He summoned a man and said, "Climb this tree and see whether anyone is in this nest."
“...or their non-existence. He replied, “Very well, Your Majesty,” and having mounted, he saw three eggs there and informed the king.
The king said, “In that case, do not release the breath from your nostrils over them,” and added, “Spread cotton wool in a basket, place those eggs right there upon it, and descend slowly.”
Having had it brought down and taking the basket in his hand, he asked his ministers, "What kind of bird's eggs are these?
They replied, "We do not know; the hunters will know. The king summoned the hunters and questioned them.
The hunters said, "Great King, among them, one is an owl's egg, one is a myna's egg, and one is a sparrow's egg."
"But how can there be three birds' eggs in a single nest? "Yes, Your Majesty;
if there is no danger from robbers, they will not perish when well-placed. The king was pleased and thought, "These shall be my sons.
He entrusted those three eggs to three ministers, saying, "These shall become my sons; you must look after them with great care."
“After you have looked after them, inform me when they have emerged from their eggshells,” he said. They guarded them with great care.
Among them, the owl’s egg broke first. The minister summoned a hunter and told him, “Find out whether it is female or male.
After the man had examined it and reported that it was a male, the minister approached the king.

“A son has been born to you, Your Majesty,” he said. The king, being delighted, gave him much wealth and, having instructed him, “Look after my little son well and give him the name Vessantara,” sent him away. He did accordingly.
Then, after a few days had passed, a sparrow’s egg was broken. That minister also had it examined by a hunter and [concluded] that it was a female.
Having heard this, he went into the presence of the king and said, "Your Majesty, a daughter has been born to you. The king was delighted;
having given him much wealth as well, he said, "Look after my daughter well, and give her the name 'Kuṇḍalinī,'" and dismissed him.
He did exactly so. Then, after a few days had passed, a quail's egg broke open. That minister—
The hunter, having examined him and being told by the king, "It is a boy," went into the presence of the king and said, "A son has been born to you, O King.

The king was delighted; he gave much wealth to the hunter as well and, saying, "Perform a blessing for my son with a great retinue and give him the name 'Jambuka'," sent him away. He did so accordingly. Thus, those three—
The birds were raised in the houses of the three ministers with the very same care afforded to the king’s own children.
The king addressed them as “my son” and “my daughter. Then the ministers mocked one another, saying, “Look, sirs, at the king’s behavior!
He goes about calling even a bird ‘my son’ and ‘my daughter.’”
Having heard this, the king thought: "These ministers do not know the perfection of wisdom of these sons of mine;
I shall make it manifest to them. Then he sent a minister to Vessantara, saying:
"Your father wishes to ask a question; when indeed will he come and ask it? That minister went and [reported to] Vessantara.
Having paid homage, he reported the message. Upon hearing it, Vessantara summoned his steward and asked, "It seems my father wishes to question me;
it is fitting that we should prepare a reception for him when he arrives here.
When will he come? The steward replied, "Let your father arrive seven days from now."
Having heard this, Vessantara said, "Let my father come here on the seventh day from now," and sent him away.
He arrived and informed the king. On the seventh day, the king had a drum beaten throughout the city and went to his son's residence.
Vessantara performed a great reception for the king, providing hospitality even to the servants and laborers.
The king, having eaten at the house of the Vessantara bird and experienced great honor, returned to his own residence.
He had a large pavilion constructed in the royal courtyard, caused a drum to be beaten throughout the city, and sat in the midst of the decorated pavilion surrounded by a great multitude.
Then he sent a minister to the presence of Vessantara with the command, "Bring Vessantara here. The minister—
Having seated Vessantara upon a golden throne, he brought him there.
Prince Vessantara sat upon his father’s lap, played with his father, and then went and sat down right there on the golden throne.
Then the king, in the midst of the great multitude, asked him about the duty of a king and spoke this first verse:
“I ask you, Vessantara, O bird—may prosperity be yours!
What indeed is the most excellent deed that must be performed by one desiring to exercise kingship?

Therein, he addresses him as “bird. “What indeed? means: “Which deed is the most excellent and supreme? Tell me, dear father, the entire duty of a king (rājadhamma). It is said that he questioned him in this manner.
Having heard this, Vessantara, without answering the question, spoke the second verse, reproaching the king for his negligence:
“After such a long time, indeed, my father Kaṃsa,
the ruler of Bārāṇasī, In his negligence, has at last exhorted me, his heedful son!”
In this context, *tātā* means father. *Kaṃsa* is his name. *Bārāṇasiggaho* means one who dwells having won over Bārāṇasī by means of the four bases of sympathy (*saṅgahavatthu*).
*Pamatto* means negligent due to not asking questions in the presence of such wise men.
*Appamattaṃ maṃ* means [the father says] "I am diligent through my possession of virtues such as moral discipline (*sīla*) and so forth. *Pitā* means a nourishing father.
"Acodayī" means that, having been mocked by his ministers with the words, "He transacts business by treating his children as mere animals," he fell into negligence;
today, after a long time, he has finally reproached him—that is what he says, meaning he asked a question.

Having thus reproached him with this verse, and having said, "Great King, a king must indeed conduct his reign righteously by abiding in three qualities," he spoke these verses while expounding the duties of a king (*rājadhamma*).
“By the very first [thought], one should restrain false anger and laughter;
thereafter, one should perform one’s duties—this, they say, is the vow of a Kshatriya.
Whatever ascetic practice you performed previously, O dear one, there is no doubt about it.”
Whatever one who is lustful or hateful might do, one should not do that again.
"For a negligent kshatriya, the prosperity of the kingdom;
all enjoyments perish—this is called the king’s calamity."
“‘Sirī and Alakkhī, when questioned by my father, replied thus:
“I delight in one who exerts effort and energy, who supports himself, and who is free from envy.
In a man who is envious, hard-hearted, and corrupt in his actions—’”
“O Great King, the ill-omened Cakkabhañjanī delights [in misfortune].
Therefore, may you be well-disposed toward all and be a protector for all.
Drive away misfortune, O Great King, and make your abode one of good fortune.”
“Endowed with fortune and wisdom, that man indeed is exalted;
he cuts off the root and the summit of his enemies, O Lord of Kāsi.
For even Sakka, the Lord of Beings, does not neglect diligence.”
Having established resolve in what is wholesome, he sets his mind upon exertion.
“Gandhabbas, fathers, and gods become companions to such a person;
the deities attend upon one who exerts himself and is heedful.”
“Therefore, my dear, being diligent and free from anger, perform your duties;
exert yourself in your tasks, for the indolent find no happiness.
Right there are the steps of your conduct; this indeed is the instruction.”
"It is enough to bring happiness to friends and suffering to enemies.
In this regard, by the first [verse] alone, "untrue" means: "My dear, a king must, from the very beginning, prohibit false speech.
For when a king is a liar, his kingdom becomes sapless; the essence of the earth [is lost] from the places where labor is performed, [yielding] no more than the seven precious gems."
If it falls below, then there is no nutritive essence (*ojā*) in food, such as oil, honey, molasses, and the like, or in medicinal herbs.
When people consume food devoid of nutritive essence, they become subject to many ailments; consequently, wealth does not arise in the kingdom’s land and water routes.
When that wealth does not arise, kings fall into poverty. Unable to maintain their servants, those servants—being unsupported—[turn against] the king...
They do not look [at it] with a heavy heart. Thus, dear son, this thing called lying is devoid of essence; it must not be committed even for the sake of one’s life.
Truth, however, is the most delicious of flavors; therefore, that alone should be accepted. Furthermore, lying is a destroyer of virtues and ends in calamity;
in the second instance of thought, it leads one to the Avīci hell. In this matter, "Dhammo... [is said].
The *Cetiya Jātaka* should be told [with the words]: "He has been killed, he is being killed.
Regarding "anger": my dear son, a king indeed should restrain even anger, which is characterized by the first arising of wrath.
For, my dear son, while the anger of others does not quickly reach its peak, it does so in the case of kings. Kings, indeed, have speech as their weapon.
By merely looking upon another with anger, they cause their destruction; therefore, a king must be even more free from anger than other men.
He should be endowed with patience, loving-kindness, and compassion, regarding the world as he would his own dear son.
My son, a king who is excessively prone to anger is unable to protect the glory that has arisen for him.
To illustrate this point, the Khantivādijātaka and the Cūḷadhammapālajātaka should be told.
For in the Cūḷadhammapālajātaka, a king named Mahāpatāpana, having caused his son to be killed, died with his heart bursting from grief for his son;
even as he was mourning the queen who had already died of a broken heart, his own heart burst as well. Then...
They too cremated those two on the very same funeral pyre. Therefore, having first abandoned false speech, the king must abandon anger as the second.

Regarding "hāsa": it means laughter; or this is simply another reading. One should restrain joking and derision—that state of mind characterized by frivolity arising from various activities—by saying:
"My dear son, one who is called a king should not be of a joking nature; he should be one who does not require others to have faith in him."
All duties must be performed through one's own direct observation. For a king whose mind is agitated, acting without deliberation on his affairs destroys the fame he has acquired.
In this regard, according to the words of the chaplain in the Sarabhaṅga Jātaka, King Daṇḍaki, having offended against Kisavaccha, was destroyed along with his kingdom and fell into the Kukkuḷa hell.

Furthermore, regarding the state of being reborn: in the *Mātaṅga-jātaka*, after following the advice of the brahmins and offending the ascetic Mātaṅga, King Majjha was destroyed along with his kingdom and reborn in hell;
and in the *Ghaṭa-paṇḍita-jātaka*, after following the words of the ten foolish royal princes and offending Kaṇhadīpāyana...
And the fact that the lineage of Vāsudeva has been destroyed must be told.

Then he should have duties performed; thus, dear son, having first avoided false speech, secondly anger, and thirdly unjust laughter, the king should thereafter have the duties to be performed for the inhabitants of the realm carried out. That, they say, is the vow of a Kṣatriya.
"O Great King, Kṣatriya, that which was spoken by me is what the ancient wise ones called 'the king’s undertaking of a vow. 'One should not do it' means:

whatever deed you have done that causes remorse later due to passion and so forth, one should not do such a deed again after having already done it before; 'do not do it, dear son! This is what is said regarding 'that which is the king's misfortune.'"

Thus it was said; in this way the ancient wise ones spoke. Regarding the word “Sirī,” Vessantara the bird spoke while bringing forward and illustrating the account that occurred previously in Bārāṇasī.
Therein, “they said” means they spoke when questioned by the merchant Suciparivāra.
“In exertion and energy” refers to a person who is established in exertion and energy, and does not [envy] the success of others.
"Having seen it, she feels envy; 'In that I delight,' she said. Thus, dear father, Sirī spoke.

But as for Alakkhī, dear father, when questioned, she said: 'I delight in one who envies the prosperity of others, who is envious at heart, evil-minded, and a defiler of wholesome deeds—one who, hating, disliking, and being distressed by wholesome deeds, does not perform them.'"
Thus, Great King, that ill-omened woman delights in destroying the wheel of skillful means, such as dwelling in a suitable locality and so forth.
"One of good heart" means one with a beautiful mind, one whose heart is intent on welfare. "Drive out" means to expel. "Into a residence" means:
"Become the established foundation for the residence of Prosperity. "He is endowed with the steadfastness of Prosperity," Great King, refers to that man, the Lord of Kāsi, who by means of wisdom—
And endowed with energy. "Magnanimous" (mahaggata) means having great aspiration;

it is said that one who seizes the thieves who are the cause [of the crime] cuts off the root of his enemies, and one who seizes the thieves themselves cuts off the head of his enemies. "Inda" means he is capable.

"Lord of Beings" (bhūtapati) is an address to the King. "In exertion" (uṭṭhāne) refers to the energy of initiative. "He does not neglect" (nappamajjati) means he does not become negligent regarding all duties.

"He applies himself. That king of the gods, directing his mind toward diligence and effort, refrains from committing evil deeds and, establishing firm resolve in virtuous meritorious actions alone, applies himself with heedfulness to exertion.
Furthermore, in order to demonstrate his state of applying energy toward virtuous deeds, [the text] mentions him together with the deities in the two heavenly worlds in the *Sarabhaṅga-jātaka*.
The following instances should be recounted: his arrival at the Kapiṭṭha Monastery, his asking of questions, and his hearing of the Dhamma;
as well as, in the Mahā-Kaṇha Jātaka, how he caused the people to be terrified by his own supernatural power so that the declining Sasana was set in motion once more, and other such matters.

As for the "Gandhabbas," they are the deities belonging to the fourfold birth (catuyonika) who dwell below the Cātumahārājika realm; it is said that they are called "Gandhabbas" precisely because of their fourfold birth.
"Named" means so-called. "Fathers" refers to the *brahmās*. "Devas" refers, by way of deities born there, to the six classes of gods belonging to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*).
"Of such a one" refers to a king who delights in wholesome deeds (*kusala*). "They become co-living" means they are to be shared in life or supported.
For kings of such a kind, when performing meritorious deeds such as giving, bestow their merit upon the deities; and those deities, having rejoiced in that merit—

Having accepted [the offerings], they increase by means of divine power. "They attend" (anutiṭṭhanti) means that when a king such as this exerts energy and applies heedfulness, the deities attend him and follow him; the meaning is that they provide righteous protection.
"He" (so) refers to you. "Exert yourself" (vāyamassu) means while performing those duties of the kingdom, do so by way of weighing, investigating, and direct personal action.

Exert energy in those various duties. "In that very place are your duties," dear son—regarding what you asked me, "What duty has been performed?"—it was in response to that very question of yours that I spoke these words, beginning with "By the first [duty] itself it is false.
These are the duties, the constituent parts of the conduct; thus, conduct yourself therein. "This" refers to that which has been explained by me to you.
"This indeed is your instruction: 'Alam'—for a king who speaks thus is sufficient, capable, and competent to bring happiness to his friends and suffering to his enemies.
Thus, having admonished the king for his negligence with this single verse, the Vessantara bird [proceeded] with eleven verses on the Dhamma.

When he had spoken thus, the great multitude, having conceived a sense of wonder and amazement at the thought, “The question has been answered with the playfulness of a Buddha,” broke into hundreds of shouts of approval.
The King, filled with joy, addressed his ministers and asked: “Sirs, ministers!
While my son Vessantara was speaking in this manner, what duty was performed by whom? “By Mahāsenagutta, O Lord,” they replied.
“Indeed, I grant him the position of Mahāsenagutta,” he said, and thus he appointed Vessantara to that office.
From then on, stationed in the post of Mahāsenagutta, he performed his father’s duties.
The Question of Vessantara is concluded.
Again, after a few days had passed, the king sent a messenger to Kuṇḍalinī in the same manner as before.
On the seventh day, he went there, returned, and sat down right there in the middle of the pavilion.
Having had Kuṇḍalinī brought and seated upon a golden throne, he asked her about the duty of kings and spoke this verse:
“O Kuṇḍalinī, you who are considered a noble lady, do you have the ability [to answer]?
What indeed is the best thing that must be done by one desiring to exercise sovereignty?
Therein, “sakkhisi” means he asks, “Will you be able to speak on the question asked by me? “Kuṇḍalinī” means...
He addresses her by the name she received from her birth-signs. It is said that on both of her ears there were two lines shaped like earrings;
therefore, they gave her the name “Kuṇḍalinī. “Maññasi” means you will understand the meaning of the question asked by me.
He addresses her thus as “Khattabandhunī” because she is the sister of Khatta, the Great General.
But why did he not ask this question of the Vessantara bird, but instead asked it of her?
Because of her female nature. For women possess limited wisdom; therefore, thinking, "If she is able, I will ask;
if not, I will not," he asked this question as a means of testing, and then asked that very same question.

When the king had thus questioned her regarding the duties of a king, she said: "Dear father, you seem to be testing me by asking, 'What will this mere woman say? I shall explain the entire duty of a king by condensing it into just two points. Having said this, she spoke:
"Dear father, there are only two points upon which everything is established:
the acquisition of what has not been gained, and the preservation of what has been gained."
“O dear father, know those ministers who are steadfast, skilled in affairs, free from deceit,
not given to drink, and non-destructive. And whoever, O dear father,
would protect you and whatever wealth you may possess— ”
Just as a charioteer holds the reins, he should cause you to perform your duties.
When those people are well-restrained, look after your own wealth yourself;
do not place your trust in another regarding your savings or your debts.
“May you yourself know income and expenditure; may you yourself know what has been done and what remains to be done.
Restrain those who deserve restraint, and encourage those who deserve encouragement.
O bull among charioteers, teach the people the true purpose of their own welfare.”
“May those unrighteous ones who are joined with you not destroy your wealth and kingdom.
Do not perform actions, nor cause them to be performed, in haste;
for an action done in haste, a fool later regrets.”
"Do not release against me a fierce and aggravated insult;
for through anger many families have flourished and yet fallen into ruin.
Do not, my dear, out of the thought 'I am the master,' act recklessly to your own harm."
May you have no ill fortune regarding women and men.
For a king who follows after sensual pleasures, even though his hair and beard have been shorn, all his enjoyments perish;
that, it is said, is the calamity of a king.
“In that very place are your duties; this indeed is the instruction:
now, O Great King, one who is skillful is a maker of merit—one who is not a drunkard and not a destroyer;
he is virtuous, whereas the immoral man goes to ruin.”
In this context, "phrases" (*padakāni*) refers to causal phrases. "Wherein" (*yattha*) means in those two phrases wherein the entire range of things conducive to welfare and happiness is established.
"Of what has not been gained" (*aladdhassa*) refers both to the acquisition of gain not previously obtained and to the preservation of that which has already been gained.
My dear, indeed, the production of gain not yet arisen is no great burden; however, [the preservation of what has arisen...]
Guarding it alone is the burden. For some, even after having acquired fame, become heedless regarding that fame;
having given rise to negligence, they commit acts such as the taking of life. Having become great thieves, they wander about plundering the kingdom.
Then kings have them seized and bring about their great ruin. Or else, being heedless regarding the arisen strands of sensual pleasure, such as forms, one engages in improper attention...
Wasting his wealth until all his property is exhausted, he becomes a pauper, clad in rags and wandering about with an alms-bowl.
Or else, having gone forth, he generates gain and honor through the mastery of the scriptures and so forth, and becoming heedless, he falls back into the lower life.
Another, although having attained the first jhāna and the others, becomes bound to such an object due to his lack of mindfulness.
One falls away from jhāna. Thus, it is indeed difficult to preserve fame that has arisen, or the attainment of jhāna and so forth.
To illustrate this point, the story of Devadatta, the *Mudulakkhaṇa-jātaka*, the *Lomasakassapa-jātaka*, the *Haritaca-jātaka*, the *Saṅkappa-jātaka*, and others should be told.
However, one person, having generated gain and honor, remained established in heedfulness.
One who performs wholesome deeds finds that their fame increases like the moon in the bright fortnight; therefore,
Great King, remaining diligent and established in the perfection of application, protect the fame that has arisen for you while ruling the kingdom according to the Dhamma.

"Know" means: attend to [the affairs] for the purpose of performing duties such as those of a storekeeper. "In gambling and cheating" means: in that which is not gambling and not cheating, being free from fraudulent practices and trickery.
"Not addicted to strong drink" means: devoid of the state of being addicted to cakes, liquor, perfumes, garlands, and strong drinks.
"Not wasteful" means: one who does not waste the wealth, grain, and so forth belonging to you. "Who" means: whichever minister. "And whatever" means: and whatever [is] in your house.
There may be wealth, and one should protect it. "Like a charioteer" means like a driver of a chariot;

just as a charioteer, restraining the horses for the sake of avoiding uneven paths, would keep the chariot under control, even so, he who is able to protect that [king] along with his possessions is called a minister.
Having recruited such a person, the king should have him perform duties such as those of a treasurer.
"O dear one, regarding 'having one's own people well-supported':

for a king whose own household folk and his personal attendants are not supported by gifts and other means, gold, silver, and so forth are lost from his inner quarters due to those unsupported people, and his household members go abroad; therefore, you must ensure that your own people are well-supported."
"Having personally examined one's own wealth, thinking 'I have this much property,' one should not do either of these two—
'let us deposit a treasure in such-and-such a place' or 'let us give a loan to such-and-such a person'— based on the trust of another; do not act out of trust in others,
but let everything be done through your own direct perception," he says.
"Income and expenditure": you yourself should know both the income arising from that [source] and the specific amounts to be given to various people, as well as the expenditures.
"What has been done and what has not been done": whether in battle, in building work, or in other duties, you yourself should know, "This was done for me by this person;
this was not done by that person"; do not be dependent on others. "Restrain," my son...
A king, having brought before him one who has committed such acts as breaking into dwellings and deserves punishment, should examine and investigate the case;
then, having cleared up the matter and reviewed the penalties established by former kings, he should punish the offender in accordance with the fault.
Furthermore, he should support one who is worthy of support—namely, one who causes dissension in an undivided enemy force, or who brings reconciliation to a divided own force.
One who brings about the acquisition of a kingdom not yet obtained, or secures its stability once obtained, or one by whom life itself has been given—
having supported such a person who is worthy of support, one should bestow upon them great honor and respect. For in this way,
others too will place their trust in him and perform what ought to be done in times of need.
"Regarding the 'country' (jānapada): instruct yourself directly on the welfare of those dwelling in the country. As for 'those appointed to unrighteousness' (adhammikā yuttā):
let not those officials appointed here and there, who break legal decisions by taking bribes, destroy your wealth and kingdom.
For this reason, being heedful, instruct [them] yourself. Regarding 'with speed' (vegena)..."
"Sahasā" means having failed to deliberate and having failed to cross over [to the other shore]. "Vegasā" means having failed to deliberate and having failed to cross over;
for an action performed impulsively under the influence of desire and so forth is neither good nor beautiful. Why is that?

Because having done such a thing, the fool later, through remorse, suffers the pain of the states of woe in this world and regrets it in the next world. This, however, is the meaning here: "In the midst of the seers..."
"Having done so, I heard [him called] 'King Bharu,'" thus it should be illustrated by the Bharu Jātaka.

"Do not release a sharp shaft against him who has transgressed," [means]: O dear one, having transgressed—that is, having exceeded—the welfare of your own heart, he has become exceedingly sharp, deeply provoked, and incensed regarding the unwholesome action of others as it proceeds.
"Do not release; do not let it settle"—this is the meaning. This is what is intended:

"Dear son, when you are presiding over a legal judgment and people bring a thief before you, saying, 'This man has killed someone or committed a burglary,' then even if your heart is greatly provoked by the words of others, do not release it through the power of anger; do not pronounce a punishment without full investigation. For what reason?"

For even a thief may be seized and brought [before you] as a "thief"; therefore, without becoming angry, listen to the accounts of both parties who are your adversaries, investigate thoroughly, and having personally verified his status as a thief, carry out what must be done according to the punishment established by tradition.
For even when anger has arisen, a king should not perform his duty without first making his heart cool.
But when his heart has become quenched and pliable, then the work of investigation should be performed.
For when the mind is harsh and boiling, the reason is not perceived, just as the reflection of a face is not seen in water that is agitated.
"By anger, my dear, for through anger many flourishing royal families have fallen into ruin and met with great destruction."
To illustrate this point, the *Khantivādijātaka*, the story of King Nāḷikera, the story of Sahassabāhu, the story of Ajjuna,
and others should be told. "Do not, dear son, thinking 'I am a lord,' incite [people] to harm"— dear son,
do not incite or lead the great multitude toward the harm of bodily misconduct and so forth, such that they would persist in adopting such harm.

"Do not do so"—this is the meaning. "May it not be yours": dear son, may there be no arising of suffering, no occurrence of pain, for those of human or animal kind, whether men or women, within your realm.
For just as under unrighteous kings the people in their realm, having committed bodily misconduct and the like, are reborn in hell, may such suffering not befall the inhabitants of your kingdom.
The meaning is: "Act in such a way that it does not come to pass.
"Free from horripilation" means one who is fearless regarding self-reproach and other such anxieties. By this, he shows the following:
"Dear son, that king who, without entertaining any suspicion toward anyone, merely follows his own desire and does whatever he wishes according to his own will..."
He does whatever he pleases; like a blind man with loose bones, or like a fierce elephant without a goad, all his wealth perishes.
That loss of wealth is called "misfortune" (*agha*) and "suffering" (*dukkha*).
In this very context, those lines of verse should be applied according to the previous method. Now, as for the words "O skillful one": "My dear, you..."
"Having heard this instruction, now, being skillful and not indolent, you should be a doer of merit by performing meritorious deeds;

you should be non-intoxicated by avoiding liquor and the like; and you should be a preserver by not destroying your welfare pertaining both to the present life and the future life. 'Be virtuous' means:
be virtuous and endowed with good conduct; having established yourself in the ten duties of a king, rule the kingdom."
“An immoral person is one who has fallen into ruin,” said she. “For, Great King, an immoral person is called ‘one who has fallen into ruin’ because he causes himself to fall into hell.
Thus Kuṇḍalinī taught the Dhamma with these eleven verses. The king, being pleased, addressed his ministers and asked:
“Sirs, ministers, when my daughter Kuṇḍalinī speaks thus, what duty should be performed for her?”
“Who said so? “The treasurer, Your Majesty. “Therefore, I shall grant him the position of treasurer,” he said, and he appointed Kuṇḍalinī to that office.
From then on, having taken up the post of treasurer, she performed her father’s work.
The Question of Kuṇḍalinī is finished.
Again, after a few days had passed, the king sent a messenger to the wise Jambuka in the same manner as before.
On the seventh day, having gone there, enjoyed the splendors, and returned, he sat down right there in the middle of the pavilion.
The minister, having seated the wise Jambuka upon a golden throne, came along carrying that throne on his head.
The wise boy, having sat on his father’s lap and played, went and sat down upon the very golden throne.
Then the King, wishing to question him, spoke this verse:
“We questioned the one of the Kosiya clan, and likewise the Kuṇḍalinī;”
"Now you speak, jackal, you who are the supreme strength among the strong.
Its meaning is this: "Dear jackal, I asked your brother Vessantara of the Kosiya clan and your sister Kuṇḍalinī about the duty of a king;
they spoke according to their own strength, but as for how I questioned them—"
"In the same way now, my son Jambuka, I ask you this: tell me what the duty of a king is, and what is the supreme strength among all strengths.
Thus the King, asking the Great Being a question, did not ask it according to the manner of questioning others, but asked it with distinction.
Then the Wise One said to him: "In that case, Great King, lend an attentive ear; I shall tell you everything."
As if placing a purse containing a thousand coins into the outstretched hands [of his audience], he began his teaching of the Dhamma:
“There are five kinds of strength in the world found in a man of great stature;
among them, what is called the strength of arms is said to be the weakest strength.”
“O Dīghāvu, the power of wealth is called the second power;
O Dīghāvu, the power of ministers is called the third power.
And the power of noble birth is certainly the fourth.”
The wise person masters all these.
"That is the best of strengths, the supreme strength is the power of wisdom;
supported by the power of wisdom, the wise person finds true welfare."
“Even if a fool should obtain the most excellent, prosperous earth,
another will take it from him by force against his will.
Even if he is of noble birth, having obtained the kingship as a kshatriya...”
For one lacking wisdom, O Lord of Kāsi, does not live even by means of everything.
Wisdom alone discerns what has been heard; wisdom increases fame and renown.
A person endowed with wisdom finds happiness even in the midst of suffering in this world.
“Indeed, no one attains wisdom who does not desire to hear,
without approaching one who is learned, established in the Dhamma, and capable of analyzing it.
But he who knows the analysis of the Dhamma, rising at the proper time and free from sloth,”
One who performs [their duty] at the proper time, for them the fruit of their action succeeds.
For one whose virtue lacks the right field, who frequents what is not the right field,
and who does not act with disenchantment, the goal of perfection does not ripen.
“For one who is devoted to the internal, who likewise cultivates the sense bases,
and who acts without weariness— the goal of perfection ripens for them.
The preservation of what has been gathered, which consists of the application of yoga...”
“Cultivate those, dear one; do not let yourself be overcome by inaction.
For through inaction, the foolish man sinks like a reed-hut.
In this context, “exalted,” O Great King, refers to a person of great aspiration in this world of beings who possesses fivefold power.
It exists. "Strength of the arms" means bodily strength. "That which is last" means that even though it is very great, it is indeed inferior. For what reason?
Because of its state as the strength of a blind fool. For if bodily strength were truly great, the strength of a little lizard would be small compared to the strength of an elephant;
yet, the strength of an elephant has become a condition for death due to its state as the strength of a blind fool.
The female jackal, through her own skill in knowledge, brought about the destruction of the elephant’s life.
Regarding this point, the following sutta should be cited: "Not everywhere is success achieved by strength alone; for the strength of a fool leads to his own destruction.
As for "the power of wealth" (*bhogabala*), it refers to all kinds of objects of enjoyment, such as gold, silver, and so forth, by way of providing support.

The power of name (*nāmabala*): this is greater than the power of the body. The power of ministers (*amaccabala*): this refers to the existence of a circle of ministers who are unbreakable in counsel, brave, and kind-hearted;
that power is greater than the previous powers due to their skill in battle. The power of noble birth (*abhijaccabala*):
this is the excellence of birth by way of the Khattiya clan, having transcended the three other clans; that [power] is [greater] than the others...
It is greater than the other powers. For only those endowed with noble birth are purified, not others. And as for these:
whatever four powers a wise person attains and surpasses through the power of wisdom (*paññā*), that power of wisdom among all powers is called the best and the foremost.
Why is that? Because supported by that power, [he stands firm].
The wise man finds profit and attains growth. To illustrate this meaning, one should relate the Puṇṇanadī Jātaka,
the Sirīkāḷakaṇṇi Pañha, the Pañcapaṇḍita Pañha, and the Sattubhasta Jātaka, the Sambhava Jātaka, the Sarabhaṅga Jātaka, and others.

The dull-witted person is a fool. "Prosperous," dear son, means that even if a person of dull wit obtains the supreme earth filled with the seven treasures, another endowed with wisdom takes possession of it by force, even against his will.
For a dull person is unable to protect the fame he has gained, or even what belongs to his family.
Even a kingdom inherited through paternal lineage cannot be attained [by one lacking wisdom]. To illustrate this point, the Pādañjali Jātaka should be told:
"Surely all those with palms joined in reverence outshine [others] by their wisdom. Regarding the phrase "even having obtained":
even after obtaining a kingdom belonging to his family by virtue of the excellence of his birth; "even by all of it" means that he does not live by that entire kingdom.
"Through lack of skill in means, one indeed fares ill.
Thus, having explained the deficiency of the unwise by this much, the Great Being now spoke the words beginning with "Wisdom" (paññā) while praising wisdom.
In that context, "learning" (suta) refers to the study of the scriptures; for it is wisdom alone that discerns them. It is "that which increases fame and renown."

It increases fame, renown, and gain. "One finds happiness even in suffering" means that even when suffering arises, one attains happiness through skill in means by remaining fearless. To illustrate this point, it is said:
"O Lord of Monkeys, he for whom these four qualities exist, just as they do in you..."
“There is no need for these mangoes, nor for the rose-apples and breadfruit”—thus, Jātaka stories such as these should be told.
“Not desiring to hear” means not attending upon wise persons and not listening to them. “Established in the Dhamma” means [established] in the nature of things.

Without relying on one who is steadfast and learned, and lacking faith in them, no one attains wisdom—neither by failing to distinguish between what is meaningful and what is meaningless, nor by failing to fathom or cross over the distinction between what is a valid reason and what is not.
"One who knows the analysis of the Dhamma" means one who is skilled in analyzing the ten courses of wholesome action. "One who rises at the proper time" means one who exerts energy.
"One who exerts energy at the proper time" means that he performs each respective task at its appropriate time.
"For him" means for that person, the fruit of his action succeeds and comes to fruition. "One whose virtue is not a proper basis" (anāyatanasīla):
"improper basis" (anāyatana) refers to misconduct, which is called the non-source of gain, fame, and happiness; "one whose virtue is such" means one who possesses that misconduct.

For such a person, dear one— one who is possessed of these traits, who associates with an immoral person who is truly no refuge, and who performs wholesome deeds while being disenchanted and wearying of them—
the purpose of his actions does not ripen rightly nor succeed; and there are three families and six...

The meaning is that one does not bring about the realms of sensual pleasure. "Internally" means for one who is devoted to the cultivation of impermanence and so forth within one's own internal domain.
"Likewise serving those who frequent the sense bases" means for one who serves persons endowed with virtue in that very way.
"It ripens" means it succeeds; it bestows great renown.
"Yogappayogasaṅkhātaṃ" means wisdom, which constitutes the application-component within the "yoga"—that is, the cause that is to be applied.
"Sambhatassa" means the protection of accumulated wealth. "Tāni tu" means:
"And these two, as well as all the aforementioned causes spoken of by me, my dear, you should practice; having taken the advice spoken by me to heart."
"Guard the wealth in your own home; do not let it be consumed by what is not work. This means: do not let it be consumed by what is improper or groundless;
do not burn up or destroy that wealth. Why? "For through non-action," meaning by performing improper deeds, a person of dull wit destroys his own wealth and later falls into misery.
"It sinks like a house of reeds": just as a house made of reeds sinks down.
Just as something decaying from its very root falls down without support, so too, by wasting wealth through improper means, one is reborn in the states of misery.
Thus, having praised the five powers by this much, and having raised up the power of wisdom as if drawing out the moon’s disk, the Bodhisatta now spoke these ten stanzas as advice to the king:
“Practice righteousness, O Great King, toward your mother and father, O Kshatriya.”
"By practicing the Dhamma here, O King, you will go to heaven.
Practice the Dhamma, Great King, toward your children and wife, O Khattiya;
by practicing the Dhamma here, O King, you will go to heaven."
“Practice Dhamma, O Great King, among your friends and ministers, O Khattiya;
having practiced Dhamma here, O King, you will go to heaven.
Practice Dhamma, O Great King, toward your mounts and your forces.”
“Having practiced the Dhamma here, O King, you will go to heaven.
‘Practice the Dhamma, Great King, in villages and in market towns;
having practiced the Dhamma here, O King, you will go to heaven.’”
“Practice the Dhamma, O Great King, throughout the kingdom and the countryside;
having practiced the Dhamma here, O King, you will go to heaven.
Practice the Dhamma, O Great King, toward recluses and brahmins.”
"Having practiced the Dhamma here, O King, you will go to heaven.
'Practice the Dhamma, Great King, toward the beasts and birds, O Kshatriya;
having practiced the Dhamma here, O King, you will go to heaven.'"
“Practice the Dhamma, O Great King; the Dhamma, when practiced, brings happiness.
Having practiced the Dhamma here, O King, you will go to heaven.
Practice the Dhamma, O Great King; [even] the gods together with Indra and Brahmā [revere it].”
"By what was well-performed they have reached heaven; O King, do not be negligent regarding the Dhamma.
Regarding this, in the first verse, "the Dhamma here" refers to the duty of attending upon one's mother and father.
This consists of rising early and performing all services for their bodies, beginning with providing them with water for the face, tooth-sticks, and so forth.
"By doing so, he fulfills [the duty]," he says. Regarding "among sons and wife":

when one restrains sons and daughters from evil, establishes them in what is wholesome, has them learn a craft, arranges their marriage with a suitable family when they have reached maturity, provides them with wealth at the proper time, and conducts himself according to the Dhamma toward his children—honoring and not disparaging his wife—he is said to practice the Dhamma among his children.
"Practicing the Dhamma toward his wives" means that he practices the Dhamma toward his wives by not being overbearing, by relinquishing authority, and by providing them with ornaments.
"Toward friends and companions" means that he practices the Dhamma toward friends and companions by gathering them together through the four bases of sympathy and by not deceiving them.
"Toward mounts and forces" refers to the mounts such as elephants and horses, and the army.
One who gives what is appropriate to be given, shows honor, and does not employ elephants, horses, and so forth in labor when they are old,
is said to practice the Dhamma toward them.
Likewise, regarding "in villages and market towns," one practices the Dhamma toward the inhabitants of those villages and towns by not oppressing them with fines or taxes.

Regarding the phrase "in the kingdoms and districts": when one oppresses both the kingdom and the district without cause, failing to maintain a benevolent mind, one is said to practice unrighteousness (*adhamma*) there;
however, when one does not oppress them but touches them with a benevolent mind, one is said to practice righteousness (*dhamma*) there.
Regarding the phrase "among recluses and brahmins": it means giving those four requisites to them...
"Among them he practices the Dhamma" means that by granting safety to all four-footed animals and birds, he is said to practice the Dhamma among them.
"The Dhamma has been practiced" means that the Dhamma of good conduct has been practiced.

"Bringing happiness" means it brings happiness in the three kinds of noble lineage and in the six celestial realms of sensual pleasure. "By what has been well-practiced" refers here to the well-practiced bodily good conduct and so forth performed in this life.
"Attained to heaven" means they have gone to the divine world, reckoned as the realm of the devas and the Brahmā-world; there they were born as recipients of divine prosperity.
"Do not neglect the Dhamma, O King"—therefore, Great King, even if you must give up your life, do not neglect the Dhamma.
Having thus spoken these ten verses on the practice of the Dhamma, he spoke this concluding verse while further exhorting him:
“In that very place are your duties; this indeed is the instruction:
association with the wise is auspicious; the self-controlled know that to be the whole.
Therein, “In that very place are your duties” is to be connected in the same manner as before. “Association with the wise is auspicious”—this too is to be understood in the same way.
"O Great King, 'the wise one knows that Sāma in its entirety'— this is what I have said. You, being a person of wisdom, should at all times associate with such individuals,
become endowed with noble qualities, and knowing for yourself through direct personal experience that Sāma is complete and perfect,
you should practice according to the instruction."
Thus the Great Being taught the Dhamma with the grace of a Buddha, as if causing the celestial Ganges to descend.
The great multitude paid him great honor and offered thousands of shouts of "Sādhu! The King, being delighted, addressed his ministers and asked:
"Gentlemen ministers, by whom was this spoken by my son, the wise Jambuka, whose beak is like the fruit of a young rose-apple tree?"
“What task was to be done has been done,” [the king said]. “It has been done, Your Majesty,” replied the general.
“Therefore, I grant him the position of general,” he said, and he appointed Jambuka to that office. From then on, standing in the position of general, he performed the duties of his father.
Great honor was accorded to the three birds. All three individuals [served] for the welfare and the Dhamma of the king.
They gave him instruction. Standing by the advice of the Great Being, the king performed meritorious deeds such as giving and became destined for heaven.
After the ministers had performed the funeral rites for the king, they informed the birds, saying, "Sire, O Jambuka bird, the king has commanded that your royal parasol be raised.
The Great Being said, "I have no need for kingship; you must be heedful."

"Rule the kingdom," he said, and having established the great multitude in the precepts, he had the law for legal decisions inscribed upon a golden plate, instructing them, "You should administer justice in this manner," and then entered the forest. His counsel prevailed for forty thousand years.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching by way of the king's instruction, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, King Ānanda was the king; Kuṇḍalinī was Uppalavaṇṇā; Vessantara was Sāriputta; and as for the jackal bird, it was I myself."
The First Exposition of the Tesakuṇa Jātaka.
[522] 2. The Exposition of the Sarabhaṅga Jātaka:
"Adorned, wearing earrings, well-robed... This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Veḷuvana concerning the Elder Mahāmoggallāna.

He spoke concerning the Parinibbāna. Having requested the Tathāgata, who was dwelling at Jetavana, to grant permission for his own Parinibbāna, the Elder Sāriputta departed and attained Parinibbāna in the birth-chamber at Nāḷaka village.
Upon hearing that he had passed away, the Teacher went to Rājagaha and resided in the Veḷuvana. At that time, the Elder Mahāmoggallāna was on the slope of Mount Isigili.
He dwelt at Kāḷasilā. By means of his power of supernormal success (*iddhi*), having reached its ultimate limit, he traveled to the celestial realms and to the Ussada hells.

Having seen the great sovereignty of the Buddha’s disciples in the celestial realms and the great suffering of the followers of other sects in the Ussada hells, he returned to the human world and said: "Such-and-such a lay follower and such-and-such a laywoman, in such-and-such a place..."
He told people, “Such-and-such a person, having been reborn in the world of the devas, enjoys great prosperity;

such-and-such a person and such-and-such a woman, among the disciples of the heretics, have been reborn in such-and-such a miserable state, such as hell. People gained confidence in the Teaching and avoided the heretics.
Great honor accrued to the Buddha’s disciples, while that of the heretics declined.
Having conceived malice toward them, they thought, "While he lives, our supporters will be divided and our honor will diminish;
we shall have him killed. For the sake of killing the Elder, they gave a thousand pieces of money to a thief named Samaṇagutta.
Thinking, "I will kill the Elder," he went to Kāḷasīla accompanied by a large retinue.
Seeing him approaching, the Elder rose up by means of his supernormal power and departed. Not seeing the Elder on that day, the robber turned back and went again on the following day;
thus he went for six days. The Elder likewise departed by means of his supernormal power each time.
But on the seventh day, the Elder’s past karma, to be experienced in a subsequent life, found its opportunity.
It is said that previously, having accepted his wife’s words and desiring to kill his mother and father, he took them by carriage into the forest.
Making a show of bandits having arisen, he beat and struck his parents. Because their vision was weak and they were deprived of sight, they did not recognize him as their own son;
perceiving them to be "merely these bandits," they cried out, "Dear one, such-and-such bandits are attacking us!"
“They are killing you; withdraw! they lamented for his sake. He thought, “Even while being beaten by me, these people are lamenting for my very sake; I am performing an improper deed.
Then, having comforted them and shown the manner of the thieves’ flight, he massaged their hands and feet and said, “Mother, father, do not be afraid; the thieves—”
Having said, “He has fled,” she brought him back to her own house once more.
That karma, having found no opportunity for so long a time, remained like a heap of glowing coals covered by ashes; now, it pursued and seized this final body.
For just as when a hunter sees a deer and releases a dog, the dog pursues the deer and—wherein... [the text continues].
It reaches its destination and seizes it right there; likewise, this karma gives its result in whatever place it finds an opportunity, and thus there is no escaping it.
Knowing that he was being dragged along by the force of his own past deed, the Elder did not go away. By the consequence of that [deed], the Elder...
He was unable to leap into the air. Even his supernormal power (iddhi), which had been capable of subduing Nandopananda and shaking the Vejayanta Palace, became weakened by the force of his karma.
The robber seized the Elder, crushed his bones until they were reduced to the size of rice grains, broke them, and ground them into powder;
having thus performed what is called "making [the body] like chaff-dust," he thought, "He is dead," and placed him in one...
Having thrown him onto the back of a bush, he departed with his retinue. The Elder, having regained mindfulness and thinking,
"I shall attain final Nibbāna after seeing the Teacher," wrapped his body in a shroud of jhāna, made it firm, leapt into the air,
and traveling through the sky to the presence of the Teacher, he paid homage to the Teacher and said, "Venerable Sir, the constituent of life..."
“I have relinquished my body; I shall attain final Nibbāna,” he said. “Will you attain final Nibbāna, Moggallāna? “Yes, venerable sir. “Where will you go to attain final Nibbāna?
“To the Black Rock Plateau, venerable sir. “In that case, Moggallāna, go and preach the Dhamma to me;
now there is no opportunity to see such a disciple as you. He replied, “So be it.”
“I shall do so, Bhante,” he said, and having paid homage to the Teacher, he leapt into the air to the height of a palm tree.
On the day of his final passing away, just like the Elder Sāriputta, he performed various kinds of miraculous powers, preached the Dhamma, and after paying homage to the Teacher,
he attained final nibbāna in the Kāḷasīla forest.
At that very moment, the six heavenly worlds were filled with a single tumultuous cry: "It is said our teacher has attained final Nibbāna!
Taking divine perfumes, garlands, incense, sandalwood powder, and various kinds of wood, they arrived. A funeral pyre was constructed of ninety-nine measures of red sandalwood.
The Teacher stood beside the Elder and oversaw the depositing of the body. All around the cremation site...
A rain of flowers fell over an area of one *yojana*. Among the gods there were humans, and among the humans there were gods.
In successive order, between the gods stood the *yakkhas*; between the *yakkhas* stood the *gandhabbas*;
between the *gandhabbas* stood the *nāgas*; and between the *nāgas* stood the *venateyyas*.
Between the *venateyya* women stood the *kinnaras*; between the *kinnaras* stood parasols; between the parasols stood golden fly-whisks;
between those stood banners; and between those stood flags.
For seven days they performed excellent festivities. The Teacher, having had the Elder take the relic, [placed it] at the gateway of the Veḷuvana monastery.

He had a cetiya constructed. At that time, the bhikkhus raised a discussion in the Dhamma hall, saying, "Friends, because the Elder Sāriputta did not attain final nibbāna in the presence of the Tathāgata, he did not receive great honor from the Buddhas;
however, the Elder Moggallāna, because he attained final nibbāna in the presence of the Buddhas, received great honor. The Teacher—
Having arrived, he asked, "Monks, with what discussion are you sitting together here now?
When they replied, "With this one," he said, "Monks, it is not only now that Moggallāna receives honor from me; he received it even in the past. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta [was conceived] in the womb of the chaplain’s Brāhmaṇī wife.
Having taken rebirth, at the end of ten months, he emerged from his mother’s womb at the time of dawn.
At that moment, in the city of Bārāṇasī, which extended twelve yojanas, all weapons burst into flame.

The chaplain, having gone outside at the moment of his son’s birth and gazing into the sky, observed the conjunction of the constellations and [thought]: “Because he was born under this constellation...”

Knowing that "this prince will become the foremost of archers in all of Jambudīpa," he went to the royal palace at an early hour and asked the king whether he had slept well. When the king replied, "How could I sleep well, teacher?
Today, throughout my entire residence, weapons have been set ablaze," [the teacher] said, "Do not fear, O King; it is not only in your residence, but throughout the entire city."
“They even blazed up; today it became thus because a prince was born in our house. “Teacher, what will become of this prince who has been born?
“Nothing at all, Great King; however, he will become the foremost of archers in the entire Jambudīpa.
“Excellent, Teacher! In that case, having looked after him, when he has reached maturity—”
Having said, "You should show it to us," he caused a thousand pieces of money—the price for the milk—to be given.

The chaplain took that and went home; having given it to his wife, on the day of the son's name-giving ceremony, because the weapons had blazed up at the moment of birth, he gave him the name Jotipāla.
Growing with such a great retinue, he became a possessor of supreme beauty at the age of sixteen.
Then his father, observing the excellence of his physical form, gave him a thousand pieces of money and said, "Dear son, go to Takkasilā and learn a craft from a world-renowned teacher.
He accepted this, saying, "Very well," and [prepared] the teacher’s fee.
Having taken leave of his parents and gone there, he paid a thousand pieces of money and began his craft; in just seven days, he reached perfection.
Then his teacher, being pleased, gave him his own precious sword, a bow with a jointed ram’s horn, a quiver with a jointed end, his own armor-garment, and a turban, saying: “Dear son,…”
“Jotipāla, I am old; now you must teach these young brahmin students,” he said, and entrusted the five hundred young brahmins to him alone.
The Bodhisatta took all the requisites, paid homage to his teacher, and returned to Bārāṇasī.
There he stood after paying homage to his parents. Then his father, having paid homage to him as he stood there, said: “Have you mastered [the arts]?”

“Those, dear father, are crafts. “Yes, dear father,” he replied. Having heard his words, he went to the royal palace and said, “Your Majesty, my son has returned after training in a craft; what should he do? “Teacher, let him attend upon us.
“Know his fee, Your Majesty. “Let him receive a thousand [pieces of money] daily. He said, “Very well.”
Having accepted [the proposal], he went home, summoned his son, and said, "Dear son, attend upon the king.
From then on, receiving a thousand [pieces of gold] every day, he waited upon the king.
The royal attendants grumbled, saying, "We see no work performed by Jotipāla, yet he receives a thousand every day."
“He takes it; we wish to see his craft. When the king heard their words, he told the chaplain.
The chaplain said, “Very well, Your Majesty,” and informed his son. The son replied, “Very well, father; I shall display my craft on the seventh day from now.
Furthermore, let the king have all the archers in his realm assembled. Having gone there, the chaplain—
He reported that matter to the king. The king had a drum beaten throughout the city and assembled the archers.

Sixty thousand archers gathered together. When the king learned that they had assembled, he had a drum beaten in the city, saying, "Let the city-dwellers witness the skill of Jotipāla," and having prepared the royal courtyard, he sat surrounded by a great multitude.
Having sat upon his excellent couch and summoned the archers, he sent word: "Let Jotipāla come.

Jotipāla placed the bow, quiver, armor, tunic, and turban given by his teacher inside his lower garment, had his sword fastened on, and went into the presence of the king in his ordinary attire, standing to one side.
The archers made an agreement, saying, “It is said that Jotipāla has come to display his skill in archery;
however, because he has come without taking up a bow, he must intend to take a bow from our hands, so we shall not give him one.
The king summoned Jotipāla and said, “Show your skill. He had a curtain drawn around and [stood] inside the curtain.
Standing there, he removed his cloth garment, put on his armor, fastened the turban upon his head,
strung the coral-colored bow with a deer-horn tip, slung his quiver over his back, placed his sword at his left side, and turning the thunderbolt-tipped iron arrow over the back of his hand,
he drew aside the curtain; then, piercing the earth, the young Naga prince appeared in full regalia.
Having emerged as if from within and gone forth, he stood after showing his respect to the king.
Seeing him, the great multitude roared, shouted, clapped their hands, and whistled. The king said, "Show your craft, Jotipāla.
"Your Majesty," he replied, "summon four of your archers—those who shoot at a fixed mark, those who shoot by sound, those who shoot by sight, and those who shoot by voice."
Then the king summoned him.
The Great Being, having drawn a circular boundary marked by four sides within the royal courtyard,
stationed four archers at the four corners and had thirty thousand arrows provided for each of them, remaining in the presence of each.

Setting aside one archer each as a marker, he himself took up a sharp-pointed iron arrow, stood in the center of the circle, and said, "Great King, let these four archers discharge their arrows at me simultaneously;
I shall ward off the arrows shot by them. The king commanded, "Do so," and the archers—
They said, “Great King, we are experts at hitting targets by sound, by the sound of a bowstring, by the sound of a reed, and by the sound of a voice;
Jotipāla is but a young boy, so we shall not miss. The Great Being said, “If you are able, then hit me.
Having agreed with “Very well,” they simultaneously discharged their arrows. The Great Being struck them all down with a single iron shaft.
Whether it fell here or there, he did not let it fall;

rather, as if surrounding the gateway of enlightenment, he made a hollow of arrows by shooting them so that they did not overstep one another—arrow against arrow, feather against feather, shaft against shaft, and barb against barb.
The archers' arrows were exhausted. Knowing that their arrows were spent, he [entered] the hollow of arrows.
Without even disappearing, he leapt up and went to stand before the king.
The great multitude raised a tumultuous clamor, shouting, cheering, clapping their hands, whistling, and snapping their fingers; they threw away their garments, ornaments, and other belongings.
Thus, there came to be a single heap of wealth numbering eighteen koṭis.
Then the king asked him, "What craft is this, Jotipāla? "It is called 'the warding off of arrows,' Your Majesty.
"Are there others who know this? "There is no one else in the whole of Jambudīpa, Your Majesty, except for me.
"Show me another, dear boy. "Your Majesty, let these four men stand at the four corners and shoot at me."
"They could not do it; however, I shall pierce these four targets with a single arrow. The archers did not dare to stand their ground.

The Great Being had four plantain trees placed at the four corners, tied a red cord to the nock of an iron shaft (*nārāca*), and aimed at one plantain tree and released it. The iron shaft pierced that plantain tree...
Then he pierced the second, then the third, then the fourth; having pierced the first one that had already been shot, it returned and rested right back in his hand.
Plantain trees stood there encircled by cords. The great multitude raised thousands of shouts.
"What kind of craft is this, dear son? asked the king. "It is called 'piercing the wheel,' O King. Furthermore—
"Show them, dear one," he said. The Great Being showed him what is called the "straight bamboo," the "bowstring of arrows," and the "arrow-shaft.
He constructed what is called an "arrow-palace," an "arrow-staircase," an "arrow-pavilion," an "arrow-rampart," and an "arrow-lotus pond.
He caused the "arrow-lotus" to bloom and made it rain "arrow-rain. Thus, these things were not shared by others.
Having displayed these twelve crafts, he further pierced seven great bodies that were unique to him alone:
he pierced a board of udumbara wood eight fingers thick, a board of asana wood four fingers thick, a copper plate two fingers thick, an iron plate one finger thick,
and having pierced through a hundred planks joined together, [he passed through] carts filled with straw, carts filled with sand, and carts filled with boards.
Having shot an arrow from the front, he caused it to emerge from the back; having shot an arrow from the back, he caused it to emerge from the front.
He sent an arrow that traveled four *usabhas* in the water and eight *usabhas* on land.

Mistaking a *vātiṅgaṇa* fruit for a bird’s nest, he pierced a single hair at a distance of one *usabha*. After the Bodhisatta had shot his arrows, [he created] palaces of arrows and other wonders in the sky.
Having done so, he caused those other notes to fall by means of a single note; thus, because he performed the breaking and the analysis [of sounds], he became renowned by the name “Sarabhaṅga.
While he was still displaying these many arts, the sun set.
Then the king, having offered him the position of commander-in-chief, said: “Jotipāla, it is late today; tomorrow you shall take up the position of commander-in-chief.”
“You shall receive an honorarium; have your hair and beard trimmed, bathe, and then come.

On that day, he gave him a hundred thousand for his expenses. The Great Being, thinking, “I have no need for this,” returned the wealth numbering eighteen koṭis to its owners, and with a great retinue, went to the river to bathe and have his hair and beard trimmed.
Having had [the preparations] made and having bathed, adorned with every ornament and endowed with incomparable splendor, he entered his residence;
there, having eaten various foods of exquisite flavor and reclined upon a magnificent couch, he slept for two watches of the night.
Waking in the final watch, he rose, folded his legs crosswise, and while sitting on the edge of the bed, he reflected upon the beginning, middle, and end of his own craft.
“From the very beginning of my craft, its ultimate result is perceived as slaughter; in the middle, it is the enjoyment of defilements;
and at the end, it is rebirth in hell. Killing living beings and excessive negligence in the enjoyment of defilements grant rebirth in hell.
Yet the king has granted me the great position of generalissimo; my power will be great.”
"I shall have many wives, sons, and daughters. Furthermore, when the basis for the defilements has reached such abundance, it is difficult to renounce them;
therefore, it is fitting for me to depart this very moment, go alone into the forest, and go forth into the ascetic life of an *isi*.
Having risen from his great couch and without informing anyone, he descended from the palace, went out through the main gate, and departed.
Alone, he entered the forest and set out toward the Kapiṭṭha Grove, three yojanas in extent, on the banks of the Godhāvarī River.
Knowing that he had departed, Sakka summoned Vissakamma and said, "Dear one, Jātipāla has gone forth into the great renunciation;
there will be a great assembly. Build a hermitage in the Kapiṭṭha Grove on the banks of the Godhāvarī River."

“Prepare the requisites for those who have gone forth,” he said. He did so accordingly. When the Great Being reached that place and saw a path used by only one person, he thought, “There must be a dwelling place for those who have gone forth. Following that path, he went there;
seeing no one, he entered a leaf-hut and, upon seeing the requisites for those who have gone forth, [thought], “Sakka, the king of the gods...”
Thinking, "He must have realized that I have departed," she removed her garment, put on a red bark-dress as an undergarment and a cloak,
draped a deerskin over one shoulder, tied her mass of matted hair into a topknot, placed a carrying-basket on her shoulder,
took up a walking-staff, and having emerged from the leaf-hut, ascended the walkway and paced back and forth several times.
Pacing back and forth, adorning the forest with the glory of his renunciation, he performed the preliminary exercises for the *kasiṇas*.

On the seventh day after his ordination, having realized the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and the five higher knowledges (*abhiññā*), he lived alone, subsisting on forest roots and fruits gathered as alms.
His mother, father, friends, kinsmen, and other circles of relatives [sought him out].
Not seeing him, they wandered about weeping and lamenting.
Then a certain forest-dweller, having entered the wilderness, saw the Great Being seated at the Kapiṭṭhaka hermitage;
recognizing him, he went to him, exchanged greetings with him, and returning to the city, [reported this] to his parents.

He reported it. They reported it to the king. The king, saying, "Come, let us see him," took his parents and, surrounded by a great multitude, reached the bank of the Godhāvarī River by the path shown by the forest-dweller.
Having arrived at the riverbank, the Bodhisatta sat in the air and taught the Dhamma; then, having led them all into the hermitage, he remained there as well.
While seated in the air, he revealed the peril of sensual pleasures and taught the Dhamma to them.
Beginning with the king, they all went forth into homelessness. The Bodhisatta remained right there, surrounded by the company of seers.
His dwelling there became famous throughout the whole of Jambudīpa. Other kings as well, together with their subjects, came into his presence.
They went forth, and there was a great gathering. Gradually, the assembly grew to consist of many hundreds of thousands.

If anyone thought sensual thoughts, thoughts of ill-will, or thoughts of cruelty, the Great Being would go before him, sit in the air, and teach the Dhamma, explaining the preliminary practice of the *kasiṇas*. By abiding in his instruction, [they attained] the eight...
Having attained the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and reached perfection in their practice, there were seven senior disciples:

Sālissara, Meṇḍissara, Pabbata, Kāḷadevila, Kisavaccha, Anusissa, and Nārada. In the course of time, the hermitage at Kapiṭṭhaka became so full that the dwelling place for the community of seers could no longer accommodate them.
Then the Great Being addressed Sālissara, saying, “Sālissara, this hermitage is no longer sufficient for the community of seers;
taking this community of seers with you, dwell near the town of Kalappacullaka within the kingdom of King Majjha.
Accepting his words with the reply, “Very well,” he took the community of many thousands of seers and departed.
He made his dwelling there. As men came and went forth into homelessness, the hermitage became full once more.
The Bodhisatta addressed Meṇḍissara, saying, “Meṇḍissara, take this company of seers and go;
in the borderlands of the Surāṭṭha country there is a river called Sātodikā; dwell on its bank. He then sent him away, and [the hermitage] became Kapiṭṭhaka-hermitage once again.
[The word] *paripūri* [means completion]. By this means, on the third occasion, he addressed the mountain:
“Mountain, there is a mountain named Añjana in the great forest; dwell depending upon it. On the fourth occasion, he addressed Kāḷadevila:
“Kāḷadevila, there is a mountain named Ghanasela in the kingdom of Avantī in the southern region; dwell depending upon it.”
He sent [them]. Once again, the Kapiṭṭhaka hermitage was filled; there were many hundreds of thousands of deer in five locations.
But Kisavaccha, having taken leave of the Great Being, dwelt in a park near the city named Kumbhavatī in the kingdom of King Daṇḍaki.
Meanwhile, Nārada was in the Middle Country, within a mountain range called Añjanagiri.
He dwelt there. The attendant, however, remained in the presence of the Great Being.
At that time, King Daṇḍaki dismissed a courtesan who had received great honor from his position.
Wandering about according to her own nature, she went to the park and, seeing the ascetic Kisavaccha, thought, "This one must be ill-omened; of him..."
Thinking, “I will wash away the stain from my body and go after bathing,” she chewed a tooth-stick and spat a large amount of saliva upon it first of all;

having spat it into the matted locks of the ascetic Kisavaccha, she even threw the tooth-stick right onto his head, and then, having washed her own head, she departed. The king, remembering her, returned to his former state.
She, being utterly deluded by ignorance, formed the perception: "Having transferred the ill omen onto the body of Kāḷakaṇṇī, the king has placed me back in my position;
I have regained my glory. Not long after that, the king dismissed the chaplain from his post.
He went to her and asked, "For what reason did you regain your position?"
Then she informed him, "Because the omen was cast upon the corpse of Kāḷakaṇṇī in the royal garden. The chaplain went and likewise cast the omen upon that corpse;
the king placed it back in its original position once more. Later on, the border regions rose in rebellion.
Surrounded by his army divisions, he set out for battle. Then the chaplain, deluded by ignorance, said to him:
Having asked, "Great King, do you desire victory, or rather defeat?
and being told, "Victory," he said, "In that case, the Kāḷakaṇṇī demon dwells in the royal garden; go after transferring your misfortune onto its body.
Taking his word, [the king] thought, "Those who come with me shall [transfer their misfortune] onto the body of the Kāḷakaṇṇī in the garden."

Having said, "Please invite me [to the meal]," he entered the garden, chewed a tooth-stick, and was the very first to spit phlegm into the matted hair of the ascetic and throw away the tooth-stick, and then washed his head. His entire retinue did likewise.
When he had departed, the general went there, saw the ascetic, removed the tooth-sticks and other refuse, and cleaned him thoroughly.
Having bathed him, she asked, "Venerable sir, what will happen to the king? He replied, "Friends, I have no ill-will in my mind;
however, the deities are angry and on the seventh day from now they will turn the entire kingdom into a wilderness.
You must take your children and wife and flee quickly elsewhere. Terrified and trembling, he went and reported this to the king. The king—
He did not accept his words. Having turned back and gone to his own home, he took his wife and children and fled, going to another kingdom.
The Teacher Sarabhaṅga, knowing this matter, dispatched two young ascetics and commanded by way of the air, "Bring Kisavaccha here on a palanquin.
The king, having fought and captured the bandits...
He returned to the city itself. Upon his arrival, the deities first caused the rain-god to send down rain;
when all the filth had been swept away by the torrent of rain, they sent down a rain of pure sand. Upon the pure sand, they sent down a rain of celestial flowers;
upon the celestial flowers, a rain of māsaka coins; and upon the māsaka coins, a rain of kahāpaṇa coins. Upon the kahāpaṇas—
A rain of divine ornaments fell; the people, filled with joy, began to seize the ornaments of gold and silver.
Then, a rain of various kinds of weapons, blazing fiercely, fell upon their bodies, and the people were cut into pieces. Then, great, glowing embers fell upon them.
Upon them fell massive, blazing mountain peaks; over these rained a shower of fine sand that filled a space sixty cubits high.
Thus, a region sixty yojanas in extent became a wasteland (*araṭṭha*), and this state of being a wasteland became known throughout the whole of Jambudīpa.
Then three kings—the Kāliṅga, Aṭṭhaka, and Bhīmaratha—who were the rulers of the kingdoms adjacent to that realm, reflected:
"It is reported that formerly in Bārāṇasī, King Kalābu Kāsika, having offended the ascetic Khantivādi, entered the earth;
likewise, King Nāḷikera had the ascetic devoured by dogs, and Sahassabāhu—"
"It is heard that Ajjuna, having offended against Aṅgīrasa, and now King Daṇḍaki, having offended against Kisavaccha, have met with destruction along with their kingdoms.
However, we do not know the place where these four kings were reborn;
there is no one capable of explaining that for us except the Teacher Sarabhaṅga. Therefore, let us approach him.
"We shall ask these questions. Thus, the three of them set out with a great retinue for the purpose of asking the questions.
However, they did not know that "so-and-so has also set out," and each one thought, "I alone am going.
Not far from the Godhāvarī river, their paths converged. Alighting from their chariots, the three of them [mounted] a single chariot.
Having ascended [the chariot], they reached the bank of the Godhāvarī River.
At that moment, Sakka, seated upon the Paṇḍukambala stone throne, reflected on seven questions and thought:
"Setting aside Teacher Sarabhaṅga, there is no one else in the world with its devas capable of answering these questions; therefore, these questions [must be asked of him]."
"I shall ask them; these three kings have also reached the bank of the Godhāvarī river to question the teacher Sarabhaṅga, and I myself shall ask them their questions as well.
Surrounded by deities from two celestial realms, he descended from the world of the gods.
On that very day, Kisavaccha passed away. To perform his funeral rites, [the people gathered] at four places.
Many thousands of seers went to that very place, erected pavilions at five locations, and having prepared a sandalwood pyre for the ascetic Kisavaccha, they cremated his body.
A rain of celestial flowers fell over an area measuring half a yojana all around the cremation site. The Great Being [performed] the deposition of his remains...
Having had the hermitage constructed, he entered it and sat down surrounded by those groups of seers.
When those kings arrived at the riverbank, there arose the sound of the trumpets of their great armies and vehicles.
Hearing that, the Great Being addressed the ascetic Anusissa, saying, "Dear son, go and find out what this sound is. He [took] a water-jar...
Having taken [the horse] and gone there, he saw those kings and spoke the first verse by way of inquiry:
“Adorned with earrings, well-dressed, with swords bound in sheaths of beryl and pearls—O bulls among chariot-warriors, who are you that stand here?
