How are you known in the world of men?”
In that context, "furnished with sword-blades bound with emeralds, pearls, and cloth" means they were equipped with precious swords adorned with beryl gems and pearl pendants.
"Stay! means "stay in one chariot. "Who are you? means "who indeed are you? How do they recognize you?"
Having heard his words, they descended from their chariots, paid homage, and stood there. Among them, King Aṭṭhaka, conversing with him, spoke this second verse:
“I am Aṭṭhaka, and this one is Bhīmaratha; this is the King of Kāliṅga, Uggata.
We have come here to see the well-restrained seers and to ask questions.”
In this context, "exalted" means as prominent and well-known as the moon or the sun. "Of the seers who are well-restrained":

"Venerable sir, we have not come here for the sake of forest sports and the like; rather, we have come here for the purpose of seeing the seers who are well-restrained in body and so forth, and endowed with virtue.
"We have come to ask about the Dhamma": [this means] to ask the Teacher Sarabhanga questions regarding the Dhamma.
“Emha” means “we have come. The letter *ya* should be understood as a euphonic conjunction (*byañjanasandhi*).
Then the ascetic said to them: “Excellent, Great Kings! You have indeed come to the very place where you ought to come.
Therefore, having bathed and rested, enter the hermitage, pay homage to the company of seers, and ask your question of the Teacher Sarabhaṅga himself.”
Having exchanged greetings with them, he lifted up the water-jar and, while wiping away the drops of water and looking up into the sky,
saw Sakka, the king of the gods, surrounded by a host of deities and mounted upon the noble back of Erāvaṇa,
descending. Addressing him, he spoke the third verse:
“You stand in the air, in the sky, like the moon on the fifteenth day of the waxing fortnight.
I ask you, O powerful yakkha: what is it that people in the world of men recognize as having been done by you?

In this context, *vehāyasaṃ* means having ascended, you stand in the sky, in the atmosphere. *Pathaddhuno* means having gone halfway along the road; the meaning is that you stand in the middle of the sky, halfway through the journey.
Having heard that, Sakka spoke the fourth verse:
“He whom they call ‘Lord of the Sujās’ among the gods, and ‘Maghavan’ in the world of men—
that King of the Devas has arrived today to see the sages who are well-restrained.”

"Therein, 'that king of the gods' refers to myself, Sakka, the king of the gods. 'Having arrived here today' means that I have come to this place today. 'For the sake of seeing' means for the purpose of seeing, for the purpose of paying homage, and for the purpose of asking questions of the Teacher Sarabhaṅga.

Then Anusissa said to him, "Very well, Great King, you may follow later," and taking the water-pot, he entered the hermitage, set the water-pot aside, and [attended] to the three kings and the king of the gods.
He informed the Great Being that they had come to ask questions. Surrounded by his company of seers, he sat down in the great spacious hall.
The three kings arrived, paid homage to the company of seers, and sat down to one side.
Sakka also descended, approached the company of seers, and standing with palms joined in reverence, he praised the company of seers and, while paying homage, spoke the fifth verse:
“From afar we have heard that the seers have assembled, possessing great supernormal power and endowed with the qualities of psychic potency.
With a heart full of faith, I pay homage to you, O noble ones, who are the best among men here in the world of the living.
Therein, “from afar we have heard” means, “Venerable sir, while we were still standing in the world of the devas, we have heard from afar that you have arrived.”
He spoke thus. This is what was meant: "These sages of ours who have gathered here are renowned far and wide, as famous as they are well-known even unto the Brahma-world.
"Of great psychic power" means possessed of great majesty. "Endowed with the qualities of psychic power" means possessed of the fivefold quality of *iddhi*.
"Ayire" means "Noble Lady. "Ye" means "you who are the best among humans in this world of living beings."
Having thus praised the company of seers, Sakka sat down to one side, avoiding the six faults of sitting. Then, seeing him seated downwind from the seers, Anusissa spoke this sixth verse:
“The fragrance of the seers who have long been ordained, issuing from their bodies, wafts away with the wind.
Departing from here, O thousand-eyed King of Gods, the fragrance of the seers is not unclean.”
In that context, "those who have long gone forth" (*ciradikkhitānaṃ*) means those who have long been ordained (*cirapabbajitānaṃ*). "Withdraw" (*paṭikkamma*) means go back; depart.
"O Thousand-eyed One" (*sahassanetta*) is a form of address. For Sakka alone perceives the matter intended by his thousand ministers;
therefore, he is called "the Thousand-eyed One. Alternatively, he is "the Thousand-eyed One" because he is capable of transcending the range of vision of the thousand-eyed gods.
"It is 'impure' because it is permeated by sweat, grime, and so forth, and thus has a foul odor; you, however, desire purity, and for that reason this smell oppresses you.
Having heard this, Sakka spoke the following verse:
"The fragrance of the seers who have long been ordained, having departed from their bodies, let it go with the wind."
“Like a garland of variegated, fragrant flowers, we expect this scent, venerable sir;
for the devas here do not perceive it as repulsive.
Therein, “let it go” means let it proceed as it pleases; the sense is: let it strike our nostrils. “We expect” (pāṭikaṅkhāma) means...
"We desire, we long for it. "In this regard," means that in this fragrance, the devas do not have a sense of disgust.
For devas feel disgust only toward those who are immoral, not toward those who are virtuous.
Having spoken thus, he said: "Venerable sir, I have come with great enthusiasm to ask a question, Anusissa."
“Grant me leave,” he said. Having heard his words, the king rose from his seat and, making way for the company of seers, spoke these two verses:
“Purindada, Lord of Beings, the illustrious Sakka, King of the Devas, Maghavan, Lord of Sujā;
that King of the Gods, the crusher of the hosts of Asuras, desires leave to ask a question.”
“Who here among these wise ones will answer the subtle questions put to him—questions concerning the three kings who rule over men, and Vāsava, the lord of the gods?
In this context, “Purindada” and the other terms are names based on Sakka’s own virtues. For he is called Purindada because he gave gifts in former times (pure).

He is the Lord of Beings (*bhūtapati*) because he is the eldest among beings; he is renowned (*yasassī*) because of his perfection of retinue; he is the Lord of the Gods (*devānamindo*) because of his supreme sovereignty;

he is Sakka because he has well performed the seven duties; he is Maghavan by virtue of his previous birth; he is the Lord of Sujā (*sujampati*) because of his status as the husband of the asura maiden Sujā;
and he is the King of the Gods (*devarājā*) because he delights the gods. "Who indeed" (*ko nu eva*) means who indeed. "In this subtle manner" (*nipuṇeti*).
Regarding these subtle and delicate questions: "Of the kings" means of the monarchs.
Having grasped the intention of these four kings, he says, "Who will explain the questions of these wise seers? Do you know anyone capable of answering their questions?
Hearing that, the host of seers said, "Venerable one, Anusissa, it is as if you were standing on the earth yet not seeing the earth."
Having said, "Who else besides the teacher Sarabhaṅga is capable of answering these questions?", he spoke this verse:
"This seer Sarabhaṅga is an ascetic, born restrained from sexual intercourse;
the son of a teacher, well-disciplined in form—he shall answer their questions."

In this context, *Sarabhaṅga* means: having shot arrows into the air and constructed celestial palaces (*pāsāda*) and other structures with them, he then caused those arrows to fall back by means of a single arrow, thereby effecting their breaking and dispersal;
thus he is called Sarabhaṅga. *From sexual intercourse* (*methunasmā*) means from the act of sexual union.

It is said that he went forth into homelessness without having indulged in sexual intercourse. *The son of the royal preceptor* (*āceraputto*) means the son of the king’s teacher, the domestic chaplain (*purohita*).
Having spoken thus, the company of seers said to Anusissa, "Friend, you yourself, having paid homage to the Teacher,
should request an opportunity for Sakka to answer the question he has asked on behalf of the company of seers. He consented, saying,
"Very well," and after paying homage to the Teacher, spoke the following verse while requesting the opportunity:
“Koṇḍañña, answer these questions; the seers of noble form entreat you.
Koṇḍañña, this is the nature among men: that when one has grown old, this burden comes upon him.
Therein, “Koṇḍañña” is an address to him by his clan name. “Dhamma” means inherent nature. “Yaṃ vuddhaṃ” means that which [comes] through wisdom.
"This burden of answering questions falls upon an elder man; this is the nature of things among human beings.
Therefore, make it manifest as if raising up a thousand suns and moons, and speak the answers to the questions of the King of Devas.
Then, granting him the opportunity, the Great Being spoke the following verse:
“Let the worthy ones ask whatever question they have desired in their minds, having been granted leave.
For I shall answer each one of you, having known this world and the world beyond by myself.
In this context, “whatever” does not refer only to you, but rather to whatever has been desired in the minds of the entire world, including its devas.

"Let your honors question me; for having realized this world and the world beyond by my own wisdom, I shall answer every question you have regarding matters pertaining to this world or the world beyond. Thus he offered his invitation as the Omniscient One.
When he had thus granted the opportunity, Sakka asked the question he had prepared himself. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
Then Maghavā Sakka, Atthadassī, and Purindada asked the first question, that which he had long desired:
"What is it that, having slain, one never grieves? What is it that the seers praise as the thing to be abandoned?"
“Kassīdha vuttaṃ pharusaṃ khametha, akkhāhi me Koṇḍañña etamatthan”ti.

Therein, “yañcāsī” means: he asked what it was that he had desired in his mind. “Etam atthan” means: regarding this matter asked by me, “tell me. Thus, with this single verse, he asked three questions.
Then, answering them, he said:
“Having slain anger, one never grieves; the seers praise the abandonment of malice.
One should forgive all harsh speech; the virtuous call this the supreme patience.
In this context, “having slain anger” means having killed and cast away anger. For it is by means of a mind of resentment that one who grieves truly grieves.
In the absence of anger, whence can there be sorrow? Therefore it is said: “He never sorrows.

Regarding the abandonment of slander (*makkhappahāna*): the seers explain this as the abandonment of slander—which is characterized by concealing one’s own virtues when they have been performed by others and is synonymous with ingratitude.
“Of all” means he should endure harsh speech from everyone, whether inferior, middling, or superior. “The peaceful ones” refers to the ancients.
The wise speak thus.
Sakka said:
"It is possible to endure the words of both one who is equal or even one who is superior;"
“How indeed could one endure the speech of an inferior? Explain this matter to me, Koṇḍañña.
Sarabhaṅga said:
“One might endure the speech of a superior out of fear; but one endures that of an equal because of provocation.”
“And whoever here would endure the words of one who is inferior—this, the virtuous say, is the highest patience.
The connection between such verses should be understood as a dialogue of question and answer. In that context, [the Buddha said]:
“Tell me, venerable Koṇḍañña, you have well explained two questions; one [question] has captured my mind.”
"He does not accept [the challenge]; how can one endure the words of one inferior to oneself?
Tell me that," he asked, speaking thus. "This forbearance"—that is, the endurance of the words of one inferior in birth, clan, and so forth—"this forbearance is supreme," say the ancient wise ones.
But as for this [other kind], out of fear of one superior in birth and so forth...
The meaning is that forbearance through seeing the danger in causing injury to an equal—characterized by the excellence of action—is what is called "forbearance as endurance" (*adhivāsanakhanti*).

When this was said, Sakka said to the Great Being: "Venerable sir, first you said, 'The virtuous call it the highest forbearance when one forgives the harsh words of all,' but now you say, 'He who here forgives the speech of an inferior...'"
“The virtuous call this patience supreme,” you say; yet your later statement does not accord with your former one.
Then the Great Being said to him, “Sakka, my later remark was made on account of my having endured harsh words after realizing, ‘This man is inferior.
For it is not possible to know whether beings are superior or otherwise by the mere sight of their physical form.”
Having said, "Therefore, the former has been stated," he spoke this verse to demonstrate that it is difficult to discern whether beings are superior,
equal, or inferior by the mere sight of their physical form,
apart from their mode of association: "How could one distinguish the fourfold appearance— whether it be superior, similar, or even inferior?"
“Virtuous ones move about in disguise; therefore, one should endure the words of all.
In this context, “disguised by the four postures” means having their true nature concealed by the four modes of conduct (*iriyāpatha*).
“In disguise” (*virūparūpena*) means that even though they possess supreme qualities, they wander about in the guise of those who are ill-favored or base persons. Regarding this matter:
The story of the Elder Majjhantika should be told.
Having heard it, Sakka became free from doubt and requested, "Venerable sir, please tell us of the benefit of this forbearance. Then the Great Being spoke this verse:
"Even a vast army, together with its king, fighting for this purpose, would not obtain such a reward."
“Whatever patient and true person may obtain, through the power of patience, enmities are stilled.
In this context, “this matter” refers to the matter characterized by the pacification of enmity and the nature of non-aversion.
When the Great Being had thus spoken on the virtues of patience, those kings thought: “Sakka has [answered] his own question...”

“He asks [us], but he will not grant us the opportunity to ask. Then, knowing their intention, Sakka set aside four questions he had himself prepared and, in order to inquire about their own doubts, spoke this verse:
“Rejoicing in your well-spoken words, I ask you another question; please, tell me that now.”
“As Daṇḍakī, Nāḷikera, Athajjuna, and King Kalābu—tell me the destiny of those who committed such evil deeds; where have those harassers of seers been reborn?
In that context, “rejoicing” refers to your [response] consisting of the answers to the three questions asked by me.
Having rejoiced in these well-spoken words— namely, how those four men came to be— and saying "And Kalābu," meaning King Kalābu,
and "Then Ajjuṇa," meaning King Ajjuṇa,
the Great Being, as he was granting him leave, spoke these five verses:
“Why is it, Vaccha, that having scattered [the dust] with a stick, you—along with your kinsmen and your entire kingdom—have been uprooted?
You are being cooked in the hell named Kukkuḷa, and sparks fall upon your body.
You who harmed those restrained ones who have gone forth, those blameless ascetics while they were preaching the Dhamma.”
The dogs gathered there and devoured that coconut while it was still quivering.
Then Ajuna fell headfirst onto a spear-point in hell with his feet upwards,
because he had reviled Gotama of the Aṅgīrasa clan, an ascetic of patience who had long practiced the holy life.
“He who had a monk— renounced in pieces, preaching patience, harmless— whoever had him cut into fragments,
is reborn in the Kalābu-vīci hell, where he is cooked in great heat, bitter and terrifying. Having heard of these hells,
and others even more wicked than these, the wise man [should refrain from such deeds].”
"One should practice the Dhamma among recluses and brahmins; by acting thus, one goes to a heavenly state.

In this context, *kisā* means having a lean body due to the lack of flesh and blood. *Avakiriya* means having scattered [the dust], that is, having cleared away the impurity from his body by spitting and throwing away the tooth-stick.
*Ucchinnamūlo* means having become one whose roots are cut off. *Sajano* means together with his retinue.
"In the hell named Kukkuḷa" refers to the hot-ashes hell (*uṇhachārika-niraya*), which is a hundred *yojanas* in extent and lasts for an eon (*kappa*).
"Sparks" (*phuliṅgāni*) means glowing embers (*vītaccitaṅgārā*).

It is said that when one is submerged there in the hot ashes, the hot ashes enter through nine openings of the body, and very large embers fall upon the head. At the moment they fall, the entire body [is consumed].
He burned like a lamp-tree, and violent pains coursed through him. Unable to endure it, he let out a great cry.
The Teacher Sarabhaṅga split open the earth and showed him being roasted there in that manner;
the great multitude fell into terror and agitation. Knowing his extreme state of fear, the Great Being made that hell vanish.
"Preaching the Dhamma" means speaking the Dhamma of the ten courses of wholesome action. "Ascetic" (samaṇa) means one who has stilled evil deeds.
"Innocent" (adūsaka) means one who is blameless. "Nāḷikera" refers to a king of that name. "In the other world" means having been reborn in hell in the next life.
"Having gathered together" means having come from here and there and torn him apart, large dogs devour him. In that...

It is said that while King Nāḷikera was ruling in the city of Dantapura in the kingdom of Kaliṅga, a certain great ascetic, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred ascetics, came from the Himālaya mountains and, having taken up residence in the royal park, taught the Dhamma to the great multitude.
People reported to the king, "A righteous ascetic is living in the park. However, the king was unrighteous.
He ruled the kingdom unrighteously. While his ministers were praising the ascetic, he thought, "I too shall listen to the Dhamma," and went to the park.

Having paid homage to the ascetic, he sat down. As the ascetic exchanged greetings with the king, he asked, "Great King, do you rule the kingdom righteously? Do you not oppress the people? Enraged at him, the king—
Thinking, "This fraudulent matted-hair ascetic has been speaking only of my faults in the presence of the city-dwellers for so long;
well, let it be, I shall find out," she invited them, saying, "Please come to our house door tomorrow.
On the following day, having filled jars with old excrement, when the ascetics arrived, she poured the excrement into their alms-bowls.
Having filled [the pit], having had the door closed, and having had the pestles and iron bars seized, he had the heads of the seers split open;

having seized them by their matted locks and dragged them out, he had them devoured by dogs. Thereupon, he himself entered the earth that had been split right there and was reborn in the Sunakha Great Hell (*Sunakha-mahāniraya*).
There, his body became three-quarters of a league (*gāvuta*) in measure. Then, very large...
Dogs the size of great elephants, of five colors, pursued him, bit him,
and having cast him down upon the glowing iron earth extending for nine yojanas, they devoured him while he writhed, tearing out his flesh until their mouths were full.
The Great Being split the earth asunder, revealed that hell, and perceiving the terror of the multitude, made it disappear.
Then Ajjuṇa, the thousand-armed king— [known as] Aṅgīrasa because he was so named due to the radiance (raṃsi) issuing forth from his limbs (aṅga)—
having harassed [him], that is, having tormented him by piercing him with a poisoned arrow and bringing him to the end of his life;
it is said that this king named Ajjuṇa, while ruling his kingdom in the capital city of Ketaka in the Mahisa country, went out hunting.
Having killed deer, he wandered about eating meat roasted on coals. Then one day, having constructed a watchtower at the place where the deer gathered, he stood there watching for them.
At that time, a certain ascetic climbed a *kāra* tree not far from the king and was plucking its fruits;
as he released a branch laden with fruit he had already gathered, it snapped loose. As it fell—
At the sound [of the arrow], the deer that had reached that place fled. The king, becoming enraged, pierced the ascetic with a poisoned shaft.
As he fell, tumbling down, he struck his head against a khadira post and died right upon the point of the stake.
At that very moment, the king split the earth asunder and was reborn in the Sattisūla Hell, which measures three gavutas in extent.
A body was formed. There, the wardens of hell, having crushed it with flaming weapons, make it ascend a mountain of glowing iron.
When it stands upon the summit of the mountain, the wind strikes it; by that gust of wind, it melts away and falls.
At that moment, below, upon a ground of glowing iron extending nine yojanas, there is a mass of fire the size of the trunk of a great *tāla* tree.
An iron stake rises up. Having reached the very tip of that stake, he stands impaled upon it.
At that moment, the earth blazes, the stake blazes, and his body blazes. There he is cooked, crying out with a great roar.
The Great Being split the earth asunder, revealed that hell, and, perceiving the state of terror in the great multitude, made himself disappear.
"Khaṇḍaso" means having cut [the victim] into pieces—hand, foot, ear, and nose—bit by bit. "Adūsakaṃ" means innocent.
Having had him thus mutilated, they had him beaten with two thousand lashes of the whip, then seized by his matted hair and dragged along, laid down face-down, and struck on the back with the heel;
thus they subjected him to great suffering. This is called the *Kalābu-vīci* hell.
*Kalābu* [was reborn] in Avīci. "Bitter" means sharp pain; having been reborn in such a hell, he is cooked between six flames.
Furthermore, the account of King Kalābu is already told in the *Khantivādijātaka*.
And as for "others even more wicked than these," this refers to having heard of other hells that are even more wicked than these [previously mentioned] hells.
"O Sakka, King of the Devas, a wise son of good family practices the Dhamma with the understanding that not only are there these four hells,
nor are these kings alone who have gone to hell; rather, knowing that there are other hells and other kings reborn in those hells,
he should practice the Dhamma toward recluses and brahmins by providing the four requisites and by establishing protection and defense in accordance with the Dhamma."
When the Great Being had thus shown the places where the four kings were reborn, the three kings became free from doubt. Then Sakka, asking the remaining four questions, spoke this verse:
“Appreciating what you have so well spoken, I ask you another question; pray, tell me that now:
What kind of person do they call virtuous? What kind of person do they call wise?”
“What kind of person do they call a true man (*sappurisa*), and what kind of person does glory (*siri*) not abandon?
Therein, “what kind of person does glory not abandon? means: what kind of person indeed, once glory has been attained, does not leave him?
Then, answering him, the Great Being spoke these four verses:
“He who is restrained in body and speech, and does no evil with the mind;
he who does not speak untruth for his own sake—they call such a person virtuous.
Contemplating a profound question with the mind, he performs no harmful or cruel deed.”
One who does not neglect a timely word of benefit— such a person they call wise.
“The one who is grateful and appreciative, the steadfast hero, who is a good friend and firm in devotion,
and who respectfully performs what must be done for the suffering person— such a person they call a true man.”
“Endowed with all these virtues—faithful, gentle, sharing, and generous;
inclusive, friendly, and soft-spoken—such a person as this, Fortune does not forsake.

In this regard, the phrases beginning with “with the body” are stated by way of the three doors of good conduct (*sucarita*). “Not for one’s own sake” is merely a conventional expression used in the teaching.

The meaning is that he does not speak falsehood for the sake of himself, or for the sake of another, or for the sake of fame, or for the sake of wealth, or for the sake of gain, or for the sake of any trifling material thing.
Granted, this meaning is already established by the phrase "restrained in speech";
however, it is stated again in this way to demonstrate the gravity of the matter, since there is no evil that a liar would not commit.
It is to be understood thus: they call that person virtuous.

"A profound question" means a question that is deep in both meaning and text—hidden, concealed, and similar to those found in the *Sattubhasta Jātaka*, the *Sambhava Jātaka*, and the *Mahāumaṅga Jātaka*. "They contemplate with the mind" means with the mind...

The meaning is: one who, having reflected upon the goal and penetrated it, is able to explain it by making it manifest as if raising up a thousand moons and a thousand suns. "Not excessively harmful" (*nāccāhitaṃ*) means not too harmful;
the meaning is: one who does not perform acts that exceed what is beneficial, nor acts that are cruel, harsh, or violent. To clarify this meaning—
“Wise people do not perform evil deeds for the sake of their own happiness;
even when touched by suffering and oppressed by it, they do not abandon the Dhamma out of desire or hatred.
Thus should the Bhūri Question be recited.

Regarding the phrase "timely" (*kālāgata*): here, one who accomplishes these things— giving at the time for giving, guarding virtue at the time for guarding virtue, observing the Uposatha at the time for observing it,
establishing oneself in the refuges at the time for doing so, going forth at the time for going forth, performing the duties of a recluse at the time for doing so,
and applying oneself to the practice of insight at the time for doing so— does not neglect, does not omit, and does not let slip the meaningful state that has arrived at its proper time.
...so it is named. "Of such a kind," O Sakka: when all-knowing Buddhas, Pacceka Buddhas, and Bodhisattas speak of one possessed of wisdom, they speak of a person of this sort.

In the verse beginning with "He who indeed," one who recognizes the virtue performed for oneself by another is called "grateful" (*kataññū*). Having recognized this, however, by means of that [virtue] of his—
One who has done a favor and, in return for that favor, acts with gratitude is called "one who knows what has been done.

Regarding "of one who is suffering": having taken upon oneself the suffering of a companion who has fallen into distress, one who personally and respectfully attends to whatever needs arise for them—the Buddhas and others describe such a person as a "true man" (sappurisa).
Furthermore, those called true men are grateful and acknowledge what has been done for them.
The *Satapatta-jātaka*, the *Cūḷahaṃsa-jātaka*, the *Mahāhaṃsa-jātaka*, and others should be recounted. By all these means:
"O Sakka, one who is endowed with all these virtues mentioned below, beginning with virtue (*sīla*); who is faithful (*saddho*), meaning possessed of the faith of conviction (*okappana-saddhā*);
who is gentle (*mudu*), meaning one who speaks kindly; and who is generous (*saṃvibhāgī*), because of delighting in the distribution of virtue and the distribution of gifts."

One who shares; one who is bountiful in speech, knowing the words of supplicants and speaking with a disposition toward giving; one who is inclusive because of gathering people together through the four bases of sympathy;

one who is sociable due to sweetness of speech, and one whose words are gentle due to smoothness of expression—will such a person not be forsaken by glory, which is to say, the excellence of attained renown and splendor? His glory shall not perish.
Thus the Great Being answered the four questions as if raising the full moon in the vault of the sky. Following that, there occurred both the asking and the answering of the remaining questions:
“Rejoicing in your well-spoken words, I ask you another thing; pray, tell me this:
among virtue, glory, the duty of the good, and wisdom—which do they say is the most excellent?”
“Wisdom is supreme, so the skilled say, like the king of stars among the constellations;
virtue, glory, and the Dhamma of the good are all followers of the wise man.
Rejoicing in what you have well spoken, I ask you another question; pray, tell me that now.”
"What must one do, what must one perform, what must one practice, and by serving whom does one obtain wisdom here?
Tell me the path for the attainment of wisdom: how acting does a mortal become wise?
"One should serve those who are mature, skillful, and learned; one should be a receiver of their teachings and a questioner."
One should listen attentively to well-spoken words; by acting accordingly, a mortal becomes wise.
That wise person contemplates the strands of sensual pleasure as impermanent, as suffering, and as a disease.
Seeing them thus, he abandons desire for those painful sensual pleasures that are fraught with great danger.
“Having become free from passion, one should dispel hatred and cultivate a measureless mind of loving-kindness;
having laid aside the rod toward all beings, the blameless one attains the Brahma-state.
In this context, *sīla* refers to the virtue of conduct (*ācāra-sīla*). *Siri* refers to the glory of sovereignty. *Satañca dhammaṃ* refers to the Dhamma of the virtuous ones (*sappurisa-dhamma*).
"Paññanti supaññaṃ": "O one of good wisdom, among these four qualities, which do they say is the most excellent?
Thus he asks. "For wisdom, Sakka, among these four qualities, that which is called wisdom is indeed the most excellent;
so the Buddhas and others who are skilled declare. For just as the hosts of stars surround the moon, and the moon alone is their [leader]...
"Supreme. Thus, virtue, glory, and the Dhamma of the good—these three are concomitants of the wise;
they follow only the wise and become the retinue of wisdom alone—this is the meaning.
"How-doing" (*kathaṃkaro*) and the following terms are merely synonyms for one another. "How-doing" means performing what kind of action, or doing what?
"By practicing what, by serving whom, by associating with whom, and by attending upon whom does one obtain wisdom in this world?
Tell me the very path to wisdom; I wish to know. How must a mortal act to be called wise?"—thus he asks.

"In those who have grown" means in the wise who have attained the increase of wisdom. "In the skillful" means in those capable of knowing subtle causes. "One who acts thus" refers to the person who...
One who associates with, frequents, and attends upon a person of such a kind as described; who learns the text;

who asks about the meaning again and again; and who—like one carving an inscription on stone or like one receiving the roar of a lion through a golden pipe—listens attentively with ears pricked for the well-spoken words: a mortal who acts in this way becomes wise.

Thus, like the sun rising from the eastern world-system, the Great Being, having explained the path of practice through wisdom (*paññā*), now spoke the words beginning with "He is wise" (*sa paññavā*) while describing the qualities of that wisdom. Therein, regarding "the strands of sensual pleasure" (*kāmaguṇe*):

he views them as impermanent in the sense of their non-existence once they have become constituent parts of sensual desire, and as the basis for the sufferings pertaining to both the present life and the future life.
He views and contemplates them as suffering and as a disease, because of the arising of eighty-nine types of diseases dependent upon sense pleasures.
Thus, through these reasons, Vipassī, seeing the impermanence and other characteristics of sense pleasures, understands:

"There is no end to the sufferings that arise dependent upon sense pleasures; the abandoning of sense pleasures alone is happiness. Having thus understood this regarding sense pleasures which are themselves suffering...

He abandons desire for great fears. Regarding him as one "free from lust," Sakka, such a person, having removed the natural defects that arise due to the nine grounds of resentment, should develop a mind of loving-kindness.
Because its object is immeasurable beings, he develops it as immeasurable;
and with his jhāna unimpaired, he is reborn in the Brahma-world, beyond reproach.

While the Great Being was thus speaking of the faults of sensual desires, the passion for the five strands of sense pleasure was abandoned by all three kings and their armies through the relinquishing of those very limbs. Knowing this, the Great Being spoke this verse in order to praise them:
“Your arrival has been for a great purpose, O Tavaṭṭhaka, Bhīmaratha, and the exalted King of Kaliṅga;
the passion for sensual pleasures has been abandoned by you all.”

In that context, "of great benefit" means having great purpose, great expansion, and great radiance. "Your eightfold [fetters]" means your eight [fetters]. "Abandoned" means abandoned by way of abandonment through the factor of its own nature (*tadaṅgappahāna*).
Having heard this, the kings, offering praise to the Great Being, spoke this verse:
"It is even so, O knower of others' minds; for all of us, sensual lust has been abandoned."
"Grant us the opportunity out of favor, so that we may attain the same destination as yours.

Therein, "out of favor" means: grant us the opportunity for the sake of our going forth. "So that we may attain the same destination as yours" means: having gone forth, may we achieve and reach your own accomplishment; they said, "May we penetrate the qualities you have penetrated.
Then, granting them the opportunity, the Great Being spoke the following verse:
“I grant you leave for the sake of favoring you, for lust for sensual pleasures has been abandoned by you.
Pervade your bodies with abundant rapture, so that you may attain my destination.
In this context, “pervade your bodies” means: pervade your bodies with the abundant rapture of jhāna.
Having heard that, accepting it, they spoke this verse:
“We shall do everything according to your instruction, whatever you shall say, O one of vast wisdom;
we shall pervade our bodies with abundant rapture so that we may attain your destination.”
Then, having caused the Great Being to grant the going-forth to all those hosts of warriors, he spoke this verse as he was dismissing the company of seers:
“Veneration has been performed for the emaciated calf; let the worthy seers depart, O noble ones.
Be always delighted in meditation and composed; this is the supreme delight for one who has gone forth.”
"Let them go there," he said, "let them go to their respective dwelling places.
The seers, having received the word of the teacher Sarabhanga with reverence upon their heads, paid him homage and, soaring into the air, departed for their own abodes.
Sakka also rose from his seat, offered praise to the Great Being, and with palms joined—
Having taken [the gift], he departed with his retinue, paying homage to the Great Being as if worshipping the sun.
Having understood this matter, the Teacher spoke these verses:
“Having heard the verses, which are endowed with the ultimate truth, well-spoken by the wise seer;”
Rejoicing in what was born from the Vedas, those renowned gods departed for the city of the gods.
“These verses, meaningful and well-phrased, were well-spoken by the wise Seer.
Whoever should listen to them with earnest intent would obtain distinction both before and after.”
“Having attained distinction between what precedes and what follows, one shall go beyond the sight of the King of Death.
In this context, “connected with the ultimate truth” means being based on Nibbāna by way of illustrating impermanence and so forth.

“These verses” was said by the Teacher while praising the well-spoken words of the teacher Sarabhaṅga, which bestow Nibbāna. In that context, “possessing meaning” is in the sense of bestowing Nibbāna.
"Based on the ultimate meaning" means having pure phrasing. "Well-spoken" means well-explained. "Making it one's concern" means making it a matter of personal need;
being one who has such need, one should listen with care. Regarding "the sequence of before and after":
the first jhāna is the prior distinction, and the second jhāna is the subsequent distinction. The second jhāna is the prior distinction, and the third jhāna...
"Further distinction" refers to the distinction established by the sequence of priority and posteriority through the eight attainments and the four paths.
"Out of sight" means that at the conclusion, having attained the further distinction of Arahantship, one reaches Nibbāna;
for a person who has reached Nibbāna is said to have gone out of sight of the King of Death.

Thus the Teacher, having reached the climax of his teaching with the attainment of Arahatship, said: "Monks, it was not only now; in the past as well, a rain of flowers fell upon Moggallāna’s funeral pyre. Having spoken thus, he proclaimed the Truths and, identifying the Jātaka, said:
"Sālissara was Sāriputta, and Meṇḍissara was Kassapa;
Pabbata was Anuruddha, and Devala was Kaccāyana."
“Ānanda was his attendant, and Kolita was Kisavaccha;
Nārada and the Elder Udāyī were the assembly—the assembly of the Buddha.
Sarabhaṅga was the Lord of the World; thus you should remember this Jātaka.”
The second is the Commentary on the Sarabhaṅga Jātaka.
[523] 3. The Commentary on the Alambusā Jātaka:
"Then he spoke"—this was related by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the seduction by his former wife.
The background story has already been explained in detail in the *Indriya-jātaka*. However, the Teacher asked that monk, “Is it true, monk, that you are dissatisfied?
When he replied, “It is true, Venerable Sir,” the Teacher said, “By whom have you been made dissatisfied?
When he replied, “By my former wife,” the Teacher said, “Monk, this woman is one who works for your harm; you [should abandon her].”
"Having destroyed his meditation by relying [on that woman], he lay deluded and unconscious for three years;
when consciousness arose, he uttered a great lamentation. Having said this, he related a story of the past:
"In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a brahmin family in the kingdom of Kāsī."
Having reached maturity and attained proficiency in all arts, he went forth into the ascetic life of an *isi* and sustained himself on roots and fruits in a forest wilderness.
Then, a certain doe, having eaten grass mixed with his excrement at the place where he had urinated and drunk water, became attached to him in mind by that alone;
she conceived a fetus, and from then on, [she stayed] nowhere else...
Without going elsewhere, she ate grass right there and wandered about in the vicinity of the hermitage.
The Great Being, observing her, understood the reason for this. Later, she gave birth to a human boy.
Out of affection for a son, the Great Being cared for him and gave him the name Isisiṅga. Then, when he had reached the age of discretion, the Great Being ordained him.
When he was advanced in years, he took his son and went to the place called Nārivana, where he exhorted him, saying:
"My son, in this Himavat there are women who resemble these flowers; when they fall under their power, they bring about great ruin.
It is not right to come under their sway. Having given this advice, he later attained rebirth in the Brahma-world.
Isisiṅga, too, dwelling in a region of the Himalayas, sported in the play of jhāna. He was one of terrible asceticism and possessed supreme mastery over his faculties.
Then, by the power of his virtue, Sakka’s palace trembled. Sakka, reflecting upon this and knowing the cause, thought: "This man might displace me from my position as Sakka;
I shall send a celestial nymph (accharā) and cause him to break his virtue. Thus he [surveyed] the entire deva-world.

While investigating, he saw that among his own two million five hundred thousand female attendants, there was no one else capable of breaking his virtue except for a single nymph named Alambusā. Having found no other, he summoned her and commanded her to break his virtue.
Explaining this matter, the Teacher spoke the first verse:
“Then the great Indra spoke: ‘Vatrabhū, the father of the victors, having struck down the daughter of the gods, [seizes] Alambusā in Sudhammā.
Therein, *brahā* means great. *Vatrabhū* means the conqueror of the asura named Vatra. *Jayataṃ pitā* means the father of the victors.
He was the father because he accomplished the duty of a father toward the remaining thirty-three sons of the gods, who were victorious and had attained victory.
"Having shattered" means having pierced their hearts as if looking within them, knowing thus: "This one is capable.
"In the Sudhammā" means in the Sudhammā assembly hall of the gods.
Seated upon the stone throne of the pale-white blanket, he summoned Alambusā and said this to her:
“Lady, the Tāvatiṃsa gods together with Indra entreat you;
go, Alambusā, to entice the seer at Isisinga.”
In this context, "misseti" means she addresses her; this is her name. However, all women are called "missā" because they are mixed with men through the mixing of defilements (*kilesa*).
Addressing her by this common name based on her qualities, he spoke thus. Regarding "isippalobhane": it means capable of enticing seers (*isi*). Regarding "isisiṅgaṃ":
it is said that on the top of her head there were two tufts of hair in the shape of a deer's horn.
They arose; therefore it is said thus.
So Sakka commanded Alambusā: "Go, approach the sage Isisinga, bring him under your power, and break his virtue.
"Lest he, who speaks and lives the holy life, should surpass us," [she thought].
“The ascetic delights in Nibbāna and has grown old; therefore, let us block his paths”—this was the speech he uttered.
In this context, “purāyanti” means that this ascetic is perfected in his conduct and lives the holy life (*brahmacariya*);
furthermore, because of his long life, he delights in the path known as Nibbāna, and he has grown old through the increase of his virtues. Therefore, as long as he does not pass us by—

"He does not overcome you and displace you from this place; therefore, go at once and block the paths leading to his world of the gods so that he does not come here—act in such a way," was the meaning.
Having heard that, Alambusā spoke these two verses:
“O King of the Gods, why do you instruct me as if you were my teacher?
Go to entice the seers; there are other apsarases as well.
There are excellent women like me in the Ashoka and Nandana groves.”
"Let there be a way for them as well; let them too go to seduction.
In this context, "What indeed do you [do]? (*kimeva tvaṃ*) illustrates: "What exactly are you doing? "You train only me" (*mameva tuvaṃ sikkhasi*):
he speaks with the intention that "In this entire world of the devas, you look only at me; you see no other. The syllable *sa-*... [is used].
In this context, there is a connection of the phrasing (*byañjanasandhikaro*). Regarding the phrase "go to Isippalobhana," the intended meaning is: "For what reason do you speak thus to me?
"And most excellent" (*pavarā ceva*) means "even more superior than I. "Free from sorrow" (*asoke*) means devoid of grief.
"Delighting" (*nandane*) means producing joy. "Turn" (*pariyāyo*) means a sequence of going.
Then Sakka spoke these three verses:
“Truly you speak the truth; there are indeed other nymphs, as excellent and sublime as these, in the sorrowless Nandana Grove.”
“Those women who have gone to serve a man do not understand it as you do, O woman beautiful in every limb.
You yourself go, O auspicious one; for you are the most excellent among women.”
"With your very complexion and form, you will bring him under your control.
In this context, "approaching a man" means that while they are approaching a male, they do not know the practice of seducing men.
"With complexion and form" refers to both the color of the body and the perfection of physical beauty. "You will bring him under your control" refers to that ascetic.
“You shall bring her under your own power.
Having heard this, Alambusā spoke two verses:
“I shall certainly go, sent by the King of the Gods;”
“I am afraid to eat this, for the brahmin’s fiery energy is intense.
Many people have fallen into hell by eating the seer’s food;
they have entered the deluded cycle of existence. Therefore, I shall pluck out my feathers.”
In this context, *na vāhanti* means "I do not go. *Vibhemīti* means "I am afraid. *Āsādun* means "to approach. This is what is meant:

"O King, it is not that I will not go because I have been sent by you; rather, I am afraid to draw near to that seer for the purpose of breaking his virtue, for he possesses fierce power (*uggatejo*).
*Āsādiya* means "having approached. *Mohasaṃsāraṃ* means "the wandering in saṃsāra through delusion," or "by means of delusion."
Sentient beings who, having lured the seer, have fallen into *saṃsāra* and are established in the suffering of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*), are beyond counting.
"Therefore" means for that reason. Regarding the phrase "I make my hairs bristle":
she says, "I make my hairs stand on end because I am thinking, 'I shall surely break his virtue.'"
Having said this, the nymph Alambusā,
possessing a form of sensual beauty, departed, desiring to mix with the sage Siṅga.
And she entered that forest protected by the sage Siṅga.
“Covered with a network of golden bells, extending for half a yojana on all sides;
at dawn, during the morning meal, at the time of the morning heat, he approached the seer Isisinga as he was tending the sacrificial fire. These are the verses of the Perfectly Enlightened One.

Regarding the phrase "she departed from there": thinking, "In that case, O King of Devas, you should reflect upon it," she entered her own bedchamber, adorned herself, and desiring to mix the sage’s horn with defilement, she departed; monks, that nymph went to his hermitage.
"Covered with a lattice of *bimbi* flowers" means covered by a grove of red sprouts. "At dawn, for breakfast" means...
“Monks, at the time for the morning meal—early in the morning, even very early; ‘at the time of dawn’ means precisely at the time of sunrise. ‘The fire-hall’ means the fire-chamber.

Having devoted himself to striving throughout the night, having bathed and performed his water-rites early in the morning, and having spent a short while in the leaf hut enjoying the bliss of jhāna, he would go out and sweep the fire-hall. Thus [he spoke] to him.
She approached Isiṅga and stood before him, displaying her feminine charms.
Then the ascetic, questioning her, said:
"Who are you that shine like lightning, like a star among the herbs?"
With her hand-ornaments shimmering and her jeweled earrings fastened,
resembling the color of the sun, fragrant with gold and sandalwood,
Māyā— of noble form, a maiden of beautiful appearance— was self-restrained.
“Your feet are firm, soft, and pure, well-placed upon the ground;
your gait is so desirable that it truly captivates my mind.
Your thighs are well-proportioned, resembling the trunk of an elephant.”
“Your well-rounded hips are smooth, like the board of a die.
Your navel is beautifully shaped, like the filaments of a blue lotus;
it will be visible from afar, like pure black collyrium.”
“Her breasts have developed in two ways: stemless and beautifully rounded;
her unyielding bosoms are like half-pumpkins.
Her long necks shine like the surface of a conch shell, resembling those of the eneya deer.”
White, free from blemish, and lovely, resembling the fourth stage of mental concentration:
“Both upper and lower, rubbed against the tips of trees;
Difficult to surpass, born of purity—your teeth are beautiful to behold.”
“Not white, but red at the edges, resembling the fruit of the *jiñjūka*;
long and wide, your eyes are beautiful to behold.
Not too long, well-groomed, and adorned with golden lashes.”
The hair on your head, your most excellent limb, is fragrant like sandalwood.
As far as the way of those who plow and guard cattle, the path of merchants,
and the striving of the sages who are self-restrained and ascetic— [all these are surpassed by yours].
“I do not see anyone equal to you on this circle of earth; who are you, whose son are you, and how may we know you?
In that context, *vicittahatthābharaṇā* means endowed with variegated hand-ornaments. *Hemacandanagandhinī* means...
Anointed with sandalwood paste fragrant as gold; "with well-restrained thighs" means possessing well-rounded, solid thighs endowed with the characteristic marks of the thighs;
"slender" means having a contracted waist; "soft" means tender and delicate; "pure" means stainless;
"well-established" means standing firmly, touching the earth evenly; "walking" means while moving; "desirable" means lovely.
"Desirable for one who desires. "They truly carry away my mind":
as you walk with such supreme feminine grace, these feet of yours truly carry away my heart. "Vimaṭṭhā" means broad. "Sussoṇī" means having beautiful hips.
Regarding the word "akkhassa," he says: "Your hips are broad like the golden plate of a beautiful-colored axle. "Like a blue lotus..."
"Kiñjakkha" means like the pericarp of a blue lotus. He spoke thus because it is covered with fine black hairs, as if with black collyrium.
Regarding the verse beginning with "Of two kinds," he spoke while describing them on the breasts. For those two, having arisen on the chest, are "stalkless" (avaṇṭa) due to the absence of a stalk;
they are "well-issued" (sādhupaccuda) because they have emerged perfectly while remaining attached to the chest; and they are called "milk-holders" (payodhara) because they sustain milk.
"Unfallen" means not fallen; because they are neither withered nor sunken, they have not entered inwardly, thus they are "unfallen.
Her breasts are like half-pumpkins because they resemble half of a golden *alābu* gourd placed upon a golden platter. "Like that of an *eṇeyyaka* deer" means:
just as the long and rounded neck of an *eṇī* deer is beautiful, so too is your neck slightly long.
“Shell-like in appearance” means the neck resembles the surface of a golden conch; this is the meaning. “With white lips” refers to the gums.
“Resembling the fourth mind” means that the “fourth mind” refers to the tongue, which is the basis for the fourth type of mental consciousness.
He says that the ends of his lips resemble the tongue because of their lovely color. “Upward-pointing” refers to the lower teeth. “Downward-pointing” refers to the upper teeth.
“Wiped with the tip of the tongue” means wiped with a tooth-stick; it is completely pure. “Twice-born” means twice-born.
“Produced from faultless [parts]” means produced from the faultless ends of the jaw-flesh.
“Not pale” means black. “Red-edged” means having red margins. “Resembling the *jiñjūka* fruit” refers to the red portion.
"Resembling the *jiñjuka* fruit. "Beautiful to behold" means they bring no satiety to those who gaze upon them, being endowed with the fivefold clarity (*pañcapasāda*).
"Not too long" means they are of appropriate measure. "Well-polished" means thoroughly polished. "Released from golden bands" (*kanakabyāsamocita*):

"golden band" (*kanakabyā*) refers to a golden ring; having been struck [with a tool] using fragrant oil by that [band], they were well-fashioned. "Agriculture and cattle-rearing": by this [phrase], both agriculture and...
He shows beings who live depending on the protection of cattle. "Whatever destination" means whatever degree of accomplishment.
"The extent of the sages' exertion" means the extent of the sages' exertion that has been carried out; the meaning is, how many sages dwell here in this Himavat.
"Not equal to them" means that among all of them, not even one is equal to you in terms of the equality of physical grace, charm, and so forth.
“I do not see anyone. Who are you?”—this he asked using masculine terminology, knowing her female state.

Thus, while the ascetics were describing their own appearance from the feet up to the hair, Alambusā remained silent. When the ascetics’ discourse had reached its natural conclusion, she perceived his state of confusion and spoke this verse:
“Venerable Kassapa, now that things have come to this, it is no longer the time for questions.”
"Come, friend, let us enjoy ourselves together in our hermitage;
come, I shall embrace you, for you are skilled in delights.

In this context, "when Kassapa had thus departed" means that when such a thought had arisen in the mind of one of the Kassapa clan, it was no longer the time for questioning. "Friend" (*samma*) is a term of address used for a companion; it is an affectionate mode of speech. "Delights" (*ratīnaṃ*) refers to the delights of the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*).
Having spoken thus, Alambusā thought: “If I remain here, he will not come within arm’s reach;
I shall act as if I am departing. Through her skill in feminine guile, she did not approach the ascetic, but set out facing the path by which he had come.
To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“Having said this, the nymph Alambusā, possessing a form of sensual beauty, departed, desiring to mix with the Sage’s horn.

Then, seeing her as she was going, the ascetic thought, “She is departing,” and cutting short his own slow progress and sluggish pace, he ran with speed and seized her by the hair with his hand. Explaining this matter, the Teacher said:
“Then, emerging with speed and abandoning his sluggish effort,
he reached for her among those most excellent braids.
That beautiful woman, turning back toward him, embraced him closely.”
They spoke of their spiritual life, just as they were satisfied with it:
"With her mind she went to Indra, who was dwelling in the Nandana grove;
and knowing her intention, Maghava, the elephant among gods—"
“Quickly send forth a couch, golden, with a canopy,
furnished with a coverlet and spread with a thousand pieces of cloth.
Place it there, holding that beautiful thing to your chest.”
Just as he had held it for a single moment, so he maintained it for three years.
After three years, the brahmin Vimada, having awakened,
saw green trees all around the Āgneyāyana fire-altar.
“Beholding the forest of fresh leaves in full bloom, resounding with the cries of flocks of cuckoos, he looked all around and wept, shedding tears.
‘I have neither offered oblations nor chanted mantras; I have abandoned the sacred fire-sacrifice.’”
"Who was it that formerly tempted my mind away from my service?
While I was dwelling in the forest, who seized the splendor that had arisen within me,
as if taking a ship filled with various jewels from the great ocean?"
In this context, "one who has approached" (*ajjhappatto*) means one who has arrived. "The beautiful woman turned back toward him" (*tamudāvatta kalyāṇī*):

having turned back—that is, having turned around—toward that seer who was standing there touching her hair, she, being beautiful to behold, was truly radiant. "She embraced him" (*palissajī*): she clasped him.
"'Then, as he fell away from the holy life, she was satisfied,' O monks; at that very moment for that seer..."
The jhāna vanished. When he had fallen away from that jhāna and from the holy life, it happened exactly as Sakka had wished.
Then, perceiving that Sakka’s aspiration had been fulfilled, that celestial maiden was satisfied;
the meaning is that she felt rapture and gladness born of that destruction of his holy life.

She went to him with her mind; having embraced him, she stood there, and because her mind was occupied with the thought, "O, would that Sakka would send me a couch," she went to Indra by means of that mental state.
"In the Nandana grove" means dwelling in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven known as the Nandana grove, due to its capacity to produce joy.
"The elephant among gods" means the best of gods. "He sent" means he dispatched. It is also read as "pāhiṇī."
*Pāṭho*: "With its carriage" means together with its retinue. "Covered with fifty canopies" means covered by fifty upper canopies.
"Spread with a thousand divine cloths" means spread with a thousand divine *kojava* cloths. "There, she...
means that she, sitting there on the divine couch, carried that Isisiṅga upon her breast. "For three years" means for one moment.
Having laid him upon her breast for three years, as if counting the number of human years, she sat there and bore him.
"Vimada" means free from intoxication or devoid of consciousness; for he lay unconscious for three years and only afterwards woke up, having regained his senses.
As he was waking, Alambusā saw the movement of his hands and other limbs.
Knowing that he had awakened, she caused her cross-legged posture to vanish and, having herself disappeared, stood there.
"He saw" means that while surveying the hermitage, he thought, "By whom have I been led to this ruin of my virtue?
and as he was lamenting with a great cry, he saw it. "The green tree" refers to the fire-hall known as Aggīyāyana.
The "green-leafed trees" are those standing surrounding him on all sides.
"A forest of fresh leaves" is a forest covered with young, new leaves.

"Weeping and lamenting" refers to his lamentation verses: "He does not sacrifice, nor does he recite mantras. "Caused to be abandoned" means abandoned; the prefix *pa-* is merely an intensifier (*upasagga*).
"Regarding 'service' (pāricariyāya)': he laments, 'Who indeed, prior to this, has enticed my mind with the service of the defilements?
Regarding 'who has seized my splendor' (yo me tejā ha sambhūtaṃ): the word *ha* is merely a particle.

He laments, 'Who is this who has seized my meditative quality—which arose through the ascetic power of a recluse and was like a great ship filled with various jewels—and brought it to destruction, as if sinking a large vessel in the great ocean?'"
Having heard that, Alambusā thought: “If I do not speak, he will curse me; well then, I shall tell him. Standing there with her body visible, she spoke this verse:
“I was sent by the King of the Gods to serve you;
I struck mind with mind; you do not realize it is negligence.”
Having heard her words and remembering the advice given by his father, he lamented, "By not following my father's word, I have met with great ruin," and spoke these four verses:
"It seems that my father Kassapa is instructing me thus:
'O young man, you must understand those women who resemble lotuses.'"
“‘Uragaṇḍāyo bujjhesi, tāyo bujjhesi māṇava’—
thus did my father instruct me, he who was compassionate toward me.
I did not disregard his word, the instruction of my aged father.”
“In this forest, devoid of humans, today I shall meditate alone.
‘I will act in such a way that woe to my life!
Either I shall become like him again, or death will be my lot.’”
In this context, "these" refers to these words. "Women resembling *kamalā* flowers": *kamalā* is said to be a flowering creeper;
women who resemble its blossoms are meant. "You should recognize them, young man"—that is, "young man, you should know them;
having known them, do not go within their sight, but drive them away. Such were the words my father instructed me at that time.
"Indeed, these are they. "Ure-gaṇḍāyī" means one who is possessed of two goiters on the chest.
"You know them well, young man," means: "Young man, you should know that these women bring about the destruction of those who have fallen under their power.
"I do not wish" means: I did not do it. "I am brooding" means: I am grieving and lamenting. "Fie upon my life! means: Fie upon this censurable life!
"My life! What is the use of my life? I shall act again so that I may become such as I was before;
having restored the lost meditative absorption (jhāna), I shall become free from passion, or else death shall come to me.

Abandoning sensual lust, he restored his meditative absorption. Then, seeing his ascetic power and knowing that he had regained his absorption, Alambusā was terrified and asked for forgiveness. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher spoke these two verses:
“Having recognized his splendor, energy, and steadfast fortitude, Alambusā grasped the feet of the sage Isisinga with her head.
‘Do not be angry with me, O Great Hero; do not be angry with me, O Great Seer.’”
“A great purpose was accomplished by me among the illustrious Thirty-three;
the entire city of the gods was shaken by you at that time.
Then, dismissing her with the words, “I forgive you, blessed lady; go as you please,” he spoke this verse:
“May the gods of the Thirty-three, and Vāsava, lord of the thirty, and you too, Bhaddā, be happy; go, maiden, as you please.
Having paid homage to him, she departed for the city of the gods on that very golden couch. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher spoke three verses:
Having grasped his feet and circumambulated him,
and having raised my hands in reverential salutation, I departed from that place.
And as for his couch, it was made of gold and well-furnished.
Adorned with fifty upper coverings and prepared with a thousand [attendants],
she ascended that very palanquin and went into the presence of the gods.
Like a flash of lightning coming forth from the darkness, she shone as she approached.
"Elated, joyful, and thrilled, the Lord of Devas granted a boon.

Herein, "he descended" is like [descending] onto an island. By the words "elated" and so forth, the manner of his satisfaction is shown; being pleased as she stood having come and paid homage, he granted her a boon.
As she was receiving the boon from him, she spoke this concluding verse:
“If you would grant me a boon, O Sakka, Lord of all beings, may I not go to Isipatana; this, Sakka, is the boon I choose.
The meaning of this is: “Sakka, King of the Devas, if you would grant me a boon, may I not go again to Isipatana; do not send me for that purpose; this is the boon I choose and request.”
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma instruction to that bhikkhu and having proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka.
At the conclusion of the Truths, that bhikkhu was established in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, Alambusā was his former wife;
Isisiṅga was the discontented bhikkhu; and as for the Great Seer who was his father, he was none other than myself.
The third *Alambusā-jātaka* commentary.
[524] 4. The *Saṅkhapāla-jātaka* commentary.
"You were one who provided space for the Noble Ones"—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the performance of the Uposatha ceremony. At that time...
Indeed, after the Teacher had gladdened the lay followers observing the Uposatha, he said, "In the past, ancient wise men abandoned great royal splendor as elephants and observed the Uposatha vows.
Being requested by them, he related a story of the past.
In the past, in Rājagaha, a king named Magadha reigned. At that time, the Bodhisatta was the chief queen of that king.
He was conceived in the womb, and they gave him the name Duryodhana.
When he reached maturity, having mastered all the arts at Takṣaśilā, he returned and demonstrated his skills to his father.
Then his father, having consecrated him in the kingdom, went forth into the ascetic life as an *īśi* and dwelt in a park. The Bodhisatta went to his father’s presence three times each day. To him—
Great gain and honor arose for him. Being unable to perform even the preliminary work on the *kasiṇas* because of that very obstacle, he thought:
"I have great gain and honor; it is not possible for me to cut off this matted hair while living here.
Without telling my son, I shall go elsewhere. Without letting anyone know, he departed from the park.
Having crossed over the Magadha country, he reached the Mahisa country.
There, near the river Kaṇṇaveṇṇā—which flows out from the Saṅkhapāla Lake—at its bend, he built a leaf-hut by the Candaka mountain.

Dwelling there, he performed the preliminary exercises for the *kasiṇas*, attained the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), and sustained himself by gleaning. Then, the Naga king named Saṅkhapāla...
Accompanied by a great retinue, he emerged from the Kaṇṇaveṇṇā River and approached him from time to time.
He taught the Dhamma to him. Then his son, desiring to see his father but not knowing where he had gone, made inquiries;
having learned that "he dwells in such-and-such a place," he went there with a large retinue for the purpose of seeing him.
Having gone to one side and put on his lower garment, he set out toward the hermitage together with several ministers.
At that moment, Saṅkhapāla was seated listening to the Dhamma with a large retinue.
Seeing the king approaching, he rose from his seat after paying homage to the seer and departed. The king paid homage to his father and exchanged greetings.
Having made his seat and sat down, he asked: "Venerable sir, which king is this who has come into your presence?
"My son, he is the Nāga King named Saṅkhapāla. Having conceived a longing for the splendor of that [kingdom] while in the abode of the Nāgas, he stayed for a few days;
then, having arranged for his father to receive a regular supply of alms-food, he returned to his own city. There, in the four...

Having caused alms-halls to be built at the gates and giving gifts throughout the whole of Jambudīpa, causing it to tremble, he guarded his virtue, performed the Uposatha rites, and aspired for the realm of the Nāgas.
At the end of his lifespan, he was reborn in the Nāga realm and became the Nāga King Saṅkhapāla.
As time passed, he became remorseful regarding that state of prosperity, and from there...

From that time on, aspiring for human birth, he observed the Uposatha fast. However, while he was living in the Nāga realm, his observance of the Uposatha did not succeed, and he fell into the destruction of his virtue.
Thereupon, departing from the Nāga realm, he went to a termite mound located between the great highway and a footpath not far from the river Kaṇṇaveṇṇā.
Having surrounded himself and resolved upon the Uposatha, he undertook the precepts and, dedicating himself as an object of generosity by saying, "Let those who need my skin, flesh, and so forth,
take them," he lay down upon the top of an anthill. While practicing the duties of a recluse,
he remained there on the fourteenth and fifteenth days, and on the first day of the lunar fortnight (pāṭipada), he went to the abode of the Nāgas.
One day, after he had thus undertaken the precepts and was lying down, sixteen inhabitants of a border village went into the forest with weapons in hand, intending to bring back meat;
having failed to find anything, they returned and saw him lying on top of the anthill, thinking, "Today we have not even caught a young lizard; let us kill this king of nāgas."
Thinking, "We shall eat it," they further considered, "If we seize it while it is large, it might escape;
therefore, we will pierce it with stakes right where it lies among the goods, weaken it, and then take it. Taking their stakes, they approached.
The Bodhisatta’s body was enormous, the size of a single-droṇa ship, and it resembled a garland of jasmine flowers arranged in a circle.
He was exceedingly beautiful, endowed with eyes resembling *jiñjuka* fruits and a head like a *jayasumana* flower.

Hearing the sound of the footsteps of those sixteen men, he drew his head out from between the rafters and, opening his red eyes, saw them approaching with spears in their hands; he then thought: "Today my wish..."

"It will reach my head; having dedicated myself to the gateway of generosity and resolved upon diligence, I shall not, out of anger, open my eyes and look at these men as they hack my body with spears until it is perforated and mangled.
Having thus made a firm resolve out of fear of breaking his own virtue, he drew his head back into the coils of the serpent.
He lay down. Then they approached him, seized him by the tail, dragged him along, and beat him against the ground.

Having pierced him with sharp spikes in eight places and thrusting thorny black rattan rods into the wounds, they took him up on a carrying-pole at eight points and set out upon the great road. From the moment the Great Being was pierced by the spikes, he—
Even in one place, out of anger, he did not look at them even after opening his eyes.
As he was being led away by eight men carrying baskets, they let his head hang down and struck it against the ground.
Then, thinking, "His head is hanging down," they laid him on the great highway, pierced his nostril with a sharp needle, inserted a cord, and lifted up his head.
Having lashed it to the tip of a pole and hoisted it up once more, they set out on the road.
At that moment, a householder named Āḷāra, a resident of the city of Mithilā in the kingdom of Videha, was traveling along in a comfortable carriage, having taken five hundred wagons with him;
he saw those sons of Bhoja carrying the Bodhisatta away in such a manner.
Having seen this, he gave each of those sixteen men sixteen oxen for transport, along with a *paṣata* of gold coins each,
and provided clothing and garments for all of them as well as for their wives;
having thus dismissed them, he then went to the Nāga-abode and, without delay, departed from there with a great retinue.
Having approached Āḷāra and spoken in praise of the Nāga realm, he took him and went to the Nāga realm;
there, having bestowed great glory upon him along with three hundred Nāga maidens, he satisfied him with divine sensual pleasures.
After Āḷāra had lived in the Nāga realm for one year, enjoying divine pleasures, he said, "Friend, I wish to go forth."
Having spoken thus to the Naga king and taken the requisites for the going-forth, he departed from the Naga abode for the region of the Himalayas.
There he went forth, and after dwelling there for a long time, he later set out on a wandering tour.
Upon reaching Bārāṇasī, he stayed in the royal park; on the following day, having entered the city for alms, he arrived at the royal gate. Then...
When the King of Bārāṇasī saw him, he was inspired with confidence by his deportment; he had him summoned, seated him on a prepared seat,
fed him various foods of exquisite flavor, and then, sitting on a lower seat,
paid homage and spoke to him, reciting the first verse:
“You have the appearance of a noble one, with clear eyes; I think you, sir, have gone forth from a family of wealth.
How indeed did you, being wise, abandon riches and enjoyments, and go forth, having departed from home?
In this context, “you have the appearance of a noble one” means you have the appearance of a faultless and beautiful body; the sense is that you are handsome. “With clear eyes” means...
"With eyes endowed with the five faculties. "From a noble family" means: "I think you have gone forth from a kshatriya family, or a brahmin family, or a merchant family.
"How indeed?"—with what cause, making what object of focus, have you abandoned wealth and enjoyments, departed from home, and gone forth? He asks this, addressing him as "one of wisdom, a wise man."
Thereafter, the connection between the verses should be understood through the exchange of words between the ascetic and the king:
“Having seen this palace, O god among men, belonging to the Mahoraga of great power;
having seen the great fruition of meritorious deeds, O King, I have gone forth out of faith.”
“Neither out of desire for sensual pleasures, nor out of fear, nor out of hatred do those who have gone forth speak a word of falsehood.
Answer me this matter when asked; having heard it, confidence will arise in me.
“O Lord of the Realm, while traveling on business, I saw the son of Bhoja on the road.”
As they went along, rejoicing, carrying that great serpent whose body was increasing in size, I approached them, O Lord of Men, and with my hair standing on end from fear, I spoke in terror:
"Where is this fearsome-bodied one being led? What will you do with this Nāga, O sons of Bhoja?"
“O son of Videha, this great serpent is being led away for the sake of food—this huge snake with a body fully grown.
Its flesh is savory, thick, and tender; yet you do not perceive its flavor.
Having gone from here to our own home, we shall take up our weapons and tear it apart.”
"We shall eat his flesh with great delight, for we are indeed the food of the serpents.
'If this great serpent is being led away for the sake of food, his body having grown large, I will give you sixteen oxen; release this nāga from his bonds!'"
“Truly, this food of ours is pleasing, and many snakes have been eaten by us before;
we will do as you say, Āḷāra, and be friends with you, son of Videha.
Then they released him from his bonds—that which was not [meant] for release from the snare.
Released from his bonds, that Naga king departed facing the east for a moment.
Having gone eastward for a moment, he looked back at me with eyes full of affection;
then I followed behind him, raising my ten-fingered hands in reverent salutation.
“Go indeed with all haste, lest your enemies seize you again;
for painful is reunion with hunters—go out of sight of the sons of Bhoja.
He went to that lake, which was serene, blue-hued, delightful, and possessed of beautiful landing places.
Covered with rose-apple trees and reeds, he crossed over and entered it, free from fear and at peace.
Not long after he had entered, O Lord of Men, that Naga appeared before me by means of his divine power;
he attended upon me as a son attends his father, speaking words that were heart-pleasing and pleasant to the ear.
“You are both mother and father to me, Āḷāra; you are my inner friend, the giver of life.
I am one who has attained his own psychic power; Āḷāra, behold my dwellings!
They abound in food and have plenty of drink and provisions, like those of Vāsava at Masakkasāra.”
In this context, "palace" refers to the golden and gem-studded palace of the Naga King Saṅkhapāla, which was endowed with hundreds of various theatrical performances.

Having seen the great fruition of the merits performed by him, and having gained faith in karma, its fruit, and the world beyond, I went forth out of that faith. "Not desiring sensual pleasures" means neither out of desire for material things nor out of fear.
"Even those who speak falsely say, 'Venerable sir, having heard your words, faith and joy will arise within me.
'Going on trade' means going with the thought, 'I shall perform the work of trade.
'We saw them on the road' means we saw people from the countryside on the main highway, traveling in comfortable carriages ahead of five hundred wagons."
I saw. "With a growing body" means with an increased body. "Taking" means having taken up with eight baskets. "I spoke" means I addressed him.
"Of terrifying body" means one whose body causes fear. "O son of a hunter!"—he addresses the hunter's son with this term of endearment.
"O son of Videha!"—they addressed Āḷāra because he was a resident of the kingdom of Videha. "Having torn apart" means having cut asunder. For we...
"We are indeed the enemies of the nāgas. "For the sake of food" means for the purpose of obtaining food.
"And be our friend" means: "Be our friend; recognize the service we have rendered you.
"Then indeed for you," O Great King, when those Bhojaputta sons had spoken thus, I [gave] them sixteen draft oxen and garments for wearing and wrapping.
I gave them a gold māsaka for every handful of grain, as well as clothing and ornaments for their wives.
Then, having laid King Saṅkhapāla, the Nāga king, upon the ground, they began to drag him along by grasping the tip of a thorny black *vetta* creeper with their own harsh hands.
Thereupon, seeing the Nāga king growing weary, and remaining unwearied myself, I [cut] that... with a sword.
Having cut the creeper, I slowly extracted it by the method of removing a bamboo splinter used for piercing children's ears,
causing him no pain; at that time, those sons of Bhoja released that serpent from the bond that had been inserted into his mouth and fastened with a snare,
and they pulled out that cord together with the snare from his nose.
He illuminated [the matter]. Thus, having released the snake and gone a short distance, they hid themselves, thinking, "This snake is weak;
we shall take it with us when it is dead.
"With eyes full of tears" means that he too, having walked for a moment facing the east, looked back at me with eyes filled with tears. At that time, they said:
"Then I shall be his. "Let him go," they said; thus they spoke to him. "The lake" refers to the Kaṇṇaveṇḍa Lake.
"Covered on both sides" means it was overspread and overspread with rose-apple trees and cane trees along both its banks.
"Having crossed over, free from fear, and delighted"—it is said that as he entered that lake, he showed great reverence to Āḷāra and descended into the water as far as his tail.
The very place he entered became free from fear; therefore, having crossed over his fear, being confident, joyful, and delighted, he entered.

"Having entered" (*pavissa*) means having gone inside. "With a divine retinue" (*dibbena me*) means that without falling into negligence in the Nāga abode, while I had not yet reached the banks of the Kaṇṇaveṇṇā River, he appeared before me with a divine retinue. "Attended upon" (*upaṭṭhahi*) means approached. "Internally" (*abbhanto*)...
It is like the flesh of the heart. "You have been very helpful to me; I shall show you honor.
Behold my dwellings"—this means, "Behold my Nāga-abode. "Like Masakkasāra"—Masakkasāra refers to Sineru, the king of mountains, by virtue of its firmness and its state of being solid and immovable.
He spoke thus with reference to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven constructed there.
"Great King! Having spoken thus, that Naga king, further describing his own Naga abode, spoke these two verses:
'That ground is endowed with excellent features; it is free from pebbles, soft, and beautiful.
The earth has low-growing grass and little dust; it is inspiring, where they abandon their grief.'"
“Free from pebbles, blue like beryl, a most delightful mango grove extending in the four directions;
with ripe and unripe fruits, well-flowered, it bears fruit throughout all seasons.
Therein, “free from pebbles” means that the ground there is devoid of stones and gravel, soft and beautiful, composed of gold, silver, and gems.
It is strewn with sand of the seven jewels. "With low grass" means it is endowed with low-lying grass that has a color like the backs of *indagopaka* insects.
"With little dust" means it is free from soil. "Where they abandon sorrow" means that as soon as they have entered [that place], they become free from grief.
