"Without hollows" means not sunken; it is without pits or unevenness on the surface, being level and well-settled. "Blue like beryl."
"Blue with beryl" means that in that Nāga abode there is a lotus pond made of beryl, with clear water, blue in luster, and covered with lotuses and water-lilies of many colors.
"In the four directions" means in the four quarters of that lotus pond.
"And ripened" means that in that mango grove, the mango trees have fruit that is fully ripe, half-ripe, and young, and are even in full bloom.
The meaning is as follows: "Ever-blossoming" means they are endowed with flowers and fruits appropriate for all six seasons.
In the midst of those forests, O god among men, was his residence, brilliant in appearance, with a silver threshold and made of gold—magnificent, it shone like lightning in the sky.
“O King, there were magnificent mansions made of jewels and gold, fashioned with many colors and always exquisitely constructed;
they were filled with adorned maidens wearing golden armlets.
That Saṅkhapāla, of extraordinary beauty, having ascended the palace in great haste,”
[He possessed] a palace with a thousand pillars and incomparable majesty, wherein his chief queen resided.
"And a certain woman, moving with great haste and taking a costly beryl [vessel],
approached the seat without being prompted, bearing a beautiful gem endowed with natural excellence."
“Then the serpent took me by the hand and seated me upon the seat facing him, saying:
‘Please sit on this seat; for you, sir, are one of my venerable elders.
And another woman, moving with haste and carrying water, approached.”
“O Lord of Men, she washed my feet just as a wife washes the feet of her own dear husband.
And another woman, moving with haste, taking up a golden bowl,
offered me food of pleasing appearance, consisting of many soups and various side dishes.”
“O Bhārata, when I had finished eating with the four [kinds of food], having perceived my husband’s intention, he approached me with even greater [generosity], with abundant divine sensual pleasures.
Therein, *nivesanaṃ* means a palace. *Bhassarasannikāsaṃ* means having a radiant appearance. *Rajataggaḷaṃ*...
The doors and panels were made of silver. There, the gabled halls and inner chambers were likewise composed of jewels. "Filled" means complete.
"That Saṅkhapāla," O Great King, refers to me; while he was thus describing the Nāga abode, I became desirous of seeing it.
Then, having led me there, that Saṅkhapāla took me by the hand and, moving with haste, [led me] past the pillars of beryl.
This indicates that having ascended the palace of a thousand pillars, he leads her to the place where his chief queen was.

"And one woman"—this means that when I had ascended the palace, a certain woman, without being told by that Nāga king, brought and spread out for me a beautiful beryl seat endowed with other gems of great purity.
"She approached" (*abbhihāsī*) means she brought it; it is said that she spread it out.
"In the foremost seat" (*pāmukhāsanasmiṃ*) means in the principal seat; the sense is that he had him sit on the highest seat. "The elders" (*garūnaṃ*):
having said, "You are one of my parents," he had him sit. "Various condiments" (*vividhaṃ viyañjanaṃ*): various condiments.
"Food of pleasing appearance" (*bhattaṃ manuññarūpaṃ*): food of a beautiful form. "O Bhārata": he addresses the king. "Having eaten" (*bhuttavantaṃ*).
"Having eaten" means having completed the meal. "They waited upon her" means they waited upon her while performing music with many hundreds of instruments.
"Knowing her husband’s mind" means knowing the heart of her own husband. "Beyond that" means beyond the performance of music.
"He approached me" means that Nāga king came near me. "A great [palace] with divine... means...
With great, sublime, divine pleasures, and with those that were no small,
he approached him and spoke this verse:
“Āḷāra, these three hundred wives of mine are all of equal status, possessing the radiance of a white lotus.”
“Aḷāra, these are yours to do with as you wish; I give them to you, so enjoy them.
In this context, *sabbattamajjhā* means all those whose waists are the measure of a hand when grasped;
however, in the commentary, the reading is *sumajjhā*. *Padumuttarābhā* means having a supreme radiance the color of a lotus, or having a supreme skin the color of a lotus.
"Use her. Having said, "Make her your personal attendant," he gave me great wealth along with three hundred women.
He said:
“Having enjoyed divine flavors for a year, you then spoke of even greater happiness.
How did this [happiness] come to the nāga, and how was it obtained? How did he attain this most excellent celestial mansion?
“Was it obtained by chance, born of transformation, self-made, or given by the gods?”
“I ask you, O King of Nagas, about this matter: how did you come to obtain this most excellent celestial mansion?

In that context, “having experienced the divine flavors” means having experienced the flavors of the divine qualities of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*). “Then indeed I was” means: at that time, I was. “Of the Naga” means:
of the auspicious-faced Saṅkhapāla, the Naga king; what is this collection of attainments? How did it come to be?
"What kind of kamma did you perform, and how was it performed, that you obtained this most excellent celestial mansion?
How did you come to possess it?"—thus I questioned him. "It was obtained by chance" means it was acquired without a specific cause.

"Born of transformation for you" means it arose from the transformation [of merit] because it had been dedicated for your sake by someone. "Self-made" means it was caused to be built by summoning craftsmen and giving them jewels.
Following that are two verses of question and answer:
“This celestial mansion was not obtained by me through supernatural power, nor born of transformation; it was not made by myself, nor given by the gods.
By my own deeds, which were blameless, and by my merits, this mansion was obtained by me.”
“What was your vow, and what was your holy life? Of what well-practiced deed is this the result?
Tell me this matter, O King of Nagas: how indeed was this celestial mansion obtained by you?
“I was once the king of the Magadhans, a lord named Duryodhana of great power.”
Thus, perceiving life to be short, impermanent, and subject to change:
“With a confident heart, I gave abundant gifts of food and drink with due respect;
my home was then like a public well, and the ascetics and brahmins were fully satisfied.”
“Garlands, perfumes, ointments, lamps, vehicles, and dwellings;
clothing, beds, and food and drink—we gave these gifts there with great care.
That was my vow, that was my holy life; this is the fruit of that well-practiced conduct.”
"By that very [merit] was this celestial mansion obtained by me, with abundant food and much drink and beverage,
adorned with dances and songs, long-lasting, yet not eternal.
Those of little power strike down you who possess great power, those lacking splendor strike down you who are radiant."
“O fang-weaponed one, what was it that you relied upon to come into the hands of the forest-dwellers?
Was a great fear pursued you, or did a fiery heat pursue you to the roots of your teeth?
O fang-weaponed one, what was it that you relied upon to fall into the power of the forest-dwellers?”
“Great fear has not come upon me; my splendor cannot be destroyed by them.
The well-proclaimed Dhammas of the virtuous are as impossible to overstep as the tide of the ocean.
Āḷāra, I always observe the Uposatha on the fourteenth and the fifteenth day.”
Then sixteen Bhoja youths arrived, taking a rope and a strong noose.
Piercing my nose and passing the rope through it, those hunters led me away while holding me firmly.
Such suffering as this I endured, not violating the Uposatha vow.
“They have seen you on that solitary path, endowed with strength and beauty beyond compare;
you are cultivated in glory and wisdom, O Naga—what do you aspire for as you perform this austerity?
It is not for the sake of sons, nor for the sake of wealth, nor even for the sake of long life, Āḷāra.”
“Longing for birth in the human womb, I therefore exert myself and practice austerity.
“You with blood-red eyes and broad chest, adorned and with hair and beard trimmed,
well-anointed with red sandalwood— you shine forth in all directions like a king of the gandhabbas.”
“You have attained divine power, O one of great majesty, and are endowed with all sensual pleasures.
I ask you this matter, O King of Nagas: in what way is the human world superior to this?
“Āḷāra, apart from the human world, neither purity nor self-restraint is truly found.”
"And having obtained a human birth, I shall bring an end to birth and death.
"One year has passed for me while dwelling in your presence; I have been served with food and drink.
Having called out, O Naga, I flee; it has been long since I last departed, O Lord of Men."
“Your sons, wives, and dependents, constantly instructed, stand before you;
I hope no one has cursed you, for I am fond of seeing you, Āḷāra.
Just as a beloved son might live established in the home of his mother and father...”
“Even better for me than that is this very thing: O Naga, your mind is well-disposed toward me.
‘I possess a ruby, a magnificent jewel-gem that brings wealth;
take it and go to your own home, and having obtained wealth, you may give up that gem.’”
In this context, "What are those vows? means: what is your undertaking of vows? "The holy life" (*brahmacariya*) means the supreme conduct. "Become a well" means:
like a lotus pond dug at a crossroads, it is a source of wealth to be enjoyed at will by righteous recluses and brahmins.
"And yet it is not eternal" means: even though it remains for a long time, he tells me, "It does not belong to me as something eternal."
"Of great power" (appānubhāvā) refers to Bhojaputta. "They struck him" means: for what reason did they strike him with spears at eight places?
"On account of what" means: with reference to what did you then come into their hands and fall under their control?
"Of the mendicants" (vanibbakānaṃ): here, the Bhojaputtas are called "mendicants. "Did not the fire follow you to the roots of your teeth?"
“Was it upon seeing your power, O son of the Bhojas, that great fear then overcame you? Or was it that the poison did not reach the roots of your teeth?
“Affliction” (*kilesa*) means suffering (*dukkha*). “In the presence of the beggars” (*vanibbakānaṃ*) means in the vicinity of the sons of the Bhojas;
the meaning is: depending upon the son of the Bhojas. “My power cannot be destroyed by them”: my own poisonous power cannot be overcome even by the power of another.

"Satā" refers to the Buddhas and others. "Dhammāni" refers to the qualities (dhammas) known as virtue (sīla), concentration (samādhi), wisdom (paññā), patience (khanti), compassion (anuddayā), and the cultivation of loving-kindness (mettābhāvanā).
"Sukittitāni" means well-praised, well-described, or well-spoken. By what means [were they praised]? It is said: "They are difficult to transgress, just like the shore of the ocean.
Thus, they were praised by those noble beings (sappurisā) as being difficult to overstep even at the cost of one's life, just as the tide cannot overstep the ocean's shore. Therefore, I...

He said this because, out of fear of breaking his virtue, he had become endowed with patience, loving-kindness, and other such qualities, and thus did not allow my anger to overstep the boundary of his moral conduct.
Furthermore, in this discourse on the Dhamma by Saṅkhapāla, all ten perfections (*pāramitā*) are found.

For at that time, the Mahāsatta’s act of relinquishing his own body was called the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*); likewise, even in the face of such fierce poison, his [maintenance of] virtue...
Unbrokenness is the perfection of virtue (*sīlapāramī*); departing from the Nāga realm to practice the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*) is the perfection of renunciation (*nekkhammapāramī*);
the deliberation, “This and that ought to be done,” is the perfection of wisdom (*paññāpāramī*); the energy of endurance is the perfection of energy (*vīriyapāramī*);
the patience of endurance is the perfection of patience (*khantipāramī*); the undertaking of truth is the perfection of truth (*saccapāramī*); and the thought, “I shall not break my virtue,” is...
“Resolution is the perfection of resolution; the state of compassion is the perfection of loving-kindness; and equanimity toward feeling is the perfection of equanimity.
Then they came: one day, seeing me lying on top of an anthill, sixteen sons of Bhoja took rough ropes, strong snares, and spears, and came into my presence. “Having pierced”—my body in eight places.
Having pierced me in several places and inserted thorny black *vetta* creepers [through the wounds], they went a short distance, thinking, "The rope has passed through his nose.
Seeing my head hanging down, they laid me down on the main road;
then, piercing my nose once more and passing a round rope through it, they fastened it to the tip of a carrying-pole (*kāja*), secured me all around, and led me away.
"I saw them, friend Saṅkhapāla. Those sons of Bhoja saw you on that narrow path for single travelers, a track for foot-passengers, endowed as you were with strength and beauty.
But you, who are cultivated and grown through sovereignty, excellence, glory, and wisdom—being such as you are, for what purpose do you practice asceticism? What do you desire?"
"You observe the Uposatha fast; you guard your virtue. There is also a reading, "addasāsiṃ" (I saw), meaning:
"I saw you on that great highway leading to a single path. "Abhipatthayāno" means desiring. "Tasmā" means:
because I desire human birth, therefore, exerting myself with vigor, I perform the practice of austerity.
"Surosito" means well-anointed. "Ito" means from this nāga-abode; [he asks] by what is the world of humans superior?
"Suddhi" refers to purification, consisting of the path, the fruit, and Nibbāna. "Saṃyamo" refers to virtue (sīla).
This he says with reference to the arising of Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas only in the human world. "Kāhāmi" refers to his own state of being without rebirth.
"Thinking, 'I shall bring an end to birth, aging, and death,' thus, Great King, did that Saṅkhapāla praise the human world.
When he was thus praising the human world, saying, 'A year for me,' I, Great King, having conceived a longing for the going-forth, said this:
'I am established there'—both with food and drink and with divine objects of sensual pleasure."
"I have been served and honored. "I am departing" means "I am going away. "It has been a long time since I left" means "I have been away from the human world for a long time.
"Has no one reviled you? he asks, meaning "I wonder if anyone among my sons and others has cursed or abused you.
There is also the reading "nābhisajjetha," which means "he did not become angry. "Attended to" means "cared for. "The jewel is mine."
"If it is so, dear Āḷāra, that you must go, then I have this ruby, a jewel that brings wealth, grants all desires, and fulfills every wish. Take this sublime gem and go to your home;
there, by its power, obtain as much wealth as you desire, and then return this gem. And when returning it, do not leave it anywhere else."
"Having said, 'You should release it into your own water-jar,' he offered me his jewel-treasure.
Having spoken thus, Āḷāra continued: "Then, Great King, I said this to the Naga king: 'Friend, I have no need for wealth;
rather, I wish to go forth. Having requested the requisites for going forth, I departed from the Naga realm together with him."
Having departed and turned him back, I entered the Himālaya mountains and went forth into homelessness. Having said this, he spoke two verses while delivering a discourse on the Dhamma to the king:
“I have seen even human sensual pleasures to be impermanent and subject to change;”
“Having seen the danger in the strands of sensual pleasure, O King, I have gone forth out of faith.
Young men and old alike fall like the fruits of a tree when their bodies break up;
seeing this too, O King, I have gone forth, for the life of a recluse is certainly better.”
In this context, "with faith" means having faith in karma, its fruit, and Nibbāna.
"They fall like the fruits of a tree" means that just as the fruits of a tree—whether ripe or unripe—fall, so too do these young men, both the youthful and the aged, fall.
"Inevitable" (apaṇṇaka) means unerring and leading to liberation. "The state of a recluse alone is better" means that the life of renunciation alone is supreme.
“Having seen the virtue in going forth, O Great King, I have gone forth.
Having heard this, the king spoke the following verse:
“Truly, those who are wise, learned, and contemplative of many matters, are indeed to be served.”
“Having heard of Nāga and your own four [qualities], I shall perform no small meritorious deeds.
In this regard, “those who consider many points” means those who know many causes. “And Nāga” means having heard the words of both the Nāga king—who likewise dwells in heedfulness—and yourself.
Then, generating enthusiasm in him, the ascetic spoke this concluding verse:
“Truly, those who are wise and deeply learned, who reflect upon many matters, should indeed be served.
Having heard of both the Naga and me, O King, perform abundant meritorious deeds.
Having thus taught the Dhamma to the king, he remained right there for four months of the rainy season and then returned to the Himalayas.
Having gone there, he developed the four divine abidings (*brahmavihāra*) for as long as he lived and was reborn in the Brahma-world.
Saṅkhapāla also, having observed the Uposatha vows for as long as he lived, and the king, having performed meritorious deeds such as giving, both departed according to their respective karma.

Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the father ascetic was Kassapa; the King of Bārāṇasī was Ānanda; Āḷāra was Sāriputta; and I myself was the Naga King Saṅkhapāla."
The Fourth: The Commentary on the Saṅkhapāla Jātaka.
[525] 5. The Commentary on the Cūḷasutasoma Jātaka:
"I summon the townsfolk"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning the perfection of renunciation (nekkhammapāramī).
The present-day narrative is exactly like the Mahānāradakassapa Jātaka.
In the past, however, there was a city named Sudassana in Bārāṇasī, where a king named Brahmadatta reigned. The Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of his chief queen;
after ten months had passed, he emerged from his mother’s womb. His splendor was like that of the full moon.
His face was handsome, so they gave him the name "Somakumāra. When he reached maturity, he was well-versed in learning and possessed a habit of listening;
therefore, they knew him as "Sutasoma. Having reached adulthood, he mastered all arts at Takkasilā and returned.
Receiving the white parasol belonging to his father, he ruled the kingdom righteously, [possessing] great...
He possessed sovereign power. He had sixteen thousand women, headed by Queen Candādevī.
Later on, as his sons and daughters increased, he became disenchanted with the household life and desired to enter the forest and go forth.
One day, he addressed his barber: "Friend, when you see grey hair upon my head, then..."
“Inform me when it has grown,” he said. The barber accepted his command, and later, seeing grey hairs, he informed him.

When the Great Being said, “In that case, my dear barber, pull them out and place them in my hand,” the barber pulled them out with golden tweezers and placed them in the king’s hand. Seeing them, the Great Being thought, “By old age, mine...”
Thinking, "My body has been overcome," he was terrified; seizing that grey hair, he descended from the palace,
sat upon the royal throne prepared in a place where the great multitude could see him, and summoned eighty thousand ministers headed by the commander-in-chief,
sixty thousand brahmins headed by the family priest, and many others, including countryfolk, provincials, and town-dwellers.
“Grey hair has grown upon my head; I am old, know that I have gone forth,” he said, and spoke this first verse:
“I address the town, my friends and relatives; I bid you farewell.”
“Gray hair has grown upon my head; now, let you find delight in the going forth.
In this context, “I address you” means “I inform you. “Let you find delight” means: “I find delight [in it]; O sirs, know that I have gone forth!
Having heard this, one among them, having attained confidence, spoke this verse:
“‘Abhuṃ me’—how indeed do you speak? ‘Sallaṃ me deva urasi kappesi’—O King, you have driven a spear into my chest.
‘Sattasatā te bhariyā, kathaṃ nu te tā bhavissantī’—you have seven hundred wives;
how indeed will they be yours? In this context, *abhuṃ* means loss or decline. *Urasī kappesi* means he thrust a well-sharpened, polished spear into his chest. *Sattasatā* means seven hundred.
This was said with reference to a Kṣatriya maiden of equal caste. "How indeed will they be for you? means:
once you have gone forth, how will those wives of yours be—left without a protector and without means?
By making them protectorless, your so-called "going forth" is not fitting.
Then the Great Being spoke the third verse:
“These young women will be seen, and others too will go there;
desiring heaven, for that reason I shall go forth.”
"In this matter, they will be known by their own deeds. [The King thought: "What am I to them? They are all young; they will go to whichever other king there may be.
Unable to give an answer to the Bodhisatta, the ministers and others went to his mother and reported the matter to her.
She came in great haste and said, "Is it true, my dear, that you wish to go forth?"
He spoke these two verses:
“Alas for me, Sutasoma, that I am your mother;
for while I lamented, O King, you went forth into homelessness without regard for me.”
“Alas, it was ill-gotten by me, O Sutasoma, that I should give birth to you;
for while I was lamenting, you have gone forth into homelessness, O Deva, without any regard for me.
In this context, *dulladdhaṃ* means: that which was obtained by me as my son, being born, was ill-gotten (*dulladdhaṃ*). That which...
"Alas! Because you wish to go forth into homelessness while I am thus distracted by various kinds of delusion, it is indeed a misfortune for me to have obtained such a son.

Even as his mother was thus lamenting, the Bodhisatta did not speak a word to her. She, having wept and wailed, stood aside by herself. Then they informed his father. He came and spoke this first verse:

“What kind of Dhamma is this, Sutasoma, and what indeed is this ‘going forth,’ that you, O Deva, being our son, go forth without regard for us when we are old and at the time when we ought to be cared for?
In this context, “yaṃ no amhe” means: that you, though being our son, [go forth] while we are old and at the time when we ought to be looked after.
"Having abandoned [your kin] without caring for them—like one casting down a stone from a precipice—you go forth as a renunciant without looking back; therefore I ask you:
what indeed is this Dhamma of yours? This was the intended meaning.
Upon hearing this, the Great Being remained silent. Then his father said to him, "Dear Sutasoma, even if it be so regarding your mother and father..."
“There is no affection [for you]; you have many young sons and daughters who will not be able to live without you.
You should go forth when they have reached maturity,” she said, and spoke the seventh verse:
“Your sons are many, still young and not yet in their prime;”
“Not seeing the Mañjū-tepita, they will, I think, undergo suffering.
In this context, “mañju” means sweet-spoken. “Nigacchanti” means they will undergo; that is, I think they will experience physical and mental suffering.
Having heard that, the Great Being spoke this verse:
“Even with these sons of mine, who are young and have not yet reached youth—
even with all of you, though you are charming— after remaining for a long time, the nature of destruction will come to pass.
In that passage, “even with all of you” means, dear ones, it is not only with my sons, but also with you and others as well.
"Even after remaining for a long time through all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), even after persisting for a vast duration, their nature of destruction is certain.
For indeed, throughout the entire world-system, there is not a single conditioned phenomenon that is called 'permanent.
Thus the Great Being spoke this Dhamma discourse to his father. Having heard his Dhamma discourse, he became silent."
Then they informed his seven hundred wives. They descended from the palace, went into his presence, took hold of his ankles, and while lamenting, spoke this verse:
“Is your heart cut out, or do you have no compassion for us?”
"O Lord, you who go forth without regard for us who lament—has your heart been severed from us because of a lack of even the slightest affection, O Sutasoma?

Or is it because of a lack of compassion that there is no pity? The meaning of this is: "Master Sutasoma, as you depart, having left us widowed, has your heart been cut off from us due to an absence of even the slightest attachment? Or rather, is it because of an absence of compassion that there is no mercy?"
"Why have you gone forth into homelessness, abandoning us as we lament thus?
Hearing the sound of their lamentation as they rolled at his feet, the Great Being spoke the following verse:
"My heart is not severed, and I still possess compassion for you."
"And aspiring for heaven, for that reason I shall go forth.
Therein, "aspiring for heaven": he reassured them, saying, "Since this going-forth has been praised by the Buddhas and others, therefore I shall go forth; do not worry," thus he comforted them.
Then they informed his chief queen. Although she was heavily pregnant with a full-term womb, she came, paid homage to the Great Being, stood to one side, and spoke three verses:
“Ill-gotten was my gain, Sutasoma, that I, though your wife,
was abandoned by you when you went forth into homelessness, O King, while I was lamenting. Ill-gotten was my gain,
Sutasoma, that I, though your wife, [was abandoned by you].”
“O King, since you have gone forth into homelessness without regard for me,
who am conceived within your womb— my pregnancy is fully developed; until I give birth to him,
let me not become a lone widow and subsequently behold sorrows.”
In that regard, "That which was mine": because you went forth without regard for me as I lamented, therefore that supreme queenhood which I obtained from you was indeed ill-obtained.
In the second verse, because you went forth without regard for me, abandoning the union of our wombs, therefore that status of being your wife which I [held]...
"Whatever has been obtained, that is ill-obtained by me"—this is the meaning. "Until when? means: "Until I give birth to that child, wait until then.
Then the Great Being spoke this verse:
"The fetus within your womb is fully matured; come now, give birth!"
“I shall go forth, leaving behind that son of extraordinary beauty.
In this context, “son,” Bhaddā, I know that your pregnancy has reached maturity;
however, when you give birth, you will give birth to a son, not a daughter. May you give birth to a son in safety, and I, together with you—
"Abandoning that son, I shall surely go forth. Hearing his words,
she was unable to restrain her grief and, saying, "From this day forward, O King,
we have no prosperity," she held her heart with both hands and, shedding tears, cried out with a great sound:
She lamented. Then, comforting her, the Great Being spoke this verse:
“Do not weep, O Canda; do not grieve, you whose eyes are blinded by the darkness of the forest.
Ascend to the excellent palace; I shall go on without looking back.”
In this regard, do not weep, O Canda; noble Queen Canda, do not weep, do not grieve.

"Vanatimiramattakkhī" means one whose eyes are like the flowers of the *girikaṇṇikā* plant. In the canonical text (*pāḷi*), however, it is written as "koviḷāratambakkhī," which means one whose reddish-brown eyes are like the *koviḷāra* flower.

Having heard his words, she was unable to remain where she was; she ascended the palace and sat down weeping. Then the Bodhisatta’s eldest son, seeing her, asked her why she was sitting there weeping, and spoke this verse:
“Mother, who has provoked you to anger? Why do you weep while looking at me so intensely?
Whom, though he is innocent, shall I have executed while my kinsmen look on?”
In that context, "Who has made you angry? means: "Mother! Who indeed has made you angry? Who has done what is unpleasant to you?
"And why do you look at me?"—the intention is: "Why do you weep while looking so intently at me? "Whom shall I execute who is not to be executed?"—he asks her:
"Tell me, whom shall I put to death even though he should not be killed, while your own kinsmen are looking on?"
Then the queen spoke this verse:
“Indeed, he who has provoked me, O dear one, cannot be slain—he is a conqueror.
My father said to me, ‘Dear one, I shall go away without looking back.’”

"In this matter, dear son, he who defeated me on this earth—that one who provoked my anger and caused grief and resentment to enter my heart through his offensive conduct—cannot be killed by you, dear son.
For it was I, dear son, who said to your father, 'I shall abandon both the glory of kingship and him, and having entered the forest, I will go forth'; this is the reason for my weeping."
Having heard her words, he lamented, saying, “Mother! What is it you say? If this is so, shall we not truly become destitute? And uttering these words, he spoke this verse:
“I who formerly used to go out to the pleasure garden and fight with rutting elephants—now that Sutasoma has gone forth into homelessness, what indeed shall I do?”
The meaning of this is: "I who formerly used to go to the pleasure grove riding in a chariot yoked with four noble steeds and adorned with every ornament,
and used to fight with rutting elephants and play other games such as horse-riding—
how shall I act now that Sutasoma has gone forth?"
Then his younger brother, who was seven years old, seeing that both were weeping, approached their mother and asked, "Mother, for what reason are you two weeping?
Having heard the matter, he said, "In that case, do not weep;
I will not allow my father to go forth. Thus he comforted them both and, together with his nurse, [went] from the palace...
Having risen and gone into his father’s presence, he said, “Father, you say that you will go forth into homelessness, leaving us behind against our will;
I shall not allow you to go forth. Grasping his father firmly by the neck, he spoke this verse:
“While my mother weeps, and my elder brother is unwilling;”
"I shall seize you by the hand; for you shall not go against our will.
The Great Being thought, "This woman is creating an obstacle for me; by what means indeed might I make her turn back?
Then, looking at the nurse, he said, "Mother! Nurse, here is this jeweled necklace; let it be yours."
"Remove the child from your hand, do not cause me an obstacle! Being unable to remove the child from her hand himself, he promised her a bribe and spoke this verse:
"Arise, nurse! Amuse this boy elsewhere."
"Do not create an obstacle for me, who aspires to heaven.
Therein, "this boy"—[the mother said], "O nurse, you must rise up, take this boy away, come back, take this jewel, and find pleasure elsewhere.
Having received the bribe, she consoled the boy, took him, went elsewhere, and while lamenting, she spoke this verse:
“What if I were to give away this light-maker? What need have I for it?
Now that Sutasoma has gone forth, what indeed shall I do with it?
The meaning of this is: “What if I were to give away this well-luminous gem, the light-maker, which was taken for the sake of a bribe?”

“I would give it away! But what need have I for this now that Sutasoma, the lord of men, has gone forth? What indeed shall I do with it? ‘When he has gone forth, I shall obtain this’—but even if I obtain it, what indeed shall I do with it?
Behold my karma! Then Mahāsenagutta thought: “This king seems to perceive that the wealth in his house is small; I shall tell him of its abundance. Rising and bowing, he spoke this verse:
“Your treasury is vast, and your storehouse is full;
the earth is conquered by you—enjoy yourself, O King, do not go forth!
Having heard this, the Great Being spoke this verse:
“My treasury is vast, my storehouse is full, and the earth is conquered by me; having abandoned all that, I shall go forth.
When he had heard this and departed, the merchant named Kulavaḍḍhana rose, paid homage, and spoke this verse:
“I too have abundant wealth, O King, such that I cannot even count it;
I give all of that to you. Enjoy yourself; do not go forth into homelessness, O King.
Having heard this, the Great Being spoke this verse:
“I know that you possess abundant wealth, O increaser of the lineage, and I am honored by you;
yet, aspiring for heaven, I shall go forth into homelessness because of that.
Having heard this, when Kulavaḍḍhana had departed, the Great Being addressed his younger brother Somadatta: “Dear brother...”
“I am distressed like a wild cock confined in a cage; a lack of delight in the household life overcomes me.
I shall go forth this very day; you take charge of this kingdom. Thus, handing over the sovereignty, he spoke this verse:
“I am deeply distressed, O Somadatta; discontent assails me.”
"Though there are many obstacles for me, this very day I shall go forth.
Having heard that, he too, desiring to go forth, spoke the following verse while explaining his situation to him:
"If this is pleasing to you, Sutasoma, then go forth this very day."
“I too shall go forth; I am not able to remain without you.
Then, having refused her, he spoke this half-verse:
“For it is not possible to go forth, for there is no cooking in the city or in the countryside.”

In this context, "for it will not cook" means: even now, as soon as they have heard my intention to go forth, in this city of Sudassana twelve leagues in extent and throughout the entire province, nothing will be cooked; no one will kindle a fire on the hearth.
Furthermore, when we two have gone forth, the inhabitants of the kingdom will become truly destitute. Therefore, it is not possible for you [to do so].
“I shall go forth myself.
When he heard this, the great multitude gathered at the feet of the Great Being and, lamenting, spoke this half-stanza:
“Now that Sutasoma has gone forth, what indeed shall we do?”

Then the Great Being said, preaching the Dhamma to the great multitude: "Enough, do not grieve! Even though I remain for a long time, I shall eventually be without you; for no conditioned phenomenon that has arisen is eternal. He spoke thus:
"I consider this life to be like a small amount of water being carried away by a rushing stream;
since life is so very brief, it is no time to be negligent."
“I think this life is being carried away like a little water in a footstep-tyre;
thus, while life is so very short, the blind fools are heedless.
They increase hell, the animal realm, and the domain of hungry ghosts.”
“Bound by the fetters of craving, they increase the host of asuras.
In this context, “this is being led away” (upanīyati) means, dear one, “I perceive that this life is being led away.
In other suttas, the meaning of *upanīyana* is “leading toward” (*upasaṃharaṇa*), but here it has the sense of “exhaustion” (*pariyādāna*). Therefore, just as a small amount of...
Water thrown into the alkaline vats of washermen is quickly consumed; so too is life.
Thus, while living beings wander about having grasped that limited formation of life within such a very brief existence, it is not the time to be negligent regarding the performance of merit;
rather, it is fitting to practice heedfulness—this is the meaning here. [As for] "the blind fools":
"They are heedless" means that, acting as if they were ageless and immortal, like pigs in a mire of excrement, they are submerged in the mud of sensual desire and thus remain heedless.
"The host of asuras" means that they increase the asura-realm of the *kāḷakañjika* asuras.
Having thus taught the Dhamma to the great multitude, the Great Being ascended to the palace named Pubbaka and, on the seventh...
Standing on the ground, he cut off his topknot with a sword and, saying, "I am nothing to you;
take your own king," he threw the bound topknot into the midst of the great multitude.
Seizing it, the multitude wailed as they rolled and turned it over upon the ground. At that spot, a great cloud of dust arose. Having retreated...

A person standing there, having observed it, lamented and spoke this verse: “A cloud of dust is rising not far away, before the palace; surely the king has had his head shaved and, together with his turban, has thrown it among the crowd, for that is why this column of dust has arisen so near the palace.
He then recited the verse: “A cloud of dust is rising not far away, before the palace;”
"I think the hair of the illustrious Dhamma-king has not been cut.
In this context, *ūhaññate* means "it rises up. *Rajaggaṃ* means a mass of dust. *Avidūre* means not far from here, from our standing place.
*Pubbakamhi* means in the vicinity of the Eastern Palace. *Maññe no* refers to the hair of our Dhamma-king.
"We think they will be cut off.
The Great Being sent a servant to fetch the requisites for one who has gone forth;
having had his hair and beard shaved by a barber and having cast his ornaments onto the surface of the bed, he tore the hems of his red garments and put on those saffron robes.
Having dressed himself, hung his clay bowl over his left shoulder, and taken up his mendicant’s staff, he walked back and forth on the upper terrace;
then, descending from the palace, he entered the street. Yet as he went, no one recognized him.
Then seven hundred noble maidens, having ascended the palace and not seeing him, [saw] only his ornaments.
Having seen this, she descended and went into the presence of the remaining sixteen thousand women;
crying out with a great lamentation, "Our beloved husband, the lord Sutasoma, has gone forth into the religious life," they emerged outside.
At that moment, the great multitude learned of his state of renunciation, and the entire city was thrown into agitation, saying, "The king, it seems..."
“Has he not gone forth? Thus the great multitude gathered at the palace gate;
thinking, “The king will be here, he will be there,” they went to the palace and other places used by the king for his enjoyment, but not seeing the king, [they said]:
“This is his palace, strewn with golden flowers and garlands;”
The king wandered about there, surrounded by the women of the harem.
This was his palace, strewn with golden flowers and garlands;
there the king wandered about, surrounded by a host of kinsmen.
“This is his gabled chamber, strewn with golden flowers and garlands;
here the king used to roam, surrounded by his women’s quarters.
This is his gabled chamber, strewn with golden flowers and garlands.”
The king wandered about here, surrounded by his circle of kinsmen:
"This is his Asoka grove, beautiful, in full bloom at all times, delightful;
here the king wandered about, surrounded by the women of the harem."
“This is his Ashoka grove, ever-blooming, delightful, and full of flowers at all times;
here the king wanders about, surrounded by a multitude of kinsmen.
This is his pleasure garden, ever-blooming, delightful, and full of flowers at all times.”
“Here the king wandered about, surrounded by his harem.
‘This is his park, always in full bloom, delightful;
here the king wandered about, surrounded by his circle of kinsmen.’”
“This is his *kaṇikāra* grove, ever-blooming and delightful in all seasons;
here the king wanders about, surrounded by his retinue of women.
This is his *kaṇikāra* grove, ever-blooming and delightful in all seasons.”
The king wandered about here, surrounded by his assembly of kinsmen:
"This is his Pāṭalivana grove, always in full bloom, delightful;
here the king wandered about, surrounded by the women of the harem."
“This is his Pāṭalī grove, ever-blooming, beautiful, and delightful,
wherein the king used to wander, surrounded by a host of kinsmen.
This is his mango grove, ever-blooming, beautiful, and delightful.”
The king wandered about here, surrounded by his womenfolk.
"This is his mango grove, ever-blooming and delightful;
where the king wandered about, surrounded by his circle of kinsmen."
“This is his lotus pond, covered and strewn with egg-born creatures,
wherein the king used to wander about, surrounded by his harem.
This is his lotus pond, covered and strewn with egg-born creatures.”
“Wandering about in grief, the king, surrounded by a multitude of kinsmen,”—thus he wandered, lamenting with these verses.
Therein, “strewn” (*vītikiṇṇa*) means covered with golden flowers and various garlands; “surrounded” (*parikiṇṇa*) means encircled.
"By women of the harem" means that women beginning with female slaves are called "women of the harem.

"By the circle of kinsmen": here, even ministers are considered kinsmen. "A gabled chamber" refers to a bedchamber within a gabled house, variegated with the seven precious gems. "An Asoka grove" is a ground consisting of an Asoka forest.
"All-seasonal" means capable of enjoyment at all times, or always in flower. "A pleasure garden" is one similar to the Nandana Grove or the Citralatāvana.
The garden. "All-season" means it is covered with flowers and fruits that arise during all six seasons.
Regarding "all-season" in the case of the *kaṇikāra* grove and others, it means that at all times they are indeed well-flowered and fruit-bearing.
"Covered" means well-covered with various kinds of water-born and land-born flowers. "Strewn with egg-born creatures" means overspread by flocks of birds.
Having thus lamented in various places, the great multitude returned again to the royal courtyard and cried out:
“Your king has indeed gone forth! Sutasoma, having abandoned this kingdom, clad in saffron robes, wanders alone like a nāga.”
Having spoken this verse, she abandoned all her wealth in her own home, took her sons and daughters by the hands, and having departed, went into the very presence of the Bodhisatta;
likewise did her parents, her children and wife, and sixteen thousand female dancers.
The entire city became as if empty, and even the inhabitants of the countryside followed after them.
Taking a retinue twelve *yojanas* in extent, the Bodhisatta set out toward the Himālaya.
Then, learning of his departure, Sakka addressed Vissakamma, saying: "Dear Vissakamma, the Great King Sutasoma has gone forth into the renunciant life;
it is necessary to find a dwelling place for him, and a great assembly will take place. Go to a region of the Himālaya..."
"Build a hermitage on the bank of the Ganges, thirty yojanas in length and fifteen yojanas in width," he sent forth.
Having done so, and having prepared the requisites for those who would go forth in that hermitage and constructed a path for a single traveler,
he departed for the world of the gods.
The Mahāsatta went by that path, entered the hermitage, and first himself went forth into homelessness;
afterwards, he caused the others to go forth as well. In later times, many went forth until the area for thirty *yojanas* was filled.
This was due to the Bodhisatta’s determination to have the hermitage established by Vissakamma and his determination that many should go forth.
The arrangement of the hermitage grounds and the rules established there should be understood according to the method described in the *Hatthipāla-jātaka*. Therein,
whenever a wrong thought such as sensual desire arose in anyone, the Great Being would approach that person through the air,
sit cross-legged in the sky, and while instructing them, spoke these two verses:
“Do not recall your former amorous play and laughter;
let not sensual desires overcome you, for the city of Sudassana is delightful.
Cultivate a mind of loving-kindness, immeasurable, by day and by night.”
"He went to the city of the gods, his dwelling place for meritorious deeds.
In this context, "pleasurable diversions" refers both to sensual pleasures and to diversions carried out by way of physical and verbal play.
"May desires not destroy you" means may you not be destroyed by either objective desires (*vatthukāma*) or defilement-desires (*kilesakāma*). "Delightful" refers to the city of Sudassana.

That [name] is delightful; do not recollect it. "A mind of loving-kindness" (*mettacitta*) is merely a term for the teaching, but he explained all four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*). "Immeasurable" (*appamāṇa*) means having immeasurable sentient beings as its object.
"You shall go" (*agacchittha*) means you will go. "To the city of the gods" (*devapura*) refers to the Brahma-world.
That company of his, too, abiding by his instruction, became destined for the Brahma-world; all this should be told according to the method set forth in the *Hatthipāla Jātaka*.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now that the Tathāgata has gone forth on the Great Renunciation;
he did so even in the past," and he identified the Jātaka, saying: "At that time, the mother and father were members of a great royal family."
"Candādevī was the mother of Rāhula; Sāriputta was the eldest son; Rāhula was the youngest son; Khujjuttarā was the nurse;
the merchant Kulavaḍḍhana was Kassapa; Mahāsenagutta was Moggallāna; Prince Somadatta was Ānanda;
the rest of the assembly was the Buddha’s retinue; and as for King Sutasoma, it was I myself."
The fifth: The Commentary on the Cūḷasutasoma Jātaka.
The summary of the Jātakas:
Suvapaṇḍita, Jambuka, Kuṇḍalinī, Varakaññā, and the Alambusa Jātaka.
The king Sutasoma, Arindama, whose fame was like that of the most excellent conch, [is here].
The commentary on the Forty-Chapter Section (Cattālīsanipāta) is finished.
18. The Fifty-Chapter Section (Paṇṇāsanipāta).
[526] 1. The Commentary on the Niḷinikā Jātaka.
"The country is burning"—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the seduction by a former wife.
And as he spoke, having asked that bhikkhu, "By whom have you been made discontented? he replied, "By my former wife."
When he had spoken thus, [the Buddha] said, "Monk, this woman has not only now been a source of harm to you;
in the past as well, by relying on her, you fell away from your meditative absorptions and met with great ruin. Having said this, he related a story of the past:
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a prominent family of northern brahmins.

Having been reborn and reached maturity, he mastered the arts, went forth as an ascetic, and having attained the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), he made his dwelling in the Himalayan region.
In accordance with the method described in the *Alambusā-jātaka*, a doe conceived a child because of him and gave birth to a son; his name was "Isisiṅga. Then his father—

Having ordained him when he had reached maturity, [the teacher] had him master the preliminary exercises for the *kasiṇas*. Before long, he had given rise to the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), and sported in the bliss of those absorptions.
He became one of fierce asceticism and supreme self-mastery. By the power of his virtue, Sakka’s abode shook.
Sakka, reflecting on this, understood the cause and thought, "I shall break his virtue by means of a stratagem," and for three years—
He stopped the rain throughout the entire kingdom of Kāsi, and the country became like a land scorched by fire.
When the crops failed and the people were oppressed by famine, they gathered together and protested in the royal courtyard.
Then the king, standing at a window, asked, "What is this? They replied, "Great King, because the rain has not fallen for three years, the entire kingdom—"
"It is burning; the people are suffering. O gods, cause the rain to fall! Although the king had undertaken the moral precepts and observed the Uposatha, he was unable to make it rain.
At that time, at the hour of midnight, Sakka entered his bedchamber, filled it with a single radiance, and stood in the air.
He stood there. When the king saw him, he asked, "Who are you? "I am Sakka," he replied. "For what purpose have you come?
"Does it rain in your kingdom, Great King? "It does not rain. "Do you know the reason why it does not rain?
"I do not know, Sakka. "Great King, in the region of the Himalayas there dwells an ascetic named Isisinga."
“He is one of terrible asceticism and supreme self-control. Because he looked up at the sky in anger while it was raining heavily upon the gods, the rain has therefore ceased.
“But what should be done here now? “When his ascetic power is broken, the rain will fall.
“But who is capable of breaking his ascetic power? “Your daughter, Great King, Niḷinikā.”
“Once you have found someone capable, summon them and send them forth with the command: ‘Go to such-and-such a place and break the ascetic’s austerity.
Having thus instructed the king, he returned to his own abode. On the following day, the king consulted with his ministers, summoned his daughter, and spoke the first verse:
“The country is burning up and the kingdom is being destroyed;
come, Niḷinikā, go and bring that brahmin to me.
In this context, “that one of mine” means: bring that brahmin who acts for my harm under your control; break his virtue by means of the pleasure of the defilements.
Having heard that, she spoke this second verse:
“O King, I am not one who endures suffering, nor am I skilled in long journeys;
how shall I go to the forest frequented by elephants?”
"In that regard, O Great King, I am not one who can endure suffering; I do not even know the length of the journey, so how shall I go?
Then the king spoke these two verses:
"Having gone to the prosperous countryside by means of both elephant and chariot..."
“Go by means of a carriage with a wooden frame, Niliṇikā;
for even if kṣatriyas go on foot, or by elephant, horse, or chariot,
they will surely bring you under their power by means of your very complexion and beauty.”
In that regard, "by means of a vehicle consisting of a wooden frame" means: "Mother Niḷinikā, you shall not go on foot;

rather, having traveled to your own country—which is prosperous, well-supplied with food, and secure—by means of elephant-vehicles and chariot-vehicles, you shall thereafter travel by a vehicle consisting of a wooden frame known as a boat, which is covered and used in open spaces and in water."
"Go! By means of your beauty and form"—meaning, by going without becoming weary, you will bring that brahmin under your control through your complexion and perfection of form.
Thus, although it was something he should not have discussed with his daughter, he spoke of it on account of protecting the kingdom. She, for her part, said, "Very well."
She accepted. Then, having given her everything that was appropriate to be given, he dismissed her along with the ministers.

The ministers, taking her with them, reached the border region; there they established a military camp, had the princess carried up, and entering the Himālayas by the path shown by a forest-dweller, they arrived at that hermitage during the morning.
They arrived nearby. At that moment, the Bodhisatta, having left his son to dwell in the hermitage, had himself entered the forest for the sake of gathering fruits.
Without going to the hermitage himself, the forester stood at a place from which he could see him and, pointing him out with his finger, spoke these two verses:
“Marked by the banner of the plantain tree, surrounded by its enclosure;
this delightful hermitage of Isisinga is visible.
This is known as the fire, and this smoke is seen.”
"I think the great-iddhi Isisiṅga does not let the fire die out.
In this context, "having the plantain as its banner-sign" means having the plantain as its mark of recognition (*paññāṇa*).
"Surrounded by *ābhujī*" means surrounded by a forest of *bhujapatta* trees. "Reckoned" means that this fire was reckoned by the meditative absorption (*jhāna*) of that Isisiṅga.
"It burns before my very eyes; I think it is not [just] a fire. I believe he does not neglect the fire, but offers oblations and tends to it.
At the moment the Bodhisatta entered the forest, the ministers surrounded the hermitage and established a guard.
Then, having had the princess assume the guise of a seer, they dressed her in a golden robe as both lower and upper garment and adorned her with all her ornaments.
Having decorated and tied it with cords, they had her take hold of the mind-ball (*cittageṇḍuka*) and sent her into the hermitage grounds; they themselves remained outside guarding her.
While she was playing with that ball, she went down to the edge of the walking-path (*caṅkama*). At that moment, Isisinga was sitting on a stone slab at the door of the leaf-hut (*paṇṇasālā*).
Seeing her approaching, he rose up in terrified alarm and entered the leaf-hut.
Having entered, he stood there. She too had merely gone to the door of his leaf-hut and was playing.
The Teacher, explaining the meaning of that and what followed it, spoke these three verses:
“Seeing her approaching, with her jeweled earrings fastened, ...”
Terrified, he entered the hermitage thatched with leaves.
At the entrance of the hermitage, she played with a ball,
displaying her limbs and revealing her private parts.
“Having seen her playing thus, the matted-hair ascetic who had gone to his leaf-hut came out from the hermitage and spoke these words.
Therein, *geṇḍukenassa* means that she was playing with a ball at the gate of the hermitage of this seer Siṅga. *Vidaṃsayantī* means...
"Revealing. "Both the secret and the revealed": the secret refers to the private parts, while the revealed refers to the face, hands, and so forth.
He said this because, it is said, while standing in the leaf-hut he thought: "If this were a *yakkha*, he would have entered the leaf-hut, crushed me, and eaten me;
this is not a *yakkha*, he must be an ascetic (*tāpasa*). Having thus emerged from the hermitage, he spoke.
Questioning him, he spoke this verse: "O friend,
what indeed is that tree whose fruit has reached such a state—
that even when cast far away, it returns, and does not depart, leaving it behind?"
In this context, "whose fruit has reached such a state" means whose delightful fruit of that tree has come to such a condition.
Thinking, "There must be a tree corresponding to that fruit," Citragenduka asks thus because he had never seen the tree before.
Then, pointing out the tree, she spoke this verse:
"O Brahmā, near my hermitage on Mount Gandhamādana there are many such trees as that from which fruit like yours has fallen."
“Even if cast far away, it returns; it does not depart leaving me behind.
Therein, “near Gandhamādana” means near my hermitage on Mount Gandhamādana. Regarding “yassa tevaṅgataṃ,” the letter *ta* is used for euphonic conjunction (*byañjanasandhi*).
Thus she spoke a falsehood. The other, having believed her and perceiving her with the thought, “This is an ascetic,” spoke this verse while offering a hospitable welcome:
“May your honor enter this hermitage and accept both drink and food;
I give them to you. Let your honor sit here on this seat; let your honor eat roots and fruits from here.
In this context, “enter this hermitage” means: may your honor enter this hermitage. “Accept” means: may he consume whatever food is available.
They go for foot-unguents; they eat sweet fruits. "Paṭicchāti" means she receives. "Idam āsanam" (this is the seat) was said at the time of entering.
Having entered her leaf-hut and sat down upon a mat of wood, her golden bark-garment split in two, revealing her body.
It was not concealed. Because the ascetic had never before seen the body of a woman, upon seeing it, he perceived it as "something beautiful" and spoke thus:
"What is this on the space between your thighs, which appears so very lustrous like black [sandalwood paste]?
Being asked, tell me the meaning of this: has your head entered into a sheath?"
In this context, "well-smeared" (*supicchita*) refers to the area between the two thighs at the time of their meeting; it is shaped like the mouth of a lute-case (*sippipuṭa*).
For one who is not endowed with the mark of beauty, that place is like a pit; for one who is so endowed, it is elevated and shaped like the mouth of a lute-case.
"Appearing blackish on both sides" means it appears as if it were dark on both flanks.
"Why has your head entered into a sheath?"—he asks this because the shape of your head as a male organ is not apparent;
he asks, "Why has it entered into that which is called your body-sheath?
Then, deceiving him, she spoke these two verses:
“While wandering in the forest searching for roots and fruits, I encountered a hyena of most terrifying form.
It suddenly pounced upon me, seized me, and having driven me off, tore out my head.
This wound of mine is eaten by maggots and itches; at no time do I find any comfort.”
"Please, sir, remove this itch; do what you have been asked for the sake of the brahmin.
Therein, "āsādayiṃ" means I struck; the meaning is that seeing him coming, I hit him with a clod of earth.
"Patitvā" means having run toward him. "Sahasājjhappatto" means suddenly arrived or reached me. "Panujja" means then...
"Having sucked me dry. "He tore it out": having plucked my head—the highest part of my body—with his mouth, he departed;
from that time on, a wound has formed in this place. "It swells": since then, this wound of mine is both eaten by flies and scratched [by insects];
because of that, I do not obtain physical or mental happiness at any time. "Pahoti" means capable.
“Capable. Regarding the phrase “the welfare of the brahmin”: she says, “May you, being entreated by me, accomplish this welfare for the brahmin; take away this suffering of mine.
Believing his falsehood to be his true nature, he said, “If it brings you such happiness, I shall do it,” and after looking toward that place, he spoke the following verse:
“Your wound is deep and bloody, with a great and putrid wound-smell;
I shall prepare for you a certain decoction so that you may become supremely happy.

In this context, “bloody” means having a red appearance. “Putrid” means free from rotten flesh. “Wound-smell” means slightly foul-smelling. “A decoction” means: “I will take certain tree-decoctions and prepare a medicinal compound for you.”
Then Niḷinikā spoke this verse:
“Neither by the application of mantras, nor by the application of astringents, nor by medicinal herbs does the itch move away from one who leads the holy life.
With that which is soft for you, relieve the itch, so that I may become supremely happy.”

In this context, "they do not work" means: "O celibate one, in this forest of mine, neither mantra-preparations, nor decoction-preparations, nor medicinal herbs such as flowers and fruits work; even when used many times, they have never previously brought about the healing of this [wound].
However, it is only when it is rubbed by that soft organ of yours that its itching subsides."
"It does not exist; therefore, remove this thorn with that.

He, perceiving that "this man speaks the truth," yet being unaware that "through sexual intercourse the virtue (*sīla*) breaks and the meditative absorption (*jhāna*) disappears"—because he had never before seen a woman and because of his lack of knowledge regarding the nature of sexual intercourse—[acted accordingly].
While she was saying, "It is medicine," he engaged in sexual intercourse with her. At that very moment his virtue (sīla) was broken and his meditative absorption (jhāna) declined.

After engaging in intercourse two or three times, becoming exhausted, he went out, descended into the lake, bathed, and having his distress subsided, returned and sat down in the leaf-hut. Again [he addressed her as] "O ascetic."
Thinking thus and asking about his dwelling place, he spoke this verse:
“By which path from here, sir, is your hermitage? I hope you find delight in the forest;
I hope your roots and fruits are abundant, and I hope that wild beasts do not harm you.”
In that context, "By which way from here? means: "In which direction from here is your hermitage, sir?
This is a form of address. Then, while hiding there, she recited four verses:
"Directly to the north from here flows the river Khemā, originating from the Himalayas."
"On its bank is my delightful hermitage; oh, may you behold my hermitage!
Mangoes, *sāla* trees, *tilaka*s, rose-apples, *uddālaka*s, and *pāṭali*s are in full bloom;
it resounds on all sides with the songs of *kimpurisa*s—oh, may you behold my hermitage!"
“Here there are palm fruits and roots, endowed with color and fragrance;
this place is further graced by its level terrain—oh, may you look upon my hermitage!
Here there are fruits and roots in abundance, endowed with color, fragrance, and flavor.”
"The hunters come to that place; let them not take my roots and fruits from there.
In this context, *uttarāyanti* means "by the north. *Khemā* is the name of a river. *Pabhāvī* means it flows forth from the Himalayas.
*Aho* is a particle used in the sense of aspiration. *Uddālakā* refers to the *vātaghātaka* trees. *Kimpurisābhigītaṃ* means [a place] resounded by the songs of kimpurisas.
It was celebrated with sweet songs by *kimpuruṣas* who surrounded it on all sides.

"Roots, tubers, and fruits are found here" means that in my hermitage there are lovely palm trees (*tāla*), as well as their roots—known as tubers—and fruits, all endowed with excellent color, fragrance, and other qualities.
"Abundant is what is found here" refers to the various fruits of many trees and the roots of forest creepers.
And there is an abundance here. Thinking, "Let them not take it from me," [I thought]:
many hunters come to my hermitage, and there is much sweet-tasting root and fruit that I have brought and set out here;
if I were to stay away for long, they might carry off the roots and fruits. Therefore, lest they should take my roots and fruits from there, even if by me—
"I wish to come along with you; come, otherwise I shall go myself," he said.
Having heard this, the ascetic spoke a verse in order to ask him to wait until his father’s return:
"My father has gone out to search for roots and fruits; he will return now at the time of evening."
“Let us both go together to that hermitage, so that my father may come for roots and fruits.
Therein, “let us both go together” means: having informed my father, we two shall go together.
Then she thought: “He has grown up entirely in the forest, and thus he does not yet know my female nature.”
"If my father were to see me here and recognize me, he would strike me with the tip of his staff and ask, 'What are you doing here?
and might even break my head. It is better for me to leave before he arrives; my business for coming here is finished.
Speaking thus, she explained the means by which he might come, and recited the other verse:
“There are many other seers of noble character who dwell along the path in groups of hundreds;
ask them about my hermitage, and they will lead you to me. Therein, “groups of hundreds” means:
friend, it is not possible for me to remain long; however, there are other seers of virtuous nature...
“Both the Brahmin and his wife live along the path to my hermitage;
I will point them out to you as I go, and you should ask them, for they will lead you into my presence.
Having thus devised a means of escape, she emerged from the leaf-hut and, even as he was looking at her, said: “You—”
Having said, "I shall return," he went back to the presence of his ministers by the same path he had come.
They took him and proceeded to the royal camp, reaching Benares in due course. On that very day, Sakka, being pleased, caused rain to fall throughout the entire kingdom;
consequently, the country became well-supplied with food. And as soon as the ascetic Isisiṅga had departed...
Thus, a burning fever arose in his body. Trembling, he entered the leaf-hut, wrapped himself in a garment of bark, and lay down in sorrow.
The Bodhisatta, returning in the evening and not seeing his son, thought, "Where has he gone?
He lowered his carrying-pole, entered the leaf-hut, and seeing him lying there, asked, "Dear one, what are you doing? as he rubbed the boy's back.
He recited three verses:
"The firewood has not been split by you, nor has water been brought by you;
even the fire has not been tended by you—why then do you meditate like one who is dull-witted?"
“The firewood is split, the fire is kindled, and the heat has been stilled by you, O celibate one.
I have my seat and water; you, having become a Brahmā, were delighted in the past.
You have not split the firewood, nor have you brought water; the fire is unkindled and your food is unprepared.”
"Today you do not speak to me; has some mental suffering been lost?"—in this context, "broken" means removed from the forest.
"Not sacrificed" means not ignited. "Broken" means that previously, at the time of my arrival, the firewood had already been removed by you.
"And the fire was sacrificed" means the fire was indeed ignited. "The burner"—means...
The heat, known as the fire of glowing embers, is already stilled and naturally provided for you.
A seat is already prepared for me to sit upon. And water—water for washing the feet—is also already set out.
You too, having become like Brahmā, being preeminent from before this, take delight in this hermitage. You have not broken the wood [for fuel].
"So now you are one whose firewood has not been gathered today. You have no cooked food," [he said].
"Nothing of our tubers, roots, or leaves has been boiled for you. "My son, why do you not speak to me today? "Have you lost something? he asked, meaning:
"What is it that you have lost, or what mental anguish is there? Tell me the reason for your lying here."
Having heard his father’s words, he spoke, explaining the reason:
“A matted-hair ascetic, a celibate student, has come here—he is beautiful to behold, with a slender body, and well-disciplined.
He is neither too tall nor too short, and his eyes are covered by very dark eyelashes.”
“Not yet grown old, his complexion fresh, and a supporting mark upon his neck;
two twin moles on his chest, well-formed, resembling golden *tinduka* fruits, radiant and glowing.
And his face is exceedingly beautiful to behold, with ears whose tips hang down in curls.”
While that young man was wandering about, his fire was burning, and his matted locks were bound with cords.
And there were four other restraints of his: blue, yellow, red, and white;
these adorned the young man as he wandered, like the *tiriṭi* flowers in the rainy season.
She wears no girdle made of *mikhala* grass or *muñja*, nor does she spread one out for the renunciant;
those bright ornaments clinging to her hips shine like lightning in the sky.
And they are without pins or stalks, fastened at the waist below the navel.
“Without being struck, they play constantly; father, what kind of tree fruits are those?
“His matted locks are most wonderful to behold, more than a hundred in number, curling at the tips and fragrant;
his head is beautifully divided into two parts—oh, would that my matted locks were likewise!”
“And when he shakes out those matted locks, which are endowed with color and fragrance, they waft away just like a blue lotus stirred by the wind; yet this man is wasting away.
And his mud is most loathsome to behold—nothing like what is found on my own body.”
Thus it blows, stirred by the Maluta wind, like a forest in full bloom at the height of summer.
It strikes down the fruit of a tree upon the earth—beautifully formed, lovely, and fair to behold;
yet when thrown, it returns again to his hand. "Alas, father! What kind of tree-fruit could that be?"
“His teeth are most beautiful to behold, pure, even, and like the finest conch shells;
when he opens his mouth, they gladden the mind. Surely he did not eat those [fruits] raw.
His speech is not harsh, it is not muffled, it is gentle, straight, not arrogant, and not fickle.”
His voice was lovely, like the song of the karavīka bird; reaching the heart, it truly delighted my mind.
"With a soft tone and speech not overly expansive, surely he has not been over-exerting himself in recitation.
I wish, sir, to see him once again; for that young man was my friend in the past."
“With my wound everywhere raw and festering, wide and well-healed yet resembling a coarse leaf,
the young man covered me with that very garment and pressed against my thighs with his hips.
Blazing, shining, and radiating light, she was like a lightning flash in the sky, brilliant and white.”
His arms were soft like the down of a collyrium-smoke cloud, and they shone with various rounded lines upon them.
Without harshness and not covered in long hair, his nails were long yet red-tipped;
embracing him with those soft arms, he of beautiful form attended upon me, bringing delight.

“Resembling cotton from a *duma* tree, radiant, with hands of golden hue, rounded and smooth—having touched me with those soft hands, he has gone from here, O father, and because of that, they burn me.
Surely he did not carry a load of salt upon his back; surely he did not break wood himself.”
“Surely he does not strike the trees with an axe, for there are no stumps in his hands.
Yet he made a wound upon my eye and said to me, ‘Make me happy.
I did so for him, and by that act I found happiness; and he too said, ‘I am happy,’ O Brahmā.”
“This *māluva*-leaf mat of yours has been scattered about by me and him;
exhausted from sporting in the water, we shall go back to the leaf-hut again and again.
O Father, today no more mantras occur to my mind, nor the fire-sacrifice, nor the ritual of sacrifice.”
Nor will I eat roots and fruits until I see that practitioner of the holy life.
"Surely you too know, dear father, in which direction the practitioner of the holy life dwells;
lead me quickly, dear father, to that direction, lest I die in your hermitage."
“I have heard of a forest in full bloom, resounded by birds and frequented by flocks of birds;
lead me quickly, dear father, to that forest, before I give up my life here in this hermitage.
In this context, *idhāgata* means, “Dear father, I have come to this hermitage site. *Sudassaneyya* means “very beautiful to behold.”
"Sutanūti" means very slender—neither too thin nor too stout. "Vineti" means that by the radiance of his own body, he leads [the hermitage] so that it appears as if filled with a single light.
Regarding the phrase "by the very black, black-hued coverings, O Sir":
dear father, by those very black, black-hued coverings—his hair, which is the color of bees—that very black head of his appears like a well-polished gem.
"Amassujāto" means that his beard has not yet grown; he is still young. "Apurāṇavaṇṇī" means one who has recently gone forth.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "he has a support for his form," it refers to a necklace worn around his neck, similar to a bowl-rest used for setting our alms-bowl;
he speaks thus with reference to a pearl necklace. "Gaṇḍā" is said with reference to his breasts.
“Beautifully formed on the chest” means they are well-formed upon the chest. There is also a reading, “from the chest. “Radiant” means endowed with luster.
There is also a reading, “pabhāsare,” meaning they shine forth.
“Exceedingly beautiful to behold” means it is most worthy of being seen. “With curled tips” is said with reference to the lion’s earring (*sihakuṇḍala*).
"And the thread" means that even the thread with which his matted hair was bound shines and emits radiance.
By the phrase "four restraints," he shows the four ornaments made of gems, gold, coral, and silver.
"They resound" means that when it rains during the rainy season, those ornaments jingle like *tiriṭisa* birds. "Mikhalanti" [means they glitter].
*Mekhalaṃ*, or rather this reading is *mekhalan*. This is said with reference to this lower garment (*nivāsana*) made of golden cloth.
*Na santhareti* means "not on woven grass. This is what is meant: "Dear one, just as we wear garments made of grass or woven grass, he does not;
rather, he wears a garment of gold. *Akhīlakānīti* means without thongs, finished, and complete. *Kaṭisamohitānīti* means fastened around the waist.
"Bound to his waist. "They play constantly" means that even when not being struck, they play at all times. "Haṃ, tāta!

means "O, dear father! "What kind of tree fruits are those?"—referring to the jeweled girdle—he asks, "Of what kind of tree are those fruits that have been strung together and bound to the waist of that young man?"
"Jaṭā" refers to the coils of hair mixed with jewels that are bound in the form of a circle of matted locks; this is what he says.
"Vellitaggā" means having curled tips. "Dvedhāsiro" means his head, having been divided into two parts, is well-distinguished by way of the matted locks bound thereon.
"Tathā" means: just as the matted locks of that young man are bound, so too have they not been bound upon me by you.
"Alas, may it be so for me too! he said, expressing this aspiration. "Endowed with beauty" (*upetarūpā*) means possessing their natural state.
"As if stirred by the wind": just as a blue lotus is stirred by the wind, even so does this hermitage in this forest grove waft [its fragrance].
"'It is not like this,' dear son: the filth upon my body is not like that on his body; for he is truly beautiful to behold."
And it was fragrant. "At the foremost time" means during the spring season.
"He struck" means he hit. "What tree’s fruit could this be? means whose tree’s fruit could that possibly be?
"Appearing like a choice conch" means resembling a well-washed conch shell. "Surely he did not eat vegetables with them" means certainly not.
That young man ate tree leaves as well as roots and various fruits with those teeth of ours, just like we do.
For while we were eating them, he pointed out that our teeth were strong and beautiful in color.
"Not harsh," dear one, refers to his speech being gentle, not rough, and not abrasive; even when speaking repeatedly, it possesses sweetness.
It is gentle because it is constant; straight because of its lack of forgetfulness; unobtrusive because of its lack of distraction; and steady because of its stability.

It is "weeping" (*rudantī*) as it speaks—that is, though it is a sound consisting of vocalization, it is as enchanting as the cry of a *karavīka* bird, possessing a beautiful tone and being very sweet.
"It truly delights" means my mind is indeed delighted. "A single-toned sound" (*bindussara*) means a unified sound. "He was a young brahmin" (*māṇavo ahū*); for he...
That young man was formerly my friend.
"Susandhi, 'smoothed all over'—my dear, there is a wound between that young man's thighs;
it is well-knit, very smooth, like the opening of a bamboo sheath, and smoothed all over on every side."
*Maṭṭhaṃ*: smooth. *Puthu*: extensive, meaning great. *Sujātaṃ*: well-formed. *Kharapattasannibhaṃ*: resembling a fully blossomed lotus bud.
*Uttariyāna*: having crossed over and spread out. *Piḷayi*: he pressed down. *Tapanti*:
the golden-colored rays streaming forth from the body of that young man were burning, shining, and radiating. *Bāhā*: his arms as well.
"Soft. "Possessing hair like collyrium" means endowed with hair resembling collyrium.
"His hands shine with various round fingers" means his hands also shine, being endowed with round fingers that possess excellent characteristics and resemble coral sprouts.
"With limbs free from harshness" means having limbs and members of the body devoid of itch, boils, and the like. "He attended, delighting me" means attending while providing me with pleasure.
He attended upon and served him. "Like cotton" is a simile for softness.

"With hands like golden bamboos, round and of beautiful complexion" means they were round and of beautiful complexion, like the surface of a golden mirror; that is, their palms were perfectly circular and their skin was lovely.
"Having touched" means having touched well, causing the sensation of his own hands to pervade my body.
"He has gone from here"—even as I was looking on, he departed from here. "They burn me with that"—by means of that touch of his hand, they now burn me;
for indeed, from the moment he left, a feverish burning has arisen in my body, and because of that, I lie down overcome with dejection.
"Surely he was not a carrier of a khāri-load, dear father; surely that young man did not wander about carrying a burden of a khāri.
'Khilāni' means 'kilāni'—this is indeed the reading. 'Sokhyaṃ' means 'sukhaṃ'. 'Spread with māluva leaves, appearing as if scattered,' dear father:
this spread of māluva leaves of yours today has been [rendered] such by our mutual touching and embracing."
As they turned about, they became as if scattered and utterly disordered. "Father, let us enter the leaf-hut again and again," he said;

"he and I, having enjoyed ourselves and become somewhat weary, shall emerge from the leaf-hut, enter the water, and after sporting until our fatigue has vanished, we shall enter this very hut again and again."
"Neither counsel nor spells": from the moment he departed today, neither counsel nor spells occur to me, do not present themselves, and do not please me.

"Neither the fire-sacrifice nor the ritual system of sacrifice": even the performance of sacrifices, such as the offering of oblations and the fanning of the flames, which ought to be done for the sake of propitiating Mahābrahmā, does not occur to me, does not present itself, and does not please me.
"Nor even those": even the roots, fruits, and grains brought by you [do not occur to me, do not present themselves, and do not please me].
“I will not eat. In whichever direction, in whichever quarter [he may be]. By “the forest,” he meant the forest standing surrounding that young man’s hermitage.
As he was thus lamenting, the Great Being, hearing his lamentation and knowing that “the virtue of this man must have been broken by a single woman,” spoke these six verses as an exhortation to him:
“In this Jotirasa forest, frequented by hosts of Gandhabbas and celestial nymphs;”
“O leaders, do not fall into such discontent while dwelling in this eternal abode of the seers.
Friends come into being and then cease to be; one shows affection toward kinsmen and friends.
But why is this person so deluded that he does not even know, ‘From where have I come?’”
“Indeed, friendships are cemented again and again through living together;
even a true friend grows old through not associating and failing to meet.
But if you should see one who leads the holy life, and if you should converse with one who leads the holy life...”
"Just as a field rich in grain is destroyed by a great flood, you will quickly lose this quality of asceticism.
If you see another practitioner of the holy life again, and if you converse with that practitioner of the holy life again,
just as a field rich in grain is destroyed by a great flood, you will quickly lose this state of inner heat."
“Beings, dear one, roam about in this world of men in various forms;
a wise person should not associate with them, for by attacking them, the practitioner of the holy life perishes.
