In this context, *imasmiṃ* means “in this. *Haṃ* is a mere particle. *Jotirasē* refers to that which is illuminated by the rays of the sacrificial fire (*joti*) being offered.
*Sanātanamhi* means "in ancient times. *Pāpuṇetha* means "he would attain. This is what is meant:
"Dear one, a wise son of good family living in such a forest as this would not attain the kind of discontent you have reached; it is not fit for him to attain it"—this is the meaning.
The Great Being spoke this verse, "Bhavanti," while still within [the forest]. This is the intended meaning here: in the world...

Among sentient beings, there are those who are friends and those who are not; among them, those who have such friendships feel affection for their own kinsmen and friends. But this one is a base deer named Jamma.
For what reason, indeed, has he become settled in that woman with the perception of her being a friend? Having been born from the womb of a doe, [he has come to this state].
Because he was raised in the forest, he does not know even his own place of origin—thinking, "From where have I come?"—let alone his kinsmen and friends.
"Again and again," my dear, means that friends are joined and united through repeated living together and association.
He alone is a friend to a man who does not go to him, who does not approach him—that is, to one who does not engage in meeting with him.

Through not living together, it withers and perishes. Therefore, dear son, if you should see him again or converse with him, then just as a mature crop is carried away by a great flood, so too will you lose and forfeit this quality of your own asceticism;
this is the meaning. "Heat" refers to the ascetic power (*śramaṇatejas*).
"By means of various forms" means by means of manifold forms. This is what is intended:
"Dear one, in the human world these beings known as yakkhinīs wander about in their own forms concealed by various shapes in order to devour those who have come under their power;
a wise person should not associate with them. For having encountered such a being and fallen into its power, even a practitioner of the holy life perishes."
"You have been seen by that female spirit (yakkhinī); you have not been eaten," he advised his son.
Having heard his father's words and thinking, "She is indeed a female spirit," the son became afraid; he turned back his mind and asked for forgiveness, saying, "Father, I will not go from here;
please forgive me. The father, in turn, comforted him, saying, "Come, young man, cultivate loving-kindness (mettā)."
“Cultivate loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity,” he said, thus explaining the cultivation of the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*).
Having practiced accordingly, he again produced the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and direct knowledges (*abhiññā*).
The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths (*sacca*), identified the Jātaka; at the conclusion of the Truths, [he made the identification].
The discontented bhikkhu was established in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, Niḷinikā was his former wife;
Isisiṅga was the discontented bhikkhu; and I myself was his father.
This concludes the first commentary, the Niḷinikājātaka.
[527] 2. The Commentary on the Ummādantī Jātaka:
"To whom does this dwelling belong, O Sunandā? This was related by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana concerning a monk who was despondent.
It is said that one day, while wandering for alms in Sāvatthī, he saw a woman fully adorned and prepared.
Having gazed upon a woman of supreme beauty, his mind became bound by passion; unable to turn back his heart, he returned to the monastery.

From that time forth, like one pierced by an arrow, afflicted by lust, resembling a startled deer, emaciated with his limbs covered in visible veins, turned pale and wan, and finding no delight, he could find no mental satisfaction even in a single act.
Having abandoned the duties toward his teacher and others, he lived devoid of application to the recitation, questioning, and the practice of meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
When his companion monks asked him, "Friend, formerly your faculties were tranquil and the color of your face was serene; now it is not so.
What is the reason? he replied, "Friends, I am dissatisfied. Then they said to him, "Be satisfied, friend, with the Teaching."
The arising of a Buddha is indeed rare, as are the hearing of the True Dhamma and the attainment of human birth.
Having attained this human birth and aspiring to the ending of suffering, why do you, having gone forth with faith after abandoning your tearful kinsmen, fall under the sway of the defilements?
For these defilements range from the gadfly and the mosquito...
Those sensual pleasures which are common to all foolish people, and even those things that serve as their basis, are of little gratification, much suffering, and much despair;

the danger therein is greater still. Sensual pleasures are like a skeleton, sensual pleasures are like a piece of meat, sensual pleasures are like a grass torch, sensual pleasures are like a pit of glowing embers, sensual pleasures are like a dream, sensual pleasures are like borrowed goods, sensual pleasures are like fruit on a tree.
“Sensual pleasures are like swords and spears; sensual pleasures are like javelins and spikes; sensual pleasures are like the heads of serpents; sensual pleasures are like masses of fire!
Having gone forth in such a teaching of the Buddha, how is it that you have fallen under the sway of these defilements that cause such harm?
Having thus admonished him, and being unable to make him accept their own counsel, they led him to the Teacher’s presence in the Dhamma Hall and asked, “What—”
When it was said, "Monks, bring that monk here even against his will," they replied, "Venerable Sir, this monk is reportedly disenchanted.

The Teacher asked, "Is it true? and when they replied, "It is true, Venerable Sir," he said, "Monks, even when ancient wise men were ruling kingdoms, when defilements arose, they did not fall under their power, but restrained their minds."
Having said, "They did not act improperly," he related a story of the past.
In the past, in the city of Ariṭṭhapura in the kingdom of Sivi, a king named Sivi reigned.
The Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of his chief queen, and they gave him the name Sivikumāra. As for the commander-in-chief...

A son was born, and they gave him the name Abhipāraka. The two of them, having become companions and growing up together, went to Takkasilā at the age of sixteen, where they mastered their arts and returned.
The king gave the kingdom to his own son, and he too, having appointed Abhipāraka to the position of general, ruled the kingdom according to the Dhamma. In that very [reign]...
In the city of Tiriṭivaccha, a daughter was born to a merchant named Tiriṭivaccha, who possessed a fortune of eight hundred million.
She was endowed with supreme beauty, attained the pinnacle of good fortune, and was possessed of auspicious marks;
on the day her name was given, they called her Ummādantī. When she reached the age of sixteen, having surpassed human beauty, she was as lovely as a celestial nymph.
She was beautiful to behold, pleasing, and endowed with the highest excellence of complexion.
Whatever ordinary worldlings saw her were unable to maintain their own composure;
intoxicated by the intoxication of the defilements as if drunk on wine, they became incapable of establishing mindfulness.
Then her father, King Tiriṭivaccha, approached the king and said, "Your Majesty, a woman-treasure has appeared in my house;
she is worthy of the king alone. Send brahmins who are experts in the science of marks to examine her, and then do as you please.
The king replied, "Very well," and dispatched the brahmins. They went to the treasurer’s house and were received with honors and hospitality.
They partook of the milk-rice. At that moment, Ummadantī, adorned with all her ornaments, approached them.
Upon seeing her, they were unable to establish mindfulness; intoxicated by the madness of defilement, they did not even realize the state of their own interrupted meal.
Some, having taken a morsel of food, [did so] with the perception, "We shall eat."
Some placed it on their heads, some threw it between their armpits, and some struck it against the wall;
they all became like madmen. Seeing them, she said, "They say these men are going to examine my marks;
seize them by the neck and drive them out! She had them expelled. Humiliated and enraged at Ummadantī, they went to the royal palace.
“Your Majesty, that woman is ill-omened; she is not suitable for you,” they said. Thinking, “She is indeed ill-omened,” the king did not summon her.
When she heard this report, she said, “I am apparently ill-omened, which is why I was not taken by the king;
yet those who are truly ill-omened do not act in such a manner. Then she added, “Very well; but if I see that king, I shall find out.”
She harbored resentment toward him. Then her father gave her to Abhipāraka, and she became dear and pleasing to him.
But by the result of what karma did she become so beautiful? It was by the result of giving a garment dyed red.
It is said that in the past, having been born into a poor family in Bārāṇasī, on a festival day, she saw virtuous women...
Having seen women playing while dressed in safflower-dyed garments and adorned with ornaments, she desired to play herself wearing such clothes.
After informing her parents, they said, "My child, we are poor; where would we get clothing like this?
She replied, "In that case, please grant me permission to work for wages at a wealthy household. They [agreed]. Her...

Having said, "We shall give [the reward] once we have recognized her virtue," they gave her permission. She approached a certain family and said, "I will work for wages with cloth dyed with safflower.
Then they said to her, "After you have worked for three years, we shall recognize your virtue and give it to you.
She consented, saying, "Very well," and undertook the work. They, having recognized her virtue—
Before even three years had elapsed, they gave her another garment along with a thick cloth dyed with safflower and sent her off, saying, "Go with your companions, bathe, and put this on.
Taking her companions, she went there and, having set aside the dyed cloth on the riverbank, she bathed.

At that moment, a disciple of Kassapa the Great Seer, who had lost his robes, arrived at that place wearing a garment made of woven twigs. Seeing him, she thought, "This venerable one must have lost his robes;
previously, because of my habit of not giving, it became difficult for me even to obtain a lower garment. Having said this, she tore the cloth into two pieces.
Thinking, "I shall give one portion to the noble sir," she climbed up, put on her own lower garment, and said, "Wait, venerable sir.
Having paid homage to the Elder, she tore the red cloth down the middle and gave him one portion.
Standing aside in a concealed spot, she discarded the broken branches and [took] one corner of it for herself.
Having dressed himself and put on one [robe], he went out. Then, by the radiance of his garment, his entire body became a single mass of light like the young sun.
Seeing him, she thought, "My noble lord did not look well at first, but now he shines like the young sun;
I shall give this too to him. Having given the second portion as well, she said, "Venerable sir, I..."
"May I, possessing supreme beauty, wander from birth to birth; may no man, upon seeing me, be unable to remain steadfast in his own nature;
and may there be no other woman more beautiful than I"—thus she made this aspiration.
The Elder, having offered words of thanksgiving, departed.
Wandering through the world of the devas, she was reborn at that time in Ariṭṭhapura and became so exceedingly beautiful.
Then, in that city, they proclaimed the Kattika festival; on the full moon day of Kattika, they adorned the city.
As Abhipāraka was going to his own guard post, he called out to her, "Bhadde, Ummādanti, today..."
"It is the festival of the Kattika full moon; as the king makes his circumambulation of the city, he will first arrive at this house door.
Do not show yourself to him, for if he sees you, he will be unable to maintain his mindfulness," she said.
She replied, "Go, my lord; I shall take care of it," and having agreed, when he had departed, she gave orders to her maidservant.
“Inform me when the King arrives at this gate of my house. Then, when the sun had set and the moon was full,
adorning the city like a celestial city (*devanagara*), with lamps burning in every direction, the King— adorned with all his ornaments,
mounted upon an excellent thoroughbred chariot, and surrounded by a host of ministers— circumambulated the city with great splendor.

He went first of all to the gate of Abhipāraka’s house. That house was surrounded by a wall the color of lapis lazuli, with its gates and watchtowers adorned, having reached the pinnacle of splendor and being most beautiful. At that moment, a maidservant informed Ummadantī.
Taking a basket of flowers and standing by the window with the grace of a *kinnarī*, she offered the flowers to the king.
He threw it. Looking up at it, intoxicated by the madness of defilements and unable to establish mindfulness, he was not even able to recognize that "this is the house of Abhipāraka.
Then, addressing his charioteer and questioning him, he spoke these two verses:
"Whose residence is this, Sunanda, protected by a rampart made of yellow bricks? ... [The rest of the verse follows] ..."
“Who is she seen from afar like a crest of flame, like a radiance upon a mountain peak in the sky?
Whose daughter is this, O Sunanda, whose daughter-in-law, or even whose wife?
Answer me quickly when asked: is she unmarried, or does she have a husband?”
In this context: "Whose is it? Whose indeed is this?"—it means made of yellow cloth (*paṇḍumaya*), that is, made of *rattiṭṭhaka* (a type of fine cotton).
"Is seen" means she is visible standing at the window. "A flame" (*accī*) refers to a mass of fire's web. "Is this perhaps a daughter?
(*dhītā nvayanti*) means "is this perhaps a daughter? "Unveiled" (*avāvaṭā*) means with the covering removed, unenclosed. "A wife" (*bhattā*) means: "If she has a husband, tell me this."
Then, explaining this to him, he spoke these two verses:
“I indeed know this, O lord of men, both by wisdom and by experience;
that man, O protector of the earth, will remain diligent for your sake day and night.”
“Prosperous, flourishing, and well-grown is one of your ministers, O lord of men;
this is his wife, Abhipāraka’s, whose name is Ummādantī, O King.
In that passage, *matyā ca petyā ca* means “from the mother’s side and from the father’s side”; I know this. Furthermore, *athopi assa* means “and also [the name] of her husband.”
She says, "I know. "Prosperous" means fully successful. "Flourishing" means well-adorned with garments and ornaments.
"Well-grown" means thoroughly increased. "By name" means by her title. For she who sees her drives one mad;
she does not allow mindfulness to be established in him, and therefore she is called "The Mad-making One" (Ummadantī).
Having heard this, the king, praising her name, spoke the following verse:
“O, how excellent is this name of hers, made both by mother and by father!
For at that time, while looking upon me, she drove me mad and maddened me.”

In that context, *matyā ca petyā ca* means "by mother and by father. *Mayhaṃ* is the dative case used in the sense of the accusative. *Avalokayantī* means "looking [at me]," the sense being: "While she was looking at me, she herself made me appear like a madman.
Having perceived his state of trembling, she closed the window and went back to the bedchamber.
From the moment the king saw her, he no longer had any intention of circumambulating the city. He addressed his charioteer:
“Friend Sunanda, turn back the chariot; this festival is not suitable for us;

it is suitable only for the general Abhipāra, and even kingship would be suitable only for him. Having had the chariot turned back, he ascended the palace, lay down upon his magnificent couch, and, lamenting, said:
“She who on the full-moon day entered [the grove], with eyes like those of a deer, her skin as beautiful as a white lotus—
seeing her, clad in the ruddy plumage of a dove, I thought there were two full-moons that day.
When she gazes at me, enticing me with her lovely, charming, and beautiful long-lashed eyes;”
“Stretching her limbs, she seems to steal my heart, like a *kimpurisa* woman born in the mountain forest.
For then that large, dark-complexioned woman, wearing earrings set with gems and clad in a single garment, looked about like a doe.”
“When indeed will a beautiful woman with copper-colored nails and fine hair, with soft arms anointed with the essence of sandalwood,
with rounded fingers and well-proportioned, firm thighs, place her head upon my feet?
When indeed will the daughter of Tirīṭi, whose waist is slender and who is draped in a golden net-like garment, [do so]?”
“He will embrace me with his tender arms, as the māluvā creeper clings to a tree born in the great forest.
When indeed will she— whose beautiful skin is red like lac-dye, whose breasts are like drops [of nectar],
and whose delicate skin is like a white lotus— press her face against my face, as one elephant pours wine from a bowl into the mouth of another?”
“When I saw him standing there, all-auspicious and heart-gladdening,
I could not perceive anything at all within my own mind.
Having seen Ummadantī, with her jeweled earrings hanging down, [I was struck by her beauty].”
“I do not sleep by day or night, as if I had been defeated by a thousand foes.
‘If Sakka were to grant me a boon, and that boon could be obtained by me:
for one night or two nights, may I be a ferryman.’”
"Having dallied with Ummādantī, Sivī the king would then [be lost].
In this context, "on the full moon night" means on a night when the moon is full.
"With eyes like those of a doe" means she has gentle eyes, like those of a female deer who, having fled out of fear of an arrow and stood within the forest, gazes back at the hunter.
"She sat down" means that, having scattered flowers with her lotus-colored palms, she sat at the window gazing at me.

"With limbs as fair as white lotuses" means her body was the color of a red lotus. "Two full moons" refers to how, on that festive day, upon seeing her dressed in red garments the color of a pigeon's foot, I gazed upon the splendor of her face.
Because two full moons had risen at the residence of one general, Abhipāraka, from the eastern world-system, I thought there were two full-moon nights.
“With wide-eyelashed” means with large lashes. “Beautiful” means pure. “Charming” means sweet in appearance.
“Beholding” refers to the moment he looks with such eyes. “Like a mountain”—

"Just as a *kimpurisa* woman, having taken up a lute in the flowering forest on the Himālaya mountains, captivates the mind of a *kimpurisa* by blending her own voice with the resonance of the strings—'In this way she truly captivates my mind,' he raves.
'Brahatī' means noble. 'Sāmā' means golden-colored. 'Ekaccavasanā' means wearing a single garment; that is, dressed in a single cloth."

The meaning is as follows: "She gazes at me, O Lord," refers to that supreme woman—possessing soft hair, a broad forehead, long eyebrows, large eyes, a prominent nose, red lips, white teeth, and sharp fangs;
with a well-rounded neck, slender arms, well-proportioned breasts, a waist like a water-jar, broad hips, and thighs like golden plantain trees—who at that moment was gazing at me out of fear.
"Having entered the forest and then turning back, she gazes at me like a bewildered doe," he says.
"With tender arms" means with soft arms. "With a well-rounded, wise gait" means with a very smooth and skillful manner of movement.
"When will that beautiful woman approach me?"—when indeed will she, with those copper-colored nails and with her well-rounded, wise manner, [begin from the head]?
"Paritosessati" means she laments while making a longing wish.
"Kañcanajāluracchadā" means adorned with golden net-like ornaments. "Vilaggamajjhā" means having a slender body and a thin waist.

"Brahāvane" means in the great forest. "Lākhārasarattasucchavī" refers to [the parts] such as the palms of the hands, the soles of the feet, the tips of the nails, the lips, and the flesh, which are beautifully colored like lac-dye.
"Red like lac juice, rubies, coral, and lotus filaments. "With breasts shaped like water-bubbles" means with breasts rounded like water-bubbles.
"From then on" means from the time I saw her standing there. "Of my own mind" means the intention is that I have become a masterless man regarding my own mind.
"Any person" means I do not know anyone by name, such as "this one is so-and-so"; I have become like a madman.
"He speaks. "He has seen" means having seen. "I do not sleep" means I obtain no rest either by night or by day.
"And may that be obtained" means: if that boon which Sakka might grant me were to be obtained, I would obtain that boon;
such is the meaning. Then those ministers informed Abhipāraka as well: "Sire, King [So-and-so], while performing the circumambulation of the city..."
“Having reached the door of your house, he turned back and ascended the palace.
Having gone to his own home, he addressed Ummadantī and asked, “My dear lady, did you show yourself to the king?
“Master, there was a man with a large belly and large teeth who arrived standing in a chariot; I do not know whether he was the king or not the king.”
"But when it was said that there is but one Lord, he stood at the window and threw flowers; he turned back and departed right then and there.

Having heard this, [the minister] thought, "I have been ruined by you," and on the following day at dawn, having ascended the royal palace and standing at the door of the inner chamber, he heard the King’s incoherent lamentations based on Ummādantī, and [realized], "This man’s heart is bound to Ummādantī."
“Having been born, he will die if he does not obtain it; therefore, having cleared away the fault of both the king and myself, it is right that I give my life to him.

Having gone to his own residence, he summoned a trusted attendant and said, “Dear son, there is a hollow tree containing a shrine at such-and-such a place; you must go there at sunset, without letting anyone know.”
Having gone there, sit within the tree; while I reach that place performing the ritual offering and paying homage to the deity, I shall say:
"O Lord, King of Devas, our king, while the festival was underway in the city, did not play but entered his inner chamber and lies there lamenting; we do not know the reason for this, O King."
‘The deities are greatly favored; every year he offers a thousand [pieces of gold] as a ritual oblation.
Tell them, “It is because of this that the king is delirious,” and I will beg them, “Grant us the gift of the king’s life.
At that moment, you must change the sound [of your voice] and say, “General, your king has no such thing as illness.”’”
"However, his heart is bound to your wife Ummadantī. If he obtains her, he will live;
if not, he will die. If you wish him to live, give Ummadantī to him.
Having thus instructed her, she sent her away.
Having gone there and sat upon that tree, on the following day, when the general—surrounded by a host of ministers—arrived at that place and made his request, he (the deity) spoke accordingly.

The general said, "Very well," paid homage to the deity, informed the ministers, entered the city, ascended to the royal palace, and knocked at the door of the inner chamber. The king [regained] mindfulness...
Having stationed him there, he asked, "Who is this? "I am Abhipāra, Your Majesty," he replied. Then the king opened the gate for him.
Having entered and paid homage to the king, he spoke this verse:
"O Lord of Beings, as I was paying homage to the beings, a *yakkha* approached me and said this:"
“The king’s mind is fixed on Ummadantī; I give her to you, so enjoy her.

In this context, “to him who pays homage” means to one who performs an offering and pays homage for the purpose of learning the cause of your lamentation. “Her” means: “I give that Ummadantī to you as your attendant.
Then the king [said], “Friend Abhipāraka, because my mind is bound to Ummadantī, she has been lamenting...”

“Do even the *yakkhas* know? he asked. “Yes, Your Majesty,” they replied. Thinking, “It seems my low character has become known to the whole world,” he established himself in a sense of shame and spoke the following verse:
“I have destroyed my merit and am not immortal; may the people know both this evil of mine and this [deed].”
"And there will be a crushing frustration for my mind, having failed to grasp her who was so dear and intoxicating.
Therein, "I shall be ruined," [he means]: "O good Abhipāraka, while sporting with her through the power of defilement (*kilesa*), I would be ruined from my merit;
yet by merely sporting with her, I do not become immortal, and the great multitude will [speak ill] of me."
If he were to recognize his lowly status, he would then reproach him, saying, "The King has done what is improper";
and because you gave that to me and later did not give your beloved wife, there would be distress for your mind—this is the meaning.
The remaining verses are both statements and counter-statements between the two.
“O Lord of Men, none other than you or me could know all that has been done by karma.
Since I have given this *ummadantī* to you, O King, eat it along with the forest trees and shrubs.
That man who performs evil deeds thinks, ‘Let others think thus of me here.’”
“Beholding beings acting thus, those men on earth who are disciplined [ask]:
‘Is there indeed any other man on earth whom you do not love in this world?
For that person, there will be intense distress when they give away their beloved, even though she was once unchaste.’”
“Truly, O Lord of Men, she is dear to me; she is not unloved by me, O Ruler of the Earth.
Go then, O Venerable One, to her who is frantic with passion, as a lion enters the cave of a mountain.
“The wise, even when oppressed by their own suffering, do not abandon karma that bears the fruit of happiness.”
“Deluded and intoxicated by pleasure, they do not even commit evil deeds.
‘For you are my mother and my father, my husband, my lord, my sustainer, and my deity;
I, along with my children and wife, am your slave. O Master, do as you wish according to your pleasure.’”
“He who commits evil thinking, ‘I am lord,’ and having done it, treats others with contempt—he does not live a long life because of that; even the gods look upon him with aversion for his evil.
“But those established in Dhamma who accept a gift given by their owners as a stranger’s offering—”
Both the recipients and the givers there perform deeds that result only in happiness.
“Was there perhaps some other man on earth, anyone in the world, who could believe that I do not love her?
And yet, my mind was deeply distressed when I gave away my beloved Ummadantī, though she had not bitten me.”
“Truly, O Lord of Men, she is dear to me; she is not unloved by me, O Protector of the Earth.
Since I gave Ummadantī to you, O King, eat of the forest fruits and enjoy yourself.
“He who, through his own suffering, [removes] the suffering of another, or through his own happiness, brings happiness to another...”
“As it is with me, so it is with others; he who knows this understands the Dhamma.
“Is there perhaps some other man on earth who could believe my words: ‘No one in the world is dear to me’?
For there would be a profound distress in his mind, having failed to give away that beloved, intoxicating woman.”
“O Lord of Men, you know that she is dear to me; she has never been unloved by me, O Protector of the Earth.
O Lord of Men, I give what is dear to you because it is dear to me; for those who give what is dear, O King, obtain what is dear.
Surely I shall now slay myself for the sake of sensual desire.”
"For I cannot bring myself to slay righteousness with unrighteousness.
But if you do not desire my life, O Lord of Men, O best of heroes among men, I shall release her for all people to see; once she is released by me, you may then summon her."
“If you, Katta, should abandon this innocent man who seeks refuge, it would lead to his own harm;
there would be great public censure for you, and he would have no allies within the city.
I myself shall endure this censure—every blame, praise, and reproach.”
“O protector of the earth, let him come here; do as you wish with him, Sivi, according to your pleasure.
“He who takes up neither blame nor praise, neither censure nor honor—glory and fortune depart from him, just as water flows away from dry land after a heavy rain.”
“Whatever suffering and pleasure there may be from this, whatever transgression of the Dhamma and mental distress,
I shall endure it all with my own breast, as the earth endures all that is stationary and mobile.
Whatever transgression of the Dhamma and mental distress, and whatever suffering I cause to others, I desire for myself.”
“I shall cast off this burden, one by one, remaining established in the Dhamma and not neglecting anything.
O Lord of Men, do not create an obstacle for me regarding this meritorious deed that leads to heaven.
With a mind full of faith, I give you Ummadantī, just as a king gives wealth to brahmins at a sacrifice.”
“Surely you, Kaccāna, are well-disposed toward me, for you and I are friends who have grown together.
All the gods and all the ancestors would censure one who perceives evil in the future life.
Indeed, O King of the Śivis, neither the townspeople nor all the people of the countryside would speak thus if this were not the Dhamma.”
“Since Ummadantī was given to you by me, O King, enjoy her in the forest grove along with your consorts.
“Surely, Katta, you have acted for my benefit; both I and Ummadantī are your friends.
And the well-proclaimed principles of the virtuous are as impossible to transgress as the shore of the ocean.”
“You are worthy of offerings, compassionate for our welfare, the sustainer and provider, and the protector of desires.
O King, what was offered to you will indeed bear great fruit; please accept me, who am maddened by passion.
Surely you are one who brings all things to fulfillment; you have practiced the Dhamma, O son of Katta.”
“Is there anyone else here in this world of living beings who, at the break of dawn, can ensure your safety, you two-legged man?
“You yourself are the best; you are unsurpassed. You are the guardian of Dhamma, the knower of Dhamma, the wise one.
As a guardian of Dhamma, may you live for a long time; teach me the Dhamma, O protector of Dhamma.”
“Therefore, Abhipāraka, listen to my words;
I shall teach you the Dhamma that has been cultivated by the virtuous.
Excellent is the king who delights in the Dhamma; excellent is the man possessed of wisdom.”
“Excellent is non-malice toward friends; the non-doing of evil is happiness.
In the victory of one who is free from anger, a king established in the Dhamma, people dwell happily, like in the cool shade of a grove.”
“I do not approve of this action performed without due consideration; it is unwholesome.
Listen to these similes of mine concerning those who act on their own knowledge:
‘If, among cattle rushing forward, the lead bull goes astray, [the whole herd follows].’”
They all go crookedly when the leader has gone crookedly.
In the same way, among human beings, if he who is considered the best practices unrighteousness,
how much more so will the rest of the people?
The entire kingdom suffers when the king acts unrighteously.
If the lead bull goes straight while the cattle are crossing,
all the cows go straight, because the leader has gone straight.
“In the same way, among humans, whoever is regarded as the best—
if he practices the Dhamma, let alone the rest of the people—
the entire kingdom dwells in happiness if the king is righteous.”
“Nor do I desire immortality through unrighteousness,
nor do I seek to conquer this entire earth.
For whatever treasure exists here among human beings— ”
“Cows, slaves, gold, clothing, and yellow sandalwood;
horses, women, jewels, and gems— even that which the sun and moon protect for me—
for the sake of these I would not walk in unrighteousness, for I was born as a bull in the midst of the Sivis.”
“Raṭṭhapāla has risen up as a leader for our welfare, honoring the Dhamma of the Sivis.
As he reflects only upon that Dhamma, he cannot be brought under the power of his own mind.
Surely, O Great King, you shall always enjoy constant prosperity and peace.”
“You shall rule for a long time, for such is your wisdom.
We rejoice in this, that you do not neglect the Dhamma;
for a kshatriya lord who neglects the Dhamma falls from his kingdom.”
“Practice the Dhamma, O Great King, toward your mother and father, O Kshatriya;
having practiced the Dhamma here, O King, you will go to heaven.
Practice the Dhamma, O Great King, toward your sons and wives, O Kshatriya.”
"Having practiced the Dhamma here, O King, you will go to heaven.
Practice the Dhamma, Great King, toward friends and companions, O Khattiya;
having practiced the Dhamma here, O King, you will go to heaven."
“Practice Dhamma, O Great King, among your mounts and your forces;
having practiced Dhamma here, O King, you will go to heaven.
Practice Dhamma, O Great King, among the villages and the market towns.”
"Having practiced the Dhamma here, O King, you will go to heaven.
Practice the Dhamma, Great King, throughout the kingdoms and the provinces;
having practiced the Dhamma here, O King, you will go to heaven."
“Practice the Dhamma, O Great King, toward recluses and brahmins;
having practiced the Dhamma here, O King, you will go to heaven.
Practice the Dhamma, O Great King, toward beasts and birds, O Kṣatriya.”
"Having practiced the Dhamma here, O King, you will go to heaven.
'Practice the Dhamma, Great King; the Dhamma practiced brings happiness.
Having practiced the Dhamma here, O King, you will go to heaven.'"
“Practice the Dhamma, O Great King; together with Indra and the gods, including Brahmā, they have attained heaven through well-practiced conduct. Do not be negligent in the Dhamma, O King.
Therein, “all of them,” O Lord of Men, means: “I alone shall conceal this and bring it back”; therefore, setting aside—
Neither you nor I, nor any other person, shall know—even in its mere outward form—this which has been done; they will not know it.
"Bhusehi" means: while enjoying yourself with her, make your own craving abundant, increase it, and fulfill your desire. "Sajāhi" means:
but having fulfilled your desire, if she does not please you, then leave her and [take her] for me alone.

Confess it. "O worthy Abhipāraka, regarding those who perform evil deeds, that person thinks and intends, 'May others here not think of me as having done this evil deed; may they not know of it. This is a wicked thought on his part. Why is that?
Because the beings—namely the Buddhas, the Paccekabuddhas, and the sons of the Buddhas—see him while he is performing it."
“Endowed with psychic power, they indeed see her. ‘She is not dear to me,’ my friend Abhipāraka—could anyone else in this world believe that even for the entire earth, Ummadantī is not dear to you?
Like a lion to his mountain cave, O Great King—if you do not bring her here, then just as a lion [is drawn] from the fever of defilements...”
"When a lioness cub has appeared, it goes to the jeweled cave where she dwells; in the same way, go to her dwelling place and there fulfill your own aspiration.

"The fruit of happiness, my dear Abhipāraka, is that when the wise are touched by their own suffering, they do not abandon the karma that yields a happy result, nor do they do so even while being deluded."
"Deluded by ignorance and intoxicated by pleasure, they do not refrain from committing evil deeds. 'Do as you please, my lord,' [she said].
'O Lord Sivirāja, there is no blame for one who enjoys his own female slave;
do as you wish, according to your pleasure and inclination, and fulfill your own desire. 'He does not live by that, my dear Abhipāraka.'"

He who commits evil thinking, “I am the lord,” and having committed it, does not fear or feel moral dread, wondering, “What will gods and humans say of me?”—by that karma he does not live for a long time; he dies quickly.
Even the deities think, “Of what use is sovereignty to this wicked king? Better for him to die with a jar of sand tied around his neck.”
They look with ordinary eyes.
"To another," Great King, means that those who abide in their own Dhamma accept a gift belonging to others, given by those owners;
for them, both the recipients and the givers, all such action results only in a happy fruit.
They perform it. For when the recipient accepts, that gift yields a great result for the donor.
"He who, O Abhipāraka, through his own suffering"—that is, he who, oppressed by his own pain, gives it to another;
having removed it from his own body, he casts it onto the body of another; or [he who seeks] his own happiness through the happiness of another.
He burns; taking the happiness of another, he casts it into himself.
Thinking, "I shall remove my own suffering," he causes another to suffer; thinking, "I shall make myself happy," he causes another to suffer;
thinking, "I shall make myself happy," he destroys the happiness of another—he does not know the Dhamma. But he who knows thus: "Just as this is for me..."
“Happiness and suffering [are experienced] by oneself, and likewise by others”—he who knows this knows the Dhamma;
such is the meaning of this verse. “I give to you out of love”: the meaning is that, desiring a beloved fruit, I give because love is the cause.
“They obtain what is dear”: as they wander through saṃsāra, they obtain only what is dear. “Caused by sensual desire,” O Abhipāraka, my friend.
Having done what is improper, rooted in sensual desire, the thought arises in me:
"I shall kill myself. "My property" means belonging to me. There is also the reading "my possession" (*mayhaṃ sati*); the meaning is:
"If you do not desire that [property], thinking 'it belongs to me'. "Of all people" means: having assembled all the guilds, for all those people.
Thinking, "This is harmful to me," I shall abandon it. Then he summoned him; that is, because he was no longer protected, you would have brought him back.
"Adūsiyaṃ" means innocent. "Kattā"—he addresses him by another name. For he performs what is beneficial for the king, and therefore he is called "Kattā.
And yet, even though he acts thus, no one in the city would say of him, "He is a doer of what ought not to be done."
There would not even be a faction [of partisans]. They do not merely criticize me with mere verbal abuse;
even if someone were to criticize or praise me face-to-face, or if they were to revile me by attributing faults to me—I would regard all that, whether it be criticism, praise, or revilement, as such.

"I shall endure all this; let it come upon me," he says. "From him"—from that man who does not accept these things such as censure and the like—"glory," which is to say sovereignty, and "fortune," which is to say wisdom, depart from their place and do not remain, just as water in the form of heavy rain flows away from dry land.
"From this"—that is, from me, because of my relinquishing of her. And "the transgression of the Dhamma."
Whatever unwholesome state has arisen by transgressing the Dhamma—whatever it may be—I shall accept it, I shall take it upon myself, and I shall bear it.

"Of the stable and the trembling" means: just as the great earth accepts and endures everything from both those whose taints are exhausted (the *khīṇāsava*) and ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*), even so shall I accept and endure all of this.
He illuminates this: "I am alone, possessed of wisdom; alone I shall carry, bear, and transport this burden of my own suffering.
"Established in the Dhamma" means being established in the Dhamma of legal adjudication, the Dhamma of traditional lineage, and the Dhamma of the three kinds of good conduct.
"Leading to heaven": O King, this meritorious deed indeed leads to heaven. "Wealth for sacrifice" means the sacrificial wealth (*yaññadhana*).
Or rather, this is the reading: "Sakhā" means that Ummadantī was my companion, and you were also my companion. "Pitaro" refers to the Brahmas.
"All" means not only the gods and Brahmas, but all the inhabitants of the kingdom as well;
they would reproach me, saying, "Look, the wife of a companion has been made a companion by him in this household. "Na hetadhammaṃ" means indeed, this is not unrighteous.
"Yaṃ te mayā" means: since she was given to you by me, therefore they will not say, "This is unrighteousness.

"Sataṃ" refers to the lineage of the Buddhas and others; for the qualities consisting of patience, the cultivation of loving-kindness, virtue, and conduct are well-praised and as difficult to overstep as the shore of the ocean.
Therefore, he says: "Just as the ocean does not transgress its shore, so shall I also not transgress the shore of my virtue."
"‘Āhuneyyo me asi,’ O Great King, means: you are worthy of my offerings and hospitality. ‘Dhātā vidhātā asi kāmapālo’ means:
you, O Lord, are my *dhātā* because of your supporting [me]; you are my *vidhātā* because of your bestowing sovereignty and happiness;
you are my *kāmapāla* because of your protecting the desires that are wished for and prayed for. ‘Tayī hutā’ means: she has been given to you. ‘Kāmena me’ means..."
"Out of desire for me, out of my aspiration, he accepts Ummadantī"—thus does the Abhipāraka give her to the king.

The king refuses, saying, "I have no need of her. Just as those throwing a bird-cage that has fallen on the ground away into the wilderness by striking it with the back of their foot, both of them likewise abandon her. Now, the king, threatening her so that she would not speak again:
He spoke the verse beginning with “Addhā hi. In this context, “Kattuputta” means his father was Katta; thus he addresses him in that way. This is what is meant:
“Surely, previously you practiced every duty toward me and acted only for my welfare and prosperity.
But now, having become an adversary, you speak much. Do not prattle on like this; is it not another [who speaks] to you?”
"A man is a two-footed creature; who in this world of the living would seek his own welfare before sunrise?
For if another king, like me, had been set on your wife with desire, he would have had your head cut off before sunrise and taken her to his own home.
But I do not do so out of fear of unwholesome karma alone; therefore, be silent, for I have no need of her."
"Enough! he rebuked him.
Having heard this, unable to say anything further, he spoke the verse beginning with "Thou indeed," as a praise of the king.
Its meaning is: O Great King, you alone are the best among all lords of men throughout the entire Jambudīpa; you are unsurpassed.

"You are a guardian of the Dhamma by protecting the Dhamma of legal adjudication, the Dhamma of traditional lineage, and the Dhamma of good conduct; you are a knower of the Dhamma through your understanding of them, and you are one of noble intelligence.
Protected by that very Dhamma which you guard, live long, O protector of the Dhamma, guardian of the Dhamma, best of kings! And teach me the Dhamma."
Then the King, teaching the Dhamma, spoke the verse beginning with “Tadiṅghā. In this context, *iṅghā* is a particle used for exhortation;
the meaning is: “Since you exhort me, therefore [I shall speak]. *Sataṃ* means practiced by true persons such as the Buddhas and others. *Sādhu* means beautiful and praised.
One who delights (*roceti*) in the Dhamma of the tradition of legal judgment and good conduct is called *dhammaruci*. For one such as that [delights] in life...
Even in his lowest state, he does not do what should not be done; therefore, it is good. "Possessed of wisdom" means endowed with knowledge.
"Not treacherous toward friends" refers to the state of being non-hostile toward a friend. "Of one established in the Dhamma" means of one who is firmly grounded in the fourfold Dhamma.
"May they sit" (*āseyuṃ*) means may they sit down (*nisīdeyyuṃ*). This is merely a conventional expression for teaching; however, the meaning here is that they may find comfort in all four postures.
The meaning is as follows. "In cool shade" means in the cool shade provided by children, wives, kinsmen, and friends.
"In his own home" (*saṅghare*) means in his own house; this shows that they might dwell happily, unoppressed by unrighteousness, forced labor, punishment, and so forth.
"And not this, friend Abhipāraka"—this refers to that unwholesome deed which was done without due consideration; this I...
"I do not approve. The intention is: "I do approve the action of those kings who, having understood, weighed, and investigated, act for themselves.
"These are similes" means: "In this matter, listen to these two similes from me. "Crooked" (*jimha*) means bent or curved.
"The leader" (*netta*) refers to that bull, the eldest, who leads the cows. "Even before" (*pageva*) [refers to] that unrighteousness.
"Others walk," meaning that while others merely walk, he walks even further; the sense is that he acts exceedingly well.

"Righteous" (*dhammika*) means ruling the kingdom according to the Dhamma, having abandoned the four ways of wrong conduct. "Immortality" (*amaratta*) means the state of a deva. "Jewels" (*ratana*) refers to both animate and inanimate jewels.
"Clothing" (*vatthiya*) refers specifically to Kāsī cloth. "Horses and women" refers to horses possessing the speed of the wind and women endowed with supreme beauty.
"Jewels and gems" refers to the seven kinds of jewels and precious articles. "Guarding" means they protect while providing light.
"Not for that" means one should not act improperly even for the sake of that universal monarch’s sovereignty.
"I am a bull" means that because I was born as the eldest king among the Sivi people, therefore—even for the sake of universal monarch sovereignty—[I would not act improperly].
The meaning is: "I do not act unfairly. He is a leader because he leads the great multitude of people by establishing them in wholesome states;
he is beneficial (*hitā*) because he acts for their welfare. He is exalted (*uggata*) because he is renowned throughout the whole of Jambudīpa as "King Sivi, it is said, is a practitioner of Dhamma.
He is the Guardian of the Realm (*Raṭṭhapāla*) because he protects the kingdom with impartiality. "Honoring" refers to the traditional law (*paveṇidhamma*) of the ancient kings of the Sivis.
“Not honoring [him]. He, that very person—namely, I—reflecting upon that very Dhamma, for that reason, do not act according to the power of my own mind.
Having thus heard the Great Being’s discourse on the Dhamma, Abhipāraka spoke the words beginning with “Assuredly” as a praise.
"Do not be negligent" means: do not neglect the Dhamma you yourself have proclaimed;
remain steadfast right there. "Neglecting the Dhamma" means: having forgotten the Dhamma, proceeding by way of a wrong course.

Having thus offered him praise, and enjoining him to practice the Dhamma with the words "Practice the Dhamma," he spoke ten further verses of advice. Their meaning has already been explained below in the *Tesakuṇa Jātaka*.
When the commander Abhipāraka had thus taught the Dhamma to the king, the king dispelled his mind’s attachment to Ummadantī.
Having delivered this Dhamma instruction, the Teacher revealed the Truths and identified the Jātaka;
at the conclusion of the Truths, that bhikkhu was established in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, the charioteer Sunanda was Ānanda, and Abhipāraka...
Sāriputta was Ummādantī, Uppalavaṇṇā was the rest of the assembly, the Buddha’s retinue, and King Sivi was I myself.
This concludes the second commentary, the Story of Ummādantī.
[528] 3. The Commentary on the Mahābodhi Jātaka.
“What indeed is the staff? What is the antelope skin?”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove concerning the perfection of wisdom.
The story will be revealed in the Mahā-Ummagga Jātaka. At that time, however, the Teacher said, “Monks, it is not only now;
in the past as well, the Tathāgata was wise and a crusher of the doctrines of others,” and he related a story of the past.

In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of eminent brahmin mahāsālas with a wealth of eight hundred million in the kingdom of Kāsi; they gave him the name Bodhikumāra.
When he reached maturity, having mastered his crafts at Takkasilā, he returned home and lived in the midst of household life, but later on, he abandoned sensual pleasures.
Having entered the region of the Himalayas and gone forth into the wandering life of a paribbājaka, he dwelt there for a long time subsisting on forest roots and fruits;
then, descending from the Himalayas during the rainy season, while wandering on his alms-round,
he eventually reached Bārāṇasī, stayed in the royal park, and on the following day went about the city for alms in the manner befitting a paribbājaka.
He arrived at the royal gate. Seeing him from his position in the lion-window, the king was inspired with confidence by his tranquility;
he had him enter his palace, seated him upon the royal throne, and after exchanging greetings and hearing a brief discourse on the Dhamma, he had various foods of exquisite flavor served to him.
Having taken the meal, the Great Being reflected: "This royal household..."
“Indeed, [this] name brings many dangers and many enemies; who now will deliver me from this arisen fear?
Seeing a favorite of the king’s—a brindled dog—standing not far away, he took a large morsel of food and made a gesture indicating his desire to give it to him.
The king, understanding this, had a bowl brought for the dog.
Having had food brought, he caused it to be given to him. The Great Being, having given it to him, finished his meal.
The king, having obtained his promise, had a leaf-hut constructed for him in the royal park within the city, provided him with the requisites of one gone forth, and settled him there;
he also went to attend upon him two or three times every day. At the time of eating—
But the Great Being sat constantly upon the royal couch itself and ate only the king’s food.
Thus twelve years passed by.
Now that king had five ministers who instructed him in both worldly affairs and the Dhamma; among them, one was a proponent of the doctrine of non-causality (ahetukavāda).

One was a proponent of creation by a Supreme Lord (Issarakatavādin), one a proponent of past-action determinism (Pubbekatavādin), one a proponent of annihilationism (Ucchedavādin), and one a proponent of the science of marks (Khattavijjavādin).
Among them, the proponent of causelessness (Ahetukavādin) taught the great multitude, saying, "These beings are purified through the cycle of existence (saṃsāra).

The proponent of creation by a Supreme Lord taught the great multitude, saying, "This world was created by a Supreme Lord. The proponent of past-action determinism [taught], "The happiness of these beings..."
Or that suffering, when it arises, arises solely because of what was done in the past”—thus he caused the great multitude to learn. The annihilationist caused the great multitude to learn:
“There is no such thing as going from this world to the next world; this world is annihilated. The proponent of the Kṣatriya-caste doctrine caused the great multitude to learn:
“Even after killing one’s mother and father, one’s own welfare must be secured. These [views] were [discussed] in the king’s court of justice.
Appointed as bribe-takers, they turned those who were not owners into owners, and those who were owners into non-owners.
Then one day, a certain man, defeated at dice, saw the Great Being entering the royal palace while wandering for alms;
having paid homage to him, he said, "Venerable sir, while you are eating in the royal palace, you [influence] the judges."

“Having seized the world and destroying it, why do you look on with indifference? Now, having accepted a bribe from the fraudulent gambler through five ministers, the rightful owner has been rendered ownerless! Thus he lamented.
Out of compassion for him, the king went to the court of justice and, having adjudicated according to the Dhamma, restored the rightful owner to his rightful status. All the people at once—
He gave a cry of "Well done! with a great sound. Hearing that sound, the king asked, "What kind of sound is this?
Upon hearing the matter, he sat down beside the Great Being who had finished his meal and asked: "Venerable sir, it is said that today your case has been decided.
"Yes, Great King," he replied. "Venerable sir, while you were deciding it, for the great multitude..."
“There will be an increase [in revenue]; from now on, you yourselves must decide these cases. “Great King, we are indeed called renunciants; this is not our business.
“Venerable sirs, it is fitting to act out of compassion for the great multitude.
Do not decide cases all day long; rather, while coming here from the pleasure grove, [decide them] at the place of judgment.”
“Having gone early in the morning, settle four legal disputes; having eaten, go to the park with four others.
In this way, there will be prosperity for the great multitude. Being entreated by him again and again, he consented, saying, “Very well,” and from then on he acted accordingly.
The fraudulent judges found no opportunity [to act]. Those ministers, having failed to receive bribes and fallen into poverty, thought:
"Ever since the time the wandering ascetic Bodhi began making decisions, we have received nothing at all.
Come now, let us say that he is an enemy of the king, create a rift between him and the monarch, and have him killed. They approached the king and said:
“Great King, this wanderer seeking enlightenment is not one who desires your welfare. When the king, not believing him, replied, “This man is virtuous and endowed with wisdom;

he would not do such a thing,” [the other said], “Great King, it is not possible for him to place all the inhabitants of the entire city in his own hands and leave only us five people behind, if our word—”
"Do not believe him; look at his retinue when he arrives here," they said. The king replied, "Very well.
Standing at the lion-window, as he watched him approaching and saw his retinue, the king—due to his own ignorance—mistook the litigants for his attendants.
He broke into a sweat, summoned those ministers, and asked, "What shall we do?"
“Have him seized, O King. “But how can we seize him when we see no grave offense?
“In that case, Great King, deprive him of his customary allowances; seeing himself deprived of those, the wise wanderer will flee of his own accord without telling anyone.”
The king said, “Very well,” and gradually caused him to lose his allowance.
On the first day, they had him sit on an empty seat. Seeing the empty seat, he realized the king’s intention;
though he went to the park himself that very day, desiring to depart immediately, he thought, “I must know for certain.”

"I shall depart," he thought, yet he did not depart. Then, on the following day, as the king sat upon his empty couch, they brought him his regular meal along with other food and gave it to him as a mixed meal.
On the third day, they did not allow him to enter the great hall, but set him down right at the foot of the staircase and gave him a mixed meal.
Taking that as well, he went to the park and performed his meal duties there.
On the fourth day, they placed him on the lower terrace and gave him a meal of broken rice and sour gruel.

Having taken that as well, he went to the pleasure garden and performed his meal duties. The king asked his ministers: "Even though his honors have been diminished, the Bodhi wanderer does not depart;
what shall we do about him? "Your Majesty, he does not wander for the sake of food, but for the sake of a parasol."
"But he wanders about. If he were to wander for the sake of food, he would have fled on the very first day. "What shall we do now?

"Tomorrow, Your Majesty, have him executed. Saying "Very well," he placed the swords in their hands and said, "Tomorrow, standing at the inner gate, cut off his head as soon as he enters, and [cut him] into pieces."
“Having done this, without letting anyone know, place it in the privy, bathe, and then return,” he said.
They agreed, saying, “Very well,” and after consulting among themselves, “We shall come tomorrow and do so,” they went to their respective homes.
The king, having eaten his evening meal, lay down upon his royal couch and recollected the virtues of the Great Being. Then, to him—
At that very moment, grief arose within him; sweat broke out from his body, and finding no comfort on the bed, he tossed and turned restlessly.
Then his chief queen approached him, but he did not engage in even the slightest conversation with her.
Thereupon she asked him, "Why is it, Great King, that you do not engage in even the slightest conversation? Is it because someone has done something to me?"
“Is there an offense? he asked. “There is none, O Queen,” [the minister] replied. “Nevertheless, it is said that the wandering ascetic Bodhi has become our enemy;
therefore, I have ordered five ministers to kill him tomorrow. They, however, will kill him, cut him into pieces, and throw him into a cesspool.
For twelve years, he has taught us much of the Dhamma.”
“I have never before seen even a single offense of his with my own eyes; yet, acting out of trust in another, I ordered his execution.

For that reason, I am grieving. Then she said to him, “If he has become your enemy, O King, why do you grieve while having him killed? One must ensure one’s own safety, even by killing a son who has become an enemy.”
“It must be done; do not grieve,” he comforted her. Finding solace by her words, he fell asleep.
At that moment, a noble brindled dog, having heard this conversation, thought, “Tomorrow it is fitting for me to give him his life through my own strength.
On the following day at dawn, he descended from the palace and went to the great gate.
Placing his head upon the threshold, he lay down watching the path by which the Great Being would arrive.
Those ministers also, having arrived at dawn with swords in hand, stood at the entrance. The Bodhisatta, having observed the time, departed from the park and came to the palace gate.
Then, seeing him, the dog opened its mouth, revealing its four fangs.
Having shown [himself], he cried out with a great voice: "Venerable sir, do you not receive alms elsewhere on the surface of Jambudīpa?
Our king has stationed five ministers with swords in their hands at the gateway for the purpose of killing you.
Do not come having Death grasped by the forehead; depart quickly! Because of his knowledge of all sounds, he understood that matter.
Having realized this, he turned back from there, went to the park, and took up his requisites for the purpose of departing.

The king, standing at the lion-window, saw him coming and going and thought, "If this man were my enemy, he would go to the park, assemble an army, and be ready for action. If not, he will take his own requisites..."
Thinking, "He will be ready to depart; I shall first learn his intention," he went to the park,
took his own requisites, and seeing the Great Being at the end of the walking path as he was leaving the leaf-hut with the thought, "I shall go," he paid homage and,
standing to one side, spoke the first verse:
“Why do you carry a staff, why a deerskin? Why an umbrella, why sandals?
Why a goad, why an alms-bowl, and also a monastic robe, O brahmin?
You appear to be hurrying—what region do you hope to reach?”
The meaning of this is: "Venerable sir, formerly when you came to our house you did not take up your staff and so forth;
but today for what reason do you take up all these requisites—your staff, deerskin, sunshade, sandals, clay bag, water-strainer, goad, clay bowl, and outer robe—with such great haste? Which one..."
When she asked, “Now you seek a direction; where do you wish to go?
the Great Being, hearing this, thought, “She does not realize what she herself has done; I shall make her know it,” and he spoke these two verses:
“Twelve years have been spent by me in your presence;”
“I do not recall ever hearing a cry from Soṇa Piṅgala.
This one is surely shouting out of pride, baring his white teeth,
having heard you and your wife, who have lost faith in me as your husband.”
In this context, "abhikūjita" means that I do not know how your dog has barked with such a great outcry.
"Ditto va" means as if arrogant. Regarding "sabharissa":
having heard you speaking of how you have commanded five ministers for the purpose of killing me, [the dog thought], "Do you not obtain alms elsewhere?"
"The king has ordered your execution; do not come here," he cried out while still intoxicated.
"Having heard my words, you who have lost faith in me"—thus he said, meaning that having heard his speech, [the elephant] roared because he had lost faith in her.
Then the king, acknowledging his own fault and seeking her forgiveness, spoke the fourth verse:
“O Brahmin, this fault has been committed as you have spoken;
I am even more pleased with this. Dwell here, O Brahmin; do not go elsewhere.
In this context, “even more” means: “It is true that I have commanded thus, and this is my fault; however, I am now even more confident in you. Dwell right here; do not go anywhere else.”

Having heard this, the Great Being said, “Great King, the wise do not dwell with one such as you, who relies on the word of others and does not act from direct experience. Then, exposing his misconduct, he spoke:
“Formerly he was all-white; even after that, he became spotted;
now he is entirely red. It is time for me to depart.”
“It was within the city, then in the middle, then outside;
before it is swept away, I shall depart by myself.
One should not associate with those devoid of faith, who are like a forest fire that consumes its fuel.”
Even if one were to dig it up moment by moment, [it would still be] water smelling of mud.
One should serve only those who have faith and avoid those who lack faith;
one should attend upon those with faith, just as one seeking water attends upon a lake.
“I honor the person who honors others; I would not associate with one who does not honor them.
That is the way of an inferior person: he who does not associate with one who honors him.
He who does not associate with one who honors him, nor serve one who serves him...”
He is indeed the most wretched of men, like a deer perched upon a branch.
"Through excessive and constant association, through lack of meeting together,
and by asking at the wrong time— by these means friendships decay."
“Therefore, one should not go too often, nor should one go after a very long interval;
one should make a request at the proper time—in this way, friends do not grow weary.
Through staying for too long, even a beloved person becomes disliked.”
"Indeed, we shall go while we are still dear to you.
In this context, "all-white," O Great King, means that previously in your residence my rice was all-white;
the meaning is that you caused only that which you yourself ate to be given to me. "Thence" means after that, [upon hearing] the words of those who were seeking to cause a rift.
"Having taken [the food], at the time you became dispassionate toward me, the mixed-rice became entirely white. 'Now' (dāni) means that it has now become entirely red.
'The time' (kālo) means that this is now the time for me to depart from you, who are ignorant of virtue.
'The interior' (abbhantaram): formerly my seat was within; it was on the royal throne itself, with its well-adorned great floor and raised white parasol."
They made me sit down. "At the top of the stairs" means at the head of the steps. "Before being driven out" means as long as one has not been dragged out by the neck.
"Digs up the mud" means that even if a man reaches a waterless well and, not seeing water, stirs up the mud...
Even if one were to stir it with a stick, that water would still smell of mud; because of its unpleasantness, one would not drink it.
In the same way, for one who attends upon those devoid of faith, even if requisites are obtained, they are meager and coarse, unpleasant, and unfit for use—this is the meaning.
"Confident" (pasanna) means established in faith. "Lake" (rahada) means a deep, great lake.
"One who associates" means one should associate with only those who associate with oneself. "One who does not associate" refers to an adversary.

"One should not associate" means one should not associate with him. "He does not associate" means that the person who does not associate with one who associates with himself—a person of benevolent mind—is said to possess the character of a non-noble person (*asappurisa*).
"A backbiter among men" means one who is base, contemptible, and the very last among all men.
"Sākhassito" means a monkey.
"Accābhikkhaṇasaṃsagga" means through excessive and constant association. "At akāle" means at an improper time;
it is said that friends decay through begging for another's beloved possessions, and you too have broken our friendship by staying with me for too long.
Therefore, because friends wear out through excessive intimacy and lack of meeting, for that reason:
"At long intervals" means having passed a long time; one should not go or approach too frequently. "When asked" means one should ask for the goods that ought to be requested at the proper time.
"They do not wear out" means that in this way, friends do not decay. "Before we become unpleasant to you"—until...
“Let us go away after having merely taken leave of you, before we become those who are no longer dear to you.
The king said:
“If, even when they are thus entreating you, you do not acknowledge their salutation with joined palms;”
“You do not act upon the words of hundreds of attendants;
thus we entreat you: please grant us this favor once more.

Therein, “you do not understand” means: Venerable sir, if you do not perceive or accept the reverential salutation made by me as I thus entreat you. “Grant us this favor once more” (pariyāyan) means: please act for one time so that we may come here again.
The Bodhisatta said:
“If we dwell in this manner, there will be no obstacle for either you or me,
O Great King, increaser of the kingdom.”
"Perhaps we might see [you] at the passing of days and nights. Therein, "If it should be so" means:
O Great King, if there is no obstacle for us who dwell thus separately, then either your life or mine will continue; this is what he indicates. "Might see" means: perhaps we might see [you].
Having spoken thus, the Great Being taught the Dhamma to the king, and saying, "Be heedful, O Great King," he departed from the park.
Having departed, he wandered for alms in a certain familiar place;
then, leaving Benares, he traveled by stages to the region of the Himalayas, where he stayed for some time. After descending again, he dwelt in a forest near a frontier village.
From the time he had left, however, those ministers sat once more at the court of justice and began their plundering.
As they were acting, they thought: “If the Great Bodhisatta wanderer returns again, there will be no life for us;
what then could we do to ensure he does not come back? Then it occurred to them:
“These beings are unable to abandon that which is called a place of attachment; what, then, is his place of attachment here? Thereupon, [they concluded]: “It is the King’s chief queen.”
Knowing this, they thought, "It is indeed possible that he might come relying on him; we must have him killed beforehand.
They said this to the king: "Your Majesty, on this day, a certain report is being heard in the city.
"What report is it? "It is said, Your Majesty, that the Great Bodhi Wanderer and the Queen have been exchanging messages with one another."
“They are sending [messages],” he said. “What have they done? It is said that the queen sent him this message:
“Is it possible, by your own power, to kill the king and give me the white parasol? She also sent him this: “The killing of the king is my task;
let the Great Bodhi Wanderer come quickly. While they were speaking thus again and again, the king—

Having placed his trust in him, he asked, "What should be done now? When it was said, "It is right to kill the queen," he did not investigate further, but said, "In that case, you yourselves must kill her, cut her into pieces, and throw her into the cesspool.
They did exactly so. The fact of her having been killed became known throughout the entire city.
Then his four sons, thinking, "By this man our innocent mother has been killed," became enemies of the king.
The king was seized by great fear. Having heard of these events through hearsay, the Great Being reflected:
"Apart from me, there is no one else capable of persuading those princes and making the king grant them pardon; and [I must save] the life of the king."
“I will give it to him and free the two boys from evil.

On the following day, he entered a border village, ate monkey meat given by the people, and having requested and taken its hide, he dried it at his hermitage, removed all odor, and used it as a lower garment, an upper robe, and even placed it over his shoulder. Why? Because [the donor] had been very helpful to him.
For the sake of his message. Taking that hide, he gradually reached Bārāṇasī, approached the princes, and said:
"The act of patricide is a terrible thing; you must not do it. There is no such thing as an immortal being.
I have come only to bring you into mutual harmony. You should come when sent for by my word."
Having instructed the prince, he entered a garden within the city, spread out a monkey skin, and sat down upon a stone slab.
Then, seeing him, the park-keeper went in haste and informed the king. Upon hearing this, the king became filled with joy;
taking those ministers with him, he went there, paid homage to the Great Being, and sat to one side. After exchanging greetings...
He began to do so. The Great Being, instead of greeting him, merely rubbed the monkey-skin.
Then he said to him: "Venerable sir, you rub the monkey-skin without even speaking to me; why is this more beneficial to you than I am?
"Yes, Great King, this monkey is very beneficial to me; I sit upon his back..."
"Having sat down, he would wander about; he brought me my water-pot, swept the dwelling place, and performed for me the duties and counter-duties of proper conduct.
But because of my own feeble state of mind, I ate his flesh, dried his skin, spread it out, and sat and lay upon it. Thus, he has been very helpful to me. In this way, he [spoke] to them.
In this debate, for the purpose of refutation, he attributed the designation "monkey" to the monkey-skin and spoke these words with reference to various circumstances.
For because he had previously lived upon it, he said, "He wandered about sitting on its back";
because he had previously carried a water-jar on his shoulder, he said, "He brought the water-jar"; and by means of that skin...
Because it had previously been swept upon the ground, he said, "I swept the dwelling place.
Because his back had previously been touched by that skin while lying down, and his feet had previously been touched by it while walking, he said, "I performed my duties and counter-duties for him.
But because he had obtained and eaten its flesh during a time of famine, he said, "However, due to the weakness of my own mind, I ate its flesh."
Hearing this, those ministers, perceiving that he had committed the taking of life, clapped their hands in derision, saying, "Look, sirs, at the deed of this renunciant!
Having killed a monkey, he wanders about eating its flesh and carrying its hide.
Seeing them acting in such a manner, the Great Being thought, "These [men] are doing this for the sake of refuting my own doctrine..."
“Since they do not know that I have come taking the hide with me, I shall make them know. Having thus addressed the proponent of causelessness, he asked:
“Friend, why do you mock me? “Because of your having committed both the act of betraying a friend and the taking of life.
Then the Great Being said: “But as for him who, having faith in both your destiny and your view, [acted] in this way...”
If one were to do so, what would be the wrong-doing? In order to refute his argument, he said:
“If the utterance follows the intention, then even against one’s will, one performs what ought not to be done, or indeed performs what ought to be done.”
One who acts against one's will— how could such a person be stained by evil here? "If this matter is both meaningful and righteous, if it is auspicious and not evil,
and if your word is true, sir, then the monkey has been well-slain by me."
“If you were to recognize the fault in your own doctrine, you would not reproach me, for such is your doctrine.
In this context, *udīraṇā* means discourse. *Saṅgatyā* means by way of association with each respective birth among the six classes of beings.

By approaching. "He conforms by way of being" means he conforms through his state of being; the dative case is used in the sense of the instrumental. "Unwillingly" means without desire or without wish.
"Whether it be what should not be done or what should be done" means either evil that ought not to be performed or wholesome merit that ought to be performed.
"He does" means he performs. "Who here? means who is there? This is what is meant: you, as a proponent of causelessness, [say] "there is no..."
"You hold such views as: 'There is no cause, there is no condition for the defilement of beings,' and so forth;
you say that this world follows and transforms according to both conjunction and intrinsic nature, and thus experiences pleasure and pain here and there;
you say that one performs evil or merit even against one's will—if that is your assertion, then if that were so, regarding that which is done against one's will..."
When evil occurs through its own inherent nature, what being here could be defiled by that evil?
For if one were defiled by evil not committed by oneself, then no one would remain undefiled.
Thus, both the meaning of your statement—which is known as the doctrine of causelessness—and the Dhamma that illuminates that meaning are excellent.

Nor is it evil. If the words of your honor—that beings are defiled without cause or condition and experience pleasure and pain—are true, then the monkey has been well-slain by me; what fault of mine is there in this?
The meaning is: "Understand, friend! For if you were to recognize the fault in your own doctrine, you would not reproach me. Why is that?"
“Indeed, your doctrine is such that you would praise me, thinking, ‘This man is engaging with my doctrine,’ yet not knowing your own doctrine, you revile me.
Having thus rebuked him, the Great Being rendered him speechless. He too, in the royal assembly, became abashed, with his shoulders drooping.
He sat down. The Great Being, having refuted his argument, addressed the proponent of the doctrine of creation by Īśvara, saying: "Friend, why do you mock me?
If you consider the doctrine of creation by Īśvara to be the truth," he said:
"If Īśvara, the Lord of all the world, ordains the life-span;..."
A man who carries out instructions regarding supernatural power, misfortune, and deeds that are either wholesome or evil, is thereby defiled as their master.
But if that purpose and that doctrine are wholesome and not evil, [he is not defiled].
“If your word is true, then the monkey has been well-slain by me.
For if you had recognized the fault in your own argument, you would not have censured me; for such is your doctrine.”
In that context, "he ordains life" means that if Brahmā or some other lord were to assign and distribute the livelihood for the entire world, saying, "You live by farming; you live by cattle-herding.

"Prosperity and misfortune" refers to prosperities such as sovereignty and the like, as well as states of misfortune such as the destruction of one's kin, and all other things, whether auspicious or evil.

If all action is fashioned and performed by the Lord alone; and if "one who acts under direction" means that some other person performs it solely according to his direction or command—then, in that case, whatever person commits an evil deed, since it was done by the Lord, the Lord alone would be smeared by that evil.
The rest should be understood in the same manner as before. And as it is here, so it is everywhere.
Thus, like one who has seized a mallet and is about to strike down a mango tree, he shattered the doctrine of creation by Īśvara through that very act of creation.
Then, addressing the proponent of past deeds, he said: "Friend, why do you mock me?
If you consider the doctrine of past deeds to be true," and having said this, he spoke as follows:
“If one undergoes pleasure and pain because of what was done in the past,
then this old evil that was committed is merely the discharge of a debt;
being released from an old debt, how could one here be tainted by evil?”
“If there is both meaning and Dhamma, if it is wholesome and not evil,
and if the word of the venerable one is true, then the monkey has been well-slain by me.
For if one were to recognize a fault in one’s own argument...”
“You should not reproach me, for such is the doctrine of my lord.
In this context, “due to past deeds” (*pubbekatahetu*) means solely because of the causes of kamma performed in previous existences.

“He is released from that debt” refers to one who undergoes suffering through execution, imprisonment, and so forth; if he [has exhausted] whatever evil was done by him in the past, [then he is released].
Now this debt is being discharged; such being the case, for me too there will be liberation from this ancient debt.
For in the past, when I was a monkey and he was a wandering ascetic (paribbājaka), he killed and ate me;
now that he has attained the state of a monkey here and I have attained the state of a wandering ascetic, he shall be killed and eaten by me. Who...?
"Here one is defiled by evil.
Thus, having refuted his doctrine as well, he turned toward the annihilationist and said:
"Friend, having spoken such things as 'a woman has been given,' you imagine that beings are annihilated right here and that there is no such thing as going to a future world."
Having rebuked him, saying, "Why do you mock me?", he said:
"From the four [elements] alone does the form of living beings arise;
and where that form arises, right there it passes away."
“The living being lives only here; having passed away, it perishes.
This world is annihilated—both the fools and the wise.
When the world is annihilated, how can one here be smeared by evil?”
“If it be so that there is both meaning and Dhamma, that it is beautiful and not evil;
and if the word of the venerable one is true, then the monkey has been well-slain by me.
For if he were to recognize the fault in his own argument...”
“You should not reproach me, for such is your own doctrine.
In this context, “of the four” refers to the primary elements (bhūta), beginning with earth. “Form” (rūpa) refers to the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha).
