“Right there” means that from where that form arises, it does not depart even at the time of its cessation. By this, [it is shown that] its nature consists of the four great elements (cātumahābhūtiko).
When this person dies, then the earth returns to and passes into the body of earth;
water... fire... wind returns to and passes into the body of wind; space takes over the sense faculties;
men carry the dead on a litter as the fifth; footprints are visible only as far as the cremation ground; and the bones turn pigeon-colored.
"Offerings become mere ashes; this so-called 'giving' is merely a prescribed formality. The talk of those who maintain the doctrine of existence is empty and false.
Both fools and the wise, upon the dissolution of the body, are cut off and perish;
they do not exist after death. Thus he established this view. "Right here" means in this very world. "The soul" (jīva).

“He lives; having died, having died, he perishes”—meaning that a being reborn in the other world does not return here by way of a destination, but perishes and is annihilated right there in the other world. When the world is thus annihilated, who here is defiled by evil?
Thus, having refuted his doctrine as well, he addressed the Khataviññā-vādī: “Friend, you [say] even one’s mother and father...”
Having spoken thus—"Why do you mock me, wandering about with the view that 'one's own interest should be pursued by killing'?"—he said:
"In this world, those who know the Kṣattṛ-veda say:
'Fools who imagine themselves wise would kill their mother, their father, and even their elder brother.'"
“...and his wife and children, if such were the purpose. In this context, *khattavidā* means *khattavijjā*;
this is indeed the reading. This is the name for those who teach the science of *khatta*.
“Fools who imagine themselves wise” means that although they are fools, they think, “We are wise,” and thus proclaim their own state of wisdom.
Thinking themselves wise and conceited, they say this: "If there were any purpose whatsoever for oneself, one should not avoid anything, but should destroy everything"—and you too are one of them.
Having thus established his position, he spoke in order to clarify his own position:
“One should not break a branch of that tree under whose shade one sits or sleeps; for the betrayer of friends is evil.
But when the need arises, one may even uproot it.”
“I have need even of the whole army; the monkey has been well-slain by me.
“If that [monkey] was for my benefit and in accordance with Dhamma, auspicious and not evil;
and if the word of the venerable one is true, then the monkey has been well-slain by me.”
“If you were to recognize the fault in your own doctrine, you would not reproach me, for such is your doctrine.
In this context, O Khaṭṭhavīda, our teachers explain it thus: [it refers to] the shadow one has enjoyed oneself.
"One would not even break a branch or a leaf of a tree. Why? Because treachery toward a friend is evil.
But you say, 'When a need arises, one should pull it out by the roots. Now, I had need for provisions;
therefore, even if he was killed by me, my purpose was served by his strength as well. The monkey has been well-slain by me."
Having thus refuted his argument as well, while those five remained speechless, he addressed the king:
"Great King, you wander about having seized these five great thieves who plunder the kingdom! Oh, how foolish you are!
For through association with such as these, a person may incur great suffering both in this present life and in the life to come. Having said this, he—
While teaching the Dhamma to the king, he said:
“The man who asserts there is no cause, the one who holds that things are made by a Supreme Lord,
the one who claims everything was done in the past, and the man who is a nihilist— [these four are the spokesmen for the world].”
“These are the base persons in the world, fools who imagine themselves wise;
such a one would commit evil, and furthermore cause others to do so.
Association with the base is the end of suffering, resulting in bitter consequences.”
In this regard, "such a person," O Great King, means that a man who is like these five types of speculative theorists would himself commit evil;
and whoever hears his words would cause another to do so as well.
"Ending in suffering" means that association with such unworthy persons results in bitter consequences, being painful both in this world and in the world beyond. Now, for this matter—
To clarify this point, the following sutta should be cited: "Bhikkhus, whatever fears arise, they all arise from the fool.
This meaning should also be illustrated by such Jātakas as the Godha-jātaka, the Sañjīva-jātaka, and the Akitti-jātaka.
Now, expanding the teaching of the Dhamma by means of an illustration, he said:
“In former times, you were a ram; unafraid, you would enter the flock of goats.
Having killed a ewe, a she-goat, or a male goat, and having terrified the rest, you would go wherever you pleased.
In that same way, certain ascetics and brahmins, having created a facade, deceive people.”
“Those who fast, sleep on the bare ground, smear themselves with dust and dirt,
exert themselves in the *ukkuṭika* posture, eat at irregular intervals, and abstain from drinks— these are of evil conduct,
yet they claim to be Arahants. These are base persons in the world, fools who imagine themselves wise.”
Such a person would commit evil, and furthermore, cause others to do so as well;
association with those who are not true persons ends in suffering and yields bitter fruit.
Those who say that there is no energy, and who proclaim that there is no cause—
Those who falsely praise both the actions of others and their own actions—
“These are the unwholesome persons in the world, fools who imagine themselves wise;
such a one might commit evil, and furthermore, cause another to do so.”
Association with those who are not true men leads to suffering and results in bitter consequences.
For if there were no energy for performing deeds,
whether good or evil, the king would not support his carpenters, nor would he have machines constructed.
“Because there exists energy for both wholesome and unwholesome deeds,
therefore the king causes machines to be made and maintains the carpenter.
Even if the rain-god does not send rain for a hundred years, nor does snow fall;”
This world would perish, this generation would be destroyed,
were it not that the rain-god sends down rain and the snow melts away;
therefore the crops ripen and the kingdom is protected for long.
“If among cattle rushing forward, the leader goes crookedly,
they all go crookedly when the leader has gone crookedly.
Even so among humans, he who is regarded as the best— ”
If he practices unrighteousness, how much more so will the rest of the people;
the entire kingdom suffers, if the king is unrighteous.
"If, when the bulls are crossing, the lead bull goes straight ahead..."
All the cows go straight when the leader has gone straight.
In the same way, among human beings, if he who is regarded as the best practices the Dhamma,
how much more so will the rest of the people?
The entire kingdom dwells in happiness if the king is righteous.
“Whoever plucks the unripe fruit from a great,
fruit-bearing tree neither knows its flavor nor destroys its seed.”
“A kingdom that rules by unrighteousness is like a great tree;
it does not know its own essence, and the kingdom perishes.
Just as one who plucks a ripe fruit from a great fruit-bearing tree [destroys it],”
He discerns its flavor, and its seed does not perish.
The kingdom which one rules by Dhamma is like a great tree;
he discerns its flavor, and the kingdom does not perish for him.
“That king, that kshatriya, who rules his realm by unrighteousness, stands in opposition to all medicinal herbs.
Likewise, he who harms the townspeople engaged in trade and commerce [stands in opposition to them].”
When the offering of strength and tribute is made, he is thwarted by his treasury.
But the king who knows the best places for attack, who has prepared his strategy in battle,
and who strikes when the enemy is on the rise, is thwarted by his own army.
“In the same way, the sage who practices violence, though restrained and living the holy life,
is opposed by the deva-world— just as a kshatriya who acts unrighteously is opposed by heaven.
And the king who stands upon unrighteousness and kills an innocent wife [is likewise opposed].”
He produces a state of conflict and is at odds with his sons.
One should practice righteousness toward the people of the countryside, toward merchants and soldiers, and one should not harm seers;
one should behave with equanimity toward one's wife and children.
“Such was that lord of the earth, Raṭṭhapāla, free from anger;
he made his enemies tremble, like Indra, the lord of the Asuras.
Regarding this, *vakassū* means *vako assu*; *assu* is merely a particle. This is what is meant: O Great King, formerly...
There was a certain crane in the form of a ram; its only long part was its tail, which it had tucked between its thighs.
Thus, unafraid in the guise of a ram, it would approach the flock of goats. There, having killed a female goat, a he-goat, or a ewe, it would depart wherever it pleased.
"Some such as these" refers to certain ascetics and brahmins who, by means of the outward mark of renunciation...
Having created a disguise and concealed themselves, they deceive the world by means of sweet words and the like, acting as if they were desirous of others' welfare.
The passage beginning with “Anāsakā” (fasting) is stated for the purpose of showing their disguise.
For some deceive people, saying, “We are fasting; we do not consume anything at all,” while others say, “We sleep on the bare ground. But for others...
Dust and dirt are their clothing; for others, there is the exertion of squatting. Even when walking, they leap up and move only while remaining in a squatting posture.
For others, there is the practice of taking food at intervals, consisting of eating once every seven or ten days;
others remain without drinking water, saying, "We do not drink water. These are called "Arahants" because they speak [of themselves as such], though they are of evil conduct.

Even after performing [these acts], they wander about saying, "We are Arahants. "These," O Great King, refers either to these five persons or to others—indeed, all those who are called "adherents of wrong views" are base individuals (*asappurisa*). "Those who say" means those who speak;
for if there were no energy, O Great King—that is, if there were no physical and mental energy associated with knowledge—

It would not exist. If even wholesome and unwholesome karma did not exist, then, such being the case, a king would not support carpenters or other craftsmen, nor would he have mechanical devices constructed—such as seven-storied palaces and the like.
For what reason? Because of the absence of both energy and karma. It would be annihilated, O Great King.
If for so long a time neither the rain were to fall nor snow were to descend, then this world would perish like at the end of an eon (*kappa*).
Yet, according to the principle taught by the proponents of annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*), there is no such thing as annihilation. "Pālite" means "he protects.
The four verses beginning with "If [there were] cows... were spoken specifically as a Dhamma teaching for the king; likewise are those beginning with "Of the great tree... and so forth.
In that context, "of the great tree" means of the sweet mango tree. "By unrighteousness" means by following an evil course.
"And he does not know its flavor" means that an unrighteous king does not know the flavor—the essence—of the kingdom; he does not obtain the prosperity of wealth.
"It perishes" means it becomes empty; people abandon the villages and market towns and take refuge in the borderlands, the mountains, and rugged wildernesses.

All sources of income are cut off. "By all medicinal herbs" means that it is counteracted by all medicinal herbs—both those consisting of roots, bark, leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth, as well as ghee, fresh butter, and the like—and these do not succeed.
For when a king is unrighteous, the earth becomes sapless; because of its lack of sap, medicinal herbs possess no vitality, and they are unable to allay diseases.
They are unable [to do so]. Thus, he is said to be at odds with them.

"Negama" refers to the householders living in the market towns (*nigama*). "Harming" means injuring and oppressing. "Those engaged" refers to those engaged in buying and selling—the sources of income consisting of sea-faring, riverine, and land-based merchants—and harming them as well.
"Offering gifts of vital essence and strength" means from here and there...

By means of seizing property, imposing taxes, and demanding tributes—both those consisting of "vitality-gifts" (*ojadāna*) and those classified as "sixth-part tributes" (*cha-bhāga-dasa-bhāga-balī*)—he oppresses them.
"He is ruined by the treasury": that unrighteous king, while destroying these people and causing his wealth and grain to diminish, is said to be "ruined by the treasury.
"One who knows the excellent target for striking": thus [he knows] the excellent targets for striking, thinking, "It is appropriate to strike at this spot."
"Those who know the field" refers to archers. "One who has performed his duty in battle" refers to a great warrior who has achieved success in combat.
"Exalted" means risen high, renowned, or a high minister. "For they lie" means that such a person either lies himself or causes others to lie.
"By force" means by means of an army. For indeed, [they would harm] such a king, thinking: "He harms even those who have been very helpful and who gave him his kingdom."
"How much less us?"—thus the remaining warriors also indeed fled. In this way, he becomes one who is opposed by his own army.

Just as seers are harmed, and just as townspeople and others are, even so a king who acts unrighteously, harming renunciants who have sought out virtuous qualities through abuse, blows, and the like, goes only to a state of misery after the breaking up of the body; he is not able to be reborn in heaven.

He is called one who is at odds with his own wealth. He slays his innocent wife—meaning he puts to death a virtuous wife who was raised under the shadow of his own arms and nurtured by his sons and daughters—by taking the words of thieves who pose as friends.
He produces a cruel state; that is, he brings about and accomplishes his own rebirth in hell. By his sons...
"And thus, even in this very life, he comes into conflict with his own sons.

In this way, having taken up the account of those five people, he spoke of the queen’s being killed and the sons’ hostility toward one another, as if seizing a thief by the topknot at the entrance of a tunnel. For the Great Being [acted] for them...
By means of a gradual discourse, he spoke on this matter for the purpose of restraining the ministers, teaching the Dhamma, and revealing to the queen that she had been killed by them;
having thus created the opportunity, he explained the facts.
Upon hearing his words, the king recognized his own transgression. Then the Great Being said to him: "From now on, O Great King, regarding such persons as these..."
Having said, "How having taken up evil deeds, you shall not do so again," he spoke the verse beginning with "One should practice the Dhamma" while giving this exhortation.
Therein, "one should practice the Dhamma": O Great King, a king indeed should practice the Dhamma within his realm without oppressing the people with unlawful taxes;
he should practice the Dhamma among the citizens without treating those who are owners as non-owners; [and] in an improper place...

Without weariness toward his duties, he should practice the Dhamma. Avoiding killing, imprisonment, abuse, and insults, and providing them with their necessary requisites, he should not harm the seers.

Establishing his daughters in suitable positions, training his sons in crafts, and properly maintaining them, as well as his wife through the relinquishing of authority, the giving of ornaments, and acts of honor—[he should act thus].
Favoring his children and wife, he should conduct himself with impartiality.

"He is such a one" means that such a king, not breaking the traditional lineage and ruling the kingdom righteously and justly, makes his enemies tremble, terrify, and shake by means of royal command and royal majesty.
The phrase "like Indra" is stated for the sake of a simile; it refers to the time beginning from when he stands having conquered and overcome the asuras.
“Inda attained the title ‘Lord of the Asuras’ because he caused the asuras, who were his own enemies, to tremble; thus he causes them to tremble.
Having thus taught the Dhamma to the king, the Great Being summoned the four princes, instructed them, explained the deed the king had committed, and asked the king’s forgiveness.
He said, “Great King, from now on, without weighing [the matter], do not listen to those who cause division...”
“Having taken their advice, how could you have committed such a reckless act? You princes as well must not be disloyal to the king!

Thus he gave this admonition to them all. Then the king said to him: “Venerable sir, it was because I had no ill will toward you or the queen that, relying on these men and taking their advice, I committed this evil deed; I shall kill even these five as well. No.
“It is possible, Great King, to do so. “In that case, have their hands and feet cut off! “Even this cannot be done.

The king, accepting [the advice] with the words, “Very well, venerable sir,” had them stripped of everything they possessed, humiliated by having their hair shorn in five tufts (*pañcacūḷaka*), being bound in a *gaddūla* rope, and being smeared with cow dung, and then banished from the kingdom.
The Bodhisatta, having stayed there for a few days, said, “Be heedful! and departed.

Having exhorted the king, he went back to the Himālayas, developed the jhānas and higher knowledges (abhiññā), and by cultivating the divine abodes (brahmavihāra) for the rest of his life, he was reborn in the Brahma-world.
Having delivered this teaching, the Teacher said: "Monks, it is not only now; in the past as well, the Tathāgata was indeed possessed of wisdom."

Having said, "It is indeed the crusher of the doctrines of others," he identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the five proponents of false views—Pūraṇa Kassapa, Makkhali Gosāla, Pakudha Kaccāyana, Ajita Kesakambalin, and Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta—were those very persons;
Piṅgala the dog was Ānanda; and the Great Bodhi Wanderer was none other than myself.
This concludes the third commentary, the Mahābodhi Jātaka.
The Summary of Birth Stories (Jātakuddāna): The first is called Saniḷīnika; the second is Saummadantivara;
the third is known as Bodhisiri; these three have been told by the Victor as beautiful.
The commentary on the Fiftieth Chapter is finished.
19. The Sixtieth Chapter. 1.
The Commentary on the Soṇaka Jātaka.
“Having heard from whom shall I give a hundred?”—this story the Teacher related while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove, concerning the perfection of renunciation (*nekkhammapāramī*).
At that time, the Blessed One, having sat down in the midst of the monks who were praising the perfection of renunciation in the Dhamma Hall, said:
“Monks, it is not only now; in the past as well, the Tathāgata indeed went forth on the Great Renunciation,” and he brought up the past.
In the past, in Rājagaha, a king named Magadha reigned. The Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of his chief queen, and on the day of his naming ceremony, they gave him the name Prince Arindama.
On the very day he was born, a son was also born to the family priest; they gave him the name Prince Soṇaka. Both of them grew up together.
Having reached maturity and possessing supreme beauty, they became indistinguishable from one another in appearance; having gone to Takkasilā and mastered their arts, they departed from there.
Thinking, "We shall learn all the crafts of every school as well as the local customs," they traveled by stages on a wandering tour until they reached Bārāṇasī.
Having stayed in the royal park, they entered the city on the following day. And on that day—
Some people, intending to perform the Brahmin recitation, prepared milk-rice and arranged seats;
seeing those princes approaching, they invited them into the house and had them sit upon the prepared seats.
There, a clean cloth was spread upon the seat prepared for the Bodhisatta, while a red woolen blanket was spread for Soṇaka. He [Soṇaka] perceived that omen.
Upon seeing him, he realized: "Today my dear friend Prince Arindama will become the King of Bārāṇasī, and he will grant me the position of commander-in-chief.
Having both finished their meal, they went to the pleasure garden.
At that time, it was the seventh day since the death of the King of Bārāṇasī, and the royal family was without an heir. The ministers and others—

At dawn, having bathed including their heads and assembled together, they harnessed the Phussa chariot with the thought, "We shall go to the presence of the one worthy of the kingdom," and sent it forth.
Having departed from the city, he proceeded by stages to the royal park;
turning back at the park gate, he stood ready for mounting. The Bodhisatta, having covered his head with a ceremonial cloth upon the auspicious stone slab, remained there.
He lay down, and Prince Soṇaka sat near him. Hearing the sound of the musical instruments, he thought, "Arinda’s Phussa-chariot is coming;
today this man will become king and grant me the position of commander-in-chief. But I have no need for sovereignty;
when he has gone, I shall depart and go forth into homelessness. Having thought thus, he stood concealed in a secluded spot. The chaplain—
Having entered the garden and seen the Great Being lying down, he had the musical instruments played.
The Great Being woke up, turned over, lay there for a short while, and then rising, sat cross-legged upon a stone slab.
Then the chaplain, raising his hands in reverent salutation, said to him: "Your Majesty, the kingdom has come to you. "Is the royal family without a son? he asked.

"So be it, Your Majesty," he replied. "Then do so, please. Then, having consecrated him right there and placed him upon a chariot, they led him into the city with a great retinue. Having circumambulated the city, he ascended the palace.
Because of the greatness of his glory, he did not even remember Prince Soṇaka.
When he too had entered that city, the other arrived later and sat down upon a stone slab.
Then, a withered leaf fell from a *sāla* tree in front of him. Upon seeing it, he thought, "Just as this has happened, so too shall my own body fall when it reaches old age.
Having thus established insight (*vipassanā*) by way of impermanence and the other characteristics, he attained *paccekabodhi*.
He attained it. At that very moment, his layman’s marks vanished and the marks of one gone forth appeared.
Uttering the exclamation, “Now there is no more renewed existence,” he went to the Nandamūlaka mountain cave.
The Great Being, after the passing of forty years, remembered him and thought, “Where indeed is my friend Soṇaka? and [sought] Soṇaka again and again.
Even while wandering, having failed to find anyone who could say, "I have heard of him or seen him," he sat upon his royal throne on a great,
adorned floor, surrounded by the dancing, singing, and music of celestial musicians (*gandhabba*) and actors, enjoying his prosperity, and thought: "To whoever hears of him from anyone and tells me,
'He named Soṇaka dwells in such-and-such a place,' I shall give him a hundred [pieces of gold]."
Having formulated this inspired utterance, "Whoever shall see it himself and report it to me, to him I shall give a thousand," and reciting that utterance by way of song, he spoke the first verse:
"Whose report shall I hear to give a hundred? He who has seen Soṇaka shall receive a thousand."
“Who will tell me of that friend with whom I played in the dust?
Then one female dancer, as if plucking it from his mouth, sang that verse for him. Then another, and yet another;
and finally, all the women of the harem sang it, saying, “This is our king’s favorite song. Gradually, even the city dwellers and the people of the countryside took it up.
They sang that very same song. The king, too, sang that very same song again and again.
After the passing of about fifty years, he had many sons and daughters; his eldest son was named Prince Dīghāvu.
At that time, the Paccekabuddha Soṇaka thought, “King Arindama desires to see me; I shall go there and [teach him] regarding sensual pleasures.”

Thinking, "I shall speak of the danger in worldly life and the benefits of renunciation, and then take the form of going forth," he came through the air by means of psychic power and sat down in the park.

At that time, a five-year-old boy with five topknots, sent by his mother to go there, was gathering wood in the park forest and was singing that same song over and over again. Then, having summoned him, he said:
“Boy, you sing only this one song without singing anything else; do you not know any other? he asked.
“I know them, venerable sir, but this alone is dear to our king, and therefore I sing it again and again.
“But have you ever seen anyone who sang a response to this song of yours? “No, venerable sir, I have never seen such a person.”
“I will teach you that; will you be able to go into the presence of the king and sing the response?
“Yes, venerable sir,” he replied. Then, explaining the response to him, he said, “Having heard from me...,” and so forth.
Having had him master it, he sent him off, saying: “Go, young man; sing this response together with the king. The king—”
"He will grant you great sovereignty; what use have you for wood? Go with haste!
Having agreed, saying "Very well," and having mastered that counter-song, he paid homage and said, "Venerable sir, please remain right here until I bring the king.
Then, going in haste to his mother, he said, "Mother, quickly bathe me and adorn me."

"Today I shall release you from this state of poverty," he said. Having bathed and adorned himself, he went to the palace gate and said, "Noble doorkeeper, inform the King that a certain boy has come and stands at the gate, saying, 'I shall sing a counter-song with you.
He went quickly and informed the King. The King, saying "Let him come," had him summoned and said, "Dear boy, you..."
“You shall sing a duet with me,” he said. “Yes, Your Majesty,” she replied. “In that case, sing then,” he said.
“Your Majesty, I will not sing in this place; rather, have the drum beaten throughout the city and assemble the great multitude, and I shall sing in the midst of the people.
The king had this done, and having seated her upon a couch in the middle of a decorated pavilion, [he provided] what was suitable for her—
Having had a seat prepared for him, he said, "Now, sing your song. "Your Majesty, you sing first, and then I shall sing in response," he replied.
Then the king, singing first, spoke this verse:
"Whose song have I heard that I give a hundred? A thousand for one seen, O Soṇaka!"
“Thus he told me of Soṇaka, my playmate from the days of playing in the dust.
In this context, *having heard* means: having heard his place of residence, namely, “Your dear friend Soṇaka lives in such-and-such a place,” to the one who reports it, I give a hundred.
*Having seen* means: having seen him, thinking, “I have seen him in such-and-such a place.”
"To whoever recites it, I shall give a thousand [pieces of gold].

Thus, having become fully enlightened, the Teacher spoke one and a half verses, illustrating how the young boy Pañcacūḷaka had responded by singing back the first verse of the *udāna* that the king had sung:
"Then the young brahmin boy, Pañcacūḷaka, spoke:"
“Having heard from me, give a hundred to one who has seen Soṇaka;
I shall provide you with Soṇaka as a companion for playing in the dust.
Now, the meaning of the verse spoken by him is this: “O Great King, regarding what you said—that you would give a hundred to one who reports having heard [of Soṇaka]—”
"You say that; give that to me as well. As for what you said—that you would give a thousand [pieces of gold] to one who points him out after seeing him—give that to me too.
Right now, they will point out your dear friend to you in person, saying, 'This is Soṇaka.
Beyond this, the verses of the Sambuddha, which are easy to understand, should be understood according to the method of the Pāḷi."
“In which country, among the kingdoms and towns, did he see Soṇaka?
Tell me that when you are asked.
“O King, it was in your own realm, in your very own park grounds.”
The great sal trees stand straight, blue-hued and enchanting;
they remain like clouds, lovely and leaning against one another.
At their roots, Soṇaka meditates, free from clinging.
While the worlds, consisting of the aggregates of clinging, were burning, he remained extinguished. Then King Pāyāsi,
having had a level road prepared with his fourfold army, went toward Soṇaka.
“Having gone to a park, while wandering in the Great Forest, he saw Soṇaka sitting there, extinguished amidst those who were burning.
In this context, *ujjuvaṃsā* means having straight trunks. *Mahāsālā* means great trees. *Meghasamānā* means resembling dark blue clouds.
"Delightful" (*rammā*) means charming. "Supported by one another" means they stand with branches interlaced with branches and roots entwined with roots.

"Of them" means beneath such *sāla* trees as these in your park-grove. "Meditates" (*jhāyati*) means he meditates by means of the meditations known as contemplation of characteristics (*lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna*) and contemplation of the object (*ārammaṇūpanijjhāna*).
"Without clinging" (*anupādāno*) means free from the clinging to sense-pleasures and so forth. "While [the trees] are burning" means while they are being consumed by the eleven fires.

"While beings are burning, he is extinguished. Having extinguished those fires, he sits upon a stone slab at the foot of a *maṅgala-sāla* tree in your park, meditating with a cool heart; this friend of yours, shining like a golden statue, awaits you.
Then, monks, having heard those words from him, King Arindama [approached] Soṇaka the Paccekabuddha.
Thinking, “I shall go forth,” he set out with a fourfold army.
Wandering about—meaning that instead of going straight, he wandered through that great forest thicket—he approached him and saw him sitting there.
Without bowing to him, he sat down to one side and, because he himself was devoted to the defilements, thinking of the other as a "miserable wretch," he spoke this verse:
“Alas, this bhikkhu is indeed pitiable! Shaven-headed and clad in the outer robe, without mother and without father, he meditates at the foot of a tree.
In this context, “he meditates” means that, being without mother and without father, he meditates having fallen into a state of compassion.
“Having heard these words, Soṇaka spoke thus:
‘O King, one does not become a pauper by practicing the Dhamma with the body.
But he who, having set aside the Dhamma, follows what is contrary to the Dhamma—’”
“That king is a miser, an evil man devoted to evil.
In this context, “this” refers to these words of reproach for the renunciate life, heard by him who delights in defilements and praises renunciation.
“He spoke this” means he spoke this while manifesting the virtues of renunciation. “Phassayanti” means while touching [the truth].
He spoke thus to show that one who has touched the Dhamma of the Noble Path with the mental body (nāmakāya) is no longer called "miserable.

"Having cast out" means having removed [the evil] from one's own personal existence (attabhāva). "Evil and intent on evil" means he is "evil" by virtue of performing evil deeds himself, and "intent on evil" by virtue of being a support for others who are doing the same.
Thus he reviled the Bodhisatta. Acting as if he did not know that he had been reviled, he stated his own name and lineage, and while exchanging greetings with him, he spoke this verse:
“Arindama is my name; I am known as the King of Kāsi.
I hope you have slept well, having arrived here with your dogs?”
In this context, "Kacci" means: "Is there anything unwell with us? He asks, however, whether it is a pleasant dwelling for the venerable one who has arrived here and is staying in this park.
Then the Paccekabuddha said to him, "Great King, not only here, but even when living elsewhere, there is nothing that is unpleasant for me," and he began the verses known as the *Samaṇabhadra-gāthā*:
"Always there is prosperity for the one without wealth, For the homeless monk."
They do not store [food] in granaries, nor in jars, nor in baskets;
seeking what has been prepared by others, those of good vows sustain themselves thereby.
And a second time, for the fortunate one who has gone forth, the homeless bhikkhu—
“Blameless almsfood should be eaten, and no one should cause obstruction.
For a third time, O Bhadda, for the houseless monk,
nibbāna-like almsfood should be eaten, and no one should cause obstruction.”
“Fourthly, for the noble one who has no possessions, the homeless monk,
who is liberated and wanders through the kingdom, in whom no attachment exists. Fifthly,
for the noble one who has no possessions, the homeless monk...”
When the city was burning, there was nothing of his that burned.
This is the sixth blessing for the bhikkhu, the houseless one who possesses good wealth:
when the kingdom is being plundered, there is nothing of his that is lost.
“Even for the seventh time, for the venerable one who has no possessions, the homeless monk—
taking his bowl and robe— he goes safely along the path guarded by thieves and those others who lie in wait as robbers, he of virtuous conduct.”
“Even for the eighth time, O Bhadda, the houseless bhikkhu who possesses nothing— whichever direction he departs, he goes without looking back. In this context,
“of the houseless one,” O Great King, means of one who has abandoned the household life and attained the state of homelessness, possessing nothing.
For a monk who possesses nothing, there is always only what is auspicious.
"They have none," O Great King—of those penniless monks, no wealth or grain is stored in storehouses, nor in jars, nor in baskets;
rather, being of virtuous conduct, they wear their outer robes and, taking up their alms-bowls, [seek] food cooked in the houses of others that has been prepared by others.
Seeking by way of the sequence of houses, they maintain their livelihood by consuming that food obtained from there after reflecting upon it in terms of the nine repulsivenesses.
"The blameless alms-food should be eaten" means that one should avoid improper seeking such as medical practice and so forth, as well as hypocrisy, hinting, and signifying.

The four requisites produced by such wrong livelihood as "squeezing" (nippesikatā)—that is, seeking gain through gain—or even those produced by right means, if used without reflection, are called "blameworthy alms-food" (sāvajjapiṇḍa).
However, having abandoned improper search and avoided wrong livelihood, those produced by right and fair means—[reflecting thus]: "Reflecting wisely upon the robe... [and so forth].
"Having reflected in the manner already described, 'I am consuming it,' that which has been consumed is called blameless alms-food (anavajjapiṇḍa).

For one by whom such blameless alms-food is to be eaten and consumed, and for those consuming such blameless alms-food, no slight defilement whatsoever arises or oppresses them by depending on the requisites; for him, this is the second [requisite]."
It is well for the poor, homeless bhikkhu. One who is "extinguished" (nibbuto) refers to a bhikkhu who is still a worldling (puthujjana);
even when he consumes alms-food obtained in accordance with the Dhamma after reflecting upon it, that is called "extinguished alms-food.
However, the alms-food of one whose taints are utterly destroyed (khīṇāsava) alone is truly called "extinguished alms-food. For what reason?

For among these four kinds of enjoyment—the enjoyment by theft, the enjoyment by debt, the enjoyment by inheritance, and the enjoyment as an owner—he enjoys it by way of enjoyment as an owner. Having transcended the slavery of craving, he enjoys it as a master;
no defilement, however slight, obstructs him on that account.
"Moving about in the realm of one who is liberated" means that his mind is unattached to families of supporters and the like;

he is like a cloud that has burst asunder, and like the stainless orb of the moon released from the mouth of Rāhu. As he moves through villages, market towns, and other places, there is not even a single attachment in him toward passion, clinging, and so forth.
For some indeed dwell in close association with families, sharing their sorrows and sharing their joys.
A certain person wanders about with a mind unattached even to his mother and father, like the young man who lived in the village of Korunagara;
for such an ordinary person (puthujjana), it is indeed well.
As for the one who thinks "nothing belongs to me," he who possesses many requisites [thinks], "Lest thieves should carry off my requisites," and thus keeps them in excess.
If one deposits robes and other requisites within the city at the house of a supporter, and then, when the city is burning,
hears that "fire has broken out in such-and-such a house" and grieves and suffers,

for such a person there is no true welfare. But as for him, O Great King, who fulfills the conduct of a bird and possesses only those requisites attached to his own body— for such a person as that, [there is no grief].
"Something was not burned; therefore, for him, even the fifth [case] is auspicious.
Regarding "while it was being plundered" (*vilumpamāne*): this means while it was being plundered; or rather, this is simply another reading. Regarding "they were seized":
just as when thieves, having emerged from mountain thickets and such, plunder a kingdom, they plunder whatever has been placed within a village belonging to one who possesses many requisites.
He carries it away; likewise, for one who has no sense of shame regarding any of his bodily requisites, even the sixth [offense] is indeed auspicious.
And "others who are highwaymen" refers to those others who have been stationed in various places for the purpose of collecting tolls.
There are highway robbers, and [the goods] are guarded by them. Regarding "bowl and robes":
a clay bowl that is of no use to thieves and exempt from customs duties, and a rag-robe (paṃsukūla) that has been strengthened by repairs;

and the eight requisites—namely, the waist-band, water-strainer, needle, knife, and needle-case—all of which are of little value—if one sets all these eight requisites upon the body and travels along the road, one will not be harmed by anyone.
He goes safely. "Virtuous" (subbata): for when thieves see robes and other such desirable things, they carry them off;
and customs officials also search his bowl, bag, and so forth, wondering, "What might he have in his hand?
But one who is virtuous and lives with few possessions goes safely even while they are looking on; therefore, this is his seventh excellence.

"He goes without looking back" means that because he possesses no requisites other than those attached to his body—having deposited everything else in the monastery—he does not look back even when returning to his place of residence. Whichever direction he wishes to go, he goes toward it without looking back;
this refers to the two who went forth in the Thūpārāma after departing from Anurādhapura.
He was like an elder among noble sons.
Thus, the Paccekabuddha Soṇaka spoke of eight auspicious qualities of a recluse.
Beyond that, he was indeed capable of speaking even a hundred, a thousand, or an immeasurable number of such auspicious qualities of a recluse. But the king, being devoted to sensual pleasures—

Having cut off his speech, he said—manifesting his own addiction to sensual pleasures with the words, "I have no need for these sham ascetics"—"There are many sham ascetics whom you praise, O bhikkhu;
yet I am greedy for sensual pleasures. What shall I do, Soṇaka?"
“Human pleasures are dear to me, and divine pleasures are dear to me as well;
by what means, then, might we obtain both worlds?
In this context, “by what means” (vaṇṇena) means by what cause (kāraṇena).
Then the Paccekabuddha said to him:
“Men who are greedy for sensual pleasures, delighting in sensual pleasures, and obsessed by sensual pleasures,
having committed evil deeds, are reborn in a state of misery.”
“Those who, having abandoned sensual desires, have gone forth free from fear from any quarter, and have attained a state of singleness—they do not go to an evil destination.
I shall give you a simile; listen to it, O Tamer of Enemies.”
In this world, some wise people understand the meaning through a simile:
"Seeing a corpse being carried away in the great ocean by the Ganges,
a crow of little wisdom and no discernment thought to himself:"
“Indeed, this vehicle has been obtained, and this food is no small amount;
my mind is devoted to that very place by night and by day.
Eating the flesh of the nāga and drinking the water of the Bhāgīrathī—”
Carefully observing the forest shrines, the bird did not flee. But the Ganges, though accessible,
was impassable for him as he descended into it— being heedless and delighting in carrion—
it carried him into the ocean, where there is no refuge for winged creatures.
“Thus, with his food exhausted, that bird flew up into the air;
neither to the west nor to the east, neither to the north nor to the south did he go.
He found no island to reach, for there was nowhere for a bird to go.”
And so he fell right there, just like the weakling. And the sea fish,
crocodiles, sharks, and *susū*— those that move with a slapping sound—
devoured him as he writhed, his wings spread wide.
“In the same way, O King, those others who enjoy sensual pleasures—
if they are greedy and do not vomit it up, they are known by the wise as having the wisdom of crows.
This simile, O King, has been made for you to demonstrate the meaning.”
"And you too will be known by that, whether you do it or not.
In this context, "evils," O Great King, refers to the fact that you, being greedy for sensual pleasures, and other men who, relying on sense-desires,
commit evils such as bodily misconduct and so forth, will go to that miserable state where neither divine nor human pleasures are obtained even in a dream.
The meaning is "they are reborn. "Having abandoned" means having cast off like a lump of spittle.
"Fearless from any quarter" means free from any fear arising from lust and the other defilements. "Attained to singleness" means attained to a state of solitude and dwelling alone.
"They do not"—such renunciants as these do not go to an evil destination.

"An illustration for you," O Great King, means: "I shall provide one illustration for you who, desiring divine and human pleasures, are like a crow clinging to a piece of elephant carrion; listen to that. *Kuṇapa* refers to an elephant's carcass.
*Mahannave* means in deep and wide water. It is said that a certain great elephant, while grazing on the bank of the Ganges, fell into the river and was unable to get out.
Being unable [to escape], he died right there and was carried away by the Ganges; it is with reference to him that this was said. "A crow" refers to a certain crow traveling through the air.
Thinking, "They are carrying a vehicle," and perching there, he thought: "I have obtained this elephant-vehicle;
hidden here, I shall move about at ease, and this itself will be a vast amount of food for me."
"Now it is not right for me to go elsewhere," he resolved.
There, "by night" means that both by night and by day his mind remained delighted right there. "He did not flee" means he did not fly up and depart.
"Descending" means descending toward the ocean. There is also the reading "carrying away" (*ohāriṇī*); that means carrying [the ship] away toward the ocean.
The meaning is as follows. "Where there is no going" refers to the middle of the ocean. "With food exhausted" means his provisions were completely spent.
"Having flown up" means that when the skin and flesh had perished, the heap of bones was shattered by the force of the waves and sank into the water.
Then that crow, unable to find a foothold in the water, flew upward; such is the meaning of "having thus flown up. "Where there is no going... [as before].
"Among the winged ones": in that middle of the ocean which is inaccessible even to winged creatures, having flown up there, he went to the western direction;
not finding a foothold there, he went to the eastern, then the northern, then the southern—having gone to all four directions, he did not find his own place of rest (*patiṭṭhāna*).
The meaning is that he did not reach it. Alternatively, [the word] *vāyasa*...
Having thus flown up, he went toward each of the directions beginning with the west, but he did not reach the island;
this is how the meaning here should be understood. *Pāpatthā* means he fell down. *Yathā dubbalako* means he fell exactly as a weakling would fall.
*Susū* refers to fierce fish named *susū*. *Pasayhakārā* means by force, even against one’s will.
"Vipakkhaka" means having one's wings destroyed.
"If the greedy ones do not vomit [them up]" means if, being greedy, they do not vomit up or cast away sensual desires.
"They have the wisdom of a crow" means that those wise ones—the Buddhas and others—know, perceive, and understand them as having wisdom equal to that of a crow.

"Meaning" (*attha*). "Showing the meaning" (*atthasandassanī*) means that which illuminates the meaning. "And you shall be known by wisdom" (*tvañ ca paññāyase*) means that you will be renowned for your wisdom.
This is what is meant: "O Great King, this advice has been given to you by me out of a desire for your welfare.
If you carry it out, you will be reborn in the world of the gods; if you do not carry it out, you will be submerged in the mire of sensual pleasures at the end of your life."
"You will be reborn in hell"—thus, for that reason or for no other reason, you alone shall be known in heaven or in hell;
but I am liberated from all states of existence and shall not undergo rebirth.
Now, while giving this instruction, the Paccekabuddha pointed out a river, and an elephant carcass being carried away by it.
The crow that eats carrion was shown; the time when it had eaten the carrion and was drinking water was shown;
the time when it was shown the delightful forest grove was shown; the entry of the carrion being carried away by the river into the ocean was shown;
and the time when the crow, finding no support upon the elephant-carrion in the middle of the ocean, met its destruction was shown.
It has been shown. In this context, the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) is to be regarded as like a river;
the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca kāmaguṇā*) within *saṃsāra* are like an elephant carcass being carried away by the river; the foolish worldling (*bālaputhujjana*) is like the crow;

and the time when the worldling experiences joy after enjoying the strands of sensual pleasure is like the time when the crow drinks water after having eaten the carcass. Just as the crow remains stuck to the carcass...
Just as seeing a beautiful grove is for an ordinary person (puthujjana) who is attached to the strands of sensual pleasure, so too is the vision of the thirty-eight objects by way of hearing;
and just as it is the time of destruction for a crow that has entered the ocean with a corpse and is unable to find a foothold,
so it is for the foolish ordinary person, greedy for the strands of sensual pleasure and intent on evil, who is unable to find a foothold in wholesome states (kusaladhamma).
"For one who is unable [to heed the advice], the attainment of great destruction in the Great Hell must be seen.
Having thus given him this exhortation by means of this simile, he now spoke this verse to make that very exhortation firm and well-established:
"A compassionate person might speak once, or even twice;..."
"One should not speak beyond that in the presence of one who does not accept the words; for speaking further than that is like being a slave in the presence of a master.
For a slave speaks even when the master accepts his words or does not accept them. Thus it was said.
“Do not speak beyond that.
Having said this, Soṇaka of immeasurable wisdom departed through the air in the sky, after having instructed the khattiya.
This is the verse of the Fully Enlightened One.
Therein, having said this—“Monks, that Paccekabuddha, possessing immeasurable supramundane wisdom, being of immeasurable intellect, having said this, rose up by means of psychic power [and declared]:
‘If you go forth, it shall be yours; if you do not go forth, it shall be yours’”—this is the meaning.
"I have given you my exhortation; be diligent," he said, and having thus instructed the kshatriya, he departed.

The Bodhisatta, standing and watching him as he traveled through the air until he passed from sight, was moved with a sense of spiritual urgency and reflected: "This brahmin, though of low birth, is unbroken..."

“He who, scattering the dust of his own feet upon my head as I was born into the khattiya lineage, flew up into the sky and departed—it is fitting that I too should go forth into homelessness this very day.

Desiring to renounce the kingdom and take ordination, he spoke these two verses: “Who indeed are these royal servants, these Śūdras who have attained such proficiency? [They have prepared the throne for me.]”
“I shall hand over the kingdom; I have no need for kingship.
This very day I will go forth into homelessness; who knows if death will come tomorrow?
Let me not, like a foolish crow, fall under the power of sensual desires.”
In that regard, who indeed knows? Where indeed are they? "The king-makers" refers to those who, having consecrated one worthy of a king, make him king.
"Sudras who have attained proficiency" refers to the Sudras and others who have attained a state of skill, such as the *mukhamangalika* (fortune-tellers).
"One who craves kingship" means one who desires kingship. "Who would know if death is tomorrow?"—that is, whether death will come today or tomorrow. This...
Who is capable of knowing this?
Having heard him thus renouncing the kingdom, the ministers said:
"You have a young son, Dīghāvu Raṭṭhavaḍḍhana."
“Consecrate him in the kingdom; he shall be our king.
Thereafter, beginning with the verse spoken by the king, the verses connected to the *udāna* should be understood according to the method of the Pāḷi itself:
“Quickly bring the prince Dīghāvu, the increaser of the realm!”
“I shall consecrate him in the kingdom; he shall be your king.
Then they brought the prince Dīghāvu, the increaser of the realm.
Seeing him, his only son, who was so delightful, the king addressed him.
“Sixty thousand villages, complete in every respect—take charge of these, my son; I entrust the kingdom to you.
This very day I shall go forth into homelessness; who knows if death will come tomorrow?”
“May I not, like a foolish crow, fall under the power of sensual desires.
Sixty thousand elephants, adorned with every ornament—
those noble steeds with golden girths, clad in cloths of gold-woven fabric.”
“Mounted by village chiefs, with spears and goads in their hands—follow them, my son; I entrust the kingdom to you.
This very day I shall go forth into homelessness; who knows if death will come tomorrow?”
“May I not, like a foolish crow, fall under the power of sensual desires.
Sixty thousand horses, all adorned with every ornament,
well-bred Sindhava steeds, swift of pace.”
“Mounted by the village chiefs bearing spears and bows—follow them, my son; I entrust the kingdom to you.
This very day I shall go forth into homelessness; for who knows if death will come tomorrow?”
“May I not, like a foolish crow, fall under the power of sensual desires.
Sixty thousand chariots, armored and with banners raised—
some adorned with leopard skins, others with tiger skins— all decorated with every kind of ornament.”
“Ascended by the village chiefs, clad in armor and with bows in hand—follow them, my son; I entrust the kingdom to you.
This very day I shall go forth into homelessness; who knows if death will come tomorrow?”
"May I not, like a foolish crow, fall under the power of sensual desires.
Rohaṇa has sixty thousand milch cows, bulls, and draft oxen;
take charge of these, my son, and I shall hand over the kingdom to you."
“I shall go forth this very day; who knows if death will come tomorrow?
Let me not, like a foolish crow, fall under the power of sensual desires.
There are sixteen thousand women, all adorned with every ornament...”
"Adorned with various garments and ornaments, wearing jeweled earrings fastened in place—my son, take charge of these; I shall hand over the kingdom to you.
"I shall go forth this very day; for who knows if death will come tomorrow?"
“May I not, like a foolish crow, fall under the power of sensual desires.
‘My mother died while I was still young, father—I have heard this;
without you, father, I would not even dare to live.’”
"Just as a young calf follows behind a forest elephant as it wanders through mountain fastnesses,
over level ground, and across uneven terrain;
even so do I follow you from behind, taking up my bowl."
“I shall be easy to support for you; I will not be difficult to support for you.
Just as when a merchant seeking wealth takes on a maritime loan for a ship, the merchants might meet with disaster therein.”
“In this very way, this wretched son is an obstacle to me;
lead this prince to the palace that increases delight.
There, with water-pots in hand, like apsarases attending upon Sakka,”
They will delight him there, and he will delight with them.
Then they led the prince to the pleasure-increasing palace;
seeing him, the maidens spoke to Dīghāvu, the increaser of the kingdom:
“Are you a deity, a gandhabba, or perhaps Sakka Purindada?
Who are you, whose son are you, and how may we know you?
“I am neither a deity nor a gandhabba, nor am I Sakka Purindada.”
“I am the son of the King of Kāsi, Dīghāvu, the increaser of the realm.
Support me—blessings be upon you—I shall be your husband.
To him there, the maidens spoke to Dīghāvu, the increaser of the realm:
“Where has the King arrived? Where has the King gone from here?
“The King has crossed over the mud; the King is established on firm ground.
He has set out upon the great path that is free of thorns and without obstruction.”
“I am one who has set out upon the path leading to an evil destination—
a path with thorns and thickets, by which those go to a state of misery.
Welcome to you, O King, as a lion to the Giribbaja cave!”
“Instruct us, O Great King; you are the sovereign over us all.
In this context, “quickly” means: therefore, bring him here swiftly. “He addressed them” means he spoke, saying, “Sixty thousand villages,” and so forth.
“Adorned with every ornament” means those nāgas were decorated with all the ornaments, beginning with those for the head.
"Hemakappanavāsasā" means those whose bodies were covered with golden ornaments (*kappana*). "Gāmaṇīyebhi" means by elephant trainers.
"Ājānīyāva" means those who indeed know what is possible and what is impossible. "Jātiyā" means of Sindhu breed; they were born in the country of Sindh, on the bank of the Indus River.
"Gāmaṇīyebhi" means by horse trainers. "Illiyā cāpadhāribhi" means those bearing the *illiyā* weapon and the bow weapon.
"By those carrying [them]. 'Lamps' (dīpā) refers to those covered with leopard skins and tiger skins.
'By village leaders' (gāmaṇīyehi) means by charioteers. 'By armored men' (vammibhī) means by those clad in armor. 'Rohaññā' means reddish-brown in color.
'Puṅgavūsabhā' means endowed with a pre-eminent bull, known as an *usabha*."
"Father, while I was still young," the prince said to him, "I heard, father, that my mother died while I was still a child;
therefore, I shall not be able to live without you. "Potaka" means a young fawn.
"Jessantaṃ" means wandering about. "Sāmuddikaṃ" means wandering upon the ocean. "Dhanesinaṃ" means of those seeking wealth.
“Vohāra” means various deceptive practices, such as a bottom-dragging fish, a water-demon, or a whirlpool.
“Tattha” means in that ocean. “The merchants might meet with disaster” means that those merchants might fall into calamity.
There is also a reading, “siyyuṃ. “Puttakali” means one who is unlucky regarding children, one who brings misfortune to his children. The prince, however, was unable to say anything further.

He could not endure it. Then the king, issuing commands to his ministers, spoke these words beginning with "This one. In this context, "with hands adorned with conchs" (*kambusahatthāya*) means that *kambu* refers to gold;
thus, the meaning is "with hands decorated with golden ornaments. "As they wish" (*yathā*) means "they act according to their desires.
Having spoken thus, the Great Being had him consecrated right there and sent him off to the city. He himself, however, remained alone.

Having departed from the park and entered the Himālaya mountains, he constructed a leaf-hut on a delightful stretch of ground, went forth into the ascetic life of an *isi*, and sustained himself by subsisting on forest roots and fruits. The great multitude also escorted the prince into Bārāṇasī;
having circumambulated the city, he ascended the palace. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said, "Then," and so forth. That...
"Having seen her, they spoke"—having seen him approaching with a great retinue and majestic splendor, those dancing girls, not even knowing his name, went up to him and said:
"Support me! means "desire me. "The mire" refers to the mire of defilements such as lust.
"The dry land" refers to the life of renunciation (*pabbajjā*). "Thornless" means free from the thorns of lust and other such afflictions.
By those very same graspings, he has reached the ungrasped. He has entered upon the "Great Path," the great road leading to heaven and liberation.
"By which"—by whichever wrong path they go to a state of misery, he says, "I have entered upon that.
Then they thought: "The King has indeed gone forth into homelessness, abandoning us; this one too appears to have a mind detached from sensual pleasures. If we do not please him..."
“Having gone forth, he will go into homelessness; we shall make him take delight [in our company].
Then, welcoming him, they spoke this concluding verse. Therein, “Giribbaja” is the dwelling place of the lion cubs, the Golden Cave;
it was as if the maned lion had come there, so a very welcome indeed is your coming, O you! “Thou art” means: thou art the lord and master of us all.
Having spoken thus, they raised all the musical instruments, and various kinds of dances and songs were performed.
There was great splendor; intoxicated by that splendor, he did not remember his father. Having ruled the kingdom according to the Dhamma, he departed according to his karma.
The Bodhisatta, too, having attained the jhānas and higher knowledges (abhiññā), at the end of his lifespan, went to the Brahma world.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now; in the past as well, the Tathāgata went forth on the Great Renunciation," and he then identified the Jātaka:
"At that time, the Paccekabuddha attained Parinibbāna; the son was Rāhula Kumāra;
the rest of the assembly were the Buddha’s own retinue; and King Arindama was none other than myself."
The First Story: The Commentary on the Soṇakajātaka.
[530] 2. The Commentary on the Saṅkiccas Jātaka:
"Having seen the king sitting... This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in Jīvakambavana concerning the patricide committed by Ajātasattu.

He spoke concerning this. For after relying on Devadatta and, at his word, having caused his father to be killed, and later, when Devadatta’s assembly had been split and a disease arose among those who had separated from him, Ajātasattu was traveling toward Sāvatthī in a palanquin, intending to ask the Tathāgata for forgiveness.
Hearing that the earth had swallowed [the palanquin] at the gate of Jetavana, he thought: "Devadatta has [done this] to the Perfectly Enlightened One..."
Having become his adversary, he entered the earth and became destined for the Avīci hell; because of him, my righteous father, the King of Dharma, was also slain.
"Shall I too enter the earth?"—thinking thus, he was terrified and found no mental delight in the glory of sovereignty.
"I will sleep a little," he thought, but as soon as he had fallen asleep, into this great earth, nine yojanas in thickness—
Having been cast down, as if being pounded with iron spikes or as if being torn apart and devoured by dogs, he rose up, crying out with a terrifying sound.
Then one day, on the full moon of the month of Kattika, surrounded by his assembly of ministers and surveying his own glory, he thought:
"The glory of my father was greater than this; yet such as I am, a king of Dharma, through reliance upon Devadatta—"
"You will kill me," he thought. As he was thinking this, a burning heat arose in his body, and his entire frame became drenched with sweat.
Then, thinking, "Who indeed will be able to dispel this fear of mine?
and realizing that there was no one other than the One of Ten Powers (the Buddha), he thought, "I have committed a great offense against the Tathāgata; who indeed will lead me [to him]?"
Thinking, "He will point [it out]," and observing that no one else could do so except Jīvaka, he took hold of him and devised a means of departure.
Uttering the inspired exclamation, "O, how delightful is this moonlit night!
and saying, "Whom indeed shall we attend today—whether a recluse or a brahmin? he [dismissed] Pūraṇa’s disciples and others from the presence of Pūraṇa and the rest.
When their virtues had been recounted, [the king], disregarding their words and questioning Jīvaka, was told by him after describing the virtues of the Tathāgata:

"May Your Majesty wait upon the Blessed One. Having thus prepared his elephant-vehicles and gone to Jīvakambavana, he approached the Tathāgata, paid homage, and was received with a friendly greeting by the Tathāgata, who spoke of the visible fruits of the spiritual life.
Having asked about the fruits of the ascetic life and heard the Tathāgata’s sweet teaching on the fruits of the ascetic life, he declared himself a lay follower at the conclusion of the discourse.

After apologizing to the Tathāgata, he departed. From that time forward, giving alms, guarding his virtue, and associating with the Tathāgata, he listened to the sweet discourse on the Dhamma; thus, through association with a spiritual friend—
Having abandoned fear and become free from horripilation, he attained mental gladness and lived happily in the four postures.
Then one day, they raised a discussion in the Dhamma Hall: "Friends, Ajātasattu, having committed the act of patricide, was overcome by fear;
lacking mental gladness due to his reliance on royal splendor, in all his postures..."
“He was experiencing suffering; now, having come to the Tathāgata and through association with a virtuous friend, he experiences the happiness of sovereignty, free from fear.
The Teacher approached and asked, “Monks, about what conversation are you sitting here gathered now?
When they replied, “About this very matter,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now that he committed the deed of patricide.”
"Having done so, rest in happiness depending upon me," he said, and then related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, he obtained a son named Prince Brahmadatta.
At that time, the Bodhisatta took rebirth in the house of the royal chaplain; as soon as he was born, he was given the name Saṅkicca Kumāra.

They gave him a name. Both of them grew up together in the royal palace. Becoming friends with one another, they reached maturity, went to Takkasilā, and having mastered all the arts, returned home. Then the king gave the vice-regency to his son.
The Bodhisatta also remained in the service of the vice-king. Then one day, the vice-king [to his father]...
Seeing the great glory of one going on a pleasure excursion, he conceived a greedy desire for it and thought:
"My father is like my brother; if I wait for his death, I will receive the kingdom in my old age.
But what is the use of a kingdom obtained then? I shall kill my father and seize the kingdom. Having thus reflected upon the Bodhisatta...
He reported that matter to him. The Bodhisatta dissuaded him, saying, “Friend, the act of patricide is a grave offense; it is a path to hell.
It cannot be done; do not do it. Although he was dissuaded by him up to three times, he spoke again and again until finally he consulted with the footmen.
They also agreed, and they investigated a means for the king’s assassination.
The Bodhisatta, having learned of this occurrence, thought, "I shall not remain together with these people.
Without even taking leave of his parents, he departed through the main gate, entered the Himalayas, and went forth into the ascetic life of an *isi*.
Having attained the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), he dwelt there subsisting on forest roots and fruits.
When he had departed, the prince also had his father killed and enjoyed great glory.
Hearing that "the youth Saṅkicca has indeed gone forth as an ascetic," many sons of good family went forth and were ordained in his presence.
Surrounded by a great company of seers, he lived there; all of them were indeed attainers of meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*). The king [also heard] about his father...
Having killed him and enjoyed the pleasures of sovereignty for only a short time, from that point on he was terrified and found no peace of mind;
he became like one condemned to perform labor in hell. Remembering the Bodhisatta, he thought:
"My friend forbade me, saying, 'The act of killing one's father is heavy [in consequence]; do not do it,' yet he tried to make me adopt his own view."
Unable to clear himself of blame, he fled. "If he were here now, he would not have been able to commit the act of patricide against me;
this too would have brought fear upon me. Where does he dwell at present?
If I knew his dwelling place, I would summon him. But who could tell me where he dwells?"
He reflected thus. From that time forward, both in the royal palace and in the king’s assembly hall, he spoke only in praise of the Bodhisatta.
When a long period had passed in this way, the Bodhisatta thought: "The King remembers me;
it is fitting for me to go there, teach him the Dhamma, and return after making him free from fear. Having lived in the Himalayas for fifty years, surrounded by five hundred ascetics, [he departed].
Having arrived through the air, he descended into a park named Dāyapassa and sat upon a stone slab, surrounded by a company of seers.
The park keeper, seeing him, asked, "Venerable sir, what is the name of this teacher of the group?
Upon hearing that he was named Saṅkicca Paṇḍita, the keeper recognized him for himself and said, "Venerable sir, please remain right here until I bring the king; our king..."
"I wish to see you," he said, and having gone swiftly to the royal palace, he informed the king of his arrival.
The king went to him, presented the appropriate offerings, and asked the question.
To explain this matter, the Teacher said:
“Having seen King Brahmadatta, that bull among charioteers, seated there,
he reported to him [the matter] for which he had been compassionate:
‘This Saṅkicca has arrived, one who is highly esteemed by the seers.’”
“Hurry forth in haste and quickly see the Great Seer!
Then the king, the bull among chariot-warriors, hurrying and mounting his harnessed chariot,
went forth surrounded by friends and ministers.
“Having set aside the five insignia of royalty—
the royal parasol, the yak-tail fan, the turban, the sword,
and the sandals— the King, the prosperer of the kingdom of Kāsī, descended from his vehicle and removed his covering.”
While [the Seer] was seated on the bank of the Dāya, Saṃkicca approached him.
Having approached, that king exchanged greetings with the seer;
after concluding his conversation, he sat down to one side.
“While sitting to one side, you then considered the time;
thereafter, you proceeded to ask about evil deeds.
‘We ask the seer Saṅkicca, who is highly esteemed by the seers.’”
To him, as he sat on the mountain slope, honored by a host of seers, [the King asked]:
“To what destination do men go after death who have transgressed the Dhamma?
I have transgressed the Dhamma; being questioned, tell me that.”
In that context, "having seen," monks, means that when the park-keeper saw the king seated in the royal assembly hall, he reported it to him;
the meaning is that he announced it by saying, "He for whom you [had concern].
"For whom you" means, O Great King, he for whom you were compassionate and kind-hearted, he whose praise you frequently uttered—that is this Saṅkicca.

"O Great King, it is considered well that this one, highly esteemed as having attained the goal, has arrived in your park and is seated upon a stone slab, surrounded by a company of seers like a golden statue.
'In a state of haste,' O Great King, means that those who have gone forth are unattached to family or faction;
they would set out even while you are still traveling. Therefore, being in a state of haste, depart quickly."
"Behold the Great Seer, because he has sought after great qualities such as virtue (sīla) and the rest.
"Thereupon, monks," [the Buddha said], "having heard those words of his, immediately after that speech, the king laid [his ornaments] aside.
It is said that as soon as he reached the gate of the park, this thought occurred to him: 'Those who have gone forth...'"
"It is not fitting for one who stands in the position of a teacher to go into the presence of the ascetic Saṅkicca in a state of arrogance.

Thus he laid aside these five royal insignia: the fly-whisk with its handle of gold inlaid with jewels, the turban made of gold, the well-adorned auspicious sword, the white parasol, and the golden sandals. Therefore it is said, "he laid aside."
"Paṭicchadanti" means having set aside that very royal insignia and placed it in the hands of the treasurer.
"Dāyapassasmiṃ" means in the garden named after that. "Atha kālaṃ amaññathā" means then he knew, "Now is the time for me to ask the question.
In the Pāḷi, however, it appears as "yathākālaṃ," which refers to asking the question in accordance with the proper time.
"Ammaññatha" means "you thought. "Paṭipajjatha" means "you practiced. "Pecca" means "having gone," or it refers to the other world;
therefore, the meaning is "in the other world. "Mayā" means "by me, Bhante. He asks: "The dharma of good conduct was transgressed by me, and the deed of patricide was committed.
Tell me that: to what destination do those who kill their fathers go, and in which hell do they suffer?"
Having heard this, the Bodhisatta said, “In that case, Great King, listen,” and first gave him this advice. The Teacher, elucidating the meaning of that matter, said:
“The Seer Saṅkicca spoke to the Prosperer of the Kingdom of Kāsī, as he sat on the bank of the Dāya river: ‘Great King, listen to me.’”
“For one who is traveling on a wrong path, if he would follow the instructions of one who points out the way, he would not stumble over a thorn on the road.
For one who has entered upon what is unrighteous, if he would follow the instructions of one who points out the Dhamma...”
"If one were to act upon his word, he would not go to an evil destination.
In this context, "by a wrong path" means by a road infested with bandits. "He instructs on the path" means he points out the safe way.
"No thorn would meet him on the path" means that for that person who follows the advice, no thorn in the form of a bandit would encounter him.

"Whoever [follows] the Dhamma" means whoever follows the Dhamma of good conduct (*sucarita-dhamma*). "He shall not" means that such a person would not go to an unhappy destination (*duggati*) divided into hell and the other realms.
For unrighteousness (*adhamma*), O Great King, is like a wrong path; the Dhamma of good conduct is like the path of safety.
Yet you previously told me, "Having killed my father, I shall be king," and though I dissuaded you, you did not act upon my words.
"Having caused your father to be killed, you now grieve; indeed, one who does not follow the advice of the wise meets with great calamity, like one who has set out upon the path of a thief.
Having thus given him this exhortation, he spoke further as he taught the Dhamma:
“Dhamma is the path, O Great King, while non-Dhamma is the by-path;
non-Dhamma leads to hell, whereas Dhamma brings one to a happy destination.
Those who act contrary to Dhamma, O King, are men who live an uneven life.”
Listen to me regarding the destination they go to after passing away, which is hell:
Sañjīva, Kālasutta, Saṅghāta, and the two Roruvas;
furthermore, Mahāvīci, Tāpana, and Patāpana.
“Thus these eight hells have been described, difficult to transcend;
crowded with those of cruel deeds, each separate and sixteenfold in its intensity.
Terrible, scorching with miserliness, blazing with flames and filled with great fear.”
And with the form of Lomahaṃsa, they are terrifying, fearsome, and painful.
"Four-cornered, with four gates, divided and measured out in sections;
surrounded by iron walls and covered over with iron."
“For them there is a ground made of iron, blazing and filled with heat;
it stands pervading a hundred yojanas in every direction at all times.
These beings fall into that hell, feet upwards and heads downwards.”
“Those who transgress against the sages— those who are self-restrained and ascetic—
those destroyers of beings, men who have committed evil deeds, are cooked for an incalculable number of years, like fish caught in a net.”
“With their limbs constantly burning both inside and out,
the denizens of hell do not reach the gate, though they seek an exit.
They run toward the east, and from there they run toward the west.”
They run toward the north, and from there they run toward the south;
for whichever gate they go to, that very one is closed.
For many thousands of years, people have been going to hell.
Raising their arms, they wail, having encountered no small suffering:
"One should not attack a person of noble character who is self-restrained and ascetic, like an enraged,
fiery venomous snake that is difficult to overcome."
“Of massive body and great archer, Ajjuna, lord of the Kekakas,
with his thousand arms lopped off, having assailed the seer Gotama—
dust-throwing Daṇḍakī, having covered him, though he was free from dust, with dust, while he was emaciated.”
Like a palmyra tree cut off at its root, that king perished along with his power.
Having struck down Mātaṅga, the illustrious one,
together with his retinue, he was destroyed in the midst of the forest.
“Having struck one another with pestles against the sage Kaṇhadīpāyana,
the Andhakaveṇḍas reached the abode of Yama. Then this being,
who formerly moved through the sky by means of the sage— ”
The official sank down to the ground, having received his humble portion.
Therefore, the wise do not praise speaking out of desire;
one should speak with a mind free from malice, uttering words joined with truth.
“If a person with a corrupted mind looks upon a sage who is perfected in true knowledge and conduct, he shall go down to hell.
Those people who, being harsh in their approach, revile the elders...”
“Without heirs and without inheritors, they become like the site of a palm tree.
But he who kills one gone forth, a great seer who has accomplished his task,
will boil for a long time in the Kāḷasutta hell.”
“The king who stands on unrighteousness, a beast who destroys his kingdom,
having scorched the countryside, is cooked in a place of scorching after death.
He is cooked for a hundred thousand celestial years.”
Overwhelmed by a multitude of fires, he experiences painful sensations.
From his body, radiant crests of flame burst forth;
from the limbs, the hair, and the nails of that one who feeds on fire, flames issue out.
“With his limbs constantly burning both inside and out,
tormented by suffering, he cries out like an elephant goaded with a hook.
That lowest of men who, out of greed or hatred, kills his own father— ”
He is cooked for a long time in the Kālasutta hell.
“Such a person is cooked in a copper cauldron, and while being cooked, they are struck by spears until their skin is stripped away.
Having been blinded and made to eat urine and excrement, such a man is submerged in caustic lye.”
“Rākṣasas, taking up a heated iron ball, long plows that have been red-hot for a long time,
and obstructing crossbars with binding ropes, enter through their wide-open mouths.
Crows, jackals, vultures, and flocks of crows— birds with iron beaks— [also enter].”
Gathering together, they devour the quivering tongue, tearing it apart along with the remnants of food and blood.
"The Rākṣasas wander about, crushing that body which is like a burnt palm tree with its limbs shattered;
for even while suffering, they find pleasure in such a hell as this."
“Whoever in this world here is a slayer of their father—
having killed his mother and gone from here to the destruction of Yama—
he undergoes intense suffering, reaping the fruit of his own actions.”
“Non-human beings of exceeding strength torment the one who gives birth to them,
repeatedly crushing her with iron-tipped hair.
She herself drinks from her own limbs the blood produced from her own body.”
They force him to drink molten copper as if it were molten tin.
Having plunged into a pool that is loathsome, putrid, foul-smelling,
a mire of excrement, resembling pus and blood, he stands there.
“Then there, worms with oversized bodies and iron mouths,
greedy for flesh and blood, pierce his skin and devour him.
And he, having reached that hell, is submerged in it to the depth of a hundred men.”
The putrid corpse stinks for a hundred yojanas all around.
For even one with keen vision is overwhelmed by that odor with his very eyes.
Such, O Brahmadatta, is the suffering a woman brings.
“Having traversed the razor-edged path, sharp and difficult to cross,
those who have miscarried fall into the treacherous river Vetaraṇī.
There are iron *simbali* trees with thorns sixteen finger-breadths long.”
They hang down on both sides over the difficult-to-cross river Vetaraṇī.
Blazing with flames, they stand at a distance like masses of fire;
set ablaze by the fire-element, they rise up a league in height.
“These go to hell, upon those sharp thorns:
women who commit adultery, and men who take another’s wife.
They fall headlong, overturned and scattered in great numbers.”
With their limbs pierced through, they cry out and remain awake for long periods at all times.
Then, at the end of the night, they enter a great iron cauldron resembling a mountain,
filled with boiling water as hot as fire.
“Thus, both by day and by night, those who are immoral and shrouded in delusion experience their own karma—
the evil deeds they themselves committed in the past.
And as for that wife who was purchased with wealth, yet treats her husband with contempt...”
