Whether it be his mother-in-law, his father-in-law, or even his eldest sister-in-law—
by means of her crooked tongue, they drag him out with all his bonds.
He sees that worm-like tongue, a fathom in length, within himself.
He is unable to persuade [others], and after passing away,
he is cooked in the cauldron. "The sheep-butchers, the pig-butchers, the fishers,
the deer-trappers, the thieves, the cow-slaughterers, the hunters, and those who praise what is blameworthy."
“Being struck by spears, iron clubs, barbed missiles, and arrows,
they fall headlong into the River of Caustic Ashes.
Morning and evening, the doer of evil deeds is struck by iron clubs.”
Then they always devour the vomit of others who have spoken ill.
"Vultures, jackals, ravens, and crows with iron beaks devour the man who has committed evil as he writhes."
“Those who kill a deer with a deer, or a bird with a bird—being unwholesome and shrouded by passion, they shall go to the overflowing hell.

In this context, “the Dhamma is the path” means that the Dhamma consisting of the ten courses of wholesome action is the secure, fearless, and auspicious path. “Those who live by wrong means” refers to...
"Those who have made their livelihood by unrighteous means—'I shall tell you of the hell where they are reborn'; listen to me.

Although the Great Being was asked by the king about the hell where patricides are reborn, he did not show that first, but spoke thus in order to show the eight great hells and the sixteen subsidiary hells. For what reason? Because, first of all, in that [hell]...
If the king were shown [these hells], he would die right then and there with his heart bursting;

however, by showing him those hells, the Buddha intends that the king—seeing the beings being cooked in these hells and following their example, thinking, "There are many other evildoers like me, and I too shall be cooked among them"—will gain support and remain healthy. Thus, he shows him those hells.
The Great Being first split the earth in two by means of his power of supernormal might (*iddhibala*) and then showed it to them.

As for the meaning of their words: "Saṃjīva" is so called because the hell-beings, having been cut into pieces and hacked to bits by the hell-wardens (*nirayapāla*) who wield various blazing weapons, are restored to life again and again there. The hell-wardens...
Roaring and crying out again and again, seizing various blazing weapons,
they pursue the hell-beings back and forth across the glowing iron earth; striking them down, they cast them onto the blazing ground, and then,
seizing flaming axes while themselves shouting loudly, they hack at those wailing with a great cry of agony as they lie on their backs.
It is called Kālasutta because they cut [the beings] there with saws having sixteen teeth. It is called Saṅghāta because great blazing mountains crush [the beings] there.
There, it is said, they force the beings into a blazing iron ground nine *yojanas* deep, up to their waists, and render them motionless.
Then, a blazing iron mountain rising from the east, like a thunderbolt—
The fierce [guardians] come and, having gone toward those beings as if grinding sesame seeds for oil-pressing, they stand in the western direction;
even when emerging from the western direction, they go in that same manner and stand in the eastern direction.
Then, two of them coming together, they crush them like stalks of sugarcane in a sugarcane press. Thus, they experience suffering there for many hundreds of thousands of years.
And there are two Roruva hells: Jālaroruva and Dhūmaroruva. Therein, Jālaroruva is filled with red iron nets that remain fixed for an eon; Dhūmaroruva is filled with alkaline smoke.
In those two, when beings are being cooked in Jālaroruva, flames enter through nine openings and burn their bodies; in Dhūmaroruva, when beings are being cooked, [the flames enter] through nine...
Alkaline smoke entering through the openings of the wounds steams the body like dough.
Because the beings at both ends wail with a great roar, both are called "Roruvā.
Or else, because there is no interval (*vīci*)—that is, no gap—between the flames or between the beings being roasted there, it is "Avīci"; and a great Avīci is "Mahāvīci."
For there, rays of light arising from the eastern and other walls strike against the western and other walls;
having pierced through those walls, they extend forward for a hundred yojanas. Rays arising from below strike against the top, and rays arising from above strike against the bottom.
Thus, in this regard, there is no "interval" (*vīci*) between the rays. However, of that—
Within a hundred yojanas, the space is filled without interval by beings like a tube filled with the paste of milk-vine;
there is no measure to the number of beings at the borders who exist in the four postures, yet they do not obstruct one another, but rather pass away right where they stand.
Thus, there is no "interval" (vīci) between beings here. However, as on the tip of the tongue—
The six drops of honey are not reckoned [as suffering] because of the power of the seventh drop of molten copper which consumes them;
likewise, there, due to that power of consumption, the remaining six types of equanimity born of unwholesome kamma-result are not reckoned [as such], and only uninterrupted suffering is perceived.
Thus, in this case, there is no so-called "interval" (vīci) of suffering. This [suffering], together with its walls...

In width it is one hundred and eighteen and three-quarter *yojanas*; in circumference, however, it is nine hundred and fifty-four *yojanas*, and including its protuberances, it is ten thousand *yojanas*.
Thus its vastness is to be understood. It "torments" (*tapati*) beings who are motionless, thus it is called "The Tormentor" (*tāpana*).
It "torments exceedingly," thus it is called "The Intense Tormentor" (*patāpana*). Regarding that, first, as for the Tormentor:
They cause beings as tall as the trunk of a palmyra tree to sit upon glowing iron spikes. Below them the earth glows, the spikes glow, and the beings themselves glow.
Thus that hell torments beings who remain motionless.
In the other [hell], however, they strike the beings born there with blazing weapons and make them climb a mountain of glowing iron. Upon the summit of that mountain...
At the time they stand there, the wind of kamma strikes them. Unable to remain steady, they fall head-first with their feet upward.
Then, from the iron ground below, glowing iron spikes rise up.
They strike those very spikes with the crown of their heads, and with their bodies pierced through them, they are roasted while burning. In this way, it torments them excessively.
The Bodhisatta, however, showing these hells, first displayed the Sañjīva hell;
seeing the beings in hell being cooked there, and when a great terror had arisen among the multitude, he made it disappear. Then, once again splitting the earth in two, he showed the Kālasutta hell;
seeing the beings being cooked there as well, and when a great terror had arisen among the multitude—

"He made even that disappear"—thus he showed it in this sequence. Then, addressing the king, he said, "Great King, having seen the beings being cooked in these eight great hells, it is fitting for you to practice heedfulness," and then, in order to further describe the functions of those very same great hells, he spoke the words beginning with "These here. In that context, "declared" (akkhātā) means...
This has been told by me, and it has indeed been told by those of old. "Crowded" means filled.

Regarding the phrase "sixteen individual *ussada* hells": for each of these hells, four at each of the four gates—making sixteen *ussada* hells per hell—all together there are one hundred and twenty-eight *ussada* hells, plus the eight great hells, totaling three hundred and thirty-six hells.
“Tormenting the stingy” means that all these are torments for the stingy. They are “terrible” because of their intense suffering.
They are “flaming” because of the presence of flames produced by kamma. They are “of great terror” because of the vastness of the fear.
They are “hair-raising” because merely seeing or hearing them causes the hair to stand on end. They are “frightful” because of their terrifying nature. They are “dreadful” because they generate fear.
They are painful because they lack happiness. "Four-cornered" means that all of them are like square boxes.
"Divided" means divided by way of four gates. "Measured in parts" means measured by establishing divisions according to the gates and the streets.
"Covered over with iron" means that all of them are concealed by an iron lid nine *yojanas* in extent. "Standing full" means that all of them are filled to this extent.

"They remain without reaching a firm footing" means that they turn over and over again in various hells, falling repeatedly with their feet upward and their heads downward; it is said with reference to those who fall thus.
"Those who speak excessively" refers to those who speak by transgressing [the bounds of decency] with harsh words. It is said that in the great hells, for the most part...
Only those who have committed offenses against righteous recluses and brahmins suffer [the consequences]; therefore, he spoke thus.
"Those who destroy" (*bhūnaha*) means those who transgress against the seers; because they have destroyed their own prosperity, they are cooked like fish cut into pieces.
"Incalculable" (*asaṅkheyya*) means impossible to count. "Evil-doers" (*kibbisakārin*) means performers of cruel deeds. "Seeking exit" (*nikkhamanesin*)...
Even though they seek and search for an exit from the hells, they do not find a door of escape.
When the eastern gate is open, they run toward it; there their skin and other parts are scorched.
And when they reach the vicinity of the gate, it closes upon them as if the western gate were open.

It appears so. This method applies everywhere. "One should not approach one who is of noble character" means that one should not approach seers of noble character as one would a snake of the kind already described, nor should one approach them by striking them with harsh words or physical acts. Why is this?
Because by offending those self-restrained ascetics, one must experience great suffering in the eight great hells.
Now, in order to show those kings who, having encountered such [a being], met with that suffering, he said, beginning with “Atikāyo.
Therein, *atikāyo* means one endowed with strength and possessing a large body. *Mahissāso* means a great archer. *Kekakādhipo* means the lord of the Kekaka country.
*Sahassabāhu* refers to [the bow] which must be strung by five hundred archers and a thousand arms.
He was called Sahassabāhu because he was capable of stringing a bow. "Vibhavaṅgato" means having reached destruction.
The background stories for these cases are detailed in the Sarabhaṅga Jātaka. "Upahacca manaṃ" means having defiled one's own mind.
"Mātaṅgasmiṃ" refers to the wise Mātaṅga; the story is described in the Mātaṅga Jātaka. "Kaṇhadīpāyanāsajja" refers to Kaṇhadīpāyana.
*Āsajja*: having approached. *Yamasādhanaṃ*: the place where the commands of King Niraya-pālaka (the Guardian of Hell) are issued.
The story is related in detail in the Ghaṭapaṇḍita Jātaka. *Isinā*: by the ascetic Kapila. *Pāvekkhi*: he entered. *Cecco*:
King Cetiya. *Hīnattā*: because his state had declined; his psychic power (*iddhi*) had vanished. *Pattapariyāyaṃ*: having reached the turn [of death], that is, the time of death. The story.
This was told in the Cetiyajāataka.
Therefore, "hi" means: because one who, being under the sway of the mind, offends against the seers (isīsu), is cooked in the eight great hells;
therefore, indeed. "Chandāgamana" refers to the fourfold going on wrong paths, beginning with desire (chanda). "Paduṭṭhena" means by one who is angry.
“He goes down to hell”: by that karma which leads downward, he goes precisely down to hell.
In the Pāḷi, however, it is written as “nirayussadaṃ”; the meaning of this is that he goes to a hell of excess (ussada-niraya).
“In old age”: both in terms of physical age and in terms of the growth of virtues. “Without offspring”: the meaning is that they do not obtain offspring or heirs even in another existence.
"Like a palmyra tree" means that even in this very life, having met with great destruction like a palmyra tree whose roots have been severed, they are reborn in hell.
"And he who kills one gone forth" refers to the foolish person who kills a recluse. "For a long time" means for a long duration.
Thus the Great Being, having shown the Paccana Hell for those who harass seers, [proceeded] to show the Paccana Hell for unrighteous kings above.
Showing this, he spoke the passage beginning with “And whoever...”. Therein, “a destroyer of the kingdom” means one who goes by way of desire and so forth and brings about the ruin of the kingdom.
“Beset by a mass of flames” means surrounded by a multitude of flames. “Of one whose food is fire” refers to one who eats only fire.
“Limbs” refers to all the major and minor parts of the body within its three-league extent. “With hair and nails” means...
Together with these, all [the terms] form a single compound. Regarding "tuttaṭṭīto":

just as an elephant pierced by *tutta* arrows cries out when being subjected to the cause of the *āneñja* (imperturbable) state, so too did the Great Being, having shown the hell of torment for unrighteous kings, now [show it] for those who have killed their fathers and so forth.
To demonstrate this, he said, "He who, out of greed," and so forth. Therein, "out of greed" means out of greed for fame and wealth. "Or out of hatred" means by way of a corrupted mind.

"Skinless" means having been boiled for many thousands of years in an iron cauldron, then having their bodies stripped of skin to the extent of three *gāvutas*, they are cast upon a blazing iron ground and pounded with sharp iron spikes.

They crush and grind him. "Having made him blind," Great King, means that the guardians of hell, having thrown that patricide down supine upon the ground of glowing iron, pierce his eyes with flaming iron spikes and thus make him blind;

then, having stuffed his mouth with warm urine and excrement and turning him over like a bundle of straw, they cause him to sink into caustic liquid and molten iron that has remained stable for an eon.
They force him to eat boiling excrement and glowing iron balls;
moreover, seeing these being brought toward him, he closes his mouth.
Then, taking long, heated, flaming ploughshares, they prop open his mouth, pry it wide, and hurl an iron hook bound with rope into it.
Having pulled out the tongue, they thrust it into that open mouth and cast that iron ball inside. "Rākṣasas" refers to the guardians of hell.

Furthermore, Great King, having dragged out the tongue of that patricide with a hook, jackals—tawny, brindled, and variegated—and dogs with iron muzzles, as well as vultures and flocks of crows, tear at the tongue which has been plunged into the earth with iron spikes.

And other birds of various kinds gather together, as if cutting with weapons, dividing [the body] into portions shaped like crow's feet, and devouring the beings as if eating the quivering, bloody remains of the feast;
this is the meaning. "That burnt palm" means that the murderer of his father has a body blazing like a burning palm tree. "With limbs shattered" means...
There, their limbs are shattered here and there. "Beating them" means striking them with blazing iron clubs.
"For that is their delight" means that for those guardians of hell, that constitutes their pleasure and sport.
"But the others are miserable" means that the other beings in hell are afflicted by suffering. "Killers of fathers" refers to patricides. Thus, this [is the fate] of the patricides.
Upon seeing the Paccana hell, the king became terrified and trembling.
Then the Great Being, having comforted him, showed him the Paccana hell for those who have murdered their mothers.
*Yamakkhayaṃ* means the abode of Yama; the sense is "hell. *Attakammaphalūpago* means one who has arrived [there] by virtue of the fruit of his own karma.
"Non-humans" refers to the guardians of hell. "They produce a slayer" means they produce one who has killed his mother.
"With iron hair" means having wrapped him with iron hair, they press him with an iron machine. "Him" refers to that slayer of his mother.
"They cause to flow" means as he is being pressed, blood flows out and fills an iron pan. Then they pull him out from the machine; at that very moment, his body—
It becomes natural. Having laid him flat on his back upon the earth, they make him drink boiling blood like molten copper.

"He stands having plunged in" means that after being crushed for many thousands of years by those who extend [the press], they throw him into a vast pit of excrement—loathsome, foul-smelling, repulsive, and thick with mud; he plunges into and submerges himself in that lake.
It remains. "Of massive bodies" means having bodies the size of a single-droṇa boat. "Iron-faced" means having faces like iron needles.
"Having pierced the skin" means starting from the skin and piercing even through to the bone, they eat even the marrow. "Greedily" means being obsessed and infatuated.
Not only do they eat, but having entered through the lower orifices and so forth, they emerge from the mouth and other openings.
Entering through the left side and other parts, they emerge from the right side and other parts;
they make the entire body perforated with holes, and there he, overcome by extreme suffering, is cooked while crying out.
And he—that killer of his mother—having reached that hell which is a thousand fathoms deep, remains submerged up to his head, and that corpse extends for a hundred leagues all around.
"Having become putrid, it blows. "Matughā" means a matricide.
Thus, having shown the Paccana hell for those who kill their mothers, the Great Being spoke this verse while further showing the Paccana hell for those who cause abortions:
"Khuradhāramanukkamma" means having passed beyond the Khuradhāra hell. Therein...
It is said that the guardians of hell spread out very large plowshares with their sharp edges facing upward; then,
they pursue those women who have caused abortions by drinking abortifacient drugs, striking them with flaming weapons as they fall into pieces upon the sharp edges of the plowshares,
where they rise again and again to face that which is so difficult to overcome.
Having stepped over the Khuradhāra hell, they are pursued by the guardians of hell and fall into the river Vetaraṇī, which is difficult, hard to cross, and uneven.
The judicial punishment therein will be made clear in the Nimijātaka.
Having thus shown the hell for those who cause abortions, the Great Being [described] where the adulterers and the unfaithful wives [suffer].
And as they fall, they are roasted; showing that hell of thorny *simbali* trees, he said, "made of iron," and so forth.
Therein, "hanging down on both sides" means that the branches of those *simbali* trees hang down from both banks of the Vetaraṇī River.
"They are radiant with flames" means that those beings, whose bodies are ablaze, remain standing while emitting fire. "A league" means three-quarters of a league (*tigāvuta*).
Their bodies, together with the flames rising from them, reach a height of one *yojana*.
"They run" means that those beings who have committed adultery with others' wives, being beaten with various kinds of weapons, ascend these *simbali* trees in hell.
"They fall" means that after they have clung to the branches and foliage of the trees and burned for many thousands of years, they are [again] by the hell-wardens...
Struck by weapons, they are overturned and, having turned over, fall with their heads downward. "Many" means numerous. "With pierced limbs":
at the time of their falling from there, spikes rise up from the iron ground below and receive their heads;
these [spikes] exit through their lower passages, and thus, with bodies pierced by spikes, they lie for a long time.

"Long indeed" means that even in dreams they do not obtain sleep, but remain awake for a long time. "At the end of the nights" means with the passing of nights, that is, after a long period has elapsed.

"They go forth" [means] toward a glowing iron cauldron sixty yojanas in size, which has persisted for an eon (*kappa*) and is filled with molten copper liquid, under the supervision of the guardians of hell (*nirayapāla*).
“They are cast down and roasted. “The immoral ones” refers to those who commit adultery with another’s wife.

Thus, having shown the Simbali Niraya of roasting for those who commit the transgression of adultery, the Great Being next spoke the words beginning with “And she who,” in order to reveal the place of roasting for those who fail to fulfill their duties toward their husband, their mother-in-law, their father-in-law, and so forth. In that context, “she despises” [is explained] in the Bhisa Jātaka.
Failing to perform the duties prescribed for a wife, she disregards them. "The eldest" means the husband’s elder brother;

"the sister-in-law" means the husband’s sister. Indeed, by failing to fulfill the duties toward any of these—such as massaging their hands and feet, bathing them, or providing food—and by failing to maintain a sense of shame and moral dread toward them, she is said to "disregard them," and she too was reborn in hell.
"By the crooked" means that those who, failing to fulfill their duties toward their husbands and so forth, revile and abuse their husbands and others, are reborn in hell;
there they are made to lie down upon the red-hot earth, their mouths are forced open with iron pikes, and their tongues are pulled out with hooks.
With ropes, they are dragged along, bound in every limb. "Filled with worms" means it is teeming with worms.

This is what is meant: Great King, that being in hell sees his own tongue—driven out to a length of one fathom by fathom—covered with worms as large as great doṇa-measures, which have grown in the places repeatedly struck by weapons.
He is unable to communicate; even though he wishes to entreat the hell-wardens, he is not able to say anything at all.
"Tāpana" means that after having been boiled there for many thousands of years in this manner, she is boiled again in the Great Niraya of Tāpana.

Thus, having shown the boiling hell for those who fail to fulfill their duties toward their husbands, mothers-in-law, and fathers-in-law, the Great Being now spoke the words beginning with "Orabbhikā" (sheep-butchers) while showing the boiling hell for those such as pig-butchers. In that context, "those who praise what is blameworthy" means:
"Those who practice slander. "The Khāranadī River": the meaning is that these butchers and others, being struck by these weapons such as spears and so forth, fall into the Vetaraṇī River.
The remaining places where the butchers and others are roasted will be made clear in the Nimijātaka. "Deceivers" (kuṭakārī):
this was said with reference to those who practice fraudulent judgment and those who employ false weights and measures. In that regard—
The *paccana* hells for those who commit fraud in judicial decisions, those who forge documents, and those who practice false weighing will be made manifest in the *Nimi-jātaka*.
"Vomited" (*vanta*) means that which has been vomited. "Of those with wretched states" (*durattānaṃ*) means of those whose personal existence (*attabhāva*) is miserable. This is what is meant:
O Great King, those beings of miserable state vomit when their heads are being split by iron spikes; then, that vomit [is caught] by glowing iron slabs.
They throw some of them into the mouths [of others], so that they are said to "eat what has been vomited by others.
*Bheraṇḍaka* means jackals. *Vipphandamānaṃ* means lying face down, with the tongue pulled out, writhing here and there. *Migena* means by a wild animal that roams alone.
*Pakkhinā* means by a bird of the same kind. *Gantā te* means those who go there. *Nirayussadaṃ* means the abundance of hell.
The Ussada Hell. In the Pāli text, however, it is written as “nirayaṃ adho” (the hell below). This hell, moreover, will be made clear in the Nimijātaka.
Thus, having shown the Great Being so many hells, he now opened up the world of the devas and, showing the king the celestial realm, said:
“The virtuous go upwards by means of well-performed deeds in this world.”
"Behold the fruit of what has been well-performed: the gods together with Indra and Brahmā.
'I tell you this, O Great King: practice that Dhamma, O Lord of the Realm.
Practice the Dhamma in such a way, O King, that you will have no regret for it hereafter.'"
In that context, "peaceful" (santa) means those who are calmed by body and so forth. "Above" (uddhaṃ) refers to the world of the devas.

"Together with their lords" (sainda) means together with the respective lords (indas) in each of those places. For when the Great Being showed the devas beginning with those of the Four Great Kings, he would say, "Great King, look at the devas of the Four Great Kings;
look at the Four Great Kings themselves; look at the Tāvatiṃsa devas; look at Sakka"—thus he showed them all.
Showing the gods, including Saindaka and Sabrahmaka, he demonstrated: "This too is the fruit of what was well-performed;

this too is the fruit. "Taṃ taṃ brūmi" means: therefore, I say that to you. "Dhammaṃ" means: from now on, having abandoned the five enmities such as the taking of life, perform meritorious deeds such as giving.
"Yathā taṃ suciṇṇaṃ nānutappeyya" means: so that you might not regret that meritorious deed of giving and so forth, which was well-performed.
Because that well-performed deed was capable of concealing the remorse caused by the act of patricide, he would not feel regret;
thus, the meaning is: "Practice such well-performed deeds and perform much merit.

Having heard the Great Being’s discourse on the Dhamma, he obtained consolation from that time forward. The Bodhisatta, however, having stayed there for some time, departed for his own dwelling place.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now that he was comforted by me;

in the past as well, he was comforted by me," and he then identified the Jātaka: "At that time, King Ajātasattu was [the king], the group of seers was the Buddha’s retinue, and the wise Saṅkicca was none other than myself."
The second commentary: the *Saṃkicca-jātaka*.
The summary of the Jātakas:
Now, listen to my words regarding the Sixty [Jātakas] in this section.
The excellent one known as the Jātakas, the one known as Soṇaka and Ariṭṭhajanaka,
and likewise the excellent duties of Vuttara, Ratha, and Isibhāsiya.
The commentary on the Sixty Sections (Saṭṭhinipāta) is finished.
20. The Section of Seventy [531] 1.
The Commentary on the Kusā Grass Birth Story.
"This realm is yours"—this was related by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a monk who was despondent.

It is said that a certain son of good family living in Sāvatthī, having gone forth after dedicating his heart to the Teaching, one day while wandering for alms in Sāvatthī, saw a well-adorned woman. Grasping at her as a sign of beauty, he gazed at her;
overcome by defilements and finding no delight in the life, he remained with long hair and nails, wearing soiled robes, turned pale and wan, with his veins standing out upon his body.
Just as five portents appear for sons of the gods who are subject to falling from the celestial realms—
namely, their garlands wither, their robes become soiled, unsightliness overtakes their bodies, sweat breaks out from both armpits,
and the deity no longer delights in his divine seat— even so it is for monks who are subject to falling away and have become disenchanted with the Dispensation.

Five portents appeared: the flowers of his faith withered, the garments of his virtue became soiled, a lack of beauty arose upon his body due to both dejection and shame, the sweat of defilement broke forth from him, and he no longer took delight in forest retreats, at the foot of trees, or in empty huts.
These same signs appeared for him as well. Then the bhikkhus led him into the presence of the Teacher and said, "This one..."
“Venerable sir, we are weary,” they said. The Teacher asked him, “Is it true, bhikkhu, that you are weary?
When he replied, “It is true, venerable sir,” the Teacher said, “Bhikkhu, do not be a slave to the defilements.
This womanhood is evil; dispel your mind’s attachment to her. Delight in the Teaching. For by being attached to womenhood—”
"Indeed, even those ancient wise men, though once possessed of splendor, became devoid of splendor and fell into ruin and calamity," he said, and then related a story of the past.
In the past, in the kingdom of Malla, in the capital city of Kusāvatī, there was a king named Okkāka who ruled his realm with righteousness and impartiality.
Among his sixteen thousand women, his chief queen, named Sīlavatī, was preeminent; she was indeed...

He obtained neither a son nor a daughter. Then the city-dwellers and the inhabitants of the kingdom gathered at the gate of the royal palace and cried out, "The kingdom will perish! The kingdom will perish!
The king opened the lion-window and asked, "While I am reigning, there is no such thing as unrighteous conduct; why do you cry out?"
“Sire, it is true that there is no such thing as acting contrary to the Dhamma; however, you have no son who will protect your lineage.
Another will seize the kingdom and destroy the realm. Therefore, pray for a son capable of ruling the kingdom according to the Dhamma.
“What must we do to pray for a son? “First, for one week, let the minor dancers—”
“Having performed the Dhamma-dance, let her go; if she conceives a son, that is well.
If not, then let her perform the Middle Dance, and after that the Senior Dance. Surely, among so many women, one who possesses merit will conceive a son.
Following their words, the king did accordingly; having enjoyed himself as he pleased for seven days, he questioned each woman as they arrived.
“Have you obtained a son? they asked. “We have not obtained one, Your Majesty,” they all replied.
The king was displeased, thinking, “A son will not be born to me. The citizens again made the same petition. The king said, “Why do you petition me?
At your request, I released the theatrical troupes, yet not even one has obtained a son; what shall we do now?”
He said: “Your Majesty, these women will be immoral and lacking in merit;
they possess no merit for obtaining a son. Even though you do not obtain a son from them, do not become indifferent.
Your chief queen is virtuous and endowed with moral conduct; release her, and a son will be born to her.”

Having agreed by saying, "Very well," he had a drum beaten, proclaiming: "It is said that on the seventh day from now, the king will release Queen Sīlavatī after making her perform a 'Dharma-dance'; let men assemble!
On the seventh day, having had the queen adorned and brought down from the royal palace, he released her. By the power of her virtue, [the light reached] Sakka’s abode.
He manifested the appearance of heat. Sakka, reflecting on the thought "What could this be?", understood that the goddess was longing for a son.
Thinking, "It is right for me to grant her a son; is there perhaps a son in the world of the gods who is suitable for her?", he searched and beheld the Bodhisatta.
It is said that at that time, having exhausted his lifespan in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, [the Bodhisatta] was in the higher celestial realms.

He desired to be reborn there. Sakka went to the door of his celestial mansion, summoned him, and said, "Mārisa, it is fitting for you to go to the human world and take rebirth in the womb of the chief queen of King Okkāka.
Having obtained his consent, he further told another son of the gods, "You too shall be her son."
Thinking, "Let no one break her virtue," he went to the gate of the king's residence in the guise of an elderly brahmin.
A great crowd of people, having bathed and adorned themselves, had gathered at the royal gate, each crying out, "I will take the queen! I will take the queen!
Upon seeing Sakka, they mocked him, asking, "Why have you come? Sakka said, "What [have I done]?"
“You may revile me; though my body has grown old, my passion does not age.
If I obtain a virtuous woman, I shall take her and depart,” he said, and by his own supernatural power, he stood right in front of everyone.
No one else was able to stand before him due to his majesty. He [then saw] her, adorned with every ornament...
Taking her by the hand as she was departing from the residence, he set out.
Then, those standing here and there reviled him, saying, "Look, sirs! This old Brahmin is taking away a queen endowed with such supreme beauty;
he does not know what is appropriate for himself. Yet the queen did not feel distressed or ashamed, thinking, "This old man is taking me away."
The king, standing at the window and looking out, wondering, "Who is taking the queen away?", saw him and became displeased.
Sakka, having taken her, departed from the city gate and, near the gate, conjured up a house with its door open and a seat prepared with a spread of grass.
Then she asked him, "Is this your dwelling? He replied, "Yes, lady."
"Previously I was alone, but now there are two of us. I shall go out for alms and bring back rice and other provisions;
you lie down on this bed of straw," he said. Then, stroking her with his soft hand and causing her to experience a divine touch, he had her lie down there.
Through the pervasion of that divine touch, she lost consciousness. Then—
By his own supernatural power, he led her to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and had her lie down upon a celestial bed in a decorated palace.
On the seventh day, having woken up and seen that splendor, she realized, "That brahmin was not a human; he must be Sakka.
At that time, Sakka was at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree, surrounded by celestial dancers.
He sat down. She rose from her bed, went to him, paid homage, and stood to one side.
Then Sakka said to her, “I grant you a boon, O Queen; choose it. “In that case, O Lord, give me a son,” she replied.
“Queen, let alone one son; I shall give you two sons. Of those two, however, one will be wise.”
"One will be ugly; one will be handsome but not wise. Which of these two do you prefer first?
"The wise one, O King," she replied. Saying "Very well," he gave her kusa-grass, divine garments, divine sandalwood, a *pāricchattaka* flower, and a lute named Kokanuda;
taking these, he entered the king’s bedchamber together with her.
Having made her lie down on the same bed, he touched her navel with his thumb.
At that moment, the Bodhisatta took conception in her womb. Sakka also returned to his own place. The wise queen knew that she was pregnant.
Then the king, having woken up and seen her, asked, "Queen, by whom were you taken? She replied, "By Sakka, Your Majesty.
He said, "I saw with my own eyes an old brahmin taking you away as he went; why do you deceive me? She said, "Believe me, Your Majesty;
Sakka took me and led me to the world of the gods. "I do not believe you, Queen," he replied. Then to him—
She showed him some *kusatṛṇa* grass given by Sakka and said, "Believe me.
The king did not believe her, thinking, "Grass called *kusatṛṇa* can be obtained from anywhere. Then she showed him celestial garments and other such things.
Having seen them and believing her, the king asked, "My lady, let Sakka take you away for now; have you obtained a son? "I have," she replied.
“Great King, I am pregnant. He was delighted and provided her with the necessary care for her pregnancy.
At the end of ten months, she gave birth to a son; they did not give him another name, but called him by the very name of the *kusaka* grass.
When Prince Kusaka reached the age of walking on his own feet, the other deva-son took rebirth in her womb. When the ten months were complete—
He gave birth to a son, and they gave him the name Jayampati. They grew up with great splendor.
The Bodhisatta was wise; without having learned any craft from a teacher, he attained mastery in all skills through his own wisdom.
Then, when he was sixteen years old, the king, desiring to give him the kingdom, addressed the queen: "My dear, for your son..."
"Once we have given him the kingdom and established the theatrical performances, we shall see him firmly established on the throne while we ourselves are still living.
Furthermore, whichever king throughout the whole of Jambudīpa desires his daughter, we shall bring her and make her his chief queen;
find out his mind—whichever princess pleases him. She agreed, saying, "Very well."
“Having reported this news to the prince, find out his mind,” he sent a female attendant.
She went and reported that news to him. Upon hearing it, the Great Being thought: “I am not handsome;
even if the princess, who is endowed with beauty, were brought here, she would see me and flee, thinking, ‘What have I to do with this ugly man? Thus, there is nothing for us to be ashamed of.”
“...there will be [a time]. What use is household life to me? Having attended upon my parents while they live, I shall go forth into homelessness after their passing.
He said, “I have no need for the kingdom, nor for the theatrical performances; I shall go forth into homelessness after my parents have passed away.
She went and reported his words to the queen, and the queen [reported them] to the king.
He reported this. The king, becoming displeased, sent a message again after a few days.
He likewise refused it. Having thus refused it up to the third time, on the fourth occasion he thought:
"It is certainly not fitting to be in a state of absolute opposition toward one's mother and father; I shall employ a stratagem."
So, having summoned the chief goldsmith and given him much gold, he sent him away with the command, "Make an image of a woman.
When the goldsmith had departed, he took other gold and made a female image himself.
For the intentions of Bodhisattas are indeed fulfilled. That golden image possessed a beauty so exquisite that it was beyond description even by the tongue. Then—
The Great Being had him dressed in linen cloth and placed him in the inner chamber of glory.
When he saw the image brought by the chief artisan, he censured it and said, "Go and bring the image that was placed in our inner chamber of glory.
Having entered the inner chamber, he saw it and thought, "A celestial nymph must have come here to sport with the prince."
Unable to stretch out his hand, he went out and said, "Your Majesty, the noble lady stands all alone in the chamber of glory;
I am not able to approach her. "Dear son, go, bring this golden image," he was sent again, and he brought it.
The prince had the image made by the smith placed in the golden chamber and had the one he himself had made adorned.
Having placed [the image] on a chariot, he sent it to his mother with the message: "If you find such a girl, take her.
She summoned the ministers and said, "Sirs, my son is of great merit and has been given by Sakka;
he will obtain a suitable maiden. If you find such a girl, you should take her. Place this image in a covered carriage..."
"Traveling throughout the whole of Jambudīpa, find a king who has such a daughter as this;
having given her to him, come back after fixing a date, saying, 'King Okkāka will enter into marriage with you.
They replied, "Very well," and taking her with them, they set out with a great retinue and wandered about until they reached a royal capital. There—

In the evening, at the place where the great multitude had gathered, they adorned that image with garments, flowers, and ornaments, placed it upon a golden palanquin, and set it down on the path leading to the ford.
The ministers themselves withdrew and stood to one side to listen to the conversations of those who came and went. When the great multitude looked at it, they perceived it as a "golden image."
Without having done so, he departs while praising her, saying: "Even though she is a human woman, she shines exceedingly like a celestial nymph;
what indeed is she standing for here, or from where has she come? There is no one of such beauty in our city.
Hearing this, the ministers said: "If there were a girl of such a kind here, [we would know her] just as we know such-and-such a king's daughter."
“They would say, ‘She is the daughter of a minister,’ yet surely there is no such person here. Taking her with them, they went to another city.
Wandering in this manner, they eventually reached the city of Sāgala in the kingdom of Madda.
There, King Madda had eight daughters who possessed supreme beauty and were like celestial nymphs; the eldest of them was Pabhāvatī.
Her name was Pabhāvati. From her body radiated a brilliance like the light of the morning sun;
even in the darkness, there was no need for a lamp within the four-cubit inner chamber, as the entire room became filled with a single uniform light. Her nurse, however, was a hunchbacked woman;
she fed Pabhāvati and, in order to bathe her head, had eight maidens of beautiful appearance take up eight jars.
In the evening, while going for water, she saw that effigy standing on the path to the bathing place;

thinking it was Pabhāvatī, she became angry, saying, "This ill-behaved woman has sent us for water, intending to bathe her head, yet she has arrived first and is standing on the path to the bathing place!
She cried out, "O you who bring shame upon the family! Having arrived before us..."
"Why are you standing here? If the king finds out, he will destroy us," she said, and as she struck the side of her cheek with her hand, it felt as if the palm of her hand were being split apart.
Then, realizing it was a "golden figure," she went toward those female attendants laughing and said, "Look at this work of mine; thinking it was my own daughter—"
“I gave her a blow; what does she count for compared to my daughter? My hand has merely been made to suffer,” he said.
Then the king’s messengers seized him and asked, “When you said, ‘My daughter is more beautiful than this,’ whom were you speaking of?
“Pabhāvati, the daughter of King Madda; this image is not even one-sixteenth part of her beauty.”
“It is not worth even a fraction. With joyful hearts, they went to the king’s gate and announced, “The messengers of King Okkāka stand at the gate.
The king rose from his seat and, while still standing, said, “Summon them!
They entered, paid homage to the king, and said, “Great King, our king inquires after your health. Having been accorded hospitality and honor, they—
When asked, “For what purpose have you come? they replied, “Our king Sīhassara has a son named Prince Kusa;
the king wishes to give him the kingdom and has sent us to you. It is said that you have a daughter named Pabhāvatī;
give her to him, and accept this golden image as a gift. And they gave that image to him.
They gave it. He too, with a joyful heart, accepted it, thinking, "There will be a marriage ceremony with such a great king.
Then the messengers said to him, "Great King, we cannot afford to delay;
we shall inform the king that the maiden has been obtained, and then he will come and take her away. He replied, "Very well."
Having spoken thus, he paid them honor and dismissed them. They went and reported this to the king and the queen.
The king, departing from Kusāvatī with a great retinue, arrived in due course at the city of Sāgala.
King Madda went out to meet him, led him into the city, and rendered him great honor.
Because she was wise, Queen Sīlavatī thought, "Who knows what might happen?
and after one or two days had passed, she said to King Madda, "Great King, we wish to see our daughter-in-law. He agreed, saying, "Very well," and had her summoned.
Pabhāvatī, adorned with all her ornaments and surrounded by her circle of attendants, arrived and paid homage to her mother-in-law. She [the queen]—her...
Having seen her, he thought: "This young woman is beautiful, while my son is ugly.
If she should see him, she will not stay even for a single day but will flee; I must devise a stratagem. He addressed the King of Madda:
"Great King, this daughter-in-law is worthy of my son; however, there is a custom handed down through our family lineage..."
“There is,” he said. “If she will conduct herself according to that custom, I shall take her away. “But what is your custom?
“In our lineage, as long as a single pregnancy has been established, a woman is not permitted to see her husband during the day.
If she acts in this manner, I shall take her away. The king asked, “What is it, my lady? Will you be able to do it?”
He asked his daughter, "Shall we speak thus? She replied, "Yes, father.
Then King Okkāka gave much wealth to the King of Madda and departed, taking her with him. The King of Madda also sent his daughter away with a great retinue.
Okkāka went to Kusāvatī, had the city decorated, released all prisoners, and performed the consecration for his son.
Having established his reign and appointed Pabhāvati as his chief queen, he caused a drum to be beaten throughout the city, proclaiming, "This is the command of King Kusa.
All the kings on the surface of Jambudīpa who had daughters sent their daughters to King Kusa;
those who had sons, desiring friendship with him, sent their sons to serve as his attendants.
The Bodhisatta had a vast retinue of dancers and ruled with great glory.
He was not permitted to see Pabhāvati by day, nor was she permitted to see him by day; for both of them, there was only meeting at night.
Therein, even the bodily radiance of Pabhāvati became indistinguishable [from his]. From the inner chamber of glory, the Bodhisatta...
He would go out only at night.
After a few days had passed, desiring to see the light by day, he informed his mother. She refused him, saying, "My dear son, do not wish for this;
wait until you have obtained a son. He, however, continued to entreat her again and again. Then—
She said to him, "In that case, go to the elephant stable and stand there in the guise of a young male elephant;
I will bring you there. Then, having filled your eyes [with collyrium], you should look about, but do not let yourself be recognized.
He agreed, saying, "Very well," and went to the elephant stable. Then his mother had the elephant stable decorated and [sent] Pabhāvati...
Saying, “Come, let us see your husband’s elephants,” she led her there and showed them to her, saying, “This elephant is named so-and-so; this elephant is named so-and-so.
There, the king saw her following behind her mother and, disguised as an elephant-keeper, struck her on the back with a lump of elephant fodder.
She became angry and thought, “I will tell the king and have his hand cut off!”
Having said this, she provoked the queen to anger. The queen mother, saying, "Do not be angry, my dear," consoled her daughter-in-law and massaged her back.
Again, the king, desiring to see her, went to the stable in the guise of a horse-keeper; seeing her there, he struck her in the same manner with a lump of horse-dung.
At that time as well, his mother-in-law consoled her when she was angry.
On another day, Pabhāvatī, desiring to see the Great Being, informed her mother-in-law;
although she was repeatedly refused with the words, "Enough, do not let it please you," she requested again and again.
Then she said to her, "In that case, tomorrow my son will perform a circumambulation of the city; you should open the lion-window and look upon him. And so it was.
Having said this, on the following day he had the city decorated, dressed Prince Jayampatika in royal attire, seated him upon the back of an elephant,
and having seated the Bodhisatta on the seat behind, he caused the city to be circumambulated clockwise.
Pabhāvati, taking [her daughter] with her, stood at the lion-window and said, "Behold the majesty and splendor of your husband!"
She said, "I have obtained a husband worthy of me," and she was delighted.

On that day, however, the Great Being, having sat in the back seat with the Jayampati in the guise of a young elephant, looked toward Pabhāvati according to his intention and displayed playful gestures according to her heart's desire through the movements of his trunk and other limbs. When the elephant had passed by, the Queen Mother—
She asked Pabhāvati, “Mother, did you see your husband? “Yes, noble lady;
however, the elephant-mendicant sitting in his rear seat was extremely ill-behaved and made gestures with his trunk toward me.
Why have they allowed such an ill-omened being to sit in the king’s rear seat? Have him removed! “Mother, in the king’s rear seat—”
“Protection indeed must be sought.
She thought: “This young elephant is exceedingly fearless; he does not even perceive the king as a ‘king.
Is this perhaps King Kusa himself? Surely he must be extremely deformed, which is why he does not [fear me].”
“...granting [this]! She then spoke into the ear of the hunchback: “Mother, go for now and find out whether the king is sitting on the front seat or the back seat. “But how shall I know?
“If he is indeed the king, he will be the first to dismount from the back of the elephant; know it by this sign.”
Having gone there, she stood to one side; first she saw the Great Being descending, and afterwards she saw Prince Jayampatika.
The Great Being, looking here and there, saw the hunchback and realized, "It must be for this very reason that she has come.
He called her over, and after firmly instructing her, "Do not speak of this matter to Pabhāvati," he sent her away.
Having gone there, she said, "The one sitting on the first seat descended first. Pabhāvatī believed her words.
The Great Being, wishing to see him again, entreated his mother.
Unable to refuse him, she said, "In that case, go to the park in an unknown guise. He went to the park and [stood] up to his neck in the lotus pond.
Having entered the water, she stood with her head covered by a lotus leaf and her face concealed by a blooming lotus.
Her mother, Pabhāvati, having led her to the garden, set out toward the edge of the lotus pond at evening time, tempting her by saying, "Look at these trees!
Look at the birds! Look at the deer! She [saw] the pond covered with five kinds of lotuses.
Having seen the lotus pond, she wished to bathe; descending into the pond with her attendants, she played there.
Seeing that lotus, she reached out her hand, desiring to pluck it. Then the king, having removed the lotus leaf, said, "I am King Kusa," and seized her by the hand.
Upon seeing his face, she cried out, "A yakkha has seized me!"
Having cried out, she fell unconscious right there. Then the king released her hand. Regaining consciousness, she thought:
"It seems King Kusarāja seized me by the hand; it was because of this that I was struck with a morsel of elephant dung from the elephant stable and a morsel of horse dung from the horse stable.
This very man sat on the hindquarters of the elephant and mocked me."
"What use have I for such a foul-faced husband? Abandoning him, while I am still alive, I shall find another husband," she thought.
Having summoned the ministers who had come with her, she said, "Prepare my carriage and conveyance;
I shall depart this very day. They reported this to the king. The king thought: "If she does not obtain permission to go..."
Thinking, "Her heart will break; let her go, and I shall bring her back again by my own power," he then gave her permission to depart. She went straight to her father’s city.
The Great Being also entered the city from the park and ascended his decorated palace. For she [had been devoted] to the Bodhisatta...
He did not desire it because of his previous aspiration; yet, due to his own past karma, he became deformed.
It is said that in the past, in the city of Bārāṇasī, in a village near the gate, two families lived—one on the upper street and one on the lower street.
One family had two sons, and the other had only one daughter. Between the two sons, the Bodhisatta was the younger. Regarding him—
They gave the maiden to the eldest brother. The youngest, not being one to support a wife, remained living right with his brother.
Then one day, they baked an excessive amount of cakes in that house. The Bodhisatta had gone out into the forest.
Having set aside a cake for him, they divided the remainder and ate it. At that moment, a Paccekabuddha came to the door of the house for alms.
The wife of the Bodhisatta’s younger brother, thinking, “I will bake another cake for my husband,” took that [dough] and gave it to the Paccekabuddha.
He too returned from the forest at that very moment. Then she said to him, “Husband, compose your mind;
your portion was given to the Paccekabuddha. He [replied], “Having eaten your portion, [he ate] my portion...”
“Desi, what shall I eat? she asked, and becoming angry, she followed the Paccekabuddha and took the cake from his bowl.
She went to her mother’s house, brought fresh, melted ghee the color of a campaka flower, and filled the Paccekabuddha’s bowl with it;
it emitted a brilliant radiance. Seeing this, she made a resolution: “Venerable Sir, by this...”
"By the power of my generosity, may my body be radiant in every place where I am reborn, may I possess the most excellent form, and may I never dwell in the same place as this unworthy man.
Thus, on account of this former aspiration, she did not desire him. The Bodhisatta, having dropped that cake into the bowl of ghee, [gave it to her].
He made this aspiration: "Venerable sir, may there be one capable of bringing even this man, though he lives a hundred leagues away, to serve as my foot-attendant.
In this regard, because of that past karma of his taking the cake while angry, he became deformed; and due to his former aspiration, she did not desire him.
When Pabhāvati had departed, he was overcome with grief; even though the other women entertained him in various ways, they were unable to make him look at them.
His entire residence, bereft of Pabhāvati, seemed empty to him.
Thinking, "She must have reached the city of Sāgala by now," he went to his mother's presence at the time of dawn.
Saying, “Mother, I shall bring Pabhāvati back; you rule the kingdom,” he spoke the first verse:
“This kingdom of yours, with its wealth and its equipment, with its own people and endowed with all objects of desire—rule this kingdom, Mother; I am going to where my beloved Pabhāvati is.”
In this context, "with its equipment" means accompanied by elephant-riders and other such gear. "With its life-force" means together with the five insignia of royalty.

"Command me, mother," he said thus because it was improper for him to take back the kingdom after having given it away; therefore, instead of entrusting it to his father or brother, he entrusted it to his mother.
Having heard his words, she said, "In that case, dear son, you must be diligent; for women are indeed impure at heart.
She then filled a golden bowl with various kinds of choice food and sent him off, saying, "Eat this on the way.
Taking it and bowing to his mother, he circumambulated her three times and said, "While living..."
Having said, "I shall see you again," he entered the inner chamber, fastened his five weapons,
tied a thousand kahāpaṇas together in a bundle along with a food bowl, took his lute Kokanuda, and departed from the city.
Setting out on the road, being of great strength and great power, he traveled fifty yojanas by midday.
Having eaten his meal, he traveled another fifty yojanas during the remainder of the day;
thus, having covered a path of one hundred yojanas in a single day, he bathed at eventide and entered the city of Sāgala.
As soon as he had entered, by the power of his majesty, Pabhāvatī was unable to remain upon the surface of her bed and descended, lying down upon the ground.
Seeing the Bodhisatta walking along the street with his faculties exhausted, a certain woman called him over, had him sit down, had his feet washed, and provided him with a bed.
With his body weary, he lay down and fell asleep.
Then, when he had fallen asleep, she prepared food, woke him, and fed him. He—
Delighted, he gave her a thousand kahāpaṇas along with the bowl of rice.
Leaving his five weapons right there and saying, "I have a place to go," he took his lute and went to the elephant stable.
He said to the elephant keepers, "Please let me stay here today; I shall perform music for you. Having been granted permission by them, he went to one side.
Having lain down and slept for a short while, his fatigue subsided;

he rose, set aside his lute, and sang while playing the instrument, saying, "Let the inhabitants of the city of Sāgala hear this sound! Pabhāvatī, lying on the ground, heard that sound and recognized it:
"This is not the sound of another's lute; without a doubt, King Kusa has come for my sake."
King Madda, too, having heard that sound, thought: "He plays with exceeding sweetness; tomorrow I shall have him summoned and have him perform music for me.
The Bodhisatta, thinking, "It is impossible for one dwelling here to see Pabhāvatī; this is not the right place," departed at dawn.
Having eaten his morning meal at the very house where he had dined in the evening, and having set aside his lute, he went into the presence of the royal potter.
Adopting the status of a pupil under him, he filled the house with clay in a single day.
Saying, "Teacher, I shall make vessels," and being told, "Yes, go ahead," he placed a lump of clay upon the wheel.
He spun the wheel; once set in motion, it continued spinning until midday had passed.
Having fashioned various small and large vessels, while he was making a vessel for Pabhāvatī’s sake, he brought forth various forms.
For the intention of Bodhisattas is indeed fulfilled; those forms [appeared] to Pabhāvatī herself.
“Let him see,” he resolved. Having dried all the vessels and baked them, he filled his house with them.
The potter took various vessels and went to the royal palace. When the king saw them, he asked, “By whom were these made?
“By me, Your Majesty. “I know they were made by you; tell me, by whom were they actually made? “By my pupil, Your Majesty.”
“He is not your pupil; he is your teacher. You should learn the craft from him.
From now on, let him make vessels for my daughters, and give him this thousand pieces.
Having had the thousand pieces given to him, she said, “Give these various colored small vessels to my daughters.”
So, having led them to those women, he said, "These small vessels are for your amusement.
They all came forward. The potter gave to Pabhāvatī only the vessel that had been made for the Great Being's sake.
She took the vessel and, upon it, [painted] the likeness of herself, of the Great Being, and of the hunchbacked woman.
Having seen it and realized, "This was not made by anyone else; it was made by King Kusarāja himself," she became angry, threw it on the ground, and said, "I have no need for this;
give it to those who want it. Then her sisters, perceiving her anger, said, "You think this small vessel was made by King Kusarāja, but it was not made by him; it was made by a potter."
“Do as he says; take it! they said, laughing at him. She did not tell them that he had done it or that he had come.
The potter gave a thousand pieces to the Bodhisatta and said, “Dear son, the king is pleased with you.
From now on, you should make vessels for the king’s daughters, and I shall carry them away for them.”
Thinking, "In this case as well, it is not possible for me to see Pabhāvati while living here," he gave those one thousand [pieces] to that very man,
went into the presence of the carpenter who was the king’s attendant, and becoming his apprentice, he made a palm-leaf fan for the sake of Pabhāvati;
and right there, taking a white parasol, a drinking-ground, and a cloth, he stood where Pabhāvati was.
He displayed various forms. The reed-worker took that and other articles he had made and went to the royal palace.
When the king saw them, he asked, "By whom were these made? and after giving a thousand pieces of money just as before, he said, "Give these reed-worker’s wares to my daughters.
He [the reed-worker] also [took] the palm-leaf fan made by the Bodhisatta for the sake of Pabhāvati.
He gave them to her alone. There, other people did not see the forms;

however, Pabhāvatī, having seen them and realized they were made by a skilled artisan, became angry and, saying, "Let those who wish to take them take them," she threw them onto the ground. Then the others mocked her.
Nalakāra brought back a thousand [pieces of gold], gave them to the Bodhisatta, and reported what had occurred.
Thinking, "This too is a point where I have no recourse," he gave a thousand pieces to that very man and went into the presence of the royal florist.

Having entered into the status of an apprentice, he fashioned various kinds of floral arrangements and made a single cushion (*cumbaṭaka*) of many colors and diverse forms for the sake of Pabhāvati. Taking all of that, the florist went to the royal palace.
The king, seeing them, asked, "By whom were these woven? "By me, Your Majesty," he replied. "I know that they were woven by you;
tell me, by whom were they actually woven? "By my pupil, Your Majesty. "He is not your pupil; he is your teacher.
You learned the craft from him. From now on, he shall [be the one] for my daughters..."
“Let him weave flowers and give him this thousand pieces,” she said, and having given the thousand, she added, “Give these flowers to my daughters.
He, for his part, gave her the head-cloth that had been made by the Bodhisatta for Pabhāvati’s sake.
There, seeing various forms together with the images of herself and the king, she recognized that it was indeed made by him.
Having realized this, he became angry and threw it on the ground. The other sisters mocked him in the same way.
The garland-maker also brought a thousand [pieces of gold], gave them to the Bodhisatta, and reported what had happened.
Thinking, "This too is a point where I have no standing," he gave the thousand to the Bodhisatta himself and went into the presence of the king’s cook.

Having gone there, he entered into the status of a pupil. Then one day, while the cook was carrying a variety of dishes for the king’s meal, he gave some bone and flesh to the Bodhisatta to cook for himself.
He prepared it in such a way that its fragrance pervaded the entire city. When the king smelled it, he asked, "Is there any other meat in your kitchen?"
“Are you cooking it? he asked. “No, Your Majesty; however, some bone and flesh were given to me for the purpose of cooking for my pupil, and that must be its scent.
The king had it brought and placed a small amount on the tip of his tongue;
immediately, it pervaded and agitated the seven thousand channels that carry the flavors. The king, bound by craving for taste, gave a thousand [pieces of gold].

Having given [the money], he said: "From now on, having have your pupil cook food for me and for my daughters, you bring it to me, and let him bring it to my daughters. The cook went and informed him. Upon hearing this, he thought:
"Now my desire has reached its fulfillment; now I shall be able to see Pabhāvati."

Satisfied, he gave that thousand pieces back to him; then, on the following day, having prepared the meal and sent the king’s food vessels, he himself took the food-basket for the princesses and ascended the palace where Pabhāvati lived.
Seeing him ascending the palace while carrying that food-basket, she thought: "This man is unworthy of himself..."

"She performs the work that must be done by slaves and laborers. However, if I remain silent for a few days, she will think, 'Now he has taken a liking to me,' and instead of going anywhere, she will stay right here looking at me.
Therefore, I shall immediately revile and scold her, not allowing her to stay here even for a moment, and drive her away. She [opened] the door.
Having opened the door halfway, he placed one hand on the doorframe, pressed the bolt with the other hand, and recited the second verse:

“O Kusa, you who carry a great burden while being crooked, whether by day or by night at the hour of midnight, return quickly to Kusāvatī! I have no desire for you while you dwell here, for you are ill-favored.”
The meaning of this is: O Great King, even if someone were to cut off your head while you were acting as a cook with a straightforward mind, you would not perform such an act for him;
yet, because you carry this great burden for my sake with a crooked mind, you will experience great suffering day and night, at all hours. What use is that to you?
"Because of the suffering you have experienced, you should return to your own city of Kusāvatī;
having made another female spirit (*yakkhinī*) who resembles you and has a face shaped like an overripe *atirasa* cake your chief queen, rule the kingdom.
"I do not wish for you to live here in such ugliness. "But I do not wish for you, being so ugly and ill-proportioned, to live here."
Thinking, "I have received this message from Pabhāvatī," his heart filled with joy, he spoke these three verses:
"I will not go from here to Kusāvatī, for I am captivated by the beauty of Pabhāvatī.
I delight in the lovely palace of Madda, having abandoned your kingdom, intent on seeing her."
“O Pabhāvatī, enticed by your beauty, I wander the earth utterly bewildered;
I know not the direction, nor from where I have come, for I am intoxicated by you, O deer-eyed one.
You, clad in golden bark-garments and wearing a beautiful girdle of gold—”
"O Sussoni, your desires are indeed [my concern], for I have no need for the kingdom.
Therein, "I delight" means I am pleased; I do not feel weary. "Being utterly deluded" means being deluded by the defilements (*kilesa*).
"I am intoxicated by you" means I am intoxicated by you, or I am maddened by you. "Clad in golden bark-garments" means wearing garments woven from cloth adorned with gold.
“I am not desirous of the kingdom” means that I have no need for the kingdom.
When this was said, she thought: “I was reviling him thinking he would feel remorse, yet he speaks as if he is already filled with passion;
what if he were to take me by the hand and say, ‘I am King Kusa’?”
“Let us shut the door and give the key so that no one may hear this conversation,” she said, and having closed the door and given the key, she stood inside.
He too brought a basket of rice, increased the amount of food, and fed the princesses.
Pabhāvatī sent the hunchback, saying, “Go and bring cooked rice from King Kusa. She brought it and said, “Eat. [He replied,] “I do not...”
"Therefore, I shall eat cooked rice; you, having eaten, take your own portion of grain, cook the rice, and bring it to me.
And do not tell anyone that King Kusara has arrived.
From then on, the hunchback brought her portion and ate herself, while she presented her own portion to her. King Kusara, from that time forward—
Not being able to see her, he thought: "Does Pabhāvati have affection for me, or does she not?
I shall test her. Having fed the princesses, he took his food-basket and set out;
at her chamber door, he struck the palace floor with his foot, rattled the vessels, and stamped his feet until he fainted.
Having offered it, he fell face down as if burnt. Hearing the sound of his groaning, she opened the door and, seeing him covered by the rice-pot, thought:
"This king, the foremost in all Jambudīpa, undergoes suffering day and night on my account;
because of his delicacy, he has fallen, covered by the rice-pot. Is he still alive, or not? She—
Having emerged from the womb, she extended her neck to look at his face in order to perceive the scent of his breath.
He took a mouthful of saliva and spat it onto her body. She rebuked him, entered the womb, and standing with the door half-open, she spoke this verse:
“Misfortune, O King, befalls him who desires what he does not wish for;
you desire the undesired, O King, and you seek to find pleasure in what is unpleasant.
In this context, *abbhūti* means *abhūti*, which signifies non-prosperity.
But because his mind was bound [to her], even though he was being reviled and insulted, he did not give rise to remorse and immediately spoke this verse:
“Whether unwillingly or willingly, the man who gains what is dear to him— In this case we praise the gain;
in that case, lack of gain is wretched.”
Even as he was speaking thus, she did not desist, but spoke even more stubborn words; wishing to deceive him, she recited the other verse:
“You are digging for the essence of stone with the wood of the *kaṇikāra* tree;
you seek to strike the wind with a net—you who desire that which does not desire you.”
In that context, "with the wood of the *kaṇikāra* tree" means with *kaṇikāra* timber. "You oppress" means you bind.
Having heard that, King Tissa spoke these three verses:
"Surely a stone has been placed within your heart, O lady of gentle marks!"
“I find no pleasure in you, having come from a foreign land.
When the princess looks at me with a frown,
I become a mere servant in King Madda’s inner palace.”
“When the princess looked at me with a smile, I was then Nāḷāgiri, and Kusa was then the king.
In this context, *mudulakkhaṇe* means endowed with the soft characteristics of a woman. *Yo* refers to me, who [came] from a foreign kingdom.
"Having come into your presence and living here, I do not receive even the pleasure of a simple welcome; thus I think:
surely a stone has been placed in your heart to prevent the arising of affection for me.
"Making a frown" means making the forehead wrinkled and uneven due to anger. "Cook" (āḷārika) means a food-preparer. At that moment, I was in the inner palace of King Madda.
"I am like a slave who prepares food," he says. "Smiling" means laughing while displaying a cheerful expression.
"I am a king"—at that moment, I am like a king ruling in the city of Kusāvatī;
why are you so harsh? From now on, do not act in such a way, my dear.
Having heard his words, she thought: "He speaks with excessive intimacy; by telling a lie, I shall use a stratagem to drive him away from here. She then spoke this verse:
"If indeed the word of the fortune-tellers should prove true, you shall not be my husband;
let them cut me into seven pieces as they please!"
The meaning of this is: "Great King, I consulted many fortune-tellers as to whether this King Kusarāja would become my husband or not;
they said, 'Even if they were to cut me into seven pieces, you certainly will not become my husband.'"
Having heard this, the king, warding her off, said: "Bhadde, I too questioned the fortune-tellers in my own kingdom;
they declared, 'There is no other husband for you but King Kusarāja Sīhasaraka.
I also spoke thus by means of the power of my own knowledge," and he spoke the following verse:
“If indeed the word of others, or my own, is true, then you have no other husband, O Kusā of lion-like voice.
The meaning of this is: whether the word of those other fortune-tellers is true, or whether my own word is true, there is no other husband for you.
Having heard his words, she thought, "It is impossible to shame him or make him flee;
what use have I for him? She closed the door and did not show herself. He too, taking up his carrying-pole, descended; from that time on, he was unable to see her.
While performing the work of a cook, he grew exceedingly exhausted; having finished his morning meal, he split firewood.
He washed the vessels, fetched water with a carrying-pole, and slept on the floor of the storehouse.
Rising early in the morning, he cooked the rice-gruel and other foods, carried them out, and fed [the family]. Driven by delight and lust (*nandirāga*), he experienced extreme suffering.
One day, seeing a hunchbacked woman passing by the door of the house where he ate, he called her to him. Out of fear of Pabhāvati, she...
Unable to go near him, she went as if in great haste. Then, approaching her with speed, he said, "Hunchback!
She turned back and stood still, saying, "Who is this? He replied, "I do not hear your voice.
Then he said to her, "Hunchback, both you and your mistress are exceedingly stiff; for all this time [you have been] in your presence..."
Vāsantī said, "I do not receive even a message regarding my health; what gift could you possibly give me?
But let that be for now—will you be able to make my humpbackedness soft and show it to me? She accepted, saying, "Very well.
Then [the other] said to her, "If you will be able to show it to me, I shall straighten your humpbackedness."
Enticing her with the words, "I will have a neck-ornament made for you," she spoke these five verses:
"O hunchback, having reached Kusāvatī, I shall have a necklace made for your neck, if you,
O radiant one with thighs like an elephant's trunk, would look upon me."
“O hunchback, having reached Kusāvatī, I shall have a necklace made for your neck, if Pabhāvatī,
whose thighs are like the trunks of elephants,
should speak to me. “O hunchback, having reached Kusāvatī, I shall have a necklace made for your neck.”
“If Pabhāvatī, whose thighs are like an elephant’s trunk,
should neglect me, I shall have a necklace made for you, O hunchback, once I have reached Kusāvatī. If Pabhāvatī,
whose thighs are like an elephant’s trunk, should neglect me...”
“I shall have a necklace made for your neck, O hunchback, once you have reached Kusāvatī—if, O you with thighs like an elephant’s trunk, you will touch me with your hands.

In this context, “I shall have a necklace made for your neck” means: “I shall have a necklace for your neck made entirely of gold. “Necklace... [The text continues as follows:]... “Necklace” (nekkhaṃ).
There is also the reading, “I will make you my neck-ornament,” which means, “I will place a necklace made of gold upon your neck.
“She might look [at me]” means, “If Pabhāvatī should look at me because of your word;
if you will be able to cause her to look at me”—the same principle applies to “she might speak to me” and so forth. In this context, however, “she might smile” refers to a gentle smile.
She would mock him. "She would mock" means she would mock by means of loud laughter.
Having heard his words, she said, "Go, Your Majesty; after a few days have passed, I shall bring her under your control;
witness my prowess! Having thus accomplished that task, she went into the presence of Pabhāvati.
Having gone to her living quarters, as if cleaning it, she left not even a fragment of a clod of earth fit for a weapon;
she removed even the sandals, swept the entire room, placed a threshold-bar across the doorway,
prepared a high seat, spread out a low stool for Pabhāvati, and said, "Come, mother, I will search your head for lice."
Having seated her there on a stool and placed her head between his own thighs, he scratched it slightly and said, "Oh, there are many lice on this woman's head!
Taking lice from his own head, he placed them in her hand and, speaking words of affection, said, "See how many lice are on your head!
Then, recounting the virtues of the Great Being, he spoke this verse:
“Surely this princess does not find even the *kusa* grass bitter;
she was supported by a wealthy master who had no need for wages.
This is its meaning: certainly, previously in the city of Kusāvatī, in the presence of King Kusa, she [enjoyed] the state of wearing garlands, perfumes, ointments, garments, and ornaments.
She finds and obtains not even the slightest pleasure; not even a mere betel leaf has ever been given to her by him before.
Why is this? For women are generally unable to break the heart of a husband who has lain upon their lap for even a single day;
yet this man, while supporting Āḷārika as his wage-earner, [neglects] both his status as a master and his duty as a provider.
"When this man arrived, though he was seeking nothing at all but the root [of the tree], you abandoned the kingdom for his sake alone and came here;
yet now that he experiences such suffering, you do not even offer him a mere greeting.
Even if, mother, you have no affection for him, you ought to give something to him, thinking: 'The supreme king of all Jambudīpa is wearying himself on my account.'"

Having heard this, she became angry with the hunchbacked woman. Then the hunchbacked woman seized her by the neck, threw her into the inner chamber, and standing outside herself, closed the door and remained there hanging from the pull-cord.
Unable to reach her, Pabhāvatī stood at the foot of the door and, reviling her, spoke this second verse:
“Surely this is not that hunchback who deserves to have her tongue cut off with a well-sharpened blade for speaking such evil words.
In this context, “well-sharpened” means with a very sharp, keen-edged blade. “Speaking such evil words” means uttering speech that is improper to hear.
Then the hunchback woman, standing while holding the pulling-rope, said: "What will your beauty avail you, O witless and ill-behaved man?
Shall we sustain ourselves by devouring your beauty? And proclaiming the virtues of the Bodhisatta with thirteen verses, she uttered what is known as the "Hunchback’s Roar":
"Do not judge her by her appearance, for she shines with noble stature.
Thinking 'she is of great lineage,' do what is pleasing and right.
Do not judge her by her appearance, for she shines with noble stature."
Thinking, "He is very wealthy," do what is pleasing and agreeable to him.
Do not defile him with your beauty, O lady of radiant splendor;
thinking, "He is very powerful," do what is pleasing and agreeable to him.
"Do not judge her by her appearance, for she shines with noble stature.
Calling her 'Mahāraṭṭhā,' do what is pleasing and dear to her.
Do not judge her by her appearance, for she shines with noble stature."
“Having addressed her as ‘Great Queen,’ do what is pleasing and agreeable to her.
Do not measure her by her physical form, O radiant one;
having addressed her as ‘Lion-voiced,’ do what is pleasing and agreeable to her.”
"Do not judge her by her appearance, for she shines with noble stature.
Having recognized her sweet voice, do what is pleasing to this lovely woman.
Do not judge her by her appearance, for she shines with noble stature."
Having made her voice sweet, O lovely one, do what is pleasing.
Do not defile her with your form, O radiant one;
having made her voice charming, O lovely one, do what is pleasing.
"Do not judge her by her appearance, for she shines with noble stature;
having recognized her sweet voice, do what is pleasing to her, O handsome one.
Do not judge her by her appearance, for she shines with noble stature."
Having designated her as "one of a hundred arts," do what is pleasing and agreeable to her.
Do not defile her on account of her beauty, O Pabhāvati;
even if she is a Kshatriya woman, do what is pleasing and agreeable to her.
"Do not judge him by his appearance, for he is distinguished by his stature;
having recognized him as King Kusa, O lovely one, do what you please.
In this regard, "Do not judge him by his appearance, for he is distinguished by his stature" means: O Pabhāvati, do not you [judge] this Lord of Men, Kusa, by his physical form.
"He measured [her] by his own form, by his height and girth; thus he took her as his measure.
Having taken it to heart that "he is of great fame" means he is of great majesty (*mahānubhāva*), one should make him dear—him who is beautiful and lovely to behold.
For his very majesty is his form; so he says. This same method applies everywhere. Furthermore, "of great fame" means having a large retinue. "Of great wealth" means...
