"Mahābhoga" means one of great wealth. "Mahabbala" means one of great power. "Mahāraṭṭha" means one whose kingdom is vast. "Mahārāja" means the preeminent king over the whole of Jambudīpa.
"Sīhassara" means one whose voice is equal to the roar of a lion. "Vaggussara" means one whose voice is endowed with grace.
"Bindussara" means one whose voice is compact and resonant. "Mañjussara" means one whose voice is beautiful. "Madhussara" means one whose voice is endowed with sweetness.
"One with a hundred crafts" means one who has accomplished many hundreds of crafts by his own power alone, without training under others.
"A khattiya" means one born in the lineage of Okkāka, an unadulterated noble. "Kusa-rāja" refers to a king whose name was identical to that of the *kusa* grass given by Sakka.
Thinking, "There is no other king such as this," the hunchback said, "Be dear to him," for so much...
She praised his virtues with verses.
Having heard her words, Pabhāvatī rebuked the hunchback, saying, "Hunchback, you boast excessively;
I shall let your husband know your true nature by reaching you with my hand. She [the hunchback] replied to her, "While I was protecting you from your father, King Kusa..."
“I did not report that he had arrived; let it be, I shall report it to the king today,” he said, and caused a great outcry.
She too, thinking “someone might hear this,” signaled to the hunchback.
The Bodhisatta, unable to see her and exhausted by poor food and a painful bed for seven months, thought: “What use have I for her? For seven...”
“Living here for a month, I have not even been able to see him; he is exceedingly harsh and violent. I shall go and see my mother and father.
At that moment, Sakka, perceiving his state of longing, thought: “The king has not been able to see Pabhāvati for seven months;
I will arrange a way for him to see her,” and he sent a messenger to King Madda.
Having sent messengers to the seven kings, he dispatched a separate message to each one, saying: "Pabhāvatī has come here, abandoning King Kusa; let them come and take Pabhāvatī.
They went with a great retinue and, upon reaching the city, did not know the reason for each other's arrival. They asked, "Why have you come? Why have you come?"
Having asked, "Have you come? and understood the matter, he became enraged and sent out proclamations, saying:
"They say he will give one daughter to seven [suitors]; behold his immodest conduct! He mocks us; seize him!
and "Let him give his daughter to all of us, or else there shall be war! Having sent these messages, they surrounded the city. King Madda, having heard the message, [acted accordingly].
Terrified and trembling, he addressed his ministers and asked, "What shall we do? Then the ministers said to him, "Your Majesty, seven kings have arrived relying upon Pabhāvati.
They say, 'If she is not given up, we will break down the wall, enter the city, and put them to death to seize her.
Therefore, while the walls are still unbreached, [seize] Pabhāvati from them."
Having said, "We shall send them," they spoke this verse:
"These elephants are steadfast; all stand here clad in armor.
Before they crush the rampart, bring her forth, O Pabhāvati!"
In that context, "upatthaddhā" means arrogant and haughty. "Ānentu etaṃ pabhāvatin" means "Bring her here, Pabhāvatī";
thus they sent messengers. Therefore [the king said], "Great King, send Pabhāvatī to them while these nāgas have not yet crushed the rampart.
Having heard this, the king thought, "If I send Pabhāvatī to one, the others will wage war; no..."
"It is possible to give [this] to one person; let him who has come here, having abandoned the supreme king of all Jambudīpa as 'ugly,' receive the fruit of his coming.
Having slain him and divided him into seven pieces, we shall send them to the seven kṣatriyas.
Speaking thus, he uttered the following verse:
“Having made seven slits, I shall reveal this splendor to the kṣatriyas who have come here to kill me.
This speech of his became known throughout the entire residence. The attendants went and said, “The king, it seems, [will reveal] you...”
“They will cut it into pieces and send them to the seven kings,” they informed Pabhāvati.
Terrified by the fear of death, she rose from her seat and, surrounded by her sisters, went to her mother’s bedchamber. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
“The princess Sāmā, dressed in fine silk, arose;”
"With eyes filled with tears, surrounded by a host of female slaves.
Therein, "Sāmā" means she who is gold-colored. "Clad in silk" means wearing garments of golden-embroidered silk.
Having gone into her mother's presence and paid homage to her mother, she spoke while lamenting:
“That face, surely once adorned with earrings, reflected in the teeth and lips of a slave-girl—
beautiful, with lovely eyes, stainless and blemishless— will now stand cast away in the forest by the kṣatriyas.
Those surely once unbound, with curled tips, soft and anointed with the essence of sandalwood;”
In the midst of the crowded charnel ground, vultures will drag her about with their feet.
"Surely those arms of mine— with copper-colored nails, fine hair, and soft as they were anointed with the essence of sandalwood—
now severed and cast away in the forest by the Kṣatriyas, are being carried off by a vulture wherever it pleases."
“Surely those breasts of yours, resembling palmyra fruits, once adorned with Kāsī sandalwood paste,
will now hang down upon my body like a young, tender fawn hanging from its mother’s udder.
Surely that broad hip of yours, so well-rounded and once graced by golden girdles— ”
When her body has been cut up by the kṣatriyas in the forest, packs of jackals will drag it away.
"Jackals, vultures, and dogs, and whatever other fanged creatures there may be—
they shall surely never grow old after devouring Pabhāvati."
“If the Kṣatriyas who have gone far away carry off my flesh,
Mother, having requested bones, you should cremate him by the roadside.
Having had fields prepared, Mother, plant saffron there.”
“When they have blossomed in the winter at the end of the frost, mother, you should remember me, saying: ‘She was so beautiful and radiant.
In this context, “rubbed with *kakkas* and ointments” refers to being rubbed with mustard-paste, salt-paste, clay-paste, sesame-paste, turmeric-paste, and facial powders.
This was treated with these five unguents. "Reflected in a mirror of ivory" means it was reflected in a mirror made of ivory;
having looked there, it was adorned. "Beautiful" means a beautiful face. "Dustless" means free from dust, stainless.
"Spotless" means free from defects such as boils or pimples. "Pure," mother—such is my face.
"Surely now, cast off by the kṣatriyas, she will remain in the forest wilderness," he lamented.
"Asitā" means black. "Vellitagga" means with tips raised up. "Sīvathikāya" means in the charnel ground.

"Parikaḍḍhissantī" means that vultures, who eat human flesh, will surely seize my hair of such a kind and drag it along, striking it with their feet. "Gayha dhaṅko" [means] having seized it, a hawk...
"He goes wherever he wishes" means, mother, surely a vulture, having seized such an arm of mine, will go wherever it pleases while tearing it off and eating it.
"Resembling a palm fruit" means like a golden palm fruit. "Anointed with Kāsī sandalwood" means rubbed with fine sandalwood.

"Regarding 'breasts': O mother, having seen me fallen in such a place as the charnel ground, the jackal will surely lap at those breasts with its mouth, just as a young son laps at his own mother's breasts. 'Soṇi' means the waist.
'Well-hacked' means well-prepared by being struck with a cow's jawbone. 'Discarded' means cast away. 'Having devoured'..."
"Mother, surely these many people will become free from old age by eating my flesh.
Mother, if those kṣatriyas, their hearts bound to me, should take my flesh,
then you must ask for the bones and burn them along the roadside— burn them between the footpaths and the great highways."
She said: "Mother, on the site where I was cremated, have flower gardens and such places constructed;
there, in these fields, plant *kaṇikāra* trees. 'When the snow has passed' means in the month of Phagguṇa, after the falling of snow. 'Remember them' means:
remember that my daughter Pabhāvatī was of such a complexion, having filled a golden casket with those flowers and placed it upon her thighs."
Thus, terrified by the fear of death, she lamented in the presence of her mother.
King Madda also gave the command: "Let the executioner come here, taking both his axe and the block.
His arrival became known throughout the entire royal palace. Then, hearing that he had arrived, Pabhāvati’s mother rose from her seat, overcome with grief, and [approached] the king...
She went into his presence. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“The mother of that maiden arose, a noblewoman with the appearance of a goddess;
seeing the sword and the slaughter-house within the king’s Madda palace, she [spoke].”
"There she stood up" means that, having risen from her seat, she went into the presence of the king and stood there.
"Seeing both the axe and the block" means that, seeing the axe and the wooden block placed before the king on the decorated terrace of the inner palace,
she spoke this verse while lamenting:
“Surely with this very sword, O Madda, having slain your daughter—so well-known and slender-waisted—you will display yourself among the kṣatriyas.

Therein, “with this sword” refers to the axe; for in this context, it is called a “sword. “Well-known and slender-waisted” means one who is well-acquainted [with virtue] and possesses a slender waist.
Then the king, seeking to persuade her, said: "Queen, what are you saying?
Your daughter has abandoned the foremost king in all of Jambudīpa as being 'ugly,' and has come back with death itself upon her forehead, leaving not even a footprint on the path she traveled;
now let her receive such a fruit for her own sake. Having heard his words, she [spoke] to her daughter...
Having approached him, she lamented and said:
"O little daughter, you did not heed my words, though I desired your welfare;
now, covered in blood, you go to the realm of Yama."
“Thus does a person come to grief and meet with misfortune,
who does not act upon the words of those who wish him well and see his true welfare.
And if today you were to take back the boy of lovely appearance— ”
A Khattiya born of a Kusa lineage, adorned with a golden girdle of jewels,
honored by his circle of kinsmen— you do not go to that destruction.
Where the kettle-drum resounds and the elephant trumpets.
"O auspicious lady of the khattiya clan, what indeed could be more pleasant than that?
The horse neighs at the gate, and the prince cries out;
O auspicious lady of the khattiya clan, what indeed could be more pleasant than that?"
“In the noble clan of the Khattiyas, resounding with the cries of peacocks and herons, and echoing with the songs of cuckoos—what indeed could be more pleasant than that?
Therein, he addresses her as “Puttike. This is what is meant: “Mother, what will you do here? [To your] husband...”
"Go into his presence; do not become intoxicated by the pride of beauty. Even though she entreated him thus, he did not heed my words.
Now, covered in blood, you go to the abode of Yama; you shall go to the realm of King Death. "And a worse state" means that she goes to a condition even more wretched than this.
"If you wear it today," [means]: "Mother, if you fall under the power of the mind..."
Having gone to King Kuśanabha and obtained a prince who, by his own form, is beautiful to behold and resembles you, you shall bear him today.

Since this is so, you would not go to the abode of Yama. Therefore, from that royal Kṣatriya family where this splendor resides—the city of Kusāvatī resounding with the sound of various drums and the trumpeting of rutting elephants—[you shall bring him forth].
"What indeed is more pleasant that you have seen, having come here? is the meaning. *Sisati* means "he laughs. *Kumāro* refers to a well-trained *gandhabba*-prince.
*Uparodeti* means he performs an offering by taking up various musical instruments.

*Kokilābhinikūjite* means in a place where cuckoos are warbling, as if competing with the offerings of dancing, singing, and instrumental music that take place morning and evening in the royal palace of Kusa.

Having conversed with her in this way through so many verses, she thought, "If only the Lord of Kuśanara were here today, he would drive away these seven kings, liberate my daughter from her suffering, and take her away. Thinking thus, she spoke this verse:
"Where indeed is the subduer of enemies, the crusher of foreign realms?"
“Of noble wisdom is he who shall release us from suffering.
Therein, “of noble wisdom” means one whose wisdom is exalted.

Then Pabhāvatī thought, “It is not fitting for my mother’s mouth to speak in praise of Kusas; I shall first tell her how he lives right here, having performed the work of a cook,” and she spoke this verse:
“Right here is that crusher of beings, the subduer of foreign realms;
he is Kusa, possessed of lofty wisdom, who shall slay them all.
Then her mother, thinking, “She is prattling on because she is terrified by the fear of death,” spoke this verse:
“Are you speaking like one who is mad? You speak like a blind fool!
If Kusa had actually arrived, how could we not know it?
In this context, “blind fools” refers to those who are deluded and lacking in knowledge. “How could we not know it? means for what reason would we fail to recognize him?
"For he would have sent us a message while still standing on the road, and the fourfold army with its raised banners would have been visible;
but you spoke out of fear of death.
When this was said, she replied, "My mother does not believe me, for she has not seen him come here and stay for seven months."
Thinking, "He knows; I shall show him," she took her mother by the hand, opened the lion-window, extended her hand, and as she showed him, she spoke this verse:
"This is the man of Āḷāra, within the maidens' quarters."
“Having firmly girt her loins, she washes the water-jar while stooping.

Regarding this: “In the midst of the maidens’ quarters” means: standing at the window, look upon her in the place where your daughters, the maidens, dwell. “Having girt her loins” means: having tied her waist-cloth, she washes the water-jar.
It is said that at that time he thought: “Today my desire will reach its fulfillment; surely, being terrified by the fear of death,”
“Pabhāvatī will tell her that I have come; I shall wash the vessels and put them away.
Having brought water, she began to wash the vessels. Then her mother, reproaching her, spoke this verse:
“You are a Veṇī, a Caṇḍālī; you are not one who brings disgrace upon the family.”
“How could you, born in the Maddakula family, make your lover a slave?

Therein, *veṇī* means a carpenter’s wife. “Are you not one who preserves the family’s honor, or are you rather a defiler of the family?”—“Lover,” he said, “how indeed could you, born in such a family, make your own husband a slave?
Then Pabhāvatī thought, “My mother does not seem to know of my living situation because of him,” and she spoke the other verse:
“I am neither a Veṇī nor a Caṇḍālī, nor am I one who brings disgrace to my clan.
O Blessed One, I am the son of Okkāka; do you perhaps think I am a slave?
Therein, “the son of Okkāka”: “Mother, he is the son of Okkāka, yet you think I am a ‘slave. Why then should I call him a ‘slave’?”
Now, describing his fame, he said:
“He who always feeds twenty thousand brahmins— O Blessed One,
do you perhaps think that Okkāka’s son is a slave?”
“O Blessed One, you who are the son of Okkāka— do you perhaps think that you are a slave to him for whom twenty thousand elephants are always harnessed?
[He] for whom twenty thousand horses are always harnessed...”
“O venerable sir, you are the son of Okkāka; do you perhaps think, ‘Are you a slave?
‘He for whom twenty thousand chariots are always harnessed— O venerable sir, you are the son of Okkāka; do you perhaps think, “Are you a slave?”’”
“O Blessed One, you who have twenty thousand bulls constantly yoked for him—
Okkāka’s son— do you perhaps think, ‘Are you a slave’?
“You who have twenty thousand milch cows constantly being milked for him— ”
“O Noble One, you are the son of Okkāka; do you perhaps consider yourself a slave?
In this way, with these five verses, her fame was extolled by the Mahāsatta. Then her mother, thinking, “This unshakable one speaks thus;
it must surely be so,” believed her and went into the presence of the king and reported the matter to him.
So, going with great speed into the presence of Pabhāvati, he asked, "Is it true, mother, that King Kusa has come here?
"Yes, dear son; today seven months have passed since you began performing the duties of a cook for your daughters.
Not believing her, he questioned Khujjā, and having heard the truth as it was, he rebuked his daughter and spoke this verse:
“Truly, O fool, you have done wrong, in that you did not declare to the mighty kshatriya that he was a naga in the guise of a frog.
In this context, *taggha* means “certainly” or “in every respect.”
Having thus reproached his daughter, he went quickly into her presence. After exchanging greetings and raising his joined palms, he confessed his own transgression and spoke this verse:
“O Great King, Bull among Charioteers, forgive our offense:
that we did not recognize you when you arrived here in disguise.”
Having heard this, the Great Being thought, "If I speak harshly, his very heart will burst right here; I shall comfort him. While still standing within the vessel, he spoke the other verse:
"It is not fitting for one such as I to be a butcher;
may you alone have confidence in me, O King; there is no fault in you."
Having received a friendly greeting from him, the king ascended the palace, summoned Pabhāvatī, and spoke this verse to send her forth to ask for forgiveness:
“Go, foolish woman, and beg forgiveness from King Kusa, who is possessed of great power;
once King Kusa has been appeased, he will grant you your life.”
Having heard her father’s words, she went into his presence, surrounded by her sisters and female attendants.
He too, remaining in the position of a laborer, having learned that she was coming to him, thought,
"Today I shall break Pabhāvati’s pride and make her lie down in the mud at my feet," and [he poured out] all the water he had brought.
Having abandoned that place which was merely a heap of chaff, she trampled it and made it into a single mass of mud.
She went to him, prostrated at his feet, and lying down upon the surface of the mud, she asked for his forgiveness. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
“Having heard her father’s words, Pabhāvatī, radiant as a goddess,”
"He seized the feet of the mighty King Kusa with his head.
Therein, "with his head" means that having prostrated with his head, he grasped the feet of King Kusa.
And having grasped him, seeking his forgiveness, she spoke these three verses:
“The watches of the night have passed, O Lord, without you.
I bow my head at your feet; do not be angry with me, O bull among chariot-warriors.
I acknowledge everything before you; Great King, listen to me.”
"And yet, I would never again do anything that is unpleasant to you.
If, despite my pleading thus, you will not do as I say,
then my father will kill me now and present me to the kshatriyas."
In this context, "nights" (*ratyo*) means nights. "All these" (*tāma*) refers to all these [nights] that have passed without you.
"I acknowledge all of this to you" (*sabbaṃ te paṭijānāmi*): "O Great King, for all this time I have done only what was unpleasant to you;
I acknowledge all of this to you. Listen further from me: from now on, I shall no longer do what is unpleasant to you. Thus, if...
“If you do not carry out my word while I am entreating you thus.

Hearing this, the king thought, “If I say, ‘You alone shall know this,’ her heart will break; I must comfort her. Having reflected thus, he said: “Since you are entreating me thus, why should I not do your bidding?”
“I am purified, O noble lady; do not fear, Pabhāvati.
‘I acknowledge everything before you; listen to me, Princess.
Furthermore, I shall never again do anything that is unpleasant to you.’”
“O lady of beautiful hips, for the sake of your desires, I shall indeed endure suffering;
having slain many members of the Madda clan, I am able to lead you away.
In this context, *kiṃ na kāhāmi* means: for what reason would I not do your bidding? *Vikuddho tyasmiṃ* means: I am free from stain.
"I am without anger toward you. "All this"—I acknowledge both your state of complete purification and your current act of making me unloved;
all of this is yours alone. "By your will"—desiring that through your desire. "They shall endure"—I accept it.
"Having slain many of the Madda clan, he is able to lead him away"—having killed many members of the royal family of the Maddas, he is capable of taking him away by force.
Then, seeing his own female attendant like a handmaid to Sakka, the king of the gods, he conceived a sense of kshatriya pride,
thinking, "While I am still living, others will take my wife and depart.
Stretching himself out in the royal courtyard like a lion, he roared, "Let all the inhabitants of the city know that I have arrived!"
Roaring, clapping his hands, and slapping his arms, he said, "Now I shall seize you alive! Let my chariots and other vehicles be yoked!
and immediately thereafter he spoke this verse:
"Let them yoke the horses to the chariot—horses of various colors, well-trained and composed."
“Then you shall behold my speed as I scatter the enemies.

In this context, “various-minded” means variegated with various ornaments. “Composed” is said with reference to the horse; the meaning is that it is well-trained and free from restlessness. “Then you shall behold my speed” means:
“Then you shall see my prowess. Taking up the enemies is my burden; go, bathe, adorn yourself, and ascend the palace.”

He sent him away. King Madda also dispatched ministers for the purpose of providing him with attendants. They surrounded the area right at the gate of his kitchen with a curtain and provided him with barbers.
Having performed his duties, bathed his head, and adorned himself with all his ornaments, he was surrounded by the ministers and others.
Thinking, "I shall ascend the palace," he looked around the directions and clapped his hands. Wherever he looked, [he saw...]
He trembled. "Now you shall see my prowess," he said. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher spoke the following verse:
"And there, within the inner palace of King Madda, they watched him, like a yawning lion, lashing his tail and doubling his forepaws."
The meaning of this is as follows: while he was yawning and snapping his fingers there, the women in the king’s inner apartments opened the windows and gazed at him.
Then King Madda sent him a magnificent, well-trained state elephant adorned with ornaments.
Ascending the back of that elephant, over which a white parasol was raised high, he had Pabhāvati seated behind him and set out with a fourfold army.
Surrounded by his army, he went out through the eastern gate, surveyed the enemy forces, and let out a lion’s roar three times, saying: “I am King Kusa!
Those who desire to live, lie down upon their breasts! Thus he crushed his enemies. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
“Having mounted the back of an elephant, and having placed Pabhāvati [upon it]...”
Having entered the battle, Kusa let out a lion’s roar.
Hearing him roaring like a lion, the other animals fled;
likewise, the kṣatriyas scattered, terrified by the sound of Kusa.
“Elephant-riders, chariot-warriors, cavalry,
and infantrymen cut one another down, trembling with the fear of the sound of the *kusa* grass.
Seeing this at the head of the battle, my mind was filled with joy.”
King Kusarāja gave the Verocana jewel to Devinda.
Having pierced through the battle and obtained the Verocana jewel,
the king, mounted upon the neck of an elephant, entered his city and capital.
“Having seized them alive and bound seven kṣatriyas, he presented them to his father-in-law, saying: ‘O King, here are your enemies.
They have all fallen under your power; your foes are utterly destroyed.’”
"Do with her as you wish—release her, or kill her.
In this context, "they fled" means that, being unable to establish mindfulness, their minds became deranged and they broke away.
"Afflicted by the fear of the sound of Kuśa" means they were overwhelmed by the terror produced by the sound of King Kuśa, their minds being bewildered.
“They cut one another” means they cut and crush each other. There is also a reading, “They split [them].

When the battle had thus been broken by the mere hearing of the Bodhisatta’s voice, Sakka, seeing that great being’s prowess at the head of the battle, was delighted in heart and gave him a mass of gems called Verojana.
"Nagaraṃ puraṃ" means the city known as the town. "Having bound them" means having bound their upper garments behind their backs.
"Kāmaṃ karohi te tayā" means: "Do as you wish; fulfill your own desire and preference, for these have indeed been made your slaves by you.
The king said:
“‘These beings belong to you alone; they are not my beings.
You alone, O Great King, are our master—either release them or kill them.
In this context, ‘You alone’ means, ‘O Great King, you alone are our lord.’”

When this was said, the Great Being thought, "What is the use of killing these? Let their coming not be in vain. Pabhāvati has seven younger sisters, daughters of the Madda king; I shall give them to these men. Having reflected thus, he spoke this verse:
"These seven daughters of yours, beautiful as celestial maidens—give one to each of them, and let them be your sons-in-law."
Then the king said to him:
"Of both ourselves and them, you are the lord of us all;
O Great King, you yourself must give to them whatever you desire."
"In that regard, O Great King Kusa, what do you say when you ask, 'Are we all yours?
You alone are the lord of these seven kings, of me, and of all these others. 'If you wish' means:
if you wish, or if you wish to give something to someone, then give it to him."
When this was said, he had them all adorned and gave one to each of those kings. To clarify this matter, the Teacher spoke these five verses:
“Sīhassara Kusā then gave one daughter of King Madda to each of those kṣatriyas, one to each.”
“Delighted by that gain, they were joyful as lions roar upon the *kuśa* grass;
at that time, seven Kṣatriyas drank from their own respective vessels.
Taking Pabhāvati and the beautiful Vairocana jewel,”
King Kusa, possessed of great power, went to Kusāvatī.
As they entered Kusāvatī in a single chariot, those two drivers,
being equal in complexion and form, did not outshine one another.
“The mother was reunited with her son, and both husband and wife were together;
they were then in harmony and dwelt upon the prosperous earth.
In this context, “satisfied” means gratified. “They drank” [the words] “Now you should be heedful,” spoken by the Kusa king.
Having been exhorted, they departed. "He departed" means that after staying for a few days, he took leave of his father-in-law, saying, "We shall go to our own kingdom," and went away.
"Traveling in a single chariot" means that both of them were traveling together, having mounted a single chariot.

"Being equal in complexion and form" means being identical in both color and physical appearance. "They did not outshine one another" means that neither surpassed the other; this was due to the power of the maṇi-jewel.
It is said that the Great Being was handsome, golden-hued, and possessed of supreme beauty;
it is said that he became so majestic through the residual merit of having offered alms-food to a Paccekabuddha in the past and through the residual merit of having commissioned a Buddha image.
"He has gathered [the people]"—thus, when his mother heard of the Great Being's arrival, she had a drum beaten throughout the city and [prepared] much for the Great Being.
Taking gifts as an offering, he went out to meet him and they came together.
He too, together with his mother, circumambulated the city and, after enjoying festivities for seven days, ascended to the decorated upper terrace of the palace.
Those two, husband and wife, were in harmony; from then on, for as long as they lived, they remained in concord, living together in mutual affection and prosperity.
"They dwelt upon the earth.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka.
At the conclusion of the Truths, the monk who was despondent was established in the fruit of Stream-entry. At that time, the parents were members of a great royal family.
The youngest was Ānanda; Khujjā was Khujjuttarā; Pabhāvatī was the mother of Rāhula; the assembly was the Buddha’s assembly;
and as for King Kusa, it was I myself who was he.
This is the first commentary on the Kusa Jātaka.
[532] 2. The Commentary on the Soṇananda Jātaka.
"Are you a deva or a gandhabba?"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a monk who supported his mother.
The background story is similar to that of the Sāma Jātaka. At that time, however, the Teacher said: "Monks, do not [reproach] this monk..."
“They grumbled, saying, ‘Even though the ancient sages obtained sovereignty over the whole of Jambudīpa, they did not take it for themselves; rather, they supported their parents alone.
Having said this, he related a story of the past:
In the past, there was a city named Brahmavaḍḍhana in Bārāṇasī. There, a king named Manoja reigned.”
He had it built. Now, there was a certain wealthy brahmin, possessing eighty crores of wealth, who was childless.
His brahmin wife, being told by him, "Lady, pray for a son," made her prayer. Then the Bodhisatta, descending from the Brahma world, took rebirth in her womb;
and when he was born, they gave him the name Soṇakumāra. Of him—
While they were traveling on foot, another being, having passed away from the Brahma-world, took rebirth in her very womb.
When he was born, they gave him the name Nandakumāra.
Once they had mastered the Vedas, attained proficiency in all arts, and reached maturity, the Brahmin, seeing their excellence of form, addressed the Brahmin woman:
“I shall bind my son, Prince Soṇa, with the bonds of the household life,” she said. Having agreed, saying “Very well,” she explained the matter to her son.
He replied, “Enough, mother; I have no need for the household life.
For as long as I live, I will care for you, and after your passing, I shall enter the Himalayas and go forth into homelessness. She then reported this matter to the brahmin.
Although they spoke thus again and again, failing to win his heart, they addressed Prince Nanda, saying, "Dear son, in that case, you must take charge of the household.
When he replied, "I will not carry on my head the spittle discarded by my brother;
after you have passed away, I too shall go forth into homelessness along with my brother," he heard their words.
Thinking, "These two, though so young, renounce sensual pleasures; how much more so should we?
Let us all go forth together," he informed the king, saying, "Father, what need have you for our going forth after our passing? We shall all go forth this very day.
Having distributed all his wealth through acts of charity and set his servants free, he [addressed] his kinsmen...

Having given what was appropriate to be given, the four people departed from the city of Brahmavaḍḍhana and, in the region of the Himalayas, established a hermitage near a lake covered with five kinds of lotuses in a delightful forest grove; having gone forth, they dwelt there.
Both brothers looked after their mother and father, providing them with tooth-sticks and [water] every morning.
Having provided water for washing the face, and having swept the leaf-hut and the surrounding courtyard, they set out drinking water and water for rinsing the mouth;
having brought sweet fruits from the forest, they feed them to their parents;
they bathe them with warm or cold water, clean their matted hair, and perform services for them such as massaging their feet.
When some time had passed in this way, the wise Nanda thought, "I shall first have my parents eat only the fruits and roots I have brought myself.
So he went ahead, and bringing whatever he had gathered from the places he had visited the day before and the day before that, he had his parents eat it at dawn.
Having eaten those things and rinsed their mouths, they observed the Uposatha. The wise Soṇa—
But having gone a long distance, he brought back fruits that were exceedingly sweet and perfectly ripe and offered them to him.
Then they said to him, "Dear one, we have already eaten what was brought by your younger brother this very morning and have become observant of the Uposatha;
there is no need for us now. Thus his various fruits did not receive their enjoyment and went to waste, even on subsequent days.
"In the same way," he said. Thus, although he had gone far by means of his five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) to fetch them, they would not eat.
Then the Great Being thought: "My parents are delicate, and Nanda brings them various fruits—some unripe, some over-ripe—and makes them eat them;
if this continues, they will not survive for long. I shall stop him."
"No," he replied. Then, addressing him, the Great Being said, "Nanda, from now on, bring various fruits and wait for my arrival;
we shall both eat together. Although this was said, Nanda, seeking his own merit, did not do as he was told.
The Great Being thought, "Since Nanda does not follow my word, he acts improperly; I shall dismiss him."
Thinking, "I shall look after my parents all by myself," he struck Nanda with his palm, saying, "Nanda, you are incorrigible;
you do not act upon the words of the wise. I am the eldest, and my parents' care is my responsibility alone.
I myself will look after them; you shall not remain here—go elsewhere!"
Thus, being dissuaded by him and unable to remain in his presence, he paid homage to him, approached his parents, and informed them of the matter.

He then entered his own leaf-hut, gazed upon the *kasiṇa*, and on that very day, having realized the five supernormal powers (*abhiññā*) and the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), he thought: "From the base of Mount Sineru, there is sand of jewels..."
"If I fetch water from a lake and, having poured it in the courtyard of my brother’s leaf-hut, am able to ask my brother for forgiveness—even this will not be fitting.
If I fetch water from Lake Anotatta and, having sprinkled it in the courtyard of my brother’s leaf-hut, am able to ask my brother for forgiveness—even this will not be fitting.
If, by means of the power of the deities, [I am able to do so] regarding my brother..."
"I shall ask for forgiveness; I am capable of bringing the Four Great Kings and Sakka to ask my brother for forgiveness, yet even so it will not be fitting.
I shall bring all the kings from the entire Jambudīpa, beginning with Manoja, the supreme king, and ask for forgiveness.
When this is done, my brother’s virtue will spread throughout the whole of Jambudīpa, like the sun and moon."

"...will appear as if [he were] there. At that very moment, he traveled by means of psychic power (*iddhi*) and, alighting at the gate of the king's palace in the city of Brahmavaḍḍhana, stood there and had it announced to the king: "It is said that a certain ascetic wishes to see you.
The king thought, "What is the use of my seeing a renunciant? He must have come for the sake of food," and sent him a meal.
He did not accept the food. Rice was sent; he did not accept the rice. Clothes were sent;
he did not accept the clothes. Betel was sent; he did not accept the betel. Then they dispatched a messenger to his presence, asking, "For what purpose have you come?
Being questioned by the messenger, he replied, "I have come to attend upon the king. When the king heard this, he—
“I have many attendants; let him practice the ascetic life himself,” he sent word.
Having heard this, the other replied, “I shall seize the sovereignty over the whole of Jambudīpa by my own power and give it to you.
Hearing this, the king thought, “Those who have gone forth are indeed wise; they will surely know some stratagem. Thus he [sent for him].

Having summoned him, seated him on a throne, and paid homage to him, he asked: "Venerable sir, it is said that you will take the entire kingdom of Jambudīpa from me and give it to me. "Yes, Great King," he replied. "How will you take it?
"Great King, by not causing even as much blood as a tiny fly might drink to be shed for anyone, and by confiscating your wealth—"
“Without using my own psychic power, I shall take it and give it to him; moreover, it is fitting that I depart this very day without making any further delay.
Trusting his words, he set out from the city surrounded by his army.
If the army became hot, Nanda the Wise created shade with his own psychic power and made it cool, even when the rain was falling.
He does not allow rain to fall upon the army; he wards off cold or heat; he causes all dangers on the road, such as stumps and thorns, to disappear;
and having leveled the path like a *kasiṇa* disk, he himself goes surrounded by the army, sitting cross-legged after spreading his leather mat in the air.

Having thus taken his army and first gone to the kingdom of Kosala, he had his camp pitched not far from the city and sent a messenger to the King of Kosala with the message: "Give us either battle or the white parasol.
The king, becoming angry and thinking, "Am I not a king?", replied, "I give you battle," and went forth at the head of his army. The two armies prepared for combat.
They began the attack. Between the two armies, the wise Nanda took his own deerskin seat, made it large, and spread it out;
he received the arrows discharged by both armies with that very skin. Not a single person in either army was pierced by an arrow;
however, when the arrows in their hands were exhausted, both armies stood there dispirited.

Nandapaṇḍita went into the presence of King Manoja and, having comforted him by saying, "Do not fear, Great King," he went into the presence of the Kosalan king and said, "Great King, do not fear; there is no obstacle for you.
Your kingdom shall remain yours alone; you need only be subject to the will of King Manoja. Having placed his trust in him, the king accepted this, saying, "Very well."
Then, having led him into the presence of Manoja, he said, "Great King, the King of Kosala is under your control;
let this kingdom belong to him alone. He accepted, saying, "Very well," brought him under his own power, and taking two armies, went to the kingdom of Aṅga.
Having seized Aṅga, he then went to the kingdom of Magadha; by this means, throughout the whole of Jambudīpa...
Having brought the kings under his own control, he then departed from them and went to the city of Brahmadatta.
He seized the kingdom after seven months and seven days more than seven years had passed.
Having caused various kinds of food and delicacies to be brought from each royal capital, he took those one hundred and one kings with him.
He drank the great draught together with them for seven days.

Thinking, "As long as the king enjoys the pleasure of sovereignty for seven days, I will not reveal myself to him," the wise man Nanda went to Uttarakuru to beg for alms and stayed for seven days at the entrance of the Golden Cave in the Himalayas. Manoja too...
On the seventh day, beholding his own great glory and prosperity, he thought: "This fame was not given to me by my parents, nor by others;
it arose in dependence upon the ascetic Nanda. Today is the seventh day since I have not seen him.
Where indeed is the giver of my glory? Thus he called to mind the wise Nanda. He [Nanda] perceived his state of recollection.
Having understood this, he came and stood in the air before him. Seeing him, the king thought:
"I do not know whether this ascetic is a deity or a human being. If he should be a human, I shall give the entire kingdom of Jambudīpa to him;
if he is a deity, I shall pay him honor. Examining him, the king spoke the first verse:
“Are you a deity, a Gandhabba, or perhaps Sakka Purindada?
Being a human endowed with psychic power, how are we to know you?
Having heard his words, speaking the truth, he spoke this second verse:
“Neither a deva nor a gandhabba, nor even Sakka Purindada,
but a human being possessed of psychic power— know it thus, Bhāradvāja.
In this context, he addresses him as “Bhāradvāja” because he bears the name of his kingdom.
Having heard this, the king thought, "This man, having become human, has indeed been so very helpful to me; I shall satisfy him with great honor. He then said:
"What kind of service was this, O sir, that was no small matter?
While the god was raining down, you made it rain-free for yourself."
“Then, when the wind and heat were fierce, you provided cool shade;
then, in the midst of enemies, you provided protection for those who sought it.
Then, you brought under your control prosperous kingdoms.”
Then he commanded one hundred charioteers: "Follow my lord.
"We have already departed from you, sir; tell us what you wish to break:
an elephant-vehicle, a horse-chariot, or adorned women?"
“Delightful dwellings we give to you, sir.
Or else in Vaṅga or Magadha, we give them to you, sir;
or else in Assaka or Avanti, we give Sumanā to you.”
“Or even half of the kingdom we shall give to you, sir;
if you have need of the kingdom, rule it as you wish.

In this context, "made of *kādamba* wood" means made from the *kādamba* tree. "It goes without touching the shoulder" means it comes of its own accord without even touching the shoulder.

When this was said, the Great Being spoke these two verses:
“I am Soṇa, O Great King, an ascetic devoted to endurance;

“Having brought fruits and roots from the forest, O Disampati, I support my mother and father, recollecting what was done in the past.
In this context, “one who associates” means he says, “I am a certain ascetic endowed with virtue and good conduct. “I support” means...
I speak thus. "Without indolence" means having become diligent. "Recalling what was done before" means recalling the virtues previously performed for me by them.
Having heard this, the king, desiring to establish a bond of trust with him, spoke the following verse:
“We wish to go to the hermitage where Kosiya finds peace;

In this context, “the hermitage” means your own hermitage site.

The meaning of this is: "Great King, this is a one-path footway;
go by it toward that direction where this cloud-colored forest, covered with blossoming *koviḷāra* trees, is seen.
There my father, of the Kosiya clan, dwells; that is his hermitage."
Having said this, the great seer departed in haste,
traveling through the air in the sky after having instructed the kshatriya.
Having swept the hermitage and prepared a seat, he sat down.
Having entered the leaf-hut, he awakened his father:
"These kings, high-born and illustrious, are approaching;
O great seer, come out from the hermitage and sit down."
“Having heard those words of his, the great seer, hurrying, departed from the hermitage and entered the gateway”—these are the verses of one who has attained full enlightenment (*abhisambuddha*).

Having gone to Anotatta and taken water, he returned even before those kings had reached the hermitage;
placing the water-jars in the water-shed, thinking, "The great multitude shall drink," he perfumed it with forest flowers,
took a broom, swept the hermitage, prepared a seat for his father at the door of the leaf-hut, entered, and announced himself to his father.
[The word] *attha* means "meaning. "He sat down" (*upāvisi*) means he sat upon a high seat.
However, the mother of the Bodhisatta sat to one side in a low place behind him. The Great Being sat on a low seat.
When Nanda Paṇḍita returned to the hermitage having taken drinking water for the Bodhisatta from Lake Anotatta, [he saw] the king...
Having arrived, he established his camp not far from the hermitage.

Then the king, having bathed and adorned himself with all his ornaments, accompanied by one hundred and one kings and taking Nanda Paṇḍita with him, entered the hermitage with great majesty and splendor to ask the Bodhisatta for forgiveness.
When the father of the Bodhisatta saw him approaching in such a manner, he questioned the Bodhisatta.
He too explained it. To clarify that matter, the Teacher said:
"Seeing him approaching, blazing as if with splendor, surrounded by a host of khattiyas, Kosika spoke thus:"
“To whom do these kettledrums and small drums, conchs, cymbals,
and tom-toms proceed before him, making the bull among charioteers laugh with joy?
To whom does this broad golden band, with its lightning-like luster, [proceed]?”
“Who is this youth coming, radiant with glory, girt with a quiver? Whose face shines so beautifully,
like a flame struck from a forge or resembling glowing acacia embers—
who is this one coming, radiant with glory?”
“Whose is this uplifted parasol, beautiful with its ribs, shielding from the rays of the sun?
Who comes here, radiant with glory?
Whose body does he embrace, holding that supreme yak-tail fan?”
They travel for a long distance upon the back of a noble elephant belonging to one of supreme merit.
“To whom do these white parasols belong, and these well-harnessed thoroughbred horses?
They scatter about on all sides; who is this coming, radiant with glory?”
“Whose hundred renowned Khattiyas, as his followers, patrol all around?
Who comes forth ablaze with glory?
His fourfold army—elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry—[surrounds him].”
“They move all around; who is this coming, ablaze with glory?
Whose is this great army that follows behind him—unshakeable and boundless, like the waves of the ocean?”
“King of kings, Mind-born, Indra, Lord of Victory;
Nanda approaches the hermitage of the celibate practitioners.
This great army follows behind him.”
“Unshakeable and boundless, like the waves of the ocean.
Herein, “as if blazing” means as though they were burning. “Proceeding” means: before whom do these musical instruments go?
“Gladdening” means delighting. “With a golden band,” dear one, [means] with a golden [band] having the color of lightning.

He asks because the forehead is encircled by a turban-band (*uṇhīsapaṭṭa*). "A youth" (*yuvā*) means one who is young. "Equipped with a quiver" (*kalāpasannaddha*) means having a bow and quiver fastened.

Endowed with four qualities: "Unshakeable" means it is impossible to shake.
"Like the ocean's" means as limitless as the waves of the ocean. "King of kings" means honored by one hundred and one kings, or a king superior to them.
"Lord of victors" means the eldest among the Tāvatiṃsa gods who have attained victory. "The inner chamber" refers to me.

“Is it well with you, sir? Is it free from ailment?

“In this forest teeming with wild beasts, is there no danger of harm?

“For many a series of years, I have dwelt here in this hermitage;

“This water is cool, brought from the heart of the mountain;
drink from it, O Great King, if you so desire.
Whatever has been given is accepted, and for all of it, the highest honor has been rendered.”
“Listen also to Nanda’s words; he will speak them.
‘We have come from Nanda’s inner chamber into the presence of the Blessed One.

Most of these [terms] have well-known connections; however, whatever here is obscure, that alone we shall explain.
"Pavedayā" means: "Tell us what is pleasing to you in this matter. "Khuddakappāni" means:
these various fruits of trees, which are sweet like small honey. "Varaṃ varaṃ" means: the most excellent among these.
“Take it and eat. “From the heart of the mountain” means from Anotatta. “The honor for all”:
that by which we were asked for permission has been accepted by us and indeed given by you; to this extent, the honor for all these people has been performed by you.
“For Nanda too”: first, everything has been done for us; now, however, for the wise Nanda...
"Listen now to the words of one who wishes to say something:

When this had been said, the wise Nanda rose from his seat, paid homage to his mother, father, and brother, and spoke while conversing with his own retinue:

and all these kshatriyas, of noble birth and renowned fame.”
And may the King Manoja grant his approval to my words:
"May those who dwell here in this hermitage,
the yakkhas of the past and the future in the forest, hear my speech."
“Having paid homage to all beings, I shall speak to the sage of excellent vows;
he, O Kosiya, is approved by me as your sacrificial fee.
To my father and my mother, since I am desirous of giving them [to you].”
“O Hero, this is a meritorious place; do not stop me, Kosiya!
This has been prescribed by the virtuous; let go of me.
For a long time you have performed service for me with diligent effort.”
“May you perform meritorious deeds for my father and mother, and become a giver of the world to me.
“In that same way, there are men who know the Dhamma and the footprints of the Dhamma—

In this context, *anumaññantu* means “may they understand”; the sense is: “having heard well, may they realize it for themselves. *Samītāro* means...

He speaks with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). "Consent" (*sammatā*) means that they are like limbs; therefore, he says to them, "I am your right arm.

"Merit is the cause that leads to heaven; do not stop me while I am performing it," he says. "By the wise" means that this service to mother and father has been devised by the wise, understood, known, and praised by them. "Relinquish this to me" means: give this up for me, release it, hand it over.

"By exertion and by service. "What has been done" means that for a long time you have performed wholesome deeds.
"Meritorious acts" means that now I desire to perform meritorious acts toward my mother and father. "The giver of my world" means that you are the one who gives me the heavenly world;
for by performing their duties and attending upon them, I shall obtain immeasurable glory in the world of the gods.
He says to him, "May you be my donor. "Just so" means:

just as you know, so too there are other men in this assembly who speak of various kinds of teachings—this portion of the Dhamma known as "reverence for one's elders. What [is that teaching]? It is: "The path to heaven..."
"Of the world": it brings happiness through both exertion and service to one's mother and father.
"That man"—even though I am practicing rightly in this way, my brother, the wise Soṇa, obstructs me from that merit. "An obstructor of the noble path":
by obstructing me in this way, this man, because of his desire to see me, becomes known as an obstructor of the path of the noble ones—that is, of the world of the Vedas.
When Nanda the scholar had spoken thus, the Great Being said, making him listen: “First you have heard his words; now listen to me as well:
‘Listen, sirs, to my words, which concern my brother’s grievance:
O Great King, you are neglecting your ancient family lineage.’”
One who acts unrighteously toward his elders is reborn in hell.
But those who are skilled in the ancient Dharma, O Lord of the Earth,
and are perfected in their conduct, do not go to a state of misery.
“Mother, father, brother, sister, kinsmen, and relatives—all these are burdens for the eldest son;
know this, O bearer of burdens. Having taken up the heavy burden, one must exert oneself like a mariner.”
"And I do not neglect the Dhamma, for I am the eldest, O bull among chariot-warriors.
Therein, "the assembly of my brother" means: "May all you noble kings who have come here as the assembly of my brother listen first to my words.
"They cause [the Dhamma] to decline" means: "I am causing it to decline. "Of the Dhamma" means: "of the Dhamma of honoring one's elder."
Of the ancestral Dhamma. "Skilled" (kusala) means clever. "And by conduct" (cārittena ca) means endowed with the virtue of right behavior.
"The burden" (bhāra): all these are his burden in the sense that they must be carried and looked after by the eldest; thus they are called his burden. "Like a ship's captain":
just as a ship's captain, having taken on a heavy load in a ship, exerts himself and strives to bring the ship safely across the middle of the ocean.
Just as all the goods and the people on board a ship become the burden of the owner alone, so too are all my kinsmen a burden for me alone;
yet I am capable and able to look after them, and I do not neglect this duty of honoring one’s elders.
Furthermore, I am the eldest not only of these, but of the entire world; therefore, I alone—along with...
"It is fitting that Nanda should look after him.
Upon hearing this, all those kings were delighted and thought, "Today we have learned that the remaining burden indeed belongs to our eldest brother.
Thus, leaving aside the wise Nanda, they took their refuge in the Great Being and offered him praise.
As they were doing so, they spoke these two verses:
“Just as the knowledge of one who has attained [the goal] is like the light of a fire,
even so has Master Kosiya revealed the Dhamma to us.”
"Just as the rising sun, Vāsudeva the light-maker,
reveals to living beings forms both beautiful and foul,
even so has Master Kosiya revealed the Dhamma to us."
In this context, "attainment" means: "Previously, while we were living under the influence of that which conceals the Dhamma of honoring one's elders, we did not know;
today, however, we have attained knowledge, like a flame from a fire. "In this very way" means:
just as a fire burning on a mountain peak in great darkness reveals forms by radiating light all around, so too for us.
The meaning is: "The venerable one of the Kosiya clan has manifested the Dhamma. As for Vāsudeva: he is Vasudeva, the "Radiant with Wealth" (vasujotana), which means the "Illuminator of Riches.

Thus, having witnessed these miracles of Nanda Paṇḍita over such a long time, and seeing that the kings had developed faith in him, the Great Being used the power of his knowledge to shatter their devotion to him and cause them all to accept his own teaching.
He looked up at his face. Then the wise Nanda thought, "My brother is wise, competent, and a preacher of the Dhamma;
he has divided all these kings and brought them over to his own side. Apart from him, I have no other refuge.
I shall entreat him alone. Having reflected thus, he spoke this verse:
“Though I entreated you thus, you did not acknowledge my salutation with palms joined;
I shall be your bound servant, rising up as your attendant. The meaning of this is:
even though I, for the sake of asking for your forgiveness, held out my joined palms to you in this manner, you did not acknowledge it.
"Do not accept [this]. You yourselves must attend upon your parents;
however, I shall be your constant companion and servant, and rising day and night with diligence, I shall look after you as your attendant.
Although the Great Being was by nature free from any ill will or enmity toward Nanda the Pandit, his words were exceedingly firm.
However, in order to humble his pride, he acted in such a way by means of a rebuke;

then, having heard his words, with a joyful heart and having conceived faith in him, he spoke to proclaim his virtue, saying: "Now I forgive you, and you shall be allowed to look after your mother and father."
“Surely you understand, Nanda, the true Dhamma taught by the virtuous;
you are noble, with noble conduct, and you are very much to my liking.
I speak to you and to the ladies: listen to my words!”
"This was not a burden to me, nor did it ever become one.
While I was thus attending to them, bringing happiness to my mother and father,
Nanda, having made a request, asked for me to attend upon him."
“Whosoever among you desires it by his own wish, choose one from among the holy ones who lead the spiritual life (brahmacārin);
let him serve Nanda. Which one shall Nanda attend upon?
In this context, *ariya* means beautiful (*sundara*). One who has become *ariyasamācāra* is one whose conduct is beautiful. *Bāḷhaṃ*—now you...
"I am very dear to you. Listen, mother and father, listen to my words.
'This is no burden'—this burden of looking after you was never a burden to me.
Without considering it a burden, while I was serving you, [I said] 'I am asking you to serve,' meaning that I am asking you to attend to me."
He requests: "Whoever desires"—for it would not be proper for me to say to you, "Serve my mother or my father," but rather I speak to that one among you celibate practitioners who desires [to do so]:
"By your desire, choose Nanda as your boon; accept this Nanda, my younger brother. Who among you shall he serve?"
"For both of us are indeed your sons.
Then his mother rose from her seat and said, "Dear wise Soṇa, your younger brother has been away for a long time;
even though he has returned after such a long absence, I did not dare to ask him [to stay]. For we were dependent upon him, but now that I have been permitted by you, I [shall take him]."
Proclaiming this meaning—“May I be allowed to embrace the celibate student with my arms and smell his head”—she spoke this verse:
“By you, dear father, we have been authorized; O Soṇa, we depend on you.
May I be allowed to touch Nanda’s head, that celibate student.”
Then the Great Being said, "In that case, mother, I give you leave;

go, embrace your son Nanda, smell his head, kiss him, and extinguish the grief in your heart. She went into his presence, embraced the wise Nanda right there in the midst of the assembly, smelled his head, kissed him, and having extinguished the grief in her heart, [she departed] with the Great Being.
Conversing with him, she said:
“Like the tender sprout of an assattha tree stirred by the wind,
my heart trembles now that I have seen Nanda after such a long time.”
“When I see Nanda come even in my dreams while asleep,
I become elated and joyful, thinking, ‘Nanda has indeed arrived.
But when I have woken up and do not see Nanda having come, [I am dejected].”
“Grief enters me all the more, along with no small measure of dejection.
‘Today, after a long time at last, I see Nanda come;
dear to both my husband and myself, yet Nanda has not entered our home.’”
“O father, let Nanda be happy, since Nanda does not dwell at home;
let Nanda obtain that, O dear one, and let Nanda attend upon me.
In this context, “stirred by the wind” means that just as the sprout of an assattha tree trembles when struck by the wind, so too [after a long time]...

"Seeing Nanda, my heart trembles today," she says. "Sutta means, dear Soṇa, that even when I see Nanda come to me in a dream while I am asleep, then too I am overjoyed. 'Bhattu cā' means he is dear to both my husband and me.
'Nando no pāvisī gharaṃ' means, dear one, let our son Nanda enter the leaf-hut. 'Yaṃ' means because."
“Your father is very dear to you; therefore, do not depart from this house again. ‘Nanda!
Dear one, let Nanda receive whatever he desires. ‘Nanda! Dear Soṇa, you attend upon your father; let Nanda attend upon me.
The Great Being, accepting his mother’s words with the reply, ‘So be it,’ said, ‘Nanda, the senior portion belongs to you.’”
Having been instructed, "She who has given birth is indeed one who performs great kindness; being heedful, you should attend to her," he spoke two verses, manifesting the virtues of a mother:
"She was compassionate and our support, and she gave us nourishment in the past."
“The path to the heavenly world—O sage, your mother chooses it for you.
‘In former times, she was a giver of flavors, O kinsman; your mother was endowed with merit.
The path to the heavenly world—O sage, your mother chooses it for you.’”
In this context, "compassionate" means one whose heart is tender. "One who formerly gave her milk" means she was the first to give her own milk, which is called *rasa*.
"My mother" means my mother does not desire me; she desires that [other child].
"Guardian" (*gottī*) means a protector (*gopāyikā*). "Endowed with merit" means supported by merit and a giver of merit.
Thus the Great Being, having praised his mother’s virtues with these two verses, returned and sat upon her seat;
then he said, "Nanda, you have obtained a mother who performed such difficult deeds for you. Both of us were raised by our mother through great hardship;
therefore, from now on, you must look after her with diligence and do not let her eat fruits that are not sweet."
In the midst of the assembly, revealing his mother’s performance of difficult austerities, he said:
“Desiring the fruit of a son, she worshipped the deities;
She consulted the constellations and the seasons and the years.”
“When she has bathed at the proper season, the emergence of the embryo occurs;
because of that she becomes desirous, and for that reason she is called ‘one who longs’ (*dohaḷinī*).
Having carried [the child] for a year or less, she gives birth.”
Because she gives birth by means of that, she is called "the mother" (*janetti*).
"With breast-milk, with song, and with a garment for her limbs, she satisfies her crying child;
because she satisfies him, she is called 'the one who satisfies' (*tosentī*)."
“Then, in the fierce wind and heat, she watches over me;
nourishing the child who does not yet understand, she is therefore called ‘Nourisher.
And whatever wealth belongs to the mother, and whatever wealth belongs to the father;”
She guards both of these as if they were not even her own son.
Thus, O son, thus, O son, does a mother grieve for one who,
having reached the prime of youth, is heedless with the wives of others at nightfall.
In the evening, the mother is distressed because her son has not returned.
Thus, a man who supports his parents with difficulty yet fails to serve his mother—
having behaved wrongly toward his mother— he is reborn in hell.
“Thus a person lives in misery, failing to serve his father;
having behaved wrongly toward his father, he is reborn in hell.
Even the wealth of those who desire wealth perishes—so have I heard.”
“Without having served his mother, he meets with hardship—or so I have heard.
Even the wealth of those who desire wealth perishes;
without having served his father, he meets with hardship.”
“Joy and gladness, and constant laughter and play—
these are obtained by one who understands, having served their mother.
“Joy and gladness, and constant laughter and play— ”
Having served one’s father, this is what may be obtained by one who understands:
“Generosity, pleasant speech, acting for the welfare of others here,
and impartiality toward all things, as is appropriate in each case;”
These indeed are the means of integration in the world, like the linchpin of a moving chariot.
If these means of integration did not exist, a mother would not receive honor or worship for the sake of her son,
nor would a father receive honor or worship for the sake of his son.
“Because the wise regard these as the means of integration,
they therefore attain greatness and become worthy of praise.
‘The parents are called Brahmā’ and ‘the former teachers’.”
They are worthy of offerings from their children and are compassionate toward their offspring.
Therefore, a wise person should indeed honor and revere them with food,
drink, clothing, and bedding.
“By anointing them, by bathing them, and by washing their feet—
by such service toward mother and father,
the wise are praised in this very world and rejoice in heaven after death.”
In this context, "the fruit known as a son" (*puttaphala*) means the fruit designated as a son.

"He pays homage to a deity" means he pays respect to and makes a request of a deity, thinking, "May a son be born to me. "He asks about the constellations" means he asks about the lunar mansions (*nakkhatta*), [inquiring]:
"By which constellation is a son born who will have a long life, and by which one who will have a short life? And "about the seasons and years" refers to... [six]...
"In which season is one born who becomes long-lived, and in which season is one born who is short-lived?
Or, from a mother of how many years of age is a son born who is long-lived, and from one of how many years is he short-lived?"—thus he asks concerning seasons and years.
"By one who has bathed in the season" means by one who has bathed when the flowers have appeared. "Deviation" refers to the threefold conjunction.
There is the descent into the womb; the embryo is established in the belly. "By that" means by means of that embryo she becomes desirous.
"By that" means that at that time, affection arises for the offspring conceived in her belly;
for that reason, she is called "one who has a fondness. "By that" means for that reason she is called both "the one who gives birth" (*janayantī*) and "the mother" (*janettī*).
"And with a limb-covering" means: having laid her down upon her chest, she causes the touch of her body to pervade him by means of that very covering which consists of her limbs.
"Delighting" means making him perceive [her affection], making him laugh. "Looking up at me as if making me hers" means:
thinking, "The wind blows upon my son; the heat of the sun falls upon him," she looks up with an affectionate heart, treating him as if he were her own.
"Both of these for him" means: the mother guards both of these riches for the sake of this son, not showing them to others, but keeping them within the inner chambers and such places.
Thus, by instructing him, saying, "O son, that [is yours]," "O son," "O blind fool, son, be thus diligent in royal households and the like;
do not perform such work," the mother is distressed and exhausted.

"Pattayobbane" means when the son has reached youth. Seeing that her son had gone to another's wife at night while intoxicated and did not return in the evening, she was distressed and exhausted, looking along the road with eyes filled with tears.
"Kicchā bhatō" means supported and nurtured with great difficulty. "Micchā caritvāna" means having failed to support his mother.
“*Dhanāpīti* means ‘wealth also’; or rather, this is the reading: *dhanampi*. This is what is meant:
‘I have heard that for those who desire wealth, even the wealth they have acquired perishes if they do not care for their mother. Or:
‘*Kicchaṃ vā so*—either his wealth perishes, or the person encounters suffering (*dukkhaṃ vāso*). ‘*Labbhametan’ti—this is obtainable both in this world and in the next world.”
And the bliss beginning with that of Ānanda is obtainable by a wise person who has served his mother; the meaning is that such a state can indeed be attained by one like him.
"And giving" means that gifts should be given to one's parents, endearing words should be spoken, and benefit should be rendered by accomplishing their needs as they arise.
"In matters" refers to the duties of honoring one's elders, whether performed here or there in the midst of an assembly.
Or, when they have gone into seclusion, one should practice equality toward them by means of salutation and so forth;
one should not perform salutations and the like in private and then fail to do so in public—one must be equal in all circumstances. "And these means of integration would not exist" means:
if these four means of integration were not present. "They regard correctly" means: they regard by way of the right method or reason.
"Greatness" means preeminence. "Brahma-like" means they are like Brahmā among their sons—supreme and best. "Ancient teachers" means the first teachers.
"Worthy of offerings" means recipients of offerings who are worthy of any kind of honor.
"With food and drink" means there is need for both food and drink. "Having passed away" means at the conclusion of death, having gone from here, one rejoices in heaven.
Thus the Great Being brought his teaching of the Dhamma to a conclusion, as if he were turning Mount Sineru. Having heard it, all those kings and their armies gained confidence.
Then, having established them in the five precepts and exhorted them, saying, "Be diligent in giving and the other perfections," he dismissed them.
All of them ruled their kingdoms according to the Dhamma, and at the end of their lives, they went to the city of the gods.
They fulfilled their duties. Both Soṇa Paṇḍita and Nanda Paṇḍita, having served their parents for as long as they lived, became destined for the Brahma-world.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka.
At the conclusion of the Truths, the monk who supported his mother was established in the fruit of Stream-entry. At that time, the parents were members of a great royal family.
Nanda the Wise was Ānanda; Manoja the King was Sāriputta; the one hundred and one kings were the eighty great elders as well as other elders;
the twenty-four unshakeable assemblies were the Buddha’s retinues; and as for Soṇa the Wise, he was none other than myself.
This is the second commentary on the Soṇananda Jātaka.
The Summary of Birth Stories (Jātakuddāna):
Now, in this excellent seventy-first chapter, the noble King Kusāvatī was in his assembly hall;
then there were the excellent Soṇa and Sunanda, and again, in the seventy-first discourse, they were consecrated.
The commentary on the Seventy-Nipāta is finished.
21. The Eighty-Nipāta [533] 1.
The Commentary on the Cūḷahaṃsa Jātaka.
"Sumukha": This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Veḷuvana concerning the sacrifice of his own life by the Venerable Ānanda.

For when the archers were dispatched by Devadatta to deprive the Tathāgata of life, the one sent first returned and said, "Venerable Sir, I am not able to deprive that Blessed One of life; he possesses great psychic power (mahiddhika)."
When it was said, "That Blessed One is of great power," Devadatta replied, "Enough, friend!
Do not you deprive the ascetic Gotama of life; I myself shall deprive the ascetic Gotama of life.

Having said this, while the Tathāgata was walking back and forth in the western shade of Vulture Peak Mountain, Devadatta himself climbed Vulture Peak Mountain and [hurled] a great [boulder] with the force of a machine.
He hurled a boulder, thinking, “With this rock I shall deprive the ascetic Gotama of life.
Then two mountain peaks came together and caught that rock. From there, a splinter flew up, struck the Blessed One’s foot, and drew blood, causing intense pain to arise.
Jīvaka then incised the Tathāgata’s foot with a knife.
Having made him vomit the foul blood, removed the putrid flesh, washed him, and anointed him with medicine, he restored him to health.
The Teacher, surrounded by the community of monks as before, moved about with the great grace of a Buddha.
Then, seeing him, Devadatta thought: "The body of the ascetic Gotama has reached the pinnacle of physical beauty."

"Seeing him thus, no human being would be able to approach; moreover, the king has an elephant named Nāḷāgiri who is fierce, cruel, and a slayer of men, and he knows nothing of the virtues of the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha; he will bring about his end.
Having gone, he reported this matter to the king. The king, accepting it with the words "Very well," [summoned] the elephant trainer...
Having summoned him, he said, "Friend, tomorrow morning, having made Nāḷāgiri intoxicated, release him onto the street by which the ascetic Gotama travels.
Devadatta then asked him, "On other days, how much liquor does the elephant drink?
When it was replied, "Eight jars, venerable sir," he said, "In that case, tomorrow you must give him sixteen jars to drink."
“You should cause Nāḷāgiri to charge head-on at the path where the ascetic Gotama has set out,” he said. He agreed, saying, “Very well.
The king had a drum beaten throughout the city, proclaiming: “Tomorrow he will intoxicate Nāḷāgiri and let him loose in the city;
therefore, citizens, having performed all your duties early in the morning, do not enter the middle streets. Then Devadatta, from the royal residence—
Having risen and gone to the elephant stable, he addressed the elephant keepers:
"Friends, we are capable of putting those in high positions in low positions, or those in low positions in high positions.
If you have need of wealth, tomorrow at dawn, having made Nāḷāgiri drink sixteen jars of strong liquor, [drive him] with goads and spears at the time of the arrival of the ascetic Gotama."

“Having pierced him, incited him to anger, and caused the elephant stable to be demolished, turn him toward the path taken by the ascetic Gotama and bring about the end of the ascetic Gotama’s life,” he said. They accepted, saying, “Very well.
That report spread throughout the entire city. When the lay followers, who were devoted to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, heard it...

Having approached the Teacher, they said, "Venerable Sir, Devadatta has allied himself with the king and will release the elephant Nāḷāgiri tomorrow on the path you have taken; therefore, do not enter for alms tomorrow, but remain right here.
We shall provide the almsfood within the monastery itself to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha."
The Teacher, however, without saying, "I will not enter for alms tomorrow," declared:

"Tomorrow, having tamed Nāḷāgiri and performed a miracle, and having crushed the heretics, I shall depart from Rājagaha for alms and, without even walking for alms in Rājagaha, I shall go out surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus and return to Veḷuvana; and the residents of Rājagaha, taking many food vessels..."
“They will come to the Bamboo Grove itself; tomorrow the meal-offering will take place right at the monastery.
For this reason, he consented to them. Having understood the Tathāgata’s consent, they brought their food vessels and departed with the thought, “We shall give our alms-gift right at the monastery.”

The Teacher, having taught the Dhamma during the first watch, answered the questions of the deities during the middle watch, and during the first portion of the last watch lay down in the lion’s posture;
having spent the second portion in the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), he entered the attainment of great compassion (*mahākaruṇāsamāpatti*) during the third portion.
Emerging from that state, he surveyed those among his kinsmen who were ready for conversion, beginning with the subduing of Nāḷāgiri.
Having seen the realization of the Dhamma by eighty-four thousand beings, and when the night had turned to dawn,
he attended to his physical needs, addressed the Venerable Ānanda, and said: “Ānanda,
announce today that all the bhikkhus residing in the eighteen great monasteries surrounding Rājagaha are to enter Rājagaha together with me.”

The Elder did accordingly. All the monks assembled at Veḷuvana. The Teacher, surrounded by a great community of monks, entered Rājagaha. Then the elephant and the bull acted according to the instructions given; there was a great gathering.
People endowed with faith thought, "Today, it is said, there will be a battle between the Elephant of the Buddha and the Elephant of the Animals."
"Let us witness the taming of Nāḷāgiri by the peerless play of the Buddha," they said, and they climbed onto the terraces, upper chambers, roofs, and other parts of the palace and stood there.
But those who were faithless and held wrong views thought, "This Nāḷāgiri is fierce, cruel, and a slayer of men;
he does not know the virtues of the Buddha and others. Today, having destroyed the golden-hued body of the ascetic Gotama..."
“He will bring about the end of his life; today we shall see the back of our enemy! Thus they stood upon their palaces and other high places.

The elephant, too, seeing the Blessed One approaching, terrifying the people, demolishing houses, and crushing wagons, raised its trunk, with its ears and tail erect, and charging like a mountain toward where the Blessed One was.
He charged toward him. Seeing him approaching, the monks said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, this Nāḷāgiri is fierce, violent, and a slayer of men; he has entered this street.
Furthermore, he does not know the virtues of the Buddha and so forth. May the Blessed One step back, venerable sir; may the Sugata step back. "Do not be afraid, monks."
“I am capable of taming Nāḷāgiri. Then the Venerable Sāriputta entreated the Teacher:
“Venerable Sir, the duty that has arisen for one’s father is the responsibility of the eldest son; I myself will tame him. Thereupon the Teacher dissuaded him, saying:
“Sāriputta, the power of a Buddha is one thing, and the power of a disciple is another; stop, Sāriputta. Thus it was.
The eighty great elders for the most part made their request. The Teacher refused them all.

Then the Venerable Ānanda, unable to endure it because of his intense affection for the Teacher, thought, "Let this elephant kill me first," and having renounced his life for the sake of the Tathāgata, he went and stood before the Teacher. Then the Teacher said to him, "Step aside, Ānanda."
"Do not stand before me," he said. "Venerable sir, this elephant is fierce, cruel, and a slayer of men; it is like the fire at the end of an eon.
Let it kill me first, and afterwards let it come into your presence. Though the Elder spoke thus up to three times, the elephant remained exactly as it was and did not retreat.
Then the Blessed One, by means of his supernormal power, caused it to retreat.
He placed [the elephant] among the monks.

At that moment, a certain woman, seeing Nāḷāgiri and terrified by the fear of death, fled while dropping the child she held in her arms between the elephant and the Tathāgata. The elephant pursued her.
Having turned back, he went into the presence of the boy. At that time, the boy let out a great cry.
The Teacher, having encompassed Nālāgiri with specific loving-kindness (*mettā*), emitted a most sweet Brahma-voice and said: "O Nālāgiri!
Those who gave you sixteen jars of liquor to drink and made you intoxicated did not do so thinking, 'He will seize another,' but rather, 'He will seize me.'"
“Do not wander about with your legs wearying for no reason; come here! he called out.
Having heard the Teacher’s words, the man opened his eyes and gazed upon the Blessed One’s glorious form.

Stricken with a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), his drunkenness severed by the Buddha’s majesty, he approached with his head hanging down and his ears flapping, and fell at the feet of the Tathāgata.
Then the Teacher said to him, "Nāḷāgiri, you are a wild elephant, while I am a Buddha-elephant;
from this day forth, do not be fierce, cruel, or a slayer of men, but cultivate a heart of loving-kindness toward all beings.
Having spoken thus, he extended his right hand, touched the elephant's forehead, and—
“Do not, O elephant, approach the Naga; for painful, O elephant, is the approach to the Naga.
For one who has been slain by the Naga, O elephant, there is no happy destination hereafter.
Do not be intoxicated, and do not be negligent; for those who are negligent do not go to a happy destination.”
“You yourself shall act in such a way that you will go to a happy destination.
Thus he taught the Dhamma.
His entire body was suffused without interruption by rapture. Had he not been an animal, it is said...
He will attain the fruit of stream-entry. When the people saw that miracle, they roared and clapped their hands;
filled with joy, they threw various ornaments, which covered the elephant’s body.
From that time on, Nāḷāgiri became known as Dhanapālaka. Now, at that gathering of Dhanapālaka...
