Eighty-four thousand beings drank the Deathless. The Teacher established Dhanapālaka in the five precepts.
Taking dust from the Blessed One’s feet with his trunk, he scattered it over his own head;
then, turning back, he stood within range of sight, paid homage to the One of Ten Powers, and returned to the elephant stable. From that time forth—
Having become one whose teeth are well-tamed, he does not harm anyone. The Teacher, his heart’s desire fulfilled, resolved:
“Let that wealth which was cast [at me] belong only to those who threw it. Having thus subdued the heretics and thinking, “Today I have performed a great miracle;
it is not fitting for me to wander for alms in this city,” he remained surrounded by the community of monks.
Like a Kṣatriya who has achieved victory, he departed from the city and went straight to the Veḷuvana.
The inhabitants of the city took abundant food, drink, and solid refreshments, went to the monastery, and offered a great almsgiving.
On that day, in the evening, the monks, having filled the Dhamma Hall and sat down together, initiated this conversation:
“Friends, a difficult deed has been done by the Venerable Ānanda in sacrificing his own life for the sake of the Tathāgata.
Even though he was turned back three times by the Teacher upon seeing Nāḷāgiri, he did not depart.
Oh, how the Venerable Ānanda is a doer of what is difficult! The Teacher thought, “A discourse on Ānanda’s virtues is underway; I must go there.”
Having emerged from the Fragrant Chamber and approached them, he asked, "Monks, with what discussion are you gathered here now?
When they replied, "With this very one," he said, "Monks, it is not only now; in the past as well, even though Ānanda was reborn in the animal realm, he sacrificed his life for my sake.
Being requested by them, he related a story of the past.
In the past, in the kingdom of Mahimsaka, in the city of Sāgala, a king named Sāgala ruled righteously.
At that time, not far from the city, in a certain fowler’s village, a particular fowler made his living by catching birds with snares and selling them in the city.
And not far from the city, at a whirlpool twelve yojanas in extent, there was a place called Mānusiyā.
There was a lotus lake covered with five-colored lotuses. Various flocks of birds descended there.

That hunter set snares there in an indiscriminate manner. At that time, Dhatarattha, the king of swans, lived in a golden cave on Mount Cittakūṭa, accompanied by a retinue of ninety-six thousand swans;
Sumukha was his commander-in-chief. Then, one day—
Then a certain number of golden swans from the flock went to Lake Mānusiya;
having wandered at their pleasure in that place of abundant food and being well-fed, they returned to Cittakūṭa and reported to Dhatarattha:
"Great King, on the human path there is a lotus lake called Mānusiya, which possesses excellent food; let us go there to gather food."
Thus, although he had refused, saying, "A 'human path' is full of danger and fear;
let it not please you," he was addressed by them again and again. Saying, "If it pleases you, let us go," he went to that lake together with his retinue.
As he descended from the sky, he stepped down while placing one foot right into a snare. Then the snare caught his foot with an iron plate.
As if pulling it, he bound and seized him. Then, as he pulled with the thought, "I shall cut it," on the first pull the skin was cut;
on the second, the flesh was cut; on the third, the sinew was cut.
The snare remained fixed against the bone, blood flowed forth, and intense pains arose.
He thought: "If I let out a cry of distress, my relatives will become terrified;
failing to gather their food, they will flee with empty stomachs and, due to their weakness, fall into the great ocean.
Enduring that pain, he allowed his kinsmen to feed as much as they required, and then, at the time when the swans were sporting, he let out a loud, continuous cry.
Hearing this, those geese, terrified by the fear of death, formed into flocks and departed toward Cittakūṭa.
When they had departed, Sumukha, the commander of the goose army, thinking, "Has this danger arisen for the Great King?
I shall find out," leaped forward with speed and, amidst the flock of geese moving ahead, [beheld] the Great Being.
Having failed to see the middle flock of swans, he searched for the last flock;

failing to see them there as well, he thought, "Without a doubt, this fear has arisen because of him," and turning back, he saw the Great Being bound in a snare, smeared with blood, afflicted by pain, and lying on the surface of the mud. Seeing him, he said, "Do not be afraid, Great King."
Saying, "I shall sacrifice my own life to release you from this snare," he descended and sat down upon the surface of the mud, comforting the Great Being.
Then, testing him, the Great Being spoke the first verse:
"O Sumukha, the birds depart without gathering [anything];"
"Go forth, you too; do not hesitate. There is no companionship for one who is bound.
In this context, "not gathering" means not looking back out of affection or attachment. "Departing" means:
"These ninety-six thousand swans, my kinsmen among birds, are leaving me behind; you too go, do not dwell here."
He said, "I desire this; for when I am bound by such a snare, there can be no companionship. Indeed, I will not now be able to perform any duty of a companion for you.
What use have you for me, who am of no service? Do not make a fuss; simply go. From here on—
“Whether I go or do not go, I shall not become immortal by that means.
Having attended upon one who is happy, how could I abandon one who is suffering?
Either death together with you, or life without you.”
“Death itself would be better for me than to live without you.
“This is not the Dhamma, O Great King, that one should abandon another who has gone such a way.
Wherever your destination is, that is my destination; this is what I desire, O Lord of Birds.”
“What other destination can there be for one bound by a snare than the great kitchen?
How is it that you, though liberated, find pleasure in such thoughts?
Or what benefit do you see, O bird, in this for both me and yourself?”
When both kinsmen and those left behind have met with the destruction of their lives—
that which is devoid of even a speck of gold, shrouded in blind darkness—
what purpose would be served by sacrificing a living being for such a thing? How could it illuminate any goal?
“How is it that you, O best of those who fly, do not understand the meaning within the Dhamma?
When the Dhamma is honored, it reveals the welfare of living beings.
Thus, looking to the Dhamma and to the welfare arising from the Dhamma—”
Beholding Bhaṭṭi with you, I do not desire life.
"Surely this is the way of the virtuous: that a friend stands by a friend in times of distress.
One would not abandon such a person even for the sake of one's own life, remembering the duty of friendship."
“This Dhamma has been practiced by you, and my devotion is known to me;
do as you wish regarding this matter of mine, for I grant you my permission to go.
However, since time has passed in this way, that which was a deficiency on my part toward my kinsmen—”
She [spoke] to him who was endowed with wisdom and supremely self-restrained.
While the noble ones, who live the noble life, were thus conversing,
the hunter appeared to them like Death approaching the sick.
“Those twice-born ones, having long observed their enemy for his welfare,
sat in silence, both of them, and did not stir from their seats.
And seeing Dhataraṭṭha rising up here and there from that place...”
“Come forth with speed, O enemy of birds, toward the lord of birds!
Having rushed forward with speed and attacked the supreme bird,
the hunter retreated, thinking, “They are caught.”
“One was sitting bound, and another, moreover, was unbound;
having approached the one sitting bound, he looked upon him without dejection.
Then, still full of doubt, he addressed Paṇḍara:”
To the lord of the flocks of birds, who sat with his body fully expanded,
[the king said]: "Since you, though bound by a great snare,
do not flee in any direction, why then, O powerful bird, do you not go away while unbound?"
"Why is it that you, a brahmin, though yourself free, gaze upon one who is bound?
While the birds depart, leaving him behind, why do you alone remain?
"He is a king, O friend of the brahmins, and a companion as dear to me as my own life."
"I shall not abandon him until the end of time.
But how was it that this bird did not see the snare set?
For this is the way of the great: they are able to perceive even their own misfortune."
“When ruin comes upon a person at the end of their life, then,
though they encounter nets and snares, they do not perceive them.
Yet even so, O one of great wisdom, various kinds of snares are spread abroad.”
"Secretly they are bound, and thus at the end of life."—The connection of these verses is to be understood according to the method of the Pāḷi itself.
Therein, "whether I go to the grove," O Great King, whether I should go from here or not, I am not [bound] by that going; nor...
"Either by not going would I be immortal; for even if I were to go from here or not go, I would still not be released from death.
But having previously attended upon her while she was happy, how could I now abandon her when she is suffering?"—thus he says.
"Or death" means that either while I do not go there would be death together with you, or while I do go there would be death apart from you.
"Life. Among those two options, the meaning is: "Death together with you is indeed better for me; that I should live without you is not better for me. "It pleases me":
whatever your destination or fate may be, that very same thing pleases me. "How so?
My dear Sumukha, while I am bound by a strong hair-rope and have fallen into the hands of another—"
"May that destination please you; but how can it please one like you—who is volitional, conscious, wise, and liberated?

'Pakkhimā' means possessing wings. 'Of both': when our two lives have come to an end, what benefit do you see for yourself or for my remaining relatives? In the word *yaṃ*, the particle *na* is used here as a particle of comparison."
*Kañcanadepiñchā* means *kañcanadvepiñcha*, or this very reading is correct;
the meaning is "having both wings like gold. *Tamasā* means "in darkness. *Gataṃ* means "done," or this very reading is correct.
This connects with the preceding *na*-sound; the meaning is "as if it were 'not done'. This is what is intended: even while you were sacrificing your life...
"Even though there is no loss to my life, this sacrifice of your life is like something done in blind darkness; it is a mere physical act whose virtue is not witnessed.
Since your sacrifice of life has such unobserved virtue, what purpose would you achieve by sacrificing your life?"
"The Dhamma, when honored, is peaceful" means the Dhamma being worshipped and revered. "It shows the goal" means it shows progress. "Looking on" means observing.
"Seeing the goal from the Dhamma" means seeing the goal that has arisen from the Dhamma. "Affection" means endearment.
"The Dhamma of the good" means the nature of the wise. "He who is a friend in misfortunes" refers to one who is a friend in times of calamity.
"One should not abandon a friend. For one who does not abandon a friend, this is indeed the nature of a friend;

truly, this is the law of the virtuous. "Known" means it has become manifest. "Do as you wish" means: do this which is my wish, that which is desired by me, my word. "But even though time has passed thus" means:
but even though time has passed thus, while I am bound here at this place with a snare. "Most perfectly restrained" means: supremely complete.
“While they were thus deliberating”—meaning while those noble ones (*ariya*), who are noble in their conduct, were saying, “Go! I will not go.
“He appeared”—meaning he came wearing saffron robes, adorned with a red garland, and carrying a club.
“To those who are afflicted”—meaning to the sick, like death itself. “He looked upon them,” monks, both of them.
Seeing the hunter approaching, they were well-disposed—meaning they were intent on each other’s welfare and possessed gentle hearts—and did not waver from their seats;
that is, they did not move from where they sat, but remained exactly as they were.
However, Sumukha thought, "Let this hunter come and strike me first," and so he sat down placing the Great Being behind him.
“Dhatarattha” refers to the swans. “Samuḍḍenta” means seeing them flying here and there out of fear of death.
“Āsajja” means having approached the other two people. “Paccakamittha” means he went back, thinking and considering whether they were bound or not;
having lost his momentum, he proceeded slowly. “Āsajja baddhamāsīnaṃ” means having approached the Great Being who was bound.
Having approached and sat down, he saw Sumukha looking at the Great Being with a look of distress;
seeing him thus, the meaning is that he became filled with doubt, thinking, "What indeed is this? Why is one who is unbound sitting near one who is bound? I shall ask the reason.
Regarding the word *paṇḍare*: it refers to swans (*haṃsa*), or alternatively, to those who are pure, stainless, and possessing the color of refined gold.
The meaning is as follows: *pavaḍḍhakāya* means having a grown body, that is, one with a large physique. *Yaṃ nū* means "since this [bird] has been bound by a great snare.
*Na kurute disaṃ* means it does not resort to even a single direction for the purpose of fleeing;

the intention is that this is appropriate. *Balī* means even though it is endowed with strength. *Pakkhī* is used as a form of address to him. *Ohāya* means having abandoned. *Yanti* refers to the remaining birds.
They go. "Avahīyasi" means you are left behind.
"Dijāmittā" means the enemies of the twice-born (the Brahmins). "Yāva kālassa pariyāyanti" means until the turn of time arrives, that is, until the time of death comes.
But how do they pass away? You say, "He is my king," yet kings are indeed wise; thus he is wise.
For what reason did he, though being equal [to others], not see the laid-out snare?
"The cause" (*padaṃ hetu*) refers to the state or cause of those who have attained greatness in self-restraint or greatness in wisdom; namely, their own awakening to misfortune.

Therefore, they are worthy of awakening to misfortune. "Failure" (*parābhava*) means decline. "Even having approached" (*āsajjāpi*) means even having drawn near, one does not awaken. "Tatā" means spread out or laid out. "Having approached the secret" (*guyhamāsajja*)—
Among those snares, they are caught by encountering that which is hidden and concealed. "Then indeed" means: "then, in this way, they are caught at the very moment their life comes to an end.
Thus, having made his heart soft through this exchange of conversation, he spoke a verse while entreating the Great Being for his life:
“Could this cohabitation with her not be of a pleasant outcome?
Would he perhaps grant us permission? Would he perhaps give us our lives?
In that context, *api nāyam* means “could this be”; *sukhudrayo* means “having a pleasant result”; and *api no anumaññāsī* refers to [granting permission for] Cittakūṭa.
"Once you have gone to see our kinsmen, you too will grant us permission. Will you not even give us our lives?
Having gained confidence through this conversation, you will not kill us.
Bound by his sweet words, he spoke this verse:
“I have not bound you, nor do I desire your death;
by all means, go quickly from here and live long, free from suffering.
Then Sumukha spoke these four verses:
“I do not desire this for him other than his life;
if you are satisfied with one, release him and eat me.
We are equal in height and girth, and we are both the same in age.”
"You have no need for life through this gain, nor for this purpose.
Therefore, look well upon it; let your greed be for wealth.
First bind me with your snare, O lord of birds, and afterwards release the king of birds."
“And only then would there be gain for you, and your request would be fulfilled;
friendship with the Dhataratthas would last as long as life.
In this context, “this” refers to that which is other than my life—apart from this life of mine, I do not desire even that. “I am equal” means...
"Samānā homa" means "let us be together. "Niminā tuvanti parivattehi tvaṃ" means "by means of a substitution, you [should say] 'Tavamhasūti'";

that is, let there be greed for us in you. He says, "What use is this to you? Produce desire for me instead. "Tāvadevāti" means "just that much. "Yācanāya cāti" means "and by my request," the sense being: "let that very request of mine be fulfilled."
Thus, by that teaching of the Dhamma, his heart became as softened as cotton wool placed in oil. Making the Great Being his gift, he gave him away and said:
"Let our great assembly behold you, released from here and gone—our friends, companions, servants, children, wives, and kinsmen."
“And there are not many such friends to be found here among the many as you are, Dhatarattha’s friend who shares his very life.
Therefore, I release your companion; let him be your follower, O King.”
"By all means, having gone quickly from here, may you shine in the midst of your kinsmen.
In this context, *no* is a mere particle. "Released by you" means that you alone are indeed releasing this [bird];
therefore, let these great assemblies of kinsmen and these friends and others see this one released by you, who has gone from here to Mount Cittakūṭa.
And here, "relatives" (*bandhavā*) refers to those connected by blood. "Exist" (*vijjati*) means they are found.
"Sharing life" (*pāṇasādhāraṇo*) means one whose life is shared, one who lives without being separated; just as you are his friend, such friends do not exist for many others.
"Following after you" (*tavānugo*) means: "As you go ahead taking this suffering person with you, let him be your follower."
Having spoken thus, the hunter’s son approached the Great Being with a mind of loving-kindness;
he cut the bonds, embraced him, led him out from the thicket, and seated him on the surface of young *dabba* grass by the edge of the forest.
Then, with a gentle heart, he slowly loosened the binding snare from the Great Being’s feet, cast it far away, and established a powerful bond of affection for the Great Being.
Taking water with a mind of loving-kindness (*mettā*), he washed away the blood and rubbed it repeatedly.
Through the power of his loving-kindness, the veins of the Bodhisatta’s foot were joined to the veins, the flesh to the flesh, and the skin to the skin;
immediately, the foot became healed, with skin and hair grown back, indistinguishable from one who had not been wounded. The Bodhisatta was at ease.
He sat down in his natural state. Then Sumukha, seeing the Great Being’s state of happiness through his own efforts, was filled with joy and offered praise to the hunter.
To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said: “Filled with devotion, out of respect for his master, he praised the one who had released him.”
Vakkanga addressed him, speaking words pleasant to the ear:
“O hunter, may you rejoice together with all your kinsmen,
just as I rejoice today, having seen the king of birds set free.”
In that context, *vakkaṅgo* means "crooked-necked.
Having thus offered praise to the hunter, Sumukha said to the Bodhisatta: "Great King, this man has done us a great service;
for he did not heed our words, but instead made us his play-geese and gave us to his masters, thereby [earning] much wealth."
"He would have gained profit; by killing me and selling my flesh, he would have obtained even the capital.
But he disregarded his own life and did our bidding. Let us take him into the presence of the king and ensure his livelihood is secure.
The Great Being agreed. Sumukha, having conversed with the Great Being in his own language, spoke again in the human tongue:
Having addressed the son of a hunter, he asked, "Friend, for what purpose have you set these snares?
When he replied, "For the sake of wealth," he said, "That being the case, take us with you, enter the city, and show us to the king; we will cause much wealth to be given to you. Then he said:
"Come, I shall instruct you so that you too may obtain it."
“Dhataraṭṭha has gained his reward; he shall see no evil whatsoever.
Quickly lead us both to the inner palace and show us to the king—unbound, natural, and standing upright like two poles set up at either side.”
“O Great King, these are the Dhataraṭṭhas, the lords of the geese;
for this one is the king of the geese, and this other is the commander-in-chief. 39.
‘Without doubt, having seen this king of geese, the lord of men—’
“Trembling, joyful, and delighted, he will give you much wealth.
In this context, “I shall train accordingly” means “I shall instruct. “Evil” means base. “Show us both to the king” means “show both of us to the king.
This was for the purpose of demonstrating the power of the Bodhisatta’s wisdom and his own quality of friendship.
He spoke thus for four reasons: for the purpose of making himself manifest, for the hunter’s acquisition of wealth, and for the purpose of establishing the king in moral virtue.
And having led them to the king, he should inform him thus:
"Great King, these two lords of swans are born of the Dhatarattha clan; of these, this one is the king, and the other is the commander-in-chief."
Thus he instructed him. The three terms beginning with “delighted” (*patīta*) are merely synonyms for states of satisfaction.
When this was said, the hunter replied, “Master, may you not find pleasure in seeing the king; kings are fickle-minded—they might turn you into game birds for sport or even have you executed.
To which [the other] said, “Friend, do not fear; I shall deal with such a cruel hunter as that...”
Having softened Lohitapāṇi with a discourse on the Dhamma, I made him prostrate at my feet.

When he said, "Kings are indeed possessed of merit and wisdom, and they know what is well-spoken and what is ill-spoken; show us to the king quickly," I replied, "In that case, do not be angry with me;
I shall certainly take you there according to your wish," and then both of them [took up] the carrying-pole.
Having placed [the child] on his shoulder and gone to the royal palace, he showed him to the king; when questioned by the king, he reported the matter exactly as it was.
To illustrate this point, the Teacher said:
“Having heard those words of his, he established [the truth] through his own deed.”
Having gone quickly to the inner palace, he showed the king the swans—
unbound and in their natural state, standing on both sides of a carrying-pole:
"O Great King, these are Dhatarattha, the lords of the swans."
“This one is indeed the king of the swans, and this other is the commander-in-chief.
How then did these birds come into your hands?
How did the hunter find such great beings here under his authority?”
“O lord of men, these snares have been set in the marshes;
whatever place I consider to be a refuge for birds becomes a trap for their lives.
Having encountered such a snare, the king of swans was caught.”
Seated there, unbound, he addressed me:
“It is most difficult for the ignoble to burn away their supreme nature;
yet this bird, devoted to the Dhamma, has exerted himself for the sake of his master.”
“Having sacrificed his own life, he who deserved to live sat there sighing and begged for the life of his master.
Hearing those words of his, I attained a state of serene confidence.”
Then I released him from the snares and gave him my permission to depart in peace.
Released by his husband, Vakkaṅga, out of reverence for his master,
spoke to him with words that were pleasing to the ear.
“Thus, hunter, rejoice together with all your kinsmen,
just as I rejoice today upon seeing the king of birds set free.
Come, I shall instruct you so that you too may obtain [this joy].”
“Dhataraṭṭha has gained his reward; he shall see no evil whatsoever.
Quickly lead us both to the inner palace and show us to the king—us two standing here on either side of the yoke-pole, unbound and in our natural state.”
“O Great King, these are the Dhataraṭṭhas, the lords of the swans;
for this one is the king of the swans, and this other is the commander-in-chief.
Without doubt, upon seeing this king of swans, the lord of men—”
“Overjoyed, happy, and delighted, he will give you much wealth.
“In accordance with his word, I have brought both of them here;
for indeed, they were right here, and both have been approved by me.”
“This bird, having thus departed, is a twice-born one of supreme virtue;
he would surely inspire gentleness even in a hunter such as I.
And I see no other gift, O King, that could be like this.”
“In the village of all the fowlers—behold that, O lord of men!
Regarding this, “he was reborn through his own karma” means that by performing what he had spoken, he brought it to completion through bodily action.
“Having gone” refers to the fact that the place where the king of swans sat was higher, while the place where the commander-in-chief sat was somewhat lower.
Having done so, they both lifted [the king] up and, shouting "The swan-king and the general are going to see the king!

Listen! Listen! as they raised the crowd, they quickly reached the inner palace while the people, their hearts melting, praised them, saying, "Never before have we seen such golden-colored swan-kings who have attained such supreme beauty."

"Having gone," means: having caused it to be announced to the king, "The swan-kings have come to see you," he was summoned by the king with a joyful mind saying, "Let them come," and having been brought forward, he showed them.
"Into his hands" (*hatthatta*) means: that which has come into the hands; "into his possession" (*patta*) is what is meant.
"Of the great ones" refers to the golden-colored Dhataraṭṭha swans who had attained greatness of glory.
He asks: "How have you, having become a hunter, attained lordship over the masters?
There is also a reading, "issaramidhamajjhagā," which means: "How have you attained sovereignty over these?
"Vihitā" means "joined. "Whatever abode one conceives of, O Great King"—that is, whatever gathering place of the birds.
I consider the obstruction of living beings to be the cause of their destruction; here and there, snares were set by me in the marshes.
"Such" refers to that kind of snare for obstructing living beings which was set by me in the human lake. "That" refers to this very thing bound there.
"He sat down" means he approached and sat down, disregarding his own life. "Mamāya" means [he thought] "me."
He addressed this general, speaking with me. "Sudukkaraṃ" means that at that moment he performed what is very difficult for ignoble persons like us.
"Kiṃ taṃ" (What is it? means: "Dahate bhāvamuttamaṃ," he reveals, burns away [the darkness], and makes manifest his own supreme intention.
"Attanāyaṃ" means belonging to himself. "Anutthunanto" means while praising the qualities of his benefactor.
Praising his life, he entreated me, saying, "Release me.
"Tassa" means "to him," who was thus entreating. "Sukhena ca" means that I permitted him, saying, "Go to Cittakūṭa as you please and see your circle of kinsmen.
"Ettheva hi" means that these two were by me [sent] right here at this Mānusī lake for the purpose of going to Cittakūṭa.
They were approved. "Thus gone" means thus fallen into the hands of the enemy.
"You should produce gentleness" means you should generate a mind of loving-kindness (*mettā*) toward yourself. "A gift" (*upāyana*) means a present. "In the entire village of fowlers":
"In every single village of fowlers, I have never before seen such a gift brought by any fowler as this. "Behold that! means look at it.
"Behold this gift brought by me, O lord of men!
Thus he praised the virtue of Sumukha even while standing there. Then the king had a costly seat provided for the king of the swans and a golden throne for Sumukha;
and when they were seated there, [he served them] with golden vessels.

Having caused parched grain, honey, molasses, and other foods to be served, and once the task of eating and drinking was finished, he raised his joined palms, requested a discourse on the Dhamma from the Great Being, and sat down upon a golden throne.
Being thus requested by him, the Great Being first engaged in polite conversation.
To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
Seeing the king seated upon a beautiful golden throne, Vakkaṅga addressed him, speaking words pleasant to the ear:
“I hope all is well with you, sir; I hope you are free from illness.”
“I hope this kingdom is prosperous, and that you govern it with righteousness.
“It is well with me, O swan, and likewise, O swan, I am free from illness;
moreover, this kingdom is prosperous as I govern it with righteousness.”
“I trust that no fault whatsoever exists among your ministers;
I trust they do not even desire your life for their own ends.
Furthermore, I trust that no fault whatsoever exists among my own ministers.”
Furthermore, they do not even desire life for the sake of their own interests.
"Is your wife like you? Is she obedient and sweet-spoken?
Is she endowed with children, beauty, and fame, and does she follow your will?"
“Moreover, my wife is like me: obedient and sweet-spoken;
endowed with the beauty of a son and fame, she follows my will and authority.
In this passage, “the king” refers to King Sāgara. “Vakkaṅga” is the name of the swan-king. “You govern by the Dhamma” means by the Dhamma...
"You instruct. "Fault" means an offense. "In your affairs" means when your affairs such as battle and so forth have arisen.
"They do not desire for themselves" means that those who give their chests and sacrifice [their lives] do not long for anything for their own life;
having abandoned their lives, they accomplish only your purpose. "Equal" means of the same kind. "Obedient" means those who accept your word. "Even in the form of sons" means...
"Endowed with sons, beauty, and fame, do they follow your will and desire?
Do they act according to your intention and remain under your control, rather than acting according to their own whims?
Thus, when the Bodhisatta had offered this hospitable greeting, the king spoke again in conversation with him:
“Did you perhaps fall into the hands of the Great Beast and undergo immense suffering during that first calamity?
Did he seize you with his machine and crush you flat with his club?”
Thus, for these people, there was such a portentous event.
“It was safe, O Great King, even while such a calamity existed;
yet no one at all acted toward us as an enemy.”
“The hunter returned and addressed him first;
then this wise Sumukha spoke in reply.
Having heard those words of his, he attained a state of serene confidence.”
Then Pāmucī released me from her bonds and permitted me to go at my ease.
"And this very thing was thought out by Sumukha himself for this purpose:
that you should come into the presence of my lord, desiring wealth for his sake."
“Welcome indeed to you both; I am delighted at the sight of you.
And may you both receive much wealth, as much as you desire.
In this context, *mahāsattuhatthattaṃ gato* means having come into the hands of a great enemy (*mahāsattu*). *Āpatitvāna* means... [having approached].
"Having run up. *Pātikanti* means "to the natural state," or this very reading (*pātikanti*) is the text itself. This is what is meant:
for these low-born men, it becomes so natural that they strike birds with sticks, bringing them to their death, and thereby receive wealth as wages.
"Kiñci rasmāsūti" means "something among us. "Sattūvāti" means "like flour. "Paccagamitthāti," O Great King—
"Seeing us, he drew back a little, thinking, 'They are bound. 'Even before,' means he was the very first to address us.
'At that time' means at that moment. 'For this purpose' means it was intended for the sake of this son of a hunter.
'Desiring wealth' means by one desiring his wealth, our coming to you was intended. 'And welcome indeed!'"
“Do not worry, sirs; your coming here is most welcome. Let him receive [what he seeks].
Having spoken thus, the king looked at one of his ministers and, when the latter asked, “What shall I do, Your Majesty?
he replied, “Have this hunter’s hair and beard trimmed, bathe and anoint him, adorn him with all ornaments, and bring him back.”
Having spoken thus, and after he had acted accordingly, the Teacher gave him— once he had been brought back— a village yielding a hundred thousand [pieces of gold] every year,
a large house situated on two streets, an excellent chariot, and much other gold and bullion.
Revealing this matter, the Teacher said:
“Having gratified the hunter with riches, the lord of men addressed Vakkanga, saying, ‘Speak words pleasant to the ear.

Then the Great Being taught the Dhamma to the king. Having heard his discourse on the Dhamma, the king, with a heart full of joy, thinking, ‘I shall pay honor to this preacher of the Dhamma,’ gave him his white parasol and, offering him the kingdom, said:”
“Whatever thing is dependent on you, over which your power prevails—may there be sovereignty for you in all respects; rule as you wish!
Whether for the sake of giving, for enjoyment, or whatever else is suitable, [may it be yours].”
“I give this wealth to you; I relinquish my sovereignty to you.
In that context, “where my authority prevails” means wherever my authority extends. “Kiñcanaṃ” refers even to that which is very slight.
“Sabbatthissariyaṃ” means let there be complete sovereignty for you alone. “And whatever else is helpful” refers to what is intended for the purpose of giving out of a desire for merit.
"Either raise the white parasol and enjoy the kingdom itself, or do whatever else pleases you;
I give this wealth to you, and I relinquish my sovereignty, including the white parasol, back into your hands.
Then the Great Being returned the white parasol given by the king to the king himself. The king also thought: "The King of the Swans..."
“I have heard the Dhamma from him, but this son of a hunter has praised him exceedingly, saying, ‘This Sumukha is sweet-spoken.
I shall listen to his Dhamma as well. While conversing with him, he spoke the following verse:
“And just as this wise Sumukha addressed me, so [should you address me].”
“If he were endowed with wisdom and would speak to me of his own accord, that would be most dear to me.
In this context, “if” means “should. This is what is meant: “If this wise Sumukha, endowed with wisdom, should address me of his own free will, that would be most dear to me.
Then Sumukha said:
“Indeed, Great King, I am a king of the nāgas dwelling in the midst of enemies;
I am not able to converse with you, for there can be no such discipline between us.
He is our superior, and you are the supreme among beings.”
“The protector of the earth, the lord of men, [is honored] with much worship for many reasons.
While the decision between those two disputants is being made,
O lords of men, the messenger must answer immediately.”
In this context, "like a king of serpents entering the interior of his enemy's cage" means like a king of serpents who has entered the inside of a basket.
"To oppose" means I am unable to speak between you two. "It would not be my [Vinaya]" means that if I were to say, "This is not mine," then it would not be my Vinaya.
"And for us" refers to the ninety-six thousand swans. "The supreme being" (uttamasatta) means the supreme person (uttamasatta).
"You both are worthy of my honor for many reasons, and indeed worthy of praise.
"By 'Pessa' is meant a servant who performs duties.
Having heard his words, the king, with a heart full of joy, said: "The son of the hunter praises you; surely there must be others like you who are sweet speakers of the Dhamma," and he spoke further:
“Indeed, by Dhamma the fowler calls him ‘wise, though born from an egg.
Such would not be the way for one who has done no good.
Thus he is of the highest nature, thus he is a most excellent being.”
“As far as I have seen, I do not see another such as you.
‘I am pleased with your natural state and with your sweet speech;
this too is my wish: that both of you may long behold one another.’”

Therein, "by way of Dhamma" means by way of its own inherent nature (*sabhāva*) as the cause. "Of one who has not accomplished his selfhood" refers to a betrayer of friends whose personal existence (*attabhāva*) has not been perfected.
"Guidance" (*naya*) means wisdom (*paññā*). "The foremost nature" (*aggapakatimā*) means the supreme intrinsic character. "The most excellent being" (*uttamasatta*) means the highest of beings.

"As far as there exists" (*yāvatatthi*) means as far as there is anything that has been seen by me. "None other" (*nāññaṃ*) means that in the place where I have looked, there is nothing else of such a kind.
"I see you. I am pleased with you by nature, O King of Swans; even before this, I was already pleased simply by the sight of you.
By your words—now I am pleased by your sweet speech. 'May I see you long'—this is my wish:
that you dwell right here and do not depart for even a moment, so that I may see you for a long time. Thus he spoke.
Then the Great Being, praising the king, said:
“That which was to be done for a supreme friend has been done by you toward us;
we have undoubtedly attained [this] because of the devotion you have for us.”
“Surely there was once a very great secret council of the assembly of kinsmen;
because we were not present at it, suffering arose among many of our people.
To dispel their sorrow, we have been permitted by you [to go].”
Having circumambulated him to the right, they would see their kinsman, O Tamer of Men:
“Surely I shall find abundant joy from seeing you;
and this great purpose shall be the consolation for our kin.”

In this context, *katamasmāsu* means "among whom?"—that is, "among us. *Pattā nissaṃsayaṃ tyāmhā* means "we have certainly been reached by you"; that is, we have indeed been attained by you without any doubt.
*Bhattirasmāsu yā tava* means "whatever devotion you have toward us"—by that devotion, we have certainly been reached by you;
we are not separated from you, nor even when parted, for we are still called your companions.
He illuminates this. "This indeed is truly great" means that this one thing is certainly very great.
"In the midst of the assembly of kinsmen" means in the interval of my assembly of kinsmen, which is now deprived of us two people; there is a gap or a void.
"Of us" means that through our absence, suffering has arisen among many birds. "May they see the Lord of Men" means may they behold him.
"O Tamer of Enemies, we are blessed by the sight of you. And this too is a great benefit:
that which consists of the reassurance to our kinsmen, known as the assembly of our relatives; this too is a great benefit.
When this was said, the king granted them permission to depart. The Great Being [then spoke] of the danger in the fivefold immorality of the king...

Having spoken thus of the benefits of virtue, and having exhorted him, saying, "Guard this virtue, rule the kingdom according to the Dhamma, and win over the people with the four means of attraction," Dhatarattha went to Cittakūṭa. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
"Having said this to the lord of men, the swan-king Dhatarattha..."
Possessing supreme speed, they approached the assembly of their kinsmen.
Seeing those two supreme birds arrived in safety, the swans cried out, "Keka! and a great clamor arose.
“Falling down, those who were devoted to their husband, out of respect for their husband,
surrounded him on all sides like birds that have found their prey.
Therein, “they approached” means that at the very time of sunrise, having consumed parched grain, honey, molasses, and so forth, by the king—
The two queens, having lifted her up with two golden palm-leaf fans and honored her with perfumes,
garlands, and other offerings, lowered her with the fans, circumambulated the king, and rose into the air. When the king, with palms joined in reverence, said, "Go,
my lords," they passed through the lion-window and, traveling with supreme speed, arrived at the company of their kinsmen.
*Paramā* means supreme. *Kekā* refers to those who, by their very nature, utter the sound "kekā.
*Bhattugāravā* means having respect for the husband. *Parikiriṃsu* means that, being delighted by the husband's state of being released [from his fetters], they surrounded that husband on all sides.
*Laddhapaccayā* means having found a firm footing.
Having thus surrounded him, those swans asked, "How were you released, Great King?
The Great Being related how he had been freed through Sumukha, and described the actions performed by Sāgara the king and the sons of the hunters.
Hearing this, the flock of swans was delighted and said, "May the commander-in-chief Sumukha, the king, and the hunter's sons live happily and free from suffering for a long time."
"May they live! he exclaimed, offering praise. To clarify this matter, the Teacher spoke the concluding verse:
"Thus, for those who possess friends, all matters turn out favorably;
Just as the swans returned to the presence of Dhatarattha, so did they approach their circle of kinsmen."

In this context, "possessing friends" refers to those endowed with virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitta*). "Favorable" means leading to the accomplishment of happiness and conducive to growth. Regarding the *Dhataraṭṭhas*:
the swan-king Sumukha was [addressed] thus by both the king and the hunter's son;
these two *Dhataraṭṭhas*, being endowed with virtuous friends, approached the assembly of their kinsmen. This constitutes the act of approaching the assembly of kinsmen.
“Their welfare has become favorable; thus, for others who possess friends as well, their welfare becomes favorable.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, “Monks, it is not only now that Ānanda sacrificed his life for my sake;
he did so in the past as well,” and he identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the hunter was Channa, and the king was Sāriputta.”
“Ānanda was Sumukha; the assembly of the Buddha consisted of ninety-six thousand swans; and as for the king of the swans, it was none other than I myself.
This concludes the first commentary, the Cūḷahaṃsa Jātaka.
2. The Commentary on the Mahāhaṃsa Jātaka.

"These swans are departing"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in the Veḷuvana grove, concerning the sacrifice of his own life by the Elder Ānanda. The background story is the same as told previously; however, here the Teacher, bringing up the past, related this:
In the past, in Bārāṇasī, King Saṃyama had a chief queen named Khemā.
At that time, the Bodhisatta lived on Mount Cittakūṭa, surrounded by ninety thousand swans. Then one day, Queen Khemā...
At the time of dawn, she saw a dream. Golden-colored swans arrived, sat upon the royal couch, and delivered a discourse on the Dhamma with sweet voices.
As the queen gave her approval and listened to the Dhamma, the night passed away while she was still unsatiated by the hearing of the Dhamma.
Having finished their discourse, the swans departed through the lion-gate.
She rose up in haste and, crying out, "Seize them, seize the swans as they flee! she woke up while still reaching out her hand.
Hearing her words, the female attendants laughed slightly, asking, "Where are the swans?
At that moment, realizing it was a dream, she thought: "I do not see what is unreal; surely there are those of golden complexion in this world."
"We shall become swans. However, if I say to the king, "We wish to hear the Dhamma of the golden swans," he will say, "Golden swans have never been seen by us before;
talk of swans is nothing but a fabrication," and he will become indifferent.
But if it is said that this is a pregnancy-longing (*dohada*), he will seek them out by whatever means possible.
"In this way, my heart's desire will be fulfilled. Having thus indicated her illness and given instructions to her attendants, she lay down.
When it was time for him to see her, the king sat upon his royal throne; not seeing her, he asked, "Where is Queen Khemā?
Hearing that she was ill, he went to her side, sat down on a part of the bed, and while massaging her back, said:
“What is it that makes you unwell? he asked. “Your Majesty, there is nothing else that makes me unwell;
rather, a longing has arisen within me. “Then speak, O Queen; whatever you desire, we shall quickly provide for you.
“Great King, I wish to perform an offering with perfumes, garlands, and other honors to a single golden swan seated upon a royal throne beneath a raised white parasol.”
“Having offered my applause, I wish to hear the discourse on the Dhamma; if I may obtain it, that is well, but if not, I have no life.
Then the King, having comforted her with the words, “If it exists in the world of men, you shall obtain it;
do not worry,” emerged from the inner chamber and consulted with his ministers: “Friends, Khemā...”
The queen said, "I shall live if I may hear the Dhamma discourse of the golden swan; if I do not receive it, there is no life for me.
"Are there indeed swans of golden hue? "Your Majesty, we have neither seen them before nor heard of them.
"Who then might know? "The brahmins, Your Majesty. The king then had the brahmins summoned.
Having paid him honor, he asked: "Are there indeed, Teacher, golden-colored swans? "Yes, Great King," [the teacher] replied.
"In our scriptures it is said that six types of beings among the animals are golden-colored: fish, crabs, turtles, deer, peacocks, and swans.
Among these, those known as the Dhataraṭṭha royal swans are wise and endowed with knowledge."
"Thus, together with humans, there are seven who possess the color of gold.
Having heard this, the king became delighted and asked, "Where do the teachers Dhataraṭṭha and Haṃsa dwell?
When they replied, "We do not know, Great King," he said, "Then who will know? When they replied, "The hunters' sons," [he went to them].
Having assembled all the hunters within his own realm, he asked them: "Dear sirs, where do those golden-colored swans known as the Dhataraṭṭha family dwell?
Then one hunter replied: "Your Majesty, it is said that they dwell on Mount Cittakūṭa in the Himālayas;
so our family tradition tells us. "But do you know a means for capturing them? "I do not know, Your Majesty."

"But who will know [of them]? "The brahmins. He summoned the wise brahmins, informed them of the existence of the golden-colored swans on Mount Cittakūṭa, and asked, "Do you know a means for capturing them?
"Your Majesty, what is the use of going to capture them? We shall bring them near the city by a stratagem and capture them."
"But what is the means? "Great King, have a lake named Khema, measuring three gavutas in extent, constructed not far to the north of the city;
fill it with water, plant various grains within it, and have it covered with five-colored lotuses.
Then, having entrusted it to a wise hunter, do not allow people to approach it for four [months]."
"Station yourselves at the ears [of the lake] and proclaim 'Fear not! Upon hearing this, various birds will descend from the ten directions;
then those swans, having heard of the safety of that lake through word of mouth, will come.
Then, having had them bound with hair-nooses, you should have them captured."

Having heard that, the king had a lake constructed in the place described by them according to the specifications mentioned; he summoned a skilled hunter, gave him a thousand [pieces of gold], and said:
"From this day forward, do not perform your own labor; I shall support your wife and children.
You must remain vigilant, protecting the secure lake and driving people away from its four corners."
“Having caused the proclamation of safety to be made, you should inform me of whatever birds come and go; when golden swans arrive, you shall receive great honor.
Having thus reassured him, he entrusted him with the protection of the safe lake. From then on, he acted there exactly according to the king’s instructions;
because he protected the safe lake, he was known as “Khemanesāda” (the Protector of the Safe Lake).
The name [“lake”] arose. From that time forth, various kinds of birds descended;
with the successive cry of “A secure and fearless lake!”, various swans arrived. First, the grass-colored swans arrived; by their cry, the pale swans came;
by their cry, the emerald-colored swans; by their cry, the white swans; by their cry—
The wild swans arrived. When they had come, Khemaka informed the king:
"Your Majesty, five-colored swans have arrived and are taking their food in the lake; because the wild swans have come, the golden swans will now arrive in just a few days.
Do not worry, Your Majesty."
Having heard this, the king caused a drum to be beaten throughout the city, proclaiming: "No one else must go there;
whoever goes shall suffer the amputation of hands and feet and the plundering of their home. From that time on, no one went there.
However, not far from Cittakūṭa, in the Kañcanaguha cave, there lived wild geese who were also very powerful.
The only distinction between them was the color of their bodies, [the others] being of the Dhatarattha lineage. However, the daughter of the king of the Pāka swans was golden-colored.
Thinking that she was a suitable match for the great lord Dhatarattha, he sent her to serve at his feet.
She became dear and pleasing to him, and for that very reason, those two swan clans became mutually trusting.
Then one day, the swans who were attendants of the Bodhisatta asked the wild-caught swans, "Where have you been seeking food during these days?
"We have been seeking food at the Khema Lake, not far from Bārāṇasī; but where have you been wandering?
When they replied, "At such-and-such a place," [the others said], "Why do you not go to the Khema Lake? It..."
"For this lake is delightful, crowded with various birds, covered with five-colored lotuses, abundant with various kinds of grain and fruit, and filled with the humming of various swarms of bees;
at its four corners, the cry of 'Fear not' resounds constantly.
There is no one capable of even approaching it, much less causing any other calamity—such is that lake."
They described Khemasara. Having heard their words, he said to Sumukha, "It seems there is a lake named Khema near Bārāṇasī where golden swans go to graze.
You should inform Dhataraṭṭha, the lord of the geese; if he grants permission, we too shall go there to graze."
They spoke. Sumukha reported this to the king. He thought: “Human beings are indeed full of guile, harsh in speech, and skilled in stratagems;
there must be a reason for this. For such a long time there was no such lake; it must have been made now for the purpose of capturing us.
He said to Sumukha: “Do not let it please you to go there; that is no lake.”

“They have done this because of their own proficiency; it was done solely for the purpose of catching us. Humans are indeed full of guile, harsh in speech, and skilled in stratagems; you should remain within your own domain.
The golden swans replied, “We wish to go to a secure lake,” and they informed Sumukha a second and even a third time.
Thus he informed the Great Being of their desire to go there.
Then the Great Being said, "Let my kinsmen not suffer because of me; therefore, let us go.
Surrounded by ninety thousand swans, he went there, gathered food, sported in swan-play, and returned to Cittakūṭa. As for Khemaka, his feeding ground was—
When they had gone after having performed their duties, he went and reported to the king that they had arrived.
The king, with a joyful heart, said, "Friend Khemaka, strive to capture one or two swans;
I will grant you great honor," and having given him travel expenses, he sent him off. He went there, sat inside a cage made of a large jar, and [waited for] the swans.

He investigated the place where they were standing. Since those who are Bodhisattas are by nature free from greed and cupidity, the Great Being proceeded by eating the rice in regular order starting from the spot where he had descended. The others wandered about, eating here and there.
Then the hunter, thinking, "This swan is free from greed and cupidity; it is right to capture him," reflected thus on the following day.
While the swans had not yet descended, the hunter sat in his wooden cage; having gone to that place, he hid himself within the cage nearby and waited, peering through a hole.
At that moment, the Great Being, preceded by ninety thousand swans, descended at the very spot where they had descended the previous day.
Having settled on the feeding ground, he proceeded while eating the rice. Through a hole in the cage, the hunter—
Looking on, he saw that the swan’s physical form had reached the pinnacle of beauty:
its body was the size of a wagon hub and golden in color; its neck was encircled by three red streaks;
three streaks descended from the throat and passed across the breast, while three emerged from the back; it was like a string of red woolen thread.
"He shines like a heap of gold set upon a base; by this it must be that he is the king, and we shall seize him alone," he thought.
The king of swans, too, having foraged extensively and sported in the water, returned to Cittakūṭa surrounded by his flock of swans.
In this very manner he took his food for five days. On the sixth day, Khemaka [prepared] a net made of the hair of black horses...

Having twisted a strong, thick rope and fashioned a snare upon a stick, he knew with certainty that "Tomorrow the king of swans will descend in this place," and so he cast the stick-snare into the water.
On the following day, as the king of swans was descending, he stepped down while his foot was already entering the snare. Then the snare caught his foot.
He seized him, binding him as if dragging him along with an iron strap. Thinking, "I shall cut him," he exerted force, pulled, and cast him down.
On the first pull, the gold-colored skin was torn; on the second pull, the wool-colored flesh was torn;
on the third pull, the sinews were torn; but on the fourth pull, [he thought], "The feet might be severed, for the king..."
However, thinking, "It is unseemly to have a deficient limb," he made no effort [to restore it], and powerful pains arose.
He reflected: "If I cry out with a loud wail, my kinsmen will become terrified;
failing to take their alms-food, they will flee while still hungry, and because of their weakness, they will fall into the ocean. Thus, enduring the pain, he remained silent.
Having turned them around by force, as if they were eating rice, he let them roam as much as they desired;

then, at the time of their swan-play, he let out a great, continuous cry with a loud sound. Hearing that, the swans, terrified by the fear of death, departed toward Cittakūṭa in flocks, just as before.

Sumukha, too, having reflected and searched in the same manner as described above, and not seeing the Great Being in any of the three places, thought, "Surely this fear has arisen for him alone," and so he turned back.
Upon seeing the Great Being bound by the snare, smeared with blood, afflicted by pain, and lying on the surface of the mud, he said, "Do not fear, O Great King; I shall sacrifice my own life."
Saying, "I shall deliver you," he descended and sat upon the surface of the mud to comfort the Great Being.
The Great Being reflected, "When ninety thousand swans abandoned me and fled, this Sumukha came alone;
will he now abandon me and flee when the hunter's son arrives, or will he not? It was for the sake of such an investigation that he remained there.
Stained with blood and still hanging from the gallows post, Tissa recited these three verses:
“Here these swans are departing, cranes driven by fear; O golden-hued one with greenish skin, fair-faced one, depart as you wish.
*Ete haṃsā pakkamanti, vakkaṅgā bhayameritā; Harittaca hemavaṇṇa, kāmaṃ sumukha pakkama.*” (SN 1.209)
“Leaving me behind, gone under the power of the snare alone, they depart without looking back—why do you despair when you are left all by yourself?
For among those who fall, the one who falls first is the best; there is no companionship for the bound.”
"Do not let me be deprived of one who is free from distress; depart as you wish, Sumukha.
In this context, "shaken by fear" means moved by fear, overcome by fear, or agitated by fear.
Regarding the third word, both "harī" and "hema" are names for gold. Because it has a golden surface, it is the color of gold (*hemavaṇṇa*); therefore, he addresses him in this way.
"Sumukha" means one with a very beautiful face. "Anapekkhamānā" means that your kinsmen, not looking toward me and having become homeless, [will depart].
"Pateva" means they will fly away immediately. "Mā anīghāya" means do not let your energy fail regarding the state of freedom from suffering that is to be attained by going from here.

Having heard this, Sumukha thought, "This king of swans does not know my status as a dear friend; he perceives me merely as a 'flatterer' (anuppiyabhāṇī). I shall demonstrate my affection for him. Having reflected thus, he spoke four verses:
“Even if I am overcome by suffering, O Dhatarattha, I will not abandon you;
whether it be life or death for me, it shall be together with you.
Even if I am overcome by suffering, O Dhatarattha, I will not abandon you.”
"You ought not to involve me in an ignoble undertaking.
I am your childhood friend, established in your heart;
I am known as the commander-in-chief, the most excellent among swans."
“How shall I boast, having gone from here into the midst of my kinsmen?
Having abandoned that which is the best among things that fall, what shall I say when I have gone from here?
Here I shall give up my life; I do not venture to act ignobly.”
In that regard, "I am not," O Great King, means that even when touched by bodily and mental suffering, I do not abandon him.
"Associated with the ignoble" means being joined with the state of ignobility through actions to be performed by those who betray friends and are shameless.
"In the act" refers to the act of abandoning him and departing. "Sakumāra" means a companion of equal age, having taken rebirth on the very same day.
The meaning is: one who has broken open the eggshell on a single day and has grown up all at once as a youth.
"I am your companion" means: I am your dear friend, equal to your right eye. "In your own mind" means: I abide in your own mind and act according to your will;
while you live, I live, and when you do not live, I do not live. There is also a reading, "saṃcitte," which means "in your mind."
"I am well-established" means I am firmly situated. "Renowned" means famous among all the swans. "They will proclaim me":
when asked, "Where is the king of swans?", what shall I say? "What shall I tell you?
means what shall I say to the flock of swans who are asking about your welfare?
When Sumukha had thus uttered his lion’s roar with these four verses, the Great Being, proclaiming his virtue, said:
“Such indeed is the Dhamma, O Sumukha, that you, standing on the path of the Noble Ones,
do not venture to abandon me, your master and friend.”
“For as I gaze upon you, no fear arises in me at all;
you shall attain life from me while I am in such a state.
In this context, “this is the Dhamma” means this is the inherent nature of the ancient wise ones. “Bhattāraṃ sakhāraṃ manti” means the husband and the master.
"And me as your companion. "No fear, no terror of mind arises within me;
I am as if standing in the midst of a flock of swans on Cittakūṭa Mountain. 'My'—that is, my life—you shall obtain.
While they were speaking thus, the hunter’s son stood at the edge of the arrow-shot range as the swans fled in three groups.
Seeing this, he wondered, "What could this be? Looking toward the place where the snare was set, he saw the Bodhisatta hanging from the snare-pole.
With joy arising within him, he fastened his loincloth firmly, took up a club, and rushed forward like the fire at the end of an eon.
Treading through the mud with his heels and walking with his head held high, he approached with speed as the deer fell before him. Regarding this matter:
Explaining this, the Teacher said:
“While the Noble Ones, who live the noble life, were thus conversing,
the hunter, taking up his staff, rushed toward them with great haste.”
Seeing him swooping down, Sumukha encouraged him greatly;
he stood before the king, the swan inspiring confidence despite the terror.
"Do not fear, O best of those who fly; for such as you do not fear."
“I shall apply myself to the yoga that is appropriate and connected with the Dhamma;
by means of that practice, you will quickly be released from the snare.
In this context, *ariyavuttinam* means “of those who abide in the conduct of the noble ones. *Bhusam* means “firmly” or “powerfully. *Atibrūhayī* means...
Speaking the words "Do not fear," which appeared in the immediately preceding verse, he raised his voice and let out a great cry.
"He stood" means that, thinking "If the hunter strikes the king, I shall receive the blow," he stood before him, having renounced his own life.
"Consoling" means inspiring confidence and providing reassurance. "Distressed" means being agitated.
He reassured the frightened king with these words, "Do not fear. "Such as you" means those like you who are endowed with wisdom and energy (*ñāṇavīriya*).
"Yoke" (*yoga*) refers to the yoke of wisdom and energy. "Appropriate" (*yutta*) means suitable. "Connected with the Dhamma" (*dhammūpasañhita*) means based on reason.
"By that expedient" (*pariyāpadānena*) means by that pure yoke employed by me. "You shall be released" (*pamokkhasi*) means you will be liberated.
Thus Sumukha, having comforted the Great Being, went into the presence of the hunter’s son and,
uttering sweet human speech, asked, “Friend, what is your name? When he replied, “Golden-hued Swan King, my name is Khemaka,” Sumukha said, “Friend Khemaka,
it was said that ‘whatever swan is caught by the hair-snare set by you, whether it be this one or another,’ yet here you are!”
"Do not form such a thought; Dhataraṭṭha, the king of swans, the preeminent leader of ninety thousand swans, has been caught in this snare.
He is endowed with wisdom, virtue, and right conduct, and stands on the side of those who provide support; it is not fitting to kill him.
I shall perform for you whatever task must be done by him. He too is golden-hued, and I am just the same; I am here for his sake."
"I shall sacrifice my own life; if you wish to take his feathers, take mine instead.
Or, if you wish to take any part of his skin, flesh, sinews, or bones, take them from my own body.
Or, if you wish to make him a pet bird, make me one instead. If you wish to sell him alive for wealth..."
"If you wish to acquire wealth, sell me while I am still alive and thereby raise the money;
do not kill this king of swans endowed with such qualities as wisdom. For if you kill him, you will not escape from hell and the other realms of suffering.
Having thus intimidated him with the fear of hell and the like, and having caused him to accept his own sweet words, he returned once more to the presence of the Bodhisatta and [addressed] him...
He stood there, offering words of consolation. Having heard his speech, the hunter thought:
"Though he is but an animal, he displays such a quality of friendship that even humans are unable to perform; even men cannot stand so firm in the duty of friendship.
Oh, how endowed with wisdom, sweet-spoken, and righteous he is! Thus, his entire body was filled with rapture and joy.

With his hair standing on end from joy, he cast aside the staff, placed his palms together in reverence upon his head, and stood there praising the virtues of Sumukha as if worshipping the sun. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“Having heard those words of his, that well-spoken speech of Sumukha...”
The hunter, his hair standing on end, bowed with palms joined in reverence:
"Never before have I heard or seen a bird speaking in human speech;
Vakkaṅga, though calling himself noble, has abandoned the human voice."
“Why indeed do you, a brahmin, remain there, released yet gazing upon one who is bound?
While the birds depart, leaving him behind, why are you alone left behind?
Therein, *añjalissa paṇāmayī* means he extended his hands in reverential salutation toward him; with the verse beginning “Not mine,” he offers praise to him.
In this context, *mānusī* means human speech; *ariya* means beautiful and faultless; *cajanto* means relinquishing.

This is what is meant: "Friend, today, while you are a bird, speaking with me in human speech, uttering words that are faultless and relinquishing your human voice, you have been seen by me face to face; but prior to this, such a marvel [had never occurred]."
“I have neither heard nor seen it. “What indeed does that protect which you revere? What indeed is this to you?

Thus questioned by the hunter with a joyful heart, Sumukha thought, “This man has become soft-hearted; now, for the sake of making him even more exceedingly gentle, I shall demonstrate my own virtue,” and he said:
“He is my king, O friend of birds; I acted as his general.”
“I am unable to abandon that lord of birds to you, O hunter.
‘My husband belongs to a great flock; let him not go to his destruction alone.
Thus, my dear friend, please lead him back so that he may rejoice with me, his wife.”
In this context, *nussahē* means “I am not able. *Mahāgaṇāya* means “of the great flock of swans.
*Mā ēkō* means “let him not go to his ruin alone while a servant like me exists. *Tathā taṃ* means “exactly as I say, so it shall be for you.
*Samma* is an address meaning “friend. *Bhattāyaṃ abhito ramē* means “this husband of mine—may I delight in his presence on all sides.”
"I rejoice; I do not feel weary.
Having heard those sweet words of his, which were grounded in the Dhamma, the hunter was filled with joy and his hair stood on end.
He thought, "If I kill this king of swans, who is endowed with such virtues as moral discipline, I shall not be released from the four states of misery."
Thinking, "Let the king do whatever he desires; I shall release him after making him a gift for Sumukha," he spoke this verse:
"O Vakkaṅga, you walk in the conduct of the Noble Ones, you who honor the alms-food."
"I release you from that husband; go, both of you, as you please.
In this context, "you possess the conduct of the noble ones" means you are endowed with the noble practice known as the observance of the duty of friendship.
"You honored the alms-food" means you honored the position of commander-in-chief obtained from your husband. "Go, both of you."
"Both of you, while making the tearful assembly of kinsmen laugh, go as you please," he said.
Having spoken thus, the hunter approached the Great Being with a gentle heart;
he lowered his staff, seated him upon the surface of the mud, released him from the snare-staff, lifted him up, drew him out from the water, and set him down upon the surface of young *darbha* grass.

Having had him sit down and having slowly loosened the snare bound around his foot, the Great Being, establishing a powerful affection toward him, took water with a mind of loving-kindness (*mettā*), washed away the blood, and rubbed it repeatedly.

Then, through the power of that loving-kindness, the veins joined with the veins, the flesh with the flesh, and the skin with the skin; his foot became as it was before, while the other remained as it was.
[The word] *nibbiseso* means "without distinction. Having attained happiness, the Bodhisatta sat down in his natural state.
Sumukha, seeing the king’s state of well-being due to himself, was filled with joy and thought: "He has done us a great service;
there is no service we have done for him in return. If he [should give us] for the sake of the king and the high ministers..."
"If he took it, he will receive much wealth after leading us to them;
if he took it for his own sake, he will surely receive wealth by selling us. Let me first ask him. Then, wishing to do him a favor, he asked:
"If, by your own effort, you have placed a swan's wing..."
“We accept this gift of fearlessness from you, friend. ‘If, by your own effort,
you had not released me— me who am like a swan with wings outstretched—
then, being powerless, O hunter, you would have committed a theft against us.’”
"In that regard, my dear hunter, if indeed by your own effort you have set a snare for the sake of your own interest for both the geese and other birds—
if, being without authority, you release us and take what belongs to him by whom you were commanded,
you would be committing theft."
Having heard this, the hunter said, "I did not capture you for my own sake; rather, I was commissioned by the King of Bārāṇasī to do so through his restraint.
Then, from the time the queen saw her dream until the king heard of their arrival, he said, "Friend Khemaka, strive to capture one or two swans; I will grant you great honor."
Having spoken thus and given him provisions, he related the entire account of how he had been sent away.
Upon hearing this, Sumukha said, "This hunter has performed a difficult deed by releasing us without regard for his own life.
If we were to go from here to Cittakūṭa, neither would the power of King Dhataraṭṭha’s wisdom be seen, nor my own duty as a friend."
Thinking, "It will become public; Luddaputta will not receive great fame; the King will not establish himself in the five precepts;
and the Queen’s desire will not reach its fulfillment," he said, "Friend, this being the case, you may not dismiss us.
Show us to the King; he will do with us as he pleases."
Explaining this matter, he spoke this verse:
“Commit this sin to that king for whom you are a servant;
there the king, as a restrainer, will act according to his own knowledge.”

In that context, "to him indeed" means go to his very presence. "There" means in that royal residence. "According to their knowledge" means according to their intention or according to their preference.
Having heard this, the hunter said: "May it not please you, venerable sirs, to see the king; kings are indeed full of danger;
they might make you a pet swan for sport, or they might even kill you. Then Sumukha said to him: "Friend hunter, do not..."
"Think this over for us: if I could produce such gentleness through a discourse on the Dhamma for one so harsh, why should I not produce it for the king?
For kings are wise and discern between what is well-spoken and what is ill-spoken. Take us quickly to the presence of the king;
but do not take us in bonds, rather take us having had us seated in a flower-cage—a flower-cage."

“Having made for Dhatarattha a large [lotus] covered with white lotuses, and for me a small one covered with red lotuses, place Dhatarattha in front and me behind at a lower level; then, taking them, lead us quickly and show them to the king,” he said.
Having heard his words, [Dhatarattha thought], “When Sumukha sees the king, my great glory—”

Thinking, "He will wish to give [them]," the hunter, filled with joy, fashioned a cage from supple creepers, covered it with lotuses, and taking them according to the aforementioned method, he departed.
To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
"Thus addressed, the hunter, [toward] those golden-hued and green-tinted [birds]..."
Gripping them both with his hands, he placed them inside a cage.
"Having taken those two birds within the cage, both of radiant complexion—
Sumukha and Dhataraṭṭha— the hunter departed."
In this context, *ajjhāvohī* means he placed or set down. *Bhassaravaṇṇine* means in one possessed of radiant beauty.

Thus, at the time of departing after taking those [birds] from Ludda, Dhataraṭṭha remembered his own wife, the daughter of the king of the Pāka swans, and addressed Sumukha, lamenting under the influence of defilement. To clarify that matter, the Teacher said:
“While being carried away, Dhataraṭṭha spoke thus to Sumukha:”
“I am greatly afraid, O Sumukha, of Sāmā with her shapely thighs;
perceiving our slaughter, she will surely destroy herself.
“O Sumukha, we are wild geese, with beautiful golden wings and golden threads [on our bodies].”
“Like a curlew on the shore of the ocean, she surely weeps piteously.
Therein, “I am afraid” means I am afraid of death. “Sāmā” means one with a golden complexion. “Lakkhaṇūruyā” means one whose thighs are endowed with auspicious marks.
“Vacamaññāya” means having understood her execution—that is, perceiving that “my beloved husband has been killed. “Vadhissati” means she will be executed.
"Of what use is life to me if my beloved husband is dead? she will think, and thus she will die.
"Pākahaṃsā" means the daughter of the king of the wild geese. "Suhemā" is her name. "Hemasuttacā" means one whose beautiful skin is like gold.
"Rucchatī" means that just as a miserable female curlew (*koñcī*) wails when her mate has died after descending into the salt sea, so indeed she will surely weep.
Having heard this, Sumukha thought: "This king of swans is fit to advise others, yet he laments out of defilement on account of a woman;
it is as if the water has become ablaze, or like the time for eating the field-crops after rising from the fence.
Suppose I were to reveal the fault of women by my own power and thus persuade him. Having reflected thus, he spoke this verse:
“Such is the greatness of the world, immeasurable and vast;
one should grieve for it alone, not as those possessed of wisdom do.
Like the wind that carries both good and bad odors, so does the wise man take up both the virtuous and the wicked.”
Like a fool with unripe fruit, like a greedy man with meat, or like a blind man;
you who do not discern the meaning of things, you have spoken to me like a dullard.
You do not know what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, yet you have arrived at the appointed time.
“One who is intoxicated with pride proclaims: ‘I consider women to be superior.
But these women are common property to many, like a tavern to drunkards.
They are mere illusion and a mirage, grief, disease, and calamity.”
“Kharā and Bandhanā, these messengers of Death dwelling in the cave—any man who places his trust in them is the lowest of men among men.
In this context, “great” means being great. “Of the world” refers to the world of swans. “Immeasurable” means [immeasurable] by way of virtues.
"Unconquerable. "A great leader" (*mahāgaṇī*) means one who possesses a large following, a teacher of a group.
"For a single woman": whatever lamentation such a person as you might direct toward a single woman, this lamentation is not like that of the wise;
with the intention, "Therefore, today I consider you a fool," he spoke thus.
"Ādeti" means he takes up. "Chekapāpakaṃ" means the beautiful and the unbeautiful. "Āmakapakkam" means both the raw and the cooked.

"Lola" means greedy for flavors. This is what is meant: O Great King, just as the wind, having struck lotus ponds and the like, [carries] fragrance, and having struck places such as rubbish heaps, [carries] stench—it carries both kinds of scent, whether fine or foul.
She takes [them] just as a foolish child sitting beneath mango and rose-apple trees reaches out his hand and,
having picked up whatever fruit has fallen— whether raw or ripe— eats it; and just as a blind man, greedy for flavor,
when food is brought before him, takes whatever morsel there is, whether with flies on it or without flies, so too do women, by way of the defilements.
They take and consort with women who are wealthy or poor, of noble birth or low birth, beautiful or ugly;
for what reason, O Great King, do you lament over such women of evil character? "Atthesu" means regarding reasons and non-reasons.
"Mando" means a dull-witted fool. "Paṭibhāsi maṃ" means it occurred to me. "Kālapariyāyaṃ" means...
"O Deva, having reached such a state at the time of death, you do not know: 'At this moment this should be done;
this should not be done; this should be said; this should not be said. "Half-intoxicated" means as if one has become half-mad. "You have uttered" means:
just as a man who has drunk liquor but is not yet excessively intoxicated prattles on about this or that, so too have you prattled; such is the meaning.
“Excellent, most supreme.
Regarding the passage beginning with “Illusion (māyā),” O King, these women are called *māyā* in the sense of deception; they are *marīci* in the sense of being ungraspable;

they are sorrows (*soka*) because they are the condition for grief and so forth; they are diseases (*roga*); they are various kinds of calamities; and they are characterized by a state of rigidity due to anger and other such passions.

They are harsh. For, because they bind one by means of fetters and the like, they are called "bonds" (*bandhanā*); and because they dwell within the cave of the body, these women are indeed called "death" (*maccu*).

This meaning should be illustrated by the sutta: "With sensual desire as cause, with sensual desire as source, with sensual desire as basis—for the sake of sensual desires alone, kings seize a thief... and so forth.
Then Dhatarattha, because his mind was bound to women, spoke thus to illustrate how "you do not know the virtue of women; only the wise know this, so they should not be censured":
"Who is worthy to censure that which has been established by the elders?
There have arisen in the world those called 'women of great power'."
“Play is directed toward them, delight is established in them;
in them seeds grow—that is, beings are born.
What man would feel revulsion for them, having struck down living beings with his hands?”
“O Sumukha, you alone, and no other, apply yourself to your duties;
yet now that danger has arisen, your mind, though terrified, does not become fearful.
For everyone who encounters uncertainty, even the coward, endures the fear.”
And wise men apply themselves to great matters that are difficult to manage.
It is for this purpose that kings desire a heroic counselor—
one who wards off the calamity that comes upon oneself through one's own course of action.
“May the king’s cooks in the kitchen not cut us today, for the color of our feet has become like that of the fruit of the bamboo.
Though set free, he did not wish to fly away; he came of his own accord to his own bonds.
"Having fallen into doubt, do not grasp at the meaning superficially.
In this context, "yaṃ" refers to that object known as the female sex, which is understood by those whose wisdom has matured and is evident to them alone, but not to fools.
"Mahābhūtā" means those of great qualities and great benefits. "Udapajjisuṃ" means that in the time of the first aeon, only the female gender...
"First" means first manifested; the meaning is that they were first produced.

"In them" means, O Sumukha, in those women, physical and verbal play was directed, applied, and established, and delight in the strands of sensual pleasure was firmly rooted. "Seeds" means that the seeds of Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, noble disciples, universal monarchs (*cakkavatti*), and so forth, grow in them.
"All these beings" refers to all these sentient beings. "They are born from their wombs" means that all of them are born from the very womb of those [women].
He illuminates it by saying "it grows. "Disgust" means one should become disgusted.
"Having assailed their life with my own life" means: even if, having assailed their life with my own lives, I were to give up my own life, who, having obtained them, would not become disgusted?
