"Not another" means no other, O Sumukha, for while I was seated in the midst of the flock of swans on the surface of Cittakūṭa, I did not see you.
When it was asked, "Where indeed is Sumukha?", they replied, "He has taken a woman and is enjoying supreme pleasure in the Golden Cave.
Thus, the meaning is: you alone among women apply yourself to these matters; you are one who is properly engaged, not another.
"Tassa tyajjā" means: for him, for you, when the fear of death has arisen today, he is—as it were—terrified by this very fear of death.
He spoke thus with the intention that "this clever mind arises for a woman in perceiving faults.
"Sabbo hi" means whoever at all. "Saṃsayaṃ patto" means one who has reached a state where life itself is in doubt.
"Bhīrū" means even though being timid, he endures fear. "Mahantāno" refers to those who are both wise and established in great positions; they are the "great ones."
They apply themselves to their purpose, striving and exerting effort; therefore, encouraging him, he says, "Do not fear, be steadfast.
This hero wards off the calamity that has come upon his master;
for this very purpose, they desire a hero who is wise. The intention is that he is also capable of providing protection for himself.
"Vikantiṃsu" means they cut. This is what is meant: "Good Sumukha, you have been placed by me in the position immediately following my own;
therefore, act in such a way that today the king’s cooks do not cut us for the sake of meat, for such is the color we have attained.
Kill him!"—and as for this color, it is just as if [it were] dependent upon a bamboo.
"The fruit that has grown destroys the bamboo itself; do not destroy it, and do not destroy me either"—it was with this intention that he spoke thus.
"Even though released" means that although he had been released and dismissed by me, the son of the hunter, saying "go to Cittakūṭa mountain as you please," he did not wish to fly away.
"He lay down" means that, desiring to see the king, he himself remained bound.
"Upagato" means that this fear of ours has come about because of him. "Sopajja" means that he too has today fallen into a state where his life is in doubt.
"Atthaṃ gaṇhāhi mā mukhaṃ" means: now take up the means for our release; strive so that we may be freed.
Speaking such words as "The wind alone carries away the fragrance," do not open your mouth for the sake of reviling women.
Having thus praised the woman and silenced Sumukha by leaving him speechless, the Great Being, perceiving his displeasure, spoke this verse to encourage him:
“Exert yourself in that practice which is appropriate and endowed with the Dhamma;
by providing for you, carry out my search for food.”
In this context, "you" means, O Sumukha, you yourself. "That practice" refers to that which you previously said, "I shall apply myself to the practice, joined with the Dhamma";
apply yourself to that now. "By your purification" means by that practice of yours which is thoroughly purified.
There is also a reading, "by your cleansing," which means by protection, because it was performed by you.
The intention was: "He seeks his own life by means of the protection provided by you.

Then Sumukha thought, "This man is exceedingly terrified of death and does not know the power of my wisdom. When he sees the king and receives a brief word from him, he will come to know; for now, I shall comfort him. Having reflected thus, he spoke this verse:
"Do not fear, O best of those who fall; for such as you do not fear."
"I shall apply myself to the yoga that is appropriate and connected with the Dhamma;
through my diligent practice, you will quickly release me from the snare.
In this context, "from the snare" means from the snare of suffering.
While they were conversing in the language of birds, the hunter’s son understood nothing at all; he merely took them on his carrying-pole and entered Bārāṇasī.

Followed by a great crowd of people who had been struck with wonder and amazement and were joining their palms in reverence, he reached the royal gate and had the king informed of his arrival. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
“Thus the hunter, in the guise of a swan, approached the king’s gate:
‘Announce me to the king, saying: “Dhataraṭṭha has arrived.
In this context, “announce me” means: “Inform the king that Khemaka has come. “To Dhataraṭṭha” means: “Announce that this Dhataraṭṭha has arrived.”
The gatekeeper went and announced him. The king, filled with joy, said, "Let him come quickly.
Surrounded by his assembly of ministers and seated upon the royal couch beneath a raised white parasol, he saw Khemaka the swan-king arrive and ascend the great terrace.
Beholding the golden-colored swans, he thought, "My heart's desire is fulfilled," and [considered] what ought to be done for him.
He commanded his ministers. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
"Seeing those two who were endowed with merit and possessed of the marks of excellence, King Saṃyama addressed his ministers."
“Give garments to the hunter, as well as food, drink, and sustenance;
let him have his fill of gold, as much as he desires.
In this context, “at the place of merit” means at a place similar to one’s own merit. “Renowned for his auspicious marks” means esteemed as excellent and well-known.
*Khalu* is a particle; its connection is with the preceding phrase, "having seen them, indeed" (*te khalu disvā*).
The words "Give! and so forth were spoken by the king as a gesture of his favor. In that context, *kāmaṅkaro hiraññassa* means "let there be for him the doing according to his desire regarding gold.
*Yāvanto* means "as much as he desires"; the sense is, "give him as much gold as he wishes."
Having thus caused him to display an appearance of confidence, and being emboldened by joy and gladness, he said, "Go, adorn him and bring him back.
Then the ministers, having brought him down from the royal residence, shaved his hair and beard, bathed and anointed him, and adorned him with every ornament, presented him to the king.
Then the king [granted] twelve villages yielding a hundred thousand [pieces of gold] per year, along with a chariot yoked with thoroughbred horses.
He caused a chariot, a great decorated mansion, and immense honor to be bestowed upon him.
Having received such great honor, he declared his own deed, saying: "O King, it was not just any goose that I brought;
this is Dhataraṭṭha by name, the king of ninety thousand geese, and this is the commander-in-chief named Sumukha. Then the king asked him: "How did you..."
“Friend, they have been caught,” he asked. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“Seeing the hunter’s state of confidence, the King of Kāsi then spoke:
‘If, friend Khemaka, this lake stands full of swans.’”
“How did he approach him who had reached such delight, holding a noose in hand?
How did he seize him who was surrounded by a host of kinsmen and had no middle ground?
Therein, *pasannattaṃ* means the state of being serene, having attained joy. “If they come, friend Khemaka, if...”
"This lotus pond of ours remains full with ninety thousand swans.
"How have you come among the Rucis?"—this being the case, how is it that you have come among those swans who are lovely to behold, surrounded by their kinsmen?
"Nimmajjhimam"—neither middle nor youngest, but the supreme king of swans. How [have you come]?
“With a noose in hand, he approached and asked, ‘How did you take it?
As he was explaining it to him, he said:
‘Today is the seventh night since I have been subsisting on food scraps.’”
“Seeking his tracks, I was diligent and exerted myself.
Then I saw his track as he moved about seeking food;
there I set a snare, and thus I caught that bird.”
In this context, *ādānāni* means "places of taking up," that is, places for seizing a feeding ground; or rather, this is the very reading [of the text].
*Upāsato* means "of one who approaches. *Padaṃ* refers to a footprint left on the ground within the feeding area. *Ghaṭassito* means having rested upon the framework of a water-jar.
*Athassa* means "then, on the sixth day, I saw the footprint of this one as he was wandering in search of food."
"‘Evaṃ tanti’ means: ‘In this way, they seized that bird,’ thus he explained the entire method of capture.
Having heard this, the king thought: ‘Even when standing at the gate, this man reported only the arrival of Dhataraṭṭha; now too, he says they seized it as one. What could be the reason for this?
Having reflected thus, he spoke this verse: ‘Hunter, you say, “These two birds, and then one”;’"
“Is your mind perverted, or what indeed do you wish to gain?

In this context, *vipariyattaṃ* means “perverted” (*vipallatthaṃ*). “Or what indeed do you wish to gain?”—that is, “Or rather, what are you thinking? Having seized one, do you intend to give it to another? Thus he asks.
Then the hunter, making it known that “Your Majesty, my mind is not perverted, nor do I wish to give the other to someone else; rather, when I lowered the snare, only one was caught,” said:
“He for whom the red palm-fruits, beautiful like refined gold,
stand pressed against his chest— he has come to my bondage.
Then this pale bird, though unbound, [approached] one distressed by being bound.”
"Declaring himself noble, he stood there, abandoning human speech.
In this context, "lohitaka" means red-colored. "Lātā" means streaks. "Uraṃ saṃhacca" means having struck the chest. This is what is meant:
O Great King, he on whose neck these three red streaks, resembling fine red gold, encircle—
"They stand pressing against my chest; he alone has come into my power. "Radiant" means pure and endowed with splendor.
"To the afflicted" means to the sick and suffering one he stood.
Then, having realized that Dhataraṭṭha was bound, [the bird] turned back, comforted him, and [waited] for the time of my arrival.

Having come forward to meet me, he stood right there in the air, engaging in sweet conversation with me and speaking in the human tongue while recounting the virtues of Dhatarattha; having softened my heart, he then stood once more before him.
Then, O King, having heard the well-spoken words of Sumukha, I released Dhatarattha with a mind full of faith.
"Thus was my release from Dhatarattha’s snare and my arrival here with these swans brought about by Sumukha alone.
In this way he spoke of Sumukha’s virtues. Upon hearing this, the king became desirous of hearing a discourse on the Dhamma from Sumukha.
Even as he was paying honor to the hunter's son, the sun set and the lamps were lit.
Many kṣatriyas and others had assembled, and Queen Khemā, accompanied by her retinue of various dancers, sat on the king’s right side.
At that moment, the king, wishing to have Sumukha speak, uttered this verse:
“Now why, O Sumukha, do you stand with your jaws clenched?”
“You have come before my assembly, yet out of fear you do not speak.

Therein, “having struck your jaw” means: you are indeed one of sweet speech; why then do you now stand with your mouth covered? “Adū” is an interrogative particle. “Out of fear” means being terrified by the dread of the assembly.
Hearing this, Sumukha spoke a verse to show that he was not afraid:
“I am not afraid, O Lord of Kāsi, having entered your assembly;
it is not out of fear that I shall not speak words regarding such a matter.
In this context, “regarding such a matter” means: “I am sitting here awaiting an opportunity to speak, thinking, ‘When a matter of such a kind arises, I shall indeed speak words.’”
Having heard that, the king, wishing to elaborate upon his words, spoke in jest:
"You see no reinforcements for him, neither chariots nor infantry;
nor do you see his armor, or even a single insect, among the armored archers."
“Neither gold nor silver, nor a well-built city,
with its moats filled in, its difficult passages, and its strong watchtowers and battlements—
wherever you have entered, O Sumukha, you do not fear what ought to be feared.”
In this context, "they rush toward" means a crowd standing around with weapons in hand for the purpose of protection;
"I do not see them. Here, *assa* is merely a particle. *Camma* refers to a shield used for protection against arrows.
*Kīṭa* refers to a small pot, a skull-cup, and so forth; he indicates that even those carrying such skull-cups are not near you. *Vammita*— [End of excerpt]
“Bound in leather. “As for ‘not gold’: I do not see even that gold upon which you rely when you are not afraid.
When the king had thus asked, “What is the reason for your lack of fear? he spoke in reply:
“I have no need for a following, nor for a city, nor for wealth.”
“Out of indifference we travel the path, for we are wanderers of the sky.
We are learned and wise, skillful and seekers of the true goal;
let us speak words endowed with meaning, established in truth.”
“And what will it avail you, who are untrue and ignoble, a liar and a cruel man—even well-spoken words?
In this context, *abhisarena* means with a retinue for protection. *Attho* means: by this, there is no purpose for me. Why? Because...
"Let us travel by a path that is not yours, a road not traveled by those like you, for we are wanderers through the sky. "We are wise," they said;
thus you have heard of us as "the Wise Ones. For that very reason, desiring to hear the Dhamma from our presence, he had us summoned.
And if you should be established in truth—meaning, if you were to stand firm in truth—then it would be meaningful.
“Let us speak words based on reason. “Asaccassa”—that is, for you who are devoid of verbal truth, what will these well-spoken words of yours avail, O shaven-headed one?
They are like a toothpick.
Hearing this, the king said, “Why do you call me a liar and ignoble? What have I done? Then Sumukha said to him, “In that case, Great King, listen,” and spoke as follows:
“Following the words of the brahmins, you had this place made secure;
and you proclaimed fearlessness throughout these ten directions.
Having plunged into that lotus pond, its pure and serene waters,”
“There is abundant food there, and harmlessness for the birds.
Having heard this report, we came into your presence;
yet those of us who were caught in your snare—this speech of yours is a lie.”
“Having placed falsehood at the forefront, along with evil desire and greed;
having transcended both connections, one is reborn in a state of suffering.
Therein, *taṃ* means “you. *Khemā* refers to the lotus pond of that name. *Ghuṭṭhaṃ* means standing at the four corners.
It was proclaimed. "In ten ways" means that while these ten directions were established, you proclaimed fearlessness.
"Having plunged in" means from those who had come after having plunged into [the pond]. "Abundant food" means abundant food such as lotus flowers, rice, and so forth.
"Having heard this" means having heard this proclamation of fearlessness from those who had come after plunging into that lotus pond.
The meaning is: "We have come to your presence, to your vicinity, to the lotus pond caused to be made by her.
"They" refers to us; "bound by your snare. "Having placed before" means having made them precede. "Craving and greed" refers to the evil greed known as craving (*icchā*).
"Both connections" refers to rebirth (*paṭisandhi*) in both the world of gods and the world of humans—having placed these evil states before [us].
“By acting thus, a person who has transcended rebirth in a happy destination is reborn in the unpleasant hell.
In this way, he put the king to shame right there in the midst of the assembly.

Then the king, making it clear that he had not caused them to be seized because he wished to eat their flesh after killing them, but rather because he had heard of their wisdom and desired to hear their well-spoken words, said:
“We did not disregard you, Sumukha, nor did we follow out of greed;
for those who have heard are wise, discerning, and thinkers of what is meaningful.
Perhaps those who have come here might speak words endowed with meaning.”
"Thus, O hunter Sumukha, you have rightly addressed me on the path.
In this context, "we do not offend": one who kills is said to offend; we do not kill. "Out of greed you caught me on the path":
desiring to eat meat, it was out of greed that you caught me, not because I am wise (*paṇḍita*). "O wise ones... [is the address].
There are eight meanings. "Thinkers of meaning" (*atthacintaka*) means thinkers of hidden meanings. "Possessing meaning" (*atthavanti*) means dependent upon a reason.
"Thus" (*tathā*) means by that reason. "Was spoken" (*vutta*) means having been spoken by me. "Sumukha, he took [you]" (*sumukha, aggahī*):
he addresses him as "Sumukha"; the letter *m* serves to join the words. "He took" (*aggahī*) means he took you in order to teach the Dhamma.
Having heard this, Sumukha said, “O Great King, you have acted improperly by desiring to hear well-spoken words [now]. He then spoke:
“O Lord of Kāsi, we are not afraid, even though our lives are at stake;
let us speak words that are meaningful, for the time has now arrived.”
“He who kills a deer with a deer, or a bird with a bird,
or buys a learned man with what he has learned— what could be more ignoble than that?
And he who utters the speech of the noble while being drenched in ignoble qualities;”
He falls away from both worlds, both here and in the world beyond.
"One who has attained fame should not become intoxicated; one who has encountered danger should not be distressed.
One should indeed strive in one's duties and guard against one's vulnerabilities."
“Those who were grown old and had passed beyond, who had reached the appointed time of death;
having practiced the Dhamma here, they have thus gone to the world of the Thirty-three.
Having heard this, O Lord of Kāsi, protect the Dhamma within yourself.”
"And release Dhataraṭṭha, O most excellent of swans.
Therein, "when brought near" means when brought into the presence of death. "At the turn of time" means that having reached the occasion of the time of death, we shall not speak.
For it is not right to bind a preacher of the Dhamma and, by threatening him with the fear of death, [make him speak] the Dhamma...
“They hear,” meaning they hear, “that which was done by you is improper. *Migena* means by a well-trained wild animal of the island.
*Hanti* means he kills. *Pakkhinā* means by a bird of the island. *Sutena* refers to a lotus pond that is renowned as safe and free from fear, similar to the wild animals and birds of the island.
*Sutaṃ* refers to a preacher of the Dhamma who has been heard of as being “wise and a versatile speaker. *Kiṇya* means “the Dhamma...”
"I shall kill," thinking thus, one might bind with a snare, pierce, harm, or oppress. Beyond that act of theirs, what indeed could be more ignoble?
One who is "noble" (ariya) speaks noble words—beautiful speech—from his mouth. One who is "drenched in ignoble qualities" (anariyadhammavassita) [is the opposite].
He is overwhelmed by ignoble states through his own karma. "From both" means from both the world of the gods and the world of humans.
"Even here" means that whether one has arisen here or arisen elsewhere, such a person, having been ruined by these two worlds of happy destiny, is reborn only in hell.
Even when facing suffering that brings a risk to life—a risk to one's very existence—one should not become weary. In restraint...
One should guard and close the openings, that is, one's own vulnerabilities and doors. "The grown" means those who have increased in virtue, the wise.
"Having transcended" means having passed beyond this human world. "The course of time" means having reached the course of time that is death.
"Thus these" means in this way they are so. "This" refers to this speech concerning the meaning uttered by me. "Dhamma" means...
[He spoke of] the dharma of the lineage and the dharma of good conduct.
Having heard this, the king said:
"Bring water for washing the feet and a costly seat."
"I shall release the illustrious Dhatarattha from the cage.
And that wise general, so skillful and mindful of his master's welfare—
who rejoices in the king’s joy and grieves when he is grieved."
“Such a one indeed deserves to eat the alms-food of his master, just as this Sumukha is the king’s life-sharing friend.
In this context, *udaka* means water for washing the feet. *Pajja* means ointment for the feet. *Sukhe* means when there is happiness.

Having heard the king’s words, they brought seats for them; when they were seated there, they washed their feet with scented water and anointed them with oil boiled a hundred times. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
“Dhatarattha sat down upon a throne made entirely of gold, Eight-legged and delightful, smooth, and covered with Kasi cloth.”
“Sumukha entered the presence of Dhatarattha, carrying a mat made entirely of gold and bordered with tiger-skin.
Taking many golden bowls from them, the people of Kasi— ”
"Among the offerings for the swans, it was presented to the supreme king.
In this context, *maṭṭhaṃ* means finished through craftsmanship. *Kāsikamatthannaṃ* means spread with Kāsī cloth.
*Kocchaṃ* means contracted in the middle. *Veyyagghaparisibbitaṃ* means bordered with tiger-skin on auspicious days.
The seat upon which the chief queen was sitting. "With golden leaves" means with golden vessels. "Many people" means numerous persons.

"Kāsis" means inhabitants of the kingdom of Kāsi. "Offered up" means they presented it. "The food sent for the King of the Swans by the King of Kāsi" refers to various foods of excellent flavor, enclosed within a golden vessel weighing eight hundred palas, which had been dispatched by the King of Kāsi as a gift for the King of the Swans.
When he had been thus presented, the King of Kāsi, in order to show them honor, himself took a golden bowl and offered it to them.
They ate the honeyed parched grain from it and drank the sweet water.
Then the Great Being, seeing the king’s gift and his graciousness, returned the greeting. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
Having seen the supreme gift brought and sent by the King of Kāsi, he who was skilled in the duties of a kshatriya then immediately asked:
"Is it well with you, sir? Are you free from illness?"
"I hope this kingdom is prosperous, and that you govern it with righteousness.
"It is indeed well with me, O swan, and likewise, O swan, I am free from illness;
furthermore, this kingdom is prosperous as I govern it with righteousness."
“Is it true that no fault whatsoever exists among your ministers?
And do they not even desire life for their own sake?
“Indeed, there is no fault whatsoever among my ministers.”
Furthermore, even for the sake of their own interests, they do not wish for [your] life.
"Is your wife like you—obedient and sweet-spoken;
endowed with sons, beauty, and fame; and following your will and authority?"
“Moreover, my wife is my equal—obedient and sweet-spoken;
endowed with the beauty and reputation of a son, she follows my will and authority.
Is the kingdom free from oppression, without calamity from any quarter?”
“You govern by means of non-coercion, by Dhamma, and with impartiality.
Furthermore, the kingdom is free from oppression and free from calamities from any quarter;
I govern it by means of non-coercion, by Dhamma, and with impartiality.”
“I hope you honor the virtuous and avoid the unvirtuous;
provided that you do not disregard the Dhamma and follow what is contrary to it.
The virtuous have been honored by me, and the unvirtuous have been avoided.”
“I follow only the Dhamma; unrighteousness has been cast out by me.
“O Khattiya, do you perhaps overlook the long duration of the future?
Are you intoxicated by intoxicants, such that you do not fear the world beyond?”
“I do not look back longingly at the past, O bird;
established in ten qualities, I do not fear the world beyond:
generosity, virtue, renunciation, uprightness, gentleness, and austerity.”
“Absence of anger, non-violence, patience, and non-opposition—
‘I see these wholesome states established within myself,’ from that joy arises in me,
along with a measureless sense of mental well-being.”
“Without reflecting, Sumukha uttered harsh words;
failing to understand the flaw in his own mind, this bird acted against us.
Enraged, he uttered harsh speech in an improper manner.”
“They are not found among us; this is not like those who possess wisdom.
Therein, *disvā* means having seen that abundant, excellent drink and food. *Pesitaṃ* means brought and presented after being caused to be fetched.
*Khattadhammānaṃ* refers to the qualities of hospitality among the first causes. *Tato pucchi anantarā* means immediately after that time, [he asked]: “Is it well?”...
"Now, sir," he asked in successive order. These six verses, however, have already had their meaning explained above.

"Are they not oppressed?"—he asks whether you do not oppress the inhabitants of the kingdom like sugarcane in a press. "Free from calamity from any quarter" (*akutoci-upaddavam*) means free from distress from any source.
"Do you govern by the Dhamma and with justice?"—he asks whether you govern your kingdom according to the Dhamma and with impartiality.
“Good men” (santā) refers to virtuous persons endowed with qualities such as moral discipline (sīla). “Having disregarded” (niraṃkatvā) means having abandoned.

“The future long” (nānāgataṃ dīghaṃ): he asks whether you do not reflect upon the duration of your own future life, thinking, “Is it long?”—that is, whether you recognize the brevity of the formations of life (āyusaṅkhārā).
“In intoxicating things” (madanīye) refers to objects of sense such as forms (rūpa) that are conducive to pride. “You do not tremble” (na santasi) means you do not fear. This...
It is said: "Having been heedless or heedful regarding the strands of sensual pleasure such as form, do you not fear the next world because of having performed wholesome deeds such as giving?

Regarding "in ten": it refers to the ten duties of a king (*rājadhamma*). Giving and so forth—namely, volition (*cetanā*) based on the ten grounds—is giving; the five precepts and the ten precepts [constitute morality].

Virtue (*sīla*), generosity through the relinquishing of things worthy of giving (*deyyadhamma*), rectitude is straightforwardness (*ajjava*), gentleness is mildness (*maddava*), the observance of the Uposatha is austerity (*tapa*), non-anger is preceded by loving-kindness (*mettā*), non-cruelty is preceded by compassion (*karuṇā*), patience is forbearance (*khanti*), and non-opposition is the absence of hostility.
"Without considering" means without considering this perfection of my qualities. "Fault of mind" means a fault of consciousness (*citta*).
"Without knowing" means not having understood. For there is no fault of mind in us;
it was simply because he did not know what we would understand that he uttered such harsh and cruel speech. "Improperly" means by an unskillful means.
"Those faults which do not exist in us"—he speaks of those defects which are not found among us. "Not this"—therefore, this speech of his does not appear like that of the wise.
Because of that, he does not appear to me as if he were wise.
Having heard this, Sumukha thought, “I have displeased the King, who is endowed with all virtues; he is angry with me, so I shall ask his forgiveness,” and he said:
“I have a severe dysentery, O Lord of Men; [it is urgent,] with speed—”
“When Dhatarattha was bound, great suffering came upon me.
‘You are like a father to us, your sons, as the earth is to all beings;
O elephant among kings, please forgive us who have transgressed against you.’”
In this context, *atisāraṃ* means "confusedly. *Vegena* means "with haste," as I spoke these words impulsively and suddenly.
*Dukkhaṃ* refers to my great mental suffering; therefore, O Great King, please forgive whatever was spoken by me under the influence of anger.
*Puttānaṃ* means "of our sons," [you are] like a father to us. *Dharaṇīriva* means "like the earth."
"You are our refuge, like the earth is the support for all living beings.
Forgive those who have transgressed"—meaning those overwhelmed by hatred and offense—thus he spoke, descending from his seat and joining his palms in reverence with his wings.
Then the king embraced him, took him, seated him upon a golden throne, and said, accepting his confession of fault:
“We rejoice in this of yours, that you do not conceal your state of being;
O bird, you break through the barrenness; you are upright, O ranger of the skies.

In this context, “we rejoice” means we forgive this fault of yours. “That” refers to the fact that you do not conceal the hidden state of your own mind. “Barrenness” (khila) means the barrenness of the mind, the stump of the mind.

Having said this, the king, being pleased with the Great Being’s discourse on the Dhamma and with Sumukha’s upright nature, thought, "One who has faith must show the appearance of faith," and so, bestowing his own royal splendor upon both of them, he said:
"Whatever jewels there are in the residence of the King of Kāsi—
silver and gold, pearls and many beryl gems."
“Jewels, conch shells, pearls, cloth, yellow sandalwood;
antelope skins, ivory goods, and much iron and black metal—this wealth I give to you; I release you from my authority.”
In this context, "pearls" refers to pearls that have been pierced or unpierced. "Jewels" refers to gemstone ornaments.

"And conch-pearls" refers to both the precious right-spiraling conch and the precious round *āmalaka*-shaped pearl. "Cloth" refers to fine Kāśī silk garments. "Antelope skin" refers to the hide of the black antelope.
"Iron" refers to both copper-colored iron and black iron. "Sovereignty" refers to the white parasol adorned with a golden wreath.
"Rule together over the city of Bārāṇasī, which is twelve yojanas in extent.
Having spoken thus, he honored both of them with white parasols and handed over the kingdom to them. Then the Great Being, conversing with the king, said:
"Surely we have been honored by you, O bull among charioteers, and duly respected."
“Among those who abide in the Dhamma, may you be our teacher.
“O Teacher, we are pleasing to you and have been approved by you;
having circumambulated you to the right, may we see our kinsman, the Lord of Men.”
In that context, "regarding the phenomena" means regarding the phenomena of the wholesome paths of action. "Teacher" means:

you are more proficient than we are, therefore you are our teacher; furthermore, because you spoke of the ten duties of a king, showed the fault of Sumukha, and accepted our confession of transgression, you are indeed our teacher, and therefore now too [you are so] by teaching us proper conduct.
"Let us become teachers," he said. "May we see the Tamer of Men (Arindama)," they replied.
He granted them permission to depart. Even as the Bodhisatta was preaching the Dhamma, the dawn broke. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
"Having reflected throughout the entire night, and having deliberated as best they could..."
“The King of Kāsi has granted permission, O most excellent of swans.

In this context, *yathākathaṃ* means whatever matter is to be considered or deliberated with them—all that having been considered and deliberated; such is the meaning. *Anuññāsi* means he gave leave, saying, “Go.
Having been thus permitted by him, the Bodhisatta advised the king, “Be diligent and rule the kingdom according to the Dhamma,” and then—

He established them in the five precepts. The king, having offered them honeyed parched grain and sweet water from golden vessels, and having honored them with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings once their meal was finished, personally lifted up the Bodhisatta with a golden hook, while Queen Khemā lifted up Sumukha.
Then, having opened the lion-window at the time of sunrise, he spoke to them.
“Go, my lords,” they dismissed him. Explaining this matter, the Teacher said:
“Then, at the end of the night, as the sun was rising, they departed from the palace while the King of Kāsi looked on.”
There, "they plunged" means they flew into the sky.
Among them, the Great Being, having leaped from his golden cage and stood in the air, comforted the king, saying, "Do not despair, Great King;
you should remain heedful and act according to our advice. Then, taking Sumukha with him, he went back to Cittakūṭa.
Then those ninety thousand swans, having emerged from the golden cave and settled on the mountain slope, saw them approaching;
they went out to meet them and surrounded them. Surrounded by their kinsmen, they entered the plateau of Cittakūṭa.
To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
“Seeing those supreme brahmins arrive safely, the swans cried out ‘Keka!
Keka! and a great sound arose.
Delighted by their master’s release, they honored him with deep respect for their master.”
“Having found their opportunity, the egg-born birds surrounded him on all sides.
Having thus encircled him, those swans asked, “How were you released, Great King?
Relying upon Sumukha, the Great Being related how he had been liberated and the deeds performed by Saṃyama, Rājā, and the son of Ludda. Having heard that, [they...]
The flocks of swans were delighted and said, "May Sumukha, the general, the king, and the hunter’s son all be happy and free from suffering, and may they live long!
To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
"Thus, for those who possess friends, all things turn out favorably."
"Just as the swans, the Dhataraṭṭhas, approached their own flock"—this has the same meaning as stated in the Cūḷahaṃsa Jātaka.
Having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said: "Monks, it is not only now; in the past as well, Ānanda acted for my sake."
Having said, "I sacrificed my own life," he identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Channa was the hunter's son;
Khemā Devī was the nun Khemā; the king was Sāriputta; Sumukha was Ānanda; the rest of the assembly were the Buddha’s retinue;
and as for Dhataraṭṭha, the king of swans, that was none other than myself."
The Second Story: The Exposition of the Mahāhaṃsa Jātaka [535].
3. The Exposition of the Sudhābhojana Jātaka:
"I neither buy nor sell"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain monk who was inclined toward giving.
He spoke concerning this. It is said that in Sāvatthī there was a certain son of good family who, having heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, became inspired with faith.

He went forth into homelessness, became one who fulfilled the precepts, was endowed with the virtues of the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), maintained a mind of loving-kindness toward his fellow celibates, was diligent in paying homage three times a day to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, and was perfect in conduct.
He had a disposition toward generosity. Being one who fulfills the qualities of kindness, even when he had already finished his own meal, he would still give to those who were present as recipients;
therefore, his inclination toward generosity and his delight in giving became well known among the Saṅgha of monks.
Then, one day, the monks initiated a discussion in the Dhamma Hall, saying, "Friends,..."
“A certain bhikkhu named So-and-so has a disposition for giving and delights in giving;
he cuts off his own greed and gives even a mere spoonful of food or a measure of water that he has received to his fellow celibates. His very disposition is like that of a Bodhisatta.
Having heard this conversation with his divine ear-element, the Teacher emerged from the fragrant chamber, approached them, and asked, “Bhikkhus, what is it that you are discussing?”

Having asked, "For what discussion are you gathered here now? and being told, "For this one," [the Buddha said], "Monks, this monk was formerly of a nature not to give, stingy, and would not give even a drop of oil on the tip of a blade of grass.
Then, having tamed him and made him free from harshness, I praised the fruit of giving and established him in generosity. He [now thinks]: 'Even a mere handful of water..."

"Having received it, I took a boon from me, saying, 'I shall not drink without having given it away. By the fruit of that, he has become one whose inclination is toward giving and who delights in generosity.
Having said this, being requested by them, he related a story of the past:
"In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, there was a householder who was wealthy, possessing eighty crores of wealth."
Then the king appointed him to the position of chief merchant (*seṭṭhi*).
Honored by the king and honored by the city-dwellers and the people of the countryside, he one day, looking upon his own prosperity, reflected:

"This fame was not obtained by me in past lives while sleeping, nor by committing bodily misconduct and the like; rather, it was obtained by fulfilling wholesome deeds (*sucarita*). In the future as well..."
“It is fitting for me to establish a foundation for my husband. He went to the king and said, “Your Majesty, there is eighty crores of wealth in my house;
please take it. When the king replied, “I have no need for your wealth;
I myself have much wealth, so take whatever you desire from here as well,” he asked, “But what, Your Majesty, am I permitted to give as my own wealth?”

He said: Then, when the king had said, "Do as you please," he had six halls for giving constructed—at the four city gates, in the center of the city, and at the door of his residence—and having established a daily expenditure of six hundred thousand [pieces of gold], he set forth a great almsgiving.
Having given gifts throughout his life, he said to his sons, "Do not let this lineage of my giving be interrupted."
Having provided instruction, at the end of his life he was reborn as Sakka. His son likewise gave alms and was reborn as Canda;
his son was reborn as Suriya; his son was reborn as Mātali;
his son was reborn as Pañcasikha; and his son, the sixth, attained the position of a chief merchant.
Having acquired it, he became known as Macchariyakosiya, possessing a fortune of eighty koṭis. Thinking, "My father and grandfather were fools;
they squandered wealth accumulated with great hardship.
But I shall protect my wealth and will not give anything to anyone," he demolished the hall for almsgiving, burned it with fire, and became a man of stubborn miserliness.
Then, beggars gathered at the door of his house and, raising their arms, lamented with a great cry: "Great merchant!

Do not destroy the tradition of giving established by your father and grandfather; give alms! Hearing this, the great multitude reviled him, saying, "The lineage of giving has been cut off by the miserly Kosiya.
Feeling ashamed, he [stood] at the door of his residence at every place where beggars arrived.
He established a guard to prevent them [from entering]. Having become destitute, they did not look toward his house door again.
From then on, he accumulated wealth alone; he neither enjoyed it himself nor gave it to his wife, children, and others.
He ate only broken rice with sour gruel and sour porridge as his sole food, and wore only coarse garments made from roots, fruits, and fibers.
He dressed himself, held a leaf-parasol over his head, and traveled in a dilapidated little chariot yoked with an old ox.
Thus, all that wealth of that wicked man had become like a coconut found by a dog.
One day, while going to attend upon the king, he thought, "I shall go taking the sub-setthi with me," and went to his house.
He arrived. At that moment, the Anuseṭṭhi was seated, surrounded by his sons, daughters, and others, eating milk-rice (pāyāsa) prepared with fresh ghee, honey, and powdered sugar.
Seeing Macchariyakosiya, he rose from his seat and said, "Come, Great Seṭṭhi; sit on this couch, and we shall eat the milk-rice together. [He offered him] the milk-rice.
Upon seeing it, saliva arose in his mouth and he desired to eat; however, he thought:
"If I eat, I will have to provide a counter-gift when the Anuseṭṭhi comes to my house, and thus my wealth will be lost;
I will not eat. Then, although he was asked again and again, he said, "I have just eaten now; I am full," and would not [eat].
He wished for it. While the king was eating the excellent rice-porridge, he watched him;

then, sitting there with saliva forming in his mouth, at the conclusion of the other’s meal, he went with him to the royal palace, saw the king, and after descending from the palace, reached his own home.
Oppressed by a craving for the rice-porridge, he thought: "If I [were to ask for] the rice-porridge..."
"I shall say, 'I wish to eat'; the great multitude will wish to eat, and many rice-grains and other provisions will be wasted;
I will not tell anyone. Thus, though he spent his days and nights thinking only of rice-milk porridge, out of fear of losing his wealth he endured his thirst without telling anyone.
Gradually, however, unable to endure it any longer, he became pale and sallow.
It happened thus. Even so, because he did not speak out for fear of losing his wealth, he later became weak and lay down, hugging his bed.
Then his wife approached him and, rubbing his back with her hand, asked, "What is it that makes you unwell, my lord?
"Make your own body unwell; there is nothing unwell with me," he replied. "My lord, you have become pale and wan."
“Is there some anxiety for you, or has the king become angry with you, or was some insult committed by your sons, or has some craving arisen?
“Yes, a craving has arisen within me. “Tell me, sir. “I will tell you, provided you are able to guard it.
“If it is something that ought to be guarded, I shall guard it. Thus, even out of fear of losing his wealth—
He did not venture to speak. Being pressed by her again and again, he said:
"My dear, one day I saw the merchant's son eating porridge prepared with fresh ghee, honey, and powdered sugar;
from that moment on, I have desired to eat such porridge. "You worthless man, are you a pauper? Among all those who dwell in Mārāṇasī..."
“I shall cook enough milk-rice for all,” she said. To him, it was as if she had struck him on the head with a staff.
He became angry with her and said, “I am well aware of your great wealth;
if you have anything brought from your family home, cook the milk-rice and give it to the citizens. She replied, “In that case, I shall cook enough for those living in one street.”

“What do you want with these? Let them eat what belongs to themselves. “Then I shall cook enough for the seven families of householders living here and there. “What do you want with those? “Then I shall cook enough for the retinue in this house.
“What do you want with that? “Then I shall cook enough for my own kinsmen. “What do you want with that?”
“Then, master, I shall cook for both you and me. “What are you? It is not right for you [to do this].
“Then, I shall cook making enough for you alone. “You must not cook for me; many are waiting for what is being cooked in the house.
But for me, take a fourth part of a measure of rice, a handful of milk, and sugar...”
“Give me a container for ghee, a container for honey, and one cooking vessel;
I shall enter the forest, cook there, and eat. She did exactly so.

He had the servant take all of it and sent her ahead, saying, “Go and stay at such-and-such a place,” while he himself, alone and with his head covered, went out in a disguise unrecognizable to others.
Having gone there, he had a hearth constructed at the foot of a bush on the riverbank and had firewood and water brought.
He then sent him off, saying, "Go, stand by a certain path, and as soon as you see anyone, give me a signal;
you must return only when I call for you. Having thus dispatched him, he lit the fire and cooked the milk-rice porridge.
At that moment, Sakka, the king of the gods, [brought] the adorned city of the gods extending ten thousand yojanas,
the golden street sixty yojanas wide, the Vejayanta palace rising a thousand yojanas high, the Sudhamma assembly hall five hundred yojanas in size, the Paṇḍukambala stone throne sixty yojanas long,
the white parasol with a golden fringe five yojanas in circumference, and [the retinue] numbering two hundred and fifty million.
The celestial nymph, beholding her own splendor—her body adorned and prepared—thought, "What indeed have I done to obtain this glory?
Looking back, she saw the gift bestowed by one who had been a merchant in Benares.
Then, looking to see where her children and others had been reborn, she saw that her son was the divine youth Canda.
Having made offerings, he was reborn; his son was Sūriya; his son was Mātali; his son was Pañcasikha.
Having seen the lineage of them all, and looking further to see what the son of Pañcasikha was like, he perceived that his own lineage had come to an end.
Then this thought occurred to him: “This unworthy man, being a miser, has not...
“He enjoys it himself and does not give to others; thus my lineage has been cut off by him. Having died, he will be reborn in hell.
I shall give him counsel, establish my lineage, and create the conditions for his rebirth in this city of the gods.
He then summoned Canda and the others, saying, “Come, we shall go to the human realm.”
"By means of his stinginess, our lineage has been severed; the hall for giving has been burnt down; he neither enjoys it himself nor gives it to others.

Yet now, desiring to eat milk-rice, thinking, 'If it is cooked at home, there will be milk-rice to give to another as well,' he enters the forest and cooks all alone. Having tamed him, [let us enjoy] the fruit of generosity."
“Having informed him, we shall return; however, if he were to die right there while being entreated by all of us together, it would be a tragedy.
Therefore, you should go first, request the milk-rice, and while you are sitting [to eat], you should come one after another in the guise of brahmins and make your request.
Having said this, he himself first approached him in the guise of a brahmin and said, “Sir, which...?”
“What is the way to go to Bārāṇasī? he asked. Then Macchariya-Kosiya said to him, “What, you madman?
Do you not even know the way to Bārāṇasī? Why have you come from here? Go back this way!
Having heard his words, Sakka, as if not hearing them, approached him again, asking, “What are you saying? He too—
“Go away, deaf Brahmin! What are you doing here? Move on! he shouted. Then Sakka said to him, “Sir, why do you shout?
Smoke is visible, fire is visible, rice porridge is being cooked; this must be a place where Brahmins are invited to dine.
I too shall receive a small portion at the time when the Brahmins eat; why do you drive me away?”
Having said this, when [the other] replied, "There is no invitation for brahmins here; go on ahead," he said, "In that case, why are you angry?
You will receive a little at the time of your own meal. Then he [the other] said to him, "I will not give you even a single grain of rice;
this is merely enough for my own sustenance, and I too obtained it only by begging from others. You [should seek] food elsewhere..."
Having said, "Go and seek one," and having spoken with reference to the fact that he had already obtained his wife by asking for her, he uttered this verse:
"I neither buy nor sell, nor do I have any store of provisions;
alas, this meager portion is so difficult to obtain—it is but a ladleful of rice, not enough for two."

Having heard that, Sakka said, “I too shall speak a single verse for you with a sweet voice; listen to it. Even as the other was warding him off, saying, “I have no need for your verse,” he recited these two stanzas:
“One should give a little from a little; one should give an average amount from an average amount;
one should give much from much. Not giving is not fitting.”
“O Kosiya, I say this to you: give gifts and enjoy them;
ascend the Noble Path. One who eats alone does not obtain happiness.
In this context, *anumajjhato majjhakaṃ* means that even a small amount, having been cut in the middle and divided into two portions...
Having given one portion, from what remains, even if one were to cut it again down the middle and give another portion,
non-giving does not apply; whether little or much has been given, it is not called "non-giving," for that too is indeed giving and possesses great fruit.
Having heard his words, he said, “What you have said is pleasing, brahmin; when the milk-rice is cooked, you shall receive a small portion.

Sit down. Sakka sat down to one side. While he was sitting there, Canda approached by that same path, engaged in the same conversation, and even as the other was trying to stop him, he recited these two verses:
“Futile indeed is his offering, and futile too his striving, who, while a guest is seated, eats his food all alone.
This I say to you, Kosiya: give gifts and enjoy them yourself.”
"Ascend the Noble Path; one who eats not alone attains happiness.
Therein, "striving" (*samīhita*) refers to the energy for the production of wealth.
Having heard his words, with great difficulty and exertion, he said: "In that case, sit down; you shall receive a small portion."

Having gone there, he sat down in the presence of Sakka. Then Sūriya approached him in that same manner, and after engaging in conversation in the same way, even as the other was trying to stop him, he recited these two verses:
“Truth is his offering; truth is also his striving;”
"When one sits down to eat a meal alone while a guest is present, I say this to you, Kosiya:
'Give gifts and enjoy the fruits of giving;
ascend the Noble Path. One who eats alone does not obtain happiness.'"
Having heard his words as well, with great difficulty and effort, he said, "In that case, sit down; you shall receive a small portion.
He went and sat down near Canda. Then Mātali approached him in the same manner, engaged in the same conversation, and even as he was trying to dissuade him, he recited these verses:
“A person may offer oblations at Sārantaṭṭha, at Gayā with its many shrines,
at Doṇa, at Timbarū’s ford, or at the great, swift-flowing river.
Yet it is here that his offering is truly made, and here that his aspiration is fulfilled.”
“Whoever eats his meal alone while a guest is seated—O Kosiya, I say this to you:
give gifts and enjoy them yourself!
Ascend the Noble Path; one who eats alone does not find happiness.”

The meaning of these [verses] is as follows: A man who, thinking "I shall perform an offering to the *nāgas*, *yakṣas*, and so forth," approaches any body of water—such as the ocean, a sandbank, or a lotus pond—and makes an offering there;
likewise, one who does so in a great river, at Gayā, at a lotus pond, or at the two fords named Doṇa and Timbaru, where the current is swift and the flow of water is vast.

And here, "if" (*assa*) means: if even in this case, regarding these guests and so forth, there is both what has been offered and what was intended by that person, it becomes fruitful and results in happiness.
When one eats a meal alone while a guest is seated, there is simply nothing to be said [of such a person];
therefore, I say this to you, Kosiya: give gifts and eat yourself as well.
"Ascend the path of the Noble Ones—the Buddhas and others—who delight in giving. For one cannot truly find happiness eating all alone.
Having heard those words, as if crushed by a mountain peak, he said with great difficulty and distress, "In that case, sit down."
“You will obtain but little,” he said. Mātali went and sat down near the Sun.
Then Pañcasikha approached him in that same manner, engaged in conversation just as before, and even while the Sun was still trying to stop him, he recited these two verses:
“For he swallows the hook along with its long line and its bait;”
“While a guest is seated, he who eats his food all alone—O Kosiya, I say this to you:
give gifts and enjoy them yourself!
Ascend the Noble Path; one who eats by himself does not obtain happiness.”
Having heard this, Macchariya Kosiya, suffering in pain and groaning, said, "In that case, sit down; you shall receive a small portion.
Pañcasikha went and sat down beside Mātali. Thus, as soon as those five brahmins had merely sat down, the milk-rice was cooked.
Then Kosiya took it down from the hearth and said, "Bring your bowls."
Without rising from their seats, they simply stretched out their hands and brought back *māluva* leaves from the Himālayas.
Seeing them, Kosiya said, "There is no rice porridge to be given to you with these leaves; bring the leaves of the *khadira* tree and others.
They brought those as well, and each leaf became as large as a shield (*yodhaphalaka*). He...
He gave milk-rice from his ladle to everyone; even at the time of giving to the very last person, no deficiency appeared in the pot.
Having given to all five, he himself took up the pot and sat down.
At that moment, Pañcasikha rose, cast off his human form, and having become a dog, went before them urinating in their presence. The brahmins—
They covered their own milk-rice with their bowls. A drop of urine fell upon Kosiya’s back.
The brahmins took water from their water-pots and, as if they were already eating, sprinkled the milk-rice over it. Kosiya said, "Give me water too;
I will wash my hands and eat. [The others replied,] "Having brought water for you, [wash your hand...]"
“Wash it,” he said. “I have given you rice porridge; give me a little water. “We do not perform the work of rinsing bowls for alms,” they replied.
“In that case, look into this pan while I wash my hands and return,” he said, and he went down into the river.
At that moment, a dog filled the pan with urine. As he was urinating—
Seeing him, he took up a large staff and came along threatening him. Having become the size of a noble thoroughbred horse, he pursued him, appearing in various colors:
he was black, white, golden-colored, and brindled; he was tall and short. Appearing thus in various colors, he pursued Macchariya-Kosiya.
Terrified by the fear of death, he approached the brahmins. They too—
Having leapt up, they stood in the air. Seeing their supernatural power, he spoke this verse:
“Indeed, these brahmins possess a magnificent appearance; and for what reason is this dog of yours?
It transforms its color and form in various ways. Tell us, O brahmins, who indeed are you?”
Having heard this, Sakka, the king of the gods, said:
“Both the Moon and the Sun have come here, and this is Mātali, the charioteer of the gods;
I am Sakka, the lord of the Thirty-three, and this one is called Pañcasikha.”
Having spoken this verse, he spoke another verse in praise of his glory:
“Hand-clappers, mridanga drums, murajas, and alambaras—
these awaken him with music, and once awakened, he rejoices.”
Having heard his words, [the King] asked: "Sakka, by doing what do you obtain such divine prosperity?
Sakka, demonstrating that those of evil character who are stingy and lack the habit of giving do not go to the world of the gods but are reborn in hell, said:
"Whosoever among these are stingy and miserly, Who revile ascetics and brahmins..."
“Having cast off this physical body right here, at the breaking up of the body, they go to hell.
Having spoken this verse, he spoke the following verse to show that those established in the Dhamma attain the world of the gods:
“Whosoever, seeking a happy destination, are established in the Dhamma, in self-restraint, and in sharing;”
“Right here, casting off the physical body, at the breaking up of the body, they go to a happy destination.

In this context, “expecting” means wishing for. Whosoever wishes for a happy destination, all of them—having established themselves in the ten precepts known as self-restraint and in the practice of giving known as sharing—cast off the body known as the physical frame right here.
The meaning is that upon the breakup of the body, they go to a happy destination.

Having said this, in order to make it known to him, "Kosiya, we have not come into your presence for the sake of rice porridge, but rather we have come out of compassion, having pity for you," he said:
"You were our kinsman in former births, yet you were miserly, irascible, and of evil character."
“We have come here for your very sake; let not one of evil nature go to hell. Therein, “he” means you.
“Let not one of evil nature” means we have come for this purpose: “May this relative of ours, being of evil nature, not go to hell.
Having heard that, Kosiya, with a joyful heart, thought, “It seems these people desire my welfare; they wish to lift me out of hell and establish me in heaven,” and he said:
“Truly, you desire my welfare, since you instruct me thus;
I shall do exactly as all that has been said by those who wish me well.
From this day forward, I shall cease from worldly activity and commit no evil whatsoever.”
"Furthermore, there is nothing that I would not give away, nor do I drink water without having given some.
And while I am giving in this way at all times, O Vāsava, these riches of mine will be exhausted.
Then, Sakka, having abandoned these sensual pleasures as they arise, I shall go forth into homelessness."
In this context: "Me" means for me; "you" means you; "what" means that with which you instruct me—therefore you are well-wishers toward me.
"So be it" means I shall do exactly as you say. "I desist" means I desist from the state of stinginess.
"There is nothing that cannot be given" means that from now on, there is not even half a mouthful of mine that is called "ungivable," nor is there anything that I would not give.
"Even if I obtain a mere mouthful of water, I shall not drink it without having given it away. "They will perish" means they will be scattered.
"As they stand" refers to the divisions as they exist, according to the categories of sense-objects (*vatthukāma*) and defilements (*kilesakāma*).
Having tamed Macchariya-Kosiya and rendered him free from stinginess, and having made him understand the fruit of giving, [the Blessed One] proceeded with a teaching of the Dhamma.
Having established them in the five precepts, he went together with them to the city of the gods. Macchariyakosiya, too,
having entered the city and obtained the king’s permission, gave wealth to the supplicants, saying, "Let them take it, filling their vessels as much as they have taken," and when that was exhausted,
he departed from there and [went] to the southern bank of the Gaṅgā from the Himālaya.
Having built a leaf-hut within a single natural lake and gone forth into homelessness, he lived there for a long time subsisting on forest roots and fruits until he reached old age.
At that time, Sakka had four daughters—Āsā, Saddhā, Sirī, and Hirī—who, taking many celestial perfumes and garlands, went to Lake Anotatta for the purpose of playing in the water. There, they...

Having played, they sat down upon the surface of the emerald stone. At that moment, a brahmin ascetic named Nārada, having gone to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven for his midday rest, spent the day in the Nandana Grove and the Cittalātāvana forest;
holding a Pāricchattaka flower like a parasol for shade, he passed over the surface of the emerald stone toward his own dwelling place.
He went to the Kañcanaguha cave. Then, seeing that flower in his hand, they entreated him for it.
Explaining this matter, the Teacher said:
“In the supreme mountain, the best of peaks, Gandhamādana, those excellent deities rejoice, protected by the Best of Gods.”
Then the supreme seer, the protector of all the world, approached, taking hold of a branch of a noble tree that was in full bloom.

"This pure, fragrant, and most excellent flower—honored by the Thirty-Three Gods and served by the foremost of the immortals—is not obtained by mortals nor even by the Dānavas; it is fit for the gods alone."
Then four women, like golden palm trees, the mistresses of pleasure, rose up before the Sage— the Goddess of Hope,
Faith, Fortune, and then Modesty— and thus spoke to the brahmin Nārada:
“If this flower of the Pāricchattaka tree, O Great Sage, has not been assigned by you, O Brahmā...”
“Grant us all our desires; may your every purpose be fulfilled, and may you be to us even as Vāsava.
Seeing them thus entreating him, Nārada spoke these words, inciting a dispute:
“I have no need for any of these things; whichever among you is the most excellent, let her adorn herself with them.”
In that context, "on the excellent mountain" (*girivare*) is a synonym for the preceding term. "Protected by the best of gods" (*devavarābhipālitā*) means guarded by Sakka.
"One who goes everywhere in all worlds" (*sabbalokagū*) means capable of traveling to all places, both in the world of the gods and in the world of humans.

"Taking a branch of the best of trees" (*dumavarasākhamādiya*) means taking a flower that has received the name "branch of the best tree" because it grew on such a branch. "Honored" (*sakkataṃ*) means having been shown respect. "By the best of the immortals" (*amaravarehi*)...
This was said with reference to Sakka. "Except by gods" means not obtained by others—whether humans, *yakkhas*, or the like—other than gods and those possessing supernormal powers (*iddhimant*).
"For that is worthy of them" means that it is indeed suitable and appropriate for them. "With skins like gold" means the skins are comparable to gold.
"Having risen" refers to the noble one who abstains from garlands, perfumes, ointments, and so forth.
"She will not wear the flower; she will throw it away in one place.

Come, let us beg it from her and wear the flower!"—saying this, they stretched out their hands and begged, and rising up all at once, [they spoke: "O Mistress of the Courtesans! O Supreme among women! O Sage! O Seer!
It was not assigned to anyone, thinking, 'I shall give it to such-and-such a person. May all your goals be fulfilled! Thus, all...
"May your heart's desire be fulfilled; may you obtain whatever you have prayed for"—thus they pronounce their blessing upon him.
"Just as Vāsava," meaning just as our father Vāsava grants whatever is desired, so may you be for us as well.
"That" refers to that flower. "Abhisamekkha" means having seen. "Saṃkala" means a dispute that increases quarrels through various assertions.
"How did he speak? [The answer is: "By these" means: "I have no need for these flowers;
I am one who abstains from wearing garlands," thus he indicates. "Whichever among you is the eldest" means: whichever is the senior among you.
"Let her wear it" means: let her put this on.
Having heard his words, all four of them spoke this verse:
“Do not look at us with partiality, Nārada; bestow [your favor] upon whichever one you desire.
For whichever among us you shall point out, O Nārada, she alone shall be considered by us as the most excellent.”
"In this matter, you alone are our supreme one"—that is to say, "O Supreme Great Sage, you alone must determine for us. Having heard their words, Nārada spoke this verse while addressing them:
"O fair-limbed ones, these words are unseemly; what brahmin would incite a quarrel?
Go and ask the Lord of Beings himself if you do not know who here is superior or inferior."
The meaning of this is as follows: "O fair ones, O you of beautiful limbs, these words spoken by you are improper for me;
for if it were so, by making one among you superior and the rest inferior, I would be increasing a quarrel.
What brahmin who has cast out evil would incite or increase a quarrel? Indeed, for such a person, the incitement of a quarrel is improper; therefore—"
"Go from here and ask your own father, Bhūtādhipa Sakka himself, if you do not know who is superior and who is inferior.
Then the Teacher spoke this verse:
"Those women, greatly incited by Nārada, were addressed while intoxicated by the pride of their beauty."
Having gone into the presence of the Thousand-Eyed One, they asked the Lord of Beings: “Which of these two is superior?
Therein, *paramappakopitā* means she was greatly provoked by him for not giving her a flower; having become angry with him, she was thus deeply offended.
*Udīritā* means she was addressed [by them], saying, “Ask the Lord of Beings himself. *Sahassacakkhunoti* means having gone into the presence of Sakka. *Kā*... [which one...]
"Among us, who is the most excellent? they asked.
Having asked this and standing there, the Lord of Creatures (Purindada), his mind captivated by seeing them, spoke thus with palms joined in reverence: "The best of gods (Devavara) said this..."
“Be all of you alike in your beautiful forms; who, O Bhaddā, has raised this quarrel?
Therein, “having seen them” means, monks, having seen all four who had come into her presence. “With intent minds” means with eager minds, with attentive hearts.
“With palms joined” means with their hands held out in reverence by the deities who were paying homage. “Alike” means—

"All of you are exactly alike. "Who indeed? means "Who, pray, is it? "He who incited the quarrel" means he spoke and increased this dispute and contention. Then, as they were speaking, they recited this verse to him:
"He who has wandered through all the worlds, the Great Sage, Nārada, who stands firm in Dhamma and is devoted to truth;"
Thus he spoke on the excellent mountain Gandhamādana: "Go and ask the Lord of Beings himself:
'If you do not know who here is the highest or the lowest.
In this context, "the departure for truth" means such an exertion.
Having heard this, Sakka thought: "These four are all my daughters. If I say, 'One among them is endowed with virtue and is the best,' the others will be angry;
it is not possible for me to decide this dispute. I shall send them to the presence of the Kosiya ascetic in the Himalayas;
he will decide their dispute. Having thus reflected, he said: "I..."
“I will not decide between you two. In the Himalayas there is an ascetic named Kosiya;
I shall send him my own food of ambrosia. He does not eat without first giving to another, and when he gives, he gives only after discerning those who possess virtue.
She among you who receives food from his hand shall be the superior one. Speaking thus, he uttered this verse:
“That great sage who wanders in the vast forest does not eat his choice food without first giving it away;
Kosiya gives gifts after careful discernment,
for she alone to whom he gives shall be most fortunate.”
In this context, "one who dwells in the great forest" means a resident of the vast wilderness.
Thus, having sent [the messenger] to the presence of the ascetic and summoned Mātali, he spoke the following verse while sending him into that ascetic's presence:
"For he who has gone to the southern direction, on the bank of the Gaṅgā, on the slopes of the Himālayas..."
“O charioteer of the gods, bestow upon that Kosiya sweet food, for he has food and drink that are difficult to obtain.
Therein, *sammati* means “dwells. *Dakkhiṇaṃ* means “to the south,” namely the southern direction of the Himālaya. *Passanī* means “on the side.
Then the Teacher said:
“Sent by the best of gods, Mātali mounted a chariot yoked with a thousand [horses];
having arrived at the hermitage very swiftly, remaining invisible, he gave sweet food to the Sage.
In this context, “remaining invisible,” monks, refers to that Mātali having accepted the word of the king of the gods.
Having gone to his hermitage and become invisible, he gave him the *sudhā* food; while giving it, he remained standing at dawn,
having practiced meditation during the night and tended the sacrificial fire, as that man stood worshipping the rising sun,
and placed the bowl of *sudhā* food into his hand.
Kosiya, having taken it, while still standing, spoke these two verses:
“While I was attending to the sacred fire, the light-maker, the supreme dispeller of the world’s darkness,
Vāsava, surpassing all beings, rained down.”
“Who is this in my hand? What is this ocean of pure water?
“A conch-like shell, white, of incomparable appearance, pure, fragrant, lovely, and wonderful;
never before seen by my eyes—what deity is this in my hand? What is this ocean of pure water?”

In this context, "having performed the water-oblation" means that after attending to the water-oblation and departing from the fire-hall, he stood at the door of the leaf-hut and worshipped the supreme sun, the light-maker who dispels the darkness of the world.
[Thinking: "Is it Vāsava, surpassing all beings and acting thus, who is offering me this ambrosia in his hands? What indeed is this?"
He recited: “Like a conch,” and so forth, praising the Sudha while remaining standing.
Then Mātali said:
“I was sent by Mahinda, the Great Seer; O Great Sage, I have hurriedly brought this Sudha.”
“You know me, Mātali, divine charioteer; eat this supreme food, do not refuse it.
“And when eaten, that best of flavors destroys twelve evils:
hunger, thirst, discontent, fatigue, anger, resentment, strife, slander, cold, heat, and drowsiness.”

"In that regard, 'I have brought this sudhā-food for you' means: 'Know me,' the sense being, 'know that I am the divine charioteer named Mātali. 'Do not withhold' means: do not refuse by saying 'I will not eat';
rather, eat without making a fuss. 'It destroys evil' means: for when this sudhā is consumed, it destroys twelve evil qualities. 'Hunger'..."
First, it dispels hunger; second, thirst for water; third, restlessness; fourth, bodily fatigue;
fifth, weariness; sixth, anger; seventh, resentment; eighth, quarreling;
ninth, slander; tenth, cold; eleventh, heat; twelfth, drowsiness and laziness.
"This is the supreme nectar, the highest flavor, the food of ambrosia; it destroys these twelve evil qualities.
Having heard this, Kosiya, declaring his own undertaking of the vow, said:
"It is not fitting for me, Mātali, to eat without first giving to others; such is my supreme vow."
“Nor does one who eats alone, nor one who honors the noble ones, nor one who does not share, find happiness.
Having spoken this verse, when asked by Mātali, “Venerable sir, seeing what fault in eating without giving to others did you undertake this vow? he replied:
“Those who strike women, those who commit adultery, those who betray friends, and those who curse the virtuous;”
"All those [who are] base, with stinginess as the fifth, therefore one should not even drink water without having given.
'Whether for a woman or for a man, I shall give a gift praised by the wise;
those who are faithful, generous, free from stinginess in this world, are considered pure and truthful.'"
In this context, *pubbe* means "first," that is, having not given [anything] previously; or alternatively, it shows:
"Indeed, this supreme vow was undertaken by me previously. *Na cāpi ekāsanamariyapūjitam* means that eating alone is not honored by the Noble Ones, such as the Buddhas and others.
*Sukham* means he does not obtain heavenly or human happiness. *Thīghātakā* means killers of women.
"Ye cime ye ca ime" means "those and these. "Sapanti" means they revile. "Subbata" refers to righteous recluses and brahmins.
"Maccharipañcamā" means those for whom a miser is the fifth; thus, they are called "maccharipañcamā. "Adhamā" means these five are indeed called unrighteous.
"Tasmā" means because, out of fear of becoming the fifth unrighteous person, I shall not even sip water or consume anything without having given [to others].
"I undertook this vow. "By a woman" means by that woman. "Praised by the wise" means praised by the wise and learned ones, such as the Buddha and others. "Reputed for purity and truthfulness":
the meaning is that those persons who are endowed with unwavering faith, who are generous, and free from stinginess, become both pure and highly esteemed.
Having heard that, Mātali stood there with his body visible. At that moment, those four celestial maidens stood in the four directions:
Sirī stood in the eastern direction, Āsā in the southern direction, Saddhā in the western direction, and Hirī in the northern direction.
To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“Then four maidens, sent by the Lord of Devas, resembling the surface of gold—
Hope, Faith, Glory, and Modesty— arrived at that hermitage where Kosiya dwelt.
Seeing them, all the peacocks of the mountain-top were filled with supreme joy because of their beautiful complexions.”
Four maidens from the four quarters spoke thus in the presence of Mātali:
“O goddess, who are you that shines toward the eastern quarter, adorned like the most excellent star, the herb?
I ask you, O one with a body like a golden vine—tell me, which goddess are you?”
“O Queen Sirī, honored by men, who always attends upon those beings free from evil;
you have come here for the sake of the ambrosia—O one of excellent wisdom, share that ambrosia with me.
“O Great Sage, the man for whom I desire the ambrosia shall rejoice in all his desires.”
“Know me as Sirī, the supreme sacrificer; O you of excellent wisdom, share with me some of this ambrosia.
In this context, *ato* means “from there. *Matā* means “approved”; thus the meaning is that she was both approved and dispatched by the chief of the gods.
*Sabbo paramappamodito* means “everyone was exceedingly delighted without exception. There is also a reading, *sāmaṃ*, referring to those deities.
"Having seen her personally"—this is the meaning. "Fourfold" (*caturo*) means clever; or this is simply the reading *cāturiya*, meaning "endowed with cleverness.
"Best of stars" (*tāravarā*) means the most excellent among the stars. "In a body like molten gold" (*kañcanavelliviggaha*) means in a physical form resembling the color of refined gold.
"By me" (*sirāhā*) means by me, Siri. "I have come to you" (*tavaṃtimāgatā*) means I have come into your presence. "Grant me [a share]" (*bhājaya*) means as you would grant me a portion of plaster...
"Serve [him], act accordingly, and give me the cream"—this is the meaning. "Jānahīti" means "know. "Jūhatuttamā" means "the best among those offering oblations into the fire.
Having heard that, Kosiya said:
"Men who are endowed with craft, with conduct and knowledge, and with wisdom, and who are proficient in their own work;"
"Deprived of her, they obtain nothing at all; this which you have done is not good.
I see a man who is lazy and gluttonous, even one of very low birth and unattractive in form;
yet, protected by you, he—though proud of his lineage—is sent like a slave by a wealthy and happy man."
“I know you to be one who clings to various falsehoods, deluded and following after those who are not wise;
such a person does not deserve a seat or water, much less ambrosia. Depart! You are not pleasing to me.
In this context, “by craft” refers to the crafts of elephants, horses, chariots, archery, and so forth. “By knowledge and conduct” refers to that which is comprised of the three Vedas.
"By means of true knowledge and virtue. "Skilled in their own work" means they are endowed with the qualities of exertion through their own personal effort.
"They obtain nothing"—they do not obtain even the slightest bit of fame or happiness.
"That which"—namely, this deficiency you have created for those who wander about having mastered various crafts for the sake of power—that was not good of you.
"Though formless, [it regards] the deformed. "Guarded by her" means protected by her.
"Even one who possesses birth" means even one endowed with noble birth, and even one endowed with craft, science, conduct, wisdom, and action. "He sends" means he makes him a messenger.

"That" (taṃ) refers to that person; therefore, "him" (taṃ). "Untrue" (asaccaṃ) means untrue because it does not abide in the truth defined as intrinsic nature, and thus it is devoid of the highest state.

"One who associates without discrimination" means one who, without having made a distinction and without knowing what is appropriate or inappropriate, serves both those endowed with crafts and skills as well as others.
"One who follows after the wise" means one who follows after the learned, acting by casting them down, striking them, and harassing them.
"How could there be fine plaster?"—for such a person devoid of virtue, how could there be a meal of fine plaster? "I do not like you; go, do not stay here."
Refused by him, she vanished right there. Then, conversing with Āsā, he said:
“Who is this fair-toothed one, adorned with earrings, wearing a golden armlet and polished shell bracelets?
You shine, embracing a color like that of a fresh rain-cloud, like a cluster of blossoms upon a red *kusam* flower.”
“O doe-eyed one, you have been startled by one who bears a bow and arrows; you look about as if bewildered.
Who is your companion here, O lady with lovely eyes? Are you not afraid, being alone in this forest grove?
In that passage, *cittaṅgadā* means “possessing variegated armlets. *Kambuvimaṭṭhadhārinī* means “wearing [ornaments] polished like conch-shell,” referring to those perfected through craftsmanship.
She wore ornaments of polished gold. "Smeared with color" refers to celestial *dukūla* cloth having the hue of a stream of poured water.
"Having wrapped herself" means both having put on a lower garment and having draped an upper robe.

"Red like a blade of kusa-grass fire" means having the color of a crest of flame from a kusa-grass fire. "Clasping a cluster of blossoms" means it is said that she had fastened an *asoka* bud, together with its sprouts, behind her ear. "Wearing a bow of autumn."
"By the hunter. "Wounded" means having received a blow. "As if slowly" means that just as that doe, standing in the middle of the forest out of fear, would look at him very slowly, so did she look.
Then Āsā said:
“O Kosiya, I have no companion here among the deities who originate from Masakkasāra.
Your hope has come to me for the sake of the ambrosia; therefore, O one of supreme wisdom, share that ambrosia with me.
In this context, “originating from Masakkasāra” means those born in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

Having heard that, Kosiya spoke, demonstrating: "It seems you grant hope to one who pleases you by fulfilling their expectation for fruit, but you do not grant it to one who does not please you; there is no one equal to you in destroying the desired object. He said:
"Merchants seeking wealth set out with hope, having boarded a ship upon the great ocean.
Sometimes they sink there, and returning with ruined wealth, they arrive with their goods lost."
“With hope, farmers plow their fields and sow seeds, employing every means;
yet, due to the onset of calamities or a lack of rain, they obtain no fruit from that labor.
Then, placing their hopes first, men seeking happiness perform services for their masters.”
Those who have overreached for the sake of their husbands, having lost everything and found nothing, flee in all directions.
Having abandoned grain, wealth, and kinsmen, seeking happiness and longing for heaven with hope, they perform even harsh austerities for a long time;
yet, having ascended a wrong path, they go to a state of misery.
“Hope is considered deceptive; abandon hope within yourself as if it were mere plaster.
One such as this does not deserve a seat or water; how much less plaster? Go away, for you are not pleasing to me.
In that context, *pavantī* means they leap forward. *Jīnādhanā* means those whose wealth has been won. Thus, by means of you, some attain success.
Some fail; he says, "There is no one like you in evil nature. They perform each task with skillful means (*upāya*).

"By the occurrence of calamities" means by the occurrence of any one of the crop-disasters, such as adverse winds, rats, locusts, *suka* insects, *pānaka* insects, white blight, or disease. "From that" means from that crop [they] do not obtain any fruit.
He says: "You yourself are the one who cuts off their hope. *Athattakārāni* means manly efforts on the fields of battle.
*Āsaṃ purakkhatvā* means having placed the hope for sovereignty before oneself. *Bhatturatthāya* means for the sake of the master.
