*Atigāḷitā* means being excessively oppressed by enemies, with their wealth plundered and their army and vehicles destroyed. *Panassanti* means they perish.
They flee. "Not having obtained anything" means not having obtained any sovereignty. Thus he says: "It is you alone who cause even these [beings] to fail to obtain sovereignty.
"Intent on heaven" means desiring to attain heaven. "Austere" means the bodily exhaustion of the five-fold heat and so forth, which is devoid of essence.
"For a long time" means for a long duration. "These hopes are considered deceptive"—thus [he speaks] regarding these beings.
"Out of hope for heaven, people go to a state of misery; therefore, you who are called 'Hope' are considered deceptive, having come to be known as a deceiver. He addressed her thus: "Āse! (O Hope!).
She too, being rejected by him, vanished. Then, conversing with Faith, he spoke this verse:
“Shining with glory, O glorious one, you stand facing the direction called by the name Jighañña.
I ask you, O you whose body is like a golden creeper: tell me, which goddess are you?

In this passage, *daddallamānā* means “shining. *Jighaññanāmavhayanaṃ* means that you stand shining while facing the direction that is addressed by such lowly names as “Aparā” (the Western) and “Pacchimā” (the West).
Then she spoke this verse:
“I am Queen Saddhā, honored by men, always serving those beings who are free from evil.
I have come to you with a request for nectar; O one of supreme wisdom, share that nectar with me.”
In this context, "faith" (saddhā) is the act of placing trust in someone's words; it may be either blameworthy or blameless.
"Worshiped" (pūjitā) means worshiped by virtue of being a blameless constituent. "One who frequents non-evil beings" (apāpasattūpanisevinī):

this is the name for a deity who, because she possesses the nature of placing trust in others through her own blameless faith and absolute trustworthiness, is capable of inspiring trust in others as well.

Then Kosiya said to him, "These beings, having placed their trust in whatever anyone says, do much more that should not be done than what should be done; all of that is as if it were caused by you. Having said this, he spoke thus:
"Sometimes, taking up generosity, self-control, renunciation, and restraint, some perform them out of faith;
yet others, once freed from you, commit theft, falsehood, fraud, and slander."
“A man who looks upon wives who are his equals—those endowed with virtue and devoted to their husbands—and having restrained even his desire for noble women, places his trust instead in a slave-girl.
You yourself, O Saddhā, are one who pursues the wives of others; you commit evil and neglect what is wholesome.”
“Such a person as you does not deserve a seat or water; how could there be fine plaster? Go away, for I do not like you.
In this context, *dāna* refers to the volition of merit consisting of the ten bases. *Dama* refers to the taming of the sense faculties. *Cāga* refers to the relinquishing of things to be given.
*Saṃyama* refers to virtue (*sīla*). *Ādāya saddhāya* means: [the words] of those who say, “These things such as giving and so forth, which bring great benefits, ought to be performed.”
Even after accepting a statement in faith, people sometimes commit such acts. "Fraud" (*kūṭa*) refers to fraudulent scales and the like, or the work of a village headman (*gāmakūṭa*).

"Some people do it" means that some individuals, having placed their trust in the words of others—thinking, "At times such as these, acts like theft must be committed for the sake of these [people]"—perform even these things.
"Again, released by them" (*puna viccutā taya*) means again...

"Even though they do not believe the words of those who say, 'These things, which result in blameworthy suffering, must not be done,' because they are infatuated by her, they nevertheless perform them.
Thus, you say that one might perform both the blameworthy and the blameless according to her will.
'Among equals' means among those who are equal in terms of birth, clan, virtue, and so forth. 'Looking' (pekkhā) is said to mean craving; thus, 'one who has craving' (sataṇho)."
Meaning: "Desire" refers to lustful desire (*chandarāga*). "He places his trust" means he places his trust even in the words of a water-carrier slave girl;

having gained confidence in her when she says, "I shall do this service for you," he abandons even women of good family and pursues her alone, thinking, "A certain woman named so-and-so has set her heart on you," even if she is a water-carrier slave girl.
It is precisely by placing faith in their words that one pursues another's wife.
Because they pursue another's wife and commit evil—abandoning what is wholesome—by trusting you and acting according to your influence, it is you alone who are the pursuer of another's wife;
you commit evils and neglect the wholesome. There is no one in the world equal to you in destroying [virtue].
“You are of evil character; go away, you are not pleasing to me.
Thereupon, she vanished right then and there. Kosiya, meanwhile, standing to the north, conversed with Hirī and spoke these two verses:
“Hungering through the night, she appears at the rising of the dawn, possessing the most excellent form and beauty;”
“O deity, you appear to me like that; tell me, who are you, what kind of nymph are you?
‘Black as a flame at the height of summer, fanned by the wind, garlanded with red leaves— Who are you standing there, looking about like a timid deer, speaking yet not releasing a word?’”
In this context, "the time when hunger is felt" means the final part of the night; the meaning is "at the conclusion of the night. "When dawn has risen" means when the sun has appeared.
"She goes"—that eastern direction which, because it is like refined gold, appears bearing a form of exquisite beauty.

"Like a black creeper in the heat" means like a black creeper (*kāḷavallī*) during the summer season. "Like a flame of fire" means like a mass of fire; that too is like a young black creeper that has just arisen in dry fields.
"Viya" means "like. "Lohitapattamālinī" means surrounded by leaves of red color. "Kā tiṭṭhasi" means:
who are you that stand there, just as a young black creeper stands, swaying with grace and beauty when stirred by the wind? "Bhāsesamānā va" means:
you appear as if desiring to speak with me, yet you do not utter a word.
Then she spoke this verse:
“I am the goddess Hirā, honored by men, who always attends upon those free from evil.
I have come here because of a dispute over nectar; as such, I am unable even to ask for nectar.”
"Like a woman who begs with her private parts exposed.
In this context, "Hirāham" means "I am Hiri. "Sudham-pīti" means that I, though being *sudhā* (ambrosia), am unable even to ask for it.
For what reason? Because begging by a woman is like exposing one's private parts (*kopīna-rūpā*); since begging by a woman is indeed like exposing one's private parts.
It is like the opening of a private part; the meaning is that she is as if shameless.
Having heard that, the ascetic spoke two verses:
“O fair-limbed one, you shall obtain it through righteousness and the proper method; for this is the Dhamma, not mere begging.”
“I invite you, whomever you seek to entreat; whatever nectar you desire, that too I shall give to you.

“Thus invited by me today to my own hermitage, O you whose form is like a golden vine—you who are worthy of being honored by me with every kind of flavor—having honored you, I shall eat even the nectar.”
In this context, "by way of Dhamma" means by way of its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
"By way of principle" means by way of reason (*kāraṇa*). For plaster is not obtained by begging; for that very reason, the other three did not obtain it. "That" (*taṃ*) refers to that [plaster].
"Whatever you desire" means: I am not merely inviting you; whatever plaster you desire, that too I shall give to you. "With a body like a polished golden bell-metal vessel."
"O you whose body is as beautiful as a heap of gold! You are indeed worthy of being honored by me not only with ambrosia, but also with all other flavors.
As for 'I shall eat': if, after honoring you with ambrosia, there should be a remainder, I too shall eat it.
Then follows another verse concerning the Perfectly Enlightened One:
“Permitted by the radiant Kosiya, she indeed entered that delightful grove of Hiri,
which possessed water, bore fruit honored by the Noble Ones, and was always frequented by beings free from evil.
There, many trees were in full bloom— mangoes, *piyāla* trees, jackfruit trees, and *kiṃsuka* trees.”
Sobhañjanas, lodhra, and also paddhaka, kekā, bhaṅgā, and tilaka in full bloom;
sāl trees, karerī, many jambu trees here, as well as assattha, nigrodha, madhuka, and vetasa;
uddālaka, pāṭali, and sinduvāraka, with delightful scents, mucalinda, and ketakī.
“Hareṇuka, veḷuka, keṇu, tinduka, millet, wild rice, and even Chinese rice;
plantains, bananas, and many kinds of śāli rice here, as well as *pavīhaya* and *ābhūjina* grains.
On its northern side, there was a pleasant lotus pond that had arisen.”
Not harsh, not steep, and free from foul odors—this is excellent.
Therein the fish delight, secure and well-fed;
there are the *siṅgu* fish, the crooked ones, the *saṃkula*, and the *rohitā* with their hundred hooks.
There were *āḷiga*, *aggara*, and *kākiṇṇa* fish, as well as *pāṭhīna* and *kākamacchaka*.
There, birds dwelt happily, secure and well-fed:
swans, cranes, peacocks, ruddy geese, and cuckoos.
In Kuṇālaka there are many colorful birds, peacocks and pheasants.
There, many diverse herds of animals come for drink:
lions, tigers, boars, bears, hyenas, and jackals.
“Palāsāda deer, gavajas, buffaloes, rohita deer, ruru deer,
eṇeyya deer, wild boars, herds of common pigs, kadalimigas,
and many cats and hares are here.”
“On the mountain slopes, carpeted with variegated flowers, resounding with the cries of birds, and frequented by flocks of birds.

Regarding this: “Radiant” means endowed with majestic power (*ānubhāva*). “He entered the hermitage” (*pāvisi yassam*); here the syllable *ya-* serves as a euphonic conjunction (*byañjanasandhikara*).
“Possessing water” means well-supplied with water in various places. “Fruitful” means endowed with many kinds of fruits. “Honored by the Noble Ones” (*ariyapūjita*)...
It is honored and praised by noble ones who have attained meditative absorption (jhāna) and are free from the faults of the hindrances (nīvaraṇa).
"Thickets of trees" refers to thickets of flowering and fruit-bearing trees. *Sobhañjana* means *siggu* trees. *Loddamatho pi paddhakā* refers to *loddarukkha* and *padumarukkha* trees.
*Kekā ca bhaṅgā* refers to trees with those very names. *Karerī* refers to *karerī* trees. *Uddālaka* refers to *vātaghātaka* trees.
*Mucalindaketakā* refers to *mucalinda* plants and the five kinds of *ketaka* grasses. *Hareṇuka* is a species of wild grain. *Veḷuka* refers to bamboo-splitting reeds.
*Keṇu* refers to forest beans. *Tinduka* refers to the *timbaru* trees. *Cīnaka* refers to small grains similar to rice. *Moca* refers to the bony plantains (*kadali*).
*Sāliyo* refers to various types of rice grown in dependence on natural ponds. *Pavīhaya* refers to...
"Various kinds of grain": *ābhūjina* means those with winged ears. "Rice": this refers to the husked grain, free from chaff and bran, consisting of the naturally grown kernels of rice.
"Of that very same," monks, means on the northern side of that very same horse-hermitage. "Lotus pond": a natural pond covered with the five kinds of lotuses. "Not harsh":
free from the harshness of fish, snails, moss, and so forth. "Not overhanging": with banks that do not slope away.
“Level” means even. “Free from stench” means endowed with water that has no repulsive odor.
“Therein” refers to that lotus pond. “Secure” means fearless. “Siṅgu” and so forth are names for those fish.
“Kuṇālaka” means cuckoos. “Citra” means those with variegated plumage. “Sikhaṇḍī” refers to peacocks with crests standing upright, or others that have crests growing on their heads.
Birds. "They come for drink" means they approach for the sake of drinking. "Palāsas" refers to rhinoceroses. "Gavajas" refers to gayals.
"Gaṇins" refers to ox-eared deer. "Kaṇṇikas" refers to the *kaṇṇika* deer. "Chamāgiris" refers to flat-topped rocks on the ground.
"Spread with variegated flowers" means spread with various kinds of flowers. "Resounded by birds" means resounded by birds with sweet voices. Such as these...
In this context, the Blessed One thus praises the hermitage of Kosiya as "the earth and the mountains.
Now, in order to show the entry and other activities of the goddess Hiri there, he said:
"Like lightning descending upon a great cloud, she approached, draped in fine cloth and hanging over trees of dark green foliage."
To her, whose head was well-bound with a wreath of *kuśa* grass, pure, fragrant, and draped with an antelope skin—this seat of *atricca* grass spoke thus with a sense of shame:
"Sit down, O auspicious lady; this seat shall bring you comfort.
Then, as she sat upon that *atricca* grass, Koṣika, who wore matted hair and an antelope skin, [approached] her who so desired.
With fresh leaves, he himself quickly offered water and food with great joy, O Great Sage.
Taking it with both hands, she spoke thus to the wearer of matted locks, her heart full of gladness:
"Now that I have been honored by you, O Brahmā, may I, victorious, go to the triple heaven."
“Permitted by the radiant Kosiya, and intoxicated with the pride of her beauty, she approached the presence of the Thousand-Eyed One and said: ‘O Vāsava, grant me this nectar and victory!
Then Sakka himself, together with the hosts of gods, honored that most excellent celestial maiden.”
“When she, worshipped by gods and humans, sat down upon a new couch with her hands joined in reverence.
In this context, *suttacā* means having beautiful skin. *Nīladumābhilambitā* means hanging from blue trees;
the meaning is that she was touching various branches of those blue trees. *Mahāmegharivā* means like the lightning of a great cloud, being invited by it.
She entered that hermitage of his as if it were her own. "Of him" means of that sense of shame (*hirī*). "Well-knit head" means a head with excellent joints.
"Made of *kuśa* grass" means made of *kuśa* grass mixed with *uśīra* and other such plants.
"Fragrant" means fragrant because it is mixed with both *uśīra* and other fragrant grasses. "Used for an antelope skin" means used as an upper covering by means of an antelope hide.
"Atricca" means having spread such a seat of grass at the door of the leaf-hut.
"Sukhayidaṃ āsanaṃ" means "sit comfortably on this seat.
"Yaṃ" means as much as is needed. "Icchamānāya" means to her who desires plaster. "Navehi pattēhi" means with fresh leaves at that very moment.
With fresh lotus leaves gathered from the pond. "They lie down" means with their own hands. "Together with water" means accompanied by the water-offering (dakkhiṇodaka).
"She brought forth fine food" means she brought the fine food. "Hurried" means hurried by the force of joy. "Handā" is a particle used for emphasis.
"The victorious one" means having attained victory.

"Permitted" means she was now authorized to go according to her own wish. "Proclaimed" means that having gone to the city of the Thirty-three, she proclaimed, "This is Sudhā," in the presence of Sakka.
"A celestial maiden" (*surakaññā*) means a daughter of the gods. "Supreme" (*uttama*) means excellent.
"With palms joined, worshipped by gods and men" means she was honored with palms joined by both deities and humans. "When" (*yadā*) refers to when [she sat] for the purpose of sitting down.
She sat down upon a new couch called the Golden Throne, which had been provided by Sakka;
then, as she sat there, Sakka and the other deities honored her with *pāricchattaka* flowers and other offerings.
Having thus paid her homage, Sakka reflected: "For what reason did Kosiya give these to her alone, without giving them to the others?"
“...gave him nectar. In order to learn the reason for this, he sent Mātali once again.
Making this matter clear, the Teacher said:
“The thousand-eyed lord of the thirty-three gods, Saṃsī, sent Mātali back once more.”
"Having gone, speak these words to Kosiya: 'O Kosiya, by what cause does hope, faith, and glory [fail];
and by what reason did Modesty receive the stain of impurity?'"—therein he spoke thus.
"My words" means: speak my words to Kosiya. "By hope, by faith, and by glory" means: by what cause indeed did Hope, Faith, and Glory receive the stain of impurity?
Having accepted his words, he mounted the Vejayanta chariot and departed. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:

“He caused that well-furnished chariot to ascend, which was resplendent like a benefactor, resembling refined gold from the Jambu River, glowing like beaten gold, and adorned as if with patterns of pure gold.”
“Many golden moons were cast down here—elephants, cattle, horses, kinkinis, tigers, and leopards;
antelopes, birds that could leap, and deer made of beryl engaged in combat.
There, they yoked a thousand swift steeds like noble stallions, resembling great tuskers.”
Adorned with a covering of golden nets, garlanded, resounding, and unobstructed—
having mounted that most excellent vehicle, Mātali caused these quarters to resound;
he made the sky, the mountains, the forest trees, and the earth together with the oceans tremble.
“Having quickly approached the hermitage, with his robe arranged over one shoulder and palms joined in reverence, Mātali, the divine brahmin, spoke thus to the learned, aged, and disciplined one:
‘Listen, Kosiya, to the words of Indra; I am his messenger, and Purindada questions you.’”
“Āsa, saddhā, sirī, and Kosiya—by what cause did Hiri obtain Sudhā?

Therein, “for the purpose of crossing that well-made boat” means for the purpose of easily crossing that Vejayanta chariot. “He brought it out” means he drew it out, lifted it up, and made it ready for travel.
“Similar to the requisites” means similar to the articles of equipment; just as...
Its implements, having a color identical to the crest of the flame, burn; the meaning is that they burn in exactly that same way.

"Made of Jambū-river gold" means made of red gold known as Jambū-nada. "Resembling a golden mosaic" means it is endowed with an eightfold auspicious design (*aṭṭhamaṅgala*) made of gold and variegated with the seven jewels. "There are golden moons" means they are made of gold.
"Candakas" here refers to chariots. "Elephants" refers to elephants made of gold, silver, and jewels; the same principle applies to the cattle and other animals as well.
"Flocks of birds made of *laṅgha* here" means that in these chariots, flocks of birds made of various gems (*nānāratana*) are also arranged in rows.
"Engaged in battle" means they are shown having been joined together with their respective weapons of war.
"Assarājaharayo" means the mind-made horse-kings of golden hue. "Susunāgasādise" means resembling young elephants in their perfection of strength.
"Kañcanajāluracchade" means endowed with breast-plate ornaments made of golden netting.
"Āveḷine" means equipped with ear-ornaments known as *āveḷas*. "Saddagame" means [moving] by sound alone, without the stroke of a goad.
"Of a nature to go. "Unrestrained" means unattached; the meaning is that they yoked such a king of horses, swift in speed, there.
"It resounded aloud" means it made a single, unified noise with the sound of the vehicle. "And the lords of the forest" means both the great trees and the forest thickets.
"It caused them to tremble" means it made them shake. In that context, by the shaking of the celestial palaces situated in the sky, the shaking of the heavens [is implied].
It should be understood. "Wearing a cloak over one shoulder" means one whose upper garment (*pāvāra*) and other robes are draped over one shoulder.
"Venerable" (*vuddha*) means increased in virtue. "Disciplined" (*vinītavant*) means endowed with disciplined conduct and behavior.
"Thus he spoke": having set the chariot in the sky and descended, he spoke thus. "A brahmin like a god" (*devabrāhmaṇa*) means a brahmin equal to a deity.
Having heard his words, he spoke this verse:
“Blind fortune appears to me, Mātali, O charioteer of the gods, for faith is impermanent.
For I consider hope to be deceptive, while modesty is established in the virtues of the Noble Ones.”
In this context, "blind" suggests to me those who, whether endowed with crafts and such skills or not, are like vessels that do not see.
"Impermanent," however, suggests to me faith, because it arises here and there after abandoning various objects, appearing in the mode of having existed and then ceased.
"Deemed deceptive," however, refers to hope, because those seeking wealth [rely] upon a ship...
Having plunged into the ocean, they return with their goods lost; therefore, she appears to me as "deceptive.
But regarding the noble quality: she is established in the noble quality known as the nature of moral shame (*hirī*) and moral dread (*ottappa*), which is utterly pure.
Now, praising her virtue, he said:
“Maidens protected by their family, those who are aged, and women who have husbands—
these restrain the high-flying desire and lust for men within their own minds through a sense of shame.
Just as those defeated at the head of the battle, falling and fleeing from swords and spears...”
"Having abandoned their lives, they turn back because of shame; those possessing shame receive [the teaching] once again.
Just as the shore restrains the waters driven by the force of the ocean, so indeed does shame restrain the evil person.
Make that shame, honored by noble ones throughout the entire world, known to Indra, O charioteer of the gods."
In this context, "the aged" refers to widows. "Those with husbands" refers to young women who have spouses. As for "of themselves":

having recognized that a powerful desire and passion for other men has arisen within themselves, they all restrain their own minds out of a sense of shame (*hirī*), thinking, "This is improper for us," and do not commit evil deeds.
"Between those falling and those fleeing" means among those who are falling and those who are running away. "Having abandoned... [the rest of the verse follows].
"Life": those who possess a sense of shame (*hiriman*) sacrifice their own lives and turn back because of that shame.
Having thus turned back, those possessing shame accept their husband once again; having rescued him from the hands of his enemies, they take him back.
"A restrainer of people from evil": it means a restrainer of people from evil; or rather, this very reading [is preferred]. "That": that shame (*hiri*). "Honored by the Noble Ones."

"It is honored by the Noble Ones, such as the Buddhas and others. It makes that known to Indra because, since it possesses such great qualities and is honored by the Noble Ones, therefore tell Indra that it is indeed called 'Supreme'.
Having heard this, Mātali spoke a verse:
“Who instilled this view in you, Kosiya? Was it Brahmā, Mahinda, or Pajāpati?
For among the gods, Hiri is esteemed as the best; she is the daughter of Mahinda and was born as the Great Queen.
In this context, “view” refers to the conviction: “Hiri is indeed a great virtue, honored by the Noble Ones. “Instilled” means he caused it to enter his heart.
"Regarded as the Best": from the moment you received the plaster in his presence, you obtained a golden throne in the presence of Indra;
being honored by all the deities, you became one who was highly esteemed as supreme.
Even as he was speaking thus, at that very moment, Kosiya’s nature subject to death arose. Then Mātali—
“Kosiya, your life-force has been relinquished; you have reached the state of being subject to death.
What use have you for the human world? Let us go to the world of the gods. Desiring to lead him there, he spoke this verse:
“Come now, depart for the triple heaven; mount this chariot that is dear to me.”
"And since you, O one of the same clan as Indra, are longing for this, you shall go this very day to the companionship of Indra.
In this context, "cherished" means dear and pleasing. "Of the same clan as Indra" means having the same lineage as Indra in a previous existence. "Longing" means he longs while desiring your arrival.
Thus, even as he was conversing with Kosiya, Kosiya passed away and became a spontaneously born son of the gods.
Having ascended the divine chariot, he stood upon it. Then Mātali led him into the presence of Sakka.
Upon seeing him, Sakka was filled with joy and gave his own daughter, the goddess Hiri, to him as his chief consort;
thus his sovereignty became immeasurable. Understanding this matter, [the Buddha said]: "The karma of extraordinary beings is purified in such a way."
The Teacher spoke this concluding verse:
“Thus are those who do no evil purified; moreover, the fruit of what is well-performed is never lost.
All those who beheld the food of ambrosia have indeed attained companionship with Indra.”
In this context, "those who have not performed evil deeds" refers to those beings who are purified in this way;
"whosoever saw that" refers to whatever beings at that time in the Himalayan region saw the food of ambrosia being given by Kosiya out of shame.
"All of them indeed" means that all of them, having rejoiced in that gift and gladdened their hearts, attained companionship with Indra.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now;
in the past as well, I tamed this one who was fond of non-giving and stubbornly stingy," and he concluded the Jātaka thus: "At that time, the goddess Hirī was Uppalavaṇṇā;
the donor Kosiya was the Bhikkhu; Pañcasikha was Anuruddha; and Mātali was Ānanda."
"Sūriya was Kassapa, Canda was Moggallāna, Nārada was Sāriputta, and Sakka was indeed myself.
This concludes the third commentary, the Sudhābhojana Jātaka.
[536] 4. The Commentary on the Kuṇāla Jātaka.
"It is declared thus": This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Kuṇāla Lake concerning five hundred bhikkhus who were oppressed by lack of joy.

Herein is the sequential account: It is said that the Sākiyas and the Koliyas had the river named Rohiṇī, which lay between the city of Kapilavatthu and the city of the Koliyas, dammed with a single embankment for the sake of their crops.
They had it done. Then, in the month of Jeṭṭhamūla, when the crops were withering, the laborers from both cities gathered together.
There, the inhabitants of the city of the Koliyans said: "If this water is drawn off from both sides, it will not suffice for either you or us;
however, our crops will be produced by this single supply of water alone."
“Give us this water. The inhabitants of Kapilavatthu replied:
“While you stand with your granaries filled, we will not be able to wander at your house doors with baskets, bags, and other such vessels in our hands, carrying red gold, blue gems, and black coins;
for even our own crops will be produced by this very same water. This—
“Give us water! “We will not give it,” they said. “Neither will we give it,” they replied.
Thus, having increased their quarrel, one rose up and struck another; he too struck another, and so on.
Striking one another in this way, they provoked the enmity of the royal families and set the conflict in motion.
The Koliyan laborers said, "Seize those Sākiyan youths living in Kapilavatthu and roar!
They lived with their own sisters like dogs, jackals, and the like;
what will their elephants, horses, and so forth, or their shields and weapons, do for us? The Sākiyan laborers replied, "Now you..."

"Seize the children of the lepers and roar! As for those who are helpless, destitute, and like animals dwelling in *kolarukka* trees—what will elephants, horses, and the like do for us, or what will shields and weapons avail them?
They went and spoke thus to the ministers appointed to that task, and the ministers spoke it to the royal families. Then...
The Sakyans, thinking, “We shall show the strength and power of those who live together with our sisters,” went forth equipped for battle.
The Koliyans also, thinking, “We shall show the strength and power of those who dwell in the Kola trees,” went forth equipped for battle.
However, other teachers say that among the slave-girls of the Sakyans and Koliyans, having gone to the river for water, [they took] their head-covers...
Having set it down on the ground, while they were seated engaged in pleasant conversation, one woman took a head-cloth thinking it was her own; because of that,
when a quarrel broke out over "my head-cloth" and "your head-cloth," eventually all the inhabitants of both cities—
including slaves and laborers, as well as servants, village headmen, ministers, and subordinate kings— went forth prepared for battle.
They say this. However, from among these methods, the former method alone is to be accepted, as it appears in many commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) and is the most appropriate.

Now, thinking that they would set out at evening time fully equipped for battle, the Blessed One—while residing in Sāvatthī—surveyed the world at dawn and saw that they had indeed set out thus equipped for battle; having seen them, he...
And while reflecting, "When I have gone there, will this quarrel be pacified or not? he considered:
"Having gone there for the sake of pacifying the quarrel, I shall relate three Jātakas; then the quarrel will be pacified.
Then, for the purpose of illustrating harmony, I shall relate two Jātakas and teach the Attadaṇḍa Sutta. Upon hearing the teaching, the inhabitants of both cities—"
"Two hundred and fifty young men will come from each family; I shall ordain them, and there will be a great gathering," he resolved.

Then, having attended to his physical needs early in the morning, he walked for alms in Sāvatthī, and upon returning from his almsround, he emerged from the Gandhakuṭī in the evening and, without informing anyone, departed.
Taking his own bowl and robe, he sat cross-legged in the air between the two armies.
To inspire a sense of spiritual urgency in them, he emitted rays of golden light to create darkness by day.
Then, as their minds were filled with agitation, he revealed himself by emitting the six-colored rays of a Buddha. The inhabitants of Kapilavatthu also—
Seeing the Blessed One, they thought, "Our preceptor, the Best of Kinsmen, has arrived; has he perhaps seen our state of quarreling?
Then they said, "Now that the Teacher has come, it is no longer possible for us to strike another's body with a weapon;
let the inhabitants of the Koliyan city kill or bind us! and so they cast away their weapons. The inhabitants of the Koliyan city did exactly the same.

Then the Blessed One, having descended, sat down upon a noble Buddha-seat prepared on a delightful stretch of sandy bank, shining with the incomparable splendor of a Buddha. Those kings also, having paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down.
Then the Teacher, though already knowing, asked them: "For what purpose have you come, Great Kings? "Not for the sake of seeing the river, venerable sir."
“Not for the sake of sport, but rather we have come here having set up a battle at this spot.
“On what account, Great King, is there this quarrel between you? “On account of water, Bhante. “What is water worth, Great King?
“It is of little value, Bhante. “What, Great King, is that which is called earth worth? “It is priceless.”
“Venerable sir,” [the king replied]. “What is the value of kshatriyas, Great King? “Kshatriyas, venerable sir, are priceless.
“Why, Great King, do you destroy priceless kshatriyas on account of water of little value?
For there is no gratification in quarreling; indeed, Great King, it was because of a quarrel that you were brought by a single tree deity into conflict with Kālasīha.”
"Having harbored enmity, he has indeed arrived here throughout this entire eon," he said, and then related the Phandana Jātaka.
Thereafter [he continued]: "O Great King, one must certainly not be one who relies on the word of others;
for by relying on the word of others, at the mere mention of a hare, the herds of four-footed creatures in the Himalayas—extending for three thousand yojanas—leapt into the great ocean."
“Therefore, one should not rely on the trust of others,” he said, and related the Daddara Jātaka.
Then he said, “Sometimes even a weak king sees a weakness in one who is very powerful, and sometimes even a very powerful one sees a weakness in a weak one;
for even the little bird Laṭukikā killed a mighty elephant,” and he related the Laṭukika Jātaka.
He related [the story]. Having thus related three Jātakas for the purpose of pacifying the quarrel, he related two Jātakas for the purpose of illustrating concord.
Saying, "For indeed, O Great King, no one is able to find a flaw in those who are in harmony," he related the Rukkhadhamma Jātaka.
Then, [saying], "O Great King, no one can find a rift in those who are in harmony..."
He was unable [to stop them]; but when they fell into mutual quarreling, a certain hunter brought about their destruction and departed with them.
Having said, "In quarreling there is no benefit," he related the Vaṭṭaka Jātaka.
Having thus related these five Jātakas, at the conclusion he related the Attadaṇḍa Sutta.
Then the kings, filled with faith, said: "If the Teacher had not come, we would have slaughtered one another and caused a river of blood to flow;
it is because of the Teacher that we have obtained our lives.

Furthermore, if the Teacher had remained in the household life, the sovereignty over the four great continents surrounded by two thousand islands would have come into our hands, along with more than a thousand [other realms]."
"If he had had sons, he would have wandered about surrounded by a retinue of kṣatriyas;
but having renounced that very prosperity and gone forth, he has attained perfect enlightenment. Let him now also wander about surrounded by a retinue of kṣatriyas!
Thinking thus, the inhabitants of both cities gave two hundred and fifty young princes each. The Blessed One ordained them.

He went to the Great Forest. From the following day onwards, surrounded by them, he wandered for alms from time to time in two cities—once in the city of Kapilavatthu and once in the city of the Koliyas. The inhabitants of both cities paid him great honor.
Out of deep reverence for him, dissatisfaction arose in those who had gone forth not out of their own inclination. It also arose in the case of his former wife.
Having said this and that to cause them dissatisfaction, they sent word to them. They became even more despondent.
The Blessed One, reflecting and perceiving their state of dissatisfaction, considered: "These monks are becoming despondent while living together with a Buddha such as I;
what kind of Dhamma discourse would be suitable for them? Thus he investigated.
He saw Kuṇāla’s teaching of the Dhamma. Then it occurred to him:

“I shall lead these bhikkhus to the Himālaya, and by recounting the story of Kuṇāla, I will reveal to them the faults of women; having brought about world-weariness, I will show them the path of stream-entry.
Having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, he entered Kapilavatthu for alms; after his meal, [he departed].
Having returned from his almsround, at the very time for his meal, he addressed those five hundred bhikkhus:
"Bhikkhus, have you ever seen the delightful region of the Himalayas? "No, venerable sir.
"Then will you go on a journey into the Himalayas? "Venerable sir, we lack supernormal powers; how shall we go? "If..."
“But if someone were to come and seize you, would you go? “Yes, Venerable Sir,” they replied.
The Teacher, having seized them all by his own psychic power, flew up into the air and went to the Himālaya. Standing in the sky, he showed them the delightful regions of the Himālaya:
the Golden Mountain, the Silver Mountain, the Jewel Mountain, the Vermilion Mountain, and the Antimony Mountain.
He showed him various mountains, including the Phalika Mountain together with its surrounding peaks; the five great rivers;
Kaṇṇamuṇḍaka, Rathakāra, Sīhapapāta, Chaddanta, Tiyaggaḷa, Anotatta, and Kuṇāladaha—the seven lakes.
And he showed him the Great Himalaya, five hundred yojanas in height and three thousand yojanas in extent, and this [region] of it...

By his own supernatural power, he showed a delightful region. There, he also showed from one side various four-footed creatures such as lions, tigers, and elephants that had made their dwellings there.

Furthermore, on the eastern slope of the Himālaya, he showed various kinds of groves and lovely places, diverse trees bearing flowers and fruits, flocks of birds of many sorts, and flowers growing both in water and on land.
He showed them a golden floor, and on the western side, a floor of vermilion.
From the moment those monks saw these delightful sights, their sensual desire for their former wives was abandoned.
Then the Teacher, taking those monks with him, descended from the sky and [landed] sixty yojanas to the west of the Himālayas.
Seated upon a surface of beryl seven yojanas in extent, beneath a *kappaṭṭhika* sal tree three yojanas high,
surrounded by those bhikkhus on a beryl floor three yojanas wide,
emitting six-colored rays of light like a blazing sun that stirs the depths of the ocean, he addressed those bhikkhus with a sweet voice: "Bhikkhus,..."
"Ask about whatever you have not previously seen here in this Himalaya," he said.
At that moment, two peacocks, each gripping a staff by its ends with their beaks, sat down in the middle with their master.
Eight peacocks stood in front, eight behind, eight to the left, eight to the right, eight below, and eight above.
Having created this shadow, they surrounded the variegated cuckoo and came through the air.
Then those bhikkhus, seeing that flock of birds, asked the Teacher: “Venerable sir, who are these birds?
“Bhikkhus, this is my ancient lineage, the tradition established by me; formerly, they served me in this very manner. At that time—
“At one time, that flock of birds was vast; three thousand five hundred female birds attended upon me.
Gradually declining, it has now become this small. “But how, venerable sir, did those female birds attend upon you in such a forest grove?
Then the Teacher, having established mindfulness by saying, “In that case, monks, listen,” said:
Bringing forth the past and showing it, he said:

"Thus it is declared, thus it is handed down: on that bearer of all medicinal herbs, strewn with many flower garlands, frequented by elephants, gavayas, lions, ruru deer, camarī deer, spotted deer, antelopes, wild oxen, bulls, tigers, leopards, dīpīs, bears, hyenas, noble kadali deer, wild cats, and sasakaṇṇika deer, and crowded with herds of great boars, elephant families, and female elephants."
In a region frequented by deer, antelope, sākha-deer, sarabha-deer, eṇī-deer, vāta-deer, pasada-deer, purisa-deer, kimpurisas, yakkhas, and rakkhasas;

a place adorned with hundreds of various minerals such as añjana, manasila, haritala, hiṅgulaka, gold, silver, and kanaka, and graced by many trees bearing clusters of blossoms and sprays of flowers that were not made of wine or spirits;
a place where flocks of birds—kuraras, cakoras, vāraṇas, peacocks, parabhutas, jīvañjīvakas, celāvakas, bhiṅkārakas, karavīkas, and intoxicated birds—were constantly crying out in harmony.
“In such a delightful grove, indeed, O sir, dwells a bird named Kuṇāla, exceedingly beautiful,
with exceedingly beautiful feathers and wings.
“Indeed, O sir, that bird Kuṇāla has three thousand five hundred female birds as his attendants.”
"Then indeed, sirs, two young female birds, having taken a stick in their beaks and caused the Kuṇāla bird to sit in the middle, flew up with him;
yet they could not prevent that fatigue from arising for the Kuṇāla bird on the long journey along the road.
"Five hundred young female birds flew up below and below [him], thinking: 'If this Kuṇāla bird should fall from his perch, we shall catch him with our wings.'"
“Five hundred female birds fly above one another, thinking, ‘May the heat not scorch this Kuṇāla bird.
Five hundred female birds fly on both sides, thinking, ‘May cold, or heat, or grass, or dust, or wind, or dew not touch this Kuṇāla bird.
Five hundred female birds fly ahead, thinking, ‘May cowherds or...’”
Cattle-herders, grass-gatherers, wood-gatherers, or forest-workers struck him with sticks,
clods of earth, hands, stones, staffs, weapons, or pebbles;
yet the bird Kuṇāla did not fly away to the bushes, creepers, trees, branches, pillars, or rocks.
"Or perhaps he will encounter powerful birds.
"Five hundred female birds fly up behind him, addressing him with soft, gentle, charming, and sweet words, thinking: 'May this bird Kuṇāla not become weary on his seat.
Five hundred female birds fly off in every direction, bringing various fruits from many different trees, thinking: 'May this bird Kuṇāla not be exhausted by hunger.'"
“Then indeed, sirs, those female birds led that Kuṇāla bird from grove to grove,
from park to park, from river-bank to river-bank, from mountain peak to mountain peak, from mango grove to mango grove,
from rose-apple grove to rose-apple grove, from breadfruit grove to breadfruit grove, and from coconut orchard to coconut orchard.”
They quickly mastered the art of moving with coconut shells for the sake of sport.
Then, indeed, Master, the bird Kuṇāla, surrounded by those young female birds throughout the day, reproached them thus:
"Perish, you outcasts! Be destroyed, you outcasts! You are thieves, harlots, unchaste, fickle-minded, and light-hearted!"
“...and its debts unrequited, it moves wherever it wishes like the wind.
Herein, this is the commentary on the meaning: “Monks, that forest grove is described thus and is renowned thus. How so?

‘Bearing all medicinal herbs upon its earth,’ and so forth. Therein, ‘bearing all medicinal herbs upon its earth’ means [the earth] which bears all medicinal herbs—roots, bark, leaves, flowers, and so on.”
The meaning is "endowed with earth" (*dharaṇī*); or alternatively, it is "bearing all medicinal herbs" (*sabbosadhayutto dharaṇidharo*).
For that region is thus declared to be "bearing the earth that holds all medicinal herbs," and it is so handed down; "in that forest thicket" is what is meant.

The same method applies to the construction of the remaining words as well. "Spread with many flower-garlands" means with both flowers produced for the sake of fruit and with garlands used for wearing.
And *vitate*. *Ruru* refers to golden-colored deer. *Uddāra* means female deer (*uddā*). *Biḷārā* means large cats (*mahābiḷārā*).
*Nelamaṇḍala* refers to a herd of young *bhiṅka* fawns. *Mahāvarāha* means great elephants;

the meaning is that it is inhabited by ten kinds of *nāga* families—such as those distinguished by their range of movement—and by herds of females (*kareṇusaṅgha*), including those with *nelamaṇḍala* herds.
The *issamiga* are black lions. The *vātamiga* are the great wind-deer. The *pasadamiga* are the spotted deer. The *purisālū* are female *yakkhinīs* with the faces of mares.

The *kimpurisā* are the various types of *kinnaras*, such as the celestial *kinnara*, the moon-*kinnara*, the tree-*kinnara*, the staff-bearing youth (*daṇḍamāṇavaka*), the *konti*-bird-eared one, the *pāvuraṇa*, and others.
It was spread over by multitudes of many trees bearing clusters of blossoms and holding flower-dust at their tips, appearing as if they were laughing.
It was overspread with many kinds of trees bearing buds, bearing flower-clusters, in full bloom, and even those that had reached the very peak of flowering.
The *vāraṇa* birds are birds with the characteristics of elephants. The *celāvakas* are also these same kinds of birds.
"Gold and kanaka" refers to two varieties of gold. With these and hundreds of other minerals, such as collyrium and so forth... [many].
In those places adorned and bound with strings of various colors (*vaṇṇadhātu-rāsī*), the address "O friend" (*bho*) is merely a form of polite speech.
"The mind" (*citta*) is variegated (*citro*) both at the tip of the mouth and in the lower part of the belly.
"Three thousand five hundred" means three thousand and five hundred; it refers to the path as a way of reckoning time (*addhāna-pariyāya-patha*).
On the path designated as a journey. *Ubbāhettha* means he obstructed. *Upapphusi* means having approached, he touched.
Regarding *pahāraṃ adaṃsu*, the meaning of the phrase *mā naṃ* should be understood according to its grammatical subject.
*Saṅgamesi* means he met. *Saṇhāhi* means with smooth [words]. *Sakhilāhi* means with affectionate [words]. *Mañjūhi* means with sweet [words]. *Madhurāhi* means...
"With sweet voices": "Attending upon" means serving by way of providing music.
"Fruit of various kinds from many trees" means fruit of diverse varieties from many trees. "As if from one grove to another" means they lead from one grove—such as a flower-grove—to another;
this is the meaning. The same principle applies to pleasure gardens and so forth. "By means of a movement like that of a coconut [fruit]" means...
Just as one coconut grove [leads] to another coconut grove. "They become exceedingly excited" means that, having led her there in this way, they quickly reach the place of pleasure.
"Heaped up throughout the day" means heaped up for the entire day. "He discourages her" means that, it is said, he [discourages] her in this manner during the day.
Having attended upon him, they descended to their dwelling tree, surrounded it, and sat upon its branches, hoping, "Perhaps we might receive some sweet words.
When they were dismissed by him, they remained there thinking, "We shall go to our own place of residence.
But King Kuṇāla, dismissing them, rebuked them with such words as, "Perish! and so forth.
In this context, "perish" means go away; "be destroyed" means perish on all sides. They are called *coriyo* (thieves) because they plunder the wealth, grain, and so forth in the home;

*dhuttiyo* (wanton women) because of their great deceitfulness; *asatiyo* (unmindful ones) because of their lack of mindfulness; *lahucittāyo* (light-minded ones) because of their lack of mental stability;
and they are those who betray friends and do not repay what has been done for them because of their self-destruction.
Having spoken thus, the Teacher removed the dissatisfaction of those bhikkhus with this discourse:
"In this way, bhikkhus, even as an animal I knew the ingratitude, the excessive pride, the lack of decorum, and the immorality of women;
therefore, instead of falling under their control, I brought them under my own control. Thus did the Teacher speak.

He remained silent. At that moment, two black cuckoos, having lifted their master with a stick, came to that place in groups of four each from the lower regions and other directions. When the monks saw them as well, they questioned the Teacher.
The Teacher said, "Monks, in the past, my friend was a Phussa cuckoo named Puṇṇamukha; this [is his companion]."
Having said, "The bamboo," when questioned by those monks in the same manner as before, he replied:
"Indeed, sirs, on the eastern side of that very Himavat, the king of mountains, there are streams flowing from the slopes of the mountain, exceedingly subtle and very refined.

In this context, they are "exceedingly subtle" (*susukhumasunipuṇa*) because of the extreme fineness and smoothness of their water; they are "mountain-born" (*girippabhava*) because the mountain is their source.

The meaning is: in which such rivers flow—rivers that are green with the currents mixed with the green grass flowing down from the Himālaya, and which approach the Kuṇāla lake by way of descending into it; these are the "very subtle and very skillful mountain-born green-flowing" rivers.
Now, describing the flowers at that Kuṇāla lake into which they flow, he said:

“In a place made delightful by the pure fragrance and beauty of water-lilies (*uppalā*), red lotuses (*padumā*), white esculent lilies (*kumudā*), blue lotuses (*nalinā*), hundred-petaled lotuses (*satapattā*), *sogandhika* lilies, and *mandālaka* lilies that have grown in full abundance. Therein, *uppala* refers to the blue lotus; *nalina* refers to the white lotus; *satapatta* refers to the lotus with its full hundred petals;
and *sampati* means [a place] where these have grown in full abundance, being newly born, and possessing a pure fragrance and beauty capable of binding the heart.
The meaning is: "endowed with a portion of a young shoot.
Now, describing the trees and so forth in that lake, he says:

"In a forest of *kuravaka*, *mucalinda*, *ketaka*, *vedisa*, *vañjula*, *puṇṇāga*, *bakula*, *tilaka*, *piyaka*, *hasana*, *sāla*, *saḷala*, *campaka*, *asoka*, *nāga* trees, *tirīṭi*, *bhujapatta*, *loddha*, and *candana* trees; and in a grove of *ogha* trees..."
In a dense thicket of black aloe, padmaka, piyaṅgu, devadāru, and kacoca;

where there were kakudha, kuṭaja, aṅkola, kaccikāra, kaṇikāra, kaṇṇikāra, kaṇavera, koraṇḍaka, koviḷāra, kiṃsuka, yodhika, vanamallikā, manaṅgaṇa, manavajja, bhaṇḍi, surucira, bhaginī, mālā, and malyadhara trees;
and which was overspread with jāti, sumana, madhugandhika, dhanu, takkāri, tālīsa, tagara, musīra, koṭṭha, and kacchu flowers.
In such a delightful grove— adorned with spreading creepers in full bloom with *atimuttaka* flowers,
resounding with the cries of swans, *pilava*, *kādamba*, and *kāraṇḍava* ducks, inhabited by hosts of *vidyādharas*, *siddhas*, ascetics, and forest-dwellers, and frequented by noble deities,
*yakṣas*, *rākṣasas*, *dānavas*, *gandharvas*, *kinnaras*, and *mahoragas*— there dwells, indeed, O sir, an exceedingly beautiful *phussa* cuckoo named Puṇṇamukha.
Sweet-voiced, with playful eyes and intoxicated gaze:
"Indeed, sir, that Phussakokila with the full face has two hundred and fifty female bird-maidens as his attendants.
Now, sir, two of those bird-maidens, having taken a stick in their beaks, [attacked] that Phussakokila..."
Having seated the Phussa cuckoo in the middle, they flew up, saying: "May no fatigue from the journey on the road overcome this full-faced Phussa cuckoo.
Fifty bird-maidens flew up below him, one after another, saying: "If this full-faced Phussa cuckoo bird should fall from his seat, we shall catch him with our wings."
“Fifty bird-maidens fly above one another, thinking: ‘May the heat not scorch this full-faced Phussakokila.
Fifty by fifty bird-maidens fly on both sides, thinking: ‘May cold, or heat, or grass, or dust, or wind, or dew not touch this full-faced Phussakokila.
Fifty bird-maidens fly ahead, thinking: ‘May cowherds [not harm] this full-faced Phussakokila.’”
Or cowherds, or grass-gatherers, or wood-gatherers, or forest-workers, might strike him with sticks,
or clods of earth, or with their hands, or with stones, or with clubs, or with staffs, or with swords, or with pebbles; yet this Puṇṇamukha, the cuckoo Phussa,
would not go against them by way of the paths, or the creepers, or the trees, or the branches, or the pillars.
“Or perhaps you will encounter rocks or powerful birds.
“Fifty female birds fly after him from behind, addressing him with soft, gentle, charming, and sweet words, thinking: ‘May this Puṇṇamukha, the Phussakokila bird, not become weary on his seat.
Fifty female birds fly off in various directions, bringing back fruits of many kinds from various trees, thinking: ‘May this Puṇṇamukha, the Phussakokila bird, not be exhausted by hunger.’”
“Then, sirs, those young female birds led that Puṇṇamukha peacock from grove to grove,
from park to park, from river-crossing to river-crossing, from mountain peak to mountain peak, from mango grove to mango grove,
from rose-apple grove to rose-apple grove, from breadfruit grove to breadfruit grove, and from coconut plantation to coconut plantation.”
They quickly master the art of moving like coconut shells for the sake of sport.
Then, indeed, Master, the peacock Phussamukha, surrounded by those bird-maidens throughout the day, praised them thus:
"Excellent, excellent, sisters! This is indeed worthy of you, sisters, daughters of noble family."
"Whomever you should serve as husband.
Then, sirs, the golden-breasted cuckoo Puṇṇamukha approached the bird Kuṇāla.
The young female birds who were Kuṇāla’s attendants saw that golden-breasted cuckoo Puṇṇamukha from afar.
Seeing him approaching, they went to where Puṇṇamukha the cuckoo was and, having approached him, said this to Puṇṇamukha the cuckoo:
“Friend Puṇṇamukha, this Kuṇāla bird is exceedingly harsh and exceedingly harsh-spoken; perhaps by coming to you, we might obtain pleasant speech once again.”
Saying, “Perhaps, sisters,” he approached where the bird Kuṇāla was;
having approached and exchanged greetings with the bird Kuṇāla, he sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, Puṇṇamukha the cuckoo said this to the bird Kuṇāla: “My dear friend Kuṇāla, why [are you thus] regarding women?”
"You are practicing wrongly toward well-born daughters of good family who are themselves practicing rightly;
indeed, my dear Kuṇāla, one must speak pleasantly even to women who speak unpleasantly, so what need is there to mention those who speak pleasantly?
When this was said, the bird Kuṇāla rebuked that Puṇṇamukha Phussakokila thus: "Begone, you!"
“‘O fellow outcaste, perish! O fellow outcaste, what wise man would have anything to do with you?
Thus insulted, Puṇṇamukha the Phussakokila bird turned back right then and there.
Then, sirs, after some time had passed, Puṇṇamukha the Phussakokila became harsh.”
An affliction arose, and severe, life-threatening pains from bloody dysentery set in.
Then, sirs, it occurred to the young female birds who were attendants upon Puṇṇamukha the cuckoo: “This Puṇṇamukha the cuckoo is afflicted;
perhaps he might recover from this illness. Thus they went to him alone, without a second.
Leaving [the palace], they approached where the bird Kuṇāla was. Kuṇāla the bird saw those female birds coming from afar;
seeing them, he said this to the female birds: “Where, you low-born women, is your husband?
“Friend Kuṇāla, Puṇṇamukha the cuckoo is ill; perhaps he might [recover] from that...”
"May my affliction be cured. When this was said, the bird Kuṇāla rebuked those young female birds thus:
"Perish, you wretches! Be destroyed, you wretches! You are thieves, harlots, ungrateful, fickle-minded, and those who do not repay what has been done for them;
like the wind, you go wherever you please! Having said this, he approached the peacock Phussamukha.
Having approached, he said this to the parrot named Puṇṇamukha:
"Ho, friend Puṇṇamukha! "Ho, friend Kuṇāla!
Then, indeed, the bird Kuṇāla [struck] that parrot named Puṇṇamukha with his wings and his beak.
Having accepted him and ordained him, she gave him various medicines to drink.
Then, sir, that affliction of Puṇṇamukha the cuckoo subsided.
In this context, *piyakā* refers to white flowers. *Hasanā*—the letter *ha* is used for euphonic junction (*sandhi*)—means simply *asanā*. *Tirīṭī* is a certain [plant].
*rukkhajāti*: species of trees. *Candana*: red fragrant sandalwood. *Oghavane*: in a forest possessed of a flood or a thicket of these [trees].
*Devadārukacocagahane*: in a dense thicket of *devadāru* trees and plantains.
*Kaccikārā*: a certain species of tree. *Kaṇikārā*: those with large flowers. *Kaṇṇikārā*: those with small flowers. *Kiṃsukā*: *vātaghātaka* trees (the "wind-killers").

*Yodhikā* means *yūthikā*. "Wearing garlands and wreaths of *vanamallikā*, *anaṅgaṇa*, *anavajja*, *bhaṇḍi*, and beautiful *bhaginī* flowers" means wearing garlands made from the flowers of *mallikā*, *anaṅgaṇa*, *anavajja*, *bhaṇḍi*, and beautiful *bhaginī* plants.
*Dhanutakkārī* means *dhanupāṭali*. *Tālīsā* refers to the *tālīsa-leaf* trees. *Kacchavitata* means...
"Spread with *jātisumana* flowers and so forth" means spread over the river-beds and mountain-clefts by these flowers.
"With blossoming creepers" refers to those places adorned and strewn with *atimuttaka* flowers and various kinds of creepers that have fully blossomed in their respective locations.
"Inhabited by hosts" means inhabited by the groups of these beings, such as the *vidyādharas* and others. "Full-faced" is due to the fullness of the face.
*Puṇṇamukho*: one with a full face. *Phussakokilo*: because it is touched by others [with joy], like the *phussa* cuckoo.
*Vilāsitanayo*: one with playful eyes (*vilāsitanetto*). *Mattakkho*: just as the eyes of those who are intoxicated are red, so too his eyes are red;
or, he has eyes of the proper measure. *Bhaginiyo*: a form of address using noble terminology. *Paricareyyātha*: you should attend upon [him] throughout the entire day.

Thus, having spoken pleasant words, he sends him away. Sometimes Kuṇāla goes with his retinue to see Puṇṇamukha, and sometimes Puṇṇamukha comes into Kuṇāla’s presence. That is why he said, "Then indeed, sir.
"Friend" means companion. "Having come" means having approached or relied upon. "May I receive" means [may I receive] pleasant speech from Kuṇāla.
"We might obtain [it]. 'Perhaps we might,'" means "perhaps you might obtain it; I shall speak. "Of those well-born" (*sujātānaṃ*) means "of those of equal birth.
"Flee" (*nassa*) means "run away. "Wretch" (*jamma*) means "vile. "Distinguished" (*viyatta*) means "who else indeed is there as distinguished as you?
"By winning his wife" (*jāyājina*) means "by having won his wife"; this is also the reading. Thus, who indeed is like you, who have been defeated by a woman?
Thinking, "Byatta is here," he rebuked him in order to prevent such speech from being uttered again. "From that very place" means:
having thought, "Kuṇāla is angry with me," he turned back right then and there;
having returned, he went back to his own residence together with his retinue.
"Appeva nāma" is a thought of doubt; having thought, "He might recover from this illness or he might not," they left him and departed. "Tumhaṃ" means "yours.
"Appeva nāma" [is used here] in the sense that he might recover from that illness or not, but by the time we arrive, he will have died.
For we know that he will die right now, and thus [we say it] regarding you.

She had come to become his attendant at the foot of the tree. "He approached her" means that these women, fearing they would become loathsome after their husband’s death, had abandoned him and departed;

meanwhile, the Great Being, possessing the strength of a nāga, having thought, "I shall go and gather various flowers, fruits, and medicinal herbs for my companion and restore him to health," sprang up into the air.
He approached where he was. *Haṃ* is a particle used when asking, "Are you alive, friend?
The other, saying to him, "I am alive," replied, "Yes, friend. *Pāyāpesī* means he caused [him] to drink. *Paṭippassambhī* means it subsided.
Those bird-maidens also arrived once he had recovered from his illness. And Kuṇāla, having filled his mouth with various fruits for several days...
After having him fed until he had regained his strength, the Great Being said to him, "My good man, you are now healthy;
dwell with your own attendants, and I too shall go to my own dwelling place.
Then he replied to him, "My good man, these women are fleeing, abandoning me while I am still grievously ill; I have no need for these harlots. Having heard that, the Great Being...
“Very well then, friend, I shall explain to you the wicked nature of women.
Having taken Puṇṇamukha by the hand, he led him to a slab of emerald on the slope of the Himālaya and sat down upon an emerald seat at the foot of a seven-yojana *sāla* tree.
On one side, Puṇṇamukha sat together with his retinue. A divine proclamation spread throughout the entire Himālaya: “Today, Kuṇāla, the king of birds...”
“Sitting upon a throne of ruby in the Himavat mountains, he will teach the Dhamma with the grace of a Buddha;
listen to that! Having heard this through the successive transmission of sound, the gods of the six sense-sphere heavens for the most part assembled there.

Many nāgas, supaṇṇas, kinnaras, vidyādharas, and other deities also proclaimed this matter. At that time, a king of vultures named Ānanda, accompanied by a retinue of ten thousand vultures, [was present].
He was residing on Mount Gijjhakūṭa. Hearing that clamor as well, he too came with his retinue, thinking, "I shall listen to the Dhamma," and sat down to one side.

Furthermore, the ascetic Nārada, a possessor of the five super-knowledges, while dwelling in a region of the Himālayas surrounded by ten thousand ascetics, heard that divine proclamation and thought, "It seems my friend Kuṇāla will speak of the faults of women."
"A great assembly will take place; it is fitting for me also to hear that teaching.

Having spoken thus, he went there by means of his psychic power (*iddhi*) together with ten thousand ascetics and sat down to one side. The great assembly was like a gathering for the preaching of the Buddhas.
Then, by means of the knowledge of recollecting past births (*jātissarañāṇa*), the Great Being [recollected] the cause seen in a previous existence connected with the fault of women.
Having made Puṇṇamukha a bodily witness, he spoke. To clarify that matter, the Teacher said:
"Then indeed, friends, the bird Kuṇāla said this to Puṇṇamukha the Phussakokila, who had recently recovered from illness and was not long risen from his sickness:
‘I have seen, friend Puṇṇamukha, Kaṇhā Dvepitikā, while she was fixing her heart upon a sixth man—namely, on Kabandha the cripple. And there is a verse regarding this:”
“Then Ajuna, Nakula, Bhimasena, Yudhitthila, and King Sahadeva—having disregarded these five husbands, that woman committed a wicked deed with a hunchbacked dwarf.
“I have seen her, my friend Puṇṇamukha. A female ascetic named Saccatapāpī, living in the midst of a charnel ground and skipping every fourth meal, committed a wicked deed with a drunken rogue.”
“Friend Puṇṇamukha, I have seen the queen named Kākavatī, who lived in the midst of the ocean as the wife of Venateyya, commit a wicked deed with Naṭakuvera.
Friend Puṇṇamukha, I have seen the queen named Kuruṅgī, whose hair was beautiful, desiring Eḷika-kumāra, commit a wicked deed with Chaḷaṅga-kumāra Dhanantevāsī.
Thus indeed have I known this regarding the mother of Brahmadatta.”
Having abandoned the King of Kosala, he committed evil with Pañcālacaṇḍa.
"They and others have committed evil; therefore, I shall neither trust nor praise women.
Just as the earth, though equally colored throughout the world, is the supporter of all beings, yet each rests upon the other."
All women are alike: unshakable and unswerving; a man should not place his trust in them.

Just as a lion, a beast of prey that feeds on blood and flesh, possessing five weapons and difficult to restrain, devours its victims by force and delights in harming others—so too should a man not place his trust in women.
“Indeed, my dear Puṇṇamukha, courtesans are not women to be approached; they are not called ‘prostitutes,’ but rather ‘slayers.

For these courtesans are like thieves in their appearance, like wine-sellers smeared with intoxicants, like merchants with flattering words, like swords turned on edge, like snakes with forked tongues, like hidden pits, like bottomless abysses difficult to fill, and like ogresses difficult to satisfy.”
They are like Yama, carrying off one side; like peacocks, devouring everything; like rivers, flowing everywhere;
like the wind, moving wherever they wish; like Mount Meru, making no distinction; and like the poison-tree, always bearing fruit. Furthermore, there is this verse on the subject:
“Like a thief, like a rogue, like a merchant who boasts;”
She turns about like the peak of Mount Issa, like a double-tongued serpent.
She is hidden like a pit, as difficult to fill as the underworld (pātāla);
she is as hard to satisfy as a rākṣasī, and like Yama, she carries away all at once.
“Like a fire, a river, or the wind, like the Nerañjarā joined with the ocean,
like a tree that constantly bears fruit— women who bring an end to wealth destroy the riches in the home.”
In this context, "one who has recovered from illness" means one who was first ill and subsequently recovered. Regarding the phrase "I saw her":

it is said that in the past, Brahmadatta, the King of Kāsi, having seized the kingdom of Kosala due to his superior strength and forces, killed the King of Kosala and took his chief queen—who was pregnant—to Bārāṇasī, where he made her his own chief queen.
In the course of time, she gave birth to a daughter. Now, it was the king’s custom that he had neither a daughter nor a son;
therefore, being delighted, he said to her, "My dear lady, choose a boon. She accepted it and set it aside. They gave the name "Kaṇhā" to that young girl.
Then, when she had reached maturity, her mother said to her: "Child, your father has granted you a boon."
“[The king] gave it; I took it and set it aside. Choose whatever boon you desire.
She said, “Mother, there is nothing else for me that does not already exist; please choose a boon yourself for my sake to receive.

Thus, due to her abundance of defilements, she broke through her sense of shame and modesty and spoke to her mother. The mother reported this to the king. The king said, “Let her take a husband according to her own wish.”
Having spoken thus, she herself caused the proclamation of the choice to be made. Many men, adorned with all manner of ornaments, assembled in the royal courtyard.
Kaṇhā, taking a basket of flowers and standing at the northern lion-window, looked out but did not find even one who pleased her.
At that time, there were these five sons of King Paṇḍu: Ajjuna, Nakula, Bhīmasena, Yudhiṭṭhila, and Sahadeva.
Having mastered their craft in the presence of a world-renowned teacher in Takkasilā, they traveled about, thinking, "We shall learn the local customs.
Upon reaching Bārāṇasī, they heard a great clamor within the city; having inquired and understood the matter, they thought, "We too shall go there.
Possessing forms equal to golden images, they went there and stood in a row. When Kaṇhā saw them, she...
With her heart bound to all five of them, she threw flower-wreaths and head-ornaments upon the heads of all five and said, "Mother, I choose these five men.

She reported this to the king. Since the boon had been granted, the king did not say, "She will not obtain them," but being displeased, he asked, "What is their caste? Whose sons are they? Upon learning that they were the sons of King Paṇḍu...
Having recognized them and paid them honor, she gave her that foot-maiden as a wife.
She took those five princes into her favor through the power of the defilements while they resided in a seven-storied palace. However, she had a personal attendant who was a hunchbacked cripple.
Having taken the five princes into her favor through the power of the defilements, when they had gone outside, she [sought] an opportunity.
Having obtained him, she did not burn with passion; instead, she committed evil with Khujja and spoke with him, saying:
"There is no one as dear to me as you; having had the princes killed, I shall smear your feet with their throat-blood.
When she later became intimate with the eldest brother, she said: "With these four..."

“You alone are dearer to me; even my own life has been surrendered for your sake, and upon the passing of my father, I shall cause the kingdom to be given to you alone,” he said. Even when she was mingled with the others, the same principle applied.
Thinking, “He loves us, and it is because of him that this sovereignty has arisen for us,” they were exceedingly pleased with her.
One day she became ill. Then her attendants gathered around her; one sat massaging her head, while the others each massaged one hand and one foot.
But the hunchback sat at the feet of her eldest brother, Prince Ajjuṇa. To him, who was massaging her head, she said:
"There is no one dearer to me than you; as long as I live, I am yours..."
"I shall live; after my father's passing, I will cause you to receive the kingdom," she said, and while signaling with her head, she took hold of him.
She signaled in the same way with her hands and feet to the others as well. But to the hunchback, she signaled with her tongue, saying, "You alone are dear to me;
for your sake I shall live. Because they had all previously spoken thus, [the king understood].
By that sign they understood the matter. Among them, the rest understood it solely by the sign given to themselves.
But Prince Ajjuṇa, seeing the movements of her hands, feet, and tongue, thought:
“Just as it was with me, so this sign must have been given to the others as well; moreover, she must have had an intimate acquaintance with the hunchback.”
The brothers took her outside and asked, "Did you see the five husbands showing me the movement of their heads?
"Yes, we saw them. "Do you know the reason for this? "We do not know. "This indeed is the reason; but do you know the reason for the signal given by your own hands and feet? "Yes, we know it."
“Did he give it to us for that very reason? Do you know the reason for the gift of recognition through the hunchback’s gesture of the tongue?

“We do not know,” they replied. Then, having explained it to them and saying, “She committed this evil deed together with him as well,” he summoned the hunchback when they did not believe him and questioned him. He related the entire occurrence.
Having heard her words, they became free from desire and passion for her and thought: "Alas! Women are indeed wicked and immoral.
Having abandoned one such as I—endowed with noble birth and possessed of great fortune—she performs evil deeds together with such a loathsome and repulsive hunchback.
What wise person indeed would associate with women so shameless and of such evil character?"
Having censured women in many ways, saying, "She will sport with him," the five men thought, "Enough for us of the household life.
They entered the Himālayas, went forth into homelessness, performed the preliminary exercises for the *kasiṇas*, and at the end of their lives, they departed according to their karma.
As for Kuṇāla, the king of birds, he was Prince Ajjuṇa at that time. Therefore, [he related] the reason he had seen himself...
Showing this, he said, "I have seen," and so forth.
Therein, "two wives" is stated by way of the King of Kosala and the King of Kāsi. "Of those with five husbands":
*pañcapatikā* (the word *ya* is merely an expletive). "Being bound": *paṭibandhantiyā*. "To the headless trunk": *kabandhe*. To him...
It is said that his neck was bent down and pressed against his chest; therefore, he appeared as if his head were severed.
"Beyond the five wise men" means having surpassed these five. "By a hunchbacked dwarf" means by one who was both hunchbacked and short.
Having said this, and wishing to show other things previously seen, he spoke again, beginning with "seen. In that regard, concerning the second case:
This is the analysis: It is said that in the past, near Bārāṇasī, a white-clad female ascetic named Saccatapāpī built a leaf-hut in a charnel ground and lived there.
She would eat only after four meal-times had passed, and she became as famous throughout the entire city as the moon or the sun.
Even when the residents of Bārāṇasī stumbled or tripped over her, they would cry out, "Homage!"...

"O you who are most truthful! they said. Then, on the first day of a festival season, some goldsmiths gathered in a group, erected a pavilion in a certain place, brought fish, meat, liquor, perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, and began drinking liquor.
At that time, one goldsmith, while throwing away the dregs of the liquor, said: "Homage to the most truthful one!"—whereupon a certain wise man...
When he was told, “O you blind fool, you pay homage to a fickle-minded woman! Oh, what a fool you are! he replied, “Friend, do not speak thus;
do not perform an action that leads to rebirth in hell. Then he said to him, “You evil-minded one, be silent!
Stake a thousand pieces of gold! On the seventh day from now, I shall give you a truly beautiful woman, adorned and ready.”
"Seated right here, I will have them bring me fermented grain-liquor and drink it; there is no such thing as a woman who is truly virtuous," he said.
[The other] replied, "You will not succeed," and made a wager of a thousand pieces with him.
He informed other goldsmiths of this matter, and on the following day at dawn, having entered the charnel ground in the guise of an ascetic, he...
He stood not far from her dwelling place, paying homage to the sun.
As she was going for alms, she saw him and thought: "This must be a powerful ascetic;
I live on the edge of the charnel ground, whereas he lives in the very center of it. There must be some noble quality within him; I shall pay him homage."
Thinking, "No," she approached and paid her respects. He neither looked at her nor spoke to her. On the second day as well, he acted in the same manner.
But on the third day, at the time of her salutation, while still with his face turned downward, he said, "Go.
On the fourth day, he offered a greeting, saying, "I hope you are not weary from begging for alms. Delighted, thinking, "I have received a greeting," she—
She departed. On the fifth day, having received even greater hospitality, she sat for a short while and then left.
But on the sixth day, when she had come, paid her respects, and was seated, [the Elder] said: "Sister, why is there today such a great sound of singing and instrumental music in Bārāṇasī?
She replied: "Venerable sir, you do not know; a festival has been proclaimed in the city, and there—"

When it was said, “This is the sound of those playing,” he acted as if he did not know where the sound came from and asked, “Sister, how many meals have you missed? “Four, noble sir; but how many have you missed?
“Seven, sister. This he spoke falsely. For he ate every day at night. He [then asked her], “How many...”
Having asked her, "Sister, how many years have you been ordained? and being told by her, "Twelve years," he asked, "How many years have you had?
She replied, "This is my sixth year. Then, having asked her, "But sister, do you possess the attainment of the peaceful Dhamma?
and being told, "I do not, Noble Sir, but you do," he said, "In my case as well..."
Having said, "There is none," he replied: "Sister, we obtain neither the pleasure of sensual desires nor the pleasure of renunciation;
why should the hell of heat belong to us alone? We shall perform service for the common people; I will become a householder.
I have wealth belonging to my mother, and I cannot endure suffering. She [then] spoke his words.
Having heard this, her own mind becoming restless and her heart bound to him, she said: "Noble sir, I too am weary of the world;
if you will not abandon me, I too shall become a householder's wife. Then he said to her, "Come, I will not abandon you;
you shall be my wife," and having brought her into the city and lived with her, [he went to] a tavern pavilion.
Having gone there, she had him take some yeast for liquor and he drank the liquor. The other [her husband] was defeated for a thousand [coins].
Because of that, she increased in the number of sons and daughters. At that time, Kuṇāla was a drunkard; therefore, revealing what he himself had seen, he said, "I saw," and so forth.

In the third case, the account of the past is explained in detail in the commentary on the Kākavativijātaka in the Catukkanipāta. At that time, Kuṇāla was a Garuḍa; therefore, revealing what he had seen himself, he said, "I saw it," and so forth.

In the fourth case, in the past, after Brahmadatta had slain the King of Kosala and seized his kingdom, he took the king's chief queen—who was pregnant—and returned to Bārāṇasī; even though he knew she was pregnant...
She made her the chief queen. When her pregnancy had reached maturity, she gave birth to a son who resembled a golden image.
Thinking, "Even when he has grown up, the King of Bārāṇasī will have him killed, saying, 'This is the son of my enemy; what is the use of him?
Let not my son die at the hands of another,'" she said to a nurse: "Mother, take this boy and [wrap him] in a rag."
"Having spread out [a cloth] and laid him down in the raw charnel ground, come back. The nurse did so, and having bathed, she returned.
The King of Kosala, having died, was reborn as a protective deity for his son.
Through his power, while a certain shepherd was grazing sheep in that place, one ewe saw the boy, and feeling affection, [she began to give] milk.
After making her drink a little and walking about, he went back again and made her drink two, three, or four times.
Seeing her actions, Eḷakapālaka went to that place; seeing the boy there, he felt maternal affection for him, took him away, and gave him to his own wife.
Since she was childless, she had no breast milk; therefore, he gave her only goat’s milk.
He gave it to her to drink. From that time on, however, two or three goats died every day.
The goat-herd thought, "If she is looked after in this way, all the goats will die; what use is she to us?
So he laid her down in a clay vessel, covered it with another, smeared the opening of the mouth with powdered rice so that it was not visible, and released her into the river.

As it was being carried along, a certain Caṇḍāla—a repairer of old buildings—along with his wife, who was childless, saw it at a lower ford near the royal palace while they were washing a monkey-fur blanket.
Running quickly, they brought it out and placed it on the bank. Opening it up and looking inside, [the husband] asked, "What is here?
and saw the boy. His wife also had no children, and a motherly affection for him arose within her.
Then, having led him home, she looked after him. From the time he was seven or eight years old, his parents would take him with them whenever they went to the royal court.
But from the time he was sixteen years old, he went there mostly on his own and performed repairs on the aging buildings.
Now, the king had a chief queen named Kuruṅgadevī, who had a daughter of exquisite beauty. From the moment she saw him—
From that time on, their minds became bound to him; finding no delight elsewhere, they would come only to the place where he performed his work.
Through their frequent meetings, their hearts became mutually attached, and misconduct arose even within the royal palace in a concealed spot.
As time passed, the female attendants, having discovered this, informed the king.
The king, becoming angry, summoned his ministers and said, "This son of a candāla has done such-and-such;
find out what should be done with him. The ministers replied, "This man has committed a great offense; it is fitting that after subjecting him to various forms of torture, he should be put to death.
At that moment, the prince’s father [was protected] by the guardian deities of that very prince.
She resolved upon her mother’s body. By the power of that deity, she approached the king and said:
“Great King, this boy is not a caṇḍāla; this boy was conceived in my womb and is the son of the King of Kosala.
I spoke a falsehood to you, saying, ‘My son is dead. I [said] of him, ‘He is the son of your enemy.’”
"After giving it to my nurse, I had it discarded in the raw charnel ground; then a certain shepherd took care of it.
When his own ewes died, he set it adrift in the river. While it was being carried away, a Caṇḍāla who repairs old buildings in your house saw it and raised it.
