If you do not believe me, summon all of them and question them."
The king summoned everyone, beginning with the nurse, and having questioned them, he heard the account exactly as it had occurred.
Delighted, thinking, "This prince is of noble birth," he bathed him, adorned him, and gave him his own daughter.
Because he had killed the female goats, they gave him the name Eḷikakumāra. Then the king, providing him with an army and vehicles, said: "Go!"
"Take over the kingdom belonging to your own father," he urged him. He too, taking Kurungadevī with him, went and established himself in the kingship.
Then the King of Bārāṇasī, thinking, "This man has not yet been trained in the arts," sent a teacher named Chaḷaṅgakumāra for the purpose of training him in the arts.
[The new king] gave him the position of general, saying, "He is my teacher."
In the course of time, Queen Kuruṅgī committed misconduct with him. The general also had an attendant named Dhanantevāsī;
he sent garments, ornaments, and other gifts for Queen Kuruṅgī through that man’s hand. She also committed evil with him.
Kuṇāla, bringing forth this matter to demonstrate it, said, “I have seen it,” and so forth.
In this context, "Lomasuddarī" means one whose belly is adorned with a line of body hair. Regarding "the student Dhana of General Chaḷaṅga Kumāra":
even while longing for the young son of Eḷika, she committed evil together with General Chaḷaṅga Kumāra and with his attendant, Dhana-antevāsī.
Thus, women who are immodest, immoral, and of evil character—I do not praise them; therefore, I said so.
The Mahāsatta brought this from the past and showed it. For he was, at that time, Prince Chaḷaṅga; therefore, he related what he himself had seen.
In the fifth instance as well, in the past, the King of Kosala seized the kingdom of Bārāṇasī and [took] the chief queen of the King of Bārāṇasī...
Having made even the pregnant woman his chief queen, he returned to his own city. Later, she gave birth to a son.
Because the king was childless, he raised the boy with the same affection as for his own son and had him trained in all the arts.
When the boy reached maturity, the king sent him forth, saying, "Take the kingdom that belongs to your father. He went there and ruled the kingdom. Then his mother—
Saying, "We wish to see our son," she took leave of the King of Kosala and, traveling with a large retinue toward Bārāṇasī, took up residence in a certain market town between the two kingdoms.
There lived a handsome young brahmin named Pañcālacaṇḍa; he presented her with a gift, and upon seeing it, her heart became bound to him.

Having committed an evil deed with him, she spent a few days right there; then, having gone to Bārāṇasī and seen her son, she quickly returned and took up residence once more in that very same market town.
After spending a few days engaging in misconduct with him, she went to the city of Kosala. From that time on, before long, for various reasons...
Having said, "I am going to my son's side," and having taken leave of the king, she went and came back,
and for about half a month she engaged in unchaste conduct with him in that town. "O Puṇṇamukha, women are indeed unvirtuous and liars"—
showing this past event as well, the Great Being said, "For it was thus," and so forth.

In this context, "the mother of Brahmadatta" refers to the mother of Prince Brahmadatta while he was ruling the kingdom of Bārāṇasī. At that time, it is said, Kuṇāla was Pañcālacaṇḍa; therefore, showing his own kinsman's reason for doing so, he spoke thus.

"And these," [he said], "my dear Puṇṇamukha, these five women alone have committed evil deeds—do not think otherwise—but rather, both these and many others are doers of evil deeds. Standing on this point, regarding those who are unchaste in the world...
The bases should be explained. Regarding "the earth":

just as the earth, known as the *jagatī*, being of the same color and free from aversion, is of one color toward all and thus serves as a foundation for both the high and the low, so too women, through the power of the defilements, serve as a foundation for all—both the high and the low.
For women, when they find an opportunity, will indeed commit evil with someone.
"All-enduring" means that just as she endures everything—neither quivering, nor becoming angry, nor wavering—so too do women endure all men by way of worldly pleasure.
If some man becomes established in their hearts, [she endures him] for the sake of protecting him.
They do not quiver, they do not shake, and they do not make a clamor.
And just as she does not become agitated or shaken, so too women are not agitated or shaken by sexual intercourse; it is impossible to fill her with it.
"Wild beast" (*vāḷamiga*) means a vicious animal. "Five-weaponed" (*pañcāvudha*) refers to this in terms of the mouth and the four feet.
It is said: "Suruddho" means well-seized or very cruel.
"Tathitthīyo" means that just as for a lion there are five weapons—namely, his mouth and his four paws—so too for women there are five weapons: visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles.
Just as he, when seizing his prey, seizes it with those five, so too do they.
When seizing its prey, it strikes with its weapons—form and so forth—and then takes hold.
Just as that [animal] is harsh and devours by force, so too these [passions] are harsh and devour by force.
Likewise, even toward a man of firm virtue, they use their own power to act with violence and bring about the destruction of his virtue. Just as that [animal] delights in harming others...
In this way, these women also delight in harming others by means of their defilements. "Tāyo" means: a man should not place his trust in those who have thus acquired such unwholesome qualities.
"Gamaniyo" refers to courtesans. This is what is meant: O Puṇṇamukha, those names given to women such as "prostitutes" (*vesiyā*) and so forth are not their natural names.
For they are not truly called "prostitutes," nor are they called "those to be approached" (*gamaniya*), nor are they "harlots" (*bandhakī*).
By name they are so called, but by way of their inherent nature, these are indeed "murderesses" (*vadhikāyo*), those women who are prostitutes and are called "those to be gone to.
"Murderesses" means those who kill their husbands. This meaning should be illustrated by the *Mahāhaṃsa-jātaka*. For it is said:
"These are like illusions and mirages, sorrows, diseases, and calamities;..."
"The harsh ones and those who bind, the snares of Death dwelling in the cave—whatever man places his trust in them, he is the lowest among men. "Veṇikatā" means those who have made a braid.
For just as a thief standing in the forest with his hair braided into a topknot plunders wealth, [so too do these].
In this way, having brought them under the power of the defilements, they plunder their wealth. "Like liquor mixed with poison" means like spirituous liquor (surā) mixed with a toxic substance.

Just as that [poisoned liquor] displays its transformation, so too these women, being infatuated with other men, not knowing what ought or ought not to be done, display a transformation by doing one thing when another was required to be done. "Flattery of speech" means, for example, as a merchant...
Just as one speaks only of the beauty of one's own goods, so too these [women], concealing their own faults, proclaim only their virtues.
"Tossing about" means that, like the horn of a deer standing turned backward, they are indeed constantly shifting due to their fickle-mindedness.
"Like a serpent" means that, because of their habitual lying, they are called "double-tongued. "Like a pit" means...
Just as a cesspool covered with grass and leaves, so too they wander about, concealed by garments and ornaments.
And just as a pit hidden by refuse, when stepped upon, causes pain to the foot, even so these [women], when approached with trust.
"Like the abyss" means that just as the abyss in the great ocean is difficult to fill, so too are these [women] with sexual intercourse.
She is difficult to satisfy by three things: by giving birth, by ornaments, and by [other means]. For this very reason it was said: “Bhikkhus, womenfolk are insatiable in three things,” and so forth.

“Like a female demon (rakkhasī)” means: just as a so-called female demon, being greedy for flesh, cannot be satisfied with wealth—rejecting even great wealth and desiring only flesh—so too these women, being greedy for sexual intercourse, [cannot be satisfied] even with much wealth.

They are not satisfied; disregarding wealth, they long only for sexual union. "Like Yama" means that just as Yama takes everything away and leaves nothing behind, so too these [passions] do not spare anyone among those endowed with noble birth and the like;

having brought about the destruction of virtue and other qualities through the power of the defilements, they lead them to hell in the second section on consciousness. "Like a flame" means that just as a flame... even if it be pure...
Just as it eats everything, even the impure, so too do these women consort with everyone, whether low or high.
The same principle applies to the simile of the river. "Yenakāmañcara" is an instrumental case used in the sense of a locative; wherever their desire lies, there they run.
*Neru* is a certain golden mountain in the Himālayas; even the crows that approach it become golden in color.
Just as he does, so too these [trees] treat one who has approached them as indistinguishable from themselves, making him exactly like them.
The *visarukkha* is a *kiṃpakkha* tree similar to a mango tree; it bears fruit constantly and is endowed with excellent color and other qualities.
Because of this, people eat it without fear and die. In the same way, those [trees] also bear fruit constantly by way of visible forms and so forth.
They appear delightful. Yet, when indulged in, they give rise to negligence and cause one to fall into the states of misery. Therefore it is said:
“He who indulges in sensual pleasures without knowing their future harm, Is struck down at their ripening, like one who has eaten the *kiṃpākaphala* fruit.”
Or, just as a poisonous tree is always laden with fruit and is perpetually harmful, so too are these [sense objects] by way of destroying virtue and the rest.
Just as the root, bark, leaf, flower, and fruit of a poisonous tree are all poison, and thus it is "always laden with fruit," even so their visible form...
down to... tangible object are all poison; thus they are "always laden with fruit" like a poisonous tree.
He spoke thus in order to make that meaning clear through the composition of a verse beginning with "Panuttaretthā.

Therein, "women who cause the destruction of treasures" refers to women who create obstacles for the treasures accumulated with great hardship by their husbands; having given these to others, they engage in unchaste conduct.
Following this, he spoke in order to demonstrate the elegance of his own discourse on the Dhamma in various ways:
“Friend Puṇṇamukha, there are these four things that, when a need arises, become harmful if they are kept in another’s family:
a bull, a milch cow, a vehicle, and a wife. A wise man should not let these four treasures stay away from his home.
And on this matter, there is also this verse:”
“One should not let a bull, a cow, a vehicle, or a wife remain in the family of relatives.
Those who do not use them break the chariot; by over-driving, they kill the draft-ox;
by milking, they kill the calf; so too, a wife corrupts herself when she stays in the family of her relatives.”
“Friend Puṇṇamukha, there are these six things that become useless when a need arises:

a bow without string, a wife from a family of kinsmen, a boat without a rudder, a vehicle with a broken axle, a friend who is far away, and an evil companion. These six things become useless when a need arises.”
“Indeed, my dear Puṇṇamukha, there are eight grounds on which a woman despises her husband:
poverty, illness, old age, drunkenness, foolishness, negligence, compliance in all matters, and the failure to provide all wealth.
Indeed, my dear Puṇṇamukha, it is on these eight grounds that a woman despises her husband. And yet, there is also [the opposite]…”
In this regard, the following statement is given:
“The poor man, the sick man, the aged man, the habitual drunkard, The heedless man,
and the foolish novice— these are excluded from all duties.”
"By granting all her desires, she treats her husband with contempt.
"Indeed, friend Puṇṇamukha, a woman brings about enmity through nine circumstances:
she is habituated to going to pleasure groves, she is habituated to going to parks, she is habituated to going to river fords, and she is habituated to going to the families of her relatives..."
She is one who goes to the families of others; she is one whose habit is to adorn herself with the finery of a slave-girl;
she is a drinker of intoxicants; she is one whose habit is to look about [lustfully]; she is one who stands at the doorway.
Indeed, my friend Puṇṇamukha, by these nine grounds does a woman bring about enmity. And regarding this, there is also this verse:
“The woman who is devoted to pleasure groves, gardens, rivers, kinsmen, and other families;
who is intent on mirrors, fine clothes, and ornaments; and who drinks intoxicants;
who has the habit of gazing [lustfully] and who stands at the threshold of the door—”
“Women bring about ill-will through nine causes.
“But, friend Puṇṇamukha, there are indeed forty-four ways in which a woman transgresses against a man:
she yawns, she bends her body, she coos, she blushes, she scratches nail against nail, she treads foot against foot, she [strikes] with a stick...”
He scratches the ground; he leaps over a boy or causes him to leap; he plays or causes him to play; he kisses or causes him to kiss;
he eats or causes him to eat; he gives or asks for; he imitates another’s actions;
he speaks loudly, speaks softly, speaks indistinctly, or speaks clearly; [he engages] in dancing, singing, instrumental music, weeping, dalliance, or adornment.
She laughs, gazes [at him], wiggles her hips, moves her private ornaments, exposes her thigh, covers her thigh,
displays her breast, displays her waistband, displays her navel, rolls her eyes,
raises her eyebrows, scratches her lip, lolls out her tongue, loosens her garment, fastens her garment, [and touches] her head.
She loosens [her hair] and ties it on her head. Indeed, my dear Puṇṇamukha, it is by these forty grounds that a woman transgresses against a man.
"Indeed, my dear Puṇṇamukha, a woman should be known as corrupted by twenty-five grounds:
she praises her husband’s absence; she does not remember him when he has departed; she does not rejoice when he has returned; she speaks ill of him..."
She speaks [to him], yet she does not speak his praise; she acts for his harm, yet she does not act for his benefit;
she does what ought not to be done for him, yet she does not do what ought to be done for him. She lies down embracing him, she lies down with her back turned to him;
she becomes restless and fidgety; she breathes deeply and experiences pain; she voids excrement and urine.
She goes frequently [to meet others], acts contrarily, and upon hearing the sound of another man's voice, she opens wide the passage of her ears;
moreover, she has squandered her wealth, forms intimate friendships with neighbors, and having set foot outside, she wanders through the streets;
indeed, she is an adulteress, constantly disrespectful toward her husband and possessed of a corrupted mind and intention.
"She stands constantly at the door; she displays her armpits, limbs, and breasts; having gone here and there, she gazes about.
Indeed, friend Puṇṇamukha, by these twenty-five points a woman may be known as corrupted.
And regarding this, there is also a further verse:
"She praises his absence from home, does not grieve when he has gone away;
upon seeing her husband returned, she does not rejoice, and never speaks in praise of her husband—
these are the signs of a woman who is corrupted."
‘She pursues what is harmful, unrestrained; she neglects her welfare, performing what ought not to be done.
She lies down with her back turned, having cast off [her husband]; these are the characteristics of one who is corrupted.
She becomes perverse and jealous; she breathes long and suffers in pain.’
She frequently goes to relieve herself of excrement and urine—these are the signs of one who is corrupted.
She behaves contrary to her nature and performs what should not be done; she listens intently to the speech of another;
and having lost her wealth, she forms intimate attachments—these are the signs of one who is corrupted.
‘She squanders with difficulty-acquired wealth, amassed through toil and gathered with pain;
she cultivates intimacy with neighbors—these are the signs of one who is corrupted.
With her feet set upon the threshold, wandering through the streets, she is constantly ill-disposed toward her husband.’
She is unfaithful and devoid of respect; these are the signs of one who is corrupted.
She stands constantly at the threshold of the door, displaying her breasts and her armpits;
she looks about in all directions with a wandering mind—these are the signs of one who is corrupted.
“All rivers flow crookedly; all forests made of wood [yield] timber;
all women commit evil when they find a secluded place.
“If one should find a moment, or privacy, or even such a secluded spot as that,”
"Could all women indeed commit evil? Or did she find another even with a cripple?
Among women who take delight in men, who are manifold-minded and unrestrained—if they should not be pleasing in every respect, one should not trust them, for women are like unstable riverbanks."
In that context, the expression "the cow [acts] with the milch-cow" is stated by means of a shift in grammatical gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*).
"She offends within the family of kinsmen" means that there, having become fearless, she engages in unchaste conduct from her youth onward even with trusted servants and others;
and although the kinsmen know of it, they do not exercise restraint, but—seeking to avoid their own ill-repute—act as if they were unaware. "Those who act for one's harm" means...
"Things not to be practiced" means things that should not be done. "Lacking virtue" means being devoid of a bowstring. "An evil companion" means a bad friend.
"By way of poverty" means through the state of being poor; the same method applies to the remaining terms as well.

In this context, because a poor person lacks ornaments and such, one is unable to win him over with defilements (or worldly charms), and thus one despises him. A sick person [is one whom one cannot win over] with material objects or sensual pleasures.
He is unable [to fulfill his duties]. Being worn out by old age, he is no longer capable of physical or verbal play and delight.

A drunkard, he even brings her hand-ornaments and other belongings right into the tavern. Foolish and blind, he is not skilled in the arts of love. Being intoxicated and addicted to female slaves, he lives with the household maidservants;
moreover, he reviles and insults his wife, thereby treating her with contempt.
She reviles and insults him who complies with all her demands, thinking, "This man is powerless; he follows me alone.
But as for him who provides all the wealth and looks after the household, his wife takes hold of all the essence of the wealth and treats that husband with contempt like a slave;
even when she desires it, she says, "What use have I for you? and excludes him from the house.
She drives [him] out. "Reached the state of blossoming" means having attained the condition of being in full bloom.
"Brings forth ill-will" means she brings forth ill-will toward her husband; she becomes corrupt, which is to say, she commits an evil deed.

"Habitual of going to the grove" means that whether with or without asking her husband's permission, she frequently goes to one of the flower-groves or similar places and there engages in improper conduct.
Having gone there, she informs her foolish husband, saying, "Today I performed an offering to the tree deity in the monastery," and so forth.
But the wise man, thinking, "Surely she is practicing misconduct there," does not allow her to go again.
The meaning should be understood in this way for all instances. "Another family" refers to the house of those who are friends, acquaintances, and so on.
She goes about saying things such as, "I have a loan invested for my growth in such-and-such a family; there is something lent on a temporary basis; I am settling that account.
Those who are "habituated to looking" (nillokanasīlā) are those whose nature it is to gaze through the openings of windows and the like.
One who "stands at the main gate" (sadvāraṭṭhāyinī) stands at the principal entrance displaying her own limbs and members.
“Transgresses” (*accācarati*) means she acts in excess; the meaning is that while standing right in the presence of her husband, she gives a signal to another man.

“Gapes” (*vijambhati*): either she has made a prior appointment, thinking, “When I see him, I shall yawn, so that by that sign you may know whether there is an opportunity or not,” or she does so even without having made such an appointment.
Thinking, “In this way he will be captivated by me,” she stands right beside her husband and stretches, displaying the act of stretching.
She bends down: having placed something slightly on the ground, she leans over as if lifting it up, showing her back.
She displays coquetry: she exhibits charm through her modes of deportment, such as walking, or through her ornaments. She feigns bashfulness:
As if feeling ashamed, she covers her body with a cloth or leans against a door or a wall.
"With the nail" means she strikes one foot-nail with a foot-nail, or one hand-nail with a hand-nail. "With a stick" means with a small rod.
"A child" means taking either her own son or another's son, she lifts him up herself or causes him to be lifted up.
"He plays" means either he plays himself or he causes a child to play. The same method applies to kissing and so forth.
"He gives" means he gives him some fruit or flower. "He asks" means he requests that very thing from him.
"He imitates" means he imitates whatever the child has done. "Loudly" means either by way of a great noise or by way of praise.
"Lowly" means lowly by way of a feeble voice, or by unpleasant speech, or by contemptuous speech. "In public" means openly in the midst of many people.
"In private" means secretly out of sight. "By dancing and so forth" means that one makes a sign by means of these things, such as dancing.
In that context, by making a sign through weeping, [one might hear it] when it is raining at night through a window.
The story of the brahmin wife of the family priest, who was led away by the merchant’s son after being mounted on an elephant, should be told.
"She laughs" means she laughs with a loud laugh; in this way, too, she makes a sign. "The armpit" means the region of the arm-pits.
"She scrapes" means she scrapes with her teeth. "The head" means the braid of hair. Thus, even by the loosening or binding of the hair, [she indicates] other men.
One makes a pretext; whether having made a determination or not having made one, thinking "someone might become infatuated," one indeed acts.
"She should be known as corrupted" means: "She is corrupted toward me, she is angry";
and having become angry, she engages in misconduct—this is how she should be understood by a wise person. "In foreign lands" means: "The wealth entrusted in such-and-such a village is lost."
Having said, “Go, accomplish that; conduct business,” and so forth, when he had departed, she—desiring to engage in improper conduct—praised living abroad.
“Disadvantage” means lack of prosperity. “Improper act” means something unfit to be done.
“Having wrapped herself” means having dressed herself tightly. “Turning this way and that” means shifting about here and there. “Becoming like saffron” means becoming full of clamor.
When she lies at his feet, the attendant makes her rise up, lights a lamp, and creates all kinds of clamor, thereby destroying his pleasure in sensual defilement (*kilesarati*).
"She experiences suffering" means she says things such as, "My head aches," and so forth.
"She acts contrary" means she behaves in opposition by giving hot food to one who desires cold food, and so forth. "Her wealth is destroyed" means...
She is one who destroys wealth that has been acquired with great difficulty by her husband through such things as excessive greed for liquor.

She "intimates" means she forms an intimacy through the influence of the defilements (*kilesa*). "With feet set forth" means having set forth her feet for the purpose of consorting with a paramour. Regarding "the husband":
due to a lack of respect for her husband and because her mind is corrupted, she becomes an adulteress.
"All women" means all women other than those whose defilements have been attenuated by insight (vipassanā) might commit evil.
"Labhamāne" means being obtained; the sense is "being found. "Nivātake" means in a place for secret consultation or for causing dissension.
"Khaṇaṃ vā rahaṃ vā" means either an opportunity or a secluded place for the purpose of committing evil. "Kayiruṃ nū" means "would they not do?"
*Ettha nū* is merely a particle. *Alatthā* means "not having obtained. Or rather, this is the reading:

"Not having obtained another accomplished person (*sampannapurisa*), they might commit evil even with a cripple (*pīṭhasappin*), even one more loathsome than that. *Ārāmakarāsū* means 'in those who cause delight.
*Aniggahāsū* means 'in those who cannot be disciplined by means of restraint. *Titthasamā* means 'like a ford' among the highest dharmas."
He does not prevent anyone from bathing; likewise, these women do not refuse anyone when there is privacy, an opportunity, or a secluded place.
For instance, in the past, in Bārāṇasī, there was a king named Kaṇḍarī who possessed supreme beauty.
Every day, his ministers brought a thousand perfume caskets for him. Having arranged them as a decorative display in his residence, [they placed] the perfume caskets...
Having split fragrant wood, they prepared it and cooked their food. His wife was also beautiful, and her name was Kinnarā.
His domestic chaplain was of the same age as him, named Pañcālacaṇḍa, and was endowed with great intelligence.
Now, near the king’s palace, a rose-apple tree grew within the inner wall, its branches hanging down over the top of the rampart. Of that tree—
In the shade lived a loathsome, misshapen cripple who was a couch-serpent (*pīṭhasappī*).

One day, a Kinnara goddess, looking out through a window, saw him and became enamored of him. Having entertained the king with pleasure that night, when the king had fallen asleep, she rose slowly from her seat, placed various kinds of choice food into golden bowls, and...
Placing him on her lap, she descended through a window by means of a rope made from her garment, climbed a rose-apple tree, and after descending onto a branch, fed the cripple.
Having committed the evil deed, she returned by the same path she had come, ascended the palace, rubbed her body with perfumes, and lay down with the king.
By this means, she constantly committed wicked acts with him; yet the king did not know it.
Thus, one day, having circumambulated the city and entering his residence, he saw a cripple lying in the shade of a rose-apple tree, overcome with extreme misery.
Seeing him, he said to the chaplain: "Look at this wretched human ghost!
"Yes, I see him, Your Majesty. "My good man, could any woman, out of desire and passion, ever find such a repulsive form as this?"
“...should approach. Having heard that, the cripple became conceited and thought, “What is this king saying?
He does not seem to know that his own queen has come into my presence.
Raising his joined palms toward the rose-apple tree, he said, “Listen, O lord, deity reborn in the rose-apple tree; apart from you, no one else knows this reason.”
He said: Having observed his behavior, the chaplain thought, "Surely the king’s chief queen has gone by way of the rose-apple tree and is committing a wicked act with him.
He asked the king, "Great King, what was the nature of your physical contact with the queen during the night?
"Friend, I saw nothing else; however, during the middle watch of the night, her body..."
“It becomes cool. “In that case, Your Majesty, let us set aside other women;
does not your chief queen, Kinnarādevī, commit wicked acts with him? “Good man, what are you saying?
How could such a woman, endowed with supreme elegance, take pleasure with one so utterly loathsome? “In that case, Your Majesty, examine her yourself.”
Saying, "Very well," he ate his evening meal that night and lay down with her.
Thinking, "I shall catch him," he acted as if he had fallen asleep at the usual time for sleep. She too rose and did exactly the same.
The king followed right after her and stood waiting in the shade of a rose-apple tree. The cripple, becoming angry with the queen—
“You have come back after staying out too long today,” he said, striking her with his hand on the earring-chain behind her ear.
Then she said to him, “Do not be angry with me, master; I was looking for the king’s sleep,” and she acted as a foot-maid in his house.
However, by that blow of his, the lion-faced earring fell from her ear and landed at the king’s feet.
The king, thinking, "It will suffice for this much," took her and departed.
She too, having committed adultery with him, went back by the same route as before and began to lie down with the king. The king refused her;
then on the following day, he commanded, "Let Queen Kinnarā come, having adorned herself with all the ornaments I gave her. She thought, "My lion-faced earrings are with the goldsmith..."

Having said, "In the presence [of the goldsmith]," she did not come; yet when she was sent for again, she returned wearing only one earring. The king asked, "Where is your earring? "It is with the goldsmith," she replied.
He summoned the goldsmith and said, "For what reason have you not given her this earring?
"I did not take it, Your Majesty," he replied. The king, becoming angry with her, said, "O wicked woman!"
“O Caṇḍālī, you ought to have been a goldsmith like me,” he said, and having thrown that earring before her, he spoke to the chaplain:
“Good sir, what you have said is true; go and have her head cut off.
He placed her in a certain spot right there in Rājagaha and, approaching the king, said: “Your Majesty, do not [punish] Queen Kinnarā...”
“Anger arose [in me], for all women are exactly like this. If you wish to know the unchaste nature of women, I shall show you both their wickedness and their great deceitfulness;
come, let us wander through the countryside in the guise of strangers.
The king said, “Very well,” and having entrusted the kingdom to his mother, he set out on a journey with him. As they traveled a league—

Having traveled along the road, while they were still seated on the highway, a certain householder, having performed an auspicious ceremony for his son’s sake, was traveling with a large retinue, having placed a young maiden in a covered carriage.
Seeing him, the chaplain said to the king: "If you wish, it is possible to cause this young maiden to commit a crime together with you."

"O King! "What are you saying? She has a large retinue; it will not be possible to do so," [the king replied]. The chaplain said, "In that case, look, Your Majesty," and going ahead, he enclosed the road with a screen at no great distance and placed the king inside the screen.
He himself sat by the side of the road weeping. Then, seeing him, the householder asked, "Dear sir, why are you weeping?"
He asked, “My wife is heavily pregnant; I have set out on the road to take her to her family home.
On the way, her womb has shifted, and she is suffering inside the carriage.
There is no woman with her, nor am I able to go there myself. I do not know what will happen; it is necessary for me to find a woman. “Do not—”
Rodī said, "I have many daughters-in-law; one will go. [The king replied,] "In that case, let this very young girl go;
she too will have good fortune. He thought, "She speaks the truth;
even for my daughter-in-law there will indeed be good fortune, for by this sign she will increase with sons and daughters. Thus he sent her. Having entered there, she [approached] the king.
Having seen him, her heart became bound to him and she committed a wicked deed. The king also gave her a signet ring.
Then, when he had finished his business and returned, they asked him, "Has she given birth? "A son of golden complexion," he replied.
The householder took him and departed. The chaplain also went into the presence of the king and said, "Your Majesty, have you seen the maiden?"
“Such is this wicked woman; how much more so, then, others? But did you give her anything? [He replied: “Yes, I gave her a finger-ring.
“I will not give it back to her,” he said, and going quickly, he took the carriage. When asked, “What is this?
he replied, “This woman has come having taken the ring placed upon my brahmin wife’s head; give it back to me, mother! and he demanded the ring.
He said: "While giving it to him, she pricked the Brahmin’s hand with her fingernail and gave it to him, saying, 'Take it, you thief!
Thus, by various means, the Brahmin showed many other unfaithful women to the king and said, 'Let this suffice for now;
we shall go elsewhere, Your Majesty. The king replied, 'Even if one were to travel throughout the whole of Jambudīpa, all [women would be like this]..."
“Women will always be like this; what use have we for them? Let us turn back! Having returned to Bārāṇasī, he said to the king:
“Great King, women are indeed of such evil nature; this is their very character. Forgive, O Lord, the Kinnarā-devī.
When thus entreated by the chaplain, the king forgave her and had her expelled from the royal palace. But having removed her from that place—
He made another woman his chief queen. Having had that cripple cast out, he had the branch of the rose-apple tree cut down.
At that time, Kuṇāla was Pañcālacaṇḍa. Thus, bringing forward the very reason he himself had witnessed, he spoke this verse:
“Indeed, having seen Kaṇḍarī and the Kinnaras, all women no longer find pleasure in the household life.”
"Having abandoned such a mortal husband, his wife saw another man, a cripple crawling on a bench.

The meaning of this is: by observing what caused King Kaṇḍarī and Queen Kinnarā—these two, Kaṇḍarī and Kinnarā—to become disenchanted, it should be understood that not all women take delight in their own husbands.

In the house. For instance, having seen another man who was a cripple crawling on his knees, the wife abandoned that king—who was such an expert in sensual pleasures—and committed a wicked act with that human *peta*.
Furthermore, in the past, in Bārāṇasī, a king named Baka ruled the kingdom according to the Dhamma. At that time, in Bārāṇasī...
A certain poor man living at the eastern gate had a daughter named Pañcapāpī.
It is said that even in the past, she was the daughter of a poor man who would knead clay and plaster the walls of her house.
Then, a certain Paccekabuddha, thinking, "Where shall I find clay for the purpose of plastering the terrace of my mountain cave," [saw] in Benares...
"Can it be obtained? Having put on his robe and holding his bowl in hand, he entered the city and stood not far from her.
She, looking up with an angry mind, said, "He is begging even for clay!
The Paccekabuddha remained perfectly still. Then, seeing that the Paccekabuddha did not move, she regained her composure and said, "O ascetic..."
Having said, "You do not even obtain clay," she brought a large lump of clay and placed it in his bowl.

He used that clay to plaster the walls of the mountain cave. Not long after, she passed away from there and took rebirth in the womb of a poor woman in a village outside the city gates of that very same town. After the lapse of ten months, she...
He emerged from his mother’s womb. By the fruit of her having offered a lump of clay, his body was endowed with exquisite touch;
however, because she had looked up in anger, his hands, feet, mouth, eyes, and nose were deformed and ugly.
Therefore, people knew him by the name "Pañcapāpī" (The Five-Ugly).
Then one day, while the King of Bārāṇasī was inspecting the city at night in an unknown guise, he arrived at that place.
That village girl, playing with her companions, took hold of the king’s hand without even realizing it was he.
Due to the touch of her hand, he was unable to maintain his composure; he felt as if he were touched by a divine contact.
Thus, being impassioned by the touch, he took her hand even though she was so ill-formed, and asked, "Whose daughter are you?
When she replied, "The daughter of a gatekeeper," he asked whether she had no husband. He said, "I shall be your husband;
go and obtain your parents' permission. She approached her parents and said, "Mother and father, a certain man desires me."
Having said, "He too will become poor; if he desires even such [a woman], very well," [the king] went and reported that he had been permitted by his parents.
He lived with her in that very house, and from then on, entering the royal palace at dawn, he went there constantly in the guise of a stranger, not desiring to look upon any other woman.

Now one day, her father developed a hemorrhage. The only medicine for this was rice gruel mixed with unbroken milk, ghee, honey, and sugar; because of his poverty, they were unable to procure it for him.
Then the mother of the five evil sons said to her daughter, "Daughter, will your husband be able to procure rice gruel? "Mother, by my husband..."
"We too must become even more wretched than this; nevertheless, I shall ask her.
Do not worry," he said, and sat down dejected at the time of her arrival. Then the king came and asked, "Why are you dejected?
She explained the matter to him. Having heard it, the king said, "My dear, this is an exceedingly potent medicine; from where [could it come]?"
Having said, "I shall obtain her," he thought: "It is not possible for me to travel in this manner at all times; dangers must be encountered along the way.

Furthermore, if I lead her to the inner palace, those who do not know of her excellence of touch will mock us, saying, 'Our king has returned having captured a female spirit (yakkhinī),' and all the inhabitants of the city [will ridicule us]."
"Having made her acknowledge the contact, I shall release her from blame. Then the king said to her, "Bhaddā, do not worry;
I will bring your father's milk-rice," and having enjoyed himself with her, he went to the royal palace.
On the following day, having had such milk-rice cooked and having had leaves brought, he made two bags and placed the milk-rice in one.
Having placed a single crest-jewel (cūḷāmaṇi) inside it, tied it up, and gone during the night, he said, "Dear lady, we are poor;
this was obtained with great difficulty. You should say to your father: 'Today eat porridge from this basket, and tomorrow from that one.
She did exactly as she was told. Then, because of the potency of the porridge, her father—
Having eaten only a little, he became satisfied. He gave the remainder to his mother and ate himself as well; thus, all three were satiated.
They then set aside the cūḷāmaṇi casket for the following day.
The king, having returned to his residence and washed his face, said, "Bring me my crest-jewel," but they replied, "We do not see it."
When they said, “O gods,” he replied, “Search the entire city. Although they searched, they did not see it.
He then said, “In that case, search outside the city, starting from the poor houses, among the rice-leaf parcels. While searching, they saw the crest-jewel in that jar;
they bound her parents, accusing them of being thieves, and led them away. Then her father said, “Sire, ...”
“We are not thieves; this jewel was brought by another,” he said. When asked, “By whom? he explained, “By my son-in-law.
When asked, “Where is he? he replied, “My daughter knows. Then he spoke with his daughter: “Dear girl, do you know your husband?
“I do not know him,” she replied. “If that is the case, we have no means of livelihood,” he said. “Father, [please tell me].”
“Having come from darkness, he goes back into darkness; therefore, I do not recognize his form, but I am able to know him by the touch of his hand.
He reported this to the king’s men, and they in turn reported it to the king. The king, acting as if he did not know, said:
“In that case, place that woman behind a curtain in the royal courtyard, leaving a space in the curtain only the width of a hand.”
"Having made a hole [in the wall], assemble the city-dwellers and seize the thief by the touch of your hands," he said.
The king's men went to her presence to do so, but upon seeing her form, they were filled with remorse;
crying out, "Shame! Shame! She is a demoness! they felt such loathing that they did not dare to touch her. However, they brought her back to the royal courtyard.
Having placed her inside the inner chamber, they assembled all the inhabitants of the city.
As each person arrived, she would take their outstretched hand through a hole and say, "It is not he. Men, caught by her touch which was like the touch of a celestial being, were unable to withdraw;
even if she were deserving of punishment, they would rather pay the fine or even enter into the state of slavery or servitude.
“We shall do this at home,” they thought. Then the king’s men beat them with sticks and drove them away.
Starting with the viceroy, they all became like madmen.
Then the king stretched out his hand, thinking, “Perhaps it might be me. Having seized him by the hand, [they cried,] “A thief!”
“I have taken her! he cried out in a loud voice. The king questioned them as well: “When you were taken by her hand, what did you think?
They reported the matter exactly as it had happened. Then the king said to them:
“I had this done so that she might be brought to my own home, thinking, ‘Lest people should despise me for not knowing her touch. Therefore, I have made all of you aware of it.”
“Tell me now, sirs, in whose house is she fit to dwell? “In yours, O King.
Then, having consecrated her, he made her his chief queen. He also granted her sovereignty over her parents.
From that time forth, being devoted to her, he neither established a court of justice nor cast even a glance at another woman. To her—
They searched for a rival. One day, having seen a sign in a dream indicating that she would become the chief queen of two kings, she informed the king.
The king summoned the interpreters of dreams and asked, "What happens when such a dream is seen?
Having received bribes from the other women, they replied, "Great King, for the queen... [to see] a completely white...
"Sitting upon the back of the elephant is a premonitory sign of your own death;
however, the moon-grasping performed while on the elephant's back is a premonitory sign that your enemy king will be brought here," he said. When asked, "What should be done now?
he replied, "Your Majesty, it is impossible to kill her; rather, having placed her on a boat, [place her] in the river..."
"It is proper to release her," they said. The king placed her on a boat together with food, clothing, and ornaments during the night and released her into the river.
As she was being carried down by the river, she came before King Bāvari, who was playing in the water in a boat in the lower reaches of the river.
They arrived. When the general saw the ship, he said, "This ship is mine.
The king, saying, "The goods on the ship are mine," saw her upon the arriving vessel and asked, "Who are you, you who resemble a female demon?
She smiled and, having declared herself the chief queen of King Baka, related the entire account of what had occurred to him.
She, however, was known throughout all of Jambudīpa as Pañcapāpī. Then the king took her by the hand and lifted her up;
at the very moment of being seized, he became impassioned with desire for her touch, ceased to perceive her as a mere woman among other women, and established her in the position of chief queen.
She became as dear to him as his own life. When Baka heard of this occurrence, he said, "I will not allow her to be his chief queen."
Thinking, "I shall give [her] to him," he gathered his army, established a camp at that landing place, and sent a message:
"Give me either my wife or battle. He replied, "I will give battle, not my wife," and prepared for war.
Both of their ministers said, "There is no need for death on account of a woman; she is the wife of the former husband..."
"It belongs to Baka, since it was obtained by the boatman Bāvarika; therefore, let there be seven days for each in their respective homes.
Having thus deliberated, the two kings informed one another. Both of them, being well-pleased, established cities at the landing-place of Titthapaṭitittha and resided there.
She served as the chief queen for both of them. Both were devoted to her.
They were [thus]. She, however, having stayed for seven days in one man’s house, was traveling by boat to the other man’s house;
while steering the boat, she committed an evil act with an old, hunchbacked boatman in the middle of the river. At that time, Kuṇāla was the king of birds, a crane.
Therefore, bringing forward this incident he had witnessed himself, he spoke this verse to show it:
“The wife of King Baka and Bāvari, who was excessively devoted to sensual pleasure, committed an impropriety toward him who followed her will;
what woman indeed would not transgress against anyone other than that?
In this context, *accantakāmānugatassa* means “of one who is excessively devoted to sensual pleasure. *Avācarī* means “she practiced an improper conduct (*anācāra*).”
"Paṭṭhavasānugassa" means of one who follows his own will, that is, in the presence of one who carries out his commands;
or, the genitive case is used in the sense of the instrumental, meaning "he committed a sin together with him.
"Tadaññaṃ" means which other man should she not transgress against? This is the meaning.
Furthermore, in the past, the chief queen of Brahmadatta, named Piṅgiyānī,
while looking out from an open window, saw the groom of the auspicious horse. At a time when the king had fallen asleep, she descended through the lattice window,
committed adultery with him, and then returned to the palace, rubbed her body with perfumes, and [rejoined] the king.
She lay down. Then one day the king thought, "Why is the queen’s body always cold at the hour of midnight?
I shall investigate her. One day, pretending to have fallen asleep, he rose and followed her as she was departing;
seeing her committing adultery with the horse-keeper, he turned back and went to his bed. She too—
Having committed adultery and returned, she lay down upon the small couch. On the following day, the king summoned her into the midst of his assembly of ministers;

having revealed that matter and declared, "All women are indeed of evil character," he pardoned her fault—which otherwise would have merited execution, imprisonment, mutilation, or dismemberment—dismissed her from her position, and appointed another as chief queen. At that time, King Kuṇāla was [the son of] Brahmadatta.
Having thus experienced it himself, he recited this verse to show what he had seen:
“Piṅgiyānī was the beloved queen of King Brahmadatta, the lord of the whole world.
She did not approach him who followed her will, nor did she, though longing for him, ever obtain him.”

In that regard, "she did not find either him" means that she, while thus transgressing, found neither that horse-keeper nor that position of chief queen; she fell away from both. "Desiring pleasures" means longing for sensual desires.
Having thus described the faults of women through these past instances of wicked-natured women, he spoke again by another method to describe their very same faults:
"Of those who are greedy, fickle-minded, ungrateful, and treacherous..."
A man who is not devoted to the gods is not worthy of trust.
They do not understand what has been done or what remains to be done, nor do they recognize their mother, father, or brother.
These ignoble ones, having transgressed the Dhamma, fall under the sway of their own minds alone.

“Even a husband who has long been devoted, dear and pleasing, compassionate, and as dear as one’s own life—people abandon him in matters of residence and duties. Therefore, I do not place my trust in women.
For the mind of women is like that of a monkey, or like the shadow of a tree shifting from branch to branch.”
The heart of women is fickle and unsteady; it revolves like the rim of a wheel.
When they see a man’s wealth, which is so desirable to behold, they lead him away with gentle words, just as the people of Kamboja lead a horse by means of a lotus flower.
“When those who look closely do not see any wealth of a man that is worth seizing,
they avoid him from every side, just as one who has crossed over and reached the further shore abandons a raft.
Like snakes, like fire that eats everything, and like rivers with swift currents, their deceit is sharp.”
These people serve both the pleasant and the unpleasant, just as a boat serves both this shore and the far shore.
They belong neither to one person nor to two; they are like a marketplace laid out for sale.
He who should think, "They are mine," would be like one trying to stop the wind with a net.
“Just as a river and a road, a tavern, an assembly hall, and a watering place—so too are women in the world;
no limit for them exists. They are like a pot placed on its stand, resembling the head of a black snake.”
As cattle graze upon the grass, they select the best for themselves.
The elephant with its temple-juice flowing, the black snake, the consecrated king, and all women—
a man should approach these with constant caution, for their true nature is indeed difficult to discern.
“Dancing women, though beautiful, are not dear to many; a courtesan is not to be resorted to.
Not for another’s wife, nor for the sake of wealth—these five kinds of women are not to be resorted to.
In this context, *luddhānaṃ* means “of those who lust. This refers to the feeling of passion even toward a bound thief, as in the case of the Kaṇavera Jātaka.
It has been said. "Of those with fickle minds" means of those whose minds change in an instant;
this should be illustrated by the *Cūḷadhanuggaha Jātaka*. Furthermore, their ingratitude should be illustrated by the *Takkāriya Jātaka* in the *Ekakanipāta*.

"Not a man possessed by a deity" means not one who is possessed by a god, nor one seized by a *yakkha*, nor one who is bewitched by a *abhūta* (phantom spirit); [such a person] [does not know] the virtuous character of women.
One does not deserve faith; rather, one who has seen the truth (bhūta-diṭṭha) would have faith. "Done" refers to the benefit performed by oneself.
"Duty" refers to the duty to be performed by oneself. "Not even mother":
having abandoned all kinsmen, because they follow only him to whom their hearts are bound, these people—mother and the rest—do not truly know him, just like Mahāpanthaka’s mother.

“Unnoble” means shameless. “Of their own” means of their own [affairs]. “In dwellings” means in times of calamity. “In duties” means in various tasks to be performed. “Ear-to-ear” means descending upon one after another.

For just as the shadow of a tree on uneven ground descends into the lowlands and ascends onto the highlands, so too the minds of these women do not bypass anyone, whether superior or inferior. “Fickle” means...
It does not rest upon even a single thing. "Like a felly" means like the felly of a chariot wheel as it moves.

"Of a form to be grasped" means of a nature that can be taken hold of. "Wealth" means riches. "They lead" means they bring [them] under their own control. "By the water-born" means by the water-born *sevāla* (aquatic moss).
It is said that when the inhabitants of the kingdom of Kamboja wish to capture horses from the forest, they [do so] at a certain place...
Having surrounded the enclosure and secured the gate, they smeared duckweed with honey at the horses' watering place;
then, starting from the grass on the bank connected to the duckweed, they smeared everything up to the enclosure and the gate.
When the horses had drunk their water, being greedy for the flavor, they ate those grasses smeared with honey and gradually reached that spot.

They enter. Thus, just as they entice horses with water-born [lotuses] and bring them under control, so too do these women, upon seeing wealth, bring a man under their power through gentle words for the sake of seizing it;
this is the meaning. "A raft" (*kulla*) refers to anything whatsoever taken up for the purpose of crossing over.
"Like glue" (*silesūpamā*): they are like glue in that they bind the hearts of men. "Sharp deceit" (*tikkhamāyā*): sharp deceit, swift deceit.
"Like a river" means that just as a mountain torrent flows swiftly, so too does she come quickly; this is the meaning.

"Like a shop" means that just as a shop with goods displayed is of benefit only to those who have the capital, so too are these women. "He who [desires] them" refers to the man who desires those women.
"He would obstruct the wind with a net" means he would try to stop the wind with a net. "No limit exists for them" means that just as for these [torrents], there is no boundary.
Regarding rivers and the like, there is no fixed time such that one must go there only at a specific hour; they may be approached at any desired moment, whether by night or by day.

Nor is there a restriction such that one must go only with such-and-such a person; rather, they are to be approached by anyone who has need of them. The meaning is that it is the same for those [meditative attainments] as well.

"They are equal to a lamp-stand" means that just as fire is not satisfied by fuel, so too these [attainments] are not satisfied by the delight of the defilements. "They are like the head of a black snake."
They are like the heads of black snakes for five reasons: on account of their anger, their harboring of resentment, their terrible venom, their forked tongues, and their treachery toward friends.

In this context, their "terrible venom" should be understood as their abundance of passion; their "forked tongues" as their malicious speech; and their "treachery toward friends" as their sexual misconduct.
"Cows [go] outside for grass alone" means that just as cows abandon the place where they have already grazed...

"Selecting the best blade of grass, whether pleasing or unpleasing, from the outside, they chew and eat it"—the meaning is that even these [women], having abandoned one who is destitute, resort only to another who possesses wealth.

"Anointed on the head" refers to a king. "And all women" means all female beings. "These" refers to these five types of persons. "From a sense of permanence" means from the perception of permanence; [this applies] to one whose mindfulness is established.
The meaning is: "having become indeed heedful. "Hard to know" means difficult to understand. "Every disposition" refers to one's underlying intention (*ajjhāsayo*).
For even a fire that has been tended for a long time burns; even an elephant that has been trusted for a long time kills; even a snake that has been familiarized for a long time bites;
even a king who has been trusted for a long time causes harm; likewise, women who have been associated with for a long time display their transformative nature.
"Of exquisite beauty" means she is handsome. "Not beloved by many" means she is not dear or pleasing to many, like the courtesan of Aḍḍhakāsi.
"Not clever" means she is not skilled in dancing and singing; for such women, being highly sought after, have many friends, and therefore they should not be cultivated.
"Not for the sake of wealth" refers to one who associates with another solely for the sake of wealth; such a woman, even if she is unmarried, [should not be relied upon].
“They should not be served, for she becomes angry when she does not obtain wealth.
When this was said, the great multitude gave the Great Being their applause, saying, “Oh, well spoken!
Having thus explained the faults of women through so many reasons, he became silent. Hearing that, Ānanda the king of vultures said, “Friend...”
“Kuṇāla, I too shall speak of the faults of women by the power of my own knowledge,” he said, and began his discourse on their faults.
To show this, the Teacher said:
“Then, indeed, O Ānanda, the vulture-king Gijjharāja, having understood the beginning, middle, and end of Kuṇāla’s discourse, at that time spoke these verses:”
“Even if a man were to give this entire earth filled with wealth to a woman he esteemed, having gained the opportunity, he might despise even her;
one should not fall under the power of those unfaithful women.
Even if she is industrious, of upright conduct, cherished since childhood, dear, and pleasing—”
They abandon one even in times of need; therefore, I do not place my trust in women.
A man should not trust thinking, "She desires me," nor should he trust thinking, "She weeps in my presence.
For these pursue both the pleasant and the unpleasant, just as a boat goes from this shore to the other.
“One should not trust one who is clothed in old branches; one should not trust an old friend who is a thief.
One should not trust a king, thinking, ‘He is my friend,’ nor should one trust a woman who is the mother of ten sons.
One should not trust women who are skilled at enchanting, even if they are of extreme virtue, for they are unrestrained.”
One should not place trust in a wife who is pursued by excessive passion, for women are like riverbanks.
They might kill, they might cut, or they might even cause one to be cut; they might even sever one’s throat and drink one’s blood.
Do not set your heart on those women who are unrestrained and full of base desires, for they are like the banks of the Ganges.
“Their falsehood is as truth, and their truth is as falsehood;
like cows in a field of grass, they devour the best of the best.
They entice them with their gait, and with their glances and smiles.”
Furthermore, even with ill-clad bodies and sweet speech,
these women are harsh thieves, wild and full of deceitful words;
there is no form of deception among men that they do not know.
“Worldly women are indeed unreliable; no fixed limit for them exists.
They are lustful and impudent, like a fire that consumes everything.
There is no such thing as a beloved among women, nor is there anyone who is not beloved.
These women serve both the beloved and the unbeloved, just as a boat goes to both this shore and the far shore.
"There is no such thing as a beloved among women, nor does an unbeloved exist;
they turn away because of wealth, like a creeper clinging to a tree."
“Women pursue the elephant-tamer, the horse-tamer, the cowherd, the man of the circle, the cremator of corpses,
and the thrower-out of flowers— even one who possesses wealth.
They abandon even a man of noble birth if he is destitute, even if he is like a mere corpse.”
“They follow and pursue [men], for women are driven by wealth.
In this context, “the beginning, middle, and end of the discourse” refers to the beginning, middle, and conclusion of the talk. “Having found the moment” means having obtained an opportunity.
“She desires me” means “she desires me”; thus, a man should not place his trust in a woman. “A mat of old branches” means...
Whether yesterday or the day before, one should not trust a seat that has been spread with old branches; one should not use it without striking it [with a staff] and without examining it.
For a long-lived serpent might have entered and remained there, or an enemy might have placed a weapon.
As for a "former friend who is an old thief," this refers to a thief stationed at a place where travelers are waylaid, whom one thinks, "He is my old friend."
One should not place trust [in them]. For those whom thieves recognize as such, they themselves kill.
Thinking "he is my friend," one quickly becomes angry; therefore, one should not trust a king, thinking "he is my friend.
One should not trust a "mother of ten," thinking, "This old woman will not now overstep me; she will protect herself. And "those who cause delight" refers to fools.
"Among those who bring pleasure. "Of exceeding virtue" means those whose virtue has transcended [ordinary bounds].
"Even if he were followed by exceeding love"—even if he were one whose love followed him excessively, he should still not trust her. Why? Because the connection is:
"For women are like a public landing-place (tittha)," meaning they are common property to all, just like a landing-place.
"Haneyyuṃ" means that being either angry or infatuated with another man, they might do all these things, such as killing and so forth.
"Mā dīnakāmāsū" means do not feel affection for those who have base inclinations or defiled intentions.
"Gaṅgatitthūpamāsū" means those who are like the fords of the Ganges in the sense of being common to all. "Musā" refers to false speech regarding them.
"Like the truth" (*saccasadisova*). Regarding the phrase "by her gait," etc.: for seduction by her gait, the *Ummadantī Jātaka* should be told;
for her ill-dressed appearance, the *Niḷinikā Jātaka*; and for her sweet speech, the story of the Elder Nanda should be related, including his saying, "Noble son, you should come quickly.
"Thieves" (*coriyo*) refers to those who plunder the wealth they have accumulated. "Hard" (*kathinā*) means those with hardened hearts.
*Vāḷā* means wild; they are of a nature to become angry even for a slight reason. *Lapasakkharā* means sweet like sugar through useless chatter.
*Asā* means base or inferior. *Sārattā* means always impassioned. *Pagabbhā* means shameless through physical immodesty and so forth.
*Yathā* means just as a fire consumes everything, so too do these consume everything. *Paṭivallanti* means they embrace [or cling to].
They embrace and entwine. "Like a creeper" means that just as a creeper, depending upon a tree, entwines the tree, so too do these women embrace a man.
In the phrase "the elephant-binder" and so forth, the word *gopurisa* refers to a cowherd. "The cremator of corpses" (*chavaḍāhaka*) means one who burns corpses.
“Cemetery-keepers” is what is meant. “Flower-scatterers” refers to those who clean latrines. “Possessing wealth”:
among these women as well, they follow only those who have wealth. “Having nothing” means being without wealth. “Equal to a scavenger” means equal and like a *caṇḍāla* who eats dog meat;
they go to and consort with even a man who is indistinguishable from him. Why? Because “women run after men for the sake of wealth.”

Thus, having established himself in his own knowledge and spoken of the faults of women, Ānanda, the king of vultures, became silent. Having heard his words, Nārada also established himself in his own knowledge and spoke of their faults. To demonstrate this, the Teacher said:
“Then indeed, sirs, Nārada the divine brahmin, having understood the beginning, middle, and end of the discourse of Ānanda the king of vultures, at that time recited these verses:
‘These four do not fulfill [their purpose]; listen to me as I speak of them. ...’”
The ocean, the brahmin, the king, the woman, and also the lord of birds.
“Whatever rivers exist upon the earth, they all flow toward the ocean;
yet they do not fill the ocean, for it is not filled because of its own vastness.”
“A Brahmin who has mastered the Veda, with its narratives as the fifth part,
should desire to hear even more, for he is not yet full because of his deficiency.
And a king [who rules] the entire earth, together with its oceans and mountains...”
Having conquered and ruled over the earth, though worthy of the seven treasures, he still longs for the further shore of the ocean; for being deficient, he is not yet full.
"If there were eight husbands for each and every woman," [he thought].
“Brave and powerful, bringing the essence of all desires, one should apply effort in the ninth [stage], for it is not filled due to its deficiency.
“All women are like fires, devouring everything; all women are like rivers, carrying everything away.”
All women are like the branches of thorny trees; all women go for the sake of wealth.
A man might grasp the wind with a net, or pour out the ocean with a single hand, or produce sound with his own hand—he who would place his trust in women.
“Among female thieves who possess many guiles, in whom truth is very difficult to find, the disposition of women is hard to comprehend, like the movement of a fish in water.
They are like fires, yet speak with gentle words; they are as difficult to satisfy as rivers.”
Knowing it, they sink down; one should avoid it from afar.
“The ensnaring Great Illusion, which disturbs the holy life—knowing it, they sink down;
one should avoid it from afar.”
“Whomever these [birds] serve, whether by desire or by wealth, they quickly consume them, just as fire consumes its own form.
Therein, “the pair of birds” refers to Kuṇāla, the eldest of the birds.
The passage beginning with “The rivers,” etc., is for the purpose of explaining the subject matter of the established outline (mātikā).
It has been said. "Deficiency" (*ūnatta*) means that [the vessel] is indeed deficient due to the vastness of the water's foundation. "Having studied" (*adhīyāna*) means having recited.

"The four Vedas with the *Vedamakkhāna* as the fifth" refers to the group of four Vedas with the *Itihāsa* (epic history) as the fifth. "Deficiency" here means that because of the vastness of his aspiration, it does not suffice for what must be learned.
"Woven with various jewels" (*anantaratanocita*) means woven and complete with various kinds of gems. "Deficiency" [refers to the fact that]...
For it is not filled because of the greatness of craving (*taṇhā*). "Siyā" means "might be," or this very reading is correct.

"Bringers of the flavor of all sensual pleasures" (*sabbakāmarasāharā*) means those which bring about the flavors of all sensual pleasures. "In the ninth" is stated for the purpose of showing that there is no satisfaction through the eight [stages].
Yet, that [craving] produces desire even in the tenth, the twentieth, or even beyond that. "Deficiency" (*ūnattā*): for that [craving] is indeed a deficiency of sensual craving.
It is not filled even by its vastness. "Like the branches of thorny trees": on a narrow path, they are like the branches of thorns.
For just as a branch, having caught [on something], drags it along, so too do these [senses] drag one away with forms and other objects.
Just as a branch, piercing the hand or other limbs, produces pain, so too do these, merely being touched, pierce the body through contact and bring about great ruin.
They cause [them] to go. "They go" means they go to another man.

"He would touch" means he would seize. "He would pour out" means that one who has entered the water to bathe would take up all the water of the entire ocean with one hand, pour it out, and discard it. "With his own" means with his own single hand; having moved that very hand—

He would raise a cry. "All existence" (*sabbabhāva*): the meaning is that when a man is told, "You alone are desirable, lovely, dear, and pleasing," and he believes it to be so, he would surrender his entire personal inclination toward women, and thus he would engage in catching the wind with nets and other such means.
"Gone" (*gata*) means going. "Free from the three fires" (*analā*): they are called *analā* because they lack the statement "fire" (*ala*) in terms of the three phenomena.
"Difficult to fill, like a great river with water"—in this way, they are difficult to fill because of their delight in the defilements (*kilesa*).
"Knowing them to be sinking"—here, *naṃ* is a mere particle; the meaning is: "knowing that women who have attached themselves to them are sinking into the four states of misery (*apāya*).
"The whirlpool"—just as a whirlpool, having deluded the hearts of the multitude, brings them under its own control, so too are these [women]; such is the sense.
It "disturbs" (*vikopanāti*) because it agitates and because it censures the holy life (*brahmacariya*). "By desire" means by association with what is dear;
"by wealth" means for the sake of wealth. "A conflagration" (*saṇṭhāna*):

just as fire (*jātavedo*), wherever it clings to its own place or any particular spot, burns that very place, so too these [passions], by way of defilement (*kilesa*), whatever person they cling to...
They cling to one another, burn with one another, and bring about great destruction.
Thus, after Nārada had explained the faults of women, the Great Being further elucidated their defects. To demonstrate this, the Teacher said:
"Then indeed, O friends, the bird Kuṇāla, having understood the beginning, middle, and end of the discourse of the divine brahmin Nārada, at that time addressed these verses:"
“A wise man should not converse even with a malevolent demon who holds a sharpened sword in his hand;
he would rather seize a serpent of fierce venom than speak alone with a single woman.
For women are the destroyers of the world’s hearts, armed with dancing, singing, and flirtatious speech.”
They afflict one whose mindfulness is unestablished, just as a host of ogresses afflicts merchants on an island.
"For them there is no discipline, nor any restraint; they delight in liquor and meat, being unrestrained.
They swallow the man's offering, just as the *timiṅgala* swallows the *makara* in the ocean."
“Those who range within the pleasant domain of the five strands of sensual pleasure— restless, undisciplined, and unrestrained— sink down into the heedless, just as rivers flow into the salt sea.
When women entice a man, whether by desire, by affection, or by wealth;
Even one who is like Jātavedas himself, such a person is consumed by the fires of lust and hatred.
Knowing that a man is wealthy and possesses great riches, they approach him with their wealth and themselves;
they entwine his impassioned mind just as the *māluva* creeper entwines a *sāla* tree in the forest.
“Adorned with various ornaments, those women with faces like variegated masks approach with manifold desire;
laughing and mocking, these women are like Śambara, experts in a hundred deceits.
Adorned with gold, gems, and pearls, these women are honored in their husbands’ families.”
Though guarded, they transgress against their husband, like a demoness dwelling within the heart.
For even a man who is majestic, discerning, honored, and revered by many people,
once fallen under the power of women, does not speak [with dignity], like the moon eclipsed by Rāhu.
“Whatever harm one might do in anger, directing it toward every quarter against an enemy who has fallen into one’s power with a wicked mind—
one meets with even greater calamity than that by being under the sway of women and full of longing for them.
Tormented by having their hair shorn and nails clipped, beaten with feet, hands, and staves;”
For women indeed resort only to what is base; they delight in it like flies on a corpse.
Whether among families or in the intervals between streets, or again in royal capitals or market towns—the wise man who seeks happiness should avoid that which is set out as the snare of Namuci.
“Having abandoned wholesome qualities and the virtues of austerity,
he who practices ignoble conduct will be cast into hell by the deities, like a merchant with a gem destined for destruction.
That fool, censured both here and in the next world, is ruined by his own karma.”
He goes aimlessly from throat to throat, like a vicious donkey-cart on a wrong path.
He enters the scorching hell, the forest of iron simbalī trees with their spears,
and having dwelt in the womb of animals, he does not escape the realm of the king of the hungry ghosts.
“The delights of divine play in the Nandana grove, and the conduct of a wheel-turning monarch among humans—
these women destroy for the heedless man, and they lead him to a state of misery.
The delights of divine play are not difficult to obtain, nor is the conduct of a wheel-turning monarch among humans.”
And the nymphs dwelling in golden palaces, who wander seeking to consume the passion of men:

for those who wander seeking to consume the passion of men, the attainment of the realm of form by transcending the realm of desire is not difficult to reach; it is rebirth in the domain of those free from lust.

“The auspicious state that transcends all suffering, which is ultimate, immovable, and unconditioned—this is not difficult to attain for those who have extinguished [defilements] and are pure, provided they wander seeking the destruction of passion.
Therein, he spoke thus: having said, “If you converse with me, I shall cause your head to fall,” he drew his sword.

Even when standing with [the victim] already seized, one should converse with a *pisāca* demon who stands there full of malice, thinking, "As soon as he has conversed, I will devour him and bring about his destruction.
One should even approach and seize a serpent of fierce power that stands there thinking, "I will bite him upon his arrival and kill him.
However, being alone, one must not converse in private with a single woman. This is because it agitates the minds of the world.
They are the heart-breakers of the world. Regarding the phrase "a host of rākṣasīs on an island":

just as a host of rākṣasīs on an island lures merchants with the guise of human beings, brings them under their power, and devours them, so too do these [sensual pleasures] bring beings under their power by means of the five strands of sensual pleasure and lead them to great ruin;
this is the meaning. Discipline (*vinaya*) is conduct (*ācāra*). Restraint (*saṃvara*) is a boundary (*mariyāda*). Of a man...
"Pābhataṃ" means wealth accumulated through suffering;
they swallow it up and lose it. "Aniyatā" means those of unsettled minds. "Loṇatoyavatiyaṃ" means possessing salty water; the meaning is "the ocean. "Āpā" means rivers (or "āpagā");
this is indeed the reading. Just as rivers flow toward the ocean, so do women toward those who are heedless.

"Meaning" (attha) refers to the purpose. "Through affection" (chandasā) means through love. "Through delight" (ratiyā) means through the delight in the five strands of sensual pleasure. "Or through wealth" (dhanena vā) means for the sake of wealth.

"Like fire" (jātavedasadisaṃ) means like a blazing fire due to the perfection of its qualities. "Destroyers of lust and hatred" (rāgadosavadhiyo) means those who kill by means of sensual lust and aversion;
there is also a reading as "those whose course is lust and hatred. "They approach" (osaranti) means they come to him with sweet words for the purpose of seizing his wealth.
They approach while binding [him]. *Sādhanā* means they accomplish [their purpose]. Or rather, this is the reading:

even after giving some of their own wealth for the sake of clothing and ornaments, they draw near; such is the meaning. *Sahattānā* means that, together with their own persons (*attabhāvena*), they act as if they are surrendering their very selves to him.
*Ativeṭhayanti* means they wrap themselves around him excessively and press upon him for the sake of obtaining wealth.
"With various charms" means in manifold ways. "With variegated bodies and faces" means that by way of adornment, they have become possessed of diverse forms and diverse faces.
"Laughing" means laughing with a loud laugh (*mahāhasita*). "Smiling" means smiling with a gentle smile (*mandahasita*).
"Like Śambara" means like the man of illusion and like the lord of the Asuras. "As if the Dānava were seated within their hearts" means just as...
“Whence have you come, sirs, you three men? Thus, even when they were within the heart and inside the belly in the Karaṇḍaka-jātaka, they overstepped the bounds of generosity;
in this way they transgressed. He shows that they were indeed unprotected.
“He does not shine” means he does not gleam, like the kings Harita, Cala, Masaka, Kassa, and Kusarāja. “Than that” means more than that calamity caused by the enemy.
"Calamity" is the meaning. "Full of longing" means possessing craving.
"Tormented by plucked hair and cut nails" means having their hair pulled out and their limbs cut with their own fingernails, being tormented and beaten with their feet and so forth.
One who, through the power of defilements, subjects even these [things] to such a state of ruin—such a person has indeed fallen into a low condition.
Women take delight [in these things], yet they do not avoid such aberrations; for what reason would they not delight in sweet conduct?
"Like flies on carrion" means that, just as flies [linger] upon a loathsome elephant carcass and the like, they likewise delight only in what is base.
"Set out" means that these are not merely women, but rather the snares of Namuci, the defilement-Māra, in these various places.
A man possessed of the eye of wisdom, desiring celestial and human happiness, would avoid a snare or a trap set by hunters for the purpose of catching birds, thinking it to be such.
"Having abandoned" means having cast aside the quality of asceticism (*tapoguṇa*), which bestows great prosperity among gods and humans. "Who" refers to that person.

He practices sensual delights among ignoble and impure objects of desire. "He will go from the world of the gods to hell" means that having transmigrated from the divine realm, he will take up residence in hell.
"Like a merchant for a glass trinket" means that just as a foolish merchant, having given away goods worth a hundred thousand, takes a glass trinket from a village, such is this person.

The meaning is "he becomes. "He" refers to that one who has fallen under the power of women. "Indeterminate" means that it is not fixed as to for how long he will be reborn in the states of misery (*apāya*).
"Gaḷāgaḷa" means that having slipped away from either the world of the gods or the human world, he goes only to the states of misery;
what is it like? It is like a chariot yoked with a vicious donkey on a wrong path; just as a chariot harnessed to a rogue donkey veers off the road.
It goes as if it were springing up; likewise. "The Simbali Forest of Spears" refers to an iron forest of *simbali* trees equipped with thorns resembling spears.
"The realm of the King of Petas" refers both to the realm of the *petas* and the realm of the *asura*s known as Kālakañcika.
"Of the negligent" means of those who are heedless; for they are negligent regarding their pleasures, [neglecting] the wholesome merit that is the root of those very attainments.
"They do not act [rightly]"—thus, all those women are said to "destroy" them.
"They lead them astray" means that by causing such a person to commit unwholesome deeds through negligence (*pamāda*), they lead him toward an unhappy rebirth (*duggati*).
"Dwellers in golden-hued mansions" refers to those who reside in palaces made of gold. "Those who have no need for women" refers to those men who, having become free from the desire for women...
They lead the holy life (*brahmacariya*). "Transcending the realm of sense-desire" (*kāmadhātusamatikkama*) refers to that destination which consists in transcending the realm of sense-desire.
