"Existence in the realm of form" (*rūpadhātuyā bhāvo*) means that existence in the realm of form, designated as the destination consisting in transcending the realm of sense-desire, is not difficult for them to attain.

"Rebirth in the sphere of those free from passion" (*vītarāgavisayūpapatti*) refers to rebirth in the Pure Abodes (*suddhāvāsa*), the world of those free from passion; that too is [not difficult] for them.

"Not difficult to obtain" means it is not hard to reach. "Absolute" (*accanta*) means beyond limits, having the nature of non-destruction. "Unshakable" (*acalita*) means unassailed by defilements (*kilesa*).

"By those who have attained extinction" (*nibbutehi*) means by those whose defilements have been extinguished. "By the pure" (*sucīhi*) means by those who are clean and thoroughly purified; for such as these, this *nibbāna* is not difficult to obtain.
Thus, having led [them] to the great *nibbāna* of the Deathless, the Great Being concluded his teaching. [There were] *kinnaras*, *mahoragas*, and others in the Himalayas.
The deities stationed in the sky gave their applause, exclaiming, "Oh, how this was spoken with the grace of a Buddha!
Then Ānanda the king of vultures, Nārada the divine brahmin, and Puṇṇamukha the Phussakokila bird, each taking his own retinue, departed for their respective abodes.
The Great Being also went to his own place. But the others, traveling at intervals, [approached] the Great Being.
Having received instruction in his presence and having remained steadfast in that instruction, they became destined for heaven.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher, identifying the Jātaka, spoke these concluding verses:
“I was Kuṇāla at that time, and Udāyī was the Phussa cuckoo.”
"Ānanda was the king of vultures, and Sāriputta was Nārada;
the assembly was the Buddha’s assembly—thus you should remember this Jātaka.
Then those monks, having gone at the time of departure by the power of the Teacher, returned at the time of arrival by their own respective powers.
They arrived. The Teacher taught them the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) right there in the Great Forest.
On that very day, they all attained Arahantship. There was a great assembly of deities. Then the Blessed One preached the Mahāsamaya Sutta to them.
This concludes the fourth commentary, the Kuṇāla Jātaka.
[537] 5. The Explanation of the Mahāsutasoma Jātaka.
"But why, O cook, do you act in such a way? This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the taming of the Elder Aṅgulimāla.
Its origin story, his going forth, and his higher ordination are found in the commentary on the Aṅgulimāla Sutta.

It should be understood in detail according to the method already stated. Having ensured the safe delivery of a woman whose fetus was obstructed by means of an act of truth (*saccakiriyā*), he thereafter became one for whom alms were easily obtained.

Cultivating seclusion, he later attained Arahatship and became renowned as one among the eighty great elders (*mahāthera*). At that time, in the Hall of Dharma (*dhammasabhā*), this conversation arose:
They raised this cry: "Friends, oh, how difficult a task has been performed by the Blessed One!
Having tamed such a fierce, blood-stained, great thief as Aṅgulimāla—rendering him harmless through neither rod nor sword—oh, truly, the Buddhas are performers of difficult deeds!
Even while standing in the Perfumed Chamber, the Teacher heard this conversation with his divine ear.
Having heard this and knowing, "Today my departure will be of great benefit;
a great discourse on the Dhamma will take place," he went to the Dhamma Hall with the incomparable grace of a Buddha.
Sitting upon the excellent seat that had been prepared, he asked, "Monks, about what talk are you gathered here now? When they replied, "About this very matter," he said, "It is not surprising..."
“Monks, it was only now that I, having attained supreme perfect enlightenment, tamed this one;
yet even while practicing my former conduct and established only in partial knowledge, I tamed him. Having said this, being requested by them, he related the past.
In the past, in the kingdom of Kuru, in the city of Indapatta, a king named Koravya ruled the realm with righteousness. At that time—
The Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of his chief queen. When ten months had passed, she gave birth to a son of golden complexion;
because of his great learning, they named him Sutasoma.
When he reached maturity, the king provided him with a thousand pieces of gold and sent him to Takkasilā to study the arts under a world-renowned teacher.
He sent him off. Taking his teacher’s fee, he departed from the city and set out on the road.
At that time, Prince Brahmadatta, the son of the King of Kāsi in Bārāṇasī, having been told the same thing and sent by his father, also departed from the city and set out on that very same road.
Then Sutasoma, having traveled along the road, stopped at a hall at the city gate to rest upon a wooden plank.
He sat down. Prince Brahmadatta also went and sat on the same plank with him.
Then Sutasoma, extending a greeting to him, asked, "Friend, you are weary from the road; where have you come from?
When he replied, "From Benares," he asked, "Whose son are you? When he said, "I am the son of the King of Kāsi," he asked, "What is your name? When he said, "I am..."
When he was told, "I am Prince Brahmadatta," [the other] asked, "For what reason have you come here? He replied, "To learn a craft.
Then, using the same method, the other asked him, "You too must be weary from the road; where do you come from?
He also explained everything to him. Both of them said, "We are both Kṣatriyas, and we have come to learn a craft from the same teacher."

Saying, "Let us go," they established a bond of friendship with one another. Having entered the city and gone to the teacher's residence, they paid homage to the teacher, recounted their own birth and lineage, and explained that they had come for the purpose of learning a craft.
He accepted, saying, "Very well. They gave him the teacher's fee and began their studies.
And not only those two, but at that time one hundred other princes in Jambudīpa were also learning the craft under him.
Sutasoma, acting as their senior pupil, attained proficiency in the craft before long while instructing them.
Without going to anyone else, he [entrusted his son] to Prince Brahmadatta alone, saying, "He is my friend."
Having gone into his presence, he became a back-tutor to him and taught him the craft. In due course, the others also completed their training.
Having been granted their leave and having paid homage to the teacher, they departed, surrounding Sutasoma.
Then Sutasoma, standing on the road and sending them off, said: "Each of you [should teach] the craft to your own fathers..."
"Once you have been established in your kingdoms, you should follow my instruction," he said.
"What is it, Teacher? "On the fortnightly Uposatha days, having observed the fast, you must not carry out executions. They accepted this, saying, "Very well.
The Bodhisatta, because he was a student of the science of bodily marks (*aṅgavijjā*), [knew that] in the future, in Bārāṇasī, Prince Brahmadatta...
Knowing that "great danger will arise because of this," he advised them thus and dismissed them.
They all returned to their respective countries, displayed their skills to their fathers, and established themselves in their kingdoms.
To inform [their fathers] of their successful establishment and their adherence to his advice, they sent letters along with gifts. The Great Being—
Having heard that news, he sent back a message saying, "Be diligent.
Among them, the King of Bārāṇasī would not eat his meal without meat. For the sake of the Uposatha day, he would even set aside meat for himself.
Then one day, that meat which had been set aside was, through the negligence of the cook, [left] in the royal palace.
The dogs of the Koliyans devoured it. The cook, unable to find that meat even while wandering about with a handful of coins, thought:
"If I serve a meal without meat, I shall have no livelihood;
what indeed shall I do? Then, thinking, "There is this expedient," he went at an improper time to the raw charnel ground, and after waiting there for a moment—
Having taken the flesh from a man's thigh and cooking it until well-done, she served the meal to the king.
As soon as a piece of meat was placed upon the tip of the king’s tongue, the seven thousand taste-carrying channels were suffused; it pervaded his entire body and remained there.
For what reason? Because of his past association with her. It is said that in the immediately preceding life, he had been a *yakkha*.
Having previously sacrificed many people and eaten their flesh, he had grown fond of it.
Thinking, "If I eat in silence, this man will not tell me about this meat," he spat it onto the ground along with his saliva.
When the man said, "Eat it, Your Majesty, for it is blameless," he had the other people cleared away and [declared], "I myself [know] its blameless nature..."
“I know; what kind of meat is this? he asked. “It is indeed the meat used for consumption on previous days, Your Majesty,” [the cook] replied.
“Is it not the case that this flavor did not exist at other times? “Today it is well-cooked, Your Majesty. “Did you not cook it exactly like this before as well?
Then, perceiving him to have become silent, [the king said]: “Tell the truth; if you do not tell it, your life—”
“There is none,” he replied. Having requested immunity from punishment, he spoke the truth as it was. The king said, “Make no noise;
you have been eating meat cooked in the ordinary way—now cook human flesh for me. “Is this not difficult, Your Majesty? “Do not fear; it is not difficult.
“From where shall I obtain it regularly, Your Majesty? “Why not from the prison?”
“There are many people. From then on, he acted accordingly.
Later, when the men in the prison had run out, he said, “Now what shall I do, Your Majesty?
He replied, “Throw a bag containing a thousand coins onto the road; whoever picks it up, seize him as a thief and have him executed. He did so.
He did accordingly. Later on, when he looked about for his thousand pieces of gold out of fear of the king but could not see them, he said, "What shall I do now?

[The other replied,] "When the city is crowded at the time of the drum-roll, you should stand at a house-door, or in an alley, or at a crossroads, kill people, and take their meat. From then on, he...
Having done so, he takes the large pieces of flesh and departs. In various places, corpses are seen.
"My mother is not to be found; my father is not to be found; my brother and sister are not to be found. The sound of people lamenting is heard.
The city-dwellers, terrified and trembling, say, "Is it a lion that is devouring these people? Or a tiger?"
Looking about, wondering, "Is it eating? Or is it a *yakkha* that is eating? they saw the entrance to the wound and thought, "A man-eating thief is eating these people.
The great multitude gathered in the royal courtyard and raised a cry of protest.
The king asked, "What is it, sirs? They replied, "Your Majesty, there is a man-eating thief in this city; please have him captured."
He said, “How shall I know him? Am I even walking about protecting the city?
The great multitude, thinking, “The king has no need for the city;
we shall inform General Kāḷahatthi,” went and told him this, saying, “It is fitting that you search for the thief. He replied, “Very well, wait for seven days.”
Having sent away the great multitude with the words, "I will find and deliver the thief," he commanded his men: "Sirs, it is said there is a man-eating thief in the city;
you must lie in wait in various places and seize him.
Accepting the order with the word "Very well," they began from then on to search the city. The cook, meanwhile, in one place...
Having concealed himself at the junction of the house, he killed a woman and began to fill a basket with her thick, dense flesh.
Then those men seized him, beat him, bound his hands behind his back, and raised a great cry, "A man-eating thief has been caught! The great multitude surrounded him. Then, having thoroughly...
Having bound him hand and foot and tied him by the neck, they took him and presented him to the commander-in-chief.
Upon seeing him, the commander-in-chief thought, "Does this man eat this meat himself, or does he sell it mixed with other meat, or does he cause others to kill for his sake?
Reflecting thus, he asked about the matter and spoke the first verse:
“But why, O cook, do you perform such extremely cruel deeds?
Deluded, you kill women and men for the sake of meat or for the sake of wealth.
Therein, he addresses the cook by the term *rasaka*.
From here on, the questions and answers with their clear connections should be understood according to the Pāli text itself:
“Neither for my own sake, nor for the sake of wealth, nor for the sake of wife, children, friends, or kinsmen;
rather, my husband is the Blessed One, the protector of the earth, and he eats meat such as this, O Venerable Sir.”
“If you are engaged for the sake of my husband and are performing these most cruel deeds,
then having reached the inner palace early in the morning, you must report that matter in the presence of the king.
“I shall do so, venerable Kāḷahatthi, exactly as you say.”
“Having reached the inner palace early in the morning, I shall speak this in the presence of the king.
In this context, “Bhagavā” is a term of reverence. “If you, however,” he said while investigating: “Does he speak the truth, or does he speak falsely out of fear of death?
In this context, “terrible deeds” refers to acts that take human life. “In the presence” [of the king].
"Standing right before him, you should speak thus. Accepting this, he recited a verse.

Then the general had him laid down with his bonds still tight; when night had turned to dawn, after consulting with the ministers and the citizens, and once they had all become of one mind and guards had been stationed at every location, [he entered] the city.
Having taken hold of him by the hand, he tied a meat-basket to the butcher’s neck, took him along, and set out for the royal palace.

The entire city cried out in lamentation. For the king, having eaten his morning meal yesterday and not receiving even his evening meal, had spent that night sitting and thinking, “The butcher will arrive now; he will arrive now,” and [he thought], “Even today the butcher—”
"He does not come, yet the great clamor of the city-dwellers is heard; what could this possibly be?
Looking out through the window, he saw him being brought in that manner. Thinking, "The reason for this has become manifest," he established mindfulness and sat cross-legged right where he was.
Kāḷahatthī approached him and questioned him, and he explained the matter to him as well. Regarding that point:
Explaining this, the Teacher said:
“Then, at the end of that night, as the sun was rising,
Kāḷa took the medicinal extract and approached the king.”
Approaching the king, he spoke these words:
"Is it true, O Great King, that you have sent a poisoner?
He kills women and men, while you eat their flesh."
“In the same way, Kāḷa, this messenger was sent by me;
why do you revile him while he is acting for my benefit?
In that context, “Kāḷa” refers to the elephant Kāḷa. “In the same way” means that the king, being urged by that powerful general, spoke falsely.
Being unable to speak further, he said this. In that context, "tathā" (thus) is a synonym for the preceding word.
"My welfare" means my prosperity. "Of one who does" means of one who is performing [it]. "What is this? means why is this? "You revile me" means: "Alas, you do a difficult thing;
you, Kāḷahatthi, having not seized another thief, seize my messenger!"—thus [he spoke] to him.
He spoke, causing fear.
Hearing this, the general thought, "This man confesses with his own mouth; oh, what a reckless fellow!
For all this time, these people have been devoured by him. I shall stop him. Having thought thus, he said, "Great King, do not speak so."
“Elephant, will you not eat human flesh? “Black-elephant, what are you saying? I am unable to desist.
“Great King, if you do not desist, you will destroy both yourself and the kingdom.
“Even if it were to be destroyed, I still cannot desist from that. Then the general, for the purpose of persuading him, related a story:
Having brought them forth, he showed them, saying: "In a past time, there were six great fish in the great ocean.
Among them, Ānanda, the Timimanta, the Ajjhāroha—these three fish were five hundred yojanas long;
the Timiṅgala, the Timirapiṅgala, and the Mahātimiṅgala—these three fish were one thousand yojanas long. All of them subsisted on stone-seaweed."
They existed. Among them, Ānanda lived on one side of the great ocean. Many fish approached him to see him, and one day, thinking, "A king is known for all bipeds and quadrupeds, yet we have no king;
let us make this one our king," they all became of one mind and made Ānanda their king.
From then on, those fish went to attend upon him every evening and morning.
Then one day, while Ānanda was eating moss from a rock on a mountain, he unknowingly ate a fish, perceiving it to be "moss.
As he was eating that meat, his entire body was convulsed with pain. He thought, "What..."
Thinking, "Is this not indeed exceedingly sweet? he drew it out and, looking at it, saw a piece of fish and meat. He thought, "I have not eaten for so long;
I shall eat one or two fish whenever they come and go at evening or morning. If I eat them openly, not even a single one will approach me."
"Everyone will flee; having remained hidden, I will strike them as they retreat one after another and eat them.
Having done so, he ate them. As the fish were approaching total exhaustion, they thought, "From where indeed will danger arise for our kinsmen?
Then a certain wise fish said, "I do not approve of this conduct of Ānanda."
Thinking, "I will catch them," he remained hidden behind Ānanda’s ear as the fish approached.
After Ānanda had sent the fish away, he ate the one that was walking last of all.
When the wise fish saw his action, he informed the others. They all fled, terrified and trembling.
From that time on, Ānanda, greedy for fish and meat, took no other food. Oppressed by hunger and exhausted, he thought, "Where have these gone?
While searching for those fish, he saw a mountain and thought, "I believe they are living here depending on this mountain out of fear of me; I shall encircle the mountain and lie down to wait."
He seized him by wrapping his tail and head around both sides.

Then, seeing his own tail encircling the mountain—thinking, "If they live here, they will flee"—the fish became enraged, realizing, "This fish has deceived me and is living in reliance upon this mountain. He then [snapped] a section of his own tail measuring fifty yojanas.
Seizing it firmly with the perception that it was another fish, he chewed and devoured it; painful sensations arose.
Attracted by the smell of blood, other fish gathered and began tearing it apart and eating it until they reached its head.
Because of its great bulk, being unable to turn over, it met its end right there, becoming a heap of bones like a mountain peak. [The birds] that move through the sky...
The ascetics and wanderers spoke among the people, and the people throughout the whole of Jambudīpa came to know it.
Bringing forward that incident to demonstrate it, Kāḷahatthi said:
“Ānanda, greedy for flavors, having eaten of all kinds of fish...”
When his retinue has perished, he dies having devoured himself.
Thus the fool, intoxicated by negligence and addicted to the pride of taste, does not understand the future;
having abandoned his sons and kinsmen who lack true Dhamma, he turns back and devours only himself.
“Having heard this, let your desire depart; O King, do not eat human flesh!
Do not, like a water-lily, make this entire kingdom empty, O Lord of Men.
In that context, “Ānanda,” O Great King, refers to one named Ānanda who, in times past, was five hundred yojanas in height in the great ocean.
The great fish, the king of all fish, stood on one side of the great ocean.
"Having eaten" means having eaten the fish of his own species out of greed for their flavor. "When the assembly of fish was exhausted" means when the multitude of fish had reached its end.
"Himself" refers to himself, who—having failed to find another feeding ground—was encircling a mountain measuring fifty yojanas.
Having eaten the tail-flesh, perceiving it as another fish, he died and passed away; now, in the great ocean, he has become a heap of bones the size of a mountain.
"Thus negligent" means: just as the great fish Ānanda was, so too have you, being greedy for the flavor of craving, become negligent and fallen into a state of negligence.
"Addicted to the taste": being addicted to the taste of human flesh, he becomes one whose mind is excessively attached to it.
"A fool": if he is a fool, one of poor wisdom, he does not perceive nor understand the suffering that will arise in the future, in a time yet to come.
"Having destroyed": having demolished and annihilated. "Sons": both sons and daughters. "And kinsmen": and other remaining relatives and friends.
The meaning is: "having abandoned his children and kinsmen. Regarding the phrase "wandering about":
being oppressed by hunger because he could not obtain any other food, he wandered throughout the entire city;
failing to find human flesh, he ate himself, just as the fish Ānanda ate only itself.

"Having heard this of yours," O Great King, means: having heard this example brought by me for you, let your desire—the desire to eat human flesh—depart, vanish, and cease. "Do not eat it," O King, means: do not eat, do not consume human flesh.
Do not you, like the water-born Ānanda fish, make this entire great ocean empty. Sir.
"O Lord of bipeds, O Sovereign of men, O Great King, do not make this entire kingdom of Kāsi and your city empty of people through truth"—this is the meaning.
Having heard that, the king said, "O Kāḷahatthi, you are not the only one who knows this simile; I too know it," and out of greed for human flesh, he spoke while citing an ancient story:
“Named Sujāta by name, his own legitimate son;
he died at the exhaustion of his lifespan in the region of Jambusanda.
In just this way, Kāḷa, having eaten food of the highest flavor, [I too have reached my end].”
"Having failed to obtain human flesh, I think I shall give up my life.

In this context, "Sujāta by name" means that while the householder Kāḷahatthi was named Sujāta, his own legitimate son, born of his body, having failed to obtain—that is, not having obtained—a rose-apple heart.
"Dead" refers to how, upon the exhaustion of that rose-apple heart...

"The son of the householder is dead; even so, having eaten and consumed the supreme flavor—the meat of humans, which is the best among all other flavors—I think, 'If I do not obtain human flesh, I shall lose my life.
It is said that in the past, in Bārāṇasī, there was a householder named Sujāta who had come from the Himālaya for the sake of consuming salt and sour gruel."
Having settled five hundred seers in his own park, he attended upon them. In his house, there was a regular supply of food for about five hundred monks.
Those ascetics would sometimes wander through the countryside for alms, and sometimes they would bring back large baskets of rose-apples (*jambu*) and eat them.
At the time when they were eating the baskets of rose-apples that had been brought back, Sujāta thought: "Today, for the venerable ones..."
“Three or four days have passed without their returning; where indeed could they have gone?
Taking his little son by the finger, he went there at the time when they were finishing their meal.

At that moment, after giving water for the elders to rinse their mouths, the youngest of all was eating a piece of rose-apple (*jambu-pesi*). Sujāta, having paid homage to the ascetics, sat down and asked: “What—”
“Venerable sir, please eat,” he asked. “It is a large jambu fruit, friend,” [the ascetic replied]. Upon hearing this, the prince felt a thirst for it.
Then the eldest of the group of ascetics gave him a small portion.
Having eaten it and becoming attached to its sweet flavor, he begged again and again, saying, “Give me a jambu fruit. While listening to the Dhamma, the householder said, “My son, do not—”

Having deceived him by saying, "Go home and you shall eat," and thinking, "The venerable ones might become weary because of this man," he went home to reassure him without having asked the company of seers for permission.
From the moment he left, his son began to lament, crying out, "Give me a rose-apple fruit!
Sujāta, thinking, "I will inform the seers as well," went to the park. They...
The seers also, thinking, "We have lived here for a long time," departed for the Himālaya itself.

Not seeing the seers in the monastery, he gave him portions of rose-apple, mango, jackfruit, and wood-apple fruits mixed with honey, sugar, and flour. As soon as these were placed upon the tip of his tongue, they became like the *halāhala* poison.
Having gone without food for seven days, he reached the end of his life. The King, bringing forward this incident to illustrate his point, spoke thus.
Then Kāḷahatthi thought, “This king is exceedingly greedy for flavors;
I shall bring him other examples as well,” and said, “Great King, desist. “I am not able to desist,” the king replied.
“Your Majesty, if you do not desist, you will fall away from both your circle of kinsmen and the glory of your kingdom. For in the past—”
"Great King, right here in Bārāṇasī there was a family of physicians who observed the five precepts.
That family had an only son, who was dear and pleasing to his parents; he was wise, competent, and a master of the three Vedas.
He associated with other youths of his own age in a group. The rest of the members of that group [consumed] fish, meat, and so forth..."
They were eating and drinking liquor. The young man did not eat meat and did not drink liquor. They deliberated:
“Because he has not drunk liquor, he does not give us our share; we shall find a way to make him drink liquor.
Having gathered together, they said, “Friend, let us play a festival game. “Friend, you drink liquor, but I do not.”
“I do not drink liquor; you go ahead,” he said. “Friend, we shall have milk brought for you to drink,” they replied.
He consented, saying, “Very well. The rogues went to the park, had sharp liquor bound inside lotus leaves, and set them aside.
Then, at the time for their drink, they brought milk to the young man. Thereupon, one rogue said, “Lotus-honey!”
"Sir, bring some," he said; and having had it brought, he made a hole at the bottom of a lotus leaf-cup, placed his fingers in his mouth, and sucked.
Likewise, they had the others brought and drank. The young man asked, "What is this? "It is called 'lotus-honey' (pokkharamadhu)," they replied.
"I too shall receive a little; give me some, sirs. They gave it to him as well. He, perceiving it to be lotus-honey—
"Drink liquor! They gave him meat roasted on coals, and he ate that as well.
As he drank again and again until he was intoxicated, they said to him, "This is not lotus-honey; this is liquor.
He said, "For all this time I did not know such a sweet flavor! Bring me some liquor, sirs! They brought it to him.
They gave him more again. His thirst became great. Then, as he asked for more once more, they told him, "It is finished.
He said, "Well then, sir, bring some more," and gave them his finger-ring.
Having drunk with them all day long, he went home intoxicated, with bloodshot eyes, trembling and lamenting, and lay down. Then his father [gave him] wine...
Knowing that he had drunk it and that his intoxication had passed, the father said, "Dear son, you have done what is improper by drinking liquor, having been born into a family of Sottiyas;
do not do so again. "Father, what fault is there in me? "The fact that you drank liquor. "Father, what are you saying?
For all this time, I have never before obtained such a sweet flavor. The Brahmin—
He begged again and again. He too said, "I cannot desist.
Then the brahmin, thinking, "If this is so, our family lineage will be cut off and our wealth will perish," spoke this verse:
"Young man, you are handsome, born into a noble Sotthiya clan;
“My dear, you do not deserve to eat what is unfit to be eaten. In this context, “young man” means:
young man, you are handsome, and you are born into a clan of Sotthiyas. “To eat what is unfit to be eaten”: my dear, you do not deserve to consume that which is improper to be consumed.
Having spoken thus, he said: “My dear, desist; if you do not desist, I shall expel you from this house.”
“I shall perform an act of banishment from your kingdom,” he said. The young man replied, “Even if that were so, I am not able to give up liquor,” and spoke these two verses:
“This is but one of the flavors; why do you restrain me?”
“I shall go there where I may find such as this.
Therefore, O Brahmin, I shall depart; I will not go into your presence, you who do not rejoice at the sight of me.”
In this context, "flavors" refers to any one of the seven flavors known as salty, sour, bitter, pungent, astringent, sweet, and alkaline; this intoxicant is called the "supreme flavor.

"Sovāhan" means "I myself. "Nippatissāmi" means "I shall go out. Having said this, he added: "I will not abstain from drinking liquor; do whatever you please. Then the brahmin, saying, "If you abandon us, we too shall abandon you," spoke this verse:
"Surely, young man, we shall obtain other heirs and sons;"
"And you, O wretch, perish; go to that place where we do not hear of you having arrived, saying, 'He lives in such-and-such a place'!
Therein, "where you have arrived" means: go to that place where we do not hear of you, saying, "He dwells in such-and-such a place.
Then, having brought him for judgment and established his state of being childless, they had him expelled. Later on, he was destitute.
A certain pauper, having dressed himself in a worn-out rag and wandering for alms with an alms-bowl in his hand, died leaning against a certain wall.
Having brought forward this instance and shown it to the king,
Kāḷahatthi said, “Great King, if you do not act according to our word, they will carry out an act of banishment against you,” and he spoke this verse:
“In this very way, O King, lord of bipeds, listen to me:
they will banish you from the kingdom, just as they did the young man Soṇḍa.
Therein, “lord of bipeds” means the chief among bipeds; “O Great King, listen to my words,” he says, “in this very way they will banish you from the kingdom, just as they did the young man Soṇḍa.”
Although the simile had been presented by Kāḷahatthi in this way, the king, being unable to desist from it, spoke further to provide another illustration:
"Sujāta by name, a disciple of one whose self was developed,
Desiring a celestial nymph, he neither ate nor drank."
“Just as one might take a drop of water on the tip of a blade of grass and measure it against the water of the ocean,
so too are human pleasures compared to divine pleasures.
In this very way, Kāḷa, having eaten food of the most excellent flavor...”
“Having failed to obtain human flesh, I think I shall give up my life.
The background story (*vatthu*) is exactly as told below.
In that context, “of those who have developed themselves” (*bhāvitattānaṃ*) means of those five hundred seers whose minds were cultivated. “As if desiring a finger-snap” (*accharaṃ kāmayanto va*)...
It is said that when he realized those seers had not arrived at the time for eating the great jambu fruit, he thought, "What could be the reason they have not come?
If they have gone somewhere, I shall find out; otherwise, I will listen to the Dhamma in their presence.
Having gone to the park, he paid homage to the group of seers and sat down right there to listen to the Dhamma from the leader of the community.
When the sun had set, although he was being urged to depart, he said, "I shall stay right here today," and after paying homage to the company of seers, he entered the leaf-hut and lay down.

In the middle of the night, Sakka, the king of the gods, surrounded by a host of celestial nymphs and his own attendants, came to pay homage to the company of seers; the entire monastery became one mass of radiance. Sujāta—
Thinking, "What indeed is this?", he rose and looked through a gap in the leaf-hut;
seeing Sakka, surrounded by celestial nymphs (*accharā*), come to pay homage to the company of seers, he became inflamed with passion at the mere sight of the nymphs.
After Sakka had sat down, listened to the discourse on the Dhamma, and departed for his own abode, the householder likewise paid homage to the company of seers on the following day.
He asked, "Venerable sir, who is this that has come to pay you homage in the middle of the night?
"It is Sakka, friend," he replied. "And who are these sitting around him? "They are called celestial nymphs. Having paid homage to the group of seers, he went home;
from the moment he arrived, he lamented, "Give me a nymph! Give me a nymph!"
His kinsmen surrounded him, wondering, "Is he possessed by a spirit? and they snapped their fingers.
He said, "I am not speaking of this *accharā*; I am speaking of a celestial nymph (*devaccharā*).
Then, looking at his wife—who had been brought there adorned as an *accharā*—and also at the courtesan, he lamented, "This is no *accharā*; she is a *yakkhinī*. Give me a celestial nymph!"
Having abstained from food, he met his end right there. Thus it is said:
“Desiring but a finger-snap, he neither ate nor drank.
O Kāḷahatthi, he who measures the water of the ocean with a mere drop taken on the tip of a blade of kusa grass— [He is like one who would measure the great ocean with a single drop.]
Having taken [that drop], one might compare it with the water in the great ocean, thinking, "The water in the great ocean may be this much," yet he would only be comparing;
for the water on the tip of the blade of *kusa* grass is exceedingly small. Just as that is, so too are human sensual pleasures compared to divine sensual pleasures.
Therefore, Sujāta did not look upon another woman; longing only for an *accharā*, he died. "In the same way," thus it was said.
"Just as he gave up his life because he did not obtain celestial pleasures, so shall I also give up my life if I do not obtain human flesh, which is the most excellent of flavors," he said.

Hearing this, Kāḷahatthi thought, "This king is exceedingly greedy for flavors; I shall instruct him. Then, in order to show that even the golden swans who travel through the sky have perished after eating the flesh of their own kind, he spoke these two verses:
“Just as those Dhataraṭṭha geese, soaring through the sky,
all came to their end because they did not eat what was offered to them;
even so, O King, lord of bipeds, listen to me.”
"O King, you ate what was not to be eaten; therefore they banish you.
In this context, "by the consumption of their own kind" means by the consumption of those of one's own species.
"Have reached their end" means that all have met with death. It is said that in the past, ninety thousand swans lived in a golden cave on Mount Cittakūṭa.
They dwell there. During the four months of the rainy season, they do not go outside;
if they were to go out, being unable to fly with their bowls full of water, they would fall right back into the great ocean. Therefore, they do not go out.
However, when the rainy season has arrived, they bring wild rice grown spontaneously from a natural lake, fill their caves with it, and eat that rice.

They lived there. However, when they had entered their cave, at the entrance of the cave there was a spider named Uṇṇanābhi, about the size of a chariot wheel, who weaves a single web every month. Each thread of his web is the thickness of a cow’s hair.
Thinking, "He will break that web," the swans gave two portions to one young swan. He—
When the rain had ceased, the leader went ahead and broke through that net; the others followed by that same path.
Then, at one time, the rains fell for five months. The swans, their food supply exhausted, deliberated, "What indeed should be done?
Thinking, "As long as we live, we shall obtain eggs," they first ate the eggs, then the chicks, and finally the aged swans.
When five months had passed, the rainy season was over. The monkey had woven five nets.
Having eaten the flesh of their own kind, the swans became weak. The young swan, who was entitled to a double share, struck the net and broke four;
he was unable to break the fifth, and it remained stuck there. Then the monkey pierced his head.
He drank the blood. Another came and struck the net; he too became stuck right there. In this way, every monkey drank the blood.
Then they say, "The lineage of Dhatarattha has been destroyed. Therefore it is said: "All have gone to their destruction.
"In the same way, you too"—just as these swans ate the forbidden flesh of their own kind, so too do you.
"You are eating; the entire city has fallen into fear. Desist, O Great King!
Because he ate the meat of his own kind, which was unfit to be eaten, therefore these city-dwellers banish him from the kingdom.
The king desired to tell another simile as well, but the citizens stood up and said, "Sir General, what are you doing?"
"Are you wandering about having seized a thief who eats human flesh?
If he does not desist, banish him from the kingdom," they said, and would not allow him to speak. Having heard the talk of many people, the king became afraid and was unable to speak again.
Once more the general asked him, "Great King, will you be able to desist, or will you not?"

Having said this, when [the king] replied, "I cannot," she placed the entire retinue of concubines, as well as her sons and daughters, all adorned with every ornament, within his sight and said, "Great King, look upon these circles of kinsmen, the assembly of ministers, and the glory of sovereignty; do not perish!
Desist from eating human flesh! The king said, "These are not dearer to me than human flesh."
When he had said this and was told, "In that case, Great King, depart from this city and kingdom," he replied, "Kāḷahatthi, I have no need for kingship;
I am departing from the city, but give me a sword, a cook, and a vessel. Then, having had a sword, a vessel for cooking meat, and a basket brought up, as well as a cook—
Having given [him] away, they performed the formal act of banishment from the kingdom.
Taking his sword and his meat-broth, he departed from the city, entered the forest, and having made a dwelling at the foot of a banyan tree, he lived there.
Standing on the forest paths, he killed men and brought them back for the sake of the broth.
He gives it to him. He, too, cooks the meat and offers it to him. Thus both of them live.
When it is time to seize humans, he says, "I am the human-thief Porisāda! and once he has spoken, no one is able to maintain their composure;
they all fall to the ground. Among them, whichever one he desires, he seizes by turning that person upside down with feet upward and head downward.
Having brought it back, he gave it to the cook. One day, having returned from the forest without finding anyone there, the king said to the cook, "What is this?
When the cook replied, "It is meat," the king said, "Place the pot on the hearth. "Where is the meat, Your Majesty? "I shall obtain the meat," he said.
Thinking, "Now my life is at an end," trembling, he lit a fire on the hearth and placed the pot upon it.
Then Porisāda killed him with a sword, cooked his flesh, and ate it. From that time on, he lived alone and cooked and ate by himself.
It became renowned throughout all of Jambudīpa that "Porisāda kills those who have set out upon the road.
At that time, a certain Brahmin of great wealth was traveling for trade from the eastern region with five hundred carts.
He wandered toward the far shore. He thought to himself: "It is said that a bandit named Porisāda murders people on this road;

I shall pay him a fee and pass through this forest. Giving a thousand pieces of money to the men living near the entrance of the forest, saying, "Please escort me through the forest," he set out on the path with them as they traveled.
The Brahmin, placing all the scriptures before him, himself bathed and anointed, adorned with every ornament,
and seated in a comfortable carriage yoked with white oxen, went last of all, surrounded by those forest-dwelling men.
At that moment, Porisāda, having climbed a tree and searching among the men, [asked] the remaining people, "What..."
Thinking, "There is something here for me to eat," his desire vanished; yet from the moment he saw the brahmin, he became eager to devour him, with saliva trickling from his mouth.
When the brahmin came near him, he descended from the tree, proclaimed his name "I am Porisāda" three times, brandished his sword, and [stood] upon the sand.
It leaped forward as if filling their eyes; not even one was able to stand, and they all fell prostrate upon the ground.
Seizing the brahmin sitting in the palanquin by the feet, he hung him upside down over his back, struck him on the head with his heels, lifted him up, and set off.
Then those men stood up and said, "Friends, we took a thousand kahāpaṇas from the hand of the brahmin;
what manliness is there in us? Let us follow them for a short distance, whether we are able or not.
Having said this, they pursued them. But the man-eater, having turned back and looked around, saw no one and proceeded slowly. In that [moment]...
At that moment, a certain brave man endowed with great strength arrived there with speed. Seeing him, he leaped over a fence and stepped upon a khadira post;
the post pierced through his back foot. As he continued leaping, blood flowed profusely from it.
Then, seeing him, [the other man] said: "Sirs, he has been pierced by me; you need only follow behind, and I shall capture him."
"No," he said. Realizing his weakness, they pursued him. Knowing that he was being followed by them, he released the brahmin and ensured his own safety.
Then, from the moment the forest-dwellers had obtained the brahmin, they turned back, saying, "What use have we for this thief?"
Purisada, too, went to his own banyan tree, entered between the shoots, and lay down, saying: "Noble tree deity,
if you are able to heal my wound within seven days, I shall wash your trunk with the blood from the throats of one hundred Kṣatriyas from all over Jambudvīpa,
encircle it with their entrails, and perform an offering ceremony for you with the five kinds of sweet meat."
“I shall do so,” he said, and made his request. Since he could obtain no food, drink, or meat, his body withered away;
yet within seven days, the wound became healed. Through the power of the deity, he perceived that it had indeed been healed.
After eating human flesh for a few days and regaining his strength, he thought: “The deity has been very helpful to me; she is my patron.”
“I shall be released. Taking his sword, he emerged from the foot of the tree and set out, thinking, “I will bring the kings here.
Then, a companion yakṣa who had eaten human flesh with him during their previous existence as yakṣas saw him wandering about;
recognizing him, thinking, “This is my friend from a past life,” he asked, “Friend, do you recognize me? “No,” [he replied].
“I recognize you. Then he told him of the deeds performed in his previous existence. Having recognized him, the other offered him hospitality.

When asked, “Where were you reborn? he related everything: the place where he was reborn, the reason for his renunciation from the kingdom, his current place of residence, how he had been pierced by a splinter, and why he had gone to the deity to seek her intercession for release.
“Even you must complete this task for me; let us both go together, friend,” he said.
“Friend, I cannot go myself, but I have a certain business.
I know a single spell called ‘The Priceless Footprint Mark’ which produces strength, speed, and sound; take that spell. He accepted, saying, “Very well.”
The yakkha, having given it to him, departed.
Having mastered the spell, from that time forth Porisāda became as swift as the wind and exceedingly brave.
Within seven days, seeing one hundred kings entering their pleasure gardens and such places, he leaped forward with the speed of the wind and cried out, "O you human thieves! I am..."
Having proclaimed his name as “Porisāda,” he roared and bellowed, striking terror into them;

seizing them by their feet and turning them upside down, he struck their heads with his heels, carried them off with the force of the wind, and—having pierced holes in the palms of their hands and bound them with ropes—he suspended them from a *nigrodha* tree, with the tips of their toes touching the ground. All those kings...
As the wind blew, they hung there swaying like garlands of *milāta* and *kuraṇḍaka* flowers. "But Sutasoma is my preceptor;
if I were to take him, the whole of Jambudīpa would become empty," he thought, and so he did not take him.
He sat down, having kindled a fire, intending to perform a sacrificial offering while carving a stake. The tree deity—
Seeing that ritual act, he thought, "He is performing a sacrificial offering for me; yet I have not provided him with any relief for his wound.
Now he will bring about the great destruction of these people—what indeed should be done?
Thinking, "I shall not be able to stop him," he went into the presence of the Four Great Kings and [reported] that matter.
Having spoken thus, he said, "Stop him! When they replied, "We will not be able to stop the work of the man-eater," he asked, "Who then can do so?
Upon hearing that it was Sakka, the king of the gods, he approached Sakka, explained the matter, and said, "Please stop him.
He too replied, "I am not able to stop him; one who is capable..."
"But I shall tell you," he said. When asked, "Who is his name? he replied: "There is no one else in the world with its devas;

however, in the city of Indapattha in the kingdom of Kuru, the son of King Koravya named Sutasoma will subdue him by making him free from cruelty, restore life to the kings, cause him to abstain from human flesh, and bring the nectar [of immortality] to all of Jambudīpa."
"He will consecrate you as king according to the Dhamma; even if he wishes to grant life to kings, tell him: 'It is necessary to bring Sutasoma back and perform the sacrificial offering.
She consented, saying, "Very well," and having returned quickly, she approached him not far away in the guise of a female renunciant.
Hearing the sound of his footsteps and thinking, "Surely some king must have fled," he looked around; seeing him, he thought, "Those who have gone forth are indeed Kṣatriyas;
having captured this one, we shall complete our hundred and perform the sacrificial offering.
Raising his sword in hand, he pursued him, but even after pursuing him for three leagues, he was unable to catch up, and sweat poured from his limbs.
He thought to himself: “In the past, I could catch even an elephant, a horse, or a chariot by pursuing them as they ran;
yet today, though I run with all my might, I cannot catch this renunciant as he goes along his own way.
What could be the reason for this? Then he thought: “Renunciants are indeed obedient to words; [if I say], ‘Stop!’...”
Thinking, "I shall seize him while he stands there," he said, "Stop, ascetic!

[The other replied,] "As for me, I have stopped, but you made an effort to run. Then, saying, "Sir, those who have gone forth do not speak falsehood even for the sake of their lives, yet you have spoken a lie," he recited this verse:
“‘Stay! was what I said to you, yet you walk away with your face turned back.
You who do not stand say, ‘I am standing,’ O female practitioner of the holy life.
This is worthy of a recluse for you: you even imagine my sword to be a heron’s feather.”
The meaning of this is as follows: "O ascetic, when you were told by me, 'Stop!', you went away with your face turned away;
O practitioner of the holy life, while you yourself were not standing, you prattled, 'I am standing'; and you thought my arrow was made of heron feathers.
Then the deity spoke these two verses:
“I stand firm among those of my own dharma, O King, and I do not change my name or clan.
Yet they call one who is a thief in this world ‘unstable’—
one who, when fallen from here, is bound for the states of deprivation and hell.”
“If you have faith, O King, accept what has been heard, O Kshatriya;
having performed a sacrifice with that, you will thus go to heaven.
In this context, “among those of like dhamma,” O Great King, means that I am established in my own ten wholesome courses of action (kusalakammapatha).

"I am; I exist. As for "name and clan": formerly, in your youth, having been Brahmadatta, you obtained the kingdom of Bārāṇasī after your father passed away and became the King of Bārāṇasī. Having abandoned that name, you became Porisāda, and now you have become Kammāsapāda.
Although born into a kṣatriya family, because you ate human flesh—which is not fit to be eaten—you are [called] thus.
Just as you have changed your own name and clan, I do not change my own name and clan.
"And a thief" means that in the world they call one who does not abide by the ten courses of wholesome action a thief.
"Fallen from here" means having fallen from here, one is established in the states of misery, in hell. O Kṣatriya, protector of the earth, Great King, [heed] my word.
“If you have faith, take Sutasoma; having performed a sacrifice with that Sutasoma, you shall thus go to heaven.

“O Porisada, liar! You promised me, ‘I will bring all the kings of Jambudīpa and perform labor for you,’ yet now you bring just these weak kings. Where is Sutasoma, the eldest king upon the surface of Jambudīpa?”
“If you do not bring him back, your word will be called a lie; therefore, take Sutasoma.
Having spoken thus, the deity made her appearance as a renunciant vanish and stood in the sky, blazing like the newly risen sun in its own splendor.
Having heard her words and beheld her form, he asked, “Who are you?”
“This is the deity born in this tree. Delighted that he had seen his own deity, he said, “O Lord, King of Devas, do not worry on account of Sutasoma;
enter your own tree. Even as he watched, the deity entered the tree. At that moment, the sun set and the moon rose. Porisāda—
Skilled in the Vedāṅgas, he knew the movement of the constellations. Looking up at the sky, he thought: "Tomorrow will be the Puṣya constellation;
Sutasoma will go to the park to bathe, and I shall seize him there. However, his protection will be great;
for three leagues around, all the city dwellers will be on guard. If the protection is not yet established, [I must act] in the very first watch of the night."
Thinking, "I shall go to Migājina’s park, descend into the auspicious lotus pond,
and stand there," he went there, entered the pond, and stood with his head concealed by a lotus leaf.
By his power, the fish, turtles, and other creatures retreated and moved about in groups along the edge of the water.
But from where was this fiery power obtained? It was through the power of past practice. For during the time of the Pacceka Buddha Kasapa, he established a distribution of milk-rice tickets;

by that merit, he became possessed of great strength. Furthermore, having had a fire-hall constructed for the sake of dispelling the cold for the Saṅgha of monks, he gave fire, wood, axes for cutting wood, and hatchets; by that merit, he became possessed of fiery power.
Thus, while he had gone into the inner garden, at the time of the powerful dawn, they established a guard extending three yojanas all around.
The king also, having eaten his morning meal early, mounted the back of a magnificent, adorned elephant and departed from the city surrounded by a fourfold army.
At that time, a brahmin named Nanda from Takkasilā [brought] four hundred [pieces of gold], each worth a hundred [pieces].
Taking twenty verses, he traversed the road of one hundred *yojanas*, reached that city, and stayed in the village near the gate.
When the sun had risen, as he was entering the city, he saw the king emerging through the eastern gate; extending his hand, he wished him victory.
The king, traveling with eyes cast toward all directions, [saw] the brahmin standing on elevated ground with his hand extended.
Having seen him, he approached him on his elephant and asked:
“In what kingdom is your birthplace, and for what purpose have you arrived here?
Tell me this matter, O brahmin; what do you desire? I shall give you today whatever you wish.”
The meaning of this is as follows: "O Brahmin, in what kingdom is your birthplace?
For what purpose, for what need, and by what cause have you arrived here in this city? O Brahmin, being asked by me, tell and explain this matter and this purpose to me;
[I shall grant] that which is desired by you, to you, this very day."
“I give; what object do you desire?
Then he spoke this verse to him:
“O Lord of the Earth, four verses of profound meaning, comparable to the excellent ocean;”
“I have come here for your very sake; listen to these verses endowed with the ultimate meaning.
In this regard, “O Lord of the Earth, O Protector of the Land”—these four verses are of what nature? They are of profoundly deep meaning, comparable to the excellent ocean.
“For your very sake”: I have arrived and am present here for your benefit alone. “Listen”: [this was said] by the Kāśyapa, the Bull of the Śākyas.
"The meaning is: ‘Listen to these four hundred valuable verses taught by the Blessed One, which are connected with the ultimate truth.
Having said this, he continued: ‘Great King, these four hundred valuable verses were taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa;
having heard that you are seekers of the Dhamma, I have come to teach them to you. The king, being delighted in heart, said: ‘Teacher, ...’"
“It is well that you have come; however, I cannot turn back. Today, on account of the conjunction with the Puṣya asterism, I have come to bathe my head.
I shall come again tomorrow and listen; do not be distressed,” he said.
Then, having commanded his ministers, “Go and prepare a bed for the brahmin in such-and-such a house, and provide him with food and clothing,” he departed.
He entered the park. It was surrounded by a wall eighteen cubits high.
Elephants surrounded it on all sides, jostling one another; then horses, then chariots, then archers, and then infantry;
the army was like a turbulent great ocean, making a loud clamor. Then the king [prepared] coarse...
Having removed his ornaments, had his beard trimmed, and rubbed his body with unguents, he bathed within the lotus pond with royal splendor.
Having emerged from the water, he put on a bathing robe and stood there. Then they brought him garments, perfumes, garlands, and ornaments.
Porisāda thought: "The king will be heavy when he is fully adorned; let me seize him while he is still light."

“I shall seize him! he cried. Roaring and bellowing, churning the fish in the water and brandishing his sword above his head like a flash of lightning, he shouted his name, “I am Porisāda, the human-thief! and raising a finger to his forehead, he emerged from the water.
Upon hearing his voice, the elephant-riders [fled] with their elephants, and the horse-riders with their horses.
The chariot-riders were carried away by their chariots. The army, casting aside the weapons they had each seized, threw themselves prostrate upon the ground.
Porisāda lifted Sutasoma up and seized him; the remaining kings he took by the feet, turned upside down, and went along striking their heads with his heel.
But approaching the Bodhisatta, he stooped down, lifted him up, and set him upon his shoulder.
Thinking, "Going through the gate will cause delay," he leaped over an eighteen-cubit wall right where it stood;
then, trampling upon the frontal globes of elephants whose rut had subsided and who were intoxicated with pride—
as if felling mountain peaks— he stepped upon the backs of swift-paced mules, knocking them down, and finally stepped upon the shafts and the poles of the chariot.
As if whirling through the air, as if crushing the blue fruit-like leaves of the *nigrodha* tree, he traveled a path of three *yojanas* in a single impulse.
Looking back to see if anyone was coming after him for the sake of Sutasoma, and seeing no one, he proceeded slowly;
then, drops of water from Sutasoma’s hair fell upon his own chest.
Seeing this, he thought, "There is no one who does not fear death; even Sutasoma, it seems, weeps out of fear of death," and said:
"Truly, the wise and discerning, those of great learning who reflect on many matters, do not weep.
For this is the supreme island for men: that the wise become dispellers of sorrow."
“Yourself, or perhaps your kinsmen, your sons and wife, grain, wealth, silver, and gold—why, O Sutasoma, do you grieve?
O best of the Koravyas, let us hear your words.
In this regard, O Great King Sutasoma, what are those who are wise? They are the intelligent ones who discern what is beneficial and what is harmful, and what is the right course and what is not.
Endowed with the wisdom of knowing, possessed of wisdom, and endowed with the wisdom of discernment;

being learned, retainers of what they have heard, thinkers on many points, and by nature inclined toward reflecting on many reasons—those wise ones, when the fear of death has arisen, do not at all weep or lament out of fear.
For, O Great King Sutasoma, "a refuge indeed... [means] hi.

But why do I say this? Because, O Great King Sutasoma, just as a great island serves as a refuge for merchants whose ships have been wrecked upon the great ocean, so too is this wise man the supreme refuge for people who are without protection.
For whatever reason, those who are wise become the dispellers of grief for grieving people; therefore, you, by reason of the fear of death...
"I think," I believe, "you are lamenting. O Great King Sutasoma, for what reason do you grieve?
Is it for the sake of yourself, or for the sake of your kinsmen, or for the sake of your wife and children, or for the sake of grain, wealth, silver, and gold?
For what kind of thing, O Best of the Kauravas, O Supreme One among the inhabitants of the Kurus, O Great King, do you thus burn with remorse again and again?
“I hear these words of yours.
Sutasoma replied:
“I do not praise myself, nor my children and wife, nor wealth, nor the kingdom.”
"The ancient Dhamma practiced by the virtuous—this is the promise that causes the brahmin remorse:
'A promise was made by me to the brahmin while I stood in the sovereignty of my own kingdom;
having given this promise to the brahmin, I shall return again, guarding my truth.'"
In this regard, "I do not reproach myself" means: first, I do not weep nor grieve for my own sake;

nor do I weep or grieve for the sake of these sons and others. Furthermore, there is an ancient dharma practiced by the wise, which is called "not repenting after having made a promise"; it is that promise of mine to the brahmin [which I now fulfill].
"I am grieving"—this is the meaning. "Guarding the truth" means protecting the truth.
For that brahmin had come from Takkaśilā having taken with him the four hundred verses on the price of a cow taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa;
and I, having made him perform the duties for a guest, entered into an agreement with him, saying, "Having bathed, you shall come and listen; wait until my return," and then he departed.
"You seized me without even allowing me to hear those verses. If you release me, I shall listen to that Dhamma and, as one who guards the truth, I will return," he said.
Then Porisāda replied to him:
“I do not believe this: that a man, having escaped from the jaws of death, could happily return to the hands of his enemies.
O best of the Kauravyas, you did not come to me [in such a state].
Having been released from the hands of Porisāda, you may go to your own palace and enjoy all your desires.”
"O King, having obtained a life that is sweet and dear, how could you come back into my presence?

In this context, "happy" means having attained happiness. "Released from the jaws of death" means that because he was released from the hands of a thief such as myself, he is called one who has escaped the mouth of death; would such a person return to the hands of an enemy? I—
I do not believe these words at all; for you, O best of the Kauravyas, did not come into my presence.
You, Sutasoma, were released from the hands of the man-eater. "To your own palace" means having gone to the royal capital residence.
"Desiring pleasures" means longing for sensual desires. "Having obtained" means having regained your life, which is exceedingly dear to you—[you who were] to me.
“From where and for what reason have you come into my presence?
Hearing this, the Great Being, as undaunted as a lion, said:
“One of pure virtue would choose death; one of evil character would not choose a life of reproach.”
For that man is not protected from miserable rebirths for whose sake one might speak a falsehood:
"Even if the wind were to blow away the mountains, and the moon and sun were to fall to the ground,
and all rivers were to flow upstream, I would never speak a lie, O King."

“The sky might split, the ocean might dry up, the earth that sustains all beings might turn back its course, and Mount Meru, the mass of rock, might fly up with its very roots; but I, O King, would never speak a falsehood.
In this context, “one might choose death” means, O Porisāda, that a man of pure virtue would not, even for the sake of his life, commit even the slightest evil.
One who does not act [righteously], though endowed with virtue, might prefer death and desire it; yet for one of evil character who is censured, that life is not better.

A person of immoral conduct might even speak a falsehood for the sake of himself or others, but such a lie does not protect that man from the miserable states of existence. Even if the wind were to blow away a mountain, O friend—
"O Porisāda, having been trained together with you in the same teacher’s school, I am such a companion that I would not speak a falsehood even for the sake of my life;

why do you not believe me? Even if a wind arising from the east or other directions were to lift a great mountain into the sky like a tuft of cotton-wool, or if the moon and the sun, along with their own celestial mansions..."
They might fall upon the earth, and all the rivers might flow upstream;

O Poriyāda, if anyone were to speak such words, they would be worthy of belief. But as for the words spoken by the people to you, saying "I am speaking a falsehood," those you must certainly not believe.
Even when this was said, he still did not believe him. Then the Bodhisatta, thinking, "This man does not believe me;
I shall make him believe by means of an oath," said, "Friend Poriṣada, first let me down from the shoulder-pole;
having made an oath, I will make you believe. When he had been lowered by him and placed on the ground, he spoke while making his oath:
“Grasping both sword and spear, I shall even take an oath upon you, my friend:
released by you and freed from debt, I will return again, guarding the truth.
The meaning of this is: O friend Poriṣāda, if you so desire, [I shall return] to a kṣatriya family protected by such weapons as these.
"May I not be reborn," thinking thus, I touch the sword and the spear.
Friend, if there is anything else that other kings would not do, or whatever else you desire, I shall even take that oath for you.
Just as I have been released by you, I shall go, become free from debt to the brahmin, and returning, I will protect the truth.
Then Porisāda thought: “This Sutasoma is making an oath that no kshatriya should ever do; what use have I for him?
Whether he comes or not, I too am a kshatriya king; I shall take my own arm-blood and perform the sacrificial offering to the deity.
He is becoming excessively exhausted. Having reflected thus—
“The promise you made to the brahmin, who stood in the sovereignty of his own kingdom—
that promise, O giver of what is excellent to brahmins, keep true and come back again. In this context,
*punarāvajassu* means “you should come back again.”

Then the Great Being said to him, "Friend, do not worry; having heard the four hundred valuable verses and having made an offering to the preacher of the Dhamma, we shall return in the morning," and he spoke this verse:
"The promise that was made by the brahmin, while he stood in the sovereignty of his own kingdom— Having fulfilled that promise to the brahmin, I, guarding the truth, shall return again."
Then Porisāda said to him, "Great King, you have taken an oath that must not be made by kshatriyas;
you should remember that. He replied, "Friend Porisāda, you have known me since my childhood;
even in jest, I have never before spoken a falsehood. Now that I am established in kingship, knowing what is right and what is wrong—"
“What falsehood shall I speak? You believe me; I will bring you the sacrificial offering tomorrow.
Thus encouraged, he said, “In that case, go, Great King. If you do not come, there will be no sacrificial offering.
The deity will not accept it without you. Do not create an obstacle for my sacrificial offering,” and he sent the Great Being away.
Thus, like the moon released from Rāhu’s jaws, Nāgabala—endowed with strength and vigor—reached the city very quickly. His army [thought]:

“King Sutasoma is wise and a sweet speaker of the Dhamma; having been permitted to speak one or two words, he will subdue Porisāda and return like an elephant in rut released from a lion’s mouth. [They said: ‘These [men] [will bring] the king [back] from Porisāda’s...”
Thinking, "The great multitude will reproach me for having come after giving [the gift]," he established his camp just outside the city and remained there.
Seeing him approaching from afar, he went out to meet him, paid homage, and offered a greeting, saying, "I hope, Great King, that you were not troubled by Porisāda?
He replied, "Porisāda has done a difficult thing to me, as well as to my mother and father; such a one..."

When he said, "Even the fierce and reckless Porisāda, having heard my discourse on the Dhamma, released me," the king adorned himself, mounted the back of an elephant, and entered the city surrounded by attendants. Seeing him, all the citizens were filled with joy.
Out of reverence for the Dhamma and a thirst for the Dhamma, he did not even look at his parents, thinking, "I shall see them later."
Having entered the royal palace and sat upon the royal throne, he summoned the brahmin, ordered his hair and beard to be trimmed,
and had him brought back after his hair and beard were shaved, he was bathed, anointed, and adorned with garments and ornaments. When the brahmin had been presented,
the king himself subsequently bathed, had the brahmin fed his own meal, and once he had finished eating, he himself...
Having eaten and having had him seated upon a magnificent couch, out of reverence for the Dhamma, he offered him worship with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings.
Then, sitting himself on a low seat, he requested: "Teacher, let us hear the verses worth a hundred pieces of gold which were brought to me by you.
To illustrate this matter, the Teacher spoke this verse:
“Released from the hands of the man-eater, he went to that brahmin and said this:
‘I shall hear the verses worth a hundred, O Brahmin, which, when heard by me, will be for my welfare.
In this context, *etadavoca* means “he said this.”
Then, at the time of being requested by the Bodhisatta, the brahmin rubbed his hands with perfumes, took out from a bag a beautiful manuscript,
and holding it with both hands, said: "In that case, Great King,

listen to these four hundred verses worthy of being remembered, taught by the Perfectly Self-Awakened One Kassapa, which intoxicate the senses with passion and the like, and lead to the attainment of the deathless, great Nibbāna."
Having spoken thus, looking down at the manuscript, he said:
“O Sutasoma, association with the virtuous occurs but once;
that association protects one, whereas frequent association with the unvirtuous does not.”
“One should associate only with the virtuous, one should cultivate intimacy with the virtuous;
by understanding the true Dharma of the good, one becomes better, not worse.
Indeed, even beautifully decorated royal chariots wear out, and the body likewise succumbs to decay.”
The Dhamma of the virtuous does not age; indeed, the virtuous proclaim it to those who are virtuous.
"The sky is far, and the earth is far; they say the further shore of the ocean is far;
yet they say that which is even further than these is the Dhamma of the virtuous compared to that of the unvirtuous, O King."
In this context, "sakideva" means only once. "Sabbhi" means by virtuous persons (sappurisa).
"Sā naṃ" means that association and meeting with those virtuous persons—even if it occurs only once—protects and guards that individual.

However, "nāsabbhi" means that association and dwelling in the same place for a very long time with non-virtuous persons (asappurisa) does not protect one; the meaning is that it does not become stable.
"Should sit together" means one should sit with them; the meaning is that one should carry out all postures (iriyāpatha) only in the company of the wise.

"Familiarity" refers to intimacy with friends. "The true Dhamma of the virtuous" refers to the true Dhamma of the wise—the Buddhas and others—consisting of the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma).
"This is better": having understood this Dhamma, there is only progress; the meaning is that there is no decline whatsoever.
*Rājaratha* means chariots fit for kings to ride in. *Sucitta* means well-adorned or well-crafted.
*Pavedayanti sabbhi* means that the Buddhas and others who are "good" (*sabbhi*)—a term used for those who are virtuous—proclaim and praise the beautiful, supreme Nibbāna.
That Dhamma of the good, known as Nibbāna, does not undergo decay; it does not age. *Nabha* means the sky. *Dūra* means far.
For the earth has a foundation and is graspable, while space is without support and without foundation;

thus, although these two are joined together, they are called "far apart" in the sense of being disconnected and in the sense of being untainted. "The further shore" means the opposite bank from this side. "So they say" means they have said that.
Thus the Brahmin, having taught four hundred verses according to the method taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa, remained silent.
It came to pass. Having heard it, the Great Being, with a heart full of joy, thought, "Truly fruitful has been my coming!
He reflected, "These verses were spoken neither by a disciple, nor by a seer, nor by anyone at all; they were spoken by the Omniscient One himself.
What indeed would be their value? Then he considered, "Even if this entire world-system, up to the Brahma-world, were filled with the seven treasures..."
"Even if he were to give [it] after having made [the preparations], he would not be able to act in a fitting manner.
However, I am capable of giving him sovereignty over the kingdom of Kururaṭṭha, three hundred yojanas in extent, in the city of Indapatta, seven yojanas in size.

Does he have the fortune to exercise sovereignty?"—thus looking with the power of the science of bodily marks (aṅgavijjā), he saw none. Then, looking at the position of commander-in-chief and so forth...
Without seeing even the fortune of a single village headman, but looking instead for the acquisition of wealth,
he looked starting from ten million pieces of gold; seeing the fortune of only four thousand kahāpaṇas, he thought,
"I shall honor him with this much," and had four bags of four thousand coins given [to him], saying, "Teacher, after you have taught these verses to other kṣatriyas..."
“How much wealth do you receive? he asked. “One hundred for each verse, Great King;
therefore they have come to be known as ‘the hundred-price’ ones. Then the Great Being said to him, “Teacher, you do not even know the value of the merchandise you yourself have taken up to sell;
from now on, let each verse be known as ‘the thousand-price’ one,” and he spoke this verse:
“‘These verses are worth a thousand; these verses are certainly not worth a hundred.
O Brahmin, quickly accept four thousand [pieces of gold]. The meaning of this is:

‘O Brahmin, these verses are worth a thousand—that is, they are worth a thousand [pieces of gold]; let it not be that these verses are worth only a hundred. O Brahmin, you should quickly accept four thousand [pieces of gold].’”
Then, having given him a comfortable carriage and commanded his men, "Escort the brahmin safely to his home," he dismissed him.

At that moment, a great sound of applause arose: "Excellent, excellent! King Sutasoma has honored the Satāraha Gāthā by making it Sahassāraha! Hearing that sound, his parents asked, "What is that sound?"
Having asked, "Is this not so? and having heard the truth of the matter, they became angry with the Great Being out of greed for their own wealth.
He, too, dismissed the brahmin and went into their presence; having paid homage, he stood there.
Then his father, without even offering him a mere word of greeting, said, "How is it, my son, that you have escaped from the hands of such a violent thief?"
Out of greed for his own wealth, he asked, "Is it true, dear son, that after hearing four verses, you gave away four thousand [pieces of gold]? When he replied, "It is true," he spoke this verse:
"Whether a verse be worth eighty, ninety, or even a hundred pieces of gold;..."
“Know for yourself alone, Sutasoma, what verse is worth a thousand. The meaning of this is:

“My dear, as for what is called a ‘verse,’ it might be worth eighty, ninety, or even a hundred [coins]; know for yourself alone: what verse is there that is worth a thousand, and in whose presence does such a one exist?
Then the Great Being, making him understand, said: “My dear, I do not desire increase through wealth; rather, I desire it through learning.”
“I desire for myself the growth of wisdom through learning, so that the virtuous may regard me as one who is peaceful.
For I am never satiated by well-spoken words, my dear, just as the great ocean is never filled by flowing rivers.
Just as a fire burning grass and wood is never sated, nor the ocean by the rivers.”
"Even so, O best of kings, those wise ones are not satiated by hearing well-spoken words.
'O Lord of Men, whenever I hear even a single meaningful verse from Sakka’s servant, I listen to it with great care;
for indeed, dear father, there is no satiety for me in regard to the Dhamma.'"
In this context, *voti* is merely a particle. "May these 'peaceful ones' associate with me"—this is what I desire. "By means of rivers" means by means of streams.
"As for my own," let alone a brahmin, Nanda; even when I hear [these words] from the mouth of my own slave:
"Father, there is no satiety for me in the teachings."
Having spoken thus, and having made an oath, saying, "Father, do not revile me on account of wealth; I will return after hearing the Dhamma," he has now come back.
"Now I shall go into the presence of Porisāda; take this kingdom of yours," he said, offering up the kingdom and reciting this verse:

“This kingdom of yours, with its wealth and its equipment, with its own life-force and endowed with all objects of desire—why, for the sake of sensual pleasures, do you revile me? I am going into the presence of Porisāda.
In this context, *ñatte* means “in the presence.”
At that moment, the heart of King Pitu grew hot. Saying, "Dear Sutasoma, what is this you say? We shall capture the bandit with a fourfold army," he spoke this verse:
"These elephant-riders, chariot-warriors, and foot-soldiers, as well as the horsemen and archers, exist for the protection of oneself;
let us employ the army and slay the enemy."

In that context, "Let us slay him" means: if the army mobilized in this manner is unable to capture him, then let us go and capture him along with all the inhabitants of the kingdom and slay the enemy; let us kill our adversary.
Then his mother and father, their faces filled with tears, weeping and lamenting, entreated him, saying, "Dear son, do not go; you must not go.
The sixteen thousand female dancers and the rest of his attendants also [cried out], "Leaving us behind as orphans..."
"Where are you going, O Lord? they lamented. No one in the entire city was able to remain composed;
everyone cried out, "It is said that Sutasoma has returned after giving his promise to the man-eater.
Now, having heard the four hundred precious stanzas and having paid honor to the preacher of the Dhamma, he will again go to the presence of the robber, having paid homage to his parents."
"He will go!"—thus the entire city was filled with a single uproar. Having heard the words of his parents, he spoke this verse:
"Porisāda performed a most difficult task when, having seized me alive, he released me.
Remembering such a prior service as that, O lords of men, how could I betray him?"

In that context, "having seized the living being" means having seized him by the life-force. "Such as that" means of such a kind as was performed by him. "Former service" means prior assistance. "O Lord of Men" is an address to his father.
Having comforted his mother and father, saying, "Mother and Father, do not worry about me;

I have performed what is wholesome, and for me the sovereignty of the peak of the six realms of existence is not difficult to obtain," he paid homage to his parents, took leave of them, and [addressed] the remaining people.
Having instructed them, he departed. To elucidate this matter, the Teacher said:
“Having paid homage to his father and mother, and having instructed the city-dwellers and the army, that speaker of truth, guarding his truthfulness, went to where Porisāda was.”
In this context, "guarding the truth" means protecting the truth.
"He went" means that having stayed at his residence that night, on the following day at the time of sunrise, he paid homage to his parents, took leave of them, and instructed the rest of the people;
then, followed by a great multitude including his wives and attendants who were weeping with tearful faces and lamenting in various ways, he departed from the city.
Being unable to turn back that crowd, he drew a horizontal line across the main road with his staff and said,
"If you have any affection for me, do not cross this. The great multitude, unable to transgress the command of one so virtuous and majestic,
wailed with a great cry and watched him as he went with the stride of a lion.
When he had passed beyond the range of sight, [Sutasoma] entered the city crying out with a single voice.
He too went into his presence by the very path by which he had come. Therefore it is said: "He went to where Porisāda was.
Then Porisāda thought: "If my friend Sutasoma wishes to come, let him come; if he does not wish to come..."
“Let the tree deity come; let her do whatever she desires for me. Having killed these kings, we shall perform a sacrificial offering with the five kinds of sweet meat.
