Having thus prepared the funeral pyre and kindled the fire, while Porisāda sat sharpening his stake, thinking, “Let it first become a heap of glowing coals,” Sutasoma arrived. Then Porisāda, seeing him, was filled with joy.
“Friend, have you gone and performed the duty that was to be done? he asked. To show, “Yes, Great King, I have heard the verses taught by the Dasa-balas Kassapa;
I have also rendered honor to the preacher of the Dhamma; therefore, it can be said that I have gone and performed the duty that was to be done,” the Great Being spoke this verse:
“A pact was made by me with the brahmin while I stood in sovereignty over my own kingdom.
To keep that pact true, O excellent giver to brahmins, I have returned.
Perform the sacrifice; eat me, Porisada!”
In that context, "yajassu" means: "Having killed me, perform a sacrifice for the deity, or eat my flesh.
Having heard this, Porisāda thought, "This king is not afraid; he speaks having become free from the fear of death.
What indeed is the power behind him? Then he reflected, "There is nothing else; this is a verse taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa."
“‘I have heard it,’ she says; surely this must be due to their supernatural power (*āsubhāva*). I too will have her speak it, and I shall hear those verses;
in this way, I too will become fearless. Having thus made his resolve, he spoke this verse:
“The food I have eaten does not diminish later; for this funeral pyre is still full of smoke.”
"In a smokeless fire, well-cooked and thoroughly ripened—may I hear verses that are worth a hundred.
In this context, "eaten" means the act of eating. That eating of mine, whether later or earlier, does not diminish;
for even later, you are indeed to be eaten by me. "Cooked in a smokeless fire" means in a fire that is smokeless and without flames.
"Meat that is well-cooked is called 'well-prepared'.
Hearing this, the Great Being thought, "This Porisāda is of evil character; having restrained him slightly and put him to shame, I shall speak. He then said:
"You are unrighteous, O Porisāda; you have fallen from your kingdom for the sake of a belly."
"These verses speak of the Dhamma; where do Dhamma and non-Dhamma coincide?
"For one who is unrighteous, cruel, and constantly blood-stained, there is no truth, much less Dhamma; what will you do with your learning?"
In this context, the verse beginning with "dhammañcima" refers to the nine supramundane states (*navalokuttaradhamma*). "Where do they meet? means where do they converge?
For the Dhamma leads to a happy destination or to Nibbāna, whereas non-Dhamma leads to an unhappy destination.

"From where is the Dhamma? means that there is not even a mere truth in speech; from where, then, could the Dhamma arise? "What is the use of what has been heard? means: what benefit do you derive from this learning?
"You will do so, for you are like a clay vessel that is not a fit receptacle for lion fat—so you are for the Dhamma.

Even when this was said, he did not become angry. Why? Because of the greatness of the Great Being’s cultivation of loving-kindness (*mettā*). Then, saying, "But friend Sutasoma, am I alone unrighteous?", he spoke this verse:
"One who would go hunting for the sake of meat, or one who would kill a man for the sake of his own self—"
"Both of them, having passed away, become equal; why then do you call me one who acts contrary to the Dhamma?

In this context, "why then" means: why do you not speak of those kings on the surface of Jambudīpa who, adorned and arrayed, accompanied by great armies, mounted on excellent chariots, go out hunting and kill deer by piercing them with sharp arrows? Why do you speak of me alone?
"He says it is unrighteous," he said. "If they are blameless, then I too am blameless," he demonstrated.
Having heard that, the Great Being spoke this verse, shattering his [the other's] dogmatic view:
"Five by five, there are no edible things for a wise Kshatriya."
"O King, you eat what is not to be eaten; therefore, you are unrighteous.

The meaning of this is: "Good Porisāda, by one who is a kṣatriya and knows the duty of a kṣatriya, ten creatures—five each such as elephants and so forth—are indeed not 'eatables' (*bhakkhā*), that is, they are not fit to be eaten for the sake of meat. 'Not...'"
Or rather, that is the reading. According to another interpretation:

when a Kshatriya knows the duty of a Kshatriya, among the five-clawed animals there are only these five creatures that are fit to be eaten—the hare, the porcupine, the monitor lizard, the monkey, and the tortoise—and no others.
Yet you eat human flesh, which is unfit to be eaten; therefore, you are unrighteous.
Thus, having been rebuked and seeing no other way out, he spoke this verse while concealing his own evil deed:
“You were released from the hands of Porisāda and went to your own palace, enjoying all your desires;
yet you have now come back into the hands of your enemy. You are not skilled in the duty of a noble king.”
In this context, "you are not skilled in the dhamma of a kshatriya" means that you are not proficient in the science of policy (nītisattha) known as the dhamma of a kshatriya;
you do not know what is beneficial or harmful for yourself, yet your reputation as a wise man has spread throughout the world without any real cause.
"But I do not see or know your state of wisdom; you are exceedingly foolish," he says.

Then the Great Being said to him, “Friend, one who is skilled in the duty of a noble (khattiya) must indeed be like me. For I know that duty, yet I do not practice for its sake,” and he spoke this verse:
“Those who are skilled in the duty of a noble generally become denizens of hell;
therefore, having abandoned the duty of a noble, I have returned here as one who guards the truth.”
“Sacrifice the sacrifice; eat me, O man-eater!

In this context, “skilled” means skilled in practicing for that purpose. “For the most part” means that the majority are destined for hell. Those, however, who are not reborn there are reborn in the remaining states of misery.
Porisāda said:
“Palaces to dwell in, lands, cattle, and horses, women as desired, and Kāsī cloth and sandalwood—all these you shall obtain there, O Lord of Men. What benefit do you see in truth?
In this passage, “palaces to dwell in” means, dear Sutasoma, celestial mansions suitable for the three seasons.
There were three palaces for her residence. "Earth, cows, and horses" means there were many earths, cows, and horses.
"Women desired" means women who were the objects of desire. "Kāsī cloth and sandalwood" means Kāsī garments and red sandalwood.
"All that and so forth" means all those things and other articles of enjoyment and utility—all of that was yours in your own city, O Mistress.
"O Lord, having become a master, you are able to enjoy everything exactly as you wish;
yet, having abandoned all this, you have come here as a guardian of truth. What benefit do you see in truth?
The Bodhisatta replied:
“Whatever flavors exist on this earth, truth is the sweetest of those flavors;
established in truth, recluses and brahmins cross to the further shore of birth and death.
In this context, “the sweetest” means that all flavors become excellent and sweet for sentient beings only at the time of truth.

Therefore, truth is the most excellent of tastes; or rather, because those who abide in the truth of abstinence and the truth of truthful speech cross over and reach the Deathless Great Nibbāna, the further shore of the threefold round of existence known as birth and death—for that reason also, it is the most excellent.
Thus the Great Being spoke of the benefits of truth. Then Porisāda [beheld] his face, which was as beautiful as a blooming lotus or the full moon.
Looking at his face, [the king] thought, “This Sutasoma sees a bed of glowing coals and a stake being carved, yet not even a trace of fear arises in his mind;
what could this be—the power of the ‘Verses Worth a Hundred Thousand,’ or the power of Truth, or perhaps some other influence?
Thinking, “I shall ask him first,” he spoke this verse as he questioned him:
“You have been released from the hands of the man-eater and, having gone to your own palace, you may enjoy all your desires;
yet you have come back again into the hands of your enemy. Surely, O Lord of Men, you have no fear of death, for you are one whose heart is undaunted and who speaks the truth.”
The Great Being, explaining this to him, said:
"Many kinds of good deeds have been performed by me, and vast, praised sacrifices have been offered;
the path to the world beyond has been purified—established in the Dhamma, who would fear death?"
“I have performed many kinds of wholesome deeds; sacrifices have been offered by me that were vast and praised.
I shall go to the next world without remorse; offer the sacrifice, O Porisada, and give me to him.
“Both my father and mother are supported by me; my sovereignty is exercised righteously and is praised.”
The path to the world beyond has been purified; established in the Dhamma, who would fear death?
"My father and mother have been supported by me, and my sovereignty was exercised in accordance with the Dhamma.
I shall go to the world beyond without remorse; perform your sacrifice, O Porisada, and give me to them."
“Services have been rendered by me to kinsmen and friends; my sovereignty has been praised through righteousness.
The path to the world beyond has been purified; established in the Dhamma, who would fear death?
Services have been rendered by me to kinsmen and friends; my sovereignty has been praised through righteousness.”
“I shall go to the next world without remorse; offer the sacrifice, O Porisada, and give me.
“Gifts have been given by me in many ways to many, and ascetics and brahmins have been satisfied;
the path to the next world has been purified. Established in the Dhamma, who would fear death?”
“I have given gifts in many ways to many people, and I have satisfied ascetics and brahmins.
Without regret, I shall go to the other world; perform your sacrifice, O Porisada, and give me as an offering.
In this context, *kalyāṇā* means those of wholesome deeds. *Anekarūpā* means manifold, by way of giving and so forth. *Yaññā* refers to the relinquishing of the ten bases for giving.

"Even sacrifices that are extremely vast, praised by the wise, and performed and offered—[if one is] 'established in the Dhamma,' who like me, thus firmly grounded in the Dhamma, would fear death? 'Without remorse' means being without regret.
'My sovereignty is praised as being according to the Dhamma' means that without violating the tenfold duty of a king, I have governed the kingdom solely through the Dhamma."
He performs duties toward kinsmen as a kinsman’s duty, and duties toward friends as a friend’s duty. "Giving" (dāna) refers to volition (cetanā) together with its physical basis.

"In many ways" (bahudhā) means by way of many modes. "To many" (bahūnaṃ) does not mean five, nor ten, but rather those to whom it has been given—whether a hundred, a thousand, or even a hundred thousand.
"Satisfied" (santappitā) means they were thoroughly gratified after being filled with whatever vessels they took.
Hearing this, Porisāda became terrified and trembling, thinking: "This Great King Sutasoma is a true man endowed with wisdom and a sweet speaker of the Dhamma;
if I were to devour him, my head would split into seven pieces, or the earth would open up and swallow me.
Saying, "Friend, you are not one fit to be eaten by me," he spoke this verse:
“A man might disregard a venomous snake, capable of killing right where it is, blazing with fierce heat;
yet his head would shatter into seven pieces if he were to disregard such a speaker of truth.

In this context, *visaṃ* refers to the halāhala poison, capable of causing death on the spot. *Jalitaṃ* means blazing with its own poisonous heat; *uggatejaṃ* means moving like a mass of fire. Or rather, he might seize the venomous snake by the neck.
Thus, having said to the Great Being, "You are like the *halāhala* poison; who would eat you?", he requested him because he wished to hear the verses.

Although the Great Being declined, saying, "You are not a vessel for such blameless verses," in order to generate reverence for the Dhamma, [the king] thought, "There is no wise man equal to this one in all Jambudīpa; if he escapes from my hands..."
Having gone there and heard those verses, he paid honor to the preacher of the Dhamma; then, taking Death upon his forehead, he returned and,
having developed an even greater reverence for hearing the Dhamma, thinking, “These verses must be exceedingly excellent,” he spoke this verse while entreating him:
“Having heard the Dhamma, men understand what is wholesome and what is evil;
even after hearing just a single verse, my mind delights in the Dhamma.

The meaning of this is: “O Sutasoma, men indeed, upon hearing the Dhamma, come to know both the auspicious and the wicked; perhaps, having heard those verses, my mind too might delight in the Dhamma of the wholesome paths of action.”
Then the Great Being, thinking, "Now Porisāda wishes to hear;
I shall speak," said, "In that case, my friend, listen well," and having made him lend an attentive ear, he praised the verses according to the very sequence spoken by the brahmin Nanda.
While a great clamor arose among the gods of the six sense-sphere heavens and the deities offered shouts of approval, he preached the Dhamma to Porisāda:
“Indeed, O Great King, there is meeting with the virtuous;
that association protects one, not frequenting the company of the unvirtuous.
One should sit together only with the virtuous; one should cultivate intimacy only with the virtuous.”
“Having understood the true Dhamma of the virtuous, one becomes better, not worse.
Indeed, even beautifully adorned royal chariots wear out, and the body likewise succumbs to decay;
but the Dhamma of the virtuous does not decay—this is what the good proclaim to the good.”
“The sky is far and the earth is far, they say the further shore of the ocean is far;
yet they say that which is even farther than those is the Dhamma of the virtuous compared to that of the wicked.
Because he had spoken so well and because of his own wisdom, those verses were [regarded] as having been spoken by an omniscient Buddha.
As he reflected thus, his entire body was filled with five-colored rapture (*pīti*);
the Bodhisatta’s heart became soft, and he regarded him as if he were his own father who had given him the white parasol.
He thought, "I see no gold or silver that I can give to Sutasoma; however, for each verse he recites, I shall grant him one boon."
Having reflected, he spoke this verse:
“O Lord of Men, having heard these verses of yours—meaningful, well-phrased, and beautifully spoken—I am joyful, glad, cheerful, and delighted. O Noble One, I grant you four boons.”
In this context, *ānandī* means "one who has become joyful. The remaining terms are synonyms for that very state. All four of these are simply modes of satisfaction.
Then the Great Being, seeking to test him by asking, "What boon indeed will you grant? spoke this verse:
"You who understand for yourself death, Benefit and harm, the states of ruin and heaven;..."
“Greedily intent on flavors and ill-conducted, what boon will you grant,
O one of evil nature? If I were to urge you, ‘Give me a boon,’ and you, having given it, were not to fulfill it—
what wise person, knowing this, would enter into such a visible quarrel and dispute as this?”
In that context, "you" refers to you who do not perceive nor understand even your own death, thinking, "I am subject to death," yet continue to perform only evil deeds.
"Beneficial and harmful" means you do not know: "This action of mine is beneficial; this is harmful;
this will lead to the lower realms; this will lead to heaven. "Taste" refers to the taste of human flesh. "Censure" means one would speak [of it as such]. Not...
"Should you refuse," means that even when spoken to with the words, "Give me a boon," having already granted it by word, you should not refuse or give it.
"Should he enter into this," means what wise person would enter into this quarrel?
Then Porisāda, thinking, "This man does not trust me; I shall make him trust me," spoke this verse:
“A person does not deserve to give that boon which, once given, one would not take back;
O noble one, give the boon without wavering, even if it means sacrificing your own life.
In this context, “without wavering” means without shrinking back.
Then the Great Being thought, "This one speaks as if he were exceedingly brave; he will surely follow my word, so I shall choose a boon.
However, if I were to request this boon first—that 'human flesh must not be eaten'—he would be greatly distressed.
Therefore, I will first take the other three boons and afterwards take this one. Having reflected thus, he said:
“The noble one’s friendship accords with the noble, the wise one’s accords with the wise;
may one see such a person healthy for a hundred years—this is the first of boons that I choose. In this context, “of the noble one” means of one who is noble in conduct.
“Friendship” means the state of a friend, the quality of a companion. “The wise one” means one possessed of wisdom.

"Endowed with knowledge. "He meets [with it]" means he flows together with it, like the waters of the Gaṅgā with the waters of the Yamunā; for beings flow together according to their elements (*dhātu*).
"He would see" means that Sutasoma, desiring long life for the man-eater, first requested the boon of his own life.
For it is improper for a wise person to say, "Give me my life"; moreover—
Thinking, "He will be pleased, thinking, 'He desires health for me alone,'" he spoke thus.
Upon hearing this, the other was delighted, thinking: "This man, having destroyed my sovereignty, now desires my very life;
to such a great thief who causes me such immense harm, he desires my life alone—oh, how he wishes me well! Thus, with a joyful mind, he deceived him.
Not knowing that the boon had already been taken, as he was about to grant that boon, he spoke this verse:
“Between the noble and the noble, friendship is fitting; between the wise and the one possessed of wisdom, it is fitting.
You have seen me for a hundred years free from illness; I grant you this first of boons.”
Therein, "of the boons" refers to the first of the four boons.
Then the Bodhisatta said:
"Those who are Kshatriyas here, protectors of the earth, consecrated on the head and given their names;"
“Do not give such a one as that to the lord of the earth; this is the second boon I choose.

In this context, “given the name ‘Muddhābhisitta’” means they were given the name “Muddhābhisitta” because they had been consecrated upon the head. “Do not give such a one” means do not give such a khattiya; do not eat him.
Thus, while taking the second boon, he chose the boon of life for hundreds of khattiyas. As the man-eater was granting it, he said:
“Those Kṣatriyas here who are protectors of the earth, consecrated on the head and given their names—I do not give such lords of the earth; this I give as the second of the boons.
But did they hear their voices, or did they not? They did not hear everything. For by Porisāda—
Fearing the danger and alarm caused by the mass of smoke from the tree, they retreated and lit a fire;
sitting between the fire and the tree, the Great Being conversed with him, so that they heard only fragments of what was said.
They reassured one another, saying, "Now Sutasoma will subdue Porisāda; do not be afraid."
At that moment, the Great Being spoke this verse:
“More than a hundred of those kṣatriyas have been captured; they are weeping, their faces bathed in tears.
Restore them to their own kingdom; this is the third boon I choose.”
In that context, "more than a hundred" means exceeding one hundred. "Taken by you" means taken by you. "Bound upon the palms" means bound upon the palms of the hands.
Thus, while taking his third boon, the Great Being chose the boon of the restoration of those kṣatriyas to their own kingdom.
For what reason? Even though he did not eat them, out of fear of enmity, he would have made them all his slaves and kept them dwelling only in the forest, having slain [their enemies].
Or he might abandon them, or take them to the borderlands and sell them; therefore, he chose the boon of returning them to their own country.
As the other was granting it, he spoke this verse:
“More than a hundred nobles have been taken by me—plunged into pits, weeping with tearful faces.”
“I shall restore your kingdom to you; this I grant as the third of your boons.
But when the Bodhisatta was about to take the fourth boon, he spoke this verse:
“Your kingdom is riven, for men are shaken by fear; many people have entered into hiding places.”
“O King, abstain from human flesh; this I choose as the fourth of the boons.
In that context, “riddled with holes” means it is not densely populated, being full of gaps here and there due to the presence of villages and such.
“Trembling with fear” means they were shaking out of terror at the thought, “Purisada will come now. “Having entered their shelter” means...
Taking the children by the hands, she entered a place of concealment such as a thicket of grass.
"Human flesh"—abandon this foul-smelling, loathsome, and repulsive human flesh. Or, [the accusative case] is used in the sense of the ablative; the meaning is: "Desist from human flesh.

When this was said, Porisāda clapped his hands and, laughing, said: "Friend Sutasoma, what is this you are saying? How could I give you this boon? If you wish to take one, take another! Having said this, he spoke this verse:
“Truly, that food is pleasing to my mind; it was for its sake that I entered this forest.
How could I desist from this? May I choose another boon as the fourth.
In this context, “this forest” refers to the fact that he has entered this forest after abandoning his kingdom.

Then the Great Being said to him, “You say, ‘Because human flesh is more dear to me, I am unable to abstain from it. For he who commits evil on account of what is dear is a fool. Having said this, he spoke the verse:
“O Lord of Men, one such as you does not truly think, ‘This is dear to me,’ yet disregarding his own self, he pursues what is dear.
One’s own self is better than anything else; what is dear may be obtained later by one who has practiced the true goal.”

In this regard, O Lord of Men, such a youth—one who is handsome and of great renown—does not, out of greed for a beloved object thinking "this indeed is dear to me," abandon himself therein, fall from all happy destinies and specific states of happiness, and cast himself into hell;
thus, he does not indulge in what is dear. And it is the supreme good: for to a person, one's own self is indeed more excellent than any supremely beloved object.

"What is the reason? [The Elder replied: "Because it is possible to obtain what is dear. For that which is called "dear" can indeed be obtained—both in this life and in the next—by means of sense objects, by merit, and by the sense of being well-established and increased, having attained the prosperity of gods and humans.

When this was said, Porisāda, overcome with fear, thought: "I am unable to relinquish the boon granted by Sutasoma, nor can I refrain from eating human flesh; what indeed shall I do? With eyes full of tears, he spoke this verse:
“Human flesh is dear to me, Sutasoma, know this;
it is not possible for me to turn back. Choose another boon, my good man.
Therein, “know this” means: you too should understand.
Then the Bodhisatta said: “He who,
thinking ‘this is dear to me,’ seeks to protect what is dear, yet disregards his own self-interest and indulges in those dear things—
he, like a drunkard who has drunk poison-mixed liquor, becomes miserable because of that very thing in the future.”
“He who here, having abandoned dear things through reflection, practices the noble Dhamma even with difficulty— he,
like one who has drunk medicines while still suffering, becomes happy thereby in the future.
In this context, “he who,” O Porisāda, refers to that person who, thinking “this is dear to me,” [abandons] himself to evil deeds...

Having abandoned dear things, he pursues them; like a drunkard who, having drunk liquor mixed with poison, suffers from that evil deed in the hells and other realms hereafter. "Having reflected" means having known and weighed.
"Having abandoned dear things" means having discarded those dear things associated with unrighteousness (*adhamma*).
When this was said, Porisāda, lamenting piteously, spoke this verse:
“Having abandoned my father and mother, and the five delightful strands of sensual pleasure, I have entered the forest for the sake of this [man]. What boon, then, will you grant me?”
In that context, "of this" refers to human flesh. "What, indeed, great? means: "Having made it so, I shall grant you that boon.
Then the Great Being spoke this verse:
"The wise do not speak words with double meaning; the virtuous remain true to their promise."
“You said to me, ‘Choose a boon, good sir,’ yet you speak thus; for it does not accord with you.
In this context, “twofold” means: good sir Poriyāda, the wise do not utter a second word that contradicts what they have already said once.
“Thus you spoke to me” means: “Good sir Sutasoma, choose a boon,” in this way you addressed me.
“Thus he spoke; therefore, that which you said then does not now accord with what you say.
Weeping again, he spoke this verse:
“Loss of merit, ill-repute, lack of fame, much evil, misconduct, and defilement—”
“I have come here for the sake of human flesh; what boon could you give me?

In this context, “evil” (*pāpa*) refers to that which has not yet reached the path of action (*kamma-patha*). “Misconduct” (*duccarita*) refers to that which has reached the path of action. “Defilement” (*kilesa*) refers to suffering (*dukkha*).
“For the sake of human flesh” means for the purpose of human flesh. “I have come” (*upāgā*) means I have approached. “That to you” (*taṃ te*) means that [boon] for you.
He said, "What boon shall I grant? Do not stop me! Have compassion and pity for me; choose another boon.
Then the Great Being said:
"A person does not deserve to grant that boon which, once granted, cannot be taken back."
“Choose a boon, O steadfast one, without wavering; even at the cost of my life, I shall grant it.
Having thus recited and shown the first verse spoken by him, he spoke these verses to encourage him in granting the boon:
“The virtuous do not sacrifice their life for the sake of wealth, nor do they sacrifice the Dhamma; the virtuous remain true to their word alone.”
“Having granted the boon, fulfill it quickly; by this means, O best of excellent kings, attain success.
“One should renounce wealth for the sake of a superior limb; one should renounce a limb while protecting one’s life;
a person, recollecting the Dhamma, should renounce even everything—limb, wealth, and life alike.”
In this context, "life" (*pāṇa*) means living. The virtuous indeed give up even their life, but not the Dhamma.
"Quickly bestow it" means, "Give it to me here quickly. "By this"—meaning by this very Dhamma and truth—be successful, accomplished, and well-established.
"O best of good kings," he addresses him while encouraging him. "Relinquish wealth, my friend."
O Porisāda, a wise man, when his limbs such as hands and feet are being severed, would sacrifice even great wealth for their protection.
"Recalling the Dhamma" means that even while renouncing limbs, wealth, and life, he recalls the Dhamma thus: "I shall not transgress the Dhamma of the virtuous."
Thus, having established him in truth by these means, the Great Being now spoke this verse to demonstrate his own venerable status:
“For when a man understands the Dhamma, and those holy ones who dispel his doubt—for that [Dhamma] is indeed his island and his refuge;
a wise man’s friendship with it shall never decay.”
In that context, "from whom" means from which person. "Dhamma" refers to the cause that indicates what is wholesome and unwholesome. "One should discern" means one should understand.
"For that indeed" means that teacher’s family is an island for this person in the sense of being a foundation, and a refuge in the sense of being a place to go when danger arises.
"Not a friend by that" means [he does not become a friend] together with that person who is the teacher.
A wise person should not, for any reason whatsoever, let friendship grow cold or perish.
Having said this, he continued: "Friend Porisāda, it is not right to break the word of a virtuous teacher;
even when I was young, I served as your personal tutor and taught you much learning."
"Even now, out of the playful grace of a Buddha, I have spoken these verses to you containing twenty stars;
therefore, you ought to do as I say," he said. Hearing this, Porisāda thought, "This Sutasoma is both my teacher and wise;
moreover, a boon has been granted to him by me. What can be done? Death is certain for at least one lifetime. Human flesh—"
“I will not eat it; I shall grant him a boon,” he said. With streams of tears flowing, he rose, fell at the feet of King Sutasoma, and as he was about to grant the boon, he spoke this verse:
“Truly, that food is pleasing to me; for the sake of it I entered the forest.”
"And if you entreat me for this matter, I shall grant you this boon as well, my good friend.
Then the Great Being said to him: "My good friend, even death is better for one established in virtue; I accept, O Great King, the boon granted by you.
From this day forward, you are established on the path of the Noble Ones. Even so, I make this request of you:"
“If you have affection for me, Great King, take the five precepts. “Very well, friend, give them to me.
“Take them, Great King. Having prostrated himself before the Great Being with the fivefold salutation, he sat down to one side.
The Great Being then established him in the five precepts. At that moment, those assembled there...
The earth-dwelling deities (bhummā devā), having conceived great joy toward the Great Being, cried out with a loud voice, making the forest resound:
"From the Avīci hell up to the peak of existence (bhavagga), there is no one else capable of restraining the man-eater Porisāda from human flesh!
Oh, what a most difficult feat has Sutasoma performed! Hearing their cry, the deities of the Four Great Kings (cātumahārājika) likewise... [and so on] up to...
A great clamor arose even as far as the Brahma-world. The kings who were clinging to the tree heard that sound of applause from the deities;
even the deity of the tree, while remaining in her own celestial mansion, gave her applause.
Thus, only the sound of the deities was heard, but their forms were not seen. Hearing the sound of the deities’ applause, the kings thought: “Sutasoma...”
“By relying on him we have obtained our lives; a difficult deed has been performed by Sutasoma in taming Porisāda,” they said, offering praise to the Bodhisatta.
Porisāda bowed at the feet of the Mahāsatta and stood to one side.
Then the Bodhisatta said to him, “Friend, release these princes. He thought, “I am their enemy, yet they have been released by me.”
“They might harm me, thinking, ‘Seize our enemy! Even if I were to give up my life, it would not be possible for me to break the virtue I received from Sutasoma;
therefore, I shall go with him and set them free, so that I will have no fear.
Then, having paid homage to the Bodhisatta, he said, “Sutasoma, let us both go and release the khattiyas,” and spoke this verse:
“You are my teacher and you are my friend; I have carried out your word, dear friend.
You too, dear friend, carry out my word; let us both go and set [him] free.
Therein, “teacher” means he is the teacher because he has shown the path to heaven, and he is a friend from the time of their youth.
Then the Bodhisatta said to him:
"I am both your teacher and your friend; you have indeed followed my word, my dear friend.
I too shall do as you say; let us both go and set [the others] free."
Having spoken thus, they approached him and said:
“We have been tormented by Kammāsapāda; submerged in the water, weeping with tearful faces, we shall never do harm to this king. Grant us your word of truth. He replied: “So be it.”
In that context, regarding the phrase "by Kammāsapāda": having accepted the proposal, "Let us both go and release them," the Great Being thought, "Kṣatriyas are indeed haughty and stubborn;
as soon as they are released, they might even beat or kill the Porisāda, thinking, 'We have been harassed by this man.
Yet he will not betray them among them; I alone shall go and give my word."

Thinking, "I shall seize them while they are still there," he went to that place and saw them clinging to the branches of the tree with their palms pressed together and their toes barely touching the ground;
as the wind blew, they were whirling about like kuraṇḍaka garlands hung on pegs. Seeing him, they thought, "Now we are safe," and all at once—
They cried out with a great roar. Then the Great Being, having comforted them by saying, "Do not be afraid," spoke thus:
"Porisāda has been subdued by me; you have received my guarantee of safety, but you must follow my word.
Regarding this, "never" (*na jātū*) means they should never, under any circumstances, act treacherously.
They said:
“We have been tormented by Kammāsapāda; we were submerged in water, weeping with tears on our faces.
We shall never do harm to this king; we promise to honor his word of truth.”
In that context, "We assent" means: "We accept and agree to this promise;
however, we are exhausted and are unable to speak. You are the refuge of all beings;
you yourselves should speak, and having heard your words, we shall give our assent."
Then the Bodhisatta said to them, "In that case, give me your promise," and spoke this verse:
"Just as a father or likewise a mother, being compassionate and desiring the welfare of their offspring,
so let it be for you with this king, and may you be to him just like sons."
Then they, accepting his proposal, spoke this verse:
"Just as a father or likewise a mother, compassionate and desiring the welfare of their offspring, so let it be for us;
and we too shall be like sons to this king."
In that context, *tumhe ca vo*—the word *vo* is a mere particle.
Thus, having obtained their promise, the Great Being summoned Porisāda and said, "Come, friend, release these kṣatriyas.
Taking up his sword, he severed the bonds of one king. That king had been without food for seven days and was overcome by intense pain.
Simultaneously with the severing of the bonds, he fainted and fell to the ground.

Seeing this, the Great Being felt compassion and, saying, "Friend Porisāda, do not cut them like that," firmly grasped one king with both hands, pressed him against his chest, and said, "Now, cut the bonds.
Porisāda cut them with his sword. Due to the Great Being's possession of great strength...
Having laid him upon his chest and lowered him to the ground with a gentle heart as if he were his own biological son, he laid him down.

Having thus laid them all upon the ground, he washed their wounds and slowly drew out the ropes from the children’s ears like threads, washing away the pus and blood until the wounds were free of infection. Then he said, "Friend Poriṣāda,..."
“Bring me a piece of tree bark, having rubbed it against a stone,” he said; and having had it brought, he performed an act of truth and smeared their palms with it.
At that very moment, the wound was healed. Porisāda took rice and cooked it in milk;
both men fed more than a hundred khattiyas. Thus they were all satisfied, and the sun set.
On the following day, they gave them only liquid to drink in the morning, at midday, and in the evening;
on the third day, they gave them rice gruel with solid food, and by then they had become healthy.
Then the Great Being asked them, "Will you be able to go? and when they said, "Let us go," he said, "Come, friend."

“Porisāda, let us go to our own kingdom,” he said. Weeping, he fell at his feet and said, “My friend, you go and take the kings; as for me, I shall remain right here, living on roots and fruits from the forest.
“My friend, what will you do here? Your kingdom is delightful; exercise sovereignty in Bārāṇasī! “My friend...”
"What are you saying? It is not possible for me to go there, for all the inhabitants of the city are my enemies.
They will revile me, saying, 'By this man my mother was eaten, my father, my brother!
They will take me by each with a staff or each with a clod of earth and deprive me of life; and as for me, yours—"
"Established in the precepts in your presence, it is not possible for me to kill another even for the sake of my own life;
therefore, I will not go. Since I have abstained from human flesh, how much longer shall I live?
Now there is no further meeting for me with you," he said, weeping. Then, having rubbed his back, the Great Being said, "You may go."
“Good Porisāda, do not worry; I am Sutasoma by name. I have disciplined such a cruel and harsh man as you.
What need is there to speak of the inhabitants of Bārāṇasī? I shall establish you there.
If I am unable to do so, I will divide my own kingdom in two and give it to you. Having said this, he added, “In your city, too, there are surely those who are my enemies.”
Having said this, he thought, "This man has performed a difficult task by carrying out my word;
I must establish him in his former glory by whatever means possible. Then, in order to entice him, he described the splendor of the city and said:
"Even the meat of four-footed birds, well-cooked and perfectly prepared by chefs—"
“Having enjoyed the nectar like Indra, why have you abandoned them and now take delight in the forest?
Those noble women, with waists as slender as a *velliviḷāka* flower, adorned and surrounding you—
just as they used to delight Indra among the gods— why have you abandoned them and now take delight in the forest?”
“Having slept comfortably in the middle of a bed, amidst a beautiful canopy supported by many pillars,
in a lovely chamber where all one’s possessions are gathered—
having abandoned that, why do you now delight in the forest?”
“Clapping hands, the kumbha drum, the niṣītha, and even musical instruments played by no one at all—
abandoning these many well-sung and well-played sounds, why do you take delight in the forest?
A city endowed with pleasure gardens, abundant garlands, furnished with deer skins, and most delightful;”
"Endowed with horses, elephants, and chariots—having abandoned these, how can you take delight in the forest?
In this context, "well-made" (sukataṃ) means well-constructed in various ways. "Well-finished" (suniṭṭhitaṃ) means well-completed through the assembly of various materials.
"How alone? (katheko): how [can it be] alone? "You take delight" (ramasī): how will you find delight while eating roots, fruits, and the like?
“Come, Great King, let us go. Regarding the phrase *vellivilākamajjhā*: here *vellī* means a heap, and *vilākamajjhā* means having a slender middle.
This indicates that she possessed the radiance of a mass of refined, dense gold and had a thin, elongated waist. Regarding the phrase *devesu*:
in the worlds of the devas, as well as in the delightful city of Bārāṇasī, celestial nymphs (accharā) formerly delighted her like Inda; having left them behind—
"What will you do here? Come, friend, let us go. "Tambūpadhāne" means on a red pillow.
"Sabbassayanamhi" means on a bed spread with all kinds of coverings. Having shown a multi-storied mansion, the meaning is:
"There you used to sleep previously, provided with half-nightly attendants. "Sukham" means having slept comfortably in the midst of such a bed.
"Now, how will you find delight in the forest? Come, let us go, my dear. "At nightfall" means during the portion of the night.
"Having abandoned" means having cast aside such prosperity as this. "Endowed with gardens and abundant garlands" means, O Great King, your garden is endowed with various kinds of flowers.
"The city is delightful and provided with deer-skins" refers to that garden named Migājina.
“Because of that, even your city is very delightful. “Having abandoned” means having discarded such a charming city.
Thus, the Great Being first tempted him with food, thinking, “Perhaps he might wish to go back, remembering the taste of the enjoyments he previously experienced”;
secondly, with sensual defilement; thirdly, with the bed; and fourthly, with dancing, singing, and instrumental music.
Having enticed him with these five things—the pleasure grove and the city—he said: "Come, Great King!
I will take you and establish you in Benares, and afterwards I shall return to my own country.
If you do not obtain the sovereignty of Benares, I will give you half the kingdom. What is the use of living in the forest? Do as I say."
He said: Having heard his words, he desired to go and thought, "Sutasoma wishes for my welfare and is compassionate;
having first established me in what is wholesome, he now says, 'I shall establish you in your former glory.
He will indeed be able to establish me in it, so it is right to go with him; what need have I for dwelling in the forest?"
Having reflected thus, with a joyful heart and wishing to speak in praise of his virtues on account of them, he said, "Friend Sutasoma,
there is nothing better than association with a virtuous friend, nor anything worse than association with an evil friend," and added:
"Just as the moon in the dark fortnight wanes day by day..."
“O King, the assembly of the wicked is like the dark fortnight of the moon.
Just as I, having approached a base and vile cook for the sake of flavor,
committed an evil deed by which I am now going to a state of misery.”
“Just as the moon in the bright fortnight increases day by day,
O King, so does the assembly of the virtuous resemble the bright fortnight. Know this, Sutasoma, through my coming to you.”
"I shall perform wholesome deeds by which I may go to a happy destination.
"Just as water fallen upon dry land, O Lord of Men, cannot be held and does not remain for long;
even so is the association with the wicked, unable to endure like water on dry land."
“Just as water rained upon a lake remains for a long time, O Lord of Men, best of heroes among men;
even so is the meeting of the virtuous, remaining for a long time like water in a lake.
The meeting of the virtuous is never-ending; as long as it lasts, it remains just so.”
“Swiftly indeed does one go away from the company of the wicked; therefore, the Dhamma of the virtuous is far removed from the unwholesome.
In this context, “day by day” means every single day. “Not fit for the journey” means not enduring the long road. “In the sea” means in the ocean.
“Best among men in heroism” means preeminent among men by virtue of their energy. “Just like water in the sea” means like the rainwater that has fallen into the ocean.
"Unfailing" means not departing. "As long as it may remain" means for as long as life remains, for that long it stays exactly so;
the friendship with the virtuous does not decay.
Thus Porisāda spoke in praise of the Great Being alone with these seven verses. And the Great Being [spoke] to Porisāda...
Taking those kings with him, he went to his own frontier village. The inhabitants of the frontier village, having seen the Great Being, went to the city and informed the ministers.
The ministers took a military force and, having gone there, surrounded him.
Accompanied by that retinue, the Great Being proceeded toward the kingdom of Bārāṇasī. Along the way, the inhabitants of the countryside [beheld] the Bodhisatta.
Having presented gifts, they followed him; there was a great retinue, and with them he reached Bārāṇasī.
At that time, the son of Porisāda was the king, and Kāḷahatthi himself was the commander-in-chief. The citizens informed the king:
"Great King, it is said that Sutasoma, having tamed Porisāda, is coming here bringing him along; let him enter the city."
"We will not give it," they said, and quickly closing the city gates, they stood there with weapons in hand.
The Great Being, realizing that the gates were closed, left behind Porisāda and the more than hundred kings and approached with only a few ministers, saying, "I am King Sutasoma;
open the gate! The men went and reported this to the king.
Thus, saying "Open it quickly," he had it opened. The Great Being entered the city.
The king and Kāḷahatthi went out to meet him, and taking him with them, they ascended to the palace.
He sat upon the royal couch and, having summoned the chief queen of the man-eater and his remaining ministers, [addressed] Kāḷahatthi...
He asked, “Kāḷahatthi, why do you not allow the king to enter the city?
“While he was ruling, he devoured many people in this city; he did what should not be done by a kshatriya; he brought disgrace upon the whole of Jambudvīpa.
Because he is such a man of evil character, for that reason [we refuse]. “Do not worry now, thinking, ‘He will act in such a way.’”
"I have tamed him and established him in the precepts; he will not harm anyone even for the sake of his own life, so you have no fear from him.
Do not act thus! Sons must indeed care for their mother and father;
for those who support their mother and father go to heaven, while others go to hell. Thus he gave this exhortation to the prince, his son, as he sat upon his royal throne.
Having given [the gift], he instructed the general as well, saying, “Kāḷahatthi, you are both a friend and a servant of the king;
the king has established you in great sovereignty, and it is fitting for you also to act for the king’s welfare.

Then he said to the queen, “Queen, you too, having come from a noble family and attained the position of chief consort in his presence, have grown old with sons and daughters; by you also [it is fitting to act for his welfare].”

"It is right to act for the welfare [of others]," he said, giving this advice to the queen as well. Then, teaching the Dhamma in order to bring that very matter to its ultimate conclusion, he spoke these verses:
"He is no king who conquers one who should not be conquered; he is no friend who betrays his friend;
she is no wife who does not stand in awe of her husband; they are no sons who do not support their parents in old age."
“That is no assembly where the virtuous are not present; those are not virtuous who do not speak the Dhamma.
Only by abandoning lust, hatred, and delusion, and speaking the Dhamma, do they become virtuous.
People do not recognize a wise man as distinct from fools as long as he remains silent.”
They know him as he speaks, teaching the deathless state:
“Let him speak and illuminate the Dhamma; let him raise high the banner of the seers.
For the well-spoken word is the banner of the seers; the Dhamma indeed is the banner of the seers.”
In this context, "invincible" refers to one's parents; one who conquers them is not truly called a king.
If you, having obtained the kingdom belonging to your father, were to become his adversary, you would be known as one who fails in his duty.
"He conquers with a straw" means he conquers by fraudulent means. If you, Kāḷahatthi, do not fulfill the duty of friendship toward the king—
"By standing in unrighteousness, you will be reborn in hell. "He does not fear" means he is not afraid.
"If you do not fear the king, you are not one who stands in the duty of a wife; you will be known as one who fails in her obligations.
"The aged" means one who is advanced in years; for at that time, sons who do not support their parents are not truly called "sons."
"There are those who are wise": those who do not speak of the Dhamma—those who, when questioned, do not speak of the true nature of reality—are not called wise.

"Speaking the Dhamma" means that only those who, having abandoned lust and the other defilements, become compassionate for the welfare of others and speak according to the true nature of things, are called wise. "Not remaining silent" means not being silent. "The deathless state."
They know him who teaches the great Nibbāna, which is the Deathless, as a "wise man.

For that very reason, Porisāda, having recognized me and with a confident heart, granted four boons and established himself in the five precepts. "Let the wise man speak"—the wise man should speak and illuminate the Dhamma.

Since the Dhamma is the banner (*dhaja*) of these [beings], such as the Buddhas and other seers, it is therefore called "having well-spoken words as its banner" (*subhāsitaddhaja*); that is, the well-spoken word.
"But fools do not take up well-spoken words.
Having heard this discourse on the Dhamma, the king, the commander-in-chief, and the queen were delighted. "Let us go, Great King; let us bring him," they said.
Having caused the drum to be beaten throughout the city and assembled the citizens, [the king] said, "Do not be afraid, you people; the king..."
"Indeed, he is established in the Dhamma; come, let us bring him here! Taking a great multitude with them and placing the Great Being at their head, they went into the presence of the king.
Having paid homage and provided a barber, they had the king’s hair and beard trimmed, bathed, anointed, and adorned him.
Then, having placed the king upon a heap of jewels and consecrated him, they led him into the city. Thus, Porisāda became king.
He caused great honor to be paid to the Great Being and to the assembled Kṣatriyas.
A great clamor arose throughout all of Jambudvīpa: “It is said that King Sutasoma, having subdued Porisāda, has been established in his kingdom.
The inhabitants of the city of Indapatta also sent a messenger, saying, “May our king come to us. Having stayed there for about a month, he said, “Friend, I am going.”
“Be heedful; have five halls of almsgiving built—at the city gates and in the center—and without violating the ten duties of a king, avoid going upon the wrong path,” he thus advised Porisāda.
From more than a hundred royal capitals, the military forces for the most part assembled. Surrounded by that army, he departed from Bārāṇasī. Porisāda also—
Having departed, he turned back halfway along the road. The Great Being gave his own mounts to the kings who had come without mounts and dismissed them.
Those kings, having exchanged greetings with him and performed salutations and other marks of respect toward the Great Being, returned each to their own country.
The Great Being also reached the city; the inhabitants of the city of Indapatta had adorned it like the city of the gods.
Having entered, he paid homage to his mother and father, exchanged pleasant greetings with them, and ascended to the great upper terrace.
While ruling the kingdom righteously, he thought: "The tree deity has been very helpful to me; I shall provide her with offerings.
He had a large pond constructed not far from that *nigrodha* tree and dispatched many families from the village [to maintain it].
He established [the settlement]. The village became great, adorned with approximately eighty thousand shops.
He also had that foot of the tree leveled from the edge of the branches downward and constructed it with a surrounding wall, a moat, and gate-towers; thus the deities were greatly pleased.
Because it was settled on the site where Kammāsapāda had been tamed, that village came to be known by the name Kammāsadamma-nigama.
All those kings, abiding by the Great Being’s counsel, performed meritorious deeds such as giving and, at the end of their lives, filled the heavenly realms.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher said, “Monks, it is not only now that I have tamed Aṅgulimāla;
he was tamed by me in the past as well,” and having spoken thus, he identified the Jātaka: “At that time, King Porisāda was...”
"Aṅgulimāla was [the Buddha], Kāḷahatthi was Sāriputta, the brahmin Nanda was Ānanda,
the tree-deity was Kassapa, Sakka was Anuruddha, the remaining kings were the Buddha’s retinue, the mother and father were royal families,
and King Sutasoma was none other than myself."
The fifth: The Explanation of the Mahāsutasoma Jātaka.
The Summary Verse (Uddāna) of the Jātakas:
Sumukha, the Great Haṃsavara, Sudhabhojanika, and another, the most excellent;
The vehicle named after the king of birds, Sakuṇāla, and the one with the most excellent name, Sutasoma—
thus ends the commentary on the Eighty Chapters (Asītinipāta).
The fifth volume is completed.
